en: *Mahāyāna-arthasamgraha*, Scroll One Cursive script confuses people and leads to grave errors; those who transmit [this text] must ensure it is authentic and take care not to use cursive script.

Dharma Master Yuan has composed this treatise in five sections: first, the Section on Teaching (*śāsana-skandha*); second, the Section on Meaning (*artha-skandha*); third, the Section on Defilement (*saṃkleśa-skandha*); fourth, the Section on Purity (*vyavadāna-skandha*).
The fifth is the miscellaneous collection (*saṃnipāta*).

Within the collection of teachings, there are three distinct sections: first, the meaning of the traces of the various sūtra teachings; second, the meaning of the Three Piṭakas; and third, the meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*).

I. The Collection of Teachings (Three Gates): 1. The Meaning of the Scriptural Traces of the Various Sutras (I). The Meaning of the Scriptural Traces of the Various Sutras is analyzed through three gates: first, recounting divergent views; second, distinguishing right from wrong; third, revealing the correct meaning. Regarding "recounting divergent views": [text follows].
There are not just one, but many differing accounts.
Liu Qiu, a recluse from Mount Wudu during the Jin dynasty, stated that these were all spoken by the Tathāgata during a single period of his transformative teaching.
There is no emergence of sudden or gradual [teachings].
Scriptures such as the Avataṃsaka are of the sudden teaching.
The remainder is called "gradual.
Within the gradual [process], there are five periods and seven stages.
As for the five periods:
When a Buddha first attains the Way,
he preaches for Trapusa and others the teachings of the human and celestial realms, consisting of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
After the two Buddhas had attained enlightenment,
for twelve years they proclaimed the various teachings of the three vehicles for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka.
For those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he teaches dependent origination. For others, he teaches the Four Noble Truths.
For those seeking the Mahāyāna,
he taught the six perfections and established the monastic discipline, but had not yet expounded the principle of emptiness.
During the thirty years following the three Buddhas' attainment of enlightenment,
they proclaimed the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Śūnyatāvāda, the Vimalakīrti, and the Saṃdhinirmocana; these were taught as the shared contemplation of the Three Vehicles.
The One Vehicle (ekayāna) that subsumes the three [vehicles] into one has not yet been taught;
furthermore, it has not yet been proclaimed that sentient beings possess buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
This was forty years after the four Buddhas had attained enlightenment.
For eight years he preached the Lotus Sūtra,
clarifying the One Vehicle and subverting the three vehicles to return them to the One.

He did not yet speak of sentient beings equally possessing Buddha-nature, but merely revealed that the Tathāgata’s past transgressions exceed the sands of the Ganges, while his future merits are twice that number.
Not understanding that the Buddha is eternal is a failure to comprehend the teaching;
thus it was said when the five Buddhas were about to enter parinirvāṇa.
For one day and one night,
he preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
clarifying that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
This is its definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
These constitute the five periods.
As for what are called the "seven stages":
In the second period, there was a distinction between the three vehicles;
this is one interpretation of the general teaching that there are seven [vehicles]. Furthermore, Master Dan said:
Buddhism is twofold: first, the sudden teaching; second, the gradual teaching.
The sudden teaching is the same as previously described.
However, within the context of gradual [enlightenment],
one cannot take those five periods as definitive;
one should simply know that all previous explanations are incomplete.
"The single proclamation at the twin śāla trees constitutes the teaching of finality; this is the second explanation.
Furthermore, Bodhiruci proclaimed that the Tathāgata’s single voice simultaneously presents both the Great and Small Vehicles in response to ten thousand occasions.
One cannot distinguish between these three teachings based on their sudden or gradual nature.
Next, we shall examine the errors [in the views] of Liu Qiu as he described them.
To say that Buddhism possesses no gates other than the sudden and the gradual is an incomplete statement.
This is evident from the Four Āgamas and the five divisions of the Vinaya as taught by the Buddha.
One should know that this is not subsumed under either the sudden or the gradual.
This is because it is said that those who have been converted by the Small Vehicle cannot be called "sudden."
The teaching of the penetration of words concerns the beginning and the end; what is taught at the time of the end is not for the purpose of entering the Great [Vehicle].
One must not say it is gradual.
Furthermore, even if there were other occasions for such practice,
sentient beings would hear of the Lesser Vehicle and attain realization therein.
Since they ultimately do not enter the Great [Vehicle], how can one speak of "gradual"?

Therefore, the categories of "sudden" and "gradual" do not exhaustively encompass all teachings; this is another fallacy. Furthermore, regarding the terminology of the "five periods" and "seven stages":
This too is erroneous and baseless.
If you say that at the beginning he taught the Dharma of humans and devas for the sake of Trapusa and Bhallika;
Regardless of their entry into the path,
whatever human or celestial teachings they rely upon,
such is the single transformation of the Tathāgata.
One teaches according to what is appropriate for each sentient being;
how could it be restricted to the initial stage?
Furthermore, the *Tiewei jing* states:
"The self of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure;
the self is fundamentally pure."
This is the emptiness of sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is taught that all phenomena ultimately revert to fundamental non-existence;
all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent.
This is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Furthermore,
Tiwei performed repentance on behalf of the assembly for the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and other offenses.
One awakens to the understanding that the four great elements and the five aggregates are fundamentally pure;
that the aggregates and their root are fundamentally pure is itself the emptiness of dharmas.
The two emptinesses are precisely the direct path for transcending the world.
Why, then, would they be called the teaching-gate of humans and devas?
Furthermore, when the Dharma was being taught:
When Trapusa and Bhallika heard the Dharma and attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
the Four Heavenly Kings attained the patience of compliance (anulomikī kṣānti), as did three hundred merchants.
They attained the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
Three hundred dragon kings attained the faculty of the patience of faith.
The asuras and others resolved their minds on bodhicitta;
likewise did the mountain deities, tree deities, water deities, fire deities, and so forth.
They all attained the ten wholesome deeds and practiced the path of the bodhisattva;
there were two hundred merchants.

The attainment of *srotāpanna* and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) refers to the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*) from the seventh stage upward.
The "patience of pliancy" (*kṣānti*) is that which is attained from the fourth stage upward.
The "patience of faith" (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) resides in the first, second, and third stages.
The root of faith and patience should reside in that final moment of mind within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*).
As for the bodhicitta:
Regarding the initial stage of understanding and practice,
those who are said to have attained the ten wholesome actions and become bodhisattvas should be understood as being at or above that level of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Furthermore, it may also be that when that Worthy One (Bhadramukha) has already departed,
one becomes a *srotāpanna*—
the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
All of these accomplish the supramundane right path.
Why, then, is it called the "Teaching Gate for Humans and Devas"?
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* clarifies this.
The Buddha bestowed upon the two men, Trapusa and Bhallika, the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood,
with the name Guhyasiddha.
This is clearly known.
What has been taught is not the instruction for humans or devas;
furthermore, Trapusa and others departed after hearing the Dharma.
He did not go to the Deer Park,
for Kāśyapa and the others had not yet been admitted to this assembly.
How this serves as a gradual progression toward what follows is extremely difficult to understand;
this is the second stage.
It is said that for twelve years the Tathāgata taught only the differentiated doctrines of the three vehicles.
On what textual evidence is this based?
In the sūtras, it is merely stated that for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the Four Noble Truths are taught;
for those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, dependent origination is taught;
and for those seeking the Mahāyāna, the six perfections are taught.
When did I ever say that it lasts for twelve years?
Furthermore, if sentient beings should wish to hear this Dharma at other times, [they may do so].
Or perhaps at this time they would prefer to hear other teachings;
how could the Buddha not have taught them?
To judge that such a principle does not exist is impossible.
However, as for the distinct teaching (biejiao),
it was taught by the Tathāgata according to what was appropriate for his single transformation;
one cannot definitively state that it occurred within twelve years.
How is this known? For instance,
the four Āgamas and the five divisions of the Vinaya are the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"For twelve years, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni briefly expounded the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* for the monastic community (*saṃgha*) that was free from business."
From this point onward,
it is explained in detail in the Ekottarika Āgama.
The same applies to this statement.
It is clearly understood that the precepts govern both the beginning and the end.
Furthermore, as for the *Cīvaravastu* of the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
it was only proclaimed at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
It is clearly known that the sutras and dharmas explain the beginning and end in their entirety;
they do not stop at merely twelve years.
Furthermore, during those five years, the Buddha preached one hundred thousand verses of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*,
elucidating the emptiness of all phenomena.
During these seven years,
he preached the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is taught that all phenomena, both form and mind, are empty.
How then can it be said that the principle of emptiness was not clarified during the twelve years [of the Buddha's teaching]?
Judging by this evidence, [the claim is untenable].
People say this is certainly erroneous.
Regarding the third stage,
it is said that within thirty years.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa*— the great chapters of the emptiness school—
he did not yet break the three [vehicles] to return to the one,
nor did he proclaim that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Since the meaning has not yet been fully understood,
that Lotus Sūtra is therefore gradual;
however, the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras—
The Buddha preached it five years after his attainment of enlightenment;
how can it be said definitively that it was in the thirtieth year?
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Rebirth" (*Upapatti-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
When the bhikṣus heard this exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā and its praise of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā),
they then removed their three robes.
Regarding the practice of giving [these robes] as alms, Nāgārjuna explains:
"The Buddha prescribed three robes."
To fail to maintain [the precepts] is a transgression.
Why, then, do you not revere the *śīlapāramitā*? To practice giving while violating the precepts is [unwholesome].
Because this occurred twelve years before the Buddha had yet established the precepts,
it was therefore not an offense; this textual evidence demonstrates that [the rule] is not restricted to the thirty-year period.
Regarding the statement that Vimalakīrti and Siyi have been [in this state] for thirty years:
on what textual evidence is this based?
We know it is merely a temporal duration established by deluded sentiment; let it be so for now.
If it is argued that the *Prajñāpāramitā* teaches the three vehicles equally and is thus a shallow teaching compared to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
one might also point out that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Because this sutra brings forth the śrāvakas, it is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka."
It is called the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka because it brings forth the pratyekabuddhas;
it is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka because it brings forth the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, within the *Siṃhanāda*, the twelve links of dependent origination are taught.
Because they observe with inferior wisdom,
there is the enlightenment of the śrāvakas; because they observe with middling wisdom, [there is the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas].
The enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha is due to observation by superior wisdom;
[as for] the enlightenment of the bodhisattva...
Regarding the contemplation of supreme,
supreme wisdom and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
that sūtra also states that the three vehicles contemplate it identically.
It should be understood as being shallow in comparison to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Furthermore, it is said in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: "The Mahāyāna..."
Since it gives birth to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas,
that sūtra should also be considered shallower than the Lotus Sūtra.
Since that [text] is profound, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) shares the same contemplation,
why should this one alone be shallow?
If one says that Prajñā does not sublate the shallow dharmas of the three vehicles,
yet in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Śāriputra asks:
"If [bodhisattvas] do not regress at all..."
Since emptiness is no different [from one another],
why is there a distinction between the three vehicles rather than only a single vehicle? Subhūti replied:
There is neither two nor three.
If one hears this and is not afraid,
one can attain bodhi.
This is no different from the Lotus Sūtra;
in what way do their words differ?
It is not that [the Lotus] refutes the three [vehicles] to return to the one.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna said:
"One should know that the Prajñā[pāramitā] [is taught] within immeasurable sūtras such as the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
It is considered the greatest;
how can you say it is shallow?
If you say that Prajñā does not speak of Buddha-nature, then it would be shallower than Nirvāṇa.
The sutras state that buddha-nature is also called prajñāpāramitā and also called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
The Prajñā and emptiness taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* are precisely the Buddha-nature.
How can it be said that they do not clarify the Buddha-nature?
Furthermore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
while explaining the True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*),
Nāgārjuna comments as follows:
Dharma is named nirvana;
it is the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Nature is named the fundamental portion.
Just as yellow stone has the nature of gold and white stone has the nature of silver,
so too all sentient beings possess the nature of nirvana.
What difference is there between this and Buddha-nature,
such that you say Buddha-nature is not being taught?
Since the words regarding their relative depth and shallowness are identical, it is inappropriate to apply them even for a moment.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra takes inconceivable liberation as its central theme;
this is among the ten types of liberation.
Regarding the first gate of liberation,
it should be known that this is the wheel of Dharma of the sudden teaching.
Why is it said that this is a sutra of provisional meaning?
The *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya* is also like this.
This is the fourth stage.
It is said that forty years later, he would proclaim the *Lotus Sūtra*,
breaking down the three vehicles to return to the one,
yet he did not yet clarify the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, it is said that even if the Tathāgata were to remain for a period exceeding the sands of the Ganges multiplied by two,
he would still be impermanent;
therefore, this serves as a gradual stage leading toward his parinirvāṇa.
The sūtra states truthfully that the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra forty years after his attainment of enlightenment; however,
its chronological relationship with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is difficult to determine.
Why is this so? The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, in his commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, states:
"Subhūti heard the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
By merely raising a hand or bowing the head,
one attains the Buddha-way;
for this reason, I now inquire into the meaning of retrogression and non-retrogression.
Based on this textual evidence,

the sequence is not fixed. If one were to say that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*— which sublates the three vehicles to return to the One— is deeper than the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [that would be incorrect].
This has already been refuted as before.
If it is argued that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is inferior to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* because it does not yet teach the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*),
this argument is incorrect.
As the sutras state, "nature" (*gotra*) is precisely the One Vehicle; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* elucidates this One Vehicle—how could it then not be "nature"?
Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
Whenever he saw the fourfold assembly, he would call out in a loud voice:
"You shall become Buddhas;
I do not slight you."
Because they know that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
it is said that "all shall become [Buddhas].
It is simply stated that "all shall become."
This clearly demonstrates the existence of the nature [of the Tathāgata].

If it is claimed that the Tathāgata’s permanence was not yet clarified prior to the period exceeding the sands of the Ganges and doubling that number of future eons, such an interpretation is incorrect.
One should know this.
That teaching describes the response seen by the Bodhisattva who has leaped forth;

it does not concern the true body (dharmakāya) when discussing the future number that exceeds the sands of the Ganges by a multiple, for if one discusses the true body, [it is beyond such calculation].
It is ultimately inexhaustible.
How can this be known? This must not be the truth.
The Sūtra says: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood,
I have expounded the Dharma to teach and transform beings,
causing Bodhisattvas to emerge."
Furthermore, he said, "I am always on Vulture Peak Mountain and other dwelling places, seen by devas and humans.
This clearly demonstrates that [the Buddha] is worthy of veneration.
Why should this future period be a multiple?
It is because the emanated bodhisattvas will,
in a future age, pass through a number of kalpas that is many times greater.
They all became Buddhas without relying on the Buddha’s transformation;
such was the case at that time for the Tathāgata.
The breath should return to its true source;
therefore, it is said that while the principle of doubling the number is real, the Buddha’s transformations are ultimately inexhaustible. Question:
If one says that those [buddhas] prior to the sands of the Ganges are conventional and not ultimate,
why does the treatise describe them as *vipāka-buddhas* (retribution buddhas)? To explain:

By means of the provisional transformation, the ultimate reality is revealed; thus, while the manifestation of the transformation has occurred for a long time, the clarification of the truth has been established for even longer.
Since that [teaching] already states that the future duration shall be double [the present], [the ultimate duration is accordingly extended].
How can there be a retribution?
This doubt is truly not resolved.
Furthermore, within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
I lament that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* possesses such great benefit;
for instance, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, eight thousand śrāvakas received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Having achieved great fruits,
and since the benefits obtained are equal,
how could what is elucidated be otherwise?
As Nāgārjuna truly said:
"The Lotus Sūtra is the most profound."
Because it is taught therein that śrāvakas can attain Buddhahood,
for this reason, all other sūtras were entrusted to Ānanda.
Since the Lotus Sūtra alone is entrusted solely to the bodhisattvas,
one must conclude from this text that it cannot be said to be shallow.
The fifth stage:
it is said that at the time of his passing, the Tathāgata preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra,
proclaiming it alone as the ultimate teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
However, while it is true that these were spoken near the end [of his life],
it is not necessarily the case that they were spoken at the very end;
they are exclusively of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Just as before the Twin Śāla Trees, he proclaimed the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Dharmaghoṣa-sūtra*, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, the *Ratnākara-sūtra*, and others;
all of these are the perfect, ultimate, definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Why is it that only *nirvāṇa* is exclusively of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
For instance, in the Buddha’s first year, he taught the *Ratnāvalī-sūtra* and [the teachings on] the Nirgranthas;
in his second year, he proclaimed the *Vaipulya-śuddha-vyūha*.
For five years he preached the Mahāprajñāpāramitā;
for seven years he preached the Pratyutpanna Samādhi;
and for nine years he preached the Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra and the Dharma-dundubhi Sūtra.
For ten years, he preached the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* and other such sūtras;
all of these are complete, ultimate, and definitive in meaning (*nītārtha*).
Why should *nirvāṇa* alone be exclusively of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
As for Master Tan’s remarks regarding the sudden and gradual [teachings],
their logic is identical to what was previously refuted.
However, in the Buddha’s single transformation,
he accords with all sentient beings;
for those who should enter the Great Vehicle, he appears accordingly.
Even if one were to explain it,
according to what has been proclaimed,
although the specific gateways differ, [the essence remains the same].
There is nothing that is not ultimate.
Why, then, would Bodhiruci alone claim that *nirvāṇa* is exclusively of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
while asserting that the Buddha’s single voice responds to myriad capacities without distinction between gradual and sudden?

This is also not the case; for although the Tathāgata responds to the ten thousand with a single voice according to the various sentient beings, there is nonetheless neither the absence of gradual nor the absence of sudden [teaching].
Indeed, there are sentient beings [who require one or the other].
Relying on shallow stages to reach the distant goal of Buddhahood, he taught the gradual path;
yet there are sentient beings who,
in a single leap, comprehend the Great [Vehicle].
The Buddha taught the sudden; how could there not be the sudden and the gradual?
To argue otherwise is incorrect.
Next, the correct meaning shall be revealed.
Within this, there are two sections:
first, the classification of the sacred teachings;
second, the determination of the specific tenets.
Although the holy teachings are numerous, they are essentially of only two kinds:
first, the mundane;
second, the supramundane.
The wholesome dharmas of the three realms of existence are called the mundane;
the paths leading out [of these realms] are the three vehicles.
It is called supramundane.
Within the supramundane,
there are further two kinds.
First is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
That which is taught for the sake of the śrāvakas is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
That which is taught for bodhisattvas is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The twelve divisions of the sūtras..."
Only the Vaipulya section constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
the remaining eleven sections do not.
This is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
That text further states:
"The Buddha [taught] for the sake of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas the path for exiting suffering."
Regarding the explanation of the sūtras:
those who compiled the scriptures collected them into two piṭakas.
The conduct of the śrāvakas constitutes the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
the conduct of the bodhisattvas constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Nāgārjuna also said:
Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the Tripiṭaka at Rājagṛha.
For the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
Mañjuśrī and Ānanda [compiled it] at Mount Cakravāḍa.
The Mahāyāna is compiled as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
this is the clear scriptural evidence of the holy teaching.
The meaning is clearly evident.
These two are also termed the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and the teachings of the Half and the Full.
[They constitute] the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
The Dharma is called "small" because it is narrow and inferior;
it is called "half" because it has not reached the ultimate.
[This refers to] the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The Dharma is vast and expansive, thus it is called "Great"; it is perfectly complete, thus it is called "Full.
Such are the distinctions within the teachings.
As for the statement regarding the definitive tenet:
The various sections of the sūtras differ in their fundamental tenets; although these tenets are numerous,
[they are categorized as follows].
There are only two kinds:
first, that which is spoken;
second, that which is indicated.
That which is spoken of refers to the practice of virtue;
that which is signified by speech refers to—
These likewise serve as manifestations of the Dharma, yet the Dharma itself is difficult to manifest;
thus it is revealed by means of its virtues.
This is the "Gate of Revealing the Virtues of the Dharma."
Because they are otherwise immeasurable, the essential tenets of the various sūtras differ from one another,
as seen in such works as the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* and others.
The generation of the bodhicitta is the primary theme [of this text], while the *Jentākasūtra* and other such works take generosity as their primary theme.
The *Śuddhaviniya-upāsaka-śīla* and other such sūtras take the precepts as their primary theme.
The *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Anantamukhasādhaka*, and other such sutras take samādhi as their primary tenet;
the *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras and others likewise do so.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other such texts take wisdom as their primary tenet; [the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*] takes liberation as its primary tenet.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and other such sutras take the Dharma-body as their primary tenet;
the Vaipulya scriptures serve as the gateway.
In such sutras as these,
the *dhāraṇī* is the central theme;
in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and others, it is likewise.
The One Vehicle is the central tenet [of the Lotus Sūtra and others].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts take the Buddha’s wondrous fruit of perfect quiescence as their central tenet.
In such sutras as these,
what is clarified differs from one to another;
nevertheless, that which they teach [is consistent].
All of these are the definitive meanings of the consummate virtues of Mahāyāna dependent origination;

The objects of cessation differ,

In various sūtras, the extinguishing of fire is termed "extinction" (*nirodha*) or "crossing over" (*pāra-gata*).

being free from all applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), it is called nirvāṇa.
A second explanation states:

The three cessations characterized by universality are called *nirodha*.

Depending on their distinctions in relation to their respective opposites (*vipakṣa*), they are designated by four meanings: the exhaustion of entities (*vastu-kṣaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), excellence (*praśānta*), and sublime emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*). Although these two differ,

The essence is not itself subject to cessation;

Therefore it is called "cessation.

It is called *vinaya* because it is that which defines what is to be practiced;

The three piṭakas all take the teaching as their essence.
What constitutes the teaching?
It consists of sounds, words, and phrases.
That which accords with the Dharma is its teaching;

Regarding the inclusion of names, phrases, and so forth within the three categories of phenomena (*triskandha-dharma*),
various treatises differ in their positions concerning whether they are subsumed under the category of form (*rūpa*).
According to the Abhidharma,
this belongs to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) among the three aggregates of phenomena.

The three types—names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*)—are comprised within that which is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), and are not associated with it (*viprayukta*).
What distinguishes them? A "syllable" (*vyañjana*) refers to the phenomena of long, short, curved, high, and low [articulations].
It is these that are called syllables.
The characters that encompass phenomena are spoken of as names;
they are mere entanglements of words.
When they are mutually connected and combined to form a textual verse,
it is called a "phrase" (pada).
It suffices for the sounds themselves to directly express the dharmas;
what need is there for letters and the like?
If it were merely the sound of the voice,
without being conjoined with the dharma of syllables and forgetting its own nature,
it would not constitute speech.
It is no different from the sounds of wind-bells and the like;
it must combine with syllables to constitute speech.
Although it combines with syllables to form speech, [it remains distinct].
If it were not associated with the named dharma (*nāmadharma*),
one could not use this to designate the preceding dharma;
precisely because it is associated with that named dharma, it is called a "designating dharma" (*vijñaptidharma*).
Although one may obtain the manifest dharmas,
if they do not correspond with the method of phrases,
the names will be dispersed and fail to constitute a textual verse.
This is because they correspond to those methods of phrasing;
thus, by incorporating syllables and so forth, the distinctions of prose, verses, stanzas, and phrases are established.
This is based on the *Asaṃprayukta-skandha* (Chapter on Non-associated Factors) of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

The "extensive" [definition] does not have the same meaning as the former. That treatise does not state that, apart from sound, there exist other entities such as letters (akṣara) that are neither matter (rūpa) nor mind (citta).

This is the nature of sound;
specifically, the function of manifesting and summoning upon that sound is designated as "syllables" (*akṣara*) and so forth.
In principle, they are not separate:
sound is always real, while phonemes and so forth are always conventional.
This is just like the distinction between matter (rūpa) and the activity of matter:
the substance itself is matter,
while the continuous movement occurring upon that matter is the activity.
The nature of form is eternally real,
while karma is eternally provisional;
by analogy with this, the meaning of other cases can be understood.
There is no need to labor over the number of their phonetic tones;
as for what distinguishes these three,
it lies precisely within the sounds themselves.

It is not as when the Tathāgata further analyzed and explained it through the Abhidharma;

The Sūtra Section.

A brief exposition is thus concluded. III. The Meaning of the Twelve Divisions of Scripture (1): A Fivefold Analysis of the Meaning of the Twelve Divisions of Scripture. I. Translation of Names and Exegesis; II. Essential Characteristics; III. Analysis According to Time; IV. Common and Specific; V. General and Particular. First: Explanation of Names.
What is called "sūtra" refers to the Dharma by way of metaphor;
it is the speech of the Noble Ones.
It can penetrate all phenomena.
As the sutras state, because it holds the warp [of the teaching], it is called a "sūtra" (thread).
Sūtras differ according to their specific meanings.
Thus, there are twelve.
As for the names of these twelve, they are:
Sūtra, Geya, Gāthā, and so forth, ending finally with Upadeśa.
"Sūtra" is a foreign term; here it is translated as "sūtra" (thread).
The speech of the Sage can penetrate all phenomena,
just as a string threads through flowers.
Therefore, it is named "Thread" (sūtra).
Its general meaning is largely similar to that of the preceding sutra.
The second is *geya*,
which is translated as "verses repeated.
It refers to the repetition in verse of the meanings of the Dharma taught within the *sūtras*.
Therefore, it is called Geya.
The third is named Vyākaraṇa; this is translated as "Prediction" (Vyākaraṇa).
To act as the cause and obtain the fruit is designated as "prediction" (vyākaraṇa).
This is what the Sage taught to reveal to people.
Therefore, it is called "bestowal" (śāstra).
The fourth type is gāthā;
this is translated as "unrepeated verse" (geya).
Because it reveals all phenomena directly through verses,
it is called gāthā. The fifth is named udāna-sūtra.
This is translated as "Spontaneous Utterance Without Inquiry," for it is proclaimed spontaneously without being requested through consultation.
Therefore, it is called the *Aparipṛcchā-svayambhūta-sūtra*.
The sixth is named the *Nidāna-sūtra*, which is translated here as the *Nidāna-sūtra* (Scripture on Causes and Conditions).
Based on the conditions of present events,
that which is taught is called the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
The seventh is named the *Avadāna-sūtra*.
This refers to parables; for example, works such as the *Śatākhyāyika* (The Hundred Parables) establish metaphors to clarify the Dharma.
The first is called the *Avadāna-sūtra*.
The eighth is called the *Itivṛttaka-sūtra*; this is named the *Vetulya* (or *Pūrvayoga*).
Because it proclaims the past events of others,
it is called Itivṛttaka (Past Deeds).
The ninth is named Jātaka (Birth Stories).
This is called a Jātaka;
it is termed a "Jātaka" because it recounts events from the past.
The tenth is named Vaipulya Sūtra; this is called Fang-kuang (Vaipulya).
"Fang" (Vipula) signifies that its principle is correct.
The meaning is complete and the names are extensive;
because the teaching follows from this profound intent, it is called the Vaipulya Sūtra.
If one relies on the Hīnayāna perspective:
"Speech" refers to what is correctly articulated;
"much" means extensive.
The eleventh is named Aputadharma.
This is translated as the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra* (The Scripture of Marvels).
It contains [the accounts of] the Blue Ox Carrying the Alms Bowl and the White Dog Listening to the Dharma.
The physical dimensions of the various devas,
the trembling of the great earth,
and other such wonders that have rarely occurred since time immemorial.
It is called "Unprecedented" because it speaks of this rare occurrence;
thus it is named the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra*.
The twelfth is called *upadeśa*. This is termed "discourse on meaning" (*vāda*),
consisting of questions and answers for the purpose of clarifying principles.
This is called the Sūtra on the Exposition of Terms;
such is the meaning of the name.
This concludes the second section.
Though varying in detail and brevity, they are indeterminate; yet in terms of their essential substance, they are one and the same,

they are divided into two types.

the principle itself is the *vaipulya*.

as for the remaining eight classes,

Regarding the reversal of the four inversions:
Because śrāvakas conceive of the Buddha as impermanent, without bliss, without self, and impure—
thereby conforming to the dharmas of ordinary worldlings—
it is said that the Tathāgata is pure, self, blissful, and permanent.
Regarding the removal of the four obstacles:
the first is the obstacle of objective signs (*nimitta*),
which refers to the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*) being removed in opposition to it.
The fruit is described as purity.
Second is the characteristic of the cause,
which refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Because of the existence of this karma,
one is subject to transformation and lacks mastery; it is for the sake of counteracting that [karma] that [this teaching is given].
It speaks of the Buddha’s true self.
Third is the characteristic of birth,
meaning that the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) is of the nature of suffering.
Because true bliss cannot be attained,
the fruit is described as bliss in order to serve as its antidote.
The fourth is the characteristic of decay,
which refers to the death of transformation;
it is the failure to attain true permanence.
In order to exclude that [view],
it is said that the fruit is permanent;
this is in contrast to the four causes.
Faith purifies the slander of the Dharma, attaining its pure fruit;
wisdom eliminates the false self, attaining the Buddha’s true self;
concentration eliminates the fear of suffering, attaining the Buddha’s true bliss.
Because they do not abandon existence through their great compassionate heart,
they attain the Buddha’s true permanence.
Furthermore, these four fruits each possess two aspects regarding their essence and characteristics.
Regarding the two aspects within purity:
the first is the characteristic of the cause,
which is primordially unstained.
Second is the superior characteristic:
purity through the removal of defilements;
this is purity by means.
Regarding my two middle [positions]:
first, I am free from the false attachment to a self held by non-Buddhists;
second, I am free from the inverted view of non-self held by śrāvakas.
Within bliss there are two aspects:
first, freedom from all suffering;
second, the elimination of afflictions.
Regarding the two aspects of "permanence":
first, it is free from the extreme of annihilation regarding conditioned phenomena;
second, it is free from the extreme of permanence regarding unconditioned phenomena.
These various distinctions are all equally results;
they are categorized according to their nature based on these results.
Therefore, it is called the nature of the fruit.
As for the nature of karma,
there are two types of the nature of karma.
First is the weariness with suffering;
second is the seeking of nirvana.
Thus, that treatise states:
The various karmas of aversion toward suffering, aspiration for nirvāṇa, and so forth,
arise and function based on the nature [of the mind].
Therefore it is called "karma.
Karma is itself its nature; thus it is called "the nature of karma" (karmatā).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If there were no Tathāgatagarbha,
one would not be able to feel various forms of weariness toward suffering nor seek the joy of Nirvāṇa."
However, the aforementioned causal nature resides in the happy realms;
as for this present karma:
The lineage prior to [the stage of] entering the path refers to the mind of aspiration and aversion toward the wholesome destinies of the Mahāyāna.
As for the nature of correspondence:
Clarifying cause and effect,
they arise from the very nature itself and are in accord with that nature.
Just as an ornament is said to possess the nature of correspondence when it is conjoined with gold,
so too is it within the context of causal correspondence.
There are three distinct meanings:
first, faith in the Mahāyāna as the cause for the Dharmakāya;
second, meditative concentration and wisdom as the causes for Buddha-knowledge.
Third, compassion serves as the cause for the great compassion of those Tathāgatas;
all of these are in accord with their nature.
Within the correspondence of results, there are likewise three kinds.
First, the five supernormal powers;
second, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows;
third, the stainlessness of the exhaustion of outflows.
These three fruits do not depart from their intrinsic nature (svabhāva); thus they are termed "concordant with the fruit.
One discerns the nature by way of this meaning of concordance.
Therefore, it is called the nature of correspondence (*samyuktatva*).
As for the nature of activity (*saṃskāratva*),
there are three distinct types of activity.
First, ordinary worldlings with false views give rise to inverted perceptions;
second, noble ones with true vision are free from the mind of delusive appearances;
third, the Tathāgata is devoid of the habit-energies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Although the three modes of practice differ,
their essential nature is non-dual;
it is just as the seed, husk, sprout, and stem are distinct from one another.
The nature of the aggregates is without distinction; however, since their nature is distinguished according to their activity,
it is called the "nature of activity."
Therefore, that treatise states:
"One who does not perceive reality is called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)."
The sages and Buddhas are able to see that the *tathatā* within the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings is without differentiation;
as for the distinction of time:
There are three kinds of time.
First is the impure time,
which is the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The second stage of purity is that of the bodhisattva;
the third stage of thorough purity is called the Tathāgata.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"There is the impure, the pure, and the thoroughly pure," and so forth,
in this sequential order.
Sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are distinguished according to their natures based on temporal differences.
This refers to the differentiation of names.
Regarding what is called "all-bases" (kṛtsnāyatana),
there are three distinct types of bases.
First, ordinary beings;
second, bodhisattvas;
third, tathāgatas.
Although these three locations differ,
their nature is omnipresent;
just as space is omnipresent despite the differences among vessels.
Therefore, it is called a "universal base" (*kṛtsnāyatana*). When its nature is defined according to the meaning of being a universal base,
it is called the "nature of the universal base."
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Just as space pervades all things yet is empty and without discrimination,
its intrinsic nature is stainless."
The mind is likewise all-pervasive and non-conceptual.
Regarding "unchanging nature," this clarifies that its nature remains unchanging throughout the three aforementioned periods.
First, during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
the essential nature remains unchanging.
There are three aspects to this immutability.
First, the thought of "I" cannot be altered by the wind.
Second, the fetters of karma.
Water cannot soak or transform it;
third, death by disease cannot burn or transform it. Fire cannot burn or transform it.
When these two were bodhisattvas,
their essential nature was unchanging.
There are two aspects to this non-changing.
First, it is unchanging throughout its entire existence;
second, it is unchanging because it is subject to cessation.
That treatise states:
The Buddha-nature of a bodhisattva is neither born nor extinguished.
Third, at the stage of Buddhahood, the essence of this nature remains unchanging.
There are four aspects of this immutability.
First, one cannot be born;
second, one cannot grow old;
third, one cannot fall ill.
The four types of death cannot cause his death.
Therefore, the Tathāgata possesses a body that is eternally constant, pure, cool, true, and unchanging.
The nature is distinguished by way of its meaning of immutability;
therefore, it is called the "immutable nature.
As for "without distinction":
To clarify its manifold meanings,
its essence is without differentiation;
thus, that treatise states:
The Dharma-body and the Tathāgata,
the Noble Truths and Nirvāṇa—
these qualities are never dissociated.
Just as light is not separate from the sun,
one should know that while these [distinctions] are explained differently according to their respective gateways,
their essence is not distinct.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha is itself Nirvāṇa;
Nirvāṇa is itself the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā)."
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is itself the true reality (*satya*).
The true reality is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Such is the case.
It is called "undifferentiated nature" because its nature is defined by way of the meaning of non-differentiation; furthermore,
it varies according to different individuals.
At times, the categories of nature are divided into thirty-three. What are they?
As explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are seven distinct meanings of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature:
first, permanence; second, bliss; third, self; fourth, purity; fifth, truth; sixth, reality; and seventh, goodness.
Regarding the meaning of the Buddha-nature of future lives, there are six distinct aspects:
first, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness; and sixth, being rarely seen.
These constitute the meaning of "I am the Buddha."
Because they cannot attain the ultimate sovereignty of a Buddha,
they do not speak of a self; rather,
they take delight in the meaning of nirvāṇa.
The nirvana of differentiated characteristics exists only at the stage of Buddhahood;
because one does not yet attain eternal peace,
it is not described as blissful.
In principle, the meaning of Buddha-nature actually pervades all nine stages.
Specifically, there are six attributes:
first, permanence; second, purity; third, truth; fourth, reality; fifth, goodness; and sixth, visibility.
In the sixth, seventh, and eighth stages, the Buddha-nature possesses five attributes:
first, truth; second, reality; third, purity; fourth, goodness; and fifth, visibility.
However, upon entering the ninth stage, [these qualities become fully manifest].
The limits of hearing and seeing are exhausted;
at the tenth stage, one sees the Tathāgata’s ultimate state with the eye of wisdom.
Therefore, it is said to be eternal.
From the eighth stage and below,
they have not yet attained equality with that [state];
thus, the meaning of permanence is briefly concealed, though it exists in reality.
From the first stage, Joy, up to the fifth stage, there are five aspects of Buddha-nature:
first, the true; second, the real; third, the pure; fourth, that which is visible; and fifth, the wholesome and unwholesome.
Because they have not yet attained the emptiness of prajñā,
they are only able to eliminate coarse afflictions while subtle hindrances remain unremoved; thus,
these are termed "wholesome" and "unwholesome."
The Buddha-nature prior to the stages is briefly without differentiation;
this [differentiation] exists from the first stage up to the Tathāgata.
Two kinds and five kinds;
two kinds and six kinds;
one kind and seven kinds.
In total, there are twenty-nine kinds.
When these are combined with the Buddha-nature of the four types of beings— the ordinary person, the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva of great power—
there are then thirty-three kinds of Buddha-nature.
Because its nature is extensively differentiated according to conditions,
it is immeasurable; thus, the Sūtra says:
Buddha-nature is not called a single dharma;
it is not called a hundred dharmas;
it is not called a thousand dharmas.
One should know that all that is wholesome and unwholesome is called the Buddha-nature;
this is from the third section.

There are four distinctions: first, clarifying existence and non-existence; second, clarifying the internal and external; third, discussing according to the world; and fourth, distinguishing between the future and the present.
Regarding "existence and non-existence," there are two gates of meaning.
First, it is discussed in terms of conditions;
second, it is analyzed according to its essence.
Regarding the discussion in terms of conditions:
The Sūtra states that there are four types:
those with icchantika-nature possess it,
while those who possess roots of goodness do not.
Those with the two roots of goodness possess it;
icchantikas do not. Those with three or two [roots] possess both.
Fourth, both are absent.
The meaning has been explained above;
now it is discussed again.
As for the existence of icchantikas,
they possess an unwholesome nature; it is through the dependent origination of buddha-nature that [this is so].
Because it is unwholesome,
the unwholesome dharma is itself the Buddha-nature.
This nature of unwholesomeness exists in icchantikas,
but not in virtuous persons.
That those with roots of goodness possess them while icchantikas lack them refers to their virtuous nature.
The Buddha-nature’s dependent origination and the untainted [dharmas] of the Three Vehicles are termed "wholesome."
Goodness is itself the nature;
therefore, it is called the "nature of goodness.
This nature exists in the noble ones but is absent in icchantikas.
As for the two who possess [it],
they equally possess the nature of reality (tathatā-gotra).
As for the two who do not possess it...
They are likewise devoid of the nature of fruition.
Regarding the statement that existence and non-existence are distinguished according to their essential nature:
as for the essence of Buddha-nature, it is...
It may be described as existent;
it may be described as non-existent;
and it may be described as neither existent nor non-existent.
That which is called "existence" refers to the Buddha-dharmas,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, within the dharmadhātu of dependent origination in the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is described as "existent.
As for what is called "non-existent," there are two meanings to be understood.
First, being devoid of characteristics is called "non-existent.
For example, although the essence of pure *sarpis* (clarified butter) exists,
it lacks characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, or white.
Furthermore, just as the substance of the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings exists,
yet possesses no characteristics such as large or small, long or short,
so too is the Buddha-nature.
Although its substance exists,
it possesses no single characteristic;
this is the meaning of "signlessness."
This is fully explained in the subsequent chapter on the eight consciousnesses.
The two types of non-nature are termed "non-existent" within the Tathāgatagarbha.
The Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
share a single essential nature and are mutually conditioned and assembled.
There is not a single dharma that maintains its own nature separately,
such that one could say those dharmas are eternal apart from all other dharmas.
There is no separate, permanent nature to be found;
all phenomena are exactly like this,
and therefore they are said to be non-existent.
Existence and non-existence are thus.
That which is neither existence nor non-existence does not refer to the two dharmas of existence and non-existence.
It is taught as being neither existent nor non-existent.
Nor is it that the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are abandoned to constitute "neither existent nor non-existent.
Nor is it that existence and non-existence combined into a single dharma constitutes "neither existent nor non-existent."
Nor is it established as a separate dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent among the two dharmas of existence and non-existence;
one should know that this is merely a case of designating that which is non-existent as existent.
If it exists, it is not existent;
one instead explains this existing dharma as non-existent.
If it is non-existent, it is not non-existent.
Therefore, names are neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, a sutra says:
"By means of existence and non-existence, one enters that which is neither existent nor non-existent."
I shall explain this by means of the analysis of characteristics (lakṣaṇa). It is wondrously transcendent of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi). What are these four?
First, it is not existent;
second, it is not non-existent;
third, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
The fourth is neither being nor non-being;
all dependently originated phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature,
the unconditioned is said to exist; because the unconditioned exists, [it is so designated].
Existence is non-existence,
because there is no nature of non-existence; thus,
existence is said to be non-existence.
Because conditioned phenomena do not exist,
their non-existence is itself not non-existent;
thus, one returns to explaining those very dharmas of existence and non-existence.
It is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is not non-existent,
nor does it possess intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Even as it is like the nature of detachment," it further explains that this is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because existence and non-existence [are mutually dependent], the phenomena of existence and non-existence are likewise unattainable.
This is precisely the Buddha-nature.
Its principle transcends form and name;
it is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
Without grasping and without abandoning;
known by right knowledge and skillfully realized through noble wisdom.
The wondrousness within this concludes the first gate.
As for the terms "inner" and "outer," they refer to two distinct gates in meaning.
First, classification according to characteristics;
second, the correspondence between principle and phenomena.
Regarding "according to characteristics":
Sentient beings are taken as the internal;
mountains, rivers, the great earth, and insentient objects are taken as the external.
If one were to speak of the nature of cause and effect therein as being restricted to sentient beings,
it could be said to be "internal."
If one speaks of the principle-nature (li-xing),
this nature pervades both the internal and the external; thus,
although it is distinguished by means of those internal and external characteristics, [it remains the same].
Yet its essence is equal,
being neither internal nor external.
To speak of its emotional and rational principles:
Those very false imaginings— the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas)—
can be said to exist "within," because they are described as having intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Yet true equanimity wondrously transcends emotional delusion;
it is designated as "external."
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"The support for conditioned phenomena— which are distinct from [the state of] abandonment and liberation—
is established as the Tathāgatagarbha."
Furthermore, a sutra states again:
"Although nature dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
it is in reality not identical to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases."
Because they are different [from the internal],
they are called "external.
They are not grasped by the emotions.
It may also be described as being neither internal nor external;
thus, a sutra says:
"The Buddha-nature of sentient beings."
It is neither internal nor external; these two gates are concluded.
As for the phrase "in terms of the world," this refers to its essential nature.
Constantly profound throughout past and present,
it is like empty space, not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The Buddha-nature is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
it is only when its nature is distinguished according to conditions that it may be said to exist within the three periods.
There are those that do not belong to the three periods of time. What are their characteristics?
For now, let us first examine their nature and characteristics with respect to the Buddha.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature,
when viewed from the perspective of its cause,
it can be said to exist in the future.
When distinguishing the effect in relation to the cause,
it can be considered as present; however,
when setting aside such relative discourse, [it is not so].
It is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
This is because the Tathāgata’s essence exhausts true nature and awakens to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally suchness;
it is not that there was first defilement which later ceases to become purity.
Because their virtue is identical to the *dharmatā*,
they do not belong to the three periods of time.
Furthermore, that which is attained...
It is eternally neither arising nor ceasing;
therefore, it does not belong to the three periods of time.
Thus, the Kāśyapa Chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is not of the past, present, or future;
it is the buddha-nature of the final body.
Judging from what precedes it, it is called "future" in relation to its name;
yet, when viewed in contrast to the Buddha,
it is called "past."
When a form precedes and faces what follows,
it is designated as "present," according to the location where it is obtained.
Being separated from arising and ceasing and in accord with suchness,
it may also be said to be not subsumed within the three periods of time.
If it were not comprised within the three periods of time,
why does the sutra state that the Buddha-nature of the final body exists in the present and the future?
Because it is seen only partially, it is called "present.
Because it is fully seen as being in the process of arising, it is called "future.
This does not contradict the statement that [the dharmas] are not of the three time periods.
In short, it is called "present" in relation to its fruit,
and it is called "future" when the fruit is designated as such in relation to its cause.
If one sets aside the opposing arguments,
then it is not [limited to] the three times;
this applies from the ninth stage of the bodhisattva downward.
When one reaches the first bhūmi and discusses its practice,
it is in reality identical to that of the ten bhūmis;
however, in the sūtras...
It is said that from the ninth stage downward, one has heard and seen the Buddha-nature but has not yet seen it with the eye;

therefore, the Buddha-nature possessed by those of the lineage (gotra) and those in the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā) is exclusively subsumed within the three periods of time.
The ultimate reality is exactly as it is described.
In the state where it is fully revealed, it is equal and free from characteristics;
it also does not belong to the three periods of time.
However, for the purpose of definitive classification, everything prior to attaining the stages is considered ordinary;
the Buddha-nature is invariably encompassed within the three periods of time,
and this remains the same even down to the icchantikas.
That which flows and turns according to its characteristics is said to be subsumed within the three periods of time;
yet its essence is neither arising nor ceasing. This concludes the section on these three gates.
Regarding the statement "should be manifested":
if explained from the perspective of ordinary beings,
the causal nature resides in the present.
The nature of the fruit exists in the future;
if one speaks in terms of the Buddha,
the nature of the fruit exists in the present.
The causal nature belongs to the past;
when speaking of its principle-nature (*li-xing*),
its purport extends to the present and the future.
The essence is neither past nor present; these four gates are concluded.
Within the fourth gate, the cause is distinguished according to its nature.
Within this, there are two gates:
first, discrimination based on objects;
second, discrimination arising from birth.
Regarding the phrase "conditioned by the correct," that which directly induces the fruit is termed the "correct cause."
That which is remote yet assists in its manifestation is called a "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu).
With respect to the Buddha-nature as it relates to the fruit,
under which category of cause is it subsumed?
The Sūtra states:
"Precisely because it is their Dharma-nature,
they look toward the Dharma-Buddha."
This is considered the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*),
just as gold within ore is the direct cause for the gold extracted from the ore.
As for the Buddha-nature of fruition (*vipāka-buddhatva*):
I further hope that you will inform the Buddha,
so that this may serve as the direct cause;
just as those seeds of a tree, being neither rotten nor damaged, possess the potential for growth.
It acts as the cause for the tree.
Such is the nature of the primary cause and its conditions.
If one regards enlightenment as a single, collective fruit, [then these factors constitute its causes].
The fundamental substance of Buddha-nature has a stronger sense of being that which gives rise to the fruit; therefore,
it is called the "direct cause."
The various perfections and equal practices, aided and brought forth by skillful means,
are taught as the contributory causes;
if one distinguishes their resultant virtues, they are as follows.
The two distinctions between intrinsic purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*) and skillful means (*upāya*) involve a mutual interchangeability of conditions and objects that is not fixed.
If viewed in relation to intrinsically pure bodhi and nirvāṇa,
then the Buddha-nature is of the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*).
The arising of the marks is taken as the direct cause (hetu-pratyaya),
while the various practices such as the perfections (pāramitās) are called the contributory causes (pratyaya-hetu).
If one looks toward the expedient means of bodhi and nirvāṇa,
the various practices such as the perfections produce fruits that are of a similar kind.
This is called the direct cause (hetu).
It is said that the principle of buddha-nature serves as the supporting condition (pratyaya).
The meaning of the "Right Condition" (pratyaya) is thus concluded in this first section of the coarse dhāraṇī.
As for the term "arising and production" (utpāda):
One aspires to the fruit of skillful means;
the nature of the Reward Buddha is its generative cause.
Within the essence of the true mind, there has been from the very beginning the principle of being able to give rise [to phenomena],
because it gives rise to those fruits.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Although the Buddha-nature is non-existent, it is not like the horn of a rabbit; even with immeasurable skillful means," [it cannot be produced].
That which cannot be produced cannot be the Buddha-nature;
the Buddha-nature can be produced, and because it can be produced, [it is the Buddha-nature].
This is called the cause of arising. Question:
For what reason is there no [existence] of a rabbit's horn?
That which is non-existent cannot be produced;
the non-existence of Buddha-nature is a non-existence that can be produced.
The commentary states:
Among the four types of non-existence, the "non-existent" (śaśaviṣāṇa) refers to absolute non-existence.
Therefore, it cannot arise when compared to the nature-pure fruit,
which is the nature of the Dharma-buddha.
However, it is a revealing cause (vijñapti-hetu),
not a producing cause (janaka-hetu).
How is it known that it is not a producing cause?
As stated in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
the cause of nirvāṇa is what is called buddha-nature.
The nature of the Buddha-nature does not arise in nirvana; therefore,
it is not a cause of arising.
What is the meaning of this?
The cause and fruit of intrinsic purity are identical in essence, with no distinction between them.
They differ according to their respective times:
when in a state of defilement, they act as causes;
when emerging from the entanglements, they act as results.
Judging from the cause,
there is no entity of a fruit that can arise apart from the cause; judging from the fruit,
[there is no cause apart from it].
Since there is no causal entity external to the fruit that can produce it,
it is not a productive cause;
rather, it is merely a revealing cause.
What is the meaning of this? The nature of all Buddhas exists as the substance of the true consciousness-mind;
from the very beginning, it has been so.
There is the sense of being able to manifest and realize a result;
therefore, it is called a "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).
It is like a lamp inside a jar which has the quality of being revealed; once the jar is broken, it becomes visible.
Because there is such a meaning that can be understood,
the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"Although the Buddha-nature differs from empty space, it is not different from it."
Although space cannot be seen despite immeasurable skillful means,
the Buddha-nature can be seen.
That which can be seen is precisely that which is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Because it can be understood, it is called the "cause of understanding" (*pariniṣpattihetu*).
Question: For what reason does the existence of space exist yet remain invisible?
The existence of Buddha-nature is such that it exists and can be seen;
thus says the commentary.
Because space is said to be non-existent, it cannot be seen;
whereas the existence of Buddha-nature is said to exist as an actual existence.
Therefore, there is that which can be seen.
Such is the meaning of the cause. If one proceeds from the perspective of the fruit-virtue (*phala-guṇa*):
Taking them all as one,
the Buddha-nature is thus described as the generative cause (janakahetu),
being of a single essential nature.
The arising of a transformed appearance is conventionally described as "birth," which differs from the cause-and-effect relationship of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Mutually distinguishing themselves from distinct entities,
the cause ceases and the fruit arises;
this is termed "arising."
The various perfections and other practices, when manifested through skillful means,
are explained as the "cause of penetration. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The Buddha-nature is like milk;
the practice of skillful means is likened to the fermenting agent, for milk can produce curd through it.
That which is called the "cause of production" refers to the conditions such as fermenting agents and heat, which manifest curd; therefore,
they are termed "causes of manifestation."
If one distinguishes between the nature-purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and the purity through application (*prayoga-viśuddhi*) in terms of the qualities of the fruition,
then the two characteristics of "arising" and "produced" are not fixed;
this is in view of the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* that are pure by nature.
The practice of the various perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth is their cause of illumination (*vyañjanahetu*).
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The fact that the perfections, such as giving (dāna),
serve as the causes of realization regarding reality is clearly demonstrated by this passage.
In relation to that fruit of intrinsic purity, the Buddha-nature is solely the direct cause;
it is neither produced nor realized.
Regarding the statement "it is not produced":
when the essence of the Buddha is latent, it is termed the cause;
this is viewed from the perspective of that cause.
Because there is no resultant entity that can arise apart from the cause,
the manifestation of time is designated as the "result";
this is stated with reference to the result.
Since there is no causal entity external to the fruit that can produce it,
it is not a productive cause.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The nature of the Buddha-nature does not arise in nirvana;
it is the dharma of nirvana.
It does not arise from causes;
yet, it is further stated that it is produced by the cause of arising.
That which is produced by the revealing cause is called "permanent."
Nirvana is attained solely through causes;
it does not arise from causes [in the sense of being produced]. Therefore, it is called "eternal."
Regarding the statement that it is not a "cause of manifestation":
the Buddha-nature, in terms of its essence,
is not a practice manifested through expedient means.
Therefore, looking toward nirvana,
it is not called the "revealing cause.
If one says that the Buddha-nature transforms according to conditions, [it is not so].
With the former ceasing and the latter arising,
one fulfills nirvana;
this may also be called "birth."
However, it is not a separate entity;
that which exists without being joined together is called "arising."
Furthermore, the Buddha-nature exists within the various stages (*bhūmi*) and is made manifest through conditions.
It is the fulfillment of nirvāṇa,
which may also be termed "clear realization";
however, it is not a distinct characteristic that manifests as nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that they are not fully realized.
However, in relation to the practices of the path of teaching— namely, skillful means, nirvana, and bodhi—
they are both generated and fully realized.
Regarding the "cause of production":
it is called "production" because one relies upon the cultivation of the various perfections (pāramitās) to give rise to those fruits of retribution.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, there is a cause of birth,
namely the six pāramitās and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding the term "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*):
it refers to the qualities of practice and the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*) accomplished throughout the preceding stages.
It is associated with its essence.
Although the essence of virtue has been established,
it remains, when compared to what follows, shrouded by the obscuration of darkness.
It cannot be clearly manifested;
within the attainment of great enlightenment,
there are various practices of skillful means that have been cultivated.
Having dispelled the obscuration of darkness and realized all the aforementioned virtues,
one attains great enlightenment.
Therefore, it is called the "revealing cause" (vijñapti-hetu). Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, there is the revealing cause."
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and Buddha-nature—
when viewed in relation to the fruits of those expedient means—
are both produced and realized.
As for what is called the "generative cause," it refers to the arising from the nature itself of the qualities of the fruit through skillful means,
just as ornamental objects arise from genuine gold.
Therefore, it is called the cause of arising.
For this reason, the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, there is a cause of arising."
This refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is itself the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Buddha-nature is named Śūraṅgama. As for what is called the "revealing cause" (vidyā-hetu):
The Buddha-nature is manifested through those expedient practices;
its essence is then clearly understood.
This nature of clear understanding—
Because it serves as the cause for the realization of the fruit of merit, it is called the "cause of illumination. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Furthermore, there is the revealing cause,
namely the Buddha-nature and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
this distinguishes the differences among causes.
This has been a brief and rough account.
Within the fifth section,
the reasons for the explanations of "nature" (*prakṛti*) found in the sūtras and śāstras are clarified.
The sutras frequently speak of emptiness,
subverting the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and teaching that all phenomena are empty.
Now, for what reason is the buddha-nature being proclaimed here?
For within the gateway of that pure dharma-realm,
all meanings are fully contained.
All phenomena arise through dependent origination;
they are mutually integrated. When one examines phenomena from the perspective of emptiness:
There are no phenomena that are not empty.
When phenomena are analyzed according to their intrinsic nature, there are no phenomena that are not of that nature.
Emptiness and nature each constitute a distinct gateway;
since these gateways differ from one another, [they are separate].
The purpose is also different:
teaching emptiness is for the sake of destroying the attachment to the existence of sentient beings;
teaching the nature (prakṛti) serves a different purpose.
The sūtras and śāstras differ.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to be free from negligence."
He proclaimed the Buddha-nature;
had he not spoken of this nature,
sentient beings would have collectively disparaged themselves.
That is to say, one considers oneself incapable of attaining great enlightenment,
lacks the resolve to enter the path,
and frequently gives rise to negligence.
Therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature and will certainly and inevitably attain realization;
this is intended to cause them to abandon negligence and to proceed accordingly toward that goal.
As stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*:
There are five reasons for this:
first, because sentient beings develop a sense of cowardice and weakness toward their own selves,
thinking that they lack the necessary nature and thus severing themselves from seeking [enlightenment].
It is taught that the Buddha-nature exists equally within all sentient beings, and they shall inevitably attain the fruit;
just as gold exists within ore and will certainly be obtained once it is smelted,
or as fire exists within wood.
If one gathers [the ingredients], it will inevitably arise;
milk possesses the nature of curd,
and when conditions are complete, it emerges.
This single principle increases their valor and their aspiration to seek Buddhahood.
It is identical to nirvāṇa.
Second, because of treating other sentient beings with contempt,
one proclaims the Buddha-nature.
He shall become a Buddha.
How, then, can he be disparaged? Therefore, in the sutra:
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging,
whenever he saw the fourfold assembly,
would cry out in a loud voice:
"You shall become a Buddha.
I do not disparage you,
for I know that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature."
Third, because sentient beings are falsely attached to a self and to living beings,
the Buddha-nature is proclaimed so that they do not grasp it through emotional attachment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is neither a self nor a sentient being."
It is neither life nor person.
Fourth, because of attachment to false dharmas,
the Buddha-nature is proclaimed.
They differ in what they grasp.
Fifth, they slander *tathatā* and Buddha-nature,
claiming that it is subject to annihilation.
Therefore, the Buddha-nature is taught as being true,
real, eternal, blissful, self, and constant. Furthermore,
it is also taught as the Buddha-nature for the sake of those sentient beings who fear annihilation and who delight in what is real and true.
The meaning of the Buddha-nature has been briefly analyzed in this manner.

5. The Meaning of Designation (Prajñapti). Section One: The Meaning of Designation Analyzed through Three Gates. I. Explaining the Name. A. The Existence or Non-existence of Designation. B. Distinguishing the Characteristics. C. First, Explaining the Name.
Regarding the term "provisional name" (prajñapti),
there are four interpretations.
First, all phenomena (dharma) are without names.
Because names are provisionally bestowed upon things, they are called "provisional names" (prajñapti).
It is like a poor and lowly person who falsely claims to be wealthy and noble;
such is the case here as well.
Second, they are designated by depending on others;
therefore, they are called "provisional names" (*prajñapti*).
For example, by depending upon the various aggregates (*skandha*), one obtains the name "sentient being."
Just as a house receives its designation based on rafters, beams, and so forth,
so it is with all such things;
furthermore, this applies to matters such as large and small, long and short.
It obtains its name by depending on others;
because the "great" depends on the "small," it acquires the name of "great."
The same applies to the "small":
because it is a long duration that is relatively short,
it receives the name "long."
The same applies to "short.
Because all things are thus, they are called provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
The designation of the three types of provisionality is termed "provisional designation."
All conventional phenomena lack a fixed nature;
they exist dependently upon other factors.
It is called a "provisional dharma.
It is a provisional designation for a tree;
therefore, it is termed a "provisional name" (prajñapti).
Fourth, all phenomena exist as provisional designations;
therefore, they are called "provisional designations.
What is the meaning of this?
The method of the Discourse on Abolishing Names holds that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations;
they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Nor is it non-existent;
nor is it non-non-existent.
There is no single, fixed characteristic by which it can be distinguished from itself.
One invokes phenomena by means of names;
phenomena follow the turning of names,
and only then do they manifest in their various forms.
The distinctions among all phenomena exist only as provisional designations; therefore,
all phenomena are said to be provisional designations.
Just as with a single dharma of form,
which inherently possesses all meanings such as suffering, impermanence, and so forth,
these are distinguished according to their respective meanings.
Apart from phenomena such as suffering and impermanence,
there is no separate intrinsic nature of form;
it is merely by conventionally applying the name "form" that one designates a collection of those phenomena.
Those dharmas, following their names, aggregate to form a single "form.
It is only when the characteristic of form is established that it is called a "dharma of form"; thus, the dharma of form exists as a conventional designation.
He then further explains that this form is impermanent and so forth,
characterizing it as suffering,
analyzing it according to its meaning.
Apart from phenomena such as the impermanence of form,
there is no separate intrinsic nature of suffering;
it is merely by provisionally applying the name "suffering" that one designates those phenomena as its collection.
Those phenomena, following their names, are integrated into a single suffering;
therefore, the phenomenon of suffering exists only as a conventional designation.
This extends even to the teaching that form is suffering, impermanent, empty, selfless, and so forth.
It is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is distinguished according to its meaning as being external to dharmas such as form.
There is no separate self-nature that is neither existent nor non-existent which can be apprehended;
it is merely by conventionally applying the name "neither existent nor non-existent" that those phenomena are designated as such.
The meanings of those various phenomena correspond to these names;
they are integrated as phenomena that are neither existent nor non-existent,
yet they are also conventionally designated as existing.
As it is with the phenomenon of form,
so it is with all phenomena;
they exist only as provisional designations.
