Therefore, they are called "provisional names" (*prajñapti*). Such is the meaning of the term.
Second, we shall distinguish the existence or non-existence of provisional phenomena, which contains two sections.
First, a general explanation;
second, a detailed analysis.
To discuss it in general terms:
The nature of provisional phenomena is not fixed. Why is it not fixed?
Because one seeks out names and grasps at phenomena.
Although the collections employ different versions,
it is not that provisional phenomena lack a nature;
thus, one may say they possess a substantial essence.
To distinguish according to reality:
if the provisional lacks its own reality, one may say it has no substance. Question: If provisional phenomena possess substance, [how can they be said to lack substance?]
Why does the sutra state that there are "only names," "only functions," and "only provisional designations," yet does not speak of a "provisional substance"?
The explanation states:
the sutra speaks of "only provisional designations."
This is precisely a conventional entity (*prajñapti-vastu*).
Since a conventional entity is not real,
it is therefore said to be merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
The general characteristics are thus.
Next, they will be discussed specifically.
There are three types of provisional phenomena.
There are three aspects: essence, function, and names.
Within these, there are four distinct meanings.
First is the subsuming of names into function.
From the perspective of its essence, it is said to be non-existent;
yet when sought through its particularities,
it is not merely that its provisional essence is empty and non-existent.
The function of names is likewise non-existent;
it is like those sentient beings who seek [the self] separately from within the aggregates.
The essence of arising cannot be apprehended.
Since there is no essence of arising,
one knows from what basis could a name be applied?
When arising functions and there is something performed,
it is merely the functioning of the aggregates;
all such cases are like this.
Therefore, in terms of substantial entity, function, and name,
all are non-existent. In the second part,
the name is said to be distinct from the entity and the function.
Seeking according to reality,
there is simply no essence or function;
it is not that conventional designations do not exist.
Why is this so? Because if one analyzes it according to its distinct parts,
the conventional entity cannot be established.
Therefore, there is no provisional substance.
Function must depend upon a substance;
since there is no substance, [there can be no function].
Since even function does not exist,
there is no provisional function;
thus, names arise based on characteristics.
It acquires its name because it does not arise based on an intrinsic essence;
it is like a person of low status who, despite lacking the essence and function of wealth and nobility, [is still designated by those terms].
They may also be conventionally designated as "wealthy" or "noble.
In all such cases, the three parts—
name, substance, and function— are distinct from the conventional entity itself.
Discussing this according to ultimate reality:
while there is no provisional substance,
it is not that names and functions do not exist.
Why is this so? Because the substance relies on its own reality, whereas the provisional is sought separately;
the provisional lacks its own reality.
Therefore, it has no substantial entity.
"Function" refers to the function of aggregation;
it is the harmonious conjunction of all dharmas.
They depend upon one another to accomplish their function; thus, there is a conventional function.
For example, a single thread alone cannot restrain an elephant, but when many are combined through mutual dependence, they possess the capacity to do so.
In all such cases, since there is a conventional function,
names are established based upon that function.
Names are not non-existent either;
the essence and function of the four means of integration follow from their names,
for there are not merely names alone.
There is also essence and function;
based on the appearance of conjunction, names arise,
and thus there are provisional designations.
By employing these provisional names,
one subsumes individual phenomena so that they all become a single totality.
Therefore, there is a provisional substance;
based on this substance, functions are applied,
and thus there are provisional functions.
Therefore, all three types exist; existence and non-existence are thus.
Third, the distinction between their characteristics and their inclusion or exclusion is not fixed.
In total, it is merely a single designation,
because all phenomena arise from the gathering of causes and conditions and are established through the conventionality of their characteristics.
Alternatively, it may be divided into two.
The second [section] has two gates:
first, the analysis of the arising of dharmas;
second, the analysis according to causes and the harmony of dharmas.

Regarding what is called "arising phenomena," there are two kinds of conventional designations: first, the conventional designation of sentient beings; [and second, the conventional designation of dharmas].
The two dharmas are provisional designations;
"sentient beings" is a provisional designation established from within.
Names are dharmas that are not exhaustive.
Why are they not exhaustive? Because they provisionally extend to both the internal and the external.
That which is internal is a sentient being;
that which is external is not a sentient being.
In the sutras, it is stated directly that "sentient being" is a mere conventional designation.
Setting aside external phenomena,
[the cause] is not exhaustive;
it may also serve as a common cause for both the internal and external aspects of sentient beings.
Within internal and external phenomena,
that which arises through the collective aggregation of general characteristics is termed a "sentient being."
Sentient beings are a mere collection;
this is called the "provisionality of sentient beings.
What are their characteristics?
There are three kinds of discrimination.
First is internal-external discrimination,
which grasps the five internal aggregates (*skandhas*).
That which constitutes sentient beings is called "internal";
it gathers the external four great elements.
They consist of grasses, trees, and so forth,
which are taken as external.
Second is the distinction between the coarse and the subtle.
Within, the aggregates are gathered to form a provisional person;
this is called "subtle. When persons form a multitude, it is called an "army."
Because this is considered coarse,
the designation is established based on the subtle;
therefore, it is specifically said that "sentient beings" are merely provisional names.
Among external objects, one grasps large-scale things such as grasses and trees and regards them as "subtle";
these grasses and trees then aggregate to form things such as groves and forests.
This is considered coarse.
Third is the distinction between defilement and purity.
"Defiled" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Purity" refers to the noble ones (ārya).
Within the phenomena of birth and death,
the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) constitute a person.
Regarding this as ordinary,
within the dharma of nirvana,
the five aggregates constitute a person.
To regard this as "sacred" is a designation based on conventional usage;
the term "dharma" is employed here as a general designation.
Regarding the existence of dharmas as entities:
all phenomena are collectively termed "dharmas.
Their essence is empty and provisional; they are designated by the provisional name "dharma."
What are their characteristics?
There are three types of discrimination:
first, internal-external discrimination.
The internal refers to the six sense faculties;
the external refers to the six sense objects.
These two are distinguished by their coarseness and subtlety.
The combination of causes is coarse;
the combination of dharmas is subtle.
This will be explained later.
Third is the discrimination between defilement and purity.
Defilement refers to saṃsāra;
purity refers to nirvāṇa.
Regarding birth-and-death and nirvana,
the sutras teach them as indeterminate;
some explain that birth-and-death is merely a provisional designation.
Nirvana is not provisional;
birth-and-death is not real.
Because they exist through being provisional and false, they are termed "provisional," such as the designation of a "provisional tree."
Therefore, it is said that they are provisional names;
the essence of nirvāṇa is real and is not a provisional name.
Because it is not provisional,
the designation "nirvāṇa" is not a mere conventional name.
This is because birth and death are merely conventional designations;
thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra speaks of "transcending birth and death."
The name transcends conventional designations.
Alternatively, some may proclaim that while nirvāṇa is a conventional designation, saṃsāra is not.
Nirvana is nameless;
names are provisionally attributed to it,
and thus it is called "provisional designation."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Nirvāṇa is nameless;
names are established for it only by force."
It is like the case of Ghaṭīkāra,
who in reality did not eat oil,
yet falsely claimed to eat oil.
The essential nature of the phenomena of birth and death is conditioned;
it is not a mere conceptual construct.
Therefore, they are not merely provisional designations.
Some, however, proclaim that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally provisional designations.
Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
None possess a fixed nature;
because they are a provisional gathering of causes and conditions, they are said to be "provisional."
A tree is a provisional designation; therefore, it is called a "provisional name" (*prajñapti-nāman*).
Likewise, the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvana exist only as provisional names.
Therefore, it is called a "provisional name" (prajñapti). Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Form is a provisional name, and so on, up to nirvāṇa—all are provisional names."
Some proclaim that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are neither conventional designations;
they discard names to seek the Dharma,
for the Dharma is free from names.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"All phenomena are devoid of an intrinsic nature apart from their names."
Question: Previously it was stated that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely provisional designations;
now you say that neither exists.
What is the reason for this?
The commentary states:
Names are used to designate all phenomena;
because phenomena follow after names, they are all merely provisional designations.
To discard names in order to seek the Dharma,
one finds that all dharmas are beyond words;
therefore, nothing at all is a provisional name.
Now, proceeding to the third [point],
the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are explained.
This concludes the section on the provisional designation of "dharmas."
Next, regarding the causes, the phenomena, and the discrimination:
as for "causes and conditions," this refers to the conventional designation of the conjunction of causes.
Regarding the "Dharma of phenomena" (dharmadharma):
this is a conventional designation based on the conjunction of phenomena. What are these two?
Regarding the boundaries of phenomena,
one gathers particulars to form a whole and combines the subtle to constitute the coarse.
A designation based on the combination of causes is a conventional construct;
it gathers particulars to form a whole,
just as the aggregates (skandhas) constitute a person.
The subtle constitutes the coarse,
just as subtle matter constitutes coarse matter and so forth;
this is the demarcation of phenomena.
The meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth,
are mutually established through their identical essence;
this is termed the provisional designation of dharmas.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
the emptiness of the combination of causes is termed the "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*),
while the emptiness of the combination of phenomena is termed the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, this same principle also exists;
the difference lies in its depth and shallowness. For instance, it may be divided into three [stages].
As stated in the "Chapter on the Three Kinds of Designation" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
first, the designation of the person (*pudgala-prajñapti*);
second, the designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*).
The third is the designation of names.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of three gates.
The first is the explanation of their names.
Second, the definition of its essential nature and characteristics;
third, the sequence of contemplative entry.
First, to explain the terminology: "provisional designation of sensation" (vedanā-prajñapti).
Because it encompasses many factors in total,
it is called "feeling" (vedanā).
Feeling is a conventional designation formed by the aggregation of many factors.

Therefore, it is called "conventional designation" (*prajñapti*). As for the term "conventional designation of phenomena" (*dharma-prajñapti*), that which possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called a phenomenon.
Because the essence of phenomena is a void collection, they are said to be "provisional as phenomena" (*dharmaprajñapti*).
As for the term "provisional as names" (*nāmaprajñapti*), it means that what manifests phenomena is called a "name."
Based on phenomena and based on conceptualization, they are provisionally established;
therefore, it is said that "name" is a provisional designation. This concludes the first section.
Next, its characteristics are analyzed.
The two gates of the dharma of reception are distinguished in relation to one another, as Nāgārjuna said:
"Provisional dharmas are reception; real dharmas are the dharma."
Although this is the general characteristic,
its meaning remains difficult to understand;
herein, it shall be briefly analyzed by means of two points.
First, directly within the context of the conjunction of causes,
one should analytically distinguish all phenomena of sensation according to their meaning.
Gathering the subtle to form the coarse,
and subsuming the particular to form the general—
all these are termed "feeling" (vedanā).
Each distinct sub-division is called a *dharma*.
It is like a person who constitutes a multitude;
the multitude itself is termed "feeling" (*vedanā*).
A person is a phenomenon; the aggregates taken together constitute a person.
Furthermore, this person is the recipient of the aggregates, and these aggregates are themselves phenomena.
It is thus for all things.
Although the dharmas of sensation differ,
they are equally established through conditions;
in their provisional aggregation, their meaning is one.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "provisional.
Second, regarding the analysis of causes, conditions, and phenomena:
all causes and conditions [are so].
To grasp individual elements and form a whole is called the conventional designation of experience (*upādāya-prajñapti*).
That all phenomena (*dharma*) are established through characteristics such as suffering and impermanence is the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*).
The Dharma of sensation is likewise.
Regarding the term "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*),
there are two explanations provided in the treatise.
First, explaining by way of general application:
the two types of names— namely "appropriation" (upādāna) and "phenomena" (dharma)—
are collectively termed "conceptual designations" (prajñapti).
Therefore, the treatise states:
"By means of their names,
one apprehends the two preceding dharmas."

This refers to the designation of names as provisional; secondly, it takes only the designation of the provisional person (pudgala-prajñapti) as the "provisional name," while the designation of dharmas (dharma-prajñapti) is the "provisional dharma."
It is judged to belong to the category of conventional designation (prajñapti). Therefore, the treatise explains:
"Upon the basis of many names, further names arise."
It is said that these are conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
For example, based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the designation "sentient being" arises;
and based on the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, the designation "tree" arises.
The multitude of trees is called a "boundary," and the grove is called "arising.
All such things are designated as conventional (prajñapti).
Such is their essential nature and characteristic; these two gates are now concluded.
Next, the sequence for discerning through contemplation and for dismantling and dispelling [misconceptions] is explained as it is stated in the treatise:
first, one dismantles the conventional designation of names.
It is simply because names are provisionally established based on phenomena and based on conceptualization.
Being floating and empty, it is easily destroyed;
therefore, it is destroyed first. Next, the conventional designation of "feeling" (vedanā) is destroyed.
Feeling is established according to the Dharma;
it is a mere collection and easily divided.
Therefore, feeling is refuted next.
Next, the provisional nature of phenomena (dharma) is refuted.
Phenomena are the fundamental basis, subtle and difficult to perceive;
they are difficult to analyze.
Therefore, it is subsequently refuted.
How is the dharma refuted? Generally, there are eight ways of explaining it.
First, refuting by examining the underlying sentiment:
as it is said, "The deluded and blind are greedily attached to a self;
the three realms are illusory, produced solely by the deluded mind."
All such cases are refuted by the wisdom of investigation.
As it is said: "The wise do not find the dharma of ignorance, for it lacks intrinsic nature."
In this way, all such [arguments] are refuted by tracing them back to their causes,
just as the nature of a sentient being is refuted by tracing it back to the causes of the aggregates (*skandha*).
By tracing back its past causes, one refutes the nature of present permanence;
all such cases are refuted by examining the effect.
Just as the future effect refutes the absence of a present cause,
so it is in all such cases; this is the fivefold refutation through mutual exclusion.
As it is said: "If there is a self, then there is what belongs to a self;
if there is no self, then there is nothing that belongs to a self.
Furthermore, as stated in a sutra:
There is bondage and there is liberation;
there is neither bondage nor liberation.
All such cases are like this.
The first is called refutation by means of logical inference (*tarka*). The second is refutation by means of reasoning (*yukti*),
such as when it is said that "the nature of all phenomena is inherently empty," and so forth.
The seventh is refutation by means of shifting the name.
For example, when one speaks of milk, one cannot apply the name "curd";
this clarifies that the nature of curd does not exist [in the milk].
All such [arguments] are refuted by the eightfold examination of reality,
just as when a person in the darkness of night sees a rope and perceives it as a snake.
To say that it is merely a rope yet perceived as the Tathāgatagarbha,
which is taken to be birth-and-death;
and to say that it is merely the Garbha and fundamentally has no birth-and-death.
All such things, which destroy all dharmas by means of these eight kinds,
are called the "falsehood of destroying the Dharma."
Having destroyed the conventional designation of phenomena, one reaches the true mark of phenomena.
This true mark of phenomena is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā) and the three [other] suchnesses; alternatively, these may be divided into four.
From its initial arising from causes up to its continuity,
this will be briefly analyzed through five gates.
First, the explanation of its name.
Second, its characteristics are defined;
third, by way of time and category,
the distinctions of its conventional designation are revealed.
Fourth, distinguishing their breadth and narrowness;
fifth, correlating them with the three types of conventional designations and subsuming them within the characteristic of suffering.
First, the explanation of the name.
What is this name? It is called "dependently produced" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) because it is a designation based on causes. It is also called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyajāta*).
Second, the provisional [nature] established through causes is also called "established through conditions" (*pratyaya-siddha*).

Third, the provisional [nature] established through mutual dependence is also called "established through relative comparison" (*apekṣā-siddha*). Fourth, the provisional [nature] of continuity (*saṃtati-siddha*).
Regarding the statement "arising from causes":
it means that from causes, effects arise,
and distinct entities and characteristics emerge.
Therefore it is said: "arising through causes.
Arising occurs dependently upon conditions;
this is called "arising through conditions" (hetu-utpāda-prajñapti).
Arising based on the collection of conditions is called "dependent origination as a designation.
As for the term "established by causes":
Phenomena (dharmas) have both general and specific aspects.
The specific serves as the cause for the general,
and the general serves as the effect of the specific.
By synthesizing those specific causes, a general effect is produced;
since the effect is dependently established upon its causes, it is termed "conceptual existence through dependence on causes" (hetu-samutthāna-prajñapti).
Furthermore, because a collective result is formed by gathering individual conditions,
it is also termed "provisional through conditional formation" (pratyaya-saṃbhūta-prajñapti). As for "provisionality through mutual dependence" (āpekṣika-prajñapti):
Matters such as long and short, large and small, high and low, and so forth,
are distinguished by comparison; they are designated as distinct only through mutual dependence.
"Nominal designation based on mutual dependence" refers to this.
As for "designation based on continuity," it refers to the transmigration of conditioned phenomena.
Tracing from the prior life to the subsequent one,
the two ends— prior and subsequent—
are called "mutual inclusion and correspondence," which is termed "continuity."
That which is called "provisional" refers to the two ends, the prior and the posterior,
which mutually depend upon one another to form a continuous succession.

This is called the "conventional designation of continuity" (saṃtāna-prajñapti). Furthermore, through continuity, a single dharma can be formed; thus, a single conventional designation is established through continuity.
This is called the "conventional designation of continuity.
The meaning of the name is thus; this concludes the first section.
Within the second section:
Distinguishing their essential natures and characteristics:
within the first category of the provisional,
there are two distinct names.
First is "arising from causes" (hetu-utpāda),
and second is "arising from conditions" (pratyaya-utpāda). Within these two, there is a fourfold analysis.
First, when a true cause produces an effect in accordance with the diversity of phenomena,
it is called "provisionality arising from causes," such as when wholesome and unwholesome karma gives rise to suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Because they arise conditioned by causes, they are termed "dependently arisen designations," such as the arising of suffering, pleasure, and so forth from afflictions.
Second, dependent origination is subsumed under causality.
All phenomena that arise from distinct natures and characteristics are termed "produced by causes.
This does not distinguish between those that are proximate and those that are remote; therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Stages of Yogic Practice):
It is taught that all phenomena arise from ten causes;
because all phenomena arise from these ten causes,
they are all termed "arisen from causes."
The three types of causes are subsumed under their effects.
The arising of the essential nature and characteristics of the effects of all phenomena is termed "dependent origination."
Without discriminating between the near and the distant,
it is taught that all phenomena arise from four conditions;
for all phenomena arise from these four conditions.
All are termed "dependently arisen.
Fourth, dependent origination collectively reveals all phenomena;
that is, all phenomena.
The arising of distinct entities and characteristics is all termed "arising from causes" and is also called "arising from conditions."
Therefore, in the sutras, the twelve links of dependent origination are collectively termed "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because causes and conditions are universal, the phenomena produced thereby—
The designation "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) arises from this; it is synonymous with "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna).
Question: [Why is this so?]
What was previously explained as phenomena arising from a primary cause is called "arising from causes";
phenomena arising from conditions are called "dependent origination. Since causes and conditions are distinct, [the two are different].
"Why are they not divided into two,
but instead combined into one?
To this, he replied:
There is no harm in establishing them separately;
however, these two arise as distinct entities,
and their meanings are similar.
Therefore, they are combined into one.
Furthermore, as previously stated, because the meanings of "dependent origination through causes" and "dependent origination through conditions" are also identical, they are treated as one.
Second, within the section on the conventional (prajñapti):
Names also have two kinds:
first, those established by causes;
second, those established by conditions.
Regarding these two,
there are four gates for distinguishing their differing meanings.
First, the gate of discourse according to the diversity of dharmas.
Within those phenomena that are formed by aggregating particulars into a whole,
phenomena of the same class constitute the coarse through the accumulation of the subtle.
Names are established based on causes,
such as coarse form being established by means of subtle form; thus,
things of different categories establish one another.
It is called "conditioned arising" (pratītyasamutpāda),
as in the case of the five aggregates forming a sentient being and so forth,
because they are of a similar kind and related by kinship.
It is said that [the cause] is established as the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) because it is heterogeneous and remote;
it is said to be established as a *pratyaya* (condition).
Second, regarding the inclusion of conditions based on causes: all phenomena,
provided they are formed by aggregating particulars into a whole, [are included].
This is called "established by cause.
Because it stands in contrast to those dharmas that are distinct entities and remote,
it is designated as a "cause."
Regarding the three ways of subsuming causes from conditions:
all phenomena that are formed by gathering distinct factors.
This is called "conditioned origination" (pratyaya-siddhi),
because it is contrasted with those past directly productive causes (janaka-hetu).
Thus, the four types of causes and conditioned origination together manifest all phenomena (dharma).
All dharmas that are established by aggregating distinct elements are collectively termed "established through causes."
The same applies to establishment by way of designation. Question:
It was stated previously that establishment by way of generic similarity is established as a conceptual construct based on causes. What is the meaning of this?
When things of different categories are established through mutual dependence, it is called a "conceptual designation established by conditions.
Since the causes and conditions are distinct,
why are they not categorized separately?
Thus, they are combined into one.
The commentary states:
"There is no harm in establishing them separately."
However, these two [categories] are combined into one because they are similar in meaning,
as both involve grasping particulars to form a whole.
Furthermore, as previously explained, both establishment by way of causes and establishment by way of conditions also have the sense of collectively manifesting all phenomena;
therefore, they are said to be one.
This is the third [section] on the conventional.
All phenomena are not one;
among them there are long and short, large and small, high and low, this and that,
coming and going, noble and base, good and evil.
All such things are mutually dependent; for instance,
if a ten-foot object does not face a five-foot object,
the characteristic of length does not arise.
The name "long" does not arise;
it is only in relation to something five chi tall that the characteristic of length is first distinguished.
The arising of long names depends on mutual dependence;
all such things are likewise conventional designations.
In the fourth provisional [teaching], dharmas are likewise not unitary;
they merely cause all dharmas to arise from the preceding to the succeeding,
in continuous succession.
All are termed "continuity.
Question: Does this continuity reside in the preceding [moment]?
If it were to exist only at the end,
how could it be called a "continuity" (saṃtati)? Since it is described as a continuity, how could it possibly be restricted to one part alone?
He asked again:
"In this tantra, why is it called 'provisional' (prajñapti)?
There are two meanings for this explanation."
First, based on both sides,
they mutually rely upon one another to establish the meaning of continuity.
Therefore, it is said to be provisional.
What are its characteristics? They are like those of the preceding moment of consciousness.
Because it relies on subsequent moments of thought,
the preceding [moment] can achieve continuity;
this refers to the phenomena of subsequent moments of thought.
Because the preceding thought serves as a condition,
the subsequent one is able to form a continuity;
this continuity formed through mutual dependence is called "conceptual continuity" (saṃtati-prajñapti).
This is one meaning.
As for the second meaning:
although the two sides are different.
Continuity constitutes a single dharma;
this single dharma is formed through continuity by depending upon its preceding and succeeding limits.
Therefore, it is called "provisional. Question:
If that is so, what is the difference between this and the formation [of phenomena] through prior and subsequent conditions?
The commentary states:
"A single essence is differentiated according to its meanings.
When these distinctions are gathered together, they form a totality from the perspective of meaning."
It is said to be "dependently established.
Regarding the aspect of the continuity of preceding and succeeding moments,
it is said to be "continuity."
Furthermore, there is another analysis which also contains slight differences.
What are these differing characteristics?
Establishment by conditions is broad;
continuity is narrow, as explained in the section on "Continuity and Establishment by Conditions."
Combining the twelve periods [of the day] forms one full day.
Within these twelve periods...
When the hours of the Tiger (寅) and Monkey (申) face each other, and those of the Rabbit (卯) and Rooster (酉) generate one another,
although they are separated and do not connect directly,
they attain harmony and together complete a single day.
Therefore, it is said to be "broad.
Within the context of the conventional designation of continuity,
although it is taught that twelve time-periods joined together constitute one day, [it is still broader].
Among these, the hours of *yin*, *shen*, *māo*, and *you* are positioned opposite one another;
since they are separated by time,
they cannot be said to form a continuous stream.
Only those that are in immediate proximity can be said to constitute a continuity;
therefore, it is called "narrow."
The essential nature and characteristics are thus; this concludes the second section.
Within the third section, the provisional distinctions are elucidated according to time and category.
Regarding the arising from causes within the conventional and the middle way, there are four distinctions.
The first is arising from causes that are of the same kind and simultaneous.
It is like the sun appearing in the sky reflected in water;
it is like an image arising from a face;
it is like an echo produced by sound.
Just as the solitary-wandering fragrance arises from a fragrant tree,
so too do all such things as forms, sounds, and fragrances arise through the production of their own specific characteristics.
Therefore, they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Because they arise simultaneously,
they are termed "simultaneous" (samakāla).
Second, arising from causes that are of the same kind but at different times,
such as barley producing barley or grain producing grain.
Third, arising from causes that are of different kinds but at the same time.
It is like visual consciousness arising from the eye and visible forms;
it is like a bell producing sound;
it is like an echo resounding from a cliff.
All such cases are like this.
Fourth, there is production from causes that are of a different category and at a different time;
for example, karma and afflictions of the past give rise to present suffering and pleasure.
This is dependent origination;
it is likewise called "origination through causes. It is the conventional reality established through conditions, situated within the middle way.
There are also four kinds. First,
formation through causes that are of the same category and simultaneous,
such as forming coarse matter by means of subtle matter.
Numerous small sounds combine to form a loud sound;
all such cases are like this.
Second, those of the same category are formed through conditions at different times.
Just as twelve hours combine to form one day,
so it is with all things:
time is formed by time.
Therefore, they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Their synthesis across preceding and succeeding moments is termed "different times" (bhinnakāla).
Third, they are established through the simultaneous conditioning of different categories.
For example, in the Mahāyāna, the five aggregates constitute a person;
it is the same in the Abhidharma.
What are called the four great elements constitute the various sense faculties and so forth.
These four are formed through the harmonious conjunction of different categories, occurring both simultaneously and sequentially.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the five aggregates constitute a person;
because the aggregates and the person are distinct, they are termed "different categories."
Because matter and mind arise together, they are said to be "simultaneous.
Because the four types of mind occur in succession, they are said to be "at different times.
This is according to other treatises.
The five aggregates constitute a person;
they exist simultaneously and unilaterally.
This is what is meant by "formation through causes" and "formation through conditions."
Within the conventional designation of mutual dependence (*apekṣā-prajñapti*), there are also four types.
The first is mutual dependence by way of being of the same kind and occurring simultaneously.
Just as in the present world people compare themselves with one another and gods compare themselves with one another—
in this same way, all such things involve two similar entities that exist at different times and depend upon one another.
Just as one compares a person of the present day with a person from the beginning of the kalpa,
so it is in all such cases.
Third, different categories [of beings] exist simultaneously in mutual dependence.
Just as in the present world, form and mind, appearance and emptiness, and existence and non-existence stand in mutual dependence,
so it is with all such things.
Fourth is mutual dependence across different categories and different times.
Just as one explains the present result based on a past cause,
so it is in all cases within the context of the conventional designation of continuity.
There are also four kinds.
First, the continuity of similar types at the same time,
such as when similar material forms in the present world mutually succeed one another.
They are joined together by cords;
all things are like this.
Second, there is the simultaneous succession of different types.
Just as in the present world various material objects are successively joined together,
such as joining a *nīpa* tree with a *khadira* tree, so it is in all cases.
Third, there is the continuity of the same kind at different times,
such as when a subsequent form arises from a preceding form;
all such cases are like this.
Fourth is the continuity of different types at different times,
such as the arising of a present effect from a past cause;
all such cases are like this.
The similarities and differences among these types have been summarized thus; this concludes the three gates.
Within the fourth gate:
Distinguishing their breadth and narrowness.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, distinguishing their breadth and narrowness in terms of existence and non-existence.
Second, distinguishing their breadth and narrowness by means of the permanent and the impermanent.
Regarding existence and non-existence,
among the four types of conventional designations:
The conditions of mutual dependence and continuity apply to both existence and non-existence;
the single type of cause that produces [an effect] is restricted to existence alone.
Question: It can be understood that the principle of mutual dependence applies to both existence and non-existence. This meaning is clear.
The middle way established through dependent origination as conventional: how does it accord with both existence and non-existence?
This is as stated in the sūtra.
Within the Great Nirvana,
all the merits of wisdom and abandonment are subsumed;
these are the merits of wisdom and abandonment.
Nirvana is established through conditions:
wisdom constitutes its existence, while the severance [of defilements] constitutes its non-existence.
Therefore, it is established through conditions and can apply to both existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The two abandonments and the two knowledges bring about the realization of bodhi; this,
too, is established through conditions.
It penetrates both existence and non-existence. Question:
How does the continuity penetrate existence and non-existence?
The commentary states:
The meaning of arising and continuity is restricted to the realm of existence (bhava).
The continuity of connection:
its meaning applies to both existence and non-existence,
just as the dharma of nirvāṇa connects with saṃsāra.
Regarding the distinction between the breadth and narrowness of "permanent" and "impermanent":
all four conventionalities (prajñapti) encompass both the permanent and the impermanent.
How do they all encompass them?
Regarding the provisional [nature] arising from causes within the Middle Way, there are four distinct categories.
The first is that impermanence gives rise to impermanence.
That is to say, within the world, there are two [views]:
first, that impermanent causes produce impermanent effects;
second, that the impermanent produces the permanent.
This means that from the mundane, impermanent goodness,
there arises the supramundane fruit of eternal enlightenment;
therefore, within the context of Nirvana, the Buddha answered Jāti.
In your doctrine, an impermanent fruit arises from a permanent nature;
in my Buddha-dharma, however, [it does not].
If a permanent effect were produced from an impermanent cause,
what fault would there be?
This would mean that the impermanent gives rise to the permanent.
Third, the constant gives rise to the constant;
that is to say, bodhi is produced from the buddha-nature.
Therefore, the sutra says:
Furthermore, there is the cause of birth,
namely the *śūraṅgama* anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the *śūraṅgama* samādhi.
This is precisely the Buddha-nature.
Fourth, the eternal gives rise to the impermanent;
that is to say, based upon the true consciousness, the deluded consciousness arises.
Based on the eternal body (nityakāya), there arise transformations, births, and cessations.
Within the provisional middle established through conditions,
there are three distinct categories of phrases.
First, impermanence results in further impermanence;
that is to say, within the world,
the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are gathered together to form a person.
Human beings become members of the assembly and so forth;
secondly, they constantly return to being constant,
which refers to that which exists within the supramundane.
The five aggregates are eternally abiding;
they constitute the attainment of Buddhahood and Bodhisattvahood;
these three—permanence, impermanence, and their harmonious integration—are established through conditions.
This means that sentient beings are composed of the eight consciousnesses;
the first seven are impermanent,
while the last one is permanent.
Within the conventional designation of mutual dependence,
there are also three phrases.
The first is that impermanence itself depends upon impermanence.
That is to say, within the world,
things are defined by long and short in relation to one another,
and by large and small in comparison to one another.
Second, the constant depends upon the constant;
that is to say, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are mutually defined by their relative positions, high and low,
and so it is in all such cases.
Third, impermanence depends upon permanence;
that is, it is in dependence upon birth and death that nirvāṇa is proclaimed.
In this way, within the conventional designation of continuity (*saṃtāna-prajñapti*),
there are four distinct categories.
First, the constant continuity of the impermanent,
which refers to the continuity of conditioned phenomena within the world;
second, the constant succession of the impermanent.
That is to say, those supramundane, eternally abiding fruits of merit confront birth and death; thus,
the three kinds of impermanence continue into permanence.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the mental consciousness that arises after emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) always continues on. It is constant.
This means that by means of a permanent cause, a permanent fruit is continuously produced.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The lineage bodhisattva possesses the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-viśeṣa*)."
They continue in succession from one to another, being the natural state since beginningless time.
A question is asked:
"If a phenomenon is eternal, it must be devoid of transition and change."
How is "continuity" explained?
The commentary states:
"The nature of permanence is without transition or change."
Therefore, it is not by means of a single dharma that the arising and ceasing are said to continue;
rather, it is because the subsequent arising connects with the preceding virtue that it is called "continuity."
Just as when the perception of permanence arises in the second stage,
it connects back to the first stage;
so it is in all such cases.
Furthermore, with respect to a single dharma that undergoes transformation according to conditions,
one may speak of "continuity," as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
The continuity of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is precisely what this refers to.
Such are the breadth and narrowness [of these categories]; thus concludes the section on these four gates.
Next, we shall subsume these under the three types of provisional designations (trividha-prajñapti) as common characteristics.
As for the "three types of provisional designations," they refer to the names of phenomena (dharmas) received as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of connection:
it is explained that within dharmas, all four types of designation (prajñapti) are fully present.
Just as when a single form-dharma arises from a preceding moment to a succeeding one,
it is a provisional designation for that which is produced by causes; once it has passed, it is no longer produced by those causes.
It is also produced by causes;
the subtle becomes the coarse.
It is established as conventional through conditions.
The characteristics of all phenomena, such as suffering and impermanence, are established through mutual dependence; they are also established through conditions.
They are defined by their relative dimensions—large and small—and compared by their degrees of coarseness and subtlety.
This is the conventional designation of mutual dependence.
The continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments is the conventional designation of continuity.
Within the conventional designation of "feeling," there are likewise four types of conventional designations,
as when one speaks of a "sentient being."
Taking this as sensation,
sentient beings each arise from past causes;
these causes give rise to what is provisional.
It is formed by gathering the aggregates;
thus it is a provisional existence established through conditions.
High and low are defined in relation to one another, as are noble and base.

This is the conventional designation of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣa-prajñapti*). The continuous succession of arising and ceasing is the conventional designation of continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*).
All such cases are likewise [conventional designations].
That [the fourth] is established through conditions is the correct meaning;
the other three are secondary.
Why is this so? That which is called "feeling" (vedanā) is a conventional designation established through conditions within the middle way.
It is called "feeling" (vedanā) because it accepts many dharmas;
such is the meaning of feeling.
It is precisely when [the object] is present as a condition that it is established; other cases do not possess the sense of being "received," and are therefore described as peripheral.
Within the conventional designation of names,
there are likewise four types of conventionality;
these are established based on the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Name has the nature of sound;
it arises from the striking together of the four great elements.
It is a designation based on causes.
Based on other treatises,
that which is called a phenomenon that is neither matter nor mind arises from perception;
it is termed a "conceptual designation arising from causes."
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"To establish and designate provisional names such as 'ground' is called the conceptualization of ground (*bhūmi-saṃjñā*)."
Therefore, one knows that names arise from conceptualization and are established based on suchness.
A name is a conventional sound;
it is formed by gathering together those actual sounds in combination.
Thus, it is a conventional construct established through conditions.
According to other treatises,
it is called a phenomenon that is neither matter nor mind;
however, this is conditioned.
Within a single moment of thought, there are the phases of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
because it is composed of these four characteristics, such as arising and abiding,
it is called a "provisional existence established by conditions."
The mutual comparison of degrees and the contrasting of good and evil constitute the "provisionality of relativity" (相待假).
The continuous succession of preceding and following moments constitutes the "provisionality of continuity" (相續假).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among these four types, it is the "conditioned continuity" (*pratyaya-saṃtati*) that is established.
This is the primary meaning, while the other two are secondary. Why is this so?
Because they state that names are merely conventional sounds.
Grasping those actual sounds,
they are successively formed; therefore,
it is precisely through conditions that a continuity is established.
The others are not correctly established;
therefore, they are said to be "lateral.
This is according to other treatises.
The correct meaning is that [arising] is established through causes and conditions,
as well as through continuity;
mutual dependence is merely incidental.

Why is this so? He explains that names are neither matter nor mind; they arise based on conceptualization (saṃjñā) and are further composed of the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Because the preceding and succeeding moments are established as a continuity, it is taught that the characteristic of continuity consists in being produced by causes and established by conditions;
this is taken as the correct meaning.
Since they are established through mutual dependence rather than by way of intrinsic nature,

It is asked:
The *Tattvasiddhi* also states that names arise based on the four great elements. Why,
then, does that school not maintain that arising from causes is the correct principle?
The commentary states:
There is a reason for this; it is because [the argument] is established within the *Tattvasiddhi*.
It is taught that sound arises from the conjunction of the four great elements;
it is through this conjunction that sound acquires its designation as "sound."
The *Śūnyatā-vibhaṅga* contains one section;
therefore, its presentation of arising is not considered the correct principle. This is as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and other such texts.
The names are proclaimed;
because they arise based on the notion of a real entity,
it is taught that arising from causes is the correct meaning.
It is not comparable to this.
[The opponent] asks:
For what reason is it said that within the conventional designation of phenomena (dharmas)?
The four provisional [designations] are all correct.
Among the two types of "receiving" (vedanā),
there are both the primary and the secondary.
The commentary states:
The Dharma is universal and thus correct in all four cases;
because the term "receiving" (śīla) is restrictive, there are both primary and secondary [forms].
According to the various treatises on phenomena,
conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are indeed immeasurable. This refers to the meaning of conventional names.

The Meaning of Entering the Gate of Non-duality (1). Entering the Gate of Non-duality: An Exegesis through Three Gates. First, defining the name;
second, discerning the characteristics.
Briefly stated, there are three distinctions. First, the explanation of the name:
"Entering the Gate of Non-duality," as taught by Vimalakīrti.
To speak of "non-duality" means the absence of difference;
it is precisely the meaning of the single reality within this sutra.
The principle of the single reality is wondrously quiescent and free from characteristics;
it is suchness, equal and impartial.
It perishes in both this and that;
therefore, it is called non-dual. Question:
All phenomena may be one, two, three, or even many;
yet the principle that overturns this teaching should logically be neither one, nor two, nor three, nor even many.
For what reason is it specifically said to be "non-dual"?
The explanation states:
it is not one, nor even many.
There is a passage in the sutras that states this;
thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"With the exception of the characteristic of a single dharma."
It is incalculable. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra also says:
"Among the manifold dharmas..."
There is not a single characteristic of any phenomenon;
nor is there even a multiplicity of characteristics within a single phenomenon.
For now, however, let us examine the principles by means of the gates of "one" and "not-two," while briefly omitting other matters.
This is because these two terms are mutually applicable to both [positions].
Therefore, it is spoken of as non-dual by way of partial contrast.
Furthermore, "duality" is the beginning of distinct phenomena;
here, this is intended to clarify that the essence of principle has no distinction.
Therefore, in contrast to duality, non-duality is taught; yet,
although non-duality is taught,
it is neither one, nor three, nor even many.
All enter therein. What is the meaning of this?
If one were to establish a single characteristic (ekalakṣaṇa).
To take one as opposed to many—
that is, for those two to each in turn oppose the other two—
is therefore called "non-duality."
If one posits many characteristics,
then pairing the many with the few results in nothing other than two.
It is called "non-dual" because it is the inverse of those two.
Furthermore, many characteristics are established.
Among many phenomena, that which stands in mutual relation to another is likewise "two"; conversely,
that which opposes those two is also so designated.
Therefore, they are non-dual.
