It is not different from the six dharmas.
As for what are called the six dharmas,
they are the five aggregates and the self.
Based on these words, they claim that there is a self;
however, as for what is called "self" within the Buddha's Dharma:
The various aggregates (skandhas) are combined;
it is a conventional designation for their collective function that they are called "self."
Their establishment of a fixed reality is a source of affliction;
for they may explain it by distinguishing it according to the aggregates (skandhas).
Regarding the views of these five persons, they differ:
some proclaim the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) to be the self,
while others [proclaim] feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Alternatively, sixteen [types] are taught, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:

first, self; second, sentient being; third, life-span possessor; fourth, living being; fifth, one who is born; sixth, nourisher; seventh, numerical category; eighth, person; ninth, agent; tenth, instigator of action; eleventh, originator; twelfth, instigator of origination; thirteenth, experiencer; fourteenth, instigator of experience; fifteenth, knower; sixteenth, seer.
This meaning will be analyzed in detail later in the section on the sixteen types of self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, depending on the distinctions among the aggregates (*skandha*), these are divided into twenty types; for example, as in the case of [the twenty types of] form (*rūpa*).
Human calculations differ;
there are four distinct types.
Some people calculate as follows:
"Form is the self"—
this is the first [view].
Or there are those who reckon:
Form is not the self; form belongs to the self.
These are the two [views].
When it is asked what constitutes the "self," and it is said that "form" is "what belongs to the self," this refers to the four aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā).
Taking this to be the self,
one need not yet analyze the place from which "mine" arises; rather, one analyzes the place from which [the notion of] arising occurs.
Among the sixty-five kinds of selfhood mentioned later,
this present discussion may suffice as a general characterization.
Some may calculate and claim:
Form is the dwelling-place of this self;
the self resides within it.
This is the third [point].
Some may calculate and say:
"The 'self' is the cave-dwelling of this form;
form dwells within it."
This is the fourth [point].
Among these four, the first is the view of a self (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
The remaining three are views of "mine. As it is with form,
so it is with feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness.
The categories are likewise equal:
five aggregates, each with four [aspects], result in twenty kinds of views.
Among these twenty,
five are the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi),
and fifteen are the view of what belongs to the self (ātmīya-dṛṣṭi).
If one possesses the basis from which conceptual discrimination arises,
there are sixty-five types of conceiving a self; for instance,
within a single form, there are thirteen such conceptions.
Form is the self; these two are one.
Form belongs to the self.
The analysis of separation is fourfold.
Some reckon that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the self,
and that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) belongs to that self which possesses sensation.
Just as a person possesses objects,
so too are there such distinctions,
even down to those who reckon consciousness to be the self.
It is taught that form is "mine" in relation to consciousness;
thus, by teaching that form is the object of that self consisting of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
it is thereby divided into four kinds.
Including the preceding [four],
there are five [types]. Some say that form serves as the dwelling place for the self consisting of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is further divided into four,
making nine in total with the preceding ones.
Some proclaim that the self of the four aggregates— feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— has form as its dwelling place.
These are further divided into four,
which together with the preceding ones total thirteen. Among these thirteen:
The first is the view of self;
the subsequent twelve are the views of what belongs to the self.
This applies to the thirteen [categories] beginning with form.
This applies likewise even to the categories of volitional formations and consciousness.
Above each of the five aggregates,
there are thirteen [factors].
In total, there are sixty-five types.
Among these sixty-five,
five are views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

To calculate [the self] as being identical with the aggregates (*skandha*) constitutes sixty types of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*); to calculate it as distinct from the aggregates constitutes [the other sixty].
The various [parts] look toward one another and are considered distinct aggregates;
they are not outside of the aggregate as a whole.
Many people have calculated this separately as sixty-five;
it is not a single person.
Such are the deluded sentiments. This concludes this section.
Next, one should examine the nature of delusive afflictions to discern the underlying principles through the observation of noble wisdom.
Knowing that there are only the aggregates (*skandhas*) and no separate self or person,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas..."
One sees the aggregates and the separation from the aggregates; the self is not to be seen.
All conditioned phenomena arise dependently.
The combination of arising and ceasing, as well as the aggregates and that which is apart from the aggregates, are devoid of a self or a person;
this is the principle. These two sections are concluded.
Next, I shall distinguish its reality:
witnessing the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas) is precisely that reality.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Once the mark of self has been eliminated,
one should give rise to the mark of dharmas."
One should form this thought:
"This body arises merely as a composite of various phenomena;
it is only phenomena that arise and cease."
Only dharmas cease.
Arising and ceasing are the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these dharmas;
therefore, they are called "real. This concludes the three gates.
As for what is called "function," it refers to the conventional designation of the collection [of factors] based on the aforementioned five aggregates; thus,
there arise distinctions such as humans, devas, men, and women.
This provisional function exists and is not a source of affliction;
therefore, the Sage always conforms to worldly convention.
The preceding four sections have explained the emptiness of the person by discussing the existence of a self, an individual, sentient beings, and a life-span.
Next, the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is explained. This consists of four sections;
first, their characteristics are distinguished.
Within the scope of the previously established emptiness,
one grasps at signs and fixates upon the determinations of the real entities and conventional functions that have been posited.
To expect that those [dharmas] are empty is entirely termed deluded sentiment;
because this is likewise an attachment to dharmas and a self, this section concludes.
Next, the principle is explained:
the Bodhisattva, through correct contemplation, knows that what was previously grasped as an object is ultimately non-existent;
it is not merely that it lacks intrinsic nature.
Characteristics also do not exist.
The absence of dharmas is precisely the principle for dispelling [deluded] attachments; these two gates are concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish their reality.
Once the characteristics of emotional attachments have been emptied and the deluded mind has ceased,
one then perceives the secret dharma-gate of the true Tathāgatagarbha-nature, the self-substance of the Dharmadhātu.
This concludes the three gates concerning its reality.
Next, its function will be distinguished.
Based on the aforementioned essence of the Tathāgatagarbha as ultimate reality:
The integration of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa is its function.
As it is said in the sūtras:
The twelve links of dependent origination are all produced by the single mind.
It is also said:
The three realms are created by a single mind.
Furthermore, it is said that the Dharma-body transmigrates through the five paths.
They are called "sentient beings.
This is the reality of the arising of birth and death.
Furthermore, as it says in the sutras:
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha manifests as the Dharmakāya;
such are the meanings [of these teachings].
It arises as nirvāṇa.
The essential nature and characteristics of non-self are roughly illustrated in this way.
Within the third section,
there are distinctions according to the tenets; therein are two parts.
First, establishing their respective categories;
second, distinguishing their differences according to those categories. Regarding the establishment of their respective categories:
There are four distinct schools of tenets:
first, the school that establishes intrinsic nature;
second, the school that refutes intrinsic nature.
Third is the School of the Destruction of Characteristics (Poxiang zong); fourth is the School of the Manifestation of Reality (Xianshi zong).
These four have been fully and extensively analyzed as previously set forth in the chapter on the Two Truths; this concludes the present section.
Next, we shall distinguish the differences according to the tenets.
Within the first tenet, only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is elucidated.
He does not teach the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Although he teaches the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*),
he merely teaches that upon the aggregates (*skandha*) there is no such self (*ātman*) or person (*pudgala*) as falsely imagined by ordinary beings.
In the second school, it is stated that the eye is empty;
however, it does not yet explain the emptiness of sentient beings as being devoid of intrinsic nature due to their causal conditions and provisional nature.
Possessing clear understanding of the two kinds of emptiness,
one perceives that the five aggregates and birth are formed by combining particulars into a whole.
This is the harmony of causes.
Within this harmony of causes,
the absence of a fixed nature is called the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*).
This differs from the previous school’s position that there is no person (pudgala) upon the aggregates, which constitutes the emptiness of sentient beings;
rather, it holds that the various phenomena are integrated through [the characteristics of] suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so forth.
It is called the conjunction of dharmas.
Within this conjunction of dharmas,
there is emptiness and no fixed nature.
This is the emptiness of dharmas.
Question: The five aggregates arise from a combination of causes and lack intrinsic nature.
How is it that one obtains the name "emptiness of sentient beings"?
The explanation says:
the five aggregates are the dharmas belonging to the self.
The name is derived from the internal;
therefore, it is called "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, all things arise collectively based on individual causes.
They are collectively termed "sentient beings.
Since those beings lack intrinsic nature,
they are called "emptiness of beings" (sattva-śūnyatā).
In the third school,
it also possesses the two kinds of emptiness, which distinguishes it from the preceding schools.
Regarding what is called the "emptiness of persons" (pudgala-śūnyatā):
The previous position directly addresses the fact that within the conjunction of causes, there is no intrinsic nature;
this is termed the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*). It is not empty, for it arises as a conventional designation.
In this school, even that which is conventionally produced does not exist; therefore,
it is called "emptiness of production."
It is like seeing a person in empty space where there is nothing;
you should know that such a person is not a person, yet is taken to be a person.
A person is not a person.
It is not by waiting for the aggregates to be separated, divided, or destroyed that one becomes a non-person.
Such is the case for all things.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"The Bodhisattva contemplates birth as being like a fifth great element or a sixth aggregate."
Regarding the statement "the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharmasūnyatā*):
within the previous school of thought,
it was merely taught that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature due to the combination of suffering, impermanence, and so forth.
Therefore, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). It is not said that phenomena which are empty and merely conventional designations do not exist;
this is what is taught in this school.
Because even provisional phenomena are empty, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
It is like flowers in the sky:
where there are no flowers, they appear as flowers.
A flower is not a flower.
It is not that it becomes a non-flower only when it is separated from its parts or destroyed by means of such qualities as suffering and impermanence;
all phenomena are like this.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti says:
"Just as a burnt seed is seen equally by both a *śrāvaka* and a *srotāpanna*,
it not only lacks inherent nature," and so forth.
Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are likewise non-existent.
Within the fourth school as well,
both types of emptiness are fully present.
This differs from what preceded;
herein, it shall be analyzed by way of two gates.
The first is the gate of support and maintenance (*ādhāra*).
Second is the gate of dependent origination.
If one discusses the basis of support,
the phenomena of delusion are empty.
The emptiness of sentient beings refers to the name;
the true quiescence upon which it depends is called the emptiness of phenomena.
It is precisely because [emptiness] arises from the deluded thoughts of sentient beings that the emptiness of deluded thought is called the emptiness of sentient beings;
its basis is the ultimate reality.
This is the intrinsic nature of phenomena; because the nature of phenomena is quiescent,
it is called the emptiness of phenomena.
If one approaches it from the perspective of the gate of ultimate dependent origination,
the quiescent essence of true suchness is termed the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā).
The quiescence of causal functioning is called the emptiness of sentient beings;
the quiescence of the true essence—
The true dharma-dhātu and the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are of one and the same essential nature.
Because they are mutually integrated and lack a separate intrinsic nature,
it is said that their essence is quiescent.
This is as when it is taught that all phenomena are eternal by virtue of this [quiescence].
According to their meaning, when analyzed,
there is no separate, permanent essence apart from all phenomena.
All categories, such as self, bliss, purity, and so forth,
are likewise the same;
there is not a single dharma that maintains its own intrinsic nature in isolation.
Therefore, all phenomena are entirely quiescent.
This quiescence of the essence of phenomena is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
As for the quiescence of conditional activity:
That tathāgatagarbha dependent origination integrates all phenomena of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
its functioning is characterized by quiescence.
This is called the emptiness of sentient beings.
It is because the functioning of causal conditions resides in persons;
therefore, the stillness of such functioning is termed the emptiness of sentient beings.
The distinctions among the schools are thus.
Within the fourth section,
they are identified and determined according to the individuals.
People refer to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
among these, the person who is a bodhisattva fully understands the two kinds of emptiness.
Regarding śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
the sūtras and śāstras differ;
such is the case in the Abhidharmakośa, the Yogācārabhūmi, the Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra, and other texts.
It is said that śrāvakas attain only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā),
and the same applies to pratyekabuddhas;
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
It is taught that śrāvakas and others can attain the two kinds of emptiness without distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that those of sharp faculties fully comprehend both types of emptiness.
As for those of dull faculties such as Śreṇika,
who understand only the emptiness of sentient beings—
what is the meaning of this?
The commentary states:
Each of these has its own underlying reason;
herein, they shall be briefly explained by way of three gates.
First, it clarifies that what the Tathāgata taught differs [according to context].
Second, it clarifies that because the faculties of the śrāvakas range from sharp to dull, their understandings differ accordingly.
Third, it correctly reconciles these statements.
Regarding the differences in what is taught:
within that school of the established nature (svabhāva-vāda), the Tathāgata taught only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Within the latter three schools,
both types of emptiness are fully explained,
as has been analyzed above.
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties: among the śrāvakas,
there are three grades of faculties.
That is to say, there are three grades— lower, middle, and superior— and these three types of persons,
upon hearing the teaching that establishes the nature of that initial thesis, [respond accordingly].
They understand only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), because within this teaching the emptiness of the essence of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) has never been proclaimed;
thus, upon hearing the second school’s teaching that refutes intrinsic nature, they are startled.
Those of dull faculties are only able to realize and understand the emptiness of persons;
those of middling and superior faculties universally understand both types of emptiness.
Upon hearing the third school,
those of middling and inferior capacity understand only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Those who benefit others all understand;
upon hearing the fourth tenet,
these three types of persons [attain realization].
They equally realize the emptiness of sentient beings,
yet do not realize the emptiness of phenomena;
for they have only attained awakening and understanding regarding the emptiness within the conceptual characteristics of emotional attachments toward sentient beings.
Next, let us reconcile these statements:
the term "Abhidharma" is based on its original foundational doctrine.
Therefore, it is proclaimed that all śrāvakas understand only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā),
whereas those of the middle and superior capacities among the adherents of the *Tattvasiddhi* school are able to understand both types of emptiness.
It is an exaggeration to say that all śrāvakas,
regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull, [possess such qualities].
Regarding the simultaneous realization of the two emptinesses,
the *Tattvasiddhi* commits the error of overextension;
this is [stated] in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
According to the third school,
it is said that those of dull faculties understand only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while those of sharp faculties understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
these are the middle and lower [capacities].
They share the same name,
"those of dull faculties. According to the fourth school,
the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* state that śrāvakas understand only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Because emptiness is realized within the midst of falsely conceived phenomena;
this may also be stated from the perspective of that initial school regarding the meaning of selflessness.
A brief judgment is thus provided. 9.

The Meaning of the Reality-Limit (bhūtakoṭi) as the Nature of Phenomena (dharmatā). Part One: Analysis and Explanation of the Name through Three Gates. 1. Distinguishing the Characteristics; 2. Great and Small, Existence and Non-existence. First, the Explanation of the Name.
This is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the meaning of the *dharmatā-bhūtakoṭi*.
These three are alternative designations for the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and so forth are synonyms for the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)."
What is called "suchness" (tathatā) is a term of equivalence;
although the characteristics of phenomena differ, [they are identical in their suchness].
In reality, they are equal;
therefore, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
As for the term "dharma-nature" (dharmatā):
The intrinsic nature is called "dharma" (phenomenon);
because it is the essential nature of phenomena,
it is termed "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena).
As for the term "actual reality" (bhūtakoṭi):
because its fundamental principle is not empty,
it is designated as "real."
Because it is the boundary of reality,
it is called a "limit" (jì).
Such is the meaning of the term.
In the second section, its essential nature and characteristics are analyzed;
therein are three parts.
First, the three gates are distinguished by means of the two truths;
second, the three gates are distinguished solely by means of the ultimate truth;
third, the three gates are distinguished by means of the entry into contemplation.
Within the first section,
the commentary provides two explanations:
first, a general discussion on the two meanings of the emptiness and existence of all phenomena.
By means of three distinct gates,
two [of them] universally address the ninefold distinctions of meaning regarding all phenomena,
thereby distinguishing them through those three gates.
Regarding the differentiation of the three based on emptiness and existence:
the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is existence,
and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is emptiness.
Just as with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and so forth,
all [categories] apply to these two.
What are their characteristics?
As stated in the treatise:
there are two kinds,
the first being mutual resemblance.
That is to say, the earth has the characteristic of solidity, water has the characteristic of moisture, and so forth. Question:
These various phenomena have distinct characteristics.
What is meant by "suchness" (tathatā)?
It is because all phenomena possess their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
and these specific characteristics are uniformly pervasive.
Because they resemble one another,
they are called "thus" (tathā).
Furthermore, within the category of earth, there are many kinds of earth.
All these are equally solid;
because their meaning of solidity is similar,
they are called "like" (*tathā*).
The same applies to water and the other elements.
Furthermore, the dharmas such as earth and so forth that have been described exist according to their actual substance;
they do not exist as they are perceived through the distorted views of a madman.
Therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā).
Second is the characteristic of reality.
As the treatise itself explains: [text follows].
Within those characteristics,
reality cannot be found when sought;
this is the meaning of emptiness.
This meaning of emptiness is that all phenomena are equal; therefore,
it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Regarding the term "dharma-nature" (dharmatā),
there are two explanations in the treatise: first,
the dharma-nature of phenomena (vastu-dharmatā).
This refers to the solidity of earth, the moisture of water, and so forth.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"One discriminates all phenomena with a mind free from attachment."
The individual intrinsic nature is called the dharma-nature of phenomena;
the second is the dharma-nature of real dharmas.
The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*) is called the true dharma-nature (*bhūta-dharmatā*).
These two types of dharma-nature are identical to those described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
As for what is termed the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*):
The treatise states:
"Dharmatā is its reality; suchness (tathatā) is also reality."
Speaking from the perspective of what follows,
"limit" (*koṭi*) refers to the boundary of realization; this is discussed in terms of emptiness and existence.
By means of three distinct gateways,
one next proceeds to the nine meanings,
again by means of three distinct gateways.
First, distinguish the nine meanings;
subsequently, apply them to differentiate the three gates.
What are these nine meanings?
As stated in the treatise:
first, the individual essence;
that is to say, all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature.
Just as that eye-faculty has pure matter derived from the four great elements as its essence,
so it is for all [the other faculties];
these two each have their respective characteristics.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to specific marks or appearances.
All phenomena possess their own respective characteristics.
Therefore, they are called "characteristics.
Third is the power of each;
"power" refers to functional efficacy.
All phenomena each possess their own functional power;
these four are each distinct causes.
This means that all phenomena each have their respective causes;
the five [aggregates] each have their respective conditions;
and all phenomena each have their respective objects of perception.
What is the distinction between cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya*)? They are distinguished by the two categories of direct and indirect.
That which produces directly is called the cause.
The term "condition" (pratyaya) refers to that which causes [a result] to arise remotely. There are six types of individual results;
that is to say, all phenomena each have their own respective results.
Seventh is the nature of each respective thing (*pratyātma-svabhāva*). "Nature" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is nothing that does not fall within the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Therefore, it is called "nature" (svabhāva).
This is not [the] substantial nature (dravyasvabhāva).
If one says that the characteristic of substance is subsumed within the preceding category of substance, [it is so].
Eighth, all phenomena each have their own limitations and obstructions;
that is to say, all phenomena each have their own specific boundaries.
For example, the aggregates (skandhas) are only five and cannot be more.
All such cases are like this. Furthermore, as with the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*),
there are only ten bases (*āyatana*) and a small portion of one [base].
There must be nothing else;
all such cases are termed "limitations and obstructions."
Ninth is the meaning of mutual accessibility (*ābhyanujñāna*). This refers to the mutual accessibility of the meanings and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*).

For example, the meaning of "form" (*rūpa*) is accessible within the ten bases (*āyatana*) and a small portion of one [base]; the mind (*citta*) is accessible within the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
All such things are thus;
these nine meanings are like the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and so forth.
All [of these] penetrate these nine.
Regarding what is called "suchness" (tathatā),
the treatise provides three explanations.
The first is the inferior suchness,
which refers to the nine preceding meanings,
each being distinct from the others.
Since they have already been described as being distinct, why are they called "suchness" (*tathatā*)?
It is because all phenomena equally possess these nine [aspects].
The first is called "suchness" (tathatā).
The second is "middle suchness," which refers to the preceding nine meanings.
All are dharmas subject to impermanence, arising and ceasing.
Third is the "superior suchness," which refers to the aforementioned nine meanings.
All are neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, and are ultimately pure.
Regarding what is called "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*),
the treatise itself explains:
The nature within the nine dharmas is called the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Within this, there are three [types].
This refers to the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior; their meaning has been explained as before.
As for what is said to be different:
To proceed directly toward that which is similar is what constitutes "suchness" (tathatā).
Now, this clarifies the essential nature of phenomena;
therefore, it is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
Regarding the term "the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi),
the treatise itself explains:
it is the realization of the fruit among the nine [stages].
It is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).
To exhaustively realize the suchness (tathatā) and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as previously described is termed the "fruit."
The meaning is thus.
Furthermore, the treatise states again:
"Among these nine dharmas..."
That which has characteristics is called "suchness" (tathatā); emptiness is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
To attain the fruit within this is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi). This concludes the first section.
Next, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are three distinct sections,
within which there are four parts.
The first is the elimination of the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
By means of three distinct gateways,
one dispels the characteristics of differentiation across the three periods of time through these three distinct gateways.
Third, regarding the meaning of the general and the specific within the principle of emptiness,
it is categorized by means of three distinct gates.
Fourth, regarding the meaning of existence and non-existence within the true nature.
By means of three distinct gates,
it is said that the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are dispelled,
as explained in the treatise.
To observe that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are empty is called "suchness" (tathatā). Question:
The Sūtras state that saṃsāra is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and impure,
whereas nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
How then can you say they are empty?
The treatise states:
In order to destroy the perverted mind,
one proclaims the suffering, impermanence, and other such characteristics of saṃsāra.
It is not intended to cause people to become attached to impermanence and so forth,

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of destroying the inverted minds of people.
He proclaims that nirvana is permanent, blissful, self, and pure,

It is precisely because all phenomena (dharmas) are ungraspable that they are called "suchness" (tathatā).
As for what is termed "the nature of phenomena" (dharmatā):
Entering into that suchness,

This dharma-nature (dharmatā) is thus by its very nature ungraspable;
therefore it is called "dharma-nature.
Thus the treatise says:
For example, it is like a small child who, seeing the moon in the water, thinks it is truly existent;

Therefore, it is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā). As for what is termed the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi),

because this true reality is the sphere realized by the Noble Ones.

Regarding the statement that it dispels the differentiated characteristics of the three periods of time,

To contemplate the phenomena of the three periods of time as neither arising nor ceasing, quiescent and equal,

This is precisely what is meant by the statement that the three periods of time are equally empty and thus called "suchness" (tathatā).
As for what is termed "dharma-nature" (dharmatā),
it is as explained in the treatise.
Dharma is named *nirvāṇa*.
The non-conceptual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is named the "original portion-seed" (*mūlabhāgīya-bīja*).

Because all phenomena possess the nature of nirvāṇa,
they are called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
As for the term "the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi):
As previously stated, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called reality;
thusness (tathatā) is likewise reality.
To speak according to what follows,
the locus of entry is called the "limit" (koṭi).
As for the statement that this is divided into general and specific categories based on the principle of emptiness:
According to the various explanations used to characterize emptiness, there are distinctions within emptiness;

Therefore, the treatise states:
"The distinctions within emptiness are called 'suchness' (tathatā). Question: [What is the meaning of this?]
Regarding the distinctions, what is meant by "suchness" (tathatā)?
It is called suchness because within all phenomena there is the common meaning of emptiness.
As for the term "dharma-nature" (dharmatā):
The logic of verbal expression is discarded;
the principle is of a single flavor.
This principle of a single flavor—
This is the essential nature of phenomena;
therefore, it is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā). Thus, the treatise states:
The totality of all things as a single emptiness is termed the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
Regarding the term "the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi),
the treatise itself explains:
Suchness and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are called "reality" (bhūta);

Regarding the statement that there is a distinction between existence and non-existence with respect to the true nature (*dharmatā*),

It is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges;

They share a single ontological nature and are mutually integrated;

Although there is no single nature,
there is no absence of nature;
there is not even a single nature that exists.
This is precisely the meaning of "suchness" (tathatā),
yet it is not a non-nature;
this is precisely the dharma-nature (dharmatā).

that which is such as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is its very reality.

As for what is called "impurity of the breath":
As stated in the treatise:

The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is as it was originally;

The treatise provides its own analogy:

All phenomena are thus;
their true nature is equal,
just as the nature of water is cold.

The true mark is as it was originally;
just as when fire has been extinguished, the water returns to its original coolness,

Based on this text, it is determined that deluded thoughts and their associated cognition are utterly extinguished.
That which is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) is...
The true mark is eternally abiding, unchanging, and immovable;

it is identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
This is precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Third, the presence or absence of the Great and Small Vehicles is clarified.

Nāgārjuna explains, saying:
In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas,
observing the arising and ceasing of phenomena is called "suchness" (tathatā);

That which is named nirvāṇa is the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa);

the phenomenon of nirvana is... [unconditioned].
That which is called "unconditioned existence" is the emptiness of the ultimate truth;
it is designated as "non-existence."
These are the three dharmas.
Regarding conditioned existence,
one neither desires nor follows it.
He establishes the gateway of wishlessness;
within the unconditioned, he has the aspiration and delight to embrace it.
Establishing the gate of signlessness, within these two,
it is neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
Regarding existence as non-existence:
because of this view, one establishes the gate of emptiness;
it is by seeing emptiness that [this is accomplished].
They do not desire nirvana;
this is called "non-aspiration.
They do not loathe birth-and-death.
It is called "not non-aspiration.
Abandoning the two previous forms of existence is called the "view of non-existence."
Second, three gateways are established according to the differences among the faculties (indriya).
There are three kinds of faculties.
That is to say, among the sharp, dull,
and middling faculties, for those of dull faculties,
the gate of wishlessness is taught.
In order to instill fear,
for those of middling faculties,
he teaches the gate of signlessness.
In order to cause them to seek [the truth],
for those of sharp faculties,
he proclaims the gate of emptiness.
This is because it causes one to realize the truth.
Third, they differ according to individual inclinations,
as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
There are three types of desire:
first, for those who delight in seclusion,
one teaches wishlessness (apraṇihita).
Second, for those who delight in tranquility,
one teaches signlessness.
Third, for those who delight in reality.
For them, he expounds the gate of emptiness.
There are four different ways of practicing this,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
There are three kinds of practice:
namely, concentration, wisdom, and equanimity. These are for the purpose of giving rise to the practice of concentration.
He proclaims the gateway of emptiness so that the mind may abide therein,
thereby giving rise to the practice of wisdom.
He teaches the gate of wishlessness so that they may observe and sever birth and death,
thereby giving rise to the practice of equanimity.
The gate of signlessness is taught so that the mind may have a basis for reliance.
Fifth, the remedies for these afflictions differ.
As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, there are two kinds of afflictions:
first, views; second, craving.
For those who act out of [wrong] views,
he proclaims the gateway of emptiness,
causing them to abandon their views.
For those who act out of craving,
he teaches the gate of wishlessness,
causing them to grow weary of birth and death and to cease their seeking and desiring.
Therefore, for those who perceive and crave [objects], he teaches signlessness (*animitta*).
He proclaims that nirvāṇa is far removed from the signs of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch,
thereby counteracting those tendencies toward craving.
It is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing;
it remedies those views and mental activities;
and it is free from the marks of male and female.
The meaning encompasses both aspects;
the distinctions among the three gates for treating afflictions are manifold,
but I shall discuss only this much for now.
Within the sixth section,
the sequence is clarified.
There are three aspects to this sequence.
First is the sequence of cultivation:
first, the wishless (apraṇihita) is taught to induce weariness with saṃsāra;
next, the signless (animitta) is taught to incite the seeking of nirvāṇa.
Later, the gate of emptiness is taught so that they may realize and witness it.
Second, according to the sequence of the ultimate and the provisional,
emptiness is the root of all virtues.
Because the Bodhisattva first contemplates this,
emptiness is explained first;
it is by seeing emptiness that [this occurs].
Because one does not perceive birth and death as something to be craved or sought after.
Next, the second [truth], wishlessness, is proclaimed;
for by realizing the meaning of emptiness, one does not perceive birth and death.
Because it is then conjoined with the signlessness of nirvāṇa,
the third [teaching] subsequently proclaims signlessness. Thirdly,
this is categorized according to the essence, characteristics, and functions of that which is empty.
To clarify their sequence,
the gate of emptiness is explained first;
it empties the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Next, the signless is explained,
which empties all dharmic signs;
subsequently, the wishless is explained.
The functions of all phenomena are empty;
the sequence is thus.
Within the seventh gate:
Regarding their classification according to their respective contexts:
within the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
it is stated that they are not fixed.
Some teachers proclaim that the three gates of liberation and the samādhis exist only in the fourth dhyāna,
the intermediate state, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), and the three formless attainments.
Because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are exclusively untainted.
As has been explained above,
the three samādhis encompass both the outflowing (sāsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava).
The untainted samādhi is like the three liberations;
as for that which is tainted:
It exists in eleven stages:

namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four fundamental dhyānas, the preliminary stage (*anāgamyāntara*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
This is according to the Mahāyāna teachings.
The three gates of liberation and the samādhis are both with outflows and without outflows.
As for those with outflows:
As previously explained,
it exists in the eleventh stage for those who are untainted (*anāsrava*).
It relies upon the ten stages, namely:
the eight dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgāmya), and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara).
If discussed comprehensively, however:
It is also based on the desire realm;
thus the Mahāyāna proclaims that within the stages of the desire realm, [this occurs].
Because there is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
the stages (*bhūmi*) are subsumed in this manner.
This concludes the eighth section.

The distinctions in meaning are fivefold: (1) listing the names and defining their characteristics; (2) the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); (3) the distinction according to persons; (4) the distinction according to realms (*dhātu*); and (5) the distinction according to stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the first of these categories, the names are first listed.
What is its name? It is called the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi) and the signlessness of signlessness (animitta-animitta).
"Desireless-desireless": this is the designation established according to its initial manifestation;
it is named the "repeated emptiness samādhi."
They may also be termed "repeated signlessness" and "repeated wishlessness.
What are their characteristics?
According to the Abhidharma:
The sixteen noble practices of those four truths are divided into three gates;
within the [gate of] suffering, there are two practices: emptiness and non-self.
It is judged as the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Next, there are ten lines,
which are explained as the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Beneath "suffering" there are two,
namely suffering and impermanence.
Beneath "origination" there are four.
The cause is the accumulation; existence is the condition.
The Path has four lower [stages];
the Path is like a track for a vehicle.
These ten types are taught as the gate of wishlessness (apraṇihita),
which extinguishes the four lower modes of activity.
Exhaustion, cessation, and wondrous emergence constitute the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*).
As for the term "repeated emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*):
An Arhat first uses the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samādhi-jñāna) to contemplate the gate of emptiness;
this is directly termed the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi).
Thereafter, by means of that impure conventional knowledge (*sāsrava-saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
one contemplates that the preceding knowledge of emptiness is also empty and selfless;
this is called the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*.
In this wisdom of contemplation, there is the emptiness of self and person,
yet the essence of wisdom is not empty;
it is the reiteration of wishlessness.
Furthermore, one first observes suffering and the other truths by means of that knowledge of non-learning (*aśaikṣajñāna*) and so forth,
which is directly termed "wishless" (*apraṇihita*);
subsequently, one observes that this very knowledge is also impermanent and thus not to be wished for or sought after.
Striking against that noble path is called the "wishless-of-the-wishless. Question:
Why is it not struck by suffering?
Because it contradicts the Noble Path;
the Path is not suffering.
If one contemplates [the aggregates] as suffering,
that is an inversion. Why, then,
does one not strike at that Noble Path by means of the causal accumulation and conditions?
The treatise states that because the factors such as the causes accord with the Noble Path,
they are not called "striking.
For what reason does one not ride upon the traces of the Path to strike that Noble Path?
The commentary states:
If one practices the contemplation of the equality of the path and so forth,
this is delighting in the noble path.
What is meant by "striking"?
Regarding the profound signlessness:
first, one employs the wisdom of the vision of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Contemplating that cessation as the ultimate exhaustion, stillness, and sublime emergence is directly termed "signlessness" (animitta).
Subsequently, contemplating this wisdom at the point where all is exhausted and ceased— this non-enumerated unconditioned state— is likewise quiescent stillness.
That which strikes down that noble path is called the signless-signless. What is this wisdom?
It is the unconditioned state beyond enumeration, wherein all [defilements] are exhausted.
What is meant by "striking"?
It is the wisdom that contemplates cessation;
it should arise, yet does not arise.
This is the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows, which is unconditioned and beyond enumeration.

Desiring to strike at that wisdom, one first contemplates the state where afflictions do not arise; this cessation through enumeration (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), being unconditioned, is its state of tranquil stillness.
Because it is tranquil,
it is desirable and delightful;
because this tranquility is desirable and delightful, [it is so].
The afflictions that are to be extinguished are objects of aversion; subsequently,
one contemplates that the state where this wisdom does not arise— the non-analytical unconditioned— is likewise tranquility.
It is desirable and pleasant,
just like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
because its state of exhaustion through wisdom is the same as that analytical cessation, it is likewise desirable and pleasant.
The wisdom that is to be extinguished is as loathsome as those afflictions themselves.
It strikes them in this manner. He asked:
"Why does it not strike that noble path with a 'wonderful exit'?"
Regarding the exclusive employment of the practice of cessation (*śamatha*),
the commentary states:
"Because it is neither numerical nor supramundane."
Why not strike it with the practice of cessation?
Because this would indiscriminately conflate it with impermanent cessation.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra):
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is called the gate of emptiness.
Within this emptiness, [all things abide].
There is no characteristic to be grasped;
this is called the gate of signlessness.
Within emptiness, there is no seeking, longing, or aspiration.
It is called the gate of wishlessness.
When a noble one contemplates the five aggregates as empty through wisdom,
it is called the samādhi of emptiness.
Furthermore, one contemplates that this wisdom is also empty;
therefore, it is called "the emptiness of emptiness. One contemplates within the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*).
There is no characteristic to be grasped;
this is called the signless samādhi.
Furthermore, one contemplates that this wisdom itself is empty and signless.
It is called "signless-signless.
Contemplating the emptiness of the aggregates,
one has no longing or aspiration.
It is called the samādhi of wishlessness.
Furthermore, observing that this wisdom is also empty and wishless is called the "wishless-of-wishlessness."
Within the Mahāyāna teachings,
there are three gates and many categories,
as fully detailed above.
Regarding the detailed discussion therein,
it is sometimes identical to the Abhidharma and sometimes resembles the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
If one explains the principle of the emptiness of birth-and-death and nirvana as three gates,
it is identical to the Abhidharma.
If one proceeds according to the principle of emptiness,
the meaning is divided into three gates,
which is the same as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
The difference lies in their depth;
as for the contemplation of the profound emptiness,
it is largely consistent with the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
For what reason does one cultivate this profound samādhi of emptiness?
The treatise states:
"It is like a person who uses a staff to burn a corpse; once the corpse is consumed, the staff must also be burned."
Wisdom is also like this:
it is first employed to sever the fetters;
once the affliction of the fetters has vanished, [wisdom remains].
Wisdom, too, must be relinquished;
thus concludes this section on cultivation. Next is the analysis according to whether they are with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava).
According to the Abhidharma,
the samādhi of the repetition of emptiness is exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
Because that which is observed by it is not the ultimate truth,
it constitutes the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, that treatise states:
Regarding the repeated concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*):
the repetition of emptiness is called "supreme.
How can it be with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
The Mahāyāna is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Having concluded these two gates according to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
we shall next discuss them in terms of persons.
In the Abhidharma system,
the samādhi of the double emptiness is attained only by Arhats of sharp faculties.
It is not for others; because those trainees still possess afflictions,
they do not attain it exclusively.
An Arhat of dull faculties does not attain mastery over the samādhis he has acquired; therefore,
he likewise cannot attain it.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all Arhats and those still in training have fully attained it.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states that even those in training attain it,
because they realize the cessation of all phenomena.
Among those of the Mahāyāna, however—
All those above the stage of spiritual lineage (gotra) attain these;
furthermore, if discussed comprehensively,
even those at the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā) ultimately attain these three gates.
Next, we shall discuss the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
According to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*):
The concentration on the profound emptiness arises only in the desire realm,
not in the two higher realms.
Within the desire realm,
the inhabitants of the three continents are able to give rise to this contemplation.
Because it is taught that [the afflictions] arise,
the *Tattvārthā* lacks textual evidence;
logically, however, this principle should apply universally.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
the Bodhisattva possesses mastery within the three realms.
Having completed these four gates, which can be cultivated anywhere at any time,
we next turn to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,
according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
The samādhi of profound emptiness is with outflows; therefore,
it extends from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The minds of all stages can all be cultivated and brought forth; however,
in the desire realm, they take as their object only the outflow-free states existing within future dhyāna.
It is for the sake of emphasizing the contemplation of emptiness.
"Non-perception" (asaṃjñā) refers exclusively to the untainted [consciousness] belonging to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
because it is proximate to it.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
because these are untainted (*anāsrava*),
they rely exclusively upon the seven meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) ranging from the first dhyāna to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
And thus they are cultivated and established:
the minds of all stages as elucidated by the Mahāyāna.
All can cultivate and give rise to the samādhi of the profound emptiness.
This brief exposition has been concluded.

11. The Meaning of the Three Conditioned Phenomena (2). The meaning of the three conditioned phenomena is explained through a twofold analysis: first, the definition of their names; second, the discernment of their characteristics. Regarding the three conditioned phenomena: [text continues].
These are the three categories of phenomena: namely, form (rūpa), mind (citta), and that which is neither form nor mind.
That which possesses substantial resistance is called form;
that which reflects and cognizes is called mind.
The formations dissociated from mind (viprayukta-saṃskāra) are the opposite of the preceding two;
they are called neither matter nor mind.
These three types [of phenomena]—
It is given the same name as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). It carries the meaning of being accumulated, arisen, and constructed.
Because phenomena are produced through conditioning, they are called "conditioned."
What is the meaning of this?
There are six ways of explaining it.
The first is to correlate the cause with the fruit.
Because all causes and conditions are able to aggregate results and are capable of performing functions,
they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Second, based on the effect in relation to the cause,
it is explained that all conditioned retributions arise from causes;
because they possess these causes, they are called "conditioned."
Third, regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing as external to phenomena,
the Abhidharma explains them in relation to the limits of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*).
Each possesses its own four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) that exist simultaneously and have distinct entities.
These four characteristics characterize phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so forth; it is by virtue of the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa) that [the phenomenon arises].
The dharmas such as form arise; likewise,
up until the presence of the fourth characteristic, namely cessation,
the dharmas such as form cease.
These four characteristics are called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) because they are capable of performing an action;
these four are applied to form and so forth in contrast to those external dharmas.
Because it explains that all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are characterized by the four marks of arising and so forth,
they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Fifth, regarding the essence of the phenomenon itself, there are the four marks before and after.
To explain "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*):

the shifting and changing of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) throughout the preceding and succeeding moments is called "conditioned. This refers to all phenomena (*dharma*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Because its substance possesses these [characteristics],
it is called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta).
Sixth, regarding the four characteristics that are simultaneous and identical in substance with the dharma itself.
To explain the conditioned:
the nature of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, is like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Their illusory existence is termed "arising."
The non-existence of illusion is called cessation;
the establishment of illusion is called abiding;
the transformation of illusion is called change.
These four are of one essence;
they arise through mutual conditioning and aggregation,
and are thus termed "becoming."
Because the intrinsic nature of phenomena such as form possesses this characteristic,
they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Such is the meaning of the term.
In the second section, its essential nature and characteristics are analyzed;
first, the material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are analyzed.
Next, the mental factors (caitta-dharma) are revealed;
subsequently, the phenomena that are neither form nor mind are explained.
Within the category of form-phenomena (rūpa-dharma):
There are two sections for analysis:
first, the discernment of essential nature and characteristics;
second, the clarification of the provisional and the real.
Regarding the essential characteristics of form (*rūpa*), the commentaries differ in their explanations.
The Abhidharma proclaims that there are eleven kinds of form.
They constitute the aggregate of form-dharmas. Which eleven?
The five faculties constitute five.
The five sense objects constitute ten;
when combined with non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), they become eleven.
The five faculties are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, which are composed of the purified four great elements.
They are produced by the four external great elements;
visible form, sound, odor, taste,
and tangibility are their five objects.
Within the actions of body and speech,
there is the non-manifestation (avijñapti) of both good and evil; this is non-manifesting form (avijñapti-rūpa).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts also speak in this same way.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* proclaims fourteen kinds of matter (*rūpa*).
They constitute an aggregate of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). Which fourteen?
The five faculties (*indriya*) constitute five.
The five sense objects become ten;
when the four great elements are added,
there are fourteen in total.
The five faculties are as described above.
As for what differs [in this context],
according to the Abhidharma method:
The substance of the five faculties is real-dharma-form (dravya-rūpa),
produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta).
It is distinct from the person,
just as a painting created by a person is distinct from that person.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
The substance of the five faculties is conventional designation and form,
composed of the four great elements;
there are no great elements external to the faculties.
Just as the aggregates constitute a person,
and there are no aggregates apart from the person,
so it is with the sense faculties.
The five aggregates are as described above. As for what differs,
in the Abhidharma system:
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is held that the derived matter (mahābhūtika-rūpa) is distinct from the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility can constitute the four great elements,
yet they do not constitute the derivatives of the great elements.
The single object of sound arises from the four great elements;
such is the distinction.
The earth, water, fire, and wind that are composed of the four objects [of sense] are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Question:
The Abhidharma speaks of non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
Why is it not discussed in the *Tattvasiddhi*?
The schools differ in their tenets,
and what they teach varies accordingly.
Within the Abhidharma system:
It is taught that non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*);
therefore, it is discussed among the categories of form.
The *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) states that it is neither form nor mind.
Therefore, it is not discussed among the [other] form-aggregates.
Furthermore, it is asked:
Why does the *Tattvasiddhi* treat the four great elements separately?
Why is it not established within the Abhidharma system?
This is also due to differences in school;
their expositions each differ.
What are the distinct characteristics?
The Abhidharma proclaims that there are four kinds of real tangibles: solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
These are considered the four great elements.
These four great elements are subsumed within the sense-object of tangibility.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, earth, water, fire, and wind are formed by gathering the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*).
They are able to bring about the five faculties.
The faculties are the cause and the objects are the fruit; thus, neither the faculties nor the objects are [inherently] grasped.
Therefore, this one section must be discussed separately.
Next, we shall distinguish between the provisional and the real according to the Abhidharma system.
The eleven kinds of form are all real dharmas;
because the Abhidharma mostly seeks them within their intrinsic nature and characteristics, there is no conventional (prajñapti) form.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
the five sense objects are real,
while the sense organs and the great elements are provisional.
By grasping objects, they become great;
because the great becomes the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
This is according to the principle of correspondence.
All things are provisional,
for they are equally phenomena that are conventionally designated through causes and conditions.
Next, the mental factors (caitta-dharma) are analyzed.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of five gates:
first, clarifying whether the essence of the mind and that of the numbers are identical or different;
second, distinguishing their characteristics through their expansion and contraction.
First, the breadth and narrowness of the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*); second, the distinction between their universal and specific applications;
third, their differing modes of association.
Regarding "identity and difference":
in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra),
the mind and its mental factors are identical in substance but distinct in their functional aspects.
It is not said that there are various categories (saṃkhyā) existing separately outside of the mind;
rather, as it is taught that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) constitutes the mind,
the others are termed categories.
Feeling is said to be mind;
the others are likewise termed mental factors. This applies to all such cases.
In the Abhidharma system,
mind (citta) and mental factors (caitasika) are distinct;
the six consciousnesses constitute the mind.
The remaining factors, such as perception and feeling,
are called mental concomitants (caitta) in the Mahāyāna teachings.
According to the end, they are distinct;
tracing them to their origin, they are one.
What is the meaning of this?
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
it is said that consciousness is threefold.
The first is the true consciousness (tathatā-vijñāna).
The mind and the mental factors are one.
Second is the deluded consciousness;
within this deluded consciousness, there are six levels of coarseness and subtlety.
Beginning from ignorance and ending with the linking consciousness,
within these six stages,
the first four stages are as follows.
In the first [category], the mind and the mental factors are one;
in the latter two categories,
the mind and the mental factors are distinct.
Because the first four mental states share the same numerical category,
the treatise describes them as "non-associated defilements."
Because the latter two are distinct,
the treatise describes them as "afflictions associated with the mind" (*citta-samprayukta-kleśa*).
Aśvaghoṣa explains, saying:
Because the mind (citta) and mental application (manasikāra) are distinct, they are said to be "associated" (samprayukta).
This meaning will be fully and extensively analyzed later in the chapter on the eight consciousnesses.
Third is the phenomenal consciousness (vastu-vijñāna).
They are exclusively simultaneous and possess all numerical categories;
this is the same as the Abhidharma.
The identity or difference between the mind and mental factors has been briefly analyzed; this concludes the first section.
Next, the opening and closing [of categories] will be analyzed.
The mental factors (caitta-dharma) may be opened or closed;
their expansion or brevity is not fixed,
and they may sometimes be consolidated into one.
That is to say, the aggregate of mind is either divided into two— namely,
mind and mental factors— or [treated as] one.
The six consciousnesses are the mind;
perception and the other [mental factors] are the formations.
Alternatively, they may be divided into four.
These are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The sovereign mind is called consciousness;
the mental factor of conceptualization is called perception.
The enumeration of sensation is called "sensation";
the remaining enumerations are called "formations.
Alternatively, they are divided into six.
These are what are called the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, according to the Abhidharma,
they constitute forty-seven mental factors (caitta-dharmas).
The mind-king is one;
among the numerical factors,
there are forty-six.
What are they? There are ten universal mental factors that pervade all stages and accompany the mind-king.
Taken together, these constitute eleven.
Regarding the ten stages common [to all],
it is as stated in that treatise.

Perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), volition (*cetanā*), liberation (*vimukti*), recollection (*anusmṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—
these are said to be universal to all stages (*sarvabhūmika*).
To grasp the characteristics of an object is called perception.
Regarding the object of desire, it is called "desire" (chanda).
That which causes the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness to come together is called "contact" (sparśa).
Regarding the determination of the object, it is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
To record and recognize without forgetting is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
To intend, wish for, and engage in the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds and so forth is called volition (*cetanā*).
To form mental signs regarding conditions and to grasp the characteristics and limits of those signs is called liberation;
if there were no such liberation, [it would not exist].
Constantly maintaining a single object without being able to abandon it;
awakening to that object is called mindfulness (smṛti).
Constantly focusing on the object without distraction is termed concentration (samādhi).
Feeling that which is agreeable or disagreeable is called "feeling" (vedanā).
These ten are universally associated with all states of mind; therefore, they are termed "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika).
There are ten wholesome stages (*kuśala-bhūmi*).
Together with the preceding [stages], they constitute twenty-one. What are they?
As stated in that treatise:
"The faculties of shame, embarrassment, faith, serenity, non-negligence, non-harming, diligence,
and equanimity are all associated with every wholesome state of mind."
Regarding the "faculties" (indriya),
they refer to the wholesome roots of non-attachment and non-hatred;
for what reason is non-delusion not mentioned?
Non-delusion is wisdom (*prajñā*);
because its essential substance is identical to the factor of wisdom within the *mahābhūmika* [mental factors],
it is not discussed here.
The absence of a mind of greedy attachment toward other sentient beings and their requisites is called non-greed (*alobha*).
This applies to both those categorized as sentient beings and those that are not.
Not harboring a mind of ill will is called non-aversion (*adveṣa*).
To feel self-reproach regarding evil is called shame (*hrī*);
to feel embarrassment before others regarding one's transgressions is called modesty (*apatrāpya*).
To have a pure mind free from doubt regarding the Three Jewels and so forth is called faith (*śraddhā*);
for body and mind to be free from evil is termed serenity (*praśrabdhi*).
To give rise to skillful means and to refrain from evil by not committing it is called non-negligence (*apramāda*).
To not oppress others is called non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
To sever evil and accumulate good,
diligently applying skillful means in practice is called diligence (*vīrya*).
It is the state of equanimity within the inner mind.
This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
These ten are present throughout all wholesome states; thus they are named the "universal wholesome factors" (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*).
Within the unwholesome stage,
there are two mental factors,
namely: lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
Combined with the preceding, there are twenty-three in total.
Within the great afflictions (*mahākleśa*),
ten are fully enumerated.
The distinct [categories] are only five;
when combined with the preceding ones, they total twenty-eight. What are these ten?
As stated in that treatise:
wrong understanding, incorrect mindfulness, non-conformity with knowledge, loss of mindfulness, lack of faith, laziness, distraction, ignorance, restlessness, and heedlessness.
These are the ground of afflictions.
Erroneous liberation is called perverse understanding;
erroneously perceiving objects is called improper mindfulness.
Perverted certainty is called non-conformable wisdom;
giving false explanations and accepting them erroneously is called loss of mindfulness regarding the Triple Gem and so forth.
Doubt regarding what is false and impurity is called lack of faith (*aśraddhā*).
Not severing evil and not cultivating good,
and lacking diligence in skillful means, is called laziness (*kausīdya*).
Being dragged by sensory objects and scattering according to various conditions is called distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Not clearly comprehending phenomena is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Restless agitation that does not cease is called *auddhatya* (restlessness).
The abandonment of skillful means is called *pramāda* (heedlessness).
These ten pervade all afflictions.
It is called the "Great Affliction Ground. Question:
Sleep also pervades all afflictions.
Why is it not called the "great ground of affliction"?
The treatise itself explains:
sleep is conducive to meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Because they can quickly induce meditative concentration, they are not mentioned; thus,
there are specifically five distinct [factors].
These five factors— namely, lack of faith, laziness, ignorance, restlessness, and heedlessness—
are distinct in essence from all other numerical categories.
Therefore, we now take these to constitute forty-seven;
as for the remaining five, they are not distinguished individually, and thus they are not mentioned.
Why are they not distinct?
As for what is called "erroneous understanding," it is numerically identical to the liberations within the *sāmānyabhūmi* (the stage of commonality).
Improper mindfulness is identical in substance to the category of mindfulness within the universal stages (*sarvabhūmika*).
Improper wisdom is...
The substance of "loss of mindfulness" (muṣitasmṛtitā) is identical to the mental factor of mindfulness (smṛti) within the universal ground.
As for "loss of mindfulness," its substance is identical to the mental factor of mindfulness within the universal ground.
The nature of distraction (*vikṣepa*) and that of the stage of access (*sāmantaka*) are identical in substance.
Question: [What about] false understanding, improper mindfulness, and so forth?
Since these are identical to the mental factors (*caitasika*) common to all stages (*sarvabhūmika*),
what is the need to laboriously designate them again as belonging to the stage of afflictions (*kleśabhūmika*)?
It is because they possess equal power to generate delusion.
Question: Among the universal [factors], why are feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), contact (sparśa),
and desire (chanda) not designated as the ground of afflictions (kleśabhūmi)?
Because they are unequal,
the great earth does not appear;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
What is meant by "unequal"?
It is when perception gives rise to strong views,
and sensation and contact give rise to desire.
Because it arises with a forceful intensity within craving,
it is said to be "unequal.
Again, he asked:
Why is volition (*cetanā*) not designated as a ground of affliction (*kleśabhūmi*)?
Since volition is the master of all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*),
it is not specifically designated as a ground of affliction.
Furthermore, volition is also powerful within the arising of craving;
therefore, it is not mentioned. Question:

If it is argued that sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), contact (*sparśa*), and so forth are not called the "ground of afflictions" (*kleśabhūmi*) because they do not uniformly give rise to delusion,
then why is wisdom (*prajñā*)— which gives rise to strong views— called the "ground of afflictions"?
The commentary states:
Since wisdom is not further discussed within the section on "seeing," it cannot be said that wisdom is predominant.
Because wisdom is not predominant,
it is called a "ground" (bhūmi).
There are ten distinctions within the ground of minor afflictions (parītta-kleśa-bhūmi).
Combined with the preceding, there are thirty-eight in total. What are they?
As that treatise states:
Anger, resentment, deceit, avarice, envy, vexation, guile, concealment, arrogance, and harmfulness—
these are said to be the minor ground [factors].
As stated in the commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya).
Regarding that which is beneficial or non-beneficial, to fail to act when one ought to act, or to act contrary to what should not be done,
while anger continues to arise— this is called *pratigha* (resentment).
It is the delighting in things that benefit others.
Suffering does not benefit others.
One ought to perform beneficial deeds,
yet one intentionally fails to do so.
If it does not benefit others and is logically improper to perform,
yet one intentionally commits it anyway.
The continuous arising of the impulse of anger is called *pratigha* (resentment).
When one feels aversion toward what is desirable or attraction toward what is undesirable, or when one persists in doing what should not be done and fails to do what should be done,
this continuous arising of resentment is termed *upanāha* (enmity).
One should delight in what others desire,
feel aversion toward what others do not desire,
and perform that which is desirable and appropriate to do.
Yet one does not intentionally perform those things that are undesirable and which,
by principle, ought not to be done.
Furthermore, to intentionally act out of anger and harbor its lingering residue is called resentment (*upanāha*).
To feign service and obedience is termed deception (*sāṭheyya*).
Avarice regarding wealth and the Dharma is called *mātsarya* (stinginess).
Envy of others' fame, profit, skills, and merit is called *īrṣyā* (envy).
The mental fever resulting from the thought of meeting with the disliked or being separated from the beloved is called *pradāśa* (vexation).
Concealing one's own nature while acting with crooked compliance to suit the occasion is called flattery (*śāṭhya*).
Hiding one's own faults is called concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Obstructing others from praising themselves is called arrogance (*mada*).
The desire to oppress others is called "harming.
These ten types exist solely on the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*).
It does not involve the five sensory consciousnesses;
it is restricted to what is abandoned through cultivation and does not involve what is abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Because they arise separately and not simultaneously,
they are called "minor grounds" (*parittabhūmi*) among the other mental factors (*caitasika*).
There are further five factors;
added to the preceding, they total forty-three.
These are: vitarka, vicāra, middha, and kaukṛtya.
Coarse thought is called *vitarka* (applied thought);
subtle thought is termed *vicāra* (sustained thought).
All afflictions [arise from these].
The state of falling asleep is called *middha* (sleep).
When the body and mind are obscured and dull,
taking up objects of perception only briefly, it is called *svapna* (dreaming).
To pursue and transform [the afflictions] is called repentance (*kaukṛtya*). Among the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*),
there are furthermore four categories.
Combined with the preceding, these total forty-seven.
That is to say: greed, hatred, pride, and doubt.
Attachment and defilement are termed "greed" (rāga).
Anger is called *dveṣa* (hatred);
to despise others is termed *māna* (pride);
to be hesitant is called *vicikitsā* (doubt).
The five views are a form of wisdom;
because they are identical in nature to the category of wisdom within the universal ground (mahābhūmika),
they are set aside and not discussed here.
The latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) is identical in number to the category of ignorance (*avidyā*) among the great afflictions;
therefore, it is not mentioned separately as this latent tendency of ignorance.
Although its substance is identical in number to that of the ignorance included among the great afflictions,
their meanings differ.
Regarding the ignorance included among the great afflictions:
While [the term] "pervasive" applies generally to all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*),
and stains (*mala*), the "underlying tendency of ignorance" (*avidyā-anuśaya*) is restricted specifically to the category of underlying tendencies.

They do not pertain to the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) or the stains (*mala*). Furthermore, among those enumerated as "universal" (*mahābhūmika*), ignorance (*avidyā*) pertains only to association (*samprayukta*),
and does not pertain to the non-common (*asādhāraṇa*).
Because it coexists with all afflictions,
the "unmanifesting" (avidyā) latent tendency encompasses both the associated and the non-shared [latent tendencies].
Among these, if there is an object of perception that is not clearly understood yet does not coexist with any of the latent proclivities (anuśaya),
this is its "unshared" [characteristic].
If it is not due to other conditions,
but rather coexists with the other nine proclivities (anuśaya),
this constitutes its association (saṃprayoga).
Such is the case in the Abhidharma;
however, in the Satyasiddhi-śāstra,
mental factors are not fixed.
Subsuming the branches within the root,
there are thirty-seven; however, when discussed according to the branches, they are enumerated separately.
Thus, they are immeasurable.
How is it that, from the beginning, there are thirty-seven?
As stated in that treatise:
In total there are ten factors:
volition, contact, mindfulness, desire, joy, faith, diligence, applied thought, sustained thought, and attention; the first four and the last one.
It is the same as the Abhidharma;
the other five [factors] differ.
As for what is called "volition" (cetanā):
As stated in the *Cintā-varga* (Chapter on Reflection):
"The longing and seeking of craving is called 'volition' (*cetanā*).

This differs from the Abhidharma position, which holds that craving is an affliction (*kleśa*) while volition is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Regarding this, the treatise states: "As for the contact [of the mind]," it says: [text follows].
The conjunction of the three is called contact (*sparśa*).
Because that mental consciousness relies upon the sense faculty and contacts the object,
it is termed contact.
It is not said that there is a separate category of "contact" (sparśa) existing apart from the mind;
in reality, the meaning of contact pervades all four types of consciousness.
Now, it is spoken of as "contact" with reference to the functioning mind.
Regarding "mindfulness" (*smṛti*), the treatise states:
"The act of bringing forth [an object] is called mindfulness; it arises after the formation of mental attention (*manasikāra*)."
It is called "initiation.
Regarding "desire" (*chanda*), the treatise states:
that which the mind requires is called desire.
Regarding "joy" (*prīti*), the treatise states:
mental pleasure is called joy;
it is designated as joy because it is predominant among the various types of desire.
This is not found in the Abhidharma.
As for "faith," the treatise states that it is necessarily termed faith.
This [category] applies to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
