The remainder is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Since the untainted exhaustion [of outflows] is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
this is what the *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims.
The emptiness of mind through cessation is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Furthermore, he taught that there are two types of cessation regarding the empty mind.

First, there is temporary cessation through the meditative attainment of extinction (*nirodhasamāpatti*); second, there is permanent cessation through the remainderless state (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Therefore, one should know that even untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*) possess cessation by calculation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is taught in the Mahāyāna has the same meaning as the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* says:
"When delusive thoughts and the fires of affliction are extinguished, that is my nirvana.
It is also said:
"To sever and eliminate the practices of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
Only then can it be called ultimate nirvāṇa. These two sections are concluded.
Next, we discuss according to the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
There are two kinds of remedies.
First, the knowledge of outflows (sāsrava-jñāna) and so forth;
second, the noble uncontaminated knowledge (anāsrava-ārya-jñāna).
This is according to the Abhidharma.
These are abandoned by conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*); there are cases where this is so and cases where it is not.
If one relies on the eight dhyānas to grasp the higher [realms] and abandon the lower ones, [this applies].
Furthermore, regarding the obstructions severed at the time of cultivating the path:
their cessation through non-enumeration occurs when, during the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one causes the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*) to never arise again.
This is not cessation through enumeration (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
All such [categories] shall be explained in detail later;
they are abandoned by the untainted [path].
There is also that which is both existent and non-existent.
The cessation of all afflictions, karma, and volitions through abandonment is what constitutes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For a person who does not regress, while on the path of cultivation,
at the moment of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), the defilements to be abandoned are rendered such that they will never arise again;
this is cessation through non-enumeration (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), not the case for a person who regresses.
Within the path of cultivation,
one reaches the stage of immovability upon the subsequent transformation of the faculties.
It causes those afflictions of the path of cultivation that were previously abandoned to never arise again;
furthermore, this is not analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). All such cases are like this.
This meaning is as explained in that *Vibhāṣā*.
It is asked: At the time when the faculties are transformed into those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), [what occurs]?
Is the root of all obstacles that are to be abandoned—namely, ignorance—a state of analytical cessation?
The explanation says: [It is not].
This is not so. He asked:
"The Abhidharma proclaims [otherwise]."
When a practitioner undergoes the transformation of their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*),
they employ one path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
this is because their fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not yet exhausted, and they seek their exhaustion with fierce vigor for the sake of attaining the superior fruit.
Because their pursuit of benefit is intense,
those beyond training (aśaikṣa) transform their faculties using nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.
Since they seek the benefit of the world through the exhaustion of their fetters,
and since these [beings] employ the unhindered knowledges and liberations to sever obstructions and ignorance,
why is that which is severed not termed "analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?
The commentary states:
"Numerical cessation" refers to that which is contrary to the characteristic of cessation;
it is not something that is non-contradictory.
Although it is abandoned, it is not extinguished;
that ignorance which is abandoned at the time of the transformation of the faculties is an outflow-free dharma.
It arises as a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) together with the subsequently attained sharp faculties and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states;
this is the efficacy of mutual support through the characteristic of its own category (*sva-bhāga*).
It resides within the advantageous;
for this reason, it is not extinguished.
Furthermore, it is the power of dull-witted wisdom to illuminate its object.
The capacity to remedy obstacles possesses both benefit and harm;
it is not entirely distinct [from other capacities].

Therefore, it is not cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). For example, when one realizes the fruit [of the path], the abandonment of the [preparatory] stages (*prayoga*) toward the outflow-free state is not called cessation through deliberation;
this case is likewise.
Question: Some say that subtle ignorance resides within the sense faculties.
It is taught that this constitutes the root of hindrances and ignorance;
the cessation of this ignorance should be termed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Why is it not so? The explanation says:
because there is subtle ignorance.
Regarding that which is described as an obstruction within the faculties: at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*),
one should abandon ignorance (*avidyā*) but not the untainted (*anāsrava*).
At the time of the transformation of the faculties,
one abandons only that which is untainted;
it is not said that there is further ignorance to be abandoned.
It is clearly known that there is no distinct ignorance herein;
it is merely dull non-outflow (anāsrava).
When sharp knowledge is obstructed by dullness,
it is called "non-knowledge.
Because the dull obstructs the sharp, it is so named.
It is taught that this constitutes an obstruction;
its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, its relinquishment is not termed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because it is through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Non-analytical cessations are numerous."
The cessation of outflows (*āsrava*) through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is narrow, as it pertains only to the cessation of those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Question: Why is this so?
Since the transformation of the faculties is not through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), what is the use of the paths of non-obstruction and liberation? To explain:
When turning [the faculties], one must necessarily contemplate the principles of the Truths;
the initial mind of contemplation is accompanied by dull acquisition (mṛdu-prāpti).
Regarding those objects of the truths,
one has not yet attained profound clarity,
nor has one attained definitive realization.
This is called "unimpededness.
At the moment of finality, one attains definitive discernment regarding the object;
this is called "liberation."
It is the same as the severing of the fetters;
therefore, with respect to the severing of the fetters, it is called "unimpeded" and it is called "liberation."
However, that which is non-existent therein is not cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Such is the Abhidharma; this is also the case in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
The abandonment of tainted knowledge is entirely not through analytical cessation;
tainted states are merely suppressed.
Because it cannot be severed [by other means],
it is only through the severance by untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) that it is called "severed and extinguished."
Within the Mahāyāna teachings,
there must be analytical distinction.
If one explains that the mundane knowledge of the eight dhyānas and so forth is "with outflows" (sāsrava), [it is because it is based on conventional reality].
That merely suppresses the fetters;
it is not analytical cessation, nor is it the permanent abandonment [of defilements] through the untainted [path].
This is precisely what constitutes their cessation through calculation. Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"If one uses conventional [wisdom] to extinguish all afflictions..."
That is not ultimate;
it is not the fruit of liberation.
Nirvāṇa is also so described.
First one moves by means of meditative concentration,
and subsequently one uproots [afflictions] by means of wisdom.
Thus, having attained nirvana, one does not abandon the world.
Realizing emptiness while following after existence is called "with outflows" (sāsrava), yet it is also capable of eternal cessation;
because it arises based on true wisdom, it is able to bring about eternal cessation.
What is it that is extinguished?
It is the view of attachment to existence and the darkness of delusion regarding emptiness; these are extinguished by the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
The deluded attachment to emptiness regarding existence and non-existence is ignorance;
wisdom can extinguish it.
Thus, these three gateways have been concluded according to their respective remedies.
Next, we discuss [cessation] in terms of time.
Time refers to the three periods.
It is by means of these three periods that one discerns the cessation of number.
According to the Abhidharma,
there are two kinds of volition (cetanā) regarding afflictions and karma:
the first is the primary essence.
Second, the accomplishment.
There are two kinds of attainment of the remedy:
first, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Second, the path of liberation:
the path of non-obstruction is able to sever [the afflictions],
and the path of liberation attains cessation.
It is also called "realizing cessation.
First, let us discuss its abandonment;
the meaning is not fixed.
If one cuts off the preceding cause so that the subsequent [effect] does not arise,
this is called "cutting off";
it refers exclusively to the cutting off of the past.
Because there is no delusion by the side of the Path,
it does not cease to manifest;
this is before delusion has arisen.
Because it has not yet arisen in the subsequent [moment],
it does not sever the present.
If one obstructs the fruit of the afflictions so that they do not arise, [this is what is meant].
This is called "abandonment.
It refers exclusively to the abandonment of future [defilements], while the possession (prāpti) of present defilements still exists.
Therefore, the present is not severed;
because the past has already arisen,
the past is not severed.
If it encompasses both cause and effect,
it is termed "severance" (prahāṇa), which universally severs [the continuity of] both the past and the future.
Correctly obstructing subsequent results so that they do not arise is called "severing the future."
Because they will not arise again,
the past afflictions do not constitute the sense of being causes.
They do not arise.
This is called the severance of the past;
at the threshold of the present path,
no delusion arises in the future.
Nor does it arise from the preceding moment;
therefore, the present is not severed. If the present were severed, attainment would be impossible.
To cause that which has not yet arisen not to arise is called "abandonment";
this constitutes the abandonment of the present.
Furthermore, it prevents the future;
it only severs the capacity for acquisition (*prāpti*), not the substance of acquisition itself.
If it is abandoned through present attainment,
such that the afflictions already acquired in the past and future no longer belong to oneself,
this is called "abandonment."
It penetrates and severs the three periods of time.
Such is the meaning of severance.
As for the attainment of cessation:
It resides in liberation;
its meaning is also not fixed,
as it is discussed in relation to its counterpart.
It is only the causes and fruits of past and future afflictions that are extinguished,
not those of the present; for in the present,
there is no acquisition of delusion (*paryavasthāna*) that can be brought to cessation.
Therefore, cessation does not apply to the present.
If one considers the essence of cessation itself,
it can only obtain the cessation of the present, and cannot obtain the cessation of the past or future.
What is the meaning of this?
The cause has passed and the effect follows; as it is currently in the process of ceasing, it is attained accordingly.
Therefore, one attains the present cessation of the presently extinguished delusions; since past [delusions] have not yet been extinguished,
one does not attain transcendence of them.
It is not that which is currently ceasing;
therefore, it cannot be "present. If one were to negate the existence of the fruit of delusion, [it would likewise be untenable].
To cause them not to arise is called "cessation";
it refers solely to the cessation of the present and future, not the past.
What is the meaning of this?
When liberation is present, afflictions do not arise;
this is called the cessation of the present.
The delusions that have been extinguished so that they do not arise again in the future are called "extinguishing the future"; as for past afflictions, [they are already extinguished].
Having already arisen,
it cannot be curtailed by the Path; therefore,
its transgression is not extinguished.
This is similar to the severance of wholesome roots within nirvāṇa;
therefore, that text states:
"Cessation is of two kinds."
First, the present [wholesome roots] are extinguished;
second, the future [wholesome roots] are obstructed.
Possessing these two types of extinction is called the severance of the wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
The severance of afflictions is likewise so:
if one causes the causal status of the various afflictions to become non-existent,
it is termed "cessation."
It penetrates and extinguishes the three periods of time.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because the antidote has become manifest.
To cause past afflictions so that they cannot give rise to subsequent ones is called "extinguishing past causes," because they do not arise in the present.
Subsequent delusions do not arise;
there is no arising of delusion in the future.
This is called the cessation of the present cause.
Subsequent delusions do not arise;
there is no arising of delusion in the future.
This is called the cessation of the cause for [future] coming.
The term "severing the roots of goodness" (kuśalamūla-ccheda) refers to severing the causes of the three periods of time within nirvāṇa;
the meaning is similar because both involve universal cessation.
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "Pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation through deliberation) is manifold; it universally encompasses the cessation of the three periods of time."
Non-analytical cessation is minimal;
it ceases only that which is future. Question:
In the Abhidharma, liberation from delusion is called "attainment of cessation.
At the time of the path of non-obstruction,
there is likewise no affliction.
For what reason is it not called "attaining cessation"?
The explanation states:
there is a reason.
At the time of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), regarding the afflictions of its own category that have not yet been abandoned,
because they have not yet arisen, they cannot be extinguished.
Although the delusions do not currently manifest,
their acquisition remains; thus,
regarding the afflictions to be abandoned within their own category:
This is not a non-existence resulting from non-practice, nor is it a non-existence resulting from abandonment;
therefore, cessation cannot be attained.
If one is a person who does not regress,
at the time of the path of non-obstruction,
the afflictions to be abandoned are rendered such that they will never arise again.
This is not cessation through deliberation;
it is not subsumed under the Truth of Cessation,
and therefore it cannot be extinguished.
Question: Does the unimpeded [knowledge] cause the defilements to be severed so that they never arise again?
If so, does it pertain to the acquisition (prāpti) of those defilements?
Why is it not extinguished?
Because the power of non-obstruction is weak and thus unable to extinguish it.
Question: Does non-obstruction cause the defilements that have been severed not to arise again?
Is it not the case that for analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), they do not arise again?
Thus, there is nothing to be attained.
For what reason is it possible to attain non-extinction?
The explanation says:
Although that which is to be acquired in the future has ceased,
the past cause still persists and gives rise to subsequent subtle afflictions;
thus, the acquisition follows that cause.
Therefore, it remains unextinguished;
such is the meaning of the cessation of afflictions.
The same applies to karmic volition (*karma-cetanā*).
Such is the Abhidharma; this is also the case in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
It merely severs the substance of afflictions, karma, and suffering;
it does not speak of severing "attainment. Even if one were to speak of attainment, [it would be as follows].
He is called a practitioner.
To accomplish that dharma is what is meant by "attainment."
The severing of afflictions is the same as in the Abhidharma;
the severing of karma is likewise so.
The retribution of the suffering of birth and death may be extinguished in the present,
so that it does not continue in the future.
This means that the knowledge of the limit (prāntakoṭika-jñāna) forcibly suppresses [the afflictions] so as to cause their cessation,
or else it causes future [afflictions] to cease by severing the present causes.
Causing them not to arise again in the future.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma,
this refers to the coarse arising of karmic fetters.
The cessation is the same as before.
However, regarding the ignorance that is of the same essence as one's own nature,
one severs only that which is present.
It causes [the afflictions] not to continue in the future;
there is no further meaning [to this].
What are their characteristics?
Because the wisdom of identical essence accords with the power of reality,
it can cause the ignorance that is the very nature of that essence never to arise again;
this is termed "severance."
This nature is ignorance;
its cessation occurs in liberation.
The method for attaining this is the same as the principle explained above. This concludes the four gates.
Next is the discussion of the stages (*avasthā*).
There are five distinct stages. The first is the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
In the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, the stages prior to the foundations of mindfulness constitute the two levels of the ordinary person within the inner stage;
in the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, the stages from the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) upward [constitute the noble path].

In the Mahāyāna Dharma, from the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) upward, there are four: first, the stage of the lineage of nature; second, the stage of the lineage of practice; third, the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); and fourth, the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the five paths of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga),
according to the Abhidharma,
there are three distinct categories in terms of their meaning.
First is the place of severance;
second is the place of attainment;
third is the place of fulfillment.
As for the stages where [defilements] are abandoned,

they occur only during the stages of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana), the path of seeing (darśanamārga), and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). Within the stage of the outer ordinary person:
Relying on mundane dhyāna,
one abandons the fetters through the six practices during the stage of seeing the truths.
One abandons the afflictions of the truths to be realized through seeing;
within the stage of the path of cultivation,
one abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
Within the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala),
although one trains in the contemplation of the truths,
one merely suppresses their active manifestation and cannot permanently sever them.
This is not discussed because those beyond training have exhausted all afflictions and there is nothing further to be severed;
therefore, it is not discussed.
Question: The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation,
thereby severing all obstacles, latent tendencies, and ignorance that he possesses.
What is non-abandonment? It is because it is not analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) at the point where the roots of obstruction are exhausted.
Therefore, it is not mentioned. If one discusses the stage where it is attained,
it occurs among the external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) during the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The external ordinary beings, those in the stages of seeing and cultivation, and those who have attained [the fruits] through abandonment,
as well as those in the stage of no-more-learning.
Within those causes, all that is to be abandoned is simultaneously and instantaneously attained,
combining to constitute the essence of the fruit.
A single stage of the inner ordinary person has nothing at all that can be attained; yet,
if one discusses the point of its accomplishment:
All five stages are accomplished;
that which is severed by the external ordinary beings is also accomplished by the internal ordinary beings.
The realization through seeing, cultivation,
and no-more-learning can be understood as being accomplished therein. This is established within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
The distinctions in meaning are twofold:
first, the locus of abandonment and attainment;
second, the locus of accomplishment.
Regarding the stage of attainment through abandonment:
it occurs within the two paths of seeing and cultivation belonging to the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Within this stage of the inner ordinary person:
Through the four minds beginning with *mṛdu*,
one gradually abandons the afflictions; therefore,
analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained.
The two types of wisdom— those derived from hearing and reflection—
can only suppress and eliminate [afflictions],
but are not yet able to exhaust them forever.
Therefore, that which is attained is not true cessation (*nirodha*).
Thus, that treatise says:
Coming from the stage of *kṣānti* and so forth,
one gradually severs the afflictions;
only upon seeing cessation (*nirodha*) are they exhausted.
It is known that although hearing and reflection cannot permanently extinguish them,
their abandonment through the two stages of seeing and cultivation can be understood.
In that school, the eight worldly dhyānas do not sever the fetters.
For external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), there is consistently neither abandonment nor attainment; for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no abandonment—
the meaning of these points can be understood accordingly.
As for their accomplishment,
those at the stage of inner ordinary beings— whether on the paths of seeing or cultivation— as well as those who are beyond training,
have all fully accomplished them.
The outer ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) are not established [as a distinct category]. Within the Mahāyāna teachings,
all those prior to the good destinies (sugati) are designated as outer ordinary beings.
Within that stage of the external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) in the fortunate realms,
one abandons the coarse [afflictions] to some extent;
thus, even in the five stages, their cessation is attained.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states that within the stage of Bhadramukha (Worthy Head), one attains ocean-seal and other samādhis as numerous as atoms;
this clarifies the manifestation of Buddhahood through the eight phases.
Within this, there is cessation and extinction;
for those within the stage of ordinary persons, there is cessation and extinction through both the paths of seeing and cultivation.

The extinction attained by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as there is nothing further to be abandoned; thus, following the analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation is now distinguished.
Within this, there is a detailed analysis according to five gates.
First, the analysis in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*).
Second, the classification according to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Third, the classification according to the internal and the external.
Fourth, the classification according to the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
The fifth [section] distinguishes [the truths] according to the three time periods.
The first [section] distinguishes them according to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Within the afflictions:

That which is prevented from arising by the power of other conditions that serve as antidotes to the unimpeded analytical knowledges and liberations is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Karma, however, is not fixed.
According to the Abhidharma system,
it refers to the volition (cetanā) of defiled karma.
They are identical to the afflictions;
all other remaining things are not analytical cessations.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is established that all karmas and the like are identical to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the retribution of suffering,
according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā),
none of these are through analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The Mahāyāna is established as being identical with the afflictions; this concludes the section on the same category.
Next, there is a distinction based on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Among the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*),
excluding those that are prevented from arising by the power of conditions such as the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the liberations (*vimokṣa*) which serve as their antidotes.
This is not cessation through deliberation;
it is untainted and indeterminate.
This is according to the Abhidharma.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
it is held that all untainted [phenomena] for which arising should have occurred but did not are not "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If the power of the Path causes the cessation of the outflows,

that is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for the case where one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and, through the power of other conditions, prevents [defilements] from arising, [that is not analytical cessation].
This is not cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). In the Mahāyāna Dharma,
it is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation of conditions.
Cessation through realization is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
the remainder is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These two categories are concluded.
Next, they are distinguished according to the internal and external.
The non-analytical unconditioned (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) universally extinguishes all dharmas, both internal and external.
External things such as grass and trees should arise but do not;
this is the cessation of external phenomena.
Regarding the internal phenomena of sentient beings:
that which should arise does not arise;
this concludes the three gateways for the cessation of internal phenomena.
Next, a distinction is made according to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)."
Within the five destinies,
all five consciousnesses attain analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
What is the meaning of this?
It refers to the five consciousnesses arising from the objects of the five sensory realms in all other locations, wherever the body may be.
Because they never arise;
these five sense-objects are here,
while sentient beings are elsewhere.
Nor can it be taken as an object.
Therefore, those five consciousnesses are also not [subject to] analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Question:
Why is the mental consciousness not discussed?
Because in all places and regarding all objects, there is this mutual relationship of mental consciousness.
They can serve as mutual objects of cognition;
it is not because they are non-arising dharmas that they are not so described.
Regarding the portion of the evil destinies,
for one who has already severed and abandoned them, there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"What practices can sever it?
The treatise states:
"There are those such as generosity, ethical discipline, hearing, reflection, cultivation, the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and so forth."
There may be those who, through the cultivation of wisdom, practice the *dhāraṇīs* and so forth, thereby severing the evil realms and attaining analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Within this, the attainment of cessation may be advanced or deferred; it is not fixed.
This applies to those who possess mastery.
By cultivating the aforementioned roots of goodness, one immediately severs the evil realms and attains analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Those of sharp faculties who do not regress are called "masters" (*vaśin*).
If one is of dull faculties,
it is only upon reaching the stage of the mind of patience (kṣānti) that cessation is first attained.
It is asked:
Regarding the three portions of the evil realms that are to be abandoned:
are they attained through non-analytical cessation all at once,
or are they attained sequentially?
Some proclaim that they are attained all at once; however,
the commentators do not reach a definitive conclusion.
If one cultivates wholesome qualities such as generosity, ethical discipline, hearing, and reflection,
one can sever what has been attained;
as for that which has not yet been severed:
Then one does not obtain it. However,
if one cultivates the untainted roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and thereby severs the paths of evil rebirths, [one obtains it].
In the three evil realms,
one simultaneously and instantaneously attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for the two realms of humans and devas:
If there is one who is able to sever [defilements] forever and will not undergo further rebirth,
they attain analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the sequence therein,
it will be discussed further in the subsequent section.
Thus concludes these four gates concerning the destinies (*gati*).
Next, regarding time: time refers to the three periods [of past, present, and future], as well as non-numerical unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
It merely extinguishes all dharmas of the future.
It does not extinguish all dharmas of the past and present.
Among future dharmas, there are two kinds:
first, those that are subject to arising.
Although they have not yet arisen in the present,
they will certainly arise in the future.
Second, dharmas that do not arise.
Because conditions are deficient, that which is easily subverted will ultimately not arise;
as for dharmas destined to arise,
although they have not yet arisen at present, [they will do so].
It will necessarily arise again later;
it is not an ultimate cessation.
Therefore, it cannot be called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Phenomena that do not arise ultimately do not originate;
they are not cessation through deliberation.
The dharmas of the past were destroyed at that very time;
this is the cessation of impermanence among the four characteristics.
It is not non-analytical cessation;
once cessation has been completed,
it is likewise not non-analytical.
Why is this so? Because that which has arisen and passed away is what constitutes the past existence.
Since its nature is established in the past and is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it is therefore not non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This refers to present phenomena.
Having arisen, it has not yet ceased;
because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Therefore, it is not analytical [cessation].
It does not extinguish the past or the present;
its essence and characteristics are thus.
This is the third section.
This clarifies the limit of attainment:
outside of space, there is no dharma that is not attained.
Now, this is set aside and not discussed.
As for the cessation of the calculable and the incalculable,
it is mostly explained with reference to the internal [self].
This is what has been attained by this person;
I shall now specifically analyze it.
Within this, there are two sub-sections.
First, the limits of the divisions are clarified in terms of afflictions;
second, they are explained in terms of retribution.
Regarding the section on afflictions:
First, the boundaries of acquisition are correctly established;
subsequently, the sequence of the acquisition of the two types of cessation is discussed.
What are these boundaries?
According to the *Vibhāṣā*,
at the stage of "increasing patience," the afflictions of the three realms that are abandoned through seeing [the truths] are eliminated.
One attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
By means of superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), one enters the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) immediately and successively;
thereby, all afflictions of the view (dṛṣṭi-āsrava) [are abandoned].
Because there is no re-arising,
it is discussed according to actual subtlety;
[this concerns] those of the highest, most superior faculties.
One who does not emerge from contemplation attains non-analytical cessation once the mind has been transformed.
Because one does not re-arise after entering the noble path from within meditative equipoise,
the treatises mostly speak from the perspective of those who are extremely dull-witted.
Therefore, it is said that through the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Within the stages of patience, there are thirty-two levels in total;
this refers to the final level.
It is called "supreme.
From the patience regarding suffering up to the mind that takes the path as its object, one attains analytical cessation,
the unimpeded [knowledges], and the right abandonments.
It is said that [the path of liberation] is "capable of attaining" [liberation], whereas the path subsequent to the path of liberation is said to be "actually attaining" it.
Question: For what reason can one who is unimpeded not yet attain [the fruit] correctly? Answer:
Because the acquisition of delusion still persists.

Question: At the time of the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) regarding the afflictions of insight (*darśana-heya*), [the seeds] have already been non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, why must it be "cessation through non-cultivation" (a-saṃskāra-nirodha)?
The commentary states:
It is not "through cultivation," but rather the cessation of future delusions.
To prevent it from arising again and to avoid extinguishing the prior cause,
it must be repeatedly extinguished.
Furthermore, analytical cessation merely extinguishes the substance of the afflictions,
ensuring they do not arise again in the future.
One does not extinguish that which has already been attained;
therefore, it is necessary to repeatedly extinguish [the afflictions]. Question:
Since the essence of the afflictions has already been extinguished by non-analytical cessation,
what further thing could be attained that would need to be extinguished again?
[If you claim] that the attainment of the preceding affliction gives rise to the subsequent one...
Because the fruit of the afflictions has not yet been extinguished.
Question: It was stated previously that it is precisely at the stage following the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained.
What is the latter?
As it is stated in the treatise:
liberation is primary.
Thereafter, at the limit of all unimpeded liberation and the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
there is the attainment of birth;
one attains the aforementioned unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is what is meant by "subsequent.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"In the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
This refers to all untainted [phenomena] subsequent to liberation,
taken as the "future" [object].
Such is the case for the delusions of view.
Next, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are discussed. In the desire realm, these afflictions are divided into nine grades according to their coarseness or subtlety,
ranging from the highest-of-the-high (ūrdhva-ūrdhva) down to the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdu-mṛdu).
The path of counteraction consists of nine preparatory stages (*prayoga-mārga*), nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
These range from the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) up to the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*).
First, the limit of attainment is explained according to the initial category;
the others may be understood by analogy.
Thus says the *Vibhāṣā*.
Among the noble ones,
there are those who possess the quality of non-retrogression yet do not give rise to contemplation.
At the time of the path of expedient means,
one attains non-analytical cessation because one does not emerge from meditative equipoise.
Because the afflictions to be abandoned never arise again, at the time of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
One correctly abandons its acquisition; one should attain cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Immediately after the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), one correctly attains cessation through deliberation.
If one who is not subject to regression gives rise to contemplation,
they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) upon reaching the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*); analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is as previously described.
In the case of one who is subject to regression,
whether they give rise to contemplation or do not give rise to it,
[this applies] from the path of preparation up to the path of non-obstruction.
There is nothing whatsoever that is attained through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
because for one who is subject to regression, there is the possibility of the dharma arising again;
it is for this reason that it is not attained.
The cessation through calculation is as described above.
Just as it is for the first category,
the same principle applies to the abandonment and attainment of the afflictions of all remaining categories, up to those of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Question: At what time does one obtain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the afflictions abandoned by one who has fallen back?
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
When a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms into one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
When the person who has attained liberation transforms into the immovable state,
it is at that time that they obtain the body of a noble being.
In the desire realm, one attains cessation by severing the fetters;
such is the body [in that realm]. It is likewise in the form realm and the formless realm.
Regarding the severance of higher-level afflictions, one need not inquire about those who have regressed;
this applies even to those who have not yet emerged from meditative observation during the stage of the path of skillful means.
One attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) when emerging from meditative absorption during the moment of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga).
One attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is because the various devas do not undergo retrogression;
thus, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) appears as it did before.
The unimpeded right abandonment attains analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) following the path of liberation;
such is the demarcation.
Next, the sequence of priority is distinguished.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, this is analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are some afflictions that are first attained as non-analytical cessations and later attained as analytical cessations.
As explained above, regarding the afflictions of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*),
at the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
One attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Only from the stage of the patience regarding suffering (duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) onward does one attain analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Furthermore, among those who cultivate the afflictions,
for a person of non-retrogression who does not emerge from meditative absorption,
at the time of the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga):
One attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Only after the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) does one attain analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). This is the first proposition.
There are some afflictions that are first extinguished through analytical cessation,
and later extinguished through non-analytical cessation.
As has been explained above,
regarding the defilements of the path of cultivation abandoned by those subject to regression,
their acquisition of cessation through analytical knowledge and liberation is occasional.
Only when the faculties are subsequently transformed does one attain the non-analytical cessation;
this is the second phrase.
There are some afflictions that are abandoned both through analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation simultaneously.
As has been explained above,
there are those of the non-retrogressive type who emerge from meditative absorption; this occurs at the time of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
One attains non-analytical cessation;
one shall attain analytical cessation.
This is the actual principle when investigated with subtlety.
First one attains non-numbering,
and subsequently one attains numbering-extinction;
these are the first two phrases.
It is described as a single gate.
Furthermore, as the treatise states:
"Among the nine grades of afflictions in that desire realm..."
The highest-of-the-high [degrees of] afflictions are severed;
these correspond with the defiled five consciousnesses regarding their objects of perception.
No longer taking it as an object,
one attains analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
because it has been subdued by the Path.
It is also attained through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This occurs at one and the same time;
the same applies to the other categories.
Up until the time when even the lowest-of-the-low grade [of defilements] is eliminated,
these associated afflictions defile the five consciousnesses with respect to their objects.
No longer taking it as an object,
one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and also attains analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
At this time, all wholesome dharmas of the desire realm,
as well as non-obscured neutral dharmas,
also attain analytical cessation because they are freed from the bonds of conditions.
When one abandons the progressively superior afflictions of the first dhyāna stage,
the three afflicted consciousnesses associated with those afflictions [are abandoned] with respect to their objects.
One no longer attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) through further conditions;
rather, that which is counteracted by the Path also attains analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Even until the time when the lowest-of-the-low level of afflictions is severed,
the three afflicted consciousnesses associated with those afflictions no longer further take their respective objects as objects.
One attains non-analytical cessation and also attains analytical cessation;
at this time, all wholesome dharmas of the first dhyāna [are attained].
Furthermore, non-obscured indeterminate dharmas also attain analytical cessation because they are free from the bonds of conditions;
this applies from the second dhyāna upward.
The five groups of consciousness do not exist [in that state], and for this reason they are not mentioned.
All of these are termed both "attainment through calculation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and "attainment without calculation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), acquired simultaneously.
This is the third alternative:
there are afflictions that are both subject to analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation.
Neither of the two is attained;
this is the one who practices constantly.
This is the fourth phrase.
This concludes the first section, which analyzes the scope of afflictions.
Next, we shall discuss the retribution of the five destinies.
There is also the sense of cessation through calculation and cessation not through calculation.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna,
one abandons the cause and becomes detached from the fruit.
That which is called cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); that which is not grasped due to other conditions is called cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is according to the Abhidharma method.
The severance of causes and the separation from fruits are both not analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
they consist in severing the delusions that moisten and sustain rebirth.
Furthermore, that which is called "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) consists in being freed from the bonds of conditions. What are its boundaries?
The retributions of the three miserable realms are established according to the *Tattvasiddhi*;
this applies from the level of the "aroused mind" (*utpāditacitta*) upward.
Because it is ultimately not received,
one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Therefore, that text states:
Those in this world who possess right view,
though they may pass through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes,
shall never fall into the evil realms.
That which is called "the burning" (*ādīpana*) and so forth is considered the supreme right view.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*,
if one says that those of sharp faculties have attained mastery:
Once the mind has departed, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This applies to those of dull faculties.
Regarding the aforementioned patience (*kṣānti*),
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Regarding the retribution of the three evil realms:
when abiding in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), it is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
this is stated from the perspective of those of dull faculties.
Because it is certain that [the afflictions] are extinguished here, it is stated many times. Question:
Regarding the retribution of the three evil realms in the future,
will it be attained through non-analytical cessation all at once,
or will it occur sequentially?
This is as explained previously.
If one cultivates wholesome qualities such as generosity, ethical discipline, hearing, and reflection,
one will eliminate and extinguish rebirth in the evil realms.
If cessation occurs through sequential cultivation and observation, then there is a sequence of before and after; if it is through the path of cultivation that they are severed and extinguished,
then their cessation is simultaneous.
At the time of the mind of patience,
one cultivates contemplation of the principle,
dwelling steadfastly without regression.
Regarding all evil realms,
there is no principle of repeated rebirth;
therefore, they cause the future infinite evil realms to be suddenly and simultaneously extinguished through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Question: Are the afflictions of the path of seeing (dṛṣṭiheya) non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained within the state of patience (kṣānti), and [is this also true for] the retribution of the three evil destinies?
Furthermore, regarding the attainment of non-analytical cessation within the stage of patience (kṣānti),
does it occur at the same time [as the patience], or does it occur sequentially?
The commentary asks:
"Regarding 'before' and 'after,' what is the meaning of this?"
Within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), regarding each of those four noble truths— both superior and inferior—
there are sixteen modes of activity (*ākāra*);
together, there are thirty-two layers of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
When first practicing the profound contemplation,
the retributions of the three evil realms are suddenly extinguished through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because there is no further layer of reception,
it is the final layer; at the time of the superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
The afflictions abandoned through seeing are not extinguished by analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) all at once,
because they do not arise again.
Question: The three miserable realms are the fruit of the delusions of view.
By what reasoning is this so?
The fruit ceases first;
the afflictions cease later.
The commentary states:
The delusions of view are of two kinds: first,
the afflictions that cause rebirth, which moisten one's birth within the three miserable realms.
Second, the afflictions that obstruct the path arise as defilements of the mind,
hindering the noble path.
The fault of rebirth is coarse;
upon first entering the stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
one is already able to prevent it from arising.
Therefore, it is caused that the evil realms are entirely not subject to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Among the delusions that obstruct the Path,
those that are subtle are difficult to abandon.
Since one has not yet reached the stage of "ultimate patience" (kṣānty-anantarya), it is possible for [the defilements] to arise momentarily; therefore,
this is not called the attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Following the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
one enters the noble path (*āryamārga*) immediately and in succession;
there is no sense of it arising again later.
At that time, one finally attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
According to the *Vibhāṣā*:
Having attained the patience regarding suffering, one attains its analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This analytical cessation consists in severing the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those afflictions that cause rebirth.

Causing the non-arising of retribution is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore, the meaning of severing the bonds of objective conditions upon retribution is also termed analytical cessation.
If the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that moisten and sustain rebirth is severed,

it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this occurs through the four dharmas of patience (*dharmakṣānti*), the mind of non-obstruction (*anantarya-citta*), and right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
Regarding the four types of dharma-knowledge, their cessation is subsequently attained.
If cessation by number (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is defined as the severing of the fetters of objects,
then there are eleven pervasive underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the realms of suffering and its origin.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are bound by conditions;
the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms is likewise bound by these conditions.
Through the patience regarding the dharma of suffering and the patience regarding the dharma of origination,
one correctly abandons those [defilements],
causing them so that they do not come again to belong to oneself.
The infinite future retributions of the three evil realms are all liberated from their causal bonds;
this occurs after the two types of dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and its origin.
Thus is the cessation through analytical discernment attained; such is the case for the evil realms.
Next, we shall discuss humans and devas.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*,
after one has attained the state of an ārya,
[the gods and humans of] the desire realm...
Each consists of seven births;
these are what must be experienced by those who have attained the stages of Srotāpanna and Sakkadāgāmin.
Once these are exhausted, [the remaining births are eliminated].
For all humans and devas,
regarding future births and deaths,
after the stage of superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti).
There is no sense of receiving [the fruit] repeatedly;
all are non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) throughout all places of birth in the realms of form and formlessness.
Each is a "single-birth portion" (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
these should be the future experiences of an *anāgāmin*,
excluding the single-birth portion itself.
Regarding all future births in the realms of form and formlessness,
after the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
there is no further possibility of receiving [rebirth].
At the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
[the defilements] are all non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) for humans and devas of the desire realm.
Each has seven births remaining.
Where is cessation attained?
By severing the fetters of the desire realm.
There are nine paths of preparation, nine paths of non-obstruction, and nine paths of liberation.
When proceeding from the stage of srotāpanna toward the stage of sakṛdāgāmin,
it does not matter whether one's faculties are sharp or dull.
There are those who attain the state of a Sakṛdāgāmin without emerging from meditative absorption.
At the time of that initial path of expedient means,
they attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the six prior factors of birth.
Because one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* without emerging from meditative absorption,
one does not undergo further births among these six realms; thus,
even if there should be regression, [rebirth is not repeated].
One does not die while regressing from the fruit,
nor is there any sense of experiencing [the fruit].
If one emerges from meditative absorption and attains the state of a Sakṛdāgāmin, [that is the case].
Prior to its attainment, there may still be the assumption of a body; therefore,
this remains the case up until the stage of the six preparatory practices (ṣaḍ-pūrvaprayoga).
One has never previously attained non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Upon reaching the sixth stage of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga),
one attains the non-analytical cessations of the six preceding births.
Following this state of non-obstruction,
one will certainly attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin and shall not undergo further rebirths.
Therefore, from the stage of the Srotāpanna heading toward the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin,
regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull,
there are those who attain the fruit of Anāgāmin without emerging from meditative absorption.
At that time of the seventh path of expedient means,
the seventh rebirth-portion among humans and devas of the desire realm attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because one attains the fruit of anāgāmin without emerging from meditative absorption,
one shall never again undergo birth and death within the desire realm.
Even if one regresses from the fruit,
one does not die nor undergo [rebirth] until it is attained;
if there are those who emerge from meditative absorption and attain the state of an Anāgāmin, [they likewise do not undergo rebirth].
Prior to its attainment,
it may allow for the assumption of a body;
however, this must continue until the moment of the ninth path of non-obstruction.
Only then does one attain the non-calculable.
Such is the non-calculable.
What is the cessation of calculation?
If one cuts off the delusions that provide moisture [to rebirth], it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the future, infinite births and deaths within the desire realm,
there are nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
Through the successive right abandonments,
one attains analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) via the nine paths of liberation.
It is not merely seven births;
if the bonds of conditions are severed,
it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Upon reaching the ninth stage of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga),
one correctly severs the fetters;
this occurs after the ninth stage of the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
All future births and deaths within the desire realm attain their cessation through analytical knowledge;
it is not limited to seven more lifetimes alone.
Question: Why is it that only the ninth unimpeded [knowledge] definitively severs the bonds of the objects of cognition,
whereas the preceding eight, though they sever them, do not yet constitute liberation?
It is for this reason that it is not mentioned;
however, because liberation occurs at this stage, the treatise discusses it.
Such is the case with the desire realm.
The body of a noble one,
while remaining in the stage of the desire realm,
severs the fetters of the first dhyāna.
Having received a body in the first dhyāna,
where is it extinguished? It is extinguished by severing the fetters of the first dhyāna.
There are also nine grades of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
If one is a person who does not regress,
they exhaust the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the first dhyāna while remaining within meditative absorption.
At the time of that initial path of skillful means,
one attains two types of birthplaces for the first dhyāna; for each,
there is a non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) pertaining to one future birth.
What are its two locations in the first dhyāna?
They are the Brahmakāyika and the Brahmapurohita, with Mahābrahmā as the third.
They are combined into a single unit.
For the Noble One, there is no principle of being born again in this state;
therefore, it is proclaimed that each constitutes a single lifetime.
After the second birth, at the stage of superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti),
it has already been non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Therefore, it is not argued that one exhausts those fetters by not emerging from meditative absorption,
nor does one subsequently fall back and undergo rebirth there. Thus,
if one were to exhaust those fetters by repeatedly emerging from absorption, [the aforementioned fault would follow].
Because they have emerged from contemplation,
during the interval before their [defilements] are exhausted,
they may relinquish their bodies of desire and be reborn in that heaven.
Therefore, up until the ninth preparatory stage (prayoga),
one cannot attain that non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of arising;
it is only upon reaching that ninth path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) that it is attained.
Only then does one attain the cessation not due to calculation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding that birth;
for after this non-obstruction,
there is no relinquishing of the body of desire to be born in that heaven.
If it is one who regresses,
they exhaust those fetters completely, whether or not they emerge from meditative absorption.
This continues up to the ninth unimpeded liberation.
One does not attain the cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding their arising;
for even though a person subject to regression has severed all fetters, [they may still regress].
Or perhaps it is because one might fall away and be reborn in that heaven;
it is not that the number [of attainments] is thus. What, then, is "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?
If one cuts off the delusions that provide moisture [to rebirth], this is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Those nine unimpeded paths (*anantarya-mārga*) are each capable of severing the infinite cycle of birth and death within the stage of the first dhyāna.
It is not merely one or two;
after the nine liberations,
one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is not merely the cessation of two places or two births;
rather, when the bonds of conditions are severed, it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This occurs at the time of the ninth path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
Having rightly severed the bonds of conditions,
after emerging from that ninth liberation,
one undergoes infinite births and deaths within the first dhyāna.
They are all subject to cessation through calculation;
it is not merely one or two.
The preceding eight are unimpeded.
Although the bonds of conditions have been severed,
they have not been severed completely;
thus, one has not yet attained liberation.
It is for this reason that it is not mentioned:
because the nine grades of fetters collectively bind all births in the first dhyāna,
even when the body resides in the desire realm.
If it is so that one attains cessation by looking toward the stage of the first dhyāna,
then it is likewise for those looking toward the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
All cases are likewise so.

They agree in saying that the states from which a person has regressed, as previously determined, are all instances where non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is not [simply] non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
When is it attained? It is said that when one who is liberated through faith transforms into one who has attained vision,
at that time it is attained.
If one does not transform the faculties,
it is attained at the time of severing the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Question:
The body of a noble one,
while still in the realm of desire, has severed the faults of desire;
even if there should be a regression, [it does not lead to rebirth].
Regarding the seven births within the sphere of what is to be abandoned,
one attains analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). For what reason?
When a person of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman) severs the higher fetters,
does he not attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding those future births?
The commentary states:
In order to establish the points where the fetters are severed and abandoned,
the two fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin are instituted.
The retrogression from the fruit is merely temporary;
it never endures through a future birth.
Therefore, one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) with respect to rebirth there.
From the severing of the fetters of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
there is no separate attainment of a fruit;
one may fall back from it, attain it again, or pass through births.
It is not that they are never experienced;
rather, it is because they cannot be attained as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
[The opponent] asks:
The body of a noble one (ārya) in the desire realm abandons the factors for rebirth in higher realms;
such is the meaning.
If one abides in the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
how does one sever the factors for rebirth in higher realms and attain cessation?
To explain:
The Noble One is born in the higher heavens;
there is no sense of regression regarding those upper stages.
In whatever stage [of defilements] they are abandoned, all factors of rebirth apply,
regardless of whether one is subject to regression or not.
All [conditioned phenomena] attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: What of the bodies of noble ones (*ārya*)?

Regarding the statement that one severs the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) while on a lower stage and attains cessation (*nirodha*), how is this to be explained?
It means that the noble ones sever the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are also nine grades of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Whether one is subject to regression or not,
there are those who, without further engaging in contemplation, exhaustively sever those fetters.
At the time of the initial path of expedient means,
those who have attained the state of being bound to one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha) obtain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
as do those who are subject to falling away.
From the stage of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
they also fully attain all previously unattained cessations not resulting from analytical deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because one attains the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) without emerging from meditative absorption,
and because one is not subject to further rebirth in any state of existence.
If there is one who, upon emerging from meditative absorption, exhausts all fetters;
because of that emergence from absorption,
[the fetters] have not yet been exhausted in the interim.
It allows for the reception of a body;
therefore, even through the nine preliminary stages (*upāya*),
one cannot attain that birth which is cessation not due to conditions (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Only upon reaching that ninth path of non-obstruction does one obtain the cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those [defilements],
as well as the person who has fallen away from them.
From the stage of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
he also attains all those previously unattained cessations not resulting from analytical deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Following this state of non-obstruction,
one will certainly attain arhatship;
one will not undergo birth again in any realm of existence.
Therefore, it is not [a matter of] enumeration in this way.
What is cessation through enumeration (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? If one cuts off the delusions that provide moisture [for rebirth], it is called cessation through enumeration.
Those nine unhindered [knowledges] are each able to sever all factors of birth within the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
they do not merely stop a single birth.
Following the nine liberations,

one sequentially attains all the unconditioned states (*asamskṛta*) consisting of the cessation of the various factors of birth within that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
rather than attaining only one.
If the bonds of the objects of perception are severed,
it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This occurs at the time of the ninth stage of the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
One then severs all fetters of objective conditions pertaining to births in the stages above the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the ninth liberation,
by which one attains the unconditioned state of the cessation of the various factors of birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It does not pertain to only one lifetime;
such is the case regarding retribution.
Within this context, one should also distinguish the sequence in which the two types of unconditioned [attainments] are acquired.
It may be understood according to the above;
the demarcations are thus.
Next are the four gates.
This clarifies that the three unconditioned phenomena differ in their respective quantities.
First, regarding their quantity:
space is the greatest in number.
There are no phenomena whatsoever.

For now, we shall briefly distinguish their quantity and smallness by means of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The meaning of this is not fixed.
According to one interpretation, the number of cessations through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is great.
Non-analytical cessation is limited,
whereas analytical cessation universally ceases the dharmas of the three periods of time;
therefore, it is called "much."
The meaning has been explained above.
Once past afflictions have been extinguished,
they cannot function as causes.
The cessation of future afflictions cannot serve as a fruit;
[likewise for] the cessation of present afflictions.
It does not involve cause and effect;
it is non-calculable and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It consists solely in the cessation of future dharmas that would otherwise have arisen.
Therefore, it is called "small.
It has one meaning: it is not that the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is numerous.
Cessation through calculation is limited;
cessation not through calculation universally extinguishes both tainted and untainted phenomena,
and is therefore called "much."
The cessation through calculation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) extinguishes only those phenomena that are subject to outflows (sāsrava);
it is therefore termed "limited.
This may be verified through such inquiry.
The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*) is certainly not analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is because these two types of cessation differ in their mutual presence or absence.
Therefore, one should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*),
as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding the first point, there are dharmas.
It is extinguished solely by analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
and not by non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
that is to say, it refers to the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the past and present.
And those that will arise in future lives as contaminated (*sāsrava*).
As for the second phrase, it refers to phenomena (*dharma*) that exist.
It is extinguished solely by non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and not by analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha);
that is to say, it refers to those untainted (anāsrava) phenomena of the future that do not arise.
The third phrase refers to those phenomena that are extinguished by both types of cessation;
these are the outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena of the future that do not arise.
The fourth phrase refers to phenomena that are not extinguished by either of the two types of cessation;
namely, past and present untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding those that will arise in future lives as untainted (*anāsrava*), their quantity is likewise thus; this concludes the first section.
Next, the differences are distinguished.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*,

the two types of cessation— cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)— are contrasted with impermanent cessation (*anityatā-nirodha*).
Now, to distinguish their differences, there are ten kinds.
The first concerns their meaning.
Distinguishing them according to whether they are conditioned or unconditioned:
cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
That which is impermanent and subject to cessation is analyzed as being, by its very nature,
a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma).
According to the Vātsīputrīyas,
the cessation of impermanence is also unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because that which is taught as the Dharma has no location for its cessation,
it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
The critics do not accept this.
The second [point] distinguishes [the types of cessation] by way of attaining liberation.
If a dharma has already ceased and liberation is attained,
that is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If, after a phenomenon has ceased,
one does not obtain the attainment of liberation,
this is not analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If phenomena are dispersed and destroyed,
one cannot attain the attainment of liberation;
this is impermanent cessation.
Third, the distinction is established in terms of bondage and liberation.
If it is the characteristic of being liberated and unconditioned,
that is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There is this liberation which is not characterized by non-bondage;
it is not analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
but rather the transcendence of future defilements.
That which never arises again is generally termed "liberation" (vimukti). There are, however,
states that possess neither the characteristic of liberation nor the characteristic of being unbound.
This statement that "it is impermanent and ceases" is not exhaustive;
in truth, it is simply impermanent.
Liberation through penetration is not liberation;
it is untainted and impermanent— this is its liberation.
That which is with outflows and impermanent is not liberation;
it is bound and unbound.
The same applies to the categories.
In the fourth section, they are distinguished according to their temporal divisions.
That which attains cessation within the phenomena of the three periods of time is cessation by enumeration (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which attains cessation within future phenomena is...
This is not cessation through calculation;
rather, that which attains cessation within currently arising phenomena is cessation through impermanence.
Fifth, the distinction is clarified by reference to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is wholesome; its acquisition (*prāpti*) is also wholesome.
It is non-analytical and indeterminate;
its acquisition is also indeterminate.
That which ceases through impermanence—
It penetrates the three natures;
attainment is likewise.
This is explained with reference to wholesome dharmas.
It is called "wholesome" when considered in relation to unwholesome phenomena; it is called "unwholesome" when considered in relation to wholesome phenomena.
The same applies to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The sixth [category] distinguishes between the bound (*baddha*) and the unbound (*abaddha*);
analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is unbound.
Because they are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*),
they can be both bound and unbound; because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), [they are bound].
That which is extinguished by the knowledge of the eight dhyānas and so forth is called a "fetter";
it is extinguished by means of the untainted (anāsrava).
It is called "unbound" because it is not a bound dharma by way of enumeration;
for it is a non-enumerated unconditioned dharma.
Attainment is exclusively a fetter,
because it is a contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon;
it is the cessation of the impermanent.
The bound and the unbound are mutually connected;
acquisition is likewise. This is explained with reference to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
It is called "bound" when speaking in terms of the tainted (*sāsrava*); it is called "unbound" when speaking in terms of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The seventh [distinction] is made based on the difference between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Cessation through calculation is not the mind;
therefore, it is neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training.
That attainment is both of one in training and of one beyond training;
it is also termed neither of one in training nor of one beyond training.
Although attainment (*prāpti*) is not itself the mind,
it is spoken of in terms of the dharmas;
it is the attainment that exists within the cause.
One is called a learner (*śaikṣa*) from the perspective of the cause,
while the attainment of the fruit constitutes the state; one is called a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) from the perspective of having attained that fruit.
The unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) attained by those [noble ones] is called "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
It is not cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner;
its acquisition is likewise so.
It is the cessation through impermanence.
These are the trainee (śaikṣa), the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither trainee nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Attainment (prāpti) is likewise.
This is explained according to the causes of the trainee.
It is called "learning" (śaikṣa);
when spoken of in relation to those beyond learning,
it is called "beyond learning" (aśaikṣa).
Regarding the explanation in terms of the contaminated (sāsrava),
it is called "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
The eighth [category] is distinguished according to the three types of abandonment (prahāṇa).
It is not severed by analytical cessation,
because it is an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛtadharma). Its attainment is indeterminate.
Some are abandoned through the path of cultivation, while others are not abandoned;
they are acquired by means of the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the outflows and so forth.
This is abandoned through the cultivation of the path;
its binding conditions are severed, and it is attained through the analytical cessation realized by untainted noble wisdom.
This is what is not abandoned.
The essence of cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is non-interrupted, because it is an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Its acquisition is invariably abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
Regarding the cessation through impermanence,
it is fully endowed with three aspects:
the destruction and extinction of the delusions of view.
That which is abandoned through seeing is the afflictions of the path of vision; that which is abandoned through cultivation is the destruction of the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
The untainted (anāsrava) destruction is its non-interruption;
attainment is also of three kinds.
This may be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
Ninth, the distinction is made in terms of the fruits of the path.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is the fruit of that path.
Up to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these serve as the seal of realization for the Path and collectively constitute the fruits of the Path.
That acquisition (prāpti) is either the path or the fruit of the path;
or it is neither the path nor the fruit of the path.
It is acquired through the power of cessation by way of the untainted cause (anāsrava-hetu).
That which is named "the Path" is the attainment within the fruits;
this is called the "fruit of the Path."
The knowledge of the outflows and so forth is acquired through analytical cessation;
it is neither the path nor the fruit.
Analytical cessation is not the fruit of the path.
That attainment is neither the path nor the fruit of the path,
because it is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma;
it is the cessation through impermanence.
