Whether it be the Path or the fruit of the non-Path— namely,
the cessation through the impermanence within the stage of "entering" (pratipannaka)—
it serves as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for that Noble Path.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "the Path.
Some things are both the Path and the fruit of the Path;
within these fruits, there is impermanence.
There are cases that are neither the path nor the fruit of the path;
they are tainted and impermanent,
and their acquisition is likewise so.
In the tenth section, the distinctions are analyzed according to the truths; [this concerns] the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is its Truth of Cessation; it is the locus of cessation through conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*),
serving as the seal of realization for the Path.
Penetration is also called cessation (*nirodha*).
Its acquisition is subsumed under the three truths of suffering, origin, and the path.
It is the acquisition belonging to the category of the extinction of outflows (*anāsrava*) through mundane and supramundane knowledge.
This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
Its cessation is attained by the noble ones;
this is the noble truth of the path.
The non-analytical unconditioned is not the truth of cessation;
it is the attainment of the truths of suffering and its origin.
The cessation of impermanence is subsumed within the three truths of suffering, its origin, and the path;
attainment is likewise so.
There are some differences;
such is their meaning.
Fifth, they are distinguished according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
"Nature" refers to dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
There are five distinct meanings [for this term].
The first is the analysis according to their essential substance (*svabhāva*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is exclusively wholesome; the other two are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
These two are further distinguished in relation to persons.
That which is conducive and beneficial is called "wholesome" (kuśala); that which is contrary and harmful is termed "unwholesome" (akuśala).
That which neither harms nor benefits is [neutral].
It is described as indeterminate (avyākṛta).
According to this principle, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is exclusively wholesome (kuśala).
Because it is conducive and beneficial,
space is unconditioned and exclusively indeterminate.
Because it is neither diminished nor increased, it is not a non-analytical unconditioned (apratisaṃkhyā-nirvāṇa).
Its meaning accords with the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The suffering retributions of the three miserable realms that are not subject to analytical cessation possess the quality of being conducive to benefit; thus,
by way of definition, they are called "wholesome."
A future pleasant fruit that is not through analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) possesses the sense of being contrary and harmful; thus,
by definition, it is called "unwholesome" (akuśala).
The others are neither beneficial nor harmful;
in meaning, they are explained as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thirdly, there is the analytical distinction according to principle.
That which accords with principle is called good;
that which opposes principle is called evil;
that which neither opposes nor accords is [neither].
It is described as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
From this perspective, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
Because it is established by being free from characteristics and in accordance with principle;
the other two are neutral because they are neither contrary nor in accordance [with principle].
Fourth, the analysis by way of causes:
that which is obtained through wholesome causes is termed "wholesome."
That which is acquired through unwholesome causes is called "unwholesome";
it is not acquired through the two types of causes, namely the adverse or the favorable.
It is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
From this perspective, the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) [is also indeterminate].
It is exclusively wholesome,
because it is obtained through wholesome causes;
it is unconditioned space.
It is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because it is not obtained through the two causes of good or evil;
it is not a non-analytical unconditioned (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirvāṇa*).
Its meaning applies to all three natures because it includes precepts, generosity, and so forth;
it prevents evil from arising.
It is called "wholesome" [only in name],
because such wrong views and the like prevent the arising of true goodness.
These are designated as "unwholesome" (akuśala);
the remainder are designated as "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
This is the fifth classification according to their fruits.
That which can produce pleasant retribution is called "wholesome" (kuśala);
that which produces suffering is called "unwholesome" (akuśala).
The remainder are termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
According to this principle, the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) [are also indeterminate].
Both are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because they do not act as causes for arising and yet result in the attainment of fruit. This is the sixth [section]:
the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The term "outflow" (āsrava) has four meanings.
First, because its substance is outflowing,
it is called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
The remainder are called untainted (*anāsrava*).
According to this principle, the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) [are also untainted].
All of these are untainted (anāsrava),
because their essence is not tainted and because they consist in the attainment of the abandonment of taints.
That which is so named is called "without outflows" (anāsrava); the remainder is called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
If one follows this meaning:
The cessation of all numerical categories is its state of being without outflows;
all others are with outflows.
The third is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava) because it is realized through outflow-free knowledge;
all others are with-outflow (sāsrava).
According to this principle,
space is not a [conditioned] number and is exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
The cessation through deliberation is not fixed;

Next, we shall distinguish the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) with respect to what has not yet come to be.
The schools differ in their tenets.

Third, there are dharmas that ought to arise in the future,
which [do not arise] due to the power of other conditions.
Causing it not to arise is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Non-existence that has not yet occurred is subsumed under the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The first is that which, being about to arise, is caused not to arise.
This very non-existence is subsumed within space. Second,
when something is about to arise, one causes it not to arise by means of the power of the Path.
This is comprised within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Third, when other conditions arise that prevent something from arising,
this is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
this "non-existence of what has not yet come to be" is identical to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*; thus ends the discussion on what has not yet come to be.
Next, regarding the mutual absence [of these factors], the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are distinguished;
their doctrinal tenets differ.
Within the *Abhidharma* tradition:
Among conditioned phenomena, there is no other dharma existing apart from one another;
according to the point of reference,
they are subsumed under the category of the conditioned.
The three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) do not mutually possess one another;
they are also subsumed under the same categories as their respective points of exposition.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is held that among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), the mutual absence of one thing within another is subsumed under space (*ākāśa*).
Because conditioned phenomena do not include the unconditioned,
and because among the three types of unconditioned phenomena there is no mutual exclusion of one another,
their definitions are not fixed.
If within space there are no other phenomena mutually present,
it is subsumed under space.
Regarding the mutual absence of other dharmas within cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), its meaning comprises two aspects:
first, looking toward the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth that are to be ceased; [second, looking toward the cessation itself].
Because it is taught that they are mutually non-existent,
this is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); it is precisely this non-existence that is correctly taught as analytical cessation.
Therefore, when these two are compared with other dharmas to distinguish their mutual absence,
they are subsumed under space (*ākāśa*);
for it is not that those [other] dharmas do not exist, as they are [merely] non-existence through calculation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there is no mutual absence of other dharmas above it;
its meaning also encompasses both aspects.
First, one should discern mutual absence by observing that which is ceased.
It is not subsumed under analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the very absence of that dharma constitutes analytical cessation.

The commentary states:
Regarding the superior analysis of mutual non-existence, there is a statement that [something] exists while [another] is said to be non-existent.

In the Mahāyāna teachings, however...

All these are cessations through calculation. Question:

Next, we shall distinguish the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) according to their ultimate nature, as the tenets of the various schools differ.

Why, then, do you now say they are absolutely non-existent?
The explanation states:
There is another interpretation: if one considers it in relation to other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), such as arising, abiding,
and ceasing, it is said to be non-existent.
These do not include one another.
If one speaks of the essence of space, non-analytical cessation, and analytical cessation as being without arising and so forth,
these are absolute non-existents.
Just as a rabbit lacks the horns found on cattle, oxen, and so forth—
this is their mutual non-existence—
the rabbit itself lacks horns.
This is ultimately non-existent.
If one speaks of the ultimate in terms of the principle of truth (satya), it is as follows.
The absence of a self, persons, and so forth,
is subsumed under the principle of truth and is what is taught in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Matters such as "turtles have no hair" are non-entities;
they are subsumed under space (*ākāśa*).
The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are themselves their own intrinsic natures.
Ultimately, that which is without arising, abiding,
and so forth, is itself subsumed within those three unconditioned phenomena among all dharmas.
Ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature,
it is subsumed within the ultimate truth;
within that ultimate truth...
One should know that the ultimate absence of all signs is likewise subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
if one considers it from the perspective of worldly convention, space is not a number and is said to be ultimately non-existent.
It is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
If one speaks of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) with respect to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
it is also subsumed under cessation through deliberation.
Regarding the distinctions therein:
the coarse aspects are the same as those of the Hīnayāna,
while the subtle aspects differ.
What is the difference?
Because the followers of the Hīnayāna have not yet realized that all phenomena are ultimately quiescent,
they do not achieve nirvāṇa within nirvāṇa.
However, while there is no arising, abiding, or ceasing with intrinsic nature,
one cannot ultimately be without all characteristics within the Mahāyāna teachings.
Seeing that all phenomena are ultimately quiescent, one thereby accomplishes nirvāṇa;
therefore, within nirvāṇa,
there is ultimately no manifestation of any worldly characteristics.
Therefore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"Worldly phenomena and nirvāṇa are ultimately not in opposition."
At the time of attaining nirvāṇa, outside of nirvāṇa,
there are no worldly phenomena that can oppose nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the cessation of enumeration is thus:
among all phenomena,
there is ultimately no intrinsic nature.
Ultimately signless, it is subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus far has this been explained.
Having completed this section by examining the four non-existences through the lens of the three non-existences,
we now proceed to examine the four non-existences through the lens of the three non-existences;
first, we shall examine the four non-existences through the lens of space (*ākāśa*).
The doctrinal systems differ.
In the Abhidharma system, space is an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
There are two types of non-inclusion:
first, mutual non-existence;
second, ultimate non-existence.
Within emptiness, there are no other phenomena such as form or mind;
this is their mutual non-existence.
The essence of emptiness is ultimately without arising, abiding, or ceasing.
This is ultimately non-existent.
Whether already existing or yet to exist—
these two types of non-existence [are likewise absent].
Space is not included [in the aggregates],
as explained in detail previously. This is established both in the *Tattvasiddhi* and in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the space that has been described,
it is entirely endowed with the four absences;
the meaning is as established above.
Next, the four types of non-existence are distinguished by means of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Within analytical cessation,
all three types of non-existence are fully subsumed.
This means that there is no ultimate mutual non-existence such that, in future lives,
defiled phenomena would not arise.
This is the non-existence of what has not yet arisen;
there are no other worldly matters.
This is their mutual non-existence.
This dharma of analytical cessation is ultimately without arising, abiding, or ceasing in its own nature;
it is absolutely non-existent,
even for dharmas that have already arisen.

It is said that because it cannot be extinguished, it already possesses the "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is not subsumed under enumeration; this non-analytical unconditioned also possesses the three absences,
identical to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), differing only in that it relies upon other conditions.
It is not that they differ in terms of the antidotes applied through the two paths of seeing and cultivation; rather,
the tenth [category] is distinguished by way of the Four Noble Truths.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path— these are the Four Noble Truths.
According to the Abhidharma:
The unconditioned nature of cessation through deliberation is not fixed;
it is sometimes subsumed within the Truth of Cessation, and at other times it is not.
There are four distinctions.
First, the analytical cessation obtained by the noble ones when their noble wisdom severs the fetters.
First, it is exclusively the truth of cessation.
Second, the noble ones' wisdom of equality abandons the fetters;
this is identical to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is attained through cultivation,
the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) that is thus obtained is also the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
Third, ordinary persons sever their fetters through mundane knowledge and attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
subsequently, they enter the Noble Path.
It is further the noble wisdom,
because it is that which is certified by realization;
it is also the truth of cessation.
What is meant by "sealing and verifying"?
There is a person who, while previously at the stage of an external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*),
used conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm.
Either having exhausted six grades,
or having exhausted nine grades,
one subsequently enters the path of seeing.
Upon reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*),
untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*) arises,
whereby one attains those unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) previously acquired during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This is called "seal of verification.
If, while still an ordinary person,
one has severed six grades [of afflictions].
By means of the wisdom comparable to the Ultimate Path, he did not realize the first fruit of a Srotāpanna,
but instead transcended to realize the second fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Regarding those who have previously severed the nine grades [of afflictions] while still an ordinary person:
upon reaching the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path,
they do not realize the fruits of *srotāpanna* or *sakṛdāgāmin*.
He directly realized the third fruit, that of a Non-returner (anāgāmin).
Why is it said only that he severed the fetters of the desire realm— either six or nine— as certified by noble wisdom, and not other categories?

The abandonment of the six grades and nine grades of fetters belonging to the desire realm constitutes the "Noble Seal" (āryamudrā), because it is the locus for the realization of the fruits [of the path];
the remainder are not such loci for the fruits.
For this reason, it is not sealed.
It is asked:
Since noble wisdom takes [phenomena] as its object, is the seal likewise an object, or is it not?
The commentary says:
It does not take [them] as an object. How is this known?
The path-comparison wisdom-mind takes the paths of the higher realms as its object and seals the non-existence of afflictions in the desire realm.
Thus, one knows that it does not take [them] as an object.
This concludes the third [section].
Fourth, at the time of being an ordinary person, conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) abandons the fetters.
Although one may attain cessation through deliberation,
one does not enter the noble path,
because it is not certified by noble wisdom.
It is not the truth of cessation; it is the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
whose essential nature is thus.
If it functions as an object,
it takes the three truths of suffering, origin, and the path as its objects;
thus one realizes nirvana.
Hearing that there is nirvana gives rise to suffering and distress;
therefore, it is the object of suffering (*duḥkha*). Due to conditions such as wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is the object of origination (*samudaya*).
Because it is the object of noble wisdom,
it can serve as the sphere of the Path;
space is not a numerical category.
Its essence is not the Four Noble Truths;
if it functions as an objective condition, it serves as an object for only two truths: Suffering and its Origin.
Since the cessation that is the object of the path is not the wisdom that takes cessation as its object,
it is not an object of cessation. Since the Truth of the Path does not take the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its objects,
it is not an object of the path.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna systems, the unconditioned state of cessation (*nirodha-asamskṛta*) is exclusively the essential substance of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
If it is taken as an object of cognition, it is the same as in the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā).
Space is not a number;
its essence is not the Four Noble Truths,
yet it can serve as the object for the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.
Those who possess pleasure find it a cause for affliction; therefore,
it constitutes the realm of suffering.

Because it is the condition for the arising of various views, greed, hatred, ignorance, and so forth, it is the object of the truth of origination (*samudaya*) in its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because it is destroyed [as such] and one enters into reality,
it is the object of the truth of the path (*mārga*).
This brief differentiation of the meaning of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) concludes here.
13. The Meaning of the Four Emptinesses (2): A Two-Gate Differentiation of the Characteristics of the Four Emptinesses. I. Subsuming the Characteristics. II. The Meaning of the Four Emptinesses.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
that which is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is a specific designation for the ultimate principle.
Because its principle transcends all marks,
it is called "emptiness. Emptiness is distinguished according to its various meanings.
It is difficult to set forth in full detail.
For now, based on a single approach, we shall discuss four types. What are these four?
First, the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena;
second, the emptiness of non-existent phenomena;
third, the emptiness of self-nature.
Fourth is the emptiness of other-phenomena (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Among these four, the first two eliminate the existence and non-existence of phenomena.
The latter two types refute emotional attachments to reveal the principle,
thereby establishing the first two gates.
Regarding the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*): it destroys the notion that phenomena possess intrinsic characteristics;
this applies to all conventional truths, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is called the general name "dharma-lakṣaṇa" (characteristics of phenomena). These characteristics of phenomena take non-existence as their dharma.
Dharmas are themselves non-dharmas;
therefore, they are called empty.
This is like the water of a mirage in the world, which is water though there is no water there.
Water is itself without water;
all phenomena are like this.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
Among all phenomena, that which is found to correspond with its own characteristic is called the emptiness of dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Question: The unconditioned emptiness of conventional truth (saṃvṛti) should be the second [emptiness],
the emptiness of non-existent dharmas (abhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā).
Now, why do you say that the characteristics of these dharmas are empty?
The explanation is:
that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That which is non-existent according to principle is also its existence;
therefore, this emptiness is called the "emptiness of dharmic characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
The conditioned and the unconditioned are called "existence";
they are devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
It is called "non-existence.
Question: Should the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not be called "non-existent"?
Why is it called "existent"?
Because this phenomenon lacks characteristics yet there is a distinction between "this" and "that," it is therefore termed "existent."
The emptiness of non-existence destroys the signlessness of phenomena;
the principle of all phenomena is empty.
That which is called "non-existence" (abhāva) is the essential nature of non-existence; this is called the characteristic of non-existence (abhāva-lakṣaṇa).
This absence of dharmic characteristics is established by way of negating existence;
it possesses no separate intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
For this reason, the Sūtra says:
"The characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Because it cannot be apprehended,
it is called the emptiness of the non-existence of dharmas. Question:
The Tathāgata has always taught the unconditioned dharma through non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing;
why then do you now say that it is empty of the characteristics of dharmas?
Nāgārjuna explains:
"In order to refute arising,
he proclaims non-arising."
Because it refutes abiding, non-abiding is proclaimed; because it refutes cessation,
[non-cessation is proclaimed].
It is taught that there is no cessation;
all these [terms] derive their names from the limits of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
It is called "empty" because it lacks a separate intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, it is said that causes and conditions are not non-existent phenomena.
To take this as "non-existence" is precisely because one takes what is not non-existent to be non-existent; thus,
non-existence is itself not non-existence.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
As for "the emptiness of its own nature," this clarifies that the dharma-nature of the two preceding types of emptiness is inherently quiescent.
It is not by means of wisdom that one forcibly contemplates [phenomena] to make them empty;
this is called the emptiness of self-nature (svabhāva-śūnyatā). That which is empty therein is the object of emptiness.
There are two kinds: first,
worldly nature, which refers to the solidity of earth, the moisture of water, and so forth.
The nature of the two types of noble beings refers to such things as the dharma-nature (dharmatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
These are the two dharma-natures.
All these are equally empty;
this is called the emptiness of self-nature and the emptiness of the nature of the world.
This is still the emptiness of dharmic characteristics mentioned previously; the emptiness of the nature of the Sage is likewise still that which was mentioned previously.
The emptiness of the marks of dharmas is already the aforementioned emptiness;
why then labor to state it again?
It is because worldly people claim that the first two kinds of emptiness are empty due to contemplation,
rather than being empty by their own nature;
it is to refute this view that [the Buddha] spoke of them again.
Regarding the emptiness of other dharmas (*itara-dharma-śūnyatā*):
there may be sentient beings who maintain that, apart from the *dharmatā* and the *bhūtakoṭi*, there exist further dharmas.
This is termed "other.
Now, in order to refute that [view],
it is clarified that there are no phenomena other than suchness and so forth.
This concludes the single section on the emptiness of other dharmas (*paradharma-śūnyatā*).
Next, the characteristics of subsumption will be analyzed regarding those eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Regarding these four kinds of emptiness,
there is no textual authority in the sūtras or śāstras concerning which characteristics they are subsumed under.
According to the principle of mutual inclusion,
the coarse [level] can also be known.
What are its characteristics?
Within the emptiness of dharmic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), eleven kinds of emptiness are subsumed, namely:

internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
By means of these eleven [categories], one equalizes them with emptiness and worldly phenomena;
therefore, they are subsumed within the emptiness of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*). Question:
Regarding the sixth, the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*):
it should be the second, the emptiness of the characteristics of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
For what reason is it subsumed within the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
The commentary states:
This emptiness is merely the emptiness of the unconditioned dharmas of conventional truth;
it is not an absence of principle.
Therefore, these are subsumed within the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*); there is no separate subsumption of the three types of emptiness.
That which is called the emptiness of emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate truth,
and the emptiness of non-existence.
Since these three types are equally non-existent according to the principle of emptiness,
they are therefore subsumed within the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
It encompasses only the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
This emptiness of intrinsic nature clarifies that the essential nature of all phenomena is inherently empty, not by the power of contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness of nature.
This meaning is identical to that of the "emptiness of self-dharmas" (svadharma-śūnyatā).
Consequently, it is subsumed within the emptiness of self-dharmas.
The preceding fifteen [factors] are subsumed according to their distinct characteristics,
while the remaining three are subsumed collectively.
Those phenomena are empty of their own characteristics; non-phenomena are empty of their own characteristics.
These two types of emptiness are subsumed together.
This refers to the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Within the emptiness of marks...
This clarifies that both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are empty. Regarding the emptiness of specific characteristics:
it clarifies that form (*rūpa*) and so forth are empty.
It is judged to belong within the first category: the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Within these, there are two types.
First, it clarifies that the common characteristics of suffering, impermanence, and so forth within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are empty and quiescent;
this emptiness is subsumed within the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Second, it clarifies the emptiness of the principle of common characteristics within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This emptiness is subsumed within the emptiness of the non-existence of phenomena (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Within that emptiness of both non-existent and existent phenomena, as for the emptiness of existent phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*):
This is the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Regarding the emptiness of non-existent phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*),
it is subsumed within the second [category], the emptiness of the characteristics of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Those phenomena are empty of their own characteristics and empty of other phenomena;
together they are subsumed within the single category of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility.
If one says that the self-characteristic of existing phenomena cannot be apprehended,

it is categorized under the first [type], the emptiness of dharmic characteristics; if one speaks of True Suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and so forth, they fall outside [the scope of those categories].
The atoms and the primordial nature (prakṛti) established by those with false views are all unfindable;
they are subsumed within the fourth emptiness, the emptiness of other-dharmas (parabhāva-śūnyatā).
The characteristics of inclusion are thus.
It is asked:
What is the relationship between these four and the eighteen emptinesses?
Since their essential nature is not different,
and the eighteen kinds of emptiness have already been explained in full detail,
why labor further to explain these four kinds of emptiness?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
There are generally four ways in which the Noble Ones teach the Dharma.
The first is to begin with a brief summary and conclude with a detailed exposition.
In order to explain the meaning,
[the teaching] is first extensive and later concise,
so that it may be easily received and maintained.
Third, brevity at the beginning and brevity at the end;
this is for those of sharp faculties.
Fourth, extensiveness at the beginning and extensiveness at the end.
Regarding those of dull faculties:
this is based on a single principle to distinguish between the sharp and the dull.
For those of sharp faculties who can understand with few words,
it is therefore taught in brief.
Those of dull faculties require many words before they attain realization; therefore,
it is explained extensively for their sake.
If it concerns many meanings and is for those of sharp faculties,
it is extensive both sequentially and simultaneously.
Because they are able to receive [the teaching],
for those of dull faculties,
both the beginning and the end are abbreviated.
Because they were unable to receive [the teaching],
that *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* was [abridged] for the sake of easy retention.
Having first extensively explained the eighteen kinds of emptiness,
he further explains the four kinds of emptiness;
the remaining [categories] are treated both extensively and concisely.
One may understand other cases by analogy with this.
This is a brief analysis of the meaning of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

14. The Meaning of the Four Upadeśas (2): An Exposition through Three Gates of Analysis. I. Explaining the Names. A. Opening and Closing; Broad and Concise. B. Detailed Explanation According to Each Particular. C. First: Explaining the Names.
There are four types of *udāna*.
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu-viniścaya-śāstra*,
"name" refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
All conditioned phenomena are suffering;
all dharmas are without self;
nirvana is tranquility and extinction.
That which arises through conditioned origination is termed "formations" (saṃskāra);
these formations flow on without constancy.
It is designated as "impermanence.
That which is oppressive and afflictive is called "suffering. The analysis of "formations" (saṃskāra) is the same as explained previously.
That which possesses its own intrinsic nature is called a dharma. Since dharmas lack an inherent, substantial nature,
they are said to be without self (anātman).
Why is it that while the first two [sections] speak of "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*),
the latter section speaks of "all phenomena" (*dharma*)?
It is because suffering and impermanence pertain exclusively to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is called "practice.
Since non-self pervades all dharmas,
one speaks of "all dharmas."
Nirvana is unconditioned;
its tranquility and detachment are called cessation (*nirodha*). As for *udāna*:
This is the language of China;
this is called a "seal" (mudrā).
Thus, it is said in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
The teachings that phenomena are impermanent, selfless, and that nirvana exists are called the Three Dharma Seals;
the *Tattvasiddhi* is likewise.
The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are firmly established;
that which signifies an unchanging meaning is called a "seal" (mudrā).
Such is the meaning of the term.
In the second section, the treatment is neither fixed as extensive nor concise;
it may encompass all phenomena in their entirety.
Taking these as one, it is called the single Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
which universally encompasses all that is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, as well as birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
They all enter therein;
therefore, the treatise states:
"One enters the great general characteristic contemplation of the dharma-realm."
Alternatively, they may be divided into two,
namely saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; by these,
all things are subsumed.
There is no dharma that is not subsumed [within this].
According to the Dharma, one distinguishes persons;
yet among these persons, there is likewise nothing that transcends the categories of ordinary being and sage.
Apart from ordinary beings and sages,
there is no third category that is neither sage nor ordinary being;
alternatively, one may further divide the dharmas.
These constitute three, namely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
the first is dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The second is false conceptualization (vikalpa),
and the third is called accomplishment (pariniṣpatti).
The former two constitute birth and death (saṃsāra).
The latter refers to nirvana;
within that cycle of birth and death,
there is no state of mind that transcends it.
Objects lack intrinsic nature;
because they arise from the gathering of conditions,
they are called "dependent origination."
When the inner mind is not true,
it is called deluded conceptualization;
this is the nature of nirvana.
Its essence is not empty or perishable;
its intrinsic nature is established as real,
and therefore it is called "established."
Alternatively, it may be divided into four,
namely these four gateways:
suffering, impermanence, and so forth, among the four [truths].
The first three are the phenomena of birth and death;
the last one is nirvana.
[The former] are impermanent and suffering.
Birth and death may be so;
the principle of non-self is universally applicable.
How, then, can they be said to be "birth and death"?
However, "self" and "non-self" are not fixed according to the Dharma;
in the sūtras, it is sometimes said that there is a self in saṃsāra and no self in nirvāṇa.
Some say that in nirvāṇa there is a self, while in saṃsāra there is no self;
others proclaim that both possess a self; and still others say that both are devoid of a self.
If one considers their actual nature,
there is a self in birth and death,
and no-self in nirvana.
Within the cycle of birth and death,
ordinary people engage in false conceptualization;
therefore, they speak of a "self."
Within nirvana, noble wisdom is free from grasping; therefore,
it is said to be selfless.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"All places of birth in the world arise from attachment to a self."
If one is free from attachment to a self,
then there is no place of birth;
this is according to the nature of phenomena.
In birth-and-death there is no self;
in nirvana there is a self.
Birth-and-death is empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, because it is not autonomous,
it is said to be non-self;
nirvāṇa is the reality.
Because it possesses the eight masteries,
it is said that there is a self.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The phenomena of birth and death are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
such is the nature of nirvana.
Regarding permanence, bliss, self, and purity:
according to the principle of emptiness,
both are devoid of self.
This is because all are phenomena that arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature. However,
if one discusses their ultimate reality,
both possess a self.
As it is said in the sutras:
"Regarding the twenty-five states of existence, is there a self or not?"
The Buddha said,
"There is a self.
This 'self' refers to the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*."
The Tathāgatagarbha is what is called Buddha-nature;
this is the sense in which there is a self within saṃsāra.
The Buddha-nature is the reality of nirvāṇa;
this is the sense in which nirvāṇa possesses a self.
It is stated thus now because it is based on a single gate.
To say that non-self constitutes birth and death is also acceptable;
among the four [truths], the first two are birth and death.
The latter refers to the single *nirvāṇa*.
The absence of self (*anātman*) applies universally;
this is indeed the principle of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*.
As in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, within the section concerning Kātyāyana,
the Dharma is divided into five aspects:
namely, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the quiescence of nirvāṇa.
From the aforementioned selflessness,
the gate of emptiness is distinguished;
this constitutes the fifth.
What is the difference between emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*), such that they constitute two distinct gateways?
This is as explained previously.
The sūtras and śāstras differ on this point.
In the Abhidharma, the aggregates (skandhas) lack the essence of a self.
It is called "non-self.
The aggregates (skandhas) are not mine;
they are described as empty.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
that which is the emptiness of sentient beings is designated as "emptiness."
The meaning of the emptiness of phenomena is explained as non-self;
as it says in the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, that which is the emptiness of sentient beings is called non-self.
That which is empty in its essential nature is explained as emptiness.
Now, based on the latter category, it is divided into two types;
thus, there are five [kinds of emptiness].
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra*,
it is also divided into five,
namely the so-called five dharmas.
First is name, second is appearance, third is false discrimination, fourth is correct wisdom, and fifth is suchness.
Among these five, the first three are the phenomena of birth and death.
The latter two types of nirvana are also acceptable;
the first three are dharmas of saṃsāra,
while the next one is nirvana.
The latter one is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
These five meanings are analyzed in detail within the subsequent chapter on the "Five Dharmas and Three Natures."
Furthermore, as in the "Skillful Means" chapter of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra,
the Dharma is divided into six aspects:
namely, birth-and-death, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity.
The Buddha-body is eternally abiding, which accords with the preceding six [meanings].
That the Buddha-body is eternally abiding is precisely the meaning of nirvāṇa as non-transmigration.
Furthermore, as in the sūtras, the dharmas are divided into eight.
There are four aspects of birth and death, namely:
suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
Nirvana has four aspects:
permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
alternatively, it may be divided into ten.
There are five aspects of birth and death:
suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
There are five aspects of nirvana.
It consists of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as existence.
Alternatively, it is divided into sixteen aspects,
with eight pertaining to nirvāṇa.
First, permanence; second, bliss; third, self; fourth, purity; fifth, truth; sixth, reality; seventh, goodness; eighth, existence.
Birth and death likewise consist of eight [aspects], which may be understood by reversing the preceding [eight].
If one wishes to analyze this extensively, it could even extend to the immeasurable;
however, for now, we shall rely on a single approach and discuss only four [categories].
In the third section,
based upon the preceding four sections,
the matter is explained in detail in successive order.
First, I shall explain impermanence.
There are three kinds of impermanence:
first, the impermanence of temporal segmentation.
Second, impermanence as the thought of non-eternality;
this is also called "for a short time.
Third, impermanence as the non-establishment of intrinsic nature.
Within this, I shall briefly analyze it by means of three sections:
first, explaining its name;
second, discerning its characteristics.
Third, regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles concerning the meanings of universality and limitation, existence and non-existence:
that which is called "segmented" refers to the causes and effects of the six realms of existence.
The differentiation of the three periods of time is called "segmentation.
Segmentation is not constant.
Therefore, it is said that all is impermanent.
To "mind impermanence" means that "minding" refers to mental attention.
The path of the mind is steep and swift;
one must believe that even within the duration of a single thought-moment,
the time for manifesting the Dharma arrives.
Therefore, it is called "mindfulness.
As it is said in the sūtras: "In the time of a finger-snap, the time of bending and extending the arm, or the time of a moment"—such are these expressions.
Relying upon their phenomenal characteristics,
the temporal divisions of the Dharma are revealed;
alternatively, they are described as a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) or a single instant (*tatkṣaṇa*), and so forth.
The mind is entrusted to the manifest,
precisely because conditioned arising and ceasing are difficult to perceive;
therefore, one relies upon form and mind to reveal their temporal divisions.
The meaning of "mindfulness" (smṛti) is as follows:
conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) shift and flow from moment to moment and are not permanent;
this is called mindfulness of impermanence (anitya-smṛti).
Regarding what is called "the lack of true establishment of intrinsic nature":
as for the two types mentioned previously, they undergo transformation and change throughout their preceding and succeeding states.
It destroys their mark of permanence;
this nature is impermanent.
It destroys their nature of permanence.

To clarify that the preceding stages of division and the dharmas of mindfulness are illusory transformations whose substantial nature lacks intrinsic reality is called "the non-establishment of nature.
Because they are not established, [they are empty].
It lacks a permanent nature;
therefore, it is called "impermanent.
Such is the meaning of the term.
What are its essential nature and characteristics?
Its essential nature and characteristics can be known as being characterized by the impermanence of disintegration.
As for those who contemplate impermanence:
conditioned phenomena, in the span of a single thought-moment, [are subject to change].
It possesses four characteristics:
first, arising; second, abiding; third, change at the end; and finally, cessation. These involve transformation and transition from the former to the latter.
Therefore, it is said that they are impermanent.
However, regarding these four characteristics,
the sūtras and śāstras differ.
As explained in the Abhidharma,
conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are by nature weak and inferior;
they cannot, of themselves, arise, abide, undergo change, or perish.
It must rely upon the simultaneous mutual interaction and transformation of the eight characteristics (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) in order to attain everything from initial birth to final cessation.
As for what are called the "eight characteristics":
Just as with a single moment of form,
there simultaneously exist the four primary characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation, as well as the four secondary characteristics.
These four secondary characteristics...
It is also called the "minor characteristic.
At the limit of that great arising,
there is a minor arising.
On one side of that great dwelling is a small dwelling;
on the other side of that great [dwelling] is another.
There is a slight difference:
where that [state] is the limit of great cessation, this is a minor cessation.
Thus, there are eight. However, these eight characteristics are named according to their capacity to act as causes.
Because it can produce others,
it is called "producing," and so on, up to "destroying others";
therefore, it is termed "destruction."
It is not meant that the arising of a phenomenon is called "birth," nor that its passing away is called "cessation.
If one discusses their essential nature:
Among the three categories of phenomena (*tri-skandha-dharma*),
it is subsumed under that which is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), namely the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding its numerical classification:
Within each of these,
there are the meanings of initial arising, subsequent abiding, final alteration, and ultimate cessation. Now,
regarding these eight types:
The essence and its nature are simultaneous,
yet their functioning is indeterminate; this refers to the functioning of their phenomenal characteristics.
The moments of striking and penetrating must coincide;
yet the application of the shifting method depends on the sequence of priority and posteriority.
When the great arising (mahābhūta) functions,
it can produce eight dharmas:
namely, the substantial entity of the characterized dharma (lakṣyadharma) and the other seven characteristics.
Taken together, these constitute eight.
These eight are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and possess the quality of being producible.
Therefore, Great Arising gives rise to that which is capable of arising;
as for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
they possess no sense of being produced.
Therefore, the "great arising" cannot arise;
it is precisely this "great arising."
It is also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and possesses the sense of being producible; therefore,
it is produced by that minor arising (*upapattibhava*).
The minor birth can only produce the major birth;
it does not produce other dharmas.
Such is the sequence.
Up until the time when the activity of great cessation arises,
it is able to extinguish the eight phenomena;
that is to say, it can extinguish the essence of the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya*) as well as the remaining seven characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
There are eight such penetrations.
These eight are conditioned;
they possess the quality of being subject to cessation.
That which can extinguish great extinction is itself great extinction;
it is also conditioned.
There is the sense of being capable of cessation;
therefore, it is in turn that which is extinguished by minor cessation.
Just as it is with form,
so it is with all conditioned phenomena;
they are all of this same nature.
Cessation and identity are characteristics that undergo transition;
only then do there arise the stages from initial birth to final extinction.
Such is the Abhidharma.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also speaks in this same way;
thus that sūtra says:
Conditioned phenomena possess the nature of arising;
therefore, arising can produce them.
Such is not the case for the phenomenon of space.
Because it is of the nature of non-arising, arising cannot produce it.
Furthermore, that sutra says:
Arising can give rise to dharmas,
but it cannot arise by itself.
Because it does not arise by itself, [it is empty].
Arising arises from arising;
arising does not arise by itself.
It arises again by depending upon arising.
This meaning is not extensively treated here as it is in the "Chapter on Non-association" (*Asaṃprayukta*) of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
That treatise proclaims:
"The arising of a dharma is called 'birth' (*jāti*)."
The cessation of phenomena is called "abiding";
the transition of phenomena is termed "change";
and the exhaustion of phenomena is named "extinction."
It is not taught that apart from dharmas there are separate characteristics or common characteristics undergoing transformation;
this same principle also applies within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Therefore, in that text, the notion of defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) as being established separately outside of the dharmas is extensively refuted;
each [of these points] constitutes the sacred teaching.
It is difficult to determine right from wrong.
Reflecting on the meaning of impermanence,
the coarse analogy is as follows.

What is called "the non-establishment of intrinsic nature" clarifies that when phenomena are simultaneous and of the same substance, their four characteristics and common characteristics are mutually sublated;
because there is no intrinsic nature of phenomena, it is called "impermanence."
What is the meaning of this?
Worldly phenomena are illusory and lack any fixed nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, characteristics have substance but no reality;
characteristics have names but no origination.
The essence is nameless and characterized by cessation; its marks have names and are subject to arising.
This is not the same as the arising that begins at a first point or emerges for the first time.
The extinction of the essence is called "extinction," which is not the same as the extinction of final dissolution where everything is reduced to ashes;
one should know that this refers to both arising and extinction.
This refers to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.
As it is said in the sutras:
"From the arising of ignorance, [all the way] up to old age and death."
This is the characteristic of arising:
from the cessation of ignorance up to old age and death.
This is the characteristic of cessation.
This arising and ceasing,
established by way of conventional designation like a magical illusion or a mirage, is what is called "abiding";
it is not the same as the abiding that persists and remains after having arisen.
Although that arising and ceasing and so forth share the same substance,
their nature and characteristics are mutually distinct.
Therefore, it is called "different.
Furthermore, it is also called "different" because it differs from the truly existent objects grasped by ordinary beings.
They differ from the subsequent decay and transformation of the state of abiding.
Such are the four characteristics;
they share a single ontological nature.
They are differentiated from one another according to their respective meanings; yet because they share the same essence,
they are said to abide, change, and perish.
Taking this as birth,
apart from abiding, change, and cessation,
there is no separate nature of birth.
Because it is of the nature of non-arising,
the nature of arising is not established;
thus, one speaks of these very dharmas of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Taking these as "abiding," there is no separate nature of abiding apart from arising and the other [characteristics].
Because there is no abiding nature,
an abiding nature is not established;
even to speak of those dharmas of arising, abiding, and change as being "destruction" [is untenable].
Therefore, apart from arising and so forth,
there is no separate nature of cessation;
for cessation lacks intrinsic nature.
The nature of cessation cannot be established.
Whether examined from the perspective of progression or regression, ultimately not a single nature can be found.
Therefore it is said that self-nature is not established as real.
Thus Vimalakīrti says:
"Neither arising nor ceasing."
This is the meaning of impermanence;
it truly lies herein.
This is what is taught in that sutra.
Arising and ceasing simultaneously;
neither arising nor ceasing.
Therefore, it is called "neither arising nor ceasing."
This does not mean that non-arising and non-ceasing are taught with reference to that single characteristic of emptiness.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"One does not know the reality that is beyond verbal expression."
There is arising and there is cessation;
contemplate the ineffable nature that all things are impermanent.
This passage also clarifies the meaning of the impermanence of nature.
A question is asked:
Impermanence is both coarse and subtle.
Arising and ceasing are coarse;
non-arising and non-ceasing are subtle.
Within suffering as well, there must likewise be both the coarse and the subtle.
One may say that being oppressed and afflicted constitutes coarse suffering;
is it not the case that being without oppression and without affliction constitutes subtle suffering?
The explanation says:
Furthermore, the meaning of affliction and coarse suffering can be understood;
yet this affliction remains in its essential nature, unimpaired.
It is not that nature is impermanent;
because it is not impermanent,
it is not called "nature as suffering."
Because it is not suffering by nature,
it is described as pleasure in conventional terms;
yet when observed in reality, it is not so.
The nature of oppression is non-oppression;
the nature of affliction is non-affliction;
its intrinsic nature is non-abiding.
This is what is called the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha) in its subtle intrinsic nature;
it is also called the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha) in its subtle accumulation of emptiness.
Such is its essential character.
Regarding the scope of these [categories],
among the three, the first two apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Within them,
the impermanence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-anityatā) exists in the Mahāyāna but not in the Hīnayāna.
Why is this so? Because sentient beings of the Hīnayāna have not yet understood the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Because it cannot destroy the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena,
it is not so described.
If the meaning of impermanence were to be distinguished through three gates:
Within the Hīnayāna, there are only the first two [aspects] and not the third;
within the suffering [of the truths], there are likewise three. Within the Hīnayāna...
It should also follow that there are two [types of suffering] which do not possess all three sufferings.
The commentary states:
"The dharma-gates are each distinct and different."
How can they be of one kind?
For instance, within the meaning of "selflessness," there are two distinct types of significance:
sentient beings of the Hīnayāna understand only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
How could it be that one might likewise attain the same as the three sufferings of the Hīnayāna, or equally realize the two kinds of selflessness?
There is no such principle in the meaning;
although we know they are not the same, [the distinction remains].
For what reason? If one were to explain it by way of general analysis,
suffering arises in dependence upon conditions.
Because its characteristics are coarse,
sentient beings of the Hīnayāna are fully able to understand and know it.
Therefore, within the Hīnayāna,
the three types of suffering are fully elucidated;
however, regarding impermanence:
The essential nature of phenomena undergoes transition and cessation; the meaning of this essential nature is subtle and difficult to discern.
Sentient beings of the Hīnayāna cannot investigate this thoroughly;
therefore, within the Hīnayāna...
The impermanence of the third nature is not clearly understood.
To discuss it separately,
this is the meaning of the three types of suffering.
The detailed exposition consists of three parts:
first, a classification according to conditions;
second, a classification according to conditions with respect to their essential nature.
Third, there is the analysis according to the three types of impermanence.
This meaning will be analyzed in detail later, within the section on "All Suffering.
As for the first two gates:
The characteristics are coarse and easy to understand;
the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is able to comprehend them.
As for the latter gate:
It is the same as impermanence.
Sentient beings of the Hīnayāna understand only the former two.
The subtle suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), which is an empty collection of intrinsic natures,
is not understood by the Hīnayāna;
therefore, within the Hīnayāna...
Not understanding that its own essence is a hollow accumulation, it is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"That which is known by wisdom within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as it has been taught."
Discrimination is suffering;
it has immeasurable varieties,
which are not understood by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
In that sutra, I did not speak of it at all;
its essential meaning is found right here.
The meaning of impermanence has been roughly illustrated in this manner; this concludes the first section.
Next, the meaning of suffering is to be analyzed.
The meaning of suffering is threefold:

namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). These three types of suffering are now to be analyzed.
Briefly, there are four gates:
first, the analysis according to conditions;
second, the analysis according to substance based on conditions.
Third, it is analyzed according to the three kinds of impermanence.
Fourth, the characteristics of its various faults are made manifest.
Regarding the phrase "in relation to conditions":
The conditions are distinguished as internal and external.
Internal refers to one's own mind;
external refers to conditions such as swords, staves, and so forth.
Within external [objects], there are again two types:
first, those that are adverse, and second, those that are favorable. Adverse refers to things such as swords and staves.
All instruments of suffering are categorized as follows: those that accord with one’s own person, life, wealth, and kin;
such are the specific conditions of suffering.
That which arises from adverse conditions is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
such as the conditions of swords, staves, and so forth.
That which can produce internal affliction is called suffering by virtue of its arising from such [affliction].
Suffering arises from suffering; therefore, it is called "the suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
It arises from those concordant conditions.
The arising of affliction due to separation from what is desired is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). When the internal mind engages with objects, [it experiences this].
This is called "volitional formations" (saṃskāra).
Dependent upon volitional formations, there arises disenchantment; through disenchantment with volitional formations, there arises suffering.
Therefore, it is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Second, regarding the distinction between the conditions and the substance:
the nature of the mind is suffering.
Based upon that suffering, one further adds the affliction of worldly affairs; thus,
suffering is added to suffering.
Therefore, it is called "the suffering of suffering.
Discussing it on this basis, the aforementioned three types of suffering [are subsumed herein].
Within this category, it is collectively termed "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), meaning that it refers to that which is suffering by its very nature.

Adding to the aforementioned suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), these are collectively termed the afflictions of phenomena (*vastuvyābādha*).
These are the conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because it arises and ceases moment by moment and is impermanent and subject to decay,
it is called the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha).
Precisely this conditioned flux is called "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Because the nature of formations is unstable, it is called the "suffering of formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding the distinction between the three types of impermanence:
with respect to the impermanence of the delimited periods of the three times,
the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is proclaimed.
The nature of the mind is suffering.
Upon this suffering, one further adds the coarse afflictions of the segmented continuity of the three periods of time.
This is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Furthermore, by means of the coarse suffering of the temporal divisions of the three periods,
the suffering of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-duḥkhatā*) is revealed.
It is also called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
With respect to the mindfulness of impermanence,
it is taught as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
That which was previously categorized as the two types of suffering within the second gate is,
in this present gate, collectively classified as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Regarding that very intrinsic nature, impermanence is not established;
thus, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is taught as being of the same substance as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
They arise together through mutual conditioning;
this is designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
These formations, being empty of collective arising, lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because its nature of conditioned activity lacks stability, it is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding what was said about the mutual illumination of the various faults:
there are three kinds of faults.
That is to say, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
To manifest suffering by means of suffering is called the "suffering of suffering" (duḥkha-duḥkhatā).

This demonstrates that the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is suffering by means of the suffering of the factual state (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). Because they are impermanent, they are suffering.
That which is called the suffering of change is suffering because of impermanence; that which is called the suffering of conditioned formations is suffering because of selflessness.
Because phenomena lack self-nature and arise through the empty convergence of causes and conditions, they are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
The meaning of suffering is thus explained; these two gates are concluded.
Next, the absence of self (*anātman*) is analyzed.
As stated in the treatise, there are two kinds of selflessness: first, the selflessness of persons;
[second, the selflessness of phenomena].
Second is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). These three gates have been fully and extensively analyzed as previously set forth in the chapter on selflessness.
Next, nirvāṇa will be examined.
As stated in the treatise,
there are two kinds of nirvāṇa:
first, that with remainder.
Second is "without remainder.
This meaning is fully explained as set forth in the Chapter on Nirvāṇa.
As for the meaning of nirvāṇa:
It is not merely the severance of the causes and effects of birth and death;
rather, its meaning as nirvana consists in being the antidote to the absence of a locus.
As it is said in the sutras:
"Phenomena are fundamentally not-arisen;
now they are also not-ceased."
This is the meaning of quiescence;
this is the meaning of the true reality of nirvāṇa.
Such is the destination of the four *upadhāna*s.

15. The Meaning of the Four *Siddhāntas* (2). The meaning of the four *siddhāntas* is explained through a fourfold analysis: 1. Defining and distinguishing their characteristics; 2. The meaning of their universal and particular scope; 3. The meaning of their mutual inclusion; 4. The meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The term 'siddhānta' is a word from the Central Kingdom (China)."
The meanings of these terms have been translated according to this region [of China], and their names are not uniform;
as it is stated in the sub-commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
It may be called the thesis (*pakṣa*),
or it may be called the proof (*sādhana*),
or it is said to be the principle (*yukti*).
Regarding what is called the "tenet" (siddhānta),
its explanation has two meanings:
first, defining the tenet in relation to the phenomena (dharma).
The Dharma gates are immeasurable,
yet the essential core resides herein; therefore,
it is proclaimed as the fundamental tenet.
Second, distinguishing the tenets in relation to the teachings.
Although the teachings are numerous and diverse,
the tenets ultimately converge upon the four categories, beginning with the world (*loka*).
Therefore, it is called a "tenet" (siddhānta).
Thus, that treatise states:
"There are four kinds of siddhāntas."
It comprehensively encompasses all twelve divisions of the sutras and the eighty-four thousand immeasurable treasuries of the Dharma;
all are true and without contradiction.
Judging by this text and looking toward the tenets of the teaching,
the meaning is not contradictory.
Therefore, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
Because it is the fundamental principle of all phenomena,
it is called "reason" (*yukti*).
The schools differ;
for now, they are divided into four types.
The first is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).
Second is the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the teaching for each individual);
third is the *pratipakṣasiddhānta* (the teaching of remedial counteraction); and fourth is the *paramārthasiddhānta* (the teaching of the ultimate truth).
Regarding the term "world" (*loka*),
as stated in the commentary on the treatise:
there are phenomena that exist by virtue of causes and conditions.
There is no separate intrinsic nature.
For example, just as the parts such as the axle, poles, spokes, and rim combine to form a chariot,
so too do the various dharmas of the five aggregates combine to form a person.
All such things exist because of the world;
this is the principle of the *loka-prasiddha-tattva* (the worldly standpoint).
What is meant by "teaching according to each individual" (*pudgala-vāda*)?
As stated in the commentary on the treatise:
the Buddha observes the differences and distinctions among people's minds and accordingly teaches the Dharma to them.
Regarding a single matter,
there may be cases where one listens or does not listen.

For example, when the Buddha addressed those sentient beings with nihilistic views who do not believe in the karmic fruits of good and evil in future lives and thus fall into the view of annihilationism.
He then speaks of mixed karma and the resulting mixed retribution for those who conceive of a self;
he then speaks of the absence of karma and the absence of one who receives retribution for those who do not so conceive.
Such matters as these are called the *puruṣa-pratipatti-siddhānta* (the established truth for the benefit of individuals).
