herein, only that which is contradictory with respect to arising is taken as the cause of contradiction.
"Non-contradictory" refers to phenomena that accord with one another and assist in the accomplishment of the preceding matter.
This is called non-contradiction of names. What is it?
If one discusses it separately:
After the tooth has grown,
the soil and water upon which it relies are not incompatible with it.
To explain this by way of analogy:
after seeds have been sown,
they depend upon the soil and water.
All are termed "non-contradictory.
These ten causes encompass and pervade all phenomena.
Now, for the time being, we shall proceed by means of the matter of causal seeds to manifest their characteristics.
Second, we shall clarify the ten causes that produce phenomena.
As stated in the treatise:
ten causes give rise to all dharmas—defiled, pure, and neutral.
First, the neutral [dharmas] are explained.
Within the indeterminate,
there is the internal and the external;
the external refers to non-sentient things.
The internal refers to sentient beings;
the ten causes within the external are explained as no different from those previously mentioned.
Within the internal [consciousness], there are four types:
first, that which is born of retribution;
second, that which pertains to deportment.
Third is the artifice;
fourth is the transformation. These constitute the single gateway of retribution-born [manifestation].
It arises from the cause of defilement and is subsumed under the category of defiled phenomena;
the remaining three types are likewise so.
This was not discussed in the treatise;
it is now appropriate to clarify it.
Regarding the mind capable of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*):
Within the sūtras and śāstras,
it is sometimes described as wholesome and sometimes designated as indeterminate.
Now, for the time being, let us proceed with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) [factors] to explain the characteristics of causes.
How are they designated?
Discourse, eloquence, majestic deportment, craftsmanship, and transformations are called the cause of conforming discourse (*anuvāda-hetu*),
because they involve that which is required and that which is to be accomplished.
The arising of these three matters is called "having causes" through the mind of skillful means.
Arising in dependence on conditions,
it is able to produce what follows;
this is called the "cause of planting seeds."
The initial expedient means that can produce what follows is called the "cause of production."
The causes subsumed under external dependent origination increase sequentially and gradually;
this is called the cause of growth.
When the arising of specific characteristics occurs,
it is called the "cause of its own seed" (*svabījanimitta*). This extends from the "cause of existence" (*astitvanimitta*) up to the "cause of its own seed."
That which is called the cause of common function is the opposite of this;
it is called the contrary cause.
Arising in accordance with [the object] without contradiction is called the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*).
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is likewise. This concludes this first section.
Regarding the causes of the phenomena of defilement,
as stated in the treatise:
they are the twelve links of dependent origination.
The differentiation according to the distinctions of words is called the cause of conventional expression (*vyavahāra-hetu*), because it possesses a cause.
There are three meanings of "explanation" (śeṣa).
First, it is explained by taking the twelve links of dependent origination as a whole and relating them to one another.
Because the preceding member exists,
the subsequent member arises;
this is called "having existence as its cause."
Second, distinguishing them in relation to cause and effect:
because there exists a causal factor with defects,
a present fruit arises.
Because there is a present cause,
the arising of future retribution occurs;
this is called "having a cause."
Third, regarding the predominance of rebirth through grasping:
it is taught that all rebirth within the three realms of existence is caused by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Only craving can cause the continuity of the various realms of existence;
for it is because of craving that existence persists."
The arising of all the links of existence is called "having existence as its cause";
this treatise relies on the latter explanation.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Through recollecting, relishing, and attachment,
the various links of existence arise."
"Existence" (bhava) is its name;
"taste" (rasa) is synonymous with craving (tṛṣṇā).
As for the "planting of the cause":
The term "releasing" (mokṣa) has two meanings.
First, it is distinguished in relation to karma and afflictions;
therein, karma constitutes the primary seed.
The afflictions act as conditions and aids;
the conjunction of these two is called the cause for planting seeds.
Second, distinguishing according to the relative distinction between the internal and external:
karma and afflictions serve as the seeds;
evil friends, false teachings, and the objects of the six sense-fields [serve as the conditions].
Taking this as a condition,
through the harmony of causes and conditions,
it is able to produce what follows.
This is called "planting.
Since the treatise relies on the latter explanation, it states:
The dharmas such as ignorance serve as the seeds for the present life;
their production of further births and deaths is termed the "cause of planting seeds."
Regarding the term "comprehending causes" (*hetu-saṃgraha*),
there are two ways of explaining it.
First, the distinction made by contrasting karma with afflictions (*kleśa*).
Karma is the primary seed;
the afflictions act as auxiliary conditions.
These are the conditions for the afflictions.
Moistening those karmic seeds and encompassing the subsequent fruits of birth is termed "encompassing the cause."
Second, regarding the distinction between the internal and external:
karma and afflictions together constitute the primary seed.
Taking evil friends, false teachings, and the objects of the six sense-fields as conditions,
they encompass ignorance and volitional formations.
Causing the subsequent fruit to arise is called "comprehending the cause" (*hetu-saṃgraha*).
This is because the treatise relies on the latter explanation.
The treatise states:
"In the present life,
one does not draw near to virtuous friends."
Not hearing the true Dharma,
they cultivate improper reflection,
whereby ignorance and the other [afflictions] arise.
These are called the "causes of grasping.
Evil friends and false teachings are like the water and soil [that nourish them].
Frequenting [such company] and listening to them,
one engages in improper reflection;
it is like the labor of a human being.
By virtue of this power,
ignorance causes formations to produce subsequent retribution;
therefore, they are called "ignorance and so forth."
The arising of these births all results from evil friends, false teachings, and improper reflection; therefore,
they are designated as the "appropriating causes."
Regarding the statement "the causes and effects of birth," there are two ways of explaining it. First,
by distinguishing between karma and afflictions in relation to one another.
Karma is the direct cause;
afflictions are the conditions.
The direct cause of karma is able to produce future results.
Therefore, it is called the cause of arising.
Second, regarding the distinction between the internal and the external:
both afflictions and karma together constitute the direct cause.
With evil friends and false teachings as conditions,
causes are able to produce effects.
Therefore, it is called the "cause of arising.
Regarding the latter explanation, the treatise states that the "causes of prolongation" refer to ignorance,
volitional formations, and so forth.
Gradually increasing,
it reaches the karmic retribution of birth and death in future worlds;
this is called the long-term cause.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"From ignorance up to renewed existence,
[the links] seek to increase."
That which leads to further births and deaths is called the "long-term cause.
This is based on the analogy of worldly cultivation and planting.
One should regard birth as the cause that leads toward aging and death;
however, the present author of the treatise [proceeds] from cause toward effect.
It is also called "long.
Why is this so? Because it is subsequently based on the internal mind.
The mind possesses the sense of gradually training toward the attainment of fruition;
because the sense of growth is manifest, it is said to "grow.
Those aforementioned external seeds are not mental phenomena.
There is no principle of gradual cultivation toward the fruit;
since its growth is not manifest,
it is not called "long."
If they mutually follow one another,
all will remain unharmed.
As for the cause of its own seed:
The seeds of the six realms of existence,
which produce their respective fruits, are called "causes of their own kind.
Therefore, the treatise states:
The arising from the various respective seeds, such as ignorance and so forth, is termed "one's own seed.
Because the causes for the six realms are distinct, it is said to be "respective.
Within each of those respective causes:
All [subsequent] fruits and retributions arise from ignorance, formative forces, and so forth; therefore,
it is said that they are produced by ignorance and the other factors.
Regarding the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*):
from "existence" (*bhava*) down to its own seed (*svabīja*),
these collectively constitute a single matter of causal conditions.
Therefore, it is called "common activity.
As for the cause according to the explanation,
it merely differentiates phenomena.
Because they cannot grow [together], they are not said to be "shared.
As for the contrary cause, it refers to the untainted factors of the path (*anāsrava-mārga-pakṣya*).
That which can oppose defiled phenomena is called a "contradictory cause" (*virodhahetu*). That which does not so oppose is [a non-contradictory cause].
This was brought forward because of the previous correspondence with factors such as existence;
thus concludes the two sections on the causes of defilement.
Next, the causes of purification are distinguished.
As stated in the treatise:
from the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to nirvāṇa,
because they are explained according to their respective designations, they are called "causes of designation" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*).
Because there is birth and death,
one joyfully seeks pure dharmas;
this is called the cause of existence.
The cause of planting and cultivation refers to the wholesome dharmas accomplished within the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi),
which are like seeds.
A virtuous friend’s correct teaching is like water and earth;
it is the beginning of understanding and practice.
Relying on prior seeds and encountering conditions, one begins to practice,
which is able to produce subsequent [results].
This is called planting the causes for the growth of the seeds:
drawing near to virtuous friends and listening to and receiving the true Dharma.
That which is capable of encompassing and giving rise to the factors of the supramundane path is called the "encompassing cause" (*saṃgrahahetu*);
it refers to that which is cultivated prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
It can produce the supramundane, untainted factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) as their generative cause (*janana-hetu*).
As for the term "sustaining cause" (*ādhāra-hetu*):
If one compares it to the worldly practice of planting seeds,
from the first bhūmi upward,
it increases more and more.
Tending toward and conforming with bodhi is called the long-term cause; if it were of the same category as defiled phenomena, [it would not be so].
From the stage of the spiritual lineage onwards,
until the gradual increase leading to the fruit of Buddhahood,
all are termed causes of growth.
The seeds of the three vehicles,
which produce their respective fruits,
are called "causes consisting of their own seeds."
From the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to its own seed (*sva-bīja*),
these are called the "causes of shared activity" (*sādhāraṇa-kārya-hetu*), as they collectively accomplish the single task of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Therefore, defiled phenomena are contrary to purity and act as opposing causes;
pure conditions accord with purity and are non-contradictory.
Thus, the treatise states:
It is contrary to the characteristics of defiled phenomena and is the cause of pure phenomena;
it is contrary to pure phenomena.
This is the cause of defiled phenomena;
the arising of phenomena is thus.
The third [section] distinguishes [the causes] by reference to two types of causes.
Regarding the two causes,
as stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
the first is the cause of production (*janakahetu*).
Second, the causal condition of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*). That which is proximate and gives rise to the essence is called the generative cause (*janana-hetu*);
that which is remote and assists in its manifestation is called the causal condition of skillful means.
The two causes are thus.
Now, their characteristics will be clarified in contrast to the ten causes,
as explained in the treatise.
The seed in relation to the sprout is called the cause of arising;
the rest are called expedient means.
However, this does not mean that only the fourth among the ten causes— the productive cause— is taken as the productive cause.
Among the ten causes,
it is simply that the seed must be able to produce the sprout.
In meaning, all these belong to the cause of arising;
the rest are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Although this is the general characteristic, [the specific details follow].
This distinction remains difficult to understand;
it is now appropriate to clarify it.
Regarding external indeterminate [dharmas]:
Among the ten causes, the single "generating cause" (janaka-hetu) is exclusively a generating cause;
it is subsumed under the "explanatory cause" (nirdeśa-hetu), the "conducive cause" (anuloma-hetu), the "contradictory cause" (virodha-hetu), and the "non-contradictory cause" (avirodha-hetu).
These five causes are merely expedient means;
as for the "cause according with the teaching":
Because it is stated that distinct dharmas do not produce dharmas,
[the cause] is not a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
Since it is subsumed under external conditions (*bāhya-pratyaya*), it is not a productive cause.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
it is only after the sprout and stem have appeared that they are designated as "growing."
Therefore, it is not a productive cause (*janakahetu*). If one proceeds from the perspective of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
the explanation is not the same as this.
As for the contradictory cause (*viruddha-hetu*),
it is simply that which can extinguish a phenomenon and serves as the means (*upāya*) for that extinction.
Because it cannot produce a phenomenon,
it is not a cause of production.
As for "non-contradiction":
Since it is identical to the cause of grasping (*parigraha-hetu*), it is not a productive cause (*janana-hetu*).
As for the remaining four causes:
The meaning encompasses both aspects;
because within the cause, it encompasses both the contributing conditions and the primary cause.
Because there is a seed,
it causes the sprout to arise;
this is its cause of arising.
Because of the presence of soil and water,
the sprout is able to grow;
this constitutes the causal condition of skillful means.
In the context of planting causes,
this also applies to both conditions and direct causes,
as a seed is to a sprout.
This is the direct cause;
soil and water for the sprout are the contributory causes.
Within the cause of its own seed,
the seed [is said to be] the sprout;
thus it is called "its own seed."
It is judged to belong to the category of productive causes (*janakahetu*). With respect to things such as stems and leaves,
the seed is judged to belong to the category of instrumental causes (*upāyahetu*) in relation to them.
Because they are not produced by a biological parent;
among the causes for shared activity,
there are likewise these two causes.
Birth and the means [of its attainment] are identical in that they exist even down to their own seeds;
these collectively encompass all of them.
The section on shared activities concludes with this single gate.
Now, we shall proceed to the internal indeterminate causes and subsume them into two categories.
The single type of productive cause is exclusively a productive cause,
because it produces its own kind.
The four types— conformable causes, inclusive causes, contradictory causes, and non-contradictory causes—
are the causes of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*).
Because within the causal state there are both types of causes,
and because one initially gives rise to an indeterminate mind.
Because it can produce what follows,
it is judged to belong to the cause of production;
this is because external objects exist.
It can give rise to the mind;
this is the cause of skillful means within the process of planting seeds.
It also possesses two causes;
it is similar [to the previous case] because it exists within the long-term cause.
It fully encompasses two causes:
first, the seeds gradually increase,
giving rise to the initial modes of conduct, crafts, and transformations.
This is the cause of its arising;
the rest are termed "expedient means.
Within the cause of one's own seeds—
It also possesses two causes:
by means of the mind of skillful means,
it is compared to the initial postures, crafts, and transformations.
Because it speaks of its own seed;
such a self-seed is precisely the cause of production.
Subsequently, through the mastery of majestic deportment, skillful arts, and transformations,
one explains one's own lineage;
this constitutes the cause of skillful means.
Because they are not produced by a biological parent;
within the causes of shared activity,
they likewise possess both types of causes.
As before, by means of "possessing" up to "one's own seeds," these [factors] are collectively subsumed for the sake of a common purpose; thus concludes this pair of gateways.
Next, the causes of defilement are subsumed into two;
among the ten causes:
The cause of arising is its own seed;
these two causes are exclusively causes of arising.
Question: Previously,
among the indeterminate dharmas, it was stated that the cause of its own seed is also a productive cause (*janakahetu*).
It is also a causal condition through skillful means.
Why, then, is it here described as being only a generative cause? To explain:
There is a reason for this:
within indeterminate phenomena,
the seed is considered in relation to the sprout.
This is also its own seed;
in relation to other stalks and so forth,
it is exclusively its own seed.
Yet it is not the cause of arising;
therefore, it possesses both meanings.
Now, within this defilement, there are fetters and karma.
From birth up to old age and death,
all are one's own seeds and are entirely causes of birth;
therefore, one's own seeds are exclusively the cause of birth.
Why is this so? Because the power of the defiled dharmas is strong;
a single cause is capable of directly producing many fruits.
Therefore, it is expected that both [the indeterminate and the wholesome] are causes for birth; however,
because the power of the indeterminate is weak,
a single type cannot directly produce many fruits.
Therefore, [factors] such as the sprout and so forth are not designated as causes of arising. If, however,
one were to maintain that within the defiled [process], [the factors] generally look toward old age and death as the cause of arising, [then...]
Why does the treatise state that the seed is called the "cause of production" (janakahetu) with respect to the sprout?
That statement is merely made from the perspective of the indeterminate (avyākṛta);
it is a conventional designation for the cause of inclusion (saṃgrahahetu), whether it be a cause of contradiction or a cause of non-contradiction.
These four types are exclusively skillful means;
their meaning is the same as explained previously.
Regarding the remaining four causes,
their meanings encompass both aspects.
Among these four causes:
The direct cause produces the fruit;
this constitutes the producing cause.
The conditional cause gives rise to the retribution.
All these are skillful means;
it is as if there were existence,
and as if there were the karma of fetters.
That which gives rise to a subsequent fruit is judged to belong to the cause of production,
because there are external conditions.
It arises as a subsequent retribution;
it is judged to belong to the stage of preparation (prayoga) within the planting of causes.
What is meant by "possessing both"?
As for the planting of the cause,
it is the conjunction of internal and external factors.
This is what is called "planting.
Within the process of planting,
one distinguishes the formation of karma that brings about future results.
That which produces [the result] is judged to belong to the cause of birth; that which produces the fruit through external conditions is judged to belong to the preparatory means.
Within the *Dīrgha-āgama*,
how are both [factors] present?
As stated in the treatise (*śāstra*).
From ignorance and formations up to old age and death,
they gradually increase;
this is called the cause of growth.
Within this process of the growth of the fruit produced in the present life,
the progression from cause to fruit is determined to belong to the producing cause (*janakahetu*).
Because causes themselves increase their fruits,
and because fruits themselves grow, they are categorized as belonging to the stage of expedient means (*upāya*). It is asked:
Why is it that the increase from cause to fruit is not considered a generative cause?
Because the cause increases by itself and the fruit grows by itself,
this process is designated as "expedient means" (*upāya*).
The commentary states:
There is a reason for this; a fruit arises from a cause.
Because the states of cause and effect are distinct,
and the characteristic of arising manifests as the cause ceases and the effect emerges,
it is called the "cause of arising."
The cause does not depend on the cause,
nor does the fruit depend on the fruit;
such a principle does not exist.
Therefore, it is not called "birth," but is merely called a "skillful means.
If one were to speak of birth in a general sense:
This principle is also unimpeachable.
Within the cause of shared activity,
how can both [aspects] be present?
If one were to further differentiate them,
they do not differ from [the categories] starting with "existence" up to "one's own seed";
these are collectively described as such.
Because they share a common objective, the defiled phenomena are thus [categorized]; this concludes the three gates.
Next, the causes of purification are subsumed.
Taking these as two,
among the ten causes, the single type known as the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) is exclusively a productive cause.
The inclusion of causes according to conventional discourse, whether they are contradictory or non-contradictory,
is merely a skillful means;
it is the inclusion of causes according to conventional discourse that is non-contradictory.
The means for its accomplishment are the causes of contradiction;
the means for its decline are the causes of regression.
As for the remaining five causes,
their meanings encompass both [aspects],
because within the category of "existence" (sat), they are included.
It penetrates both the internal and external,
for by virtue of possessing the seeds of the initial factors of the path,
it gives rise to the subsequent factors of the path.
It is judged to belong to the category of productive causes (*janaka-hetu*), because external conditions exist that are capable of producing the path to liberation.
It is judged to belong to the category of skillful means.
The same applies to planting;
it is the internal and external factors acting in harmony.
This is called "planting.
Within this process, that portion which takes up the seeds of the path capable of producing a subsequent result is determined to be the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
The appropriation of external conditions that can produce a subsequent [result] is called the "expedient means" (upāya) within the long-term causes.
Proceeding from the path toward the path,
gradually increasing therein—
this is the cause of its arising.
Increasing toward cessation is the causal condition for skillful means. Question:
For what reason is it that within defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*),
the movement from cause toward fruit is termed the "cause of arising" (*utpatti-hetu*),
whereas in pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*), the movement toward the fruit is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*)?
The commentary states: There is a reason for this;
the fruit of defiled phenomena is what is called birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Birth-and-death is conditioned;
because it is a phenomenon capable of arising,
one constantly tends toward it.
This is the cause of its arising and the fruit of pure dharmas, namely, nirvana.
Nirvāṇa is unconditioned;
it is not a dharma that can be produced.
Therefore, it increases through long-term causes.
Regarding that, it is merely termed a "skillful means. Question:
What was the cause of the previously mentioned defiled dharmas?
The mutual arising of causes and conditions is merely termed a "skillful means.
For what reason is the path that increases within purity said to be the "cause of production"?
The commentary states:
Defilements are coarse; proceeding from cause toward fruit, the characteristic of arising manifests.
Therefore, it is called the cause of arising (*utpatti-hetu*). This is because, in contrast to that coarse and manifest arising,
the cause arises as a causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), and thus the characteristic of arising itself is not manifest.
It is not called a cause of arising.
Pure dharmas proceed toward cessation through the subtle path;
they never lead to arising.
This is because it is directed toward that which is not a produced phenomenon (*anutpanna-dharma*).
Thus, the arising of the characteristics of the Path is proclaimed as the cause of production.
Within the context of its own seeds (*svabīja-hetu*), the Path is taught in relation to the Path itself as its own seed.
This is the cause of its arising.
With respect to the path and cessation,
it is taught as having its own seed.
This is the cause of skillful means.
Within the cause of common activity,
it likewise possesses two causes.
If one were to further analyze them, there is no difference from [the categories] ranging from "existence" (sattva) to "one's own seed" (svabīja).
These six are subsumed together as common factors; thus, the two causes are as described.
In the fourth section, the meaning of the complete inclusion of the six causes according to their characteristics is presented;
this is also analyzed in detail in the *Abhidharma-mahāmati-śāstra*.
What are the six names?
First is the cause of production (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
which refers to the time when a phenomenon arises.
The fact that all phenomena do not obstruct one another is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
This is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The first is called the unobstructed cause (*anāvaraṇa-hetu*).
The second is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
which refers to the time when various phenomena arise.
The principle of coexistence refers to phenomena such as arising, abiding, and ceasing that mutually assist one another in their formation;
this is termed the "coexistent cause" (sahabhū-hetu).
Third, the cause of its own kind (*sabhāga-hetu*):
all phenomena produce their own kind.
It is called the "self-cause" (*svabhāva-hetu*);
in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
it is called the "seed-of-itself cause" (*svabīja-hetu*).
Fourth is the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
The eleven pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that increase all defiled phenomena are called the pervasive cause.
What are the eleven?
The five views of the lower realm, doubt,
and ignorance constitute seven.
The four— namely, the two views [of self-identity and extremes], false view, adherence to views, doubt, and ignorance—
are added to the previous eleven, making fifteen in total.
Fifth is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
All minds and mental factors that associate with one another while apprehending an object are called the associated cause.
The previously mentioned co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) is established based on the nature of mutual dependence;
this is the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu).
Sixth is the cause of retribution: all karmas and afflictions. These are mutually dependent and functional.
The attainment of suffering and pleasure is termed the "retributive cause" (*vipāka-hetu*).
This meaning is explained in detail in the chapter on the six causes.
Now, [it is discussed] in relation to the ten causes.
They are subsumed by their common characteristics.
Among these, first, with respect to external indeterminate causes,
they are subsumed as six.
Among these ten,
with the exception of the contradictory cause, the remaining nine are subsumed within the three causes.
Among those remaining nine:
The inclusion of causes according to their description and their non-contradiction—
these three types are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). They are the generative cause (*janana-hetu*),
the developmental cause (*vṛddhi-hetu*), and the cause of its own seed (*svabīja-hetu*).
These three types are the causes of their own kind (*svabhāva-hetu*),
because they arise from their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as phenomena of the same class (*sabhāga-dharma*).
Because within the cause,
three types of causes are fully present:
first, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu).
Because there is soil and water,
sprouts, stalks, and so forth arise;
this is called the "cause of action within existence."
Second is the common cause (sādhāraṇa-hetu),
namely the four characteristics such as arising (jāti) and so forth within external matter,
which [act] upon that external matter.
Supporting one another so that the body stands is called the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Third is the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Because a preceding form gives rise to a subsequent form,
it is called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) among the planted causes.
It possesses two causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
These are the seed and that water and soil.
The coming together [of conditions] is called "planting.
In relation to the sprout and so forth,
the seed is its own specific cause (*svabhāva-hetu*).
The moisture of the soil and water;
looking toward those sprouts and so forth, these are called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
As for the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-hetu*):
There are three types:
namely, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), and the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu). If further analyzed:
From "not different" up to "because of its own seed," these six [factors] are subsumed as common causes; thus concludes this section.
Next, regarding the ten causes of the neutral internal dharmas:
The possession of characteristics functions as a subsumptive cause; it excludes contrary causes,
while the remaining nine causes apply to all other cases.
It is subsumed under four causes:
namely, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
What are their characteristics?
The "cause that accords with what is taught" (*yathā-vāda-saṃgrāhaka-hetu*) and the "non-contradictory cause" (*avirodha-hetu*): these three types are the "causes of activity" (*kāritra-hetu*).
The "cause of production" (*janana-hetu*) is a single type.
This is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because within the category of "existent causes," all four types of causes are fully present.
Because the six sense faculties and external objects exist,
an indeterminate mind arises;
this is the cause of its activity.
Because there are various mental factors and so forth that arise simultaneously and mutually assist one another in their accomplishment,
they constitute a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
That which arises earlier gives rise to what follows;
this is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all minds and mental factors.
The condition of association is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Among the causes of planting, it is included therein.
It fully encompasses both causes;
within the process of planting, it distinguishes that the seed is capable of producing what follows.
This is the self-nature cause (svabhāva-hetu).
Taking up the six sense faculties and external objects is the productive cause (kāraṇa-hetu).
Within the long-term cause,
there are likewise two causes:
those that arise from similar types.
This is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The successive succession of moments of mind is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
the same applies to their own seeds.
Within the cause of co-existent activity, there are four causes,
as previously stated: from "because it exists" up to "its own seed."
These six are subsumed together because they share a common function.
As for the contradictory cause (*virodhahetu*),
it acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) for the destruction of that phenomenon.
Because they are not dharmas that are retributive, they lack a cause of retribution;
because they are not defiled dharmas, they lack a pervasive cause. These three sections are concluded.
Next, we shall clarify their mutual inclusion by contrasting them with the causes of defilement.
Excluding those that are contradictory,
the remaining nine are subsumed under these six causes;
they are explained accordingly as being included within the causes and as being non-contradictory.
These three types are the efficient causes (*kārana-hetu*).
The productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) arises from its own seed;
this is its retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because within causes there exist six types of causes,
and because there exist faculties and objects.
The afflictions that give rise to karma are called the "causes of what is done" (kṛtakāraṇa),
such as the mind, mental factors, and so forth.
Supporting one another so that the body stands is called the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and suffering arise from one another as homogeneous types.
That which arises prior to another is called its "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because through its pervasive influence, it causes all defiled phenomena to increase.
This is the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
There are mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) that arise simultaneously,
which act as conditions through association (samprayoga).
It is called the cause of correspondence (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Because karma and afflictions produce their corresponding future fruits,
it is the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
Within the causal stage of planting,
both types of causes are fully subsumed:
namely, the retributive cause and the contributory cause.
This refers to karma and afflictions;
when they arise in the presence of conditions and are capable of producing future results,
this is termed "planting."
The planting of karma and afflictions therein gives rise to future fruits;
this is precisely the cause of retribution.
External conditions that produce a fruit are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Among the causes of growth, [this is included].
It possesses three causes:
the afflictions, karma, and suffering that increase within their respective categories are its own-part causes (*svabhāva-hetu*).
The afflictions increase,
giving rise to the karma of body and speech;
this is the cause of what is produced.
Karmic activity and afflictions increase the suffering of birth;
these are its causes of retribution.
As for the cause of co-existence (*sahabhū-hetu*),
it fully subsumes the six causes;
if one were to further differentiate them:
Because they are not different, up to and including their own seeds, these are collectively subsumed as common objects; thus concludes the section on these three gates.
Next, the characteristics are clarified through their inclusion within the causes of purity.
Excluding those that are contradictory,
the remaining nine are subsumed under these four causes;
they are explained as being included within the causes of "conducive" (*anuloma*) and "non-contradictory" (*aviruddha*).
This is the "cause of what is produced" (*kṛtaka-hetu*). Because within this cause,
all four causes are fully subsumed.
This refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
By relying on virtuous friends and the correct teaching of the Dharma,
one increases the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
This is the cause of what is produced.
Among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas),
the former arises before the latter.
Arising from causes of the same category is the cause of its own kind (*sabhāga-hetu*). At the same time,
it possesses both the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mārga*) and non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
This is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The associated mental factors (*citta-dharma*) that arise together with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) constitute the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Within the causal stage of planting,
there are two types of causes:
namely, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Among these cultivated seeds,
the initial factors of enlightenment arise in response to conditions.
This is called planting;
among these plantings, it is the foremost category of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
After being born as a similar type,
it is its own cause; when arising from a dissimilar type, it is its mutual cause.
This is the cause of its production;
through conditions such as virtuous friends,
it is able to arise in the future.
This is also that which is produced;
the causes of arising are not fixed within the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
The seeds of pure dharmas must be with-outflows (sāsrava),
for it is by means of these seeds that the supramundane, outflow-free (anāsrava) path is produced.
The arising of dissimilar types is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, this refers to the seeds of pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma-bīja*).
It must be untainted (anāsrava),
for it is by means of this seed that the path leading out [of suffering] arises;
they arise from one another as homogeneous types.
This is its own-nature cause (*svabhāva-hetu*).
Within the causes of duration, if there is a path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), [it is also its own-nature cause].
If it is the untainted path,
it increases within its own category;
this is its cause of its own kind.
If one proceeds from the contaminated toward the uncontaminated, or from the path toward cessation,
this is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Within the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is as follows:
The seeds of the Hīnayāna,
when compared to the path leading out [of saṃsāra] and when compared to nirvāṇa,
are said to be their own seeds.
When dissimilar categories are viewed in relation to one another,
these are the efficient causes (kāraṇa-hetu) for the seeds of the Mahāyāna.
Looking toward the path of transcendence,
one explains one's own category; thus, they are mutually related as being of the same kind.
This is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
In relation to nirvāṇa, it is described as its own seed;
this is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Within the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
all four causes are fully subsumed; namely,
the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
If one were to analyze them in detail,
they are not different from "existence" (*sat*) up to their own seeds (*svabīja*),
as these collectively subsume them for the sake of a common purpose.
Because it is not a defiled dharma,
it lacks a pervasive cause; because it is not a retributive dharma, [it lacks a homogeneous cause].
There is no cause for its retribution.
Fifth, it is distinguished by way of the four conditions,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichizhi).
What are the four conditions?
First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
second, the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Third is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
fourth is the sovereign condition (adhipati-pratyaya). Among the six causes:
The associated cause, the coexistent cause, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause,
and the retributive cause— these five types constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Within the causes that produce [an effect],
they are divided into three conditions;
this is with respect to the produced [effect].
The six sense objects give rise to the mind;
these constitute its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The mental factors follow in immediate succession.
The preceding [moment] lending itself to the succeeding one is the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
All other phenomena do not obstruct it.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This meaning is explained in detail in the chapter on the four conditions.
Now, these ten causes are collectively subsumed; therein,
first, the external indeterminate causes are subsumed as the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Among the ten causes,
with the exception of the contradictory cause,
there are the remaining nine causes.
It is subsumed under two conditions,
namely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among the nine [causes], three are causal factors (*hetu*).
These are exclusively subsumed under the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That is to say, they are subsumed under the "conformity-to-explanation" cause (*anuvāda-hetu*) and the "non-contradiction" cause (*avirodha-hetu*).
These three causes are exclusively subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
These are the generative cause (*janakahetu*), the developmental cause (*poṣakahetu*), and the specific-seed cause (*svabījhetu*).
This is because they are subsumed within the "own-part" (*svabhāga*) among the six causes;
the remaining three causes are excluded.

The second is that which is subsumed under conditions, namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the planting condition (*āvāpaka-pratyaya*), and the co-operative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). These eight may be seen within the causal condition:
by means of the presence of soil and water, the sprout is able to arise.
This is the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya),
for it is by virtue of the existence of the seed that the sprout is caused to arise.
This is the causal condition,
because it is comprised within one's own continuum;
it is planted within the cause.
The appropriation of the seed,
in relation to the arising of that sprout,
constitutes its causal condition.
Because it is appropriated by itself,
the soil and water that are taken up can produce a sprout;
this is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Within the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
there are likewise two conditions;
as before, these range from "because it exists" up to its own seed.
These are subsumed together for the sake of a common purpose.
As for the contradictory cause:
The aspiration to destroy those phenomena serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); this concludes one section.
Next, the ten causes of neutral internal phenomena are explained as the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
Among these ten, with the exception of the contradictory cause,
the remaining nine causes [are as follows].
It is subsumed under the four conditions.
As for the "cause according to designation," it is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Since the "cause with a basis" (sahetu) fully encompasses the four conditions,
one selects from among them the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu), the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), and the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
They are considered the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) give rise to the mind;
these are the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The six sense objects give rise to the mind;
these constitute its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The mental factors follow in succession.
That which arises after what has previously arisen is the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).
This is established within the context of planting the cause.
It fully encompasses the four conditions;
that which takes up the seeds and is able to produce subsequent [states] is its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because they are comprised within oneself,
the six sense organs give rise to the mind;
thus, they are the predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
External conditions give rise to the mind;
these are its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
From the initial planting of the seed, the subsequent mind arises in succession.
This is the sequential condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
It causes its own seeds to grow and develop,
fully encompassing both conditions.
The arising of similar types constitutes their causal condition;
they arise in successive order.
This is the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). It subsumes the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) without contradiction;
each possesses two conditions.
These are the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The six sense faculties give rise to the mind;
this is the dominant condition.
The six sense objects give rise to the mind;
these are its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
As for the common causal factors (sahakāri-hetu):
It fully encompasses the four conditions.
As before, by means of "existence" up to "one's own seeds," it collectively subsumes all of them.
Regarding the cause of contradiction, it is that which, with respect to those phenomena,
aims to destroy them for the sake of a common purpose.
This concludes the two gates concerning the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Next, the causes of defilement are subsumed under the four conditions.
Within these causes of defilement:
Furthermore, by excluding the contradictory [causes],
the remaining nine causes are subsumed within the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
The "cause according to description" is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
because it is that which possesses the cause.
It is subsumed within the four conditions;
because there are fetters and karma,
they are able to produce future results.
This is its causal condition:
because there is the preceding mind,
the succeeding mind arises.
This is the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya). Because the six sense objects exist,
the six consciousnesses arise.
This is their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
because there are the six sense faculties,
the six consciousnesses arise.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because of having evil friends who teach the Dharma erroneously and so forth,
one increases the fetters and karma.
That which arises as a subsequent result is also a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for the planting cause (*ropaṇa-hetu*):
It is subsumed under the four conditions.
The formation of results through fetters and karma constitutes its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The successive arising of moments of mind constitutes the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
One associates with evil friends.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Listening to and receiving false teachings is its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The productive cause arises from its own seed and is comprised of two conditions;
the retributive cause produces its fruit.
This is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That minds arise in succession from one another is the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
It is subsumed under two conditions: the cause of grasping and the non-contradictory cause.
It consists in associating with evil friends.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Listening to and receiving false teachings is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Within the long-term causes,
there are three conditions: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
From ignorance comes volitional formations;
these increase and produce fruits,
which constitute their causes and conditions.
Because they are subsumed under the cause of retribution: from cause arises cause,
and from fruit arises fruit.
This is also a causal condition,
because it is comprised within its own category;
thus, from ignorance up to birth-and-death.
The successive arising of mind-moments constitutes the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*). From afflictions, wholesome karma arises.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Within the cause of common activity (*sahabhū-hetu*),
all four conditions are fully subsumed.
If one were to analyze further,
all these [categories] are subsumed within the range from "existence" (sat) up to "one's own seed" (svabīja), without distinction.
Regarding the cause of contradiction for a shared purpose:
it is the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to the destruction of that phenomenon. These three gates are now concluded.
Next, the causes for purification are subsumed as four conditions,
excluding the contradictory cause.
The remaining nine causes are subsumed within the four conditions;
regarding these nine:
The "cause according to verbal designation" is the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya),
because it exists within the [category of] causes.
It fully encompasses the four conditions,
because the preceding path gives rise to the subsequent path.
This is the cause and condition:
because they are comprised within their own category,
there exist simultaneously the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
This is also a causal condition,
because it is subsumed under association;
it precedes that which arises later.
This is the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
Because there exists the dharma of the Path, the Path arises by taking it as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
This is its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
because there are virtuous friends who correctly teach the Dharma and so forth,
they gather sentient beings and lead them toward the Path.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Within the causal seed that is planted,
it fully encompasses all four conditions.
Within the context of cultivation,
one selects the very first category of the untainted path-factors (*anāsrava-mārga-pakṣya*),
which is capable of giving rise to those that follow.
This is the causal condition:
because it is comprised within one's own continuum,
the mind arises in relation to its object.
This is its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The six sense faculties giving rise to the mind constitute its dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The successive arising of mind-moments constitutes the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
It serves as the cause of production, the cause of growth, and the cause of its own seed.
It is subsumed by three conditions;
that similar types arise from one another is its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because it is comprised within oneself,
that which arises from a different category is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Within this path, the successive arising of mind-moments constitutes the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
The non-contradictory cause (aviruddha-hetu) is subsumed under two conditions: namely,
the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) and the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Associating with spiritual friends gives rise to the Path;
this is the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya). With the Dharma as its object-condition (ālambanapratyaya), the Path arises.
This is its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the "cause of shared activity" (*sahakāri-hetu*),
it fully encompasses the four conditions.
The same applies to the inclusion [of factors] up to their own seeds;
they are collectively subsumed for the sake of a common purpose.
As for the contradictory cause,
it acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to the destruction of that phenomenon.
The four conditions are thus.
Question: In the *Mukha-śāstra*, those ten causes are subsumed under the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*) and the "instrumental cause" (*upāya-hetu*).
These two causes are subsumed as two conditions.
As for the cause of production:
It is explained as the causal condition (*nidāna-pratyaya*).
The instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*) is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Now, why is it said that the four conditions (pratyaya) are fully subsumed within the ten causes (hetu)?
The commentary explains:
This determination was made by the author of the treatise because he considers those external phenomena produced by neutral (avyākṛta) causes.
If one considers internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*),
they likewise possess four conditions;
thus, that treatise states:
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) that is the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is subsumed under mental factors (caitta). Such are the four conditions.
This concludes the sixth section.
Regarding the classification by way of results:
if categorized according to the ten causes,
there are likewise ten results.
What are the ten fruits?
They correspond to the respective functions performed within the aforementioned causes.
Thus, the characteristics of the ten fruits can be clearly understood.
Furthermore, that treatise explains five fruits:
first, the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
Second is the fruit of retribution;
third is the fruit of the person;
fourth is the dominant fruit.
Regarding the five fruits of liberation,
as for what is called the "fruit of reliance" (niśraya-phala), it is as explained in the treatise.
The practice of good increases good;
the practice of evil increases evil.
In this way, all things arise from their own corresponding types.
This is called the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*). As for what is called the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*),
it refers to tainted (*sāsrava*) karma.
The suffering and pleasure that arise [therefrom] are called the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
As for the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*):
In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
it is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
"human" (*puruṣa*) refers to a person (*pudgala*).
Whatever actions a person undertakes,
all such matters are each successfully accomplished.
The fruits of a great man are called the twenty-two faculties;
these are termed "predominant."
Each has its own fruit that arises,
which is called the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
This explanation is made for the time being with reference to internal phenomena (*ādhyātmikadharma*).
Among external phenomena,
one should know that there is a predominant conditionality.
It is also called the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Through the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-mārga-pakṣa*),
one attains the realization of liberation.
This is called the fruit of liberation;
it is the mundane severance of fetters,
not their ultimate exhaustion.
It is not the fruit of liberation.
These are the five fruits;
now, in contrast to these fruits:
This clarifies what is obtained through causes.
Within this, first, regarding external indeterminate causes,
it clarifies the attainment of results.
Among the ten causes,
with the exception of the contradictory cause,
the remaining nine causes [are to be understood].
It is able to obtain three fruits, namely:
the fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
These correspondingly explain the causes of inclusion and the causes of non-contradiction.
These three causes obtain the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
because by having planted the seeds, one is able to obtain these three fruits.
That which takes up the seeds capable of producing a subsequent [result] obtains its *niśraya-phala* (supporting fruit).
That which takes up the water and soil capable of producing a subsequent [result]...
One obtains the predominant fruit (adhipatiphala),
shares in human effort,
and is able to accomplish external affairs.
This is called the fruit of a great man (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Through the causes of production, the causes of growth, and the cause of its own seed,
it is able to obtain the fruit of reliance (*adhipati-phala*).
Because phenomena of the same class arise from one another in succession,
they are the causes for their common activity.
It can produce the three fruits,
because it shares with them the possession of their own seeds up to the point of continuity,
and because it serves as a common basis for connecting with them.
Regarding the discordant cause (*visabhāga-hetu*):
with respect to the destruction of that dharma, it is its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*);
however, this [destruction] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it is not a retributive cause (vipāka-hetu),
it lacks a retributive fruit (vipāka-phala).
This is when viewed from the perspective of karmic activity (karma-saṃskāra).
It is described as the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support),
as explained later in the section on the two causes of defilement and purity;
this is because it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).
The section on the fruit of non-liberation concludes this first gate.
Next, regarding the ten internal causes of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
the attainment of the fruit is explained.
Excluding the contradictory cause,
the remaining nine causes are capable of producing the three results.
That is to say: the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
In accordance with these explanations, the causes of inclusion (*saṃgraha-hetu*) and non-contradiction (*avirodha-hetu*) obtain the sovereign fruit.
Because there are causes,
one is able to obtain the three fruits;
because there are the six sense faculties and external objects.
The arising of an indeterminate mind is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala),
because it is produced by a person.
This is the fruit of the person (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Because the former gives rise to the latter,
it is its fruit of reliance (*adhipatiphala*).
As for the planting of causes,
one is able to obtain three fruits;
they are identical in their existence.
The generative cause (*janakahetu*), the developmental cause (*poṣakahetu*), and the specific-seed cause (*svabījāhetu*) can obtain the fruit of support (*niśrayaphala*),
because they arise as similar types.
As for the cause of co-existent activity,
it also obtains three fruits;
as before, this is because [the cause] exists up to its own seed.
As for the contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*),
with respect to the destruction of that phenomenon,
it serves as the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
However, because this indeterminate [state] is not a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
it lacks a retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*); furthermore, because it is not untainted (*anāsrava*), it lacks such a fruit.
The section on the absence of the fruit of liberation concludes these two gates.
Next, the five fruits are explained in relation to the causes of defilement.
Within the causes of defilement:
Excluding those that are contradictory,
the remaining nine causes are capable of attaining the four fruits.
Excluding the fruit of liberation,
that which accords with the teaching of the cause obtains the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
Because they possess causes,
they are able to produce four fruits:
ignorance gives rise to volitional formations, and so forth.
The later arises based on the former,
thereby obtaining its fruit of support;
this is because there are karmas associated with fetters.
Because it can produce subsequent effects,
there is a retributive fruit;
for there exist sentient beings.
