first, in terms of its essential substance (*dravya*).
Arising from conditions is termed "formations" (saṃskāra).
Second, in terms of their functional capacity.
Because they give rise to subsequent results,
they are called "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*);
such is the meaning of the term.
What are its essential characteristics?
Within this, it is analyzed by means of seven categories.
First, analysis according to its nature.
Although conduct is immeasurable, it essentially consists only of good and evil;
thus, there are two types of karma: good and evil.
Because they are able to obtain retribution,
[the indeterminate] is without retribution; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Second, the classification according to possession,
which refers to all actions of body, speech, and mind. Third,
the classification according to fruit.
As stated in the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra),
these are what are called the immovable karmas of sin and merit,
as well as the evil karma of the three miserable realms.

That which is called "sin" refers to the unwholesome karma of beings within the realms of the desire realm. That which is called "merit" refers to the wholesome karma of humans and devas within the same desire realm.
The eight types of determinate karma within the two upper realms are called "immovable" (āniñjya).
They are distinguished according to four pairs of retributions.
That which is called suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure:
these are the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
Their karma is distinguished according to five bases.
This refers to those bound to the three realms.
When categorized according to time, there are six types:
namely, karma that ripens in the present life, karma that ripens in the next life, karma that ripens in subsequent lives, and indeterminate karma.
Seventh, the analysis according to secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). There are four distinct types of characteristics:
first, black; second, white; third, a mixture of black and white; and fourth, neither black nor white.
Among these four, the first three are the causes of contaminated, fragmented existence;
the last one is the cause of uncontaminated, transformational existence.
The activities of karma are immeasurable;
I have discussed them here only briefly.
A detailed analysis of these will be provided later within the section on the accumulation of karma.
What is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) has the meaning of discrimination.
Within that, there are three kinds of discrimination.
The seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*),
which exists from after the formation of karmic formations until before the actualization of rebirth.
Because it is perfumed and activated by karma and afflictions,
it is able to produce future results; therefore,
it is designated as the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, if discussed comprehensively,
all consciousness within ignorance and formations is also the link of consciousness.
Second is the consciousness seeking rebirth,
which exists in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Third is the consciousness of taking birth.
This is called the limb of consciousness (vijñāna-anga),
referring to the first moment of defiled mind at the time of taking birth.
Regarding the matter of the parents' semen, blood, and so forth,
delusive thoughts give rise to attachment toward things such as a lotus pond,
rather than giving rise to sexual desire.
Regarding the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*):
because the mind is designated by means of verbal expressions, it is called "name";
the physical body, characterized by material obstruction, is called "form."
It is designated as "form" (rūpa).
This is because mental phenomena (citta-dharma) are profound and obscure, making them difficult to manifest clearly.
Without expression, there is no discernment;
therefore, we designate things as "names" based on their expressions.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* says:
The four formless aggregates are designated as "name" (nāma) because they are proclaimed by means of names;
whereas the characteristic of form (rūpa) manifests as physical shape.
This can be directly perceived through the characteristics of name-and-form and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Discussing them collectively,
they are all name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
This is because, in this link, matter and mind are first fully present.
Because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is divided into distinct segments,
it is specifically termed a "limb" (aṅga).
As for the "six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana):
The place where consciousness arises is called an "entry" (āyatana).
These entries differ from one another.
There are six kinds of separations, namely:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These are preceded by the increase of form.
Now they constitute five bases (*āyatana*).
What was previously called the base of increase (*vṛddhyāyatana*) is now termed the mind base (*manāyatana*).
That which is called "contact" (sparśa) refers to the coming together with sensory objects;
this is designated as contact.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
contact (*sparśa*) is designated as perception (*saṃjñā*) with reference to the subsequent member of feeling (*vedanā*);
because it is the initial stage of the conventional designation of contact, it is called "contact."
According to the Abhidharma,
"contact" (sparśa) is defined as the factor of contact among the mental factors (caitasika-dharma). This factor of contact—
Based on the sense faculties and directed toward their objects, it causes the faculty and the object to come into mutual contact; therefore,
it is called "contact" (sparśa).
The same is taught in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
However, there are five types of contact (*sparśa*).
The first is designation-contact (*adhivacana-sparśa*).
This refers to the contact of the mental level (*manobhūmi*), which is capable of giving rise to mental factors (*dharma*).
Second is the contact with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*),
which refers to the contact associated with the five consciousnesses that comes into contact with present objects.
Therefore, it is called "with resistance.
Third is the contact of clarity,
which refers to untainted (anāsrava) contact.
Fourth is the contact of ignorance,
which refers to contact associated with the various afflictions.
Fifth is the neutral contact.
This refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) contacts.
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The sphere of the designation (*adhivacana*), the sphere of resistance (*pratigha*), and those of clarity (*vidyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the intermediate state."
Of these five, the first two are distinguished by way of their faculties;
the latter three [are distinguished] as follows.
They are distinguished according to their respective natures. These five types differ in scale;
what is taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle is not fixed.
If one takes the contact that results from retribution as the factor of contact,
then verbal contact, physical contact, and intermediate contact constitute this factor of contact.
The other two are not [the contact factor],
because clarity and ignorance are not resultant phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*).
If one were to say that all contaminated contacts (*sāsrava-sparśa*) constitute the contact factor, [it would be incorrect].
Excluding that contact of clarity, the remaining four are all [contact].
Contact of clarity is untainted (*anāsrava*);
therefore, it is not included.
What is taught in the Mahāyāna dharma is not fixed.
If one speaks of "segmented" [death],
it is the same as in the Hīnayāna.
If one speaks of the twelve links of dependent origination in terms of transformation,
all five types of contact are subsumed within the link of contact.
As for what is called "feeling":
Experiencing [an object] is called feeling (*vedanā*).
Within this, there are various classifications—detailed, abbreviated, or indefinite;
alternatively, they may be summarized into two categories.
Alternatively, it may be divided into two:
first, bodily sensation;
second, mental sensation.
That which is associated with the five consciousnesses is called bodily sensation; that which is associated with the mental consciousness is [mental sensation].
This is called mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*).
Alternatively, it is said to be threefold:
namely, suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Some speak of five feelings, namely:
suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
Others speak of six feelings.
This refers to the sensations (vedanā) produced within the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya).
Alternatively, eighteen are taught, because each of the six sense faculties is further divided into three types of sensation: painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Alternatively, thirty-six feelings are taught by dividing the preceding eighteen into defiled and pure categories;
or one hundred and eight are taught.
As Nāgārjuna has said,
the first thirty-six [factors] are divided according to the three periods of time;
thus, there are one hundred and eight.
As for what is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*):
it is the defilement toward an object that is named craving.
Within the present life, afflictions (*kleśa*) are not of a single kind.
For what reason is it specifically termed "craving"?
It is because future birth and death are drawn forth and produced by craving.
The power of craving is particularly strong;
therefore, it is explained specifically. Although only craving is mentioned, [it implies the other links as well].
The remaining fetters all follow along,
just as when a king comes or goes in the world, the rest of the multitude follows him;
herein lies the distinction.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, attachment to one's own body;
second, attachment to what is required.
There are five broad categories:
first, the arising of a desire to obtain and a craving for things that are agreeable but not yet acquired;
second, the arising of a craving to prevent the loss of things that are agreeable and already acquired.
Third, the arising of the craving for non-attainment toward objects that are disagreeable and not yet acquired;
fourth, the arising of the craving for abandonment toward objects that are disagreeable and already acquired;
fifth, the arising of neutral craving toward objects that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable.
Because it does not give rise to revulsion, as it is not extremely contrary to one's feelings.
What is called "grasping" (upādāna) is dominated by the preceding craving (tṛṣṇā).
Because one grasps and clings to sense objects, it is called "clinging" (upādāna).
To analyze it in detail,
there are four kinds of clinging.
First is attachment to precepts and rituals;
second is attachment to views;
third is attachment to sensual desires.
The fourth is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). These four types of doctrines differ;
according to the Abhidharma:
The mind that clings to precepts within the entire triple world is called the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). All views of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) within the entire triple world [are likewise so designated].

All dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) of the desire realm are collectively termed "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). All [afflictions] of the desire realm are collectively termed "clinging to desire" (*kāmayoga*).
The various dull afflictions within the two upper realms that arise taking one's own person as their object are collectively termed "clinging to self" (*ātma-grāha*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the single underlying tendency of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is called the grasping at the discourse of self (*ātmavādopādāna*).
In reality, there is no essence of a self;
it is merely attached to the name "self," and is therefore called "discourse on self" (ātmavāda).
Based on this view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), one gives rise to the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi),
grasping at either annihilationism or eternalism.
If one views [the self] as annihilated:
To be attached to the five desires is called "clinging to desire.
[They hold that] there is no future life.
Because they crave present pleasure,
if one perceives [the self] as permanent,
there are those who are sharp-witted and those who are dull-witted.
If one is of dull faculties,
they will grasp at and maintain the precepts with the hope of attaining happiness in future lives.
This is called the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
If one of sharp faculties reckons that the self (*ātman*) is eternal and that pleasure and pain do not change, then there would be neither sin nor merit.
Therefore, one gives rise to false views;
these are designated as "adherence to views.
According to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), however:
To speak directly, if the four types of clinging are taken as the member of clinging,
then all afflictions are fully subsumed.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The four types of grasping do not include the dull afflictions;
thus, the link of grasping (upādāna) universally includes the four graspings as well as all other dull afflictions.
As for what is called "existence" (bhava):
Present karma and its activities are capable of producing their corresponding fruits; therefore,
they are called "existence" (bhava).
Since this is karma,
why is it not called "karma," but rather "existence" (*bhava*)?
The future fruit does not yet exist;
it is said to "exist" only in terms of its functional capacity because it exists by virtue of karma.
As for its actual essence and characteristics:
It is the same as the link of becoming (*bhava*).
As for what is called "birth" (*jāti*),
it is said to be "birth" because the retribution of the future existence first arises.
The nature and characteristics of birth are the same as the consciousness that arises through sensation within the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As for what is called "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*):
The process of decay, transformation, exhaustion, and destruction is called old age and death;
it is the same as the preceding factors such as name-and-form and the six sense bases.
These twelve factors are mutually dependent and rely upon one another.
Therefore, it is called "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya).
As discussed regarding causal conditions within the context of the Four Noble Truths,
karma is that which can produce [results] directly.
It is said that [karma] is the cause,
while the afflictions are the remote assistance;
thus they are said to be the conditions.
This is not the case here;
do not inquire whether all afflictions, karma,
and suffering arise from the former to the latter.
This concludes the brief analysis of the names,
meanings, entities, and characteristics of causes and conditions.
In the second section, through opening and closing, expansion and abbreviation,
the characteristics of causes and conditions are clarified.
Such is the dharma of causes and conditions.
The extent of the exposition is not fixed,
as stated in the "Chapter on the Holy Life" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*;
sometimes it is taught as being one.
That is to say, the twelve links of dependent origination are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Alternatively, they are said to be twofold,
namely, the twelve links as solely causes and effects.
The past [factors] of ignorance and formations,
and the present [factors] of craving, grasping,
and becoming— these constitute the causal portion.
Present consciousness and so forth,
as well as future birth and death,
constitute its fruit-portion.
Alternatively, it is explained as threefold;
within this, there are three different gateways.
The first is the differentiation according to the three time periods.
Ignorance and formations refer to the past;
the link of consciousness is not fixed [to a specific time].
If one takes the seed-consciousness within the cause as the member of consciousness,
it belongs to the past.
If one takes the very first consciousness at the moment of rebirth as the constituent of consciousness (vijñāna-anga),
it belongs to the present.
If one says that the mind-consciousness which seeks birth is "consciousness," the meaning is not fixed.
In relation to its past causes,
it is described as being present; in relation to its present retribution, [it is described as being future].
It is said that [the factors] from name-and-form and the six sense bases up to contact and feeling belong exclusively to the present.
There are three types of craving and grasping;
their meanings are not fixed,
but when one discusses their essential nature:
Its arising occurs in the present;
it is judged to belong to the present when its functional power is considered.
It can possess its corresponding fruit;
since the cause follows from the fruit,
it is categorized as belonging to the future.
According to this teaching within the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, if it is so, then...
Why are past causes not determined as present based on their effects? To this,
it is explained:
There is a reason for this: once the arising [of an effect] has been determined by means of past causes and present effects, it is fixed.
Therefore, they differ according to the world;
they are not described as following one another.
The future does not yet exist.
Because it exists by virtue of causes,
it is therefore subsumed under the cause;
it is considered from the perspective of the fruit as yet to come.
The two links of birth and death definitely belong to the future.
This is the first analysis of the three periods of time.
The classification of the three and two paths is as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*: ignorance (*avidyā*),
craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
This is the path of afflictions.
The two links of volitional formations and consciousness constitute the path of karma.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death—
these seven factors are taught as the path of suffering.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping [are the remaining links].
All of these are afflictions.
For what reason is ignorance mentioned separately?
The manifestation of craving and grasping is evident;
this principle should be applied equally.
However, it is now distinguished for the sake of differentiating the three periods of time.
The mutual discussion of concealment and manifestation equally distributes [the dharmas] across the three periods of time;
this is not without its underlying reason.
There are two meanings to this explanation.
First, the distinction between the root and the branches: ignorance is the root.
Principle is manifested first;
this was taught in the past.
Craving and grasping are the secondary branches.
The principle will be discussed later;
for now, we shall explain it by distinguishing between the two types of strength and weakness.
The affliction of ignorance deludes one regarding the fundamental limit,
thereby establishing and accumulating birth and death.
The power and efficacy of these are strong;
this was taught in the past regarding craving and grasping.
It draws forth future existence;
its power is predominant,
and it is described in terms of the present.
The two factors of "volitional formations" (saṃskāra) are both equally karma.
For what reason is the name "volitional formation" specifically applied to those in the past?
The principle that they exist in the present should likewise apply to the other times;
it is merely for the sake of distinguishing the different names for the divisions of the three periods of time.
The three periods of time are equalized;
this is not without cause.
Within the past, that which has been accumulated and arisen is already determined.
The marks, names, and formations are present;
the future does not yet exist,
but it comes into being through karma.
Therefore, they are said to exist only in terms of their functional capacity.
The five fruits, such as consciousness, and the two retributions of birth and death are all equally suffering.
For what reason are consciousness and the other aggregates manifested,
yet birth and death have not yet been explained?
The principle should likewise be uniform;
it is only to distinguish the divisions of the world that different names for concealment and manifestation are employed.
The equal distribution across the three periods of time also has its reason: it is because the present retribution has already arisen and reached its conclusion.
Therefore, they are designated as "consciousness" and so forth with reference to their resultant essence;
as for the future, which has not yet arisen,
it is named by way of the past.
In order to cause beings to develop revulsion, the cycle of birth and death is taught.
This is the second [section]: the differentiation of the three paths and the differentiation of the three types of suffering.
As stated in the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*,
ignorance, formations, consciousness, and so forth up to the six sense bases are termed "suffering due to conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The two links of contact and feeling are called the suffering of suffering;
the remaining causal factors are called the suffering of change.
The three types of suffering are mutually pervasive. Why is this so?
Because, in principle, they are actually equally pervasive.
However, I shall now clarify how the two factors of contact and sensation manifest as dependent origination.
The nature of the mind is suffering;
upon that suffering, one further adds the afflictions of present circumstances.
Suffering upon suffering; therefore, it is called "the suffering of suffering.
Ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth arise in the present.
Because its meaning is manifest, it is called "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*).

Since the essence of conditioned formations is suffering, they are termed "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). This refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), and so forth.
They tend toward the future fruits of decay, such as birth, old age, and death.
Therefore it is called "disintegration.
The essence of disintegration is suffering; thus it is called the "suffering of disintegration" (vipariṇāma-duḥkha).
This has been discussed according to the coarse and subtle, or the manifest and hidden;
it does not exhaust the underlying principles.
This is a threefold classification by way of increasing numbers.
Alternatively, it is explained as fourfold,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
namely, ignorance, formations, birth, and old age and death.
Craving and grasping are subsumed within ignorance;
existence is subsumed within formations.
The five fruits, beginning with consciousness,
are subsumed within birth and death;
therefore, four are taught.
Alternatively, they are divided into five,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
namely, feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), and birth (*jāti*).
The five fruits beginning with consciousness are subsumed within sensation (*vedanā*);
ignorance (*avidyā*) is subsumed within craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
They enter into existence through action,
and they enter into birth through death;
therefore, five [aggregates] are taught.
Alternatively, it is explained as sixfold,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
namely, the causes and effects of the three periods of time.
Alternatively, it is explained as seven,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The rest is omitted for brevity.
Alternatively, they are said to be eight,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
That is to say, from consciousness through name-and-form up to existence:
ignorance is subsumed within craving and grasping,
while formations are subsumed within existence.
Since birth and death are subsumed within the links such as consciousness,
they are spoken of as only eight,
or sometimes as nine.
As stated in the *Nagaropama-sūtra*,
excluding the first three factors, it teaches the remaining nine;
alternatively, it teaches eleven.
As it was taught to Satyaka Nirgranthaputra:
setting aside the single dharma of birth, the remaining eleven were taught.
Satyaka Nirgranthaputra was born together with his sister.
The Buddha protected his intention and did not speak of the members of dependent origination; however,
at other times, he fully explained the twelve links of dependent origination.
The details are as explained in the sutra.
These variations in elaboration and brevity are thus according to the needs of those being transformed.
In the third section,
there is a classification according to time;
therein are six [categories].
1. Analysis according to the three times;
2. Analysis according to the three times;
3. Analysis according to two times.
Fourth, the analysis according to the sequence of before and after within a single lifetime;
fifth, the analysis according to simultaneous distinct entities;
sixth, the analysis according to simultaneous identical entities.
Regarding the "five lifetimes," as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
two branches are established for the past of the past.
As that sutra states:
"Afflictions arise from the causal conditions of afflictions";
this is the first [point].
Karma gives rise to afflictions; this is the second.
This clarifies the afflictions and karma within the past, the bygone eon.
Birth arises from the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) within its preceding past life.
Furthermore, two factors are established in that past life,
as stated in that sutra.
The arising of afflictions produces karma;
this is the first [link].
That is to say, it transcends ignorance.
Birth arises from the link of formations;
karma gives rise to suffering— these are the two.
This means that from past formations, five present fruits arise;
four members are established in the present,
as explained in that sutra.
The arising of suffering and afflictions is the first [of these].
This proceeds from the five present fruits.
Birth arises from the affliction of craving; this is the second [link].
From craving, grasping arises.
The arising of existence through the afflictions is the third;
from grasping, existence arises.
That there is suffering due to conditions is the fourth [link].
From the existing link (bhava), [arises birth].
It gives rise to future suffering.
Following that, in the future,
three members are established.
As stated in that sutra:
"Karma arises from the condition of karma"—
this is the first [point].
This refers to the mutual arising of karma and karma in future lives;
for example, bodily and vocal karma are produced from mental karma,
and karma gives rise to afflictions.
This is the second [type].
It refers to future karma,
which gives rise to the afflictions that lead to rebirth in the future.
The arising of afflictions leads to suffering;
this is the third [point].
That is to say, it refers to the afflictions from which one undergoes rebirth in the future.
Regarding birth in the future, within the future branch of arising (*jāti*),
only one branch is established in the future.
As that sutra says:
"Suffering arises conditioned by suffering"—
this is the first [point].
From that branch of birth arise old age, death, and so forth;
it is solely these twelve links of dependent origination across the three times that give rise to old age and death.
It should consist of two branches;
however, those [teachers] establish twelve branches based solely on the perspective of the causes and conditions that produce [the result].
Because one does not grasp at what is produced,
old age and death arise from the branch of birth;
this consists solely of the single branch of name-and-form.
The five periods are thus concluded in this first section.
Next, regarding the analysis by way of the three periods of time:
the essence of the dharma of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) extends throughout both the past and the future.
Now, judging according to the theory of the manifestation and concealment across the three periods of time:
all afflictions prior to the creation of karma in the past life are categorized as ignorance (*avidyā*).
The link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) is not fixed.
If one takes the seed-consciousness within the causal state as the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*),
then the link of volitional formations is short.
At the time of performing an action,
it is called the limb of volitional formations (saṃskāra); after the action has been performed, [it is called the limb of existence].
It is judged to belong to the *vijñāna* link.
If one takes the mind that seeks birth and the mind that undergoes birth as the *vijñāna* link,
[it would be incorrect].
The link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) is long;
from the time after one has performed an action until before death,
this belongs to the link of volitional formations.
The link of consciousness (vijñāna) is indeterminate.
If one speaks of the seed-consciousness as consciousness,
it exists from after the karma has been performed in the past until before death.
If one says that the mind-consciousness seeking birth is "consciousness," it abides in the intermediate state (antarābhava) where its destination is not yet fixed.
In relation to past causes,
it is called "present"; in relation to present effects, [it is called "past"].
If it is said to be past;
or if the very first consciousness at the moment of rebirth is taken as the member of consciousness (vijñāna-anga),
it necessarily belongs to the present.
The two links of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are not fixed in their temporal sequence.
If one takes the seed-consciousness within the causal state as the link of consciousness, [it belongs to the past].
The link of consciousness is long,
while the link of volitional formations is short;
this refers to the time when karma is being created.
It is designated as the link of volitional formations (saṃskāra).
From the time after karma has been performed until before birth is received,
it is classified as belonging to the link of consciousness (vijñāna).
If one takes the very first consciousness at the moment of rebirth as the link of consciousness,
then the link of formations would be too long.
The link of consciousness (vijñāna) is short;
the period from after the performance of karma until before rebirth is categorized as belonging to the link of formations (saṃskāra).
The very first moment of consciousness at the time of rebirth is categorized as belonging to the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Therefore, the treatise states:
Birth-existence (upapatti-bhava) and death-existence (maraṇa-bhava) should be known as a single moment.
As for the limb of name-and-form (nāmarūpa):

there is a slight trace of this shallow breath;

The stages of the fragmented [birth-and-death] are thus. Regarding the causes and conditions of the transformative [birth-and-death],
ordinary beings possess only the single link of ignorance.
Because the ground of abiding in ignorance has been established first,
persons of the two vehicles possess both ignorance and formative action.
Yet the retribution has not yet been experienced.
When will he experience it?
One who is not deluded regarding the Dharma.
Once this body has perished,
one will be born in a pure land and immediately receive [a new body].
Those of foolish nature will only receive it when the thought-mind arises after their parinirvāṇa in the future.
Among those in the Mahāyāna,
those at the stage of the Ten Abodes and above still possess ignorance and formative action;
those at the stage of the Spiritual Lineage and above undergo the fruits of birth and death.
It reaches its ultimate exhaustion only at Buddhahood.
Thus concludes this first section. Next, the arising and ceasing [of the mind] is explained.
First, we shall discuss the stage of birth-and-death with temporal limits (*paricchinna-bheda*). For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the causes and conditions for this stage arise and do not cease;
for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*), they seek its cessation and cannot learn to give rise to it.
For those of the Mahāyāna,
there is both cessation and arising: it ceases because they have severed [afflictions] for themselves,
and it arises because they transform others.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Nor does one ultimately extinguish conditioned phenomena,
for the sake of transforming sentient beings."
Next, we discuss transformation.
For ordinary beings, the causes and conditions for that transformation have neither arisen nor ceased.
The learning of the two vehicles arises but has not yet been extinguished.
It is asked:
"Can the two vehicles also extinguish wisdom and enter parinirvāṇa?"
How is it that they do not extinguish?
The explanation states:
although those of the two vehicles temporarily extinguish their wisdom, [it is not ultimate].
Because they will inevitably be reborn later and are not eternally extinguished,
they are not called "extinction."
Those of the Mahāyāna also arise and cease; they arise because they are beginners in their practice.
Because they reach their ultimate end, these two gates are extinguished.
Next, we shall distinguish dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by way of what is understood.
Within that dharma of dependent origination, ordinary worldlings—
When one perceives a self or a person, the twelve links of dependent origination arise even without the actual process of transmigration. Because a self exists,
the causal conditions that arise thereby become bound together.
This is called "what belongs to me.
Those of the Two Vehicles understand and know that there is no self and no person;
rather, it is merely the collective arising of various causes and conditions.
Because there is no self,
the phenomena of causes and conditions have nothing to which they are attached.
Therefore, it is not "mine. Those of the Mahāyāna deeply understand that dependent origination is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is free from the two extremes.
How is this meaning analyzed as being threefold?
First, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is clarified that they are neither existent nor non-existent.
The twelvefold chain of dependent origination arises from the gathering of conditions;
it is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is not existent,
because it arises from the gathering of conditions;
yet it cannot be said to be non-existent.
To see that phenomena are not existent is the contemplation of reversal;
to see that phenomena are not non-existent [is likewise].
This is its sequential contemplation.
The two characteristics are truly relative,
clarifying that they are neither existent nor non-existent.
The twelvefold chain of dependent origination arising from deluded perceptions is termed "characteristics," while that which serves as its basis is the ultimate truth.
It is taught as being real.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The twelve links of dependent origination."
All depend upon the one mind.
When appearances arise based on the emotional mind,
they are said to be "not non-existent."
According to reality, it is fundamentally quiescent;
thus it is said to be non-existent.
Seeing that it is non-existent in reality, [one realizes this].

This is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein the characteristics of understanding are not non-existent. This is the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Third, within the reality of the ultimate, there is a distinction between essence and function.
Ultimate truth is eternally quiescent;
since no conditions can be apprehended,
it is called "non-existent."
This very true consciousness,
following along with delusion, undergoes transmigration and gives rise to the twelve links of dependent origination.
It is said that they are not non-existent.
Furthermore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest their activities in accordance with the world;
these too are called "not non-existent."
To see that phenomena do not exist is the contemplation of their true nature;
to know that phenomena are not non-existent [is likewise].
This is the contemplation of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Regarding persons, it is thus.
In the eighth section:
Regarding the classification by way of knowledge,
the gateways of knowledge are not one.
For now, we shall proceed by means of those forty-four knowledges and seventy-seven knowledges.
To discern the characteristics of causes and conditions,
they are briefly analyzed herein by way of five gates.
First, the three contemplations are established;
second, the seven stages of expedient means are explained;
third, the meaning of those seven stages of expedient means is analyzed.
It clarifies the distinctions among the forty-four types of knowledge.
Fourthly, it clarifies the differences among the seventy-seven types of knowledge by means of the meanings of the three preceding modes of contemplation and the seven stages of expedient means.
Fifth, distinguishing the differences according to the person.
Regarding the "three contemplations," if one follows the *Abhidharma*:
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are explained as the three contemplations;
these contemplations reside within the stage of the foundations of mindfulness.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is explained that the contemplation of impermanence, non-self,
and suffering constitutes three distinct clarifications.
The four contemplations are contained within the four patiences of the present; this concludes that section.
Regarding the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), we shall first discuss them in terms of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the subsequent categories of phenomena,
what are these seven names?
The first is the contemplation of form (*rūpa*).
Second, observing the arising of form;
third, observing the cessation of form;
fourth, observing the path regarding form.
Fifth, contemplate the taste of form;
sixth, contemplate its faults;
seventh, contemplate the emergence from form.
As for "observing form," it means observing the retribution of form;
this is the contemplation of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
To contemplate the arising of form is to contemplate the causes and conditions of form;
this is the contemplation of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya). To contemplate the cessation of form is...

To contemplate the cessation of form as the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the contemplation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). To contemplate the path regarding form is [the contemplation of the Truth of the Path].
To contemplate form as its antidote is the path that is untainted;
this is the contemplation of the Truth of the Path.
To contemplate the gratification of form is—
To observe that prior forms can give rise to the flavor of attachment is to observe the faults of form;
to observe that prior forms can give rise to the fault of suffering is likewise to observe the faults of form.
Regarding the observation of the emergence of form:
one observes that the cessation of form leads to liberation from birth and death.
Why, then, is it not said that observing the arising of form constitutes the path?
The commentary states:
The path of arising is precisely the eighth, the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For this reason, it is not discussed [separately].
As it is with form,
so it is with all phenomena;
these seven serve as the skillful means for the contemplation of the ultimate truth.
These are called the stages of skillful means.
In what locations do these seven stages reside?
According to the Abhidharma,
the four preceding stages of application consist of the four types of receptivity to the present [truths] and the path of vision.
The latter three are situated within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, these seven gates belong to the stages of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī bhūmi*). These two gates are now concluded.
Next, the distinctions among the forty-four knowledges are explained.
These forty-four knowledges are as described in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
This is still the contemplation of the first four gates among the aforementioned seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*).
Because these four contemplations are applied to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*),
there are forty-four distinct types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
The twelve links of dependent origination arise sequentially,
forming eleven pairs of interconnected causes and effects.
Regarding these eleven:
Seeking the root from the end,
one traces it back in reverse order;
first, one establishes four [links] by correlating old age and death with birth.
First, contemplate the suffering of old age and death;
second, contemplate the origin of old age and death;
third, contemplate the cessation of old age and death.
Fourth, one contemplates the path of old age and death,
tracing it back in reverse order as far as the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*),
in contrast to the preceding ignorance (*avidyā*).
There are likewise these four:
namely, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of origination, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of the path leading to cessation.
This is in relation to ignorance as compared to what precedes it.
There is no further cause for accumulation;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
For what reason is there a reverse contemplation?
Having sought the cause by means of the fruit and practiced contemplation in accordance with the truths, these three gates are concluded.
Next, the distinctions among the seventy-seven knowledges are explained.
There are seventy-seven knowledges,
as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The treatise merely states:
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"In the present world, old age and death have birth as their condition;
they do not exist apart from birth as their condition."
The same applies to the past and the future.
This is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*). As for the contemplation of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*):
This is the wisdom of nirvāṇa.
In this same sequence, it applies to everything down to ignorance; all are exactly like this.
I shall not elaborate extensively,
as this has already been exhaustively analyzed through the various divergent interpretations of the masters regarding the essential nature and characteristics of this wisdom.
This is still subsumed under the second stage of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*),
namely the contemplation of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-vipaśyanā*), as well as the three contemplations beginning with impermanence (*anitya*). For what reason?
Among the seven stages of expedient means, this treatise focuses specifically on the contemplation of accumulation;
it takes the twelvefold dependent origination as its fundamental principle.
"Arising" (samudaya) has the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya); therefore, this is treated specifically [as such].
Within the contemplation of arising, there are sixty-six [subdivisions].
Within the three contemplations, there are eleven [aspects].
When these are combined with those [of the other two], there are seventy-seven in total;
of these, sixty-six are as previously stated.
To contemplate how causes produce effects and that they abide and are maintained without ceasing is called the knowledge of the persistence of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
The latter eleven [realizations] involve contemplating suffering, impermanence, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth,
and thus tending toward nirvana.
It is called the wisdom of nirvāṇa;
therefore, the treatise says:
"It increases birth and death."
Knowledge of the persistence of phenomena is called the wisdom of abiding in the Dharma; that which diminishes birth and death is called the wisdom of Nirvana.
What are their characteristics?
In the present world,
the twelve links of dependent origination arise in successive order.
The mutual connection between cause and effect consists of eleven pairs;
this is likewise true for the past and the future.
Thus, there are thirty-three pairs of causes and conditions.
Now, first, within those three periods of time, we shall examine the characteristics of the observation regarding birth as the condition for old age and death.
The other categories may be understood accordingly.
Within the present life, there are two types of contemplation on the accumulation of birth as the condition for aging and death.
First, aging and death have birth as their condition;
second, aging and death are not separate from having birth as their condition.
What is the difference between these two?
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "The former is correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*);
the latter is analytical contemplation (*pravicaya-darśana*)."
Why must this be examined?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
"The various non-Buddhist practitioners..."
There are many delusions regarding causes and conditions;
some say that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause of sentient beings,
while others say that Brahmā is the cause, and so forth.
The Buddha refuted this in order to demonstrate that cause produces effect as a reality that is not false;
thus he taught that within the present life, conditioned by birth, there arise aging and death.
Since these two exist,
the same applies to the past and future; thus,
they are divided into six.
These six contemplations on accumulation belong to the stages of hearing and reflection;
within the four patiences of the present,
they contemplate birth-conditions and old age and death across the three periods of time in their entirety.
One performs three kinds of contemplation, namely:
impermanence, suffering, and emptiness and non-self.
Although these three contemplations differ, [they are unified].
They share the same destination of nirvana;
taken together as one, it is called the knowledge of nirvana (nirvāṇa-jñāna).
Including this with the preceding ones,
there are a total of seven knowledges. Question:
For what reason, within the contemplation of origination (*samudaya*),
are the three periods of time divided into six,
whereas in the knowledge of *nirvāṇa* they are not?
The three periods of time are one.
The commentary states:
"Collectively observing that the observation of causes gives rise to effects."
The fruits of birth are not the same;
they are distinguished according to the world.
This is the wisdom of Nirvana.
Destroying the marks of birth and death,
one proceeds toward quiescence;
quiescence is equality.
The three periods of time are unified as one.
Within these three periods, there arise birth, old age, and death.
Since these seven factors exist, [the cycle continues].
Tracing back in reverse order, it is likewise for the conditionality of ignorance giving rise to volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*).
Within these eleven pairs,
there are seven types of knowledge in each.
Therefore, there are seventy-seven knowledges in total.
Question: Why does it not proceed from ignorance and formations all the way to old age and death?
First, within the law of dependent origination, there are two sequences, from old age and death back to ignorance and formations.
First is the direct order and second is the reverse order.
From beginning to end,
this is the sequential order.
From end to beginning is the reverse order;
there are many ways of contemplating phenomena.
It cannot be fixed as such;
furthermore, this is the method of contemplation for śrāvakas,
and śrāvakas possess dull faculties.
Seeking the root from the branches makes the contemplation easy to accomplish;
it is for this reason that it is so.
He asked again:
"The arising of phenomena through causes and conditions is inexhaustible;
with regard to old age and death, what follows after them?"
Why is the meaning of dependent origination not explained?
Because beyond old age and death,
there is nothing further that arises.
For this reason, it was not mentioned.
If that is so, why was it declared in the *Bhūmi-sūtra* that old age and death act as the cause for what follows?
The commentary states:
Old age and death further look toward the future;
thus, there is indeed the sense of a cause.
Because Bodhisattvas are able to see this, it is taught by them.
The seventy-seven knowledges of the Śrāvakas contemplate phenomena,
taking old age and death as their cause.
The śrāvakas do not perceive this;
therefore, it is not discussed here.
Furthermore, the śrāvakas also understand the subsequent meaning that old age and death are conditioned by birth.
For now, this has been stated based on only one portion;
therefore, the exposition of these four gates has not yet been concluded.
It shall be distinguished according to persons.
Discussing them collectively:
the forty-seven knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges arise identically for the three vehicles.
To discuss them individually:
the forty-four knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges are all methods of contemplative practice for śrāvakas.
According to the treatise,
among the śrāvakas there are those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties;
[for these] there are forty-four knowledges.
The contemplative practice of those of dull faculties consists of seventy-seven knowledges;
the contemplative practice of those of sharp faculties [is as follows].
Why is this so? Because the preceding forty-four [verses] contemplate the effect by means of the cause.
Because it is easy to accomplish through contemplation and can be practiced by those of dull faculties, it is said to be "for the dull.
There are seventy-seven knowledges.
Observing that causes produce effects,
one observes what is difficult to mature;
because it is only those capable of benefiting others who are fit for this, it is taught as being for the benefit of Bodhisattvas within these laws of causes and conditions.
The gateways of contemplation are boundless;
as detailed extensively in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*,
they cannot be fully distinguished here.
The meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) has been roughly explained in its general direction.

28. The Meaning of the Eighteen Emptinesses (4). The Meaning of the Eighteen Emptinesses is analyzed through three gates: first, their similarities and differences; second, the sequence of cultivation and entry; third, the first [gate], the analysis of their characteristics. First: Analysis of Characteristics.
The meaning of the eighteen kinds of emptiness is set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty and tranquil.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
This emptiness is the meaning of one gate within the gateway of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Although the individual gates differ, [they share this same essence].
The wondrous principle is empty and harmonious; its meaning is not absent from anything.
Because it is not absent from anything, there is no dharma that is not empty.
For this reason, the sutras sometimes speak of the emptiness of form,
even proceeding to proclaim the emptiness of all phenomena;
this is because there are no phenomena that are not empty.
Therefore, as they are distinguished according to their respective designations,
it is difficult to determine whether they are extensive or concise. For this reason, the sūtras sometimes speak of one, two, or even many.
As for what is called "one":
setting aside the discursive explanations,
emptiness is of a single flavor.
The single flavor of emptiness is wondrously transcendent of all marks;
therefore, it is called "one."
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of it as "sole emptiness" (*kevala-śūnyatā*).
"Sole" is another term for non-duality (*advaya*).
In other sūtras, emptiness is sometimes spoken of as being twofold.
These are what are called the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
Alternatively, they are said to be threefold:
namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Question: The gate of emptiness may be called "emptiness," but what of the signless and the wishless?
"What is meant by 'emptiness'?
Nāgārjuna explains:
"These three types are one in essence."
There is a differentiation according to the mode of practice.
When the practitioner contemplates emptiness as being without marks that can be grasped,
this is the gate of emptiness.
It is renamed "signlessness.
Within the contemplation of signlessness,
the arising [of phenomena] is found to be unattainable.
At that time, the signless (animitta) is further named the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra);
although the name has changed, [the essence remains the same].
Their essence is not different;
therefore, these three are all equally empty,
just like a single wisdom.
It is sometimes called the foundations of mindfulness, sometimes the right path,
and sometimes the factors of enlightenment.
It is sometimes called power,
sometimes called fearlessness,
and sometimes called unimpededness.
This is also like this.
In the sūtras, emptiness is sometimes further explained as fourfold,
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
First, the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena;
second, the emptiness of non-existent phenomena;
third, the emptiness of self-nature.
Fourth is the emptiness of other-dharmas (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*). This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed in the previous chapter on the four emptinesses.
Alternatively, it is taught as fivefold.
This refers to the emptiness of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Alternatively, it may be divided into six, namely:
the emptiness of the five aggregates and the emptiness of sentient beings (sattva-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on Practice and Response" (*Xiying pin*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,

emptiness is explained as sevenfold: namely, the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
These seven are none other than the final seven among the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
For what reason are these seven specifically taught?
The treatise itself explains:
Extensively, there are eighteen;
briefly, they are condensed into seven emptinesses.
This is analogous to the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga).
In its extensive form, it comprises the thirty-seven factors;
in its abbreviated form, it consists of only the seven factors of awakening. This case is likewise.
Because these seven types [of beings] bring great benefit to sentient beings,
they are specifically taught.
Regarding its essential nature and characteristics,
it is similar to the latter seven among the eighteen [dhātus].
Furthermore, as stated in the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*, space is enumerated as one of the ten [unconditioned phenomena].

That is to say: emptiness of belief, emptiness of nature, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the great ultimate, emptiness of conjunction, emptiness of arising, emptiness of non-discrimination according to reality, emptiness of non-abandonment, and the emptiness of detachment through non-detachment.
This is analyzed in detail in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages);
furthermore, the ten equalities mentioned in the sixth stage are also the ten emptinesses.
As stated in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
there are eleven kinds of emptiness; these are the eleven.
This has been explained in detail in the preceding chapter.
Furthermore, it is as stated in the "Praise of Purity" (*Śuklavidarśanā*) chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which speaks of the thirteen emptinesses (*trayodaśa-śūnyatā*).

That is to say: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, and the emptiness of characteristics.
Nevertheless, these are still the first thirteen of the eighteen kinds of emptiness;
if they were explained further,
they would not differ from those.
Question: For what reason are these [emptinesses] specifically mentioned among the eighteen emptinesses?
Setting aside the other five,
the treatise itself explains:
"These thirteen emptinesses."
Because it exhaustively refutes all phenomena,
it is explained specifically;
there are five other kinds of emptiness.
Emptiness is explained in its general characteristics;
there are no other distinct dharmas.
Therefore, they are not discussed separately.
Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on the Mutual Inclusion of the Six Perfections" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
there are fourteen kinds of emptiness; above the first thirteen emptinesses, [the fourteenth is taught].
Furthermore, there is one more type: the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
This constitutes fourteen [types of emptiness].
This is the emptiness of all things.
Among the eighteen [elements], the latter five emptinesses are collectively termed "all.
Question: [Why is this so?]
Why are these fourteen [emptinesses] taught and not eighteen?
The treatise itself explains:
"Among the fourteen emptinesses..."
All phenomena are empty; this encompasses all phenomena exhaustively. Even if there were any remaining forms of emptiness, they would be included herein.
All [factors] are included therein;
for this reason, only these fourteen are mentioned.
In some sutras, however, only eighteen are mentioned.

That is to say: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.
The names are thus; however,
these eighteen [elements] follow the distinctions of their designations.
This is not a matter of observing the sequence of shallow and deep entry.
As for what is called "internal emptiness" (adhyātma-śūnyatā),
it is as explained in the treatise:
The six sense bases, beginning with the eye,
are called "internal. Among these internal phenomena, [the following occurs].
It is called "empty" because it is devoid of self and what belongs to self, as well as being devoid of the eye and so forth.
As for the term "external emptiness":
As stated in the commentary on the treatise:
"The six sense bases, such as form and so forth,
are designated as 'external.'"
Within these external phenomena,
there is no self or what belongs to a self,
nor is there form and so forth.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
As for "internal and external emptiness," it refers to the general contemplation of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) mentioned previously.
The absence of self and what belongs to self,
as well as the absence of those phenomena,
is called internal and external emptiness (adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, regarding "internal and external" and so forth,
it is as explained in the *Smṛtyupasthāna* [Sūtra].
Why is there a specific treatment first and a general treatment later?
This meaning has been extensively analyzed as previously set forth in the eleven types of emptiness.
Regarding "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*),
it is as explained in the treatise:
One uses emptiness to dismantle emptiness;
therefore, it is called "the emptiness of emptiness.
What kind of emptiness is being dismantled?
According to the analysis in the treatise,
it refutes the three preceding types of emptiness; therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
It is not equal to *nirvāṇa*.
To simultaneously dispel both existence and non-existence is what is meant by "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Another explanation follows.
Because it destroys the other seventeen kinds of emptiness,
it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). This refers to phenomena that possess characteristics (*sanimitta-dharma*).
It must be destroyed by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Emptiness is a principle of reality (*dharmatā*);
why should it need to be destroyed?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"It is like a person taking medicine to eliminate various illnesses;
once those illnesses have been eliminated, the medicine should also be expelled."
If the medicine does not leave,
the medicine itself becomes a further affliction;
such is the case for the practitioner.
First, one uses the meaning of emptiness to counteract afflictions;
yet if one further clings to "emptiness-emptiness," that too becomes a source of suffering,
and therefore it must be dismantled.
Regarding what is called "great emptiness," as stated in the commentary on the treatise:
within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas...
He proclaims the emptiness of dharmas as the Great Emptiness within the Mahāyāna.
It is taught that the emptiness of the ten directions constitutes the "Great Emptiness," which shatters the realms of the ten directions.
Vast, manifold, and boundless,
it is called "Great.
One shatters that Great Space.
Therefore, it is called "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā). Question:
The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) proclaim that there exists a spatial direction (dig).
The Buddha-dharma is not like that.
How is it then that you now say there are the ten directions?
He analyzes it and finds it to be empty.
Nāgārjuna explains that within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas:
Although it is not explicitly taught that beyond the three-thousandfold world system there are further infinite worlds in the ten directions within the Mahāyāna dharma, [it is so].
In accordance with conventional truth,
beyond the three thousandfold world system,
there are further infinite worlds in the ten directions.
According to ultimate truth,
it is analyzed and shown to be empty. What, then, is that which is so?
This means that within the combination of the four great elements,
one discriminates between "this" and "that"; therefore,
it is said that there are directions.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the four great elements are fundamentally non-existent.
Based upon what, then, could one speak of "directions"?
For this reason, they are called empty (*śūnya*).

Question: If it is because that direction does not exist within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that it is called "great emptiness," then what is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?
It should be called "Great Emptiness.
The treatise itself explains:
"The ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)."
In reality, it is indeed "great" because it receives that name first;
the others are not called "great."
Question: For what reason is "great emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) taught to refute all directions?
The treatise says:
It is for the sake of destroying great false views,
such as those held by the various non-Buddhists who reckon that fixed directions exist substantially and are not empty.
Therefore, emptiness must be taught to refute those fixed views;
furthermore, it is taught as "directional emptiness" (dig-śūnyatā) in order to eliminate the extreme views of existence and non-existence,
just as one who cultivates loving-kindness does.
Taking the worlds of the ten directions as their object,
they cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward those in the ten directions.
If one claims there is exhaustion,
one falls into the view of finitude;
if one claims there is no exhaustion...
They fall into the view of extremes.
By means of these two views,
they immediately lose their mind of loving-kindness.
Therefore, it is said that space is directional;
this eliminates those two views and ensures that compassion remains unimpaired.
Question: For what reason does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explain that the emptiness of *prajñā* constitutes the "Great Emptiness"?
In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
it is taught that the emptiness of true consciousness constitutes the "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
In that *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
it is taught that the emptiness of the ten directions constitutes the "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The commentary explains:
In the eleven emptinesses of nirvāṇa,
both characteristics and reality are discussed;
those are the ten preceding emptinesses.
This is the emptiness of characteristics;
the latter, the "Great Emptiness," is the true emptiness.
Within the essence of true wisdom,
the entire dharma-realm is fully contained;
the dharma-realm is entirely suchness.
Therefore, it is called "Great Emptiness.
The *Dì jīng* (Earth Sūtra) is likewise;
it first explains the emptiness of sentient beings, the emptiness of phenomena, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
That its characteristics are empty is the emptiness of the ālayavijñāna;
this is its true emptiness.
Within the ālayavijñāna,
the entire dharma-dhātu is subsumed;
the dharma-dhātu is entirely suchness.
Therefore, it is called "Great.
The eighteen kinds of emptiness found in that *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Daipin) are all instances of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
This is not true emptiness.
Because it is not true,
it cannot be designated as "great emptiness" based on its reality.
However, the mere negation of the great elements is called "great emptiness.
Because these eighteen [emptinesses] are not ultimate true emptiness,
Nāgārjuna described them as the gateway to limited wisdom.
Because the essence of prajñā is quiescent and is true emptiness,
Nāgārjuna describes it as the gateway to great wisdom.
As for this gateway to great wisdom:
This is precisely the Great Emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā) spoken of in the Nirvāṇa-sūtra;
it is called "Small" because it employs the principle of the eighteen emptinesses to dismantle phenomenal characteristics,
whereas this is the True Illumination of Prajñā.
Because it accords with reality and is free from marks, it is called "Great.
Why is it named the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?
As stated in the commentary on the treatise:
"The true nature of all phenomena is the ultimate truth."
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is also empty;
this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).
What is the true mark? It is the reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is called the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Because it is the essential nature of that reality, it is named the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Since the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the reality of all phenomena, how can it be empty?
The treatise itself explains:
Because it is truly not something to which one can cling, it is said to be empty;
for it is taught that all phenomena constitute the true nature (dharmatā).
Apart from these phenomena, [there is nothing else].
No distinct, real self-nature can be apprehended;
therefore, it is called "empty.
Furthermore, nirvana is said to be the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
This emptiness of nirvana is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

As for the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), it refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth.
Because they arise through the gathering of causes and conditions, they are called "conditioned.
As for what is called "emptiness":
The commentary provides two explanations.
First, within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), there is no self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*),
and because they are devoid of the characteristic of permanence, they are called "empty" (*śūnya*).
Second, because the characteristics of conditioned causal phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are termed "empty.
Within the first gate, one is detached from self and what belongs to self.
That which is subsumed under the emptiness of beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and is free from the characteristic of permanence is also the emptiness of beings.
This is also the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Therefore, the treatise explains:
"If one says that the self is permanent..."
That which is eternally empty enters into the emptiness of arising.
If one says that the aggregates are eternal, they are eternally empty.
Thus one enters the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Within the second gate, there is no characteristic of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).
It is exclusively subsumed under the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

This differs from the case of *nirvāṇa*, where, regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one clarifies only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); as for the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), it is likewise [subsumed under the emptiness of phenomena].
One attains the true reality of dharmas,
which is free from arising, abiding,
and ceasing, and realizes and witnesses nirvana.
It is called an unconditioned dharma;
yet within the reality-mark of dharmas,
even the self-characteristic of the unconditioned cannot be apprehended.
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned. Question:
If one speaks of the emptiness of the unconditioned, [how is this so?]
What difference is there between this and those people of wrong views who slander [the Dharma] by claiming that nirvāṇa does not exist?
The treatise itself explains:
"Those people of wrong views..."
Having no faith in nirvāṇa,
they subsequently give rise to the thought of slandering it, claiming that nirvāṇa does not exist.
As for the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*):
it merely negates the fixed grasping at the characteristics of nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is called "emptiness."
This is not the same as wrong views;
rather, this emptiness destroys the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena.
The "emptiness of the eleven [aspects] distinct from nirvāṇa" clarifies that among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there is no self or person,
and thus it is taught as emptiness. As for "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), as the treatise explains:
It is called ultimate emptiness because it is destroyed by the emptiness of the conditioned and the emptiness of the unconditioned, leaving nothing whatsoever remaining.
For example, an arhat who has forever exhausted all outflows is called "ultimate purity.
This emptiness is likewise so.
As for "emptiness of that which is without beginning":
The arising of dharmas is not of this present moment;
it is called "beginningless.
The emptiness of beginningless dharmas is called "emptiness of the beginningless" (anavarāgra-śūnyatā).
Why is it that "emptiness with a beginning" is not mentioned?
The treatise itself explains:
there is a great delusion that has a beginning.
Because it asserts that there is a beginning,
the very first body would then be without causes and conditions.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
First, abandon these faults.
Contemplate that phenomena are beginningless;
contemplate this beginninglessness.
Since that which has a beginning has already been discarded,
there is no need to speak of "emptiness of that which has a beginning.
Rather, it concerns only those phenomena without beginning that are being examined.
Because the grasping at signs has not yet been relinquished,
I now proclaim the emptiness of phenomena that are beginningless.
As for what is called "emptiness of dispersion":
As stated in the commentary on the treatise:
"Scattering" (saṃvarta) means separation.
For example, it is like the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), which, when combined, constitute a person.
If the five aggregates are divided,
separated, torn asunder, and dispersed,
the person cannot be found.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
All such things are thus; that which is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (prakṛti-śūnyatā) refers to this.
As stated in the *Śāstra*:
"The nature of all phenomena is called 'emptiness of nature' because it is empty of itself."
Just as the nature of water in the world is not hot,
even if it is temporarily heated by great heat through artificial means, it returns to cold once that state ceases;
so too must it be with all phenomena.
Although it appears to exist through the provisional combination of various conditions,
its nature cannot be found if one is separated from those conditions;
therefore, we know this.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
Question: As for the "ultimate emptiness" mentioned previously:
This is precisely the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Why is this emptiness of intrinsic nature stated again here?
The treatise itself explains:
Now, as for "the emptiness of nature," it negates the inherent nature of all phenomena;
it is like how there is no quality of heat in water, yet the characteristic of water is not absent.
Ultimate emptiness means that the characteristics of all phenomena are destroyed,
such that even the characteristics of the phenomena of causes and conditions do not exist.
Furthermore, "emptiness of nature" is that which is practiced by Bodhisattvas;
"ultimate emptiness" is...
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
Regarding the emptiness of self-characteristics,
there are two kinds of characteristics.
The first is the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), also called the general characteristic (samudāya-lakṣaṇa).
The second is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
It is also called "dissimilar characteristics" (visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa). Suffering, impermanence,
and so forth are its "similar characteristics" (sādharmya).
Form, fragrance, taste, and so forth are their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The fact that both of these are empty is called the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
What is the distinction between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such that they are divided into two kinds of emptiness?
The treatise states there is no distinction;
it is merely a difference in name.
Furthermore, "nature" (svabhāva) refers to the essence,
while "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to external appearance.
For example, a bhikṣu’s observance of the prohibitive precepts constitutes his nature as a bhikṣu.
Shaving the head and donning dyed robes are the marks of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, it is like a brahmin who receives his own dharma and takes it as his nature.
He has a topknot on his head and holds a three-pronged staff as his emblem;
he is also like the element of fire.
Heat is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
red color is its characteristic mark (lakṣaṇa).
Thus, because all such natures and characteristics are distinct.
This is divided into two types of emptiness.
A question is asked:
"Is it not sufficient to speak directly of the emptiness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā) alone?"
Why is it necessary to proclaim the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics?
It is spoken of as "intrinsic" precisely to clarify that the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
As for the emptiness of all phenomena:
The aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) are called "all phenomena" (dharmas). Among these phenomena,
their various distinct characteristics are all empty.
This is called the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Question:
If one says that all phenomena are empty, [then...]
This interpretation is not correct.
All dharmas each possess their own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
What is meant by "emptiness"?
The answer is:
the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) are not fixed.
Therefore, it is said to be empty.
As for "the emptiness of the unapprehendable," this refers to all phenomena, including both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The nature and characteristics are quiescent;
they cannot be found through seeking.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness."
Within this, there are three points. First,
within those aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana),
a self cannot be found when sought.
This is called emptiness.
Second, within those various causes and conditions,
the intrinsic nature of phenomena cannot be found.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
Just as one cannot find a fist when searching among the five fingers,
so too the causes and conditions of dharmas cannot be found upon threefold investigation.
This is called emptiness. Question:
Is it because of inferior wisdom that one seeks the Dharma but does not attain it?
Because [the dharma] does not truly exist, one cannot obtain the dharma when seeking it.
The treatise itself explains:
"Because the dharma does not truly exist."
It cannot be found when sought.
However, this emptiness is identical to ultimate emptiness and the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics.
What is the distinction [between them] such that they are further explained?
The treatise says:
There are those who, upon hearing it said that space is empty,
give rise to fear in their hearts;
for this reason, it is now explained.
Because it cannot be found when sought within causes and conditions, it is said to be empty.
As for the emptiness of non-existent phenomena:
As stated in the commentary on the treatise:
"When all phenomena have ceased, they are called 'non-existent dharmas.
This non-existence has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and is likewise unapprehendable."
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
Regarding the emptiness of existing phenomena:
all phenomena exist merely through causes and conditions.
Existence is itself non-existence;
therefore, it is called emptiness.
As for the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas:
Because some people grasp at the two phenomena of existence and non-existence and find them to be unattainable when sought,
it is said that there is the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.
The two preceding emptinesses refute existence and non-existence individually; here,
they are refuted collectively.
Furthermore, while the previous two types of emptiness refute the phenomena that are grasped (the apprehended),
this present one refutes the subjective mind that grasps (the grasper).
Furthermore, as explained in the treatise:
"The emptiness of dharmas" (dharmāśūnyatā) refutes the arising and abiding of dharmas.
Regarding the emptiness of non-existence:
when phenomena are destroyed and cease,
this present emptiness of both non-existence and existence [is established].
This refutes [the opposing views] both preceding and following [it].
Furthermore, as explained in the treatise,
one contemplates present phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
That all things are empty is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
To contemplate that past and future phenomena are empty is called the emptiness of non-existing phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
Because they are not perceived in the present,
one contemplates that all phenomena of the three periods of time as well as unconditioned phenomena are entirely empty.
