When a noble being is born within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they can attain the untainted faculty of joy (anāsrava-prīti-indriya) belonging to the lower stages.
In this state of joy, the sense faculties such as the eye do not exist;
one is born above the first dhyāna.
There are no male or female faculties, nor the faculty of grief or the faculty of suffering.
This applies to those who have severed their roots of goodness while in the desire realm.
There are no faculties such as faith;
all ordinary worldlings lack the three untainted [faculties].
Therefore, it is not fixed.
If the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is present,
one necessarily possesses seven faculties.
These are the faculty of suffering, the faculties of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, as well as the faculties of body, mind, and life.
All others are indeterminate.
This refers to those who lack certain faculties.
Then there would be no sense organs such as the eyes, ears, nose,
or tongue; for that which is formless possesses neither male nor female faculties.
Within the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
an anāgāmin or arhat possesses no faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*); if they possess the faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*), it is likewise present.
Only the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is established;
the others are indeterminate. This is the case if one is in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
There are no seven material faculties.
If one enters the meditative attainment of cessation while in the desire or form realms, [these do not exist].
Then there would be neither the mind-faculty nor other mental factors;
however, if the body-faculty exists,
one necessarily possesses two faculties.
The body faculty and the life faculty;
all others are indeterminate.
If one lacks these faculties...
Then there are no faculties such as the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue.
If one is in the form realm (rūpadhātu) or among those who are formless (ārūpya),
there are no male or female faculties.
If one enters the meditative attainment of cessation,
then the mental faculty and the other mental factors are absent; however,
if there is the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses three faculties.
This refers to the eye, the body, and life.
Since the eye must depend upon the body, there is a body.
Life-force is born of retribution;
therefore, there is the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
All others are indeterminate.
If one is deficient in faculties,
lacking ears, nose, or tongue;
or if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or is formless (*arūpin*).
There are no male or female faculties.
For one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation,
there are likewise no mental faculty or other mental factors.
Regarding the faculties of the ear, nose,
and tongue: even if only one is present,
they all constitute three faculties.
This can be understood by analogy with the eye-faculty.
If the mind-faculty is present,
it must necessarily possess all three faculties.
That is to say, the faculties of mind, life, and equanimity;
all others are indeterminate.
Within the formless realm, the eye and other such faculties do not exist.
When ordinary persons are born in the stages above the fourth dhyāna,
they possess no faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
When one is born above the third dhyāna,
there is no faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
When one is born above the first dhyāna...
There are no male or female faculties, nor the faculty of grief or the faculty of suffering.
Among those in the realm of desire who have severed their roots of goodness,
there are no faculties such as faith and the rest.
Ordinary beings in the three realms possess neither the three nor the untainted [faculties].
If they possess the faculty of equanimity, [they possess it].
It necessarily possesses three faculties,
the same as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); if it possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukha-indriya*), [it likewise possesses the other two].
It must possess four faculties:
namely, the faculty of pleasure, the mental faculty, the life faculty, and the faculty of equanimity.
Pleasure necessarily depends upon the mind.
Therefore, there is the faculty of mind;
since life is the master of retribution,
there is the faculty of life.
When one is in a state of inferiority,
one must necessarily accomplish the superior Dharma; therefore,
there is the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
Question: It is asked, "How can one who dwells below necessarily achieve the equanimity of those above?
The explanation provides three meanings.
First, all "tasting" concentrations (*āsvādanasamādhi*) belonging to a lower stage that have not yet been abandoned within a higher stage.
Because all are fully accomplished, they exist.
Second, they reside in the lower stages.
The pure meditative concentrations cultivated in the higher stages are all fully accomplished;
as for the person of the third stage of holiness, they reside in a lower stage.
When severing the fetters of the upper realms by means of the pure meditative concentration of the upper realm and the untainted [concentration] of the lower realm,
they are identical because they cultivate the same antidote.
One attains all pure concentrations (*śuddhadhyāna*) and untainted concentrations (*anāsravadhyāna*) of the higher stages;
therefore, wherever there is pleasure, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is necessarily present.
In other cases, it is not fixed.
What is meant by "indeterminate"?
When a noble one is born in the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu),
at that time they possess the untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya) belonging to the stage of the third dhyāna.
Because the untainted [faculties] arise in higher realms without losing those of the lower,
there are no faculties such as the eye at the limit of that faculty of pleasure.
When ordinary beings are born in the third dhyāna or above,
they lack the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). This is because those with outflows (*sāsrava*) who are born in higher realms [no longer possess it].
This is because they have lost the lower [faculties].
Ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) in the first dhyāna and above lack the male and female faculties,
as well as the faculty of grief and the faculty of suffering.
If one in the desire realm has severed the roots of goodness,
they lack the faculties such as faith.
All ordinary beings lack the three kinds of untainted [dharmas];
therefore, they are not fixed.
If one possesses the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses five faculties:

namely, joy, pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), the mental faculty (*manas*), and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If there is the life-faculty, there are the life-faculty, the mental faculty, and equanimity.
The meaning is the same as for "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
How is it that joy (*prīti*) necessarily constitutes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
There are also three reasons.
First, all "tasting" concentrations (*āsvādanasamādhi*) belonging to a lower stage that have not yet been abandoned within a higher stage.
Since all are fully accomplished,
there is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
These two exist in the lower stages.
In the higher stages,
the pure meditative concentrations (śuddha-samādhi) that are cultivated are all fully accomplished; therefore,
there is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).

Third, when a noble person residing in a lower stage uses a higher pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) and a lower untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) to sever the fetters of the higher realms.
Because they repair what was previously damaged,
they attain the mundane pure concentration (*laukika-śuddha-samādhi*) and the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the higher stages; therefore,
they possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
By this principle, wherever there is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya),
there must necessarily be the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
The rest are all indeterminate.
Why are they indeterminate?
Because noble ones are born within the four formless realms.
At that time, there is no faculty of pleasure, nor the faculties of the eye and so forth;
having been born above the First Dhyāna,
there are no male or female faculties, nor the faculty of grief or the faculty of suffering.
If one in the desire realm has severed the roots of goodness,
they lack the faculties such as faith;
this applies to all ordinary worldlings.
There are no three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya); therefore, it is not fixed.
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya), one necessarily possesses seven faculties.
These are the faculty of suffering, the faculties of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, as well as the faculties of body, mind, and life.
All others are indeterminate.
As for those who lack these faculties:
Then there would be no sense organs such as the eyes, ears, nose,
or tongue; for that which is formless possesses neither male nor female organs.
Within the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), neither the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) nor the arhat possesses the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
[Question: Why is this so?
If the anāgāmin and arhat lack the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya),
they should likewise lack suffering (duḥkha). For what reason?
It is possible to possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) without possessing the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The commentary explains:
"Grief arises because of attachment to sensual desires."
Therefore, for those who are non-returners and arhats,
there is suffering but no sorrow,
because they have already abandoned desire.
When one sees the destruction of the pleasures of the five desires,
no sorrow or affliction arises; however,
this is not the case with suffering.
It does not arise from the discrimination of attachment to desire;
therefore, for those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) and arhats,
there is suffering but no sorrow.
One who has severed the roots of goodness lacks the faculties such as faith;
such is the ordinary person.
There are no three untainted [roots].
Therefore, it is indeterminate. If there is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), [it is likewise].
They necessarily possess eight faculties:
namely, the five feeling faculties, the body faculty, the mind faculty, and the life faculty.
All others are indeterminate.
As stated in the section on suffering:
if one possesses the male faculty,
one necessarily possesses eight faculties.
That is to say: the male faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, and the faculties of suffering, pleasure, joy, and equanimity;
all others are indeterminate.
This refers to those who lack these faculties.
There are no faculties such as the eye;
for one who is a male with a single sexual organ, there is no female faculty.
Among those who have attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), arhatship, or who are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) possessing the eight dhyānas,
there is no faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya). This is because those who have severed the roots of goodness (samucchinnakuśalamūla) [also lack it].
There are no faculties such as faith;
ordinary persons lack the three untainted [faculties].
If one possesses the female faculty,
they possess eight faculties at most,
provided they lack the male faculty.
The rest are all the same as before.
If one possesses the faculty of faith,
then eight faculties are established.
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the faculties of mind,
life, and equanimity; all others are indeterminate for those born in the formless realm.
Ordinary persons who lack the faculties of the eye and so forth are born in the stages above the fourth dhyāna.
Then there is no faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
When born above the third dhyāna,
there is no faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Above the first dhyāna,
there are no male or female faculties, nor the faculty of sorrow or the faculty of suffering;
this applies to all ordinary beings.
The three untainted faculties— vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and up to the faculty of wisdom—
are all identical to the faculty of faith.
If one possesses the faculty of knowledge, one necessarily possesses eleven faculties.

These are the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya), the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā), the faculties of joy (saumanasya), pleasure (sukha), and equanimity (upekṣā), the mental faculty (manas), and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
All others are indeterminate.
In what way are they indeterminate?
Those born in the formless realm lack the sense organs such as the eye;
those born above the first dhyāna likewise lack them.
There are no male or female faculties, nor the faculty of sorrow or the faculty of suffering,

because they exist only on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). There are also no faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
Question: It was previously stated that the Srotāpanna and Anāgāmin attain their results through nine faculties;
why is it now said that they necessarily accomplish them through eleven?
The commentary states:
There is a reason for this;
the preceding [passage] relies upon current usage.
Because joy, pleasure, equanimity,
and so forth cannot be employed simultaneously,
there are nine faculties.
Now, because this treatise discusses [the faculties] as they are accomplished, there are eleven.
Since the faculty of "I do not know" exists,
there are eleven faculties in total.
It is the same as the aforementioned faculty of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), with the exception that the faculty of knowledge is excluded and the faculty of non-knowledge (*ajñānendriya*) is added.
If one possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), one necessarily possesses thirteen faculties:
the eleven mentioned previously, plus two from the higher [stages].

Furthermore, when entering the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), one necessarily abides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, the faculty of body (*kāyendriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) are present.
The others are all indeterminate.
If one is deficient in faculties,
then they lack the four faculties of the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue.
The two faculties of male and female differ according to individuals;
their presence or absence is not fixed.
If one enters the path of seeing the truths based on the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna,
then the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) is absent.
Therefore, it is said to be indeterminate.
Within the seventh gate,
its sequential order is clarified.
All embodied existence has the six sense faculties as its substance;
therefore, they are discussed first. Since these six sense faculties exist, [the subsequent discussion follows].
One can thus distinguish between the male and female characteristics;
therefore, next, the two faculties of male and female are explained. These faculties are mutually inclusive within the system of the various faculties.
Because it is neither interrupted nor severed,
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is explained next;
it is that which enables the various faculties to encounter their objects and give rise to cognitive awareness.
Therefore, next come the five feelings.
These aforementioned defiled dharmas must have antidotes,
as defilement necessarily entails its remedy.
"Cultivation" refers to pure dharmas.
All pure dharmas arise with faith and the other [faculties] as their cause.
Therefore, one clearly understands faith and the other [faculties]. Because of faith and the others,
the Noble Path is brought forth.
The noble stages consist of three levels;
therefore, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are taught last among the twenty-two faculties.
This is a brief summary.
*Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Four;
*Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Six.

In this fascicle of the *Ranfa ju fan nao yi* (The Collection on the Meaning of Afflictions) compiled by Dharma Master Yuan, there are seven sections: the meaning of the ten fetters (*daśa-saṃyojana*), the meaning of the ten entanglements (*daśa-paryavasthāna*), the meaning of the ten obstacles (*daśa-āvaraṇa*),

the meaning of the fourteen difficult questions (*catur-daśa-dur-vicāra*), the meaning of the sixteen divine selves (*ṣoḍaśa-puruṣa*), the meaning of the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), and the meaning of the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*caturaśīti-sahasra-kleśa*).

53. The Meaning of the Ten Latent Tendencies (6): An Exposition through Ten Gates of Analysis on the Meaning of the Ten Latent Tendencies. I. Analysis of the Three Natures; II. Analysis of the Sharp and Dull Faculties, and of Seeing and Cultivation; III. Analysis of Different Modes of Association; IV. Analysis according to Objects and the Corresponding Realms; V. Analysis of the Ninety-eight Latent Tendencies and so forth; VI. Analysis of Different Modes of Bondage through Conditions; VII. Analysis of the Distinctions in the Formation of Meaning; VIII. Analysis of the Arising of Karma and the Moistening of Rebirth; IX. Analysis of the Sequence of Causal Origination. Section One: [The First Gate].
First, the names are explained in general;
second, their characteristics are distinguished.
As for what is called a "messenger":
As stated in the *Dilun*,
that which follows along with and binds is called an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).
Thus, the afflictions are named by means of this analogy:
just as worldly public officials pursue a criminal and, finding an opportunity, bind him,
so too do the afflictions.
They have long followed along with the practitioner,
binding them to the three realms of existence and preventing their transcendence; therefore, they are called "proclivities" (anuśaya).
The *Abhidharmapitaka* and the *Tattvasiddhi* also maintain this view.
Thus, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"It causes [the afflictions] to follow along."
Just as a bird follows its shadow or water follows its course,
the *Tattvasiddhi* states that it causes [the mind] to follow after it.
It is like a mother following her child;
it is also like a malarial fever or the poison of a rat that has not yet manifested;
it is like the black mark on heated iron.
Like a sprout within a seed,
or like a debt not yet repaid—
these are all examples of the meaning of "following along" (anubandha).
Some commentators explain that "to dispatch" (shǐ) means to employ as a servant;
this interpretation is not at variance with the meaning.
However, this is not found in the sūtras or śāstras;
such is the meaning of the name.
Next, its characteristics will be distinguished.
The meanings of these [afflictions] may be opened or closed, expanded or abbreviated, without fixed limits.
Now, proceeding by way of a single approach, we shall briefly discuss ten types:

namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Regarding what is called the view of a body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), it is also termed the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
The five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are called the "body."
Within the body, the grasping of a self is clearly perceived;
because it arises from that which is delusive, it is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
To scrutinize and recklessly designate [a self] within the five aggregates is the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
because one perceives a self therein.
That which is established from this perspective is also called the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
What are its characteristics? There are two types of the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
First, sentient beings are attached to a self;
second, phenomena are attached to a self within the five aggregates.
To establish the notions of "self" and "person" is called the sentient being's attachment to a self within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Grasping at the nature [of things] and clinging to their characteristics is called the attachment to a self in phenomena (*dharmātmagrāha*).
These two have been fully and extensively analyzed as before in the chapter on selflessness (*anātman*).
Regarding the term "extreme view" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*):
because it deviates from the Middle Way by falling into either annihilationism or eternalism, it is called an extreme view.
What are their characteristics?
According to the Abhidharma,
they consist solely in reckoning the impermanent as permanent within the context of suffering.
This is called the view of extremes.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among all phenomena:
Grasping at annihilationism and grasping at eternalism are both termed "extreme views. Thus,
the *Tattvasiddhi*, in its chapter on extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), states:

This is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

[One claims that] after death, one is created anew.

it is the same as in the Abhidharma.
As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the upper realms are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
when analyzed according to principle, their meaning is the same as that established in the *Tattvasiddhi*.

All ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are unwholesome. Regarding the third [category], there is a distinction between those that are sharp and those that are dull, as well as between those abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
First, the sharp and dull are distinguished.
According to the Abhidharma,
the first five are "investigative" (vitarka) because their nature is that of seeking.
The latter five are dull,
because they do not involve investigative inquiry.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however...
Taken as general characteristics and including their specific divisions, they are the same as in the Abhidharma;
however, if analyzed according to actual subtle reality,
the first five are exclusively beneficial.
Among the latter five types [of afflictions], greed, anger, pride, and doubt are invariably dull;
ignorance is not fixed.
This is said with reference to ignorance as it pertains to the five views.
Ignorance (avidyā) is sharp;
they explain that false knowledge is ignorance.
Therefore, this is stated from the perspective of others.
Ignorance is dull;
this characteristic exists in both [Hīnayāna and] Mahāyāna teachings.
Furthermore, if discussed generally,
among the ten proclivities (daśānuśaya),
there are both sharp and dull varieties.
Those with many [defilements] are called "sharp," while those with few are called "dull. This concludes this section.
Next, the division between those who see and those who cultivate.
As stated in the Abhidharma,
the period from the moment of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*) up until the fifteenth moment of mind is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
From the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, culminating in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.

When contemplating the truths through their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), one cannot say that [the stage] from the "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) onward constitutes the path of seeing; rather,
it can only be said that the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) is called the path of seeing.
The cultivation of the path is as previously described.
Within the Mahāyāna dharma,
this occurs from the first bhūmi, the path of seeing, up through the second bhūmi and above.
This is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Such is the nature of the paths of seeing and cultivation.
Within the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*):
The five views and doubt obstruct only the vision of the truths; therefore,
they are called "afflictions of view."
Greed, hatred, pride, and delusion universally obstruct both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Regarding those that obstruct the vision of the truths:
Those that obstruct the path of seeing are judged to be afflictions of seeing; those that obstruct the path of cultivation are judged to be afflictions of cultivation.
In the Abhidharma system,
greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit that arise based on [wrong] views are able to obstruct the realization of the truths.
That which arises conditioned by objects can obstruct the cultivation of the path;
this is established within the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and pride all possess the nature of grasping (*upādāna*).
When this nature of grasping is predominant,
it is able to obstruct the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Those whose grasping nature is subtle can obstruct the path of cultivation;
these are all the afflictions described in the Mahāyāna.
There is nothing that does not involve delusion regarding the principle;
among these, the coarse types are judged to be afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
The subtle [afflictions] constitute the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation. Question: Where do these two arise?
According to the Abhidharma,
prior to the path of vision (darśanamārga),
both wheels arise simultaneously.
From the stage of Srotāpanna upward,
one cultivates the afflictions of the realm of existence independently; this is according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
The textual accounts do not provide a definitive classification; they are distinguished according to their underlying meaning.
Prior to the path of vision (darśana-mārga),...
In the stage of Srotāpanna and above, one may give rise solely to the afflictions of view while the afflictions of cultivation are present as potentialities but do not manifest;
in the stages from Srotāpanna upward, one may give rise solely to the afflictions of cultivation.
Question: For what reason, in the Abhidharma system,
do both wheels arise together prior to the realization of the truths?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains that while the former [school] asserts that the afflictions of view arise independently,
the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) classifies these afflictions according to their objects.
Those arising from delusion regarding principles are judged to be afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); those arising from attachment to objects are [afflictions of conduct].
They are judged to be afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Ordinary beings inherently and constantly possess these two;
therefore, they arise simultaneously.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) possess the nature of grasping.
Since all are deluded regarding the principle,
these two afflictions are distinguished merely by their relative gravity.
All afflictions arising in ordinary beings [are categorized in this way].
The nature of grasping is heavy in the mind;
when entering the path of seeing,
this heavy grasping is forever extinguished.
Therefore, all that arises is termed "delusion through views.
In the afflictions of the sages, the grasping nature is light and thin;
in ordinary beings, when they give rise to delusion, it cannot be so.
Therefore, ordinary persons do not give rise to the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
they can only achieve them. Question:
Since the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have not yet arisen from the beginning, how can they be possessed?
To explain this:
The afflictions of view are the causes for the afflictions of cultivation;
because the fruit of cultivation necessarily arises when the cause of view exists,
they are said to be "accomplished."
Question: The *Tattvasiddhi* refutes the Sarvāstivādins' position that one has already attained the accomplishment of the first dhyāna even before the desire for the desire realm has been abandoned.
That text refutes it as follows:
What is meant by "not having entered [the path] yet having attained accomplishment"?
It is like a person who does not recognize a single character, yet claims to understand writing; this is improper.
According to that category of afflictions,
it should not be the case that they are already accomplished before they have arisen. To explain:
The deluded mind and the wholesome mind are different;
they cannot be treated as analogous.
Delusion has been practiced for a long time and is firm and strong, making it difficult to sever.
Although it has not yet arisen,
it will certainly be produced; therefore,
it is said to be "accomplished."
Wholesome dharmas are difficult to produce;
for although there may be prior causes,
they do not necessarily arise.
That which has not yet arisen is not called "accomplished.
This distinction applies here as well; in the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are two types of afflictions: those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation.
At all times they arise simultaneously;
for the ground of the dwelling of ignorance has been functioning from the very beginning.
Once the truths have been realized,
one gives rise only to the afflictions abandoned through cultivation. Such are the paths of seeing and cultivation.
The fourth section clarifies the differences in the association with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This contains two parts:
first, the clarification of the differences in the association with the various latent dispositions by way of the six consciousnesses.
According to the Abhidharma,
the two underlying tendencies of greed and hatred, as well as the associated ignorance,
all pertain to the six consciousnesses.
The non-associated ignorance and the other seven latent proclivities exist only in the mental stage;
this is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The nature of grasping and ignorance pervades all six consciousnesses; as for all others, it is not so.
It exists only on the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
it is explained in the same manner as the *Abhidharma*.
Second, by correlating [the proclivities] with the five feelings, the distinctions in their association are clarified.
As for the "five feelings," they are:
suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
In the stage of the five consciousnesses, that which is oppressive and distressing is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
that which is pleasant is called pleasure (*sukha*).
In the stage of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), sorrow and affliction are called grief (*daurmanasya*).
Rejoicing is called joy (*prīti*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) pervades all six consciousnesses.
Thus are the five feelings.
What is meant by "conjunction" (saṃprayoga)?
According to the Abhidharma,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are simultaneously conjoined with the five types of sensation (vedanā).
He says that the desire realm possesses all five types of sensation;
with respect to this stage:
The non-associated ignorance is associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) is associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity,
because it causes mental distress.
It is associated with sorrow;
at the time of cessation, it abides in equanimity.
Therefore, the *Śāstra on Equanimity* states:
In the desire realm, joy (*prīti*) is coarse while doubt (*vicikitsā*) is subtle;
therefore, it is not associated with the feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*),
because it belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
It is not associated with the two feelings of suffering or pleasure;
rather, the two views of self-existence and extremes, the two graspings of precepts and views,
and the underlying tendency of pride are associated with joy and equanimity.
Because divergent views have been dispelled and the mind’s arrogance and conceit have been measured,
there is joy associated with [the mind];
this is accompanied by tranquility and equanimity.
Therefore, it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and not with the mode of mental distress (*daurmanasya*);
for this reason, it is not associated with sorrow or suffering (*duḥkha*).
Because it belongs to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*),
it is not associated with pleasure; it consists of the single underlying tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*).
It is associated with the three feelings of sorrow, joy, and equanimity.
When those people of wrong view hear that there is cause and effect, they give rise to sorrow and distress.
Therefore, it is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*). Upon hearing that [suffering] does not exist, one rejoices; therefore, it is associated with joy (*saumanasya*).
Because cessation is conjoined with equanimity (*upekṣā*), it is associated with the perception of equanimity.
Because it belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*),
it is not associated with the two feelings of suffering and pleasure.
Greed is associated with the feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity.
Because it penetrates the defiled and attached activities of the six consciousnesses,
it is associated with joy and pleasure;
because it rests in equanimity, it is associated with tranquility.
It is associated with equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) and does not involve modes of opposition or affliction; therefore,
it is not associated with sorrow (daurmanasya) or suffering (duḥkha).
Hatred is associated with the feelings of mental distress and equanimity;
it may be understood as being analogous to greed.
It is also associated with ignorance.
It is associated with the five feelings because it is permanent and pervasive;
so they say.
In the first dhyāna, there is neither sorrow nor suffering;
there are the remaining three feelings.
These consist of the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body.
Within the body there is still pleasant feeling;
within concentration there is joy,
and outside of concentration there is equanimity.
Within this stage, non-common ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā) is associated exclusively with equanimity (upekṣā).
The five views, doubt, pride, joy, and equanimity are associated [with these feelings],
because they belong to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Question:
In the desire realm, doubt and joy do not coexist.
Why, then, is doubt associated with joy in the first dhyāna?
The treatise states:
In this state, there are no other faculties;
therefore, it is associated [with them].
That [text] states that within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are no other faculties.
Setting aside the discussion of meditative concentration,
it is asked: Why is the mind hesitant and unable to reach a decision?
It should be vexed.
How can it be associated with the feeling of joy?
The commentary explains:
This joy is not the joy of understanding the principle;
therefore, it can be associated with [the mind].
Although it is associated, [it is so].
There is only the substance of joy (prīti) but no function of joy;
the same applies to the remaining dhyānas.
This also includes the latent tendency of greed (rāgānuśaya) and the ignorance (avidyā) associated with it.
It is associated with the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity;
since it lacks the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), it is not mentioned [in that context].
In the stage of the second dhyāna,
there is only joy and equanimity;
within this stage, [these two alone exist].
The unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā) is associated only with equanimity (upekṣā).
All others are associated with both joy (prīti) and equanimity.
Within the stage of the third dhyāna,
there is only pleasure and equanimity;
in this stage, [these two alone exist].
The non-associated ignorance is associated exclusively with equanimity;
all others are associated with everything.
It is associated with equanimity (upekṣā).
From the fourth dhyāna upward,
there is only the feeling of equanimity.
All afflictions are associated with abandonment;
according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, they are associated sequentially.
They do not exist simultaneously;
from the preceding receiving consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the subsequent ten afflictions (*kleśa*) arise,
remaining associated and not abandoned.
Therefore, it is called "associated. He says:
from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
All possess the five types of feeling;
among them, the latent tendency of greed is associated with joy and pleasure.
The latent tendency of aversion is associated with that [feeling] of mental grief and suffering;
the remaining eight latent tendencies are associated with the feeling of equanimity.
The nature of grasping is ignorance associated with the five feelings;
it exists from the sphere of infinite space upward.
There is neither suffering nor pleasure;
there are three remaining feelings,
among which the latent tendency of greed resides.
It is associated exclusively with joy.
The latent tendency of aversion is associated exclusively with the feeling of grief.
As for the remaining eight latent tendencies:
It is associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Its nature as grasping (*upādāna*) is universally pervasive; this is established by considering feeling (*vedanā*) in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This analysis is merely cursory.
Fifth, there is the classification according to objects and realms.
First, we shall discuss it in relation to objects.
The "object" (viṣaya) refers to principle and phenomena.
Principle refers to the Four Noble Truths;
phenomena refer to all aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so forth.
According to the Abhidharma,
the two views of self-identity and extreme views are deluded only regarding the Truth of Suffering.
Because they arise in relation to the fruit, the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is next broader in scope;
it is deluded regarding both suffering and the path.
They are not deluded regarding the origin and cessation [of suffering]. Why is this so?
Because people of the world...
Many claim that ascetic practices can exhaust past karma; therefore,
they are said to be deluded regarding suffering,
such as Subhadra and others.
Furthermore, there may be some individuals who cling to various views, as well as to practices such as giving and morality,
which are not the true Dharma of the Path.
They take this to be the true path and claim it can bring about purification;
thus they are deluded and obscured regarding the true path.
Therefore, it is said that they are deluded regarding the path. For this reason, the treatise states:
"Those who are internally deluded."
Seeing suffering, one cuts it off;
those who are externally deluded remove it only upon seeing the Path.
What are the internal and external?
Furthermore, it is said that one is deluded regarding the internal and deluded regarding the external. To explain:
The grasping at precepts and observances conditions the arising of outflows (*āsrava*).
The Truth of Suffering is the principle within these phenomena characterized by outflows.
Because it is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is designated as "internal."
Because the Truth of the Path is the rational nature external to those phenomena that possess outflows (*sāsrava*),
it is described as "external.
If one were to simply claim that one attains liberation by experiencing the fruit of suffering in the present as retribution for past causes, [it would not be so].
This is called internal delusion.
It is because one cannot destroy the obstacles to attaining liberation while undergoing suffering that [suffering] is taken as that which can destroy them.
To grasp [these] as being capable of liberation is therefore called delusion.
If a person grasps at such practices as the observance of precepts and so forth...
They take this to be the true path and claim it can bring about purification;
thus they are deluded and obscured regarding the true path.
Therefore, these are called external delusions.
As for those internal delusions,
at the time of seeing suffering:
Knowing suffering cannot destroy the obstacles to liberation;
those views must first be severed.
This refers to those who are externally deluded.
Only when one perceives the true path does one come to know that the precepts and so forth are not the true path; therefore,
those views are severed precisely at that moment.
Therefore, it is said that this is the purification of the path and the non-path.
Since no one in the world can purify through grasping at accumulation,
one does not become deluded regarding accumulation.
One who clings to precepts,
seeking the fruit of cessation,
never takes cessation itself as the cause for purification.
Therefore, there is no confusion regarding cessation.
Furthermore, it is said that the truth of cessation is free from faults.
Purity is not a perverted view; therefore, one is not deluded regarding cessation.
[The opponent] asks:
Worldly people take up asceticism (duḥkha) as the means to purification; those who are deluded regarding suffering are called "those who grasp at asceticism" (śīlavrataparāmarśin).
Such persons take up the grasping at precepts and vows, the grasping at ritual offerings, and various views, regarding them as the means to purification.
Since the essence of that morality, generosity,
and so forth is precisely the accumulation (*saṃudaya*), why can it not be said to be delusion regarding accumulation?
The commentary states:
There is an interpretation that the non-Buddhists take suffering itself to be the means of purification.
Therefore, it is called "delusion regarding suffering.
Although the essence of precepts, giving, and various views is actually the origin [of suffering],
for those who are non-Buddhists...
It is not said that the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) themselves are the means of purification;
rather, when they are transformed into the Path (*mārga*), only then can they be said to be the means of purification.
Therefore, it can only be said that they are deluded regarding the Path;
they are not called deluded regarding Origination. Why is this so?
The mind that clings to precepts arises mostly from secondary teachings;
within the Noble Teachings, it does not.
It is taught that through diligent effort one can emerge from birth and death;
therefore, suffering itself is taken as the means for purification within the Buddha's sutras.
It is not said that the cause of origination is that which can purify;
rather, it is said that the cultivation of the path is what can purify.
Therefore, [this is] not the teaching of the non-Buddhists.
Not grasping is explained as the "origin" [of purification],
while transforming it is explained as the "path" that is capable of purifying.
The dissimilarity lies herein.
It is asked:
Although the non-Buddhists adopt precepts and so forth and take them to be the Path, [they differ from us].
Originally, it does not take the Path as its object;
how, then, can it be called "delusion regarding the Truth of the Path"?
To hold this [view] is to deviate from that [reality].
Therefore, it is said to be delusion. Question:
The Abhidharma states:
The principle of the origin of suffering is the Truth of the Origin of Suffering;
this does not depend on its specific manifestation.
The same applies to cessation and the path.
Furthermore, that which those non-Buddhists take to be asceticism capable of purifying is merely a matter of practicing painful austerities,
such as the observance of precepts and so forth.
To take this as the Way is to be deluded regarding the practice of the Way,
rather than being deluded regarding its principle.
How is it that they are called "deluded regarding the truth of the path"?
The explanation states: there is one interpretation.
Although they are deluded regarding phenomena,
because they infer the principle from the phenomenon,
they can be said to be deluded regarding the Truth of the Path that leads to suffering.
How is this so? Just as the fact that suffering can remedy past karma is established,
it is likewise logical that this must be the case.
Therefore, it is said that there is delusion regarding the principle; it is likewise on the path.
As the Buddha has taught:
Since the path of remedial action is not the true path,
it follows by principle that it is likewise not [the ultimate].
Therefore, it is said that there is delusion regarding principle.
What is the factual suffering and the factual path?
What is the principled suffering and the principled path?
Furthermore, it is said that delusion regarding phenomena is a category of delusion regarding principle;
from those causes of past karma and afflictions,
one receives retribution within the six destinies.
This is called the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Conditioned dharmas arise and perish from moment to moment.
The former being able to produce the latter is explained as "origination" (samudaya);
the latter arising from the former is explained as "suffering" (duḥkha).
This is suffering by principle (*li*).
The distinct retributions within the six realms of existence are termed suffering by fact (*shi*).
All conditioned and out-flowing phenomena arise solely from what preceded them,
regardless of whether the interval is distant or near;
these are termed "fruits."
Regarding this fruit,
the four meanings such as suffering and impermanence cannot be universally designated as the principle of suffering;
rather, they pertain to the thirty-seven factors within that path.
Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are called the path of phenomena (*vastumārga*).
Within those very phenomena, the Middle Way is established according to the four meanings of the *yāna* (vehicle) as a trace.
Generally speaking, this is called the path of principle (*li*).
Such is the relationship between principle and phenomena (*shi*); therefore, it is said that phenomena cause delusion regarding principle.
The grasping at precepts and observances is likewise.
False view, the grasping at views, and the underlying tendency of doubt all universally delude one regarding the Four Noble Truths.
With a mind of false views,
they slander the Four Noble Truths; therefore,
this is called universal delusion.
One perceives with a mind of false grasping that the five aggregates of the fruit are the foremost.
This is called delusion regarding suffering;
one grasps at the five aggregates as the primary cause.
This is called being deluded regarding the origin [of suffering].
Taking the Brahma heavens and the like, or the heavens of non-perception and the like, to be nirvana.
This is called the delusion of extinction.
Regarding the path established by that adherence to precepts and observances,
one grasps it as being supreme.
This is called being lost on the path.
Furthermore, they take the inferior views and other such states of mind regarding the Four Noble Truths to be supreme.
From the perspective of what is grasped,
this is also called being deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths.
It is asked:
If one were to take the various views regarding the Four Noble Truths as superior,
one would then be deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths by virtue of that which is grasped;
likewise, the attachment to precepts and observances also takes the views regarding the Four Noble Truths as being capable of purifying.
Why is it not said that they are deluded regarding the Four Truths?
The explanation states:
because they are not analogous.
Those who hold to views as supreme grasp those very views and take them to be the foremost.
Only that which does not turn back toward the path is called "supreme";
therefore, clinging to names leads to delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths, whereas clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is not like this.
When these are transformed into the Path,
they are then said to be able to purify;
therefore, according to the names established for them, one is deluded regarding the Truth of the Path.
Question: The treatise explains that there are three views and three corresponding [afflictions]:

the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) correspond with doubt; false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) corresponds with [the affliction of] attachment to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa); and the view of grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) corresponds with [the affliction of] attachment to views (dṛṣṭyupādāna).

How is it that the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is exclusively deluded regarding the path to suffering, while the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) pertains to all four [truths]? Regarding the word "respectively" (yathāyogam): [it means] as follows.
This is merely a partial statement.
Regarding the lower part of the path of suffering,
it can be said that the grasping for views arises following the grasping for precepts and vows.
Under the truths of the origin and cessation [of suffering],
one merely follows wrong views;
as for the latent tendency of doubt, it is discussed separately.
Doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths is pervasive;
all other afflictions— greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—
are likewise pervasive delusions concerning the Four Noble Truths.
And those that obstruct the path of cultivation.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
these are the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
This applies to all delusions regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Miscellaneous Questions," states: "All fetters..."
They are abandoned at the time of seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Since "cessation" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths,
these [afflictions] are delusions regarding the truths in general.
How is that explained? It is like the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
which arises with respect to the locus of the fruit.
This is delusion regarding suffering.
To view the self as permanent and not produced from causes and conditions is delusion regarding the origin [of suffering].
To say "I do not perish" is itself delusion regarding perishing;
for by reckoning the self as eternal, one lacks the path capable of removing [this delusion].
This is precisely delusion regarding the Path.
The same applies to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Among the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), [the same principle holds].
This means that suffering serves as the remedy;
it is precisely because one is deluded regarding suffering,
failing to recognize that improper conduct is the causal condition for suffering.
This is delusion regarding the origin [of suffering]:
falsely grasping at wrong conduct as being that which can bring about purification.
This is delusion regarding the path.
Because they teach that deviant conduct is the correct path,
they lack the intention to sever [afflictions] and proceed toward the truth of cessation;
this is precisely delusion regarding cessation.
The remaining proclivities are as described above.
False view, adherence to views, and doubt are deluded only with respect to the Four Truths.
Greed, anger, ignorance, and pride delude both the paths of seeing and cultivation;
the same applies to the Mahāyāna. This concludes this section.
Next, we shall discuss the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā):
Among the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), hatred (*pratigha*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the remaining proclivities pertain to all realms.
Why is this so? As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:

"In the higher realms, there are no [afflictions] of the nature of the six vexations—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and suffering (*duḥkha*)."
Therefore, by attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and tranquility (*śamatha*) to nourish the body,
one is free from ill-will. Furthermore,
because compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) is perfected, one is free from ill-will.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all ten afflictions (*āśrava*) are universal;
thus, its "Chapter on Miscellaneous Questions" states:
The higher realms also possess envy, jealousy, and so forth;
therefore, they possess anger. How is this known?
Just as that Brahmā King spoke to the assembly of Brahmās:
"If you simply abide in this foundation,
it will enable you to reach the end of old age and death."
"Do not go to the Gautama;
this is precisely jealousy.
Jealousy is that which is encompassed by the latent tendency of hatred."

Fifth, based on the ninety-eight, the meaning of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) is analyzed and elucidated.

The meaning of the distinctions among the types of ignorance has been determined as previously explained.

Question: Why are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) excluded?
This is because they arise within the fruit-stage of their own level.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,

With a mind of anger and resentment toward the higher stages,

That text further states:

The schools differ in their tenets;

There are four meanings of "relinquishment" (śeṣa):

It briefly eliminates the outflow-tainted proclivities (anuśaya) that take as their object craving, hatred, pride, and so forth, within the realm of the path.
Second, regarding the nature of the path of cessation: that which is exhausted is called "cessation."
The term "all" excludes the afflictions associated with the truths of suffering and its origin;
the term "three" excludes the affliction of clinging to precepts and rituals associated with the truth of the path.
Deluded by the clinging to precepts and rituals, one does not penetrate the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is called "incomplete.
These four alone constitute the heads [of the fetters].

because cessation and the path are the foremost dharmas within that body,

It is not the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
That which is called "pure" refers to the purity of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
Taking them as pure is not the clinging to precepts; therefore,
only false view, ignorance, and the latent tendency of doubt are mentioned.
They take the untainted as their object; although they do so,
they are not bound by them.
It is untainted and subtle,
because its object cannot be apprehended.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of affliction universally take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects,

It is known that greed and the others also have uncontaminated objects as their conditions;

In the upper realms, with the exception of hatred, fourteen latent proclivities (anuśaya) take this as their object; thus concludes this first section.
Next, the different meanings of the bondage of the various latent proclivities will be explained.
There are two kinds of bondage.
First is the bond of conditions;
second is the bond of association.
These are distinguished according to two meanings.
A pair of non-outflows serves to distinguish between the two fetters and the ten outflow-afflictions.
To take the six external sense objects as conditions;
being bound by these conditions is called "bondage through conditions. Simultaneously—
The binding of mental factors such as perception and feeling is called "associated bondage" (saṃprayukta-bandhana).
Second, the mutual relationship among the various latent tendencies (anuśaya).
To distinguish between these two types of bondage,
they are briefly analyzed here by means of four propositions.
The first is that which is a bondage of conditions but not a bondage of association.
Second, those that are bound by association but not by object-condition;
third, those that are bound both by object-condition and by association;
fourth, those that are neither bound by object-condition nor by association.
Regarding the initial statement that "those bound by objects are not associated," this refers to those latent proclivities (anuśaya) which have out-flowing objects; from among them,
one excludes the ignorance that is associated with its own category.
All others, when mutually compared,
obtain the status of being mutual conditions (*ālambana*).
This is called the bond of conditions;
because they do not exist simultaneously,
it is not the bond of association.
The proclivities that have outflowing objects are also bonds by way of being objects with respect to those that have non-outflowing objects,
because one acquires them by taking those as objects.
It is not a bond of association,
because they do not exist simultaneously.
As for the statement that it is a bond of association and not a bond of object-conditioning:
Among those [afflictions] having untainted objects,
wrong view and doubt are "associated fetters" (saṃprayoga-bandhana) in relation to the ignorance associated with their own respective categories.
Because they are simultaneous,
they are not bound by conditions;

Regarding what is called "bondage by object" (*ālambana-bandhana*) and also "associated" (*samprayukta*):
this refers to those among the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*).
Excluding the unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā),
all other [ignorances], in relation to the ignorance associated with their own respective categories, [are mutually concomitant].
It is also a bond of conditions and a bond of association,
just like that view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
That which has arisen previously has already ceased;
that which arises subsequently takes as its object the ignorance associated with the views of the preceding body.
This is called "bondage by conditions.
Subsequently, the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity arises;
that which takes the preceding view of a self-identity as its object is likewise bondage by conditions.

how can it apprehend the views of a preceding life?
Because it is associated with and takes as its object the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in a future life,
the ignorance that arises simultaneously with the view of a self-identity is called "bondage by association" (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
All the proclivities (anuśaya) are thus;
non-associated ignorance (apratisaṃyukta-avidyā), when compared with associated ignorance (saṃprayukta-avidyā), [is distinct].
There is no sense of association.
Therefore, excluding that, the two types of ignorance do not coexist simultaneously;
thus, moreover, the unique ignorance (āveṇika-avidyā) is distinguished from the other latent tendencies (anuśaya).
Furthermore, there is no sense of association [with them];
therefore, they are excluded. These are the proclivities (anuśaya) that have untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana).
They do not take contaminated phenomena as their object; for this reason, they are not mentioned.
As for the statement that they are neither bound by objects nor associated [with them]:
Among those [afflictions] that take the untainted as their object, the unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā),
when compared with the associated ignorance and the other latent dispositions (anuśaya),
is not a binding by way of an object-condition (ālambana-bandhana).
Because they have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object,
they are not bound by association;
because they do not exist simultaneously.
Among those with uncontaminated objects, wrong view and doubt—
excluding the associated ignorance—
are considered in relation to the remaining latent proclivities.
Nor is it bound by conditions,
because its conditions are untainted (anāsrava).
Nor is it bound by association (saṃprayoga).
Since they do not occur simultaneously, these two sections are concluded.
Next, regarding the distinctions in the objects of the various latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) and their bonds (*bandhana*), there are three parts.
First, clarifying the general and specific objects of bondage by the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Second, clarifying the differences in bondage according to the three periods of time.
Third, clarifying the variations in bondage according to the six consciousnesses.

according to the Abhidharma,
these refer to greed, hatred, and pride.

What is their specific characteristic?

such as that mind of greed.
One gives rise to a mind of craving toward objects that are seen and heard;

As it is with the mind of greed,
so it is with hatred and pride.
What is their common characteristic?
The views, doubts, and ignorance are called "common characteristics" because they arise by taking all objective phenomena as their collective object;
this is according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Miscellaneous Questions."
This should not be the meaning.

those that are general are all termed "common" (sādhāraṇa).

one must not speak of them in isolation.
For example, when the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*) sometimes arises by taking the four continents as its object in their entirety.
What is the distinction between meditative concentration? Furthermore, in that treatise,
the *Dīrghanakha-sūtra* is cited as proof regarding desire, hatred, and so forth.
This is a general affliction,
just as when a person hears of "all that exists" (sarvabhāva) while holding the view of a self (ātman).
All give rise to a mind of patience;
patience is itself craving.
Upon hearing that all things are mindless, they cannot endure it.
Intolerance is anger (*dveṣa*).
To grasp at a self with arrogance is called pride (*māna*).
Furthermore, there are those with wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Upon hearing that all things are non-existent,
the mind becomes greedy and joyful;
upon hearing that all things exist, the mind becomes angry and distressed.
To rely on this and exalt oneself is precisely pride (*māna*). How,
then, are they distinguished?
One should know that regarding view, doubt, and ignorance,
there is also the sense of having distinct conditions. Why, then,
are they fixed as being universal?
Therefore, each of the ten afflictions (daśa-āsrava) possesses both general and specific aspects;
it is thus established in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
In reality, it is the doctrine of the *Abhidharma* that all ten afflictions possess both general and specific aspects.
This is merely a matter of many words.
Next, we shall clarify the differences in bondage according to the three periods of time,
as explained in the Abhidharma.
Regarding the underlying tendencies of greed, hatred, and pride: if they are past,
they exist within those contaminated phenomena of the three times.
Only that which is bound by those fetters has the sense of being bound; for that which is not taken as an object lacks the meaning of bondage,
because its objects are fixed.
If it were present, then among the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three times,
it would only bind those [phenomena] that are its objects of focus (*ālambana*), and not those that are not its objects of focus.
If it is projected, it is not bound,
because its object is fixed.
As for that which exists in the future:
There is birth and non-birth.
If there were no birth, one would not be bound by the conditions of all contaminated phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
Because they have not yet arisen,
all contaminated phenomena of the three times possess the quality of being capable of binding.
As for those who are born,
they are bound individually according to their conditions;
it is like a person shooting arrows from afar at many people simultaneously.
If the arrow has not yet been released, many people all possess the status of being "shootable.
Once it has been released, however, only that which it strikes is said to be "shot";
those others it does not strike are not said to be shot.
The same applies to greed and the other afflictions;
those that have not yet arisen bind all [beings] universally.
As for those that arise,
they bind separately according to conditions;
as for the remaining seven latent tendencies (anuśaya), [they function similarly].
Whether occurring in the past, present, or future,
they all bind all that is with outflows throughout the three periods of time,
because those views and so forth act as fetters that bind together.
This is a statement regarding general characteristics;
it is not a statement regarding specific characteristics or differentiated characteristics.
As explained in the subsequent section,
according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) across the three time periods.
Each and every one binds the outflows (*āsrava*) existing throughout the three periods of time.
Subsequently, there are differences in the "binding by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-bandhana*) according to the six consciousnesses,
as explained in the treatise.
Regarding the afflictions of greed and hatred within the five consciousnesses:
