However, pride is of three kinds:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Of these, the aforementioned pride regarding the Dharma is considered the superior type.
It obstructs the mind of "inferior patience" on the fourth stage;
with the purification of the body, it becomes "middling.
It obstructs the understanding of "middle patience" on the fifth stage.
Grasping at defilement and purity is the lowest form of pride;
it obstructs the wisdom of superior patience within the sixth stage.
It is eliminated by the sixth stage;
compared to the preceding [stages],
it is therefore described as "subtle."
The nature [of these afflictions] consists of the dharmas that constitute the obstacles of pride and delusion;
they are described as "distress" (*nīrṇāma*) in terms of their transgression, yet they are based on subtle afflictions.
This clarifies the inferior, middling,
and superior types; the same applies to their categories,
as they are all equally afflictions.
Why are the first two described as pride?
Because they obstruct that which transcends the world; they are the very obstacles to be eliminated.
Adhering to [the view] in accordance with the Path is a minor fault;
it is not the same as the previous three cases, where both the nature and the characteristics are contradicted.
Therefore, by summarizing the objects of grasping to distinguish their respective hindrances, they are described as types of pride (*māna*).
This applies to the first hindrance; all subsequent cases are likewise so.
However, this subtle [state] is the residual energy of that coarse [state];
therefore, it is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). As for the habitual tendency of subtle characteristics:
This refers to the initiation of superior practice in the seventh stage.
It is taught that attachment to emptiness constitutes an obstacle within the sixth stage,
because in the sixth stage one attains equality regarding phenomena and dwells with delight in emptiness.
Being unable to immediately give rise to superior practice within emptiness constitutes an obstacle; thus,
grasping at conditioned phenomena is considered coarse.
Attachment to emptiness is subtle; the characteristics of this subtlety are called "marks" (lakṣaṇa).
The residual traces remaining within the coarse state are designated as "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā).
However, although their respective apprehensions differ— being either emptiness or existence—
their adherence to intrinsic nature is the same.
It may still be described as the habitual tendencies of a coarse family.
Regarding the statement that there are obstacles to practice within the signless (*animitta*):
this refers to the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of the eighth stage.
It is taught that within the seven stages, effort constitutes an obstacle;
in the eighth stage, however,
spontaneous conduct becomes fully matured.
The relinquishing of effort is called "signlessness" (animitta);
in comparison to signlessness, [it is so designated].
This is called "cultivation with effort," for it involves active practice and is thus obstructed by the signless (*animitta*).
Therefore, it is termed an "obstruction.
As for the obstruction of being unable to properly benefit sentient beings,
this refers to the unimpeded preaching of the Dharma on the ninth stage.
Because those [defilements] cannot act as obstacles in the eighth stage;
although one can purify the buddha-field and transform sentient beings within the preceding eight stages, [the remaining defilements persist].
To be unable to benefit sentient beings through unimpeded eloquence is called "incapacity.
Because of this incapacity, [one is so designated].
It is described as an obstruction.
To say that one lacks mastery over all phenomena refers to [the lack of] the wisdom of mastery pertaining to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
It is taught that within the nine stages, ignorance serves as an obstruction;
for although one may possess unimpeded eloquence and preach the Dharma throughout those first nine stages, [ignorance remains].
Being unable to employ unimpeded illumination regarding the profound Dharma known by the Buddha is called "lack of mastery.
Furthermore, one is unable to receive the Tathāgata’s cloud-and-rain style of preaching the Dharma.
To pour down the rain of the Dharma, extinguishing evil and giving rise to good,
is called "lack of mastery.
Because of this lack of mastery, it is described as an obstacle.
The second [section] clarifies the basis upon which these obstructions are established.
Upon what does the author of the treatise rely in establishing these ten obstructions?
This is based on the twenty-two delusions (*moha*) within the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
These ten obstacles, together with the eleventh, the subtle obstacle of knowledge,
constitute the twenty-two; of these,
there are two in the first stage.
Up to the stage of Buddhahood, there are two types for each;
therefore, in total, there are twenty-two.
Regarding the two types of the first stage:
First, there are sentient beings who are attached to a self and to phenomena; this is attachment to the delusion of a self, which is a primary affliction.
Second, there is the arising of afflictions in the higher and middle evil destinies.
There are three types of afflictions:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior. [This refers to] middling and superior afflictions.
It can give rise to evil karma and cause one to undergo retribution in the evil realms; thus,
in relation to the fruit, it is called the cause.
These are called the "predominant afflictions of the evil destinies.
The author of the treatise explains that, regarding the first [of these], they constitute the obstacle of the ordinary person's notion of a self (*pṛthagjana-ātmagrāha*).
Regarding the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), there are two types of ignorance (*moha*).
First is the delusion regarding the practice of subtle transgressions of the precepts;
this is an obstacle to the ethical discipline of restraint in that second bhūmi.
Second is the delusion regarding the practice of various courses of action.
These are the two types of obstacles to practice in those two stages: the obstacle to gathering wholesome qualities and the obstacle to gathering sentient beings.
Because one does not know the various kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karma, one is unable to gather wholesome qualities.
One is unable to sustain living beings.
The Master of the Treatise explains this, based on the first [point], as the obstacle of improper physical conduct and so forth.
Regarding the two types of delusion in the third bhūmi:
First, the delusion regarding the fulfillment of hearing and retention,
which obstructs the mind that understands the Dharma upon the third bhūmi;
second, the delusion regarding desire and attachment.
It obstructs the eight dhyāna-samādhis and so forth of that third bhūmi.
The Master of the Treatise explains it as having the characteristic of darkness with respect to its obstruction of hearing and so forth.
Regarding the two [obstructions] of the fourth bhūmi:
First is the delusion regarding craving for dharmas:
this is the mind that craves the understanding of the Dharma heard within the three stages.
Second is the delusion regarding meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In the third stage (*bhūmi*), there are practices such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) speaks of these from the perspective of the first [stage] as the fourth obstacle of pride regarding the understanding of the Dharma (*dharmāvabodha-māna-āvaraṇa*).
Regarding the two [obstacles] in the fifth stage:
First, the folly of turning one's back on saṃsāra and heading toward nirvāṇa:
this refers to the pride of grasping at purity during the fourth bhūmi,
which obstructs the ten kinds of equanimity in that fifth bhūmi.
Furthermore, it obstructs the practice of great compassion and other deeds for the benefit of sentient beings belonging to that stage.
Second, being exclusively turned away from nirvana and toward worldly delusion obstructs the practice of the contemplation of the truths and so forth belonging to the fifth stage.
The author of the treatise explains that, regarding the first [topic], it constitutes the fifth obstacle of pride concerning the purity of the body.
As for the two [obstacles] of the sixth stage:
first is the delusion regarding the predominance of mental aspects (*ākāra*).
This refers to the grasping at the characteristics of discrimination regarding defilement and purity within the fifth stage,
which obstructs the tenfold equality of dharmas in the sixth stage.
Second, the inability to observe the arising of manifold formations produces delusion,
which obstructs the contemplation of causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) on the sixth stage.
The Master of the Treatise, speaking from the perspective of the former, designates this as the sixth subtle afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the two types of delusion in the seventh stage:
first is the delusion regarding the practice of subtle characteristics,
which refers to the mind that delights in emptiness during the sixth stage.

The first is the delusion regarding the skillful means of contemplation on signlessness, which obstructs the initiation of superior practices through the ten types of skillful means wisdom within the seventh stage.
The second is the delusion regarding the practice of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*),
which obstructs the cultivation of effortlessness within the seventh stage.
The Master of the Treatise explains that, regarding the first [of the two], it is the seventh subtle characteristic—the obstacle of habitual tendencies.
Regarding the eighth stage, there are two types:
first, the delusion of non-manifestation within signlessness.
This refers to the mind of effortful practice within the seven stages,
which constitutes the delusion regarding the two types of mastery that obstructs effortless practice in the eighth stage.
It obstructs the practice of purifying buddha-fields and the three types of mastery within the eighth stage, as well as the ten masteries;
the author of the treatise refers to this initial [obstruction] as the "eighth obstacle to practice."
Regarding the two types of ignorance on the ninth stage:
first, there is the ignorance concerning the lack of mastery over the dhāraṇīs of all phenomena and their names.
This obstructs the practice that accomplishes the wisdom of the ninth stage.
The second is the delusion regarding the mastery of delighting in preaching the Dharma.
It obstructs the attainment of mastery in preaching and so forth within the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*).
The author of the treatise, referring to the latter, designates it as the ninth obstruction: the inability to effectively benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the two [types of ignorance] concerning the ten stages (*bhūmi*): the first is the ignorance regarding great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
This refers to that which obstructs the unsurpassed and superior practice of the supernormal powers of the ten stages.
The second is the delusion regarding subtle and secret practices,
which refers to the obstacles to the sevenfold wisdoms of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The author of the treatise, speaking from the latter perspective, designates this as the obstacle to mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) also have two types of delusion (*moha*) in relation to Buddhahood.
The first is the delusion regarding all subtle meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
which refers to the stage of ignorance (*avidyābhūmi*).
It obstructs the Tathāgata’s merit of all-knowledge.
Second is the delusion of obstruction,
which refers to ignorance regarding phenomena.
Regarding the obstruction of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*),
the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states that there is an obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) in the tenth stage.
One should know that this is the delusion of the obstacle;
it establishes the basis for the obstacle.
This brief analysis of it is thus concluded.
Within the third section,
regarding the "discernment of characteristics," the manner of opening and closing is not fixed.
Some say there is one, two, or even many.
As for what is called "one," it means that all afflictions collectively constitute a single hindrance.
Alternatively, they may be divided into two categories,

namely those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Among the ten [afflictions], the first one is an affliction abandoned through seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*).
The remaining nine types are afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding their activity as afflictions,
they can also be divided into two categories.
The second and eighth are karmic obstacles (karmāvaraṇa);
the others are afflictions (kleśa).
Alternatively, they are said to be threefold.
These are what are called craving with views and ignorance.
The first is [craving with] views;
the second can give rise to the violation of precepts.
The afflictions are precisely that craving;
the latter eight are ignorance,
or they are said to be six.
There are three [realms] in the world;
it is the same for that which transcends the world.
From the third stage downward, they are called mundane.
From the fourth stage upward, it is called "transcending the world.
Regarding the three within the world,
the first is the obstacle to liberation.
That is to say, the grasping at a self-mind obstructs the understanding of non-self;
second is the obstruction of practice,
which refers to improper conduct obstructing the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The third is an obstruction to the functioning of wisdom;
specifically, the characteristic of darkness obstructs the luminous and pure knowledge of that third stage.
Regarding the three supramundane [stages]:
From the initial understanding of phenomena down to their subtle characteristics,
these constitute the obstacles to that understanding, which consist of the conceptual discrimination between existence and non-existence.
The first is the obstacle to the understanding that [reality] is neither existent nor non-existent.
The second is the obstacle to practice,
which refers to the obstacle of having practice directed toward the signless (animitta).
These obstruct the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of that eighth stage;
the remaining two types are obstructions to the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-prayoga*).
They are unable to benefit sentient beings because they do not understand the Dharma;
alternatively, they are said to be ten.
Beginning from the mark of self (*ātman*) up to the dharmas, one does not attain mastery.
Alternatively, twenty [types of delusion] are taught; these twenty delusions are explained in detail as above.
If one were to analyze them in detail,
their specific enumerations would be difficult to exhaust.
Such are the characteristics of these hindrances.
The fourth section clarifies the locus of their abandonment;
herein there are five parts.
First, the introduction of divergent views.
Second, refuting erroneous attachments;
third, establishing the correct meaning;
fourth, challenging the correct meaning.
The fifth [section] provides an explanation to resolve [objections].
Regarding the term "alternative explanations," some say:
Among these ten hindrances, that which obstructs the first bhūmi consists of the initial mind of the first bhūmi’s unimpeded right abandonment;
this continues up to that which obstructs the tenth bhūmi.
The beginning mind of the ten stages is the unimpeded right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
How is this known? It is because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that those who initially rely on the bodhisattva path are considered ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
It is known from the fact that they possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one does not sever them at all;
this is also proclaimed in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* regarding those prior to the stages.
This is considered the "patience of submissiveness" (伏忍).
Thus, one knows that [the afflictions] are not severed.
Furthermore, it is as stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) regarding the third stage.
Those bound by various views are severed at the time of the first bhūmi;
this is clearly known.
First, the obstacles to the first stage are initially removed.
Furthermore, within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there are the afflictions that obstruct the vision of the truths (darśana-heya-kleśa).
Once the patience regarding suffering has departed, there is unimpeded right abandonment;
this is the unimpeded right remedy that follows the practice of the once-returner, which eliminates the afflictions obstructing the path of cultivation.
Using the small to categorize the great,
their meanings are similar; it is only the obstacle to the stage of Buddhahood [that differs].
At the final moment of the tenth stage, there is unimpeded right abandonment;
in the stage of the Tathāgata, this is realized as liberation through elimination,
because the Buddha is beyond training and is pure, being external to all residual afflictions.
This is one treatise.
Furthermore, others say:
"The obstacles to the first stage."
At the initial moment of the first bhūmi, there is unimpeded right abandonment;
this continues until the obstacles that hinder the Buddha-bhūmi are removed,
at which point the Buddha-wisdom first arises as unimpeded right abandonment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The ground of the abiding of ignorance is severed by the Bodhi of the Buddha."
These are the two treatises.
Such are the differing explanations; this concludes the first section.
Next, the refutation of false attachments follows.
If one says that the initial obstacle is the unimpeded and correct abandonment at the very first moment of the first stage,
continuing thus up to the tenth.
The claim that "at the initial moment of the tenth stage,
there is unimpeded severance" is not correct. Why is it not correct?
As stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages),
eleven stages are taught in correspondence with the eleven hindrances.
It describes the first stage by means of distancing oneself from the first obstacle,
up to distancing oneself from the eleventh obstacle.
The stage of the Tathāgata is explained;
furthermore, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*,
it is taught in contrast to those twenty-two kinds of delusion.
The eleven purities and the twenty-two delusions are fully detailed as listed above.
Regarding the first two delusions,
the purity of the first stage is taught;
this continues up to the final two delusions of that [stage].
It is taught that the Buddha-ground is pure.
If it is said that the ten grounds constitute the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the correct abandonment of the ten obstacles,
then the Tathāgata-ground should likewise be so.
Furthermore, when the stage of the Tathāgata is compared to the liberation from even those subtle obscurations and the realization of their abandonment, it is unimpeded;
the same applies to the ten stages.
Why trouble yourself with doubt?

If one says that the Buddha-ground is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa), then its external evidence of exhaustion differs entirely from the ten grounds; for the ten grounds, when compared to what precedes them, [are still subject to training].
Having attained their respective stages and no longer advancing in practice,
they are also those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
How is this different from the Buddha?
Furthermore, if it were the stage of a Buddha,
it would therefore be beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

In the context of the Bodhisattva’s training, the stages (*bhūmi*) are explained according to their manifestation; in the context of abandonment, the stages are explained according to their cessation.
This is the stage of Buddhahood;
because it is beyond training, it is the liberation that transcends all states of existence.
When a bodhisattva is still in training,
what should be severed is spoken of as liberation; although cause and effect differ, [they are nonetheless connected].
Since both take "emerging" (*niṣkramaṇa*) as the path to liberation,
although their causes and effects differ,
why should they not equally be designated as "stages" (*bhūmi*) based on that act of emerging?
If it is argued that the Sūtras state that a bodhisattva who initially relies on a nature possessed of afflictions does not completely sever them prior to the stages,
this is precisely what is proclaimed in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
although one has not yet reached the first stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), prior to the stages...
Yet it is able to destroy all birth and death;
for this reason, it is called inconceivable.
Why is it not severed?
Furthermore, in the Great Nirvana, there is the non-attainment of attainment.
That which is called "non-attainment" refers to the Great Nirvana.
As for what is meant by "arriving," it is because the Bodhisattva has forever severed greed, hatred,
and delusion; therefore, they are able to arrive.
With body, speech, and mind purified,
and not having committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes,
one is thus able to reach the point of not slandering the Vaipulya sutras.
It is not for icchantikas that they seek this;
therefore, they are able to reach it.
Where do bodhisattvas, having eternally severed greed and the other afflictions, attain great parinirvāṇa?
Regarding those above the stage of spiritual lineage (gotra), how is this known?
It is from that very scriptural passage.
The *srotāpanna* reaches [the goal] after eighty thousand *kalpas*,
up to the *pratyekabuddha*, who reaches it after ten thousand *kalpas*.
As for this term "reaches":
They reach the nirvana attained by the bodhisattvas before them;
yet the srotāpannas reach it after eighty thousand kalpas,
and even the pratyekabuddhas reach it after ten thousand kalpas.
Upon reaching the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*),
it is called "reaching nirvāṇa. Therefore,
we know that when a bodhisattva permanently destroys greed and the other afflictions, they reach nirvāṇa.
From the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, one eternally severs craving and so forth, attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Why, then, would one not sever them?
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), stating:
It is said that as soon as a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, they attain perfect awakening,
perceive the true reality of phenomena, and become fully endowed with the body of wisdom, equal to all Tathāgatas. Why, then,
would they not sever [the afflictions]?
Furthermore, it is proclaimed in the *Avataṃsaka* that there is permanent abandonment prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Why, then, do you not rely on that text? How can this be?
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is analyzed.
The position of these ten stages belongs to the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*).
That verse states:
The fourth is the noble son born of excellence, truly a child of the Buddha;
born from the true Dharma of all the noble ones,
they do not cling to either extreme of existence or non-existence.
"One is eternally free from birth and death and has emerged from the triple world.
How could it not be eternal?
Furthermore, it is proclaimed in the *Bhūmivastu*:
How is it that the purification of the two obstacles within the spiritual lineage (gotra) is not severed?
If one says that what is called "subduing patience" (kṣānti) prior to the stages constitutes non-severance,
this is precisely what is taught in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (Renwang jing).
Up to the stage of the Vajra, all are termed "subdued";
only the Buddha alone is able to effect their permanent eradication.
Even at the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), these [defilements] are not yet permanently severed.
Although the Sūtra speaks of their "subduing," the proponent of the preceding thesis maintains that on the stages above [the seventh], they are termed "permanent."
Although he explains that the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi constitute "subduing," how could there be no permanent abandonment whatsoever therein?
Furthermore, if it is explained that the stages prior to the bhūmi constitute "subduing,"...
Within this, there is no permanence.
The Benevolent King Sūtra proclaims that the first, second, and third stages are considered the stage of faith and patience (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
One should be without realization;
that is called "patience through faith.
Within this, there is realization.
Although he speaks of "subduing," what prevents it from being "permanent"?
Furthermore, if it is taught that the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi constitutes subduing, [then...]
Within this, there is no permanence;
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* proclaims that all stages from the third downward are entirely mundane.
However, if aversion does not sever [the defilements],
one must return to the three stages, and there would likewise be no permanent severance;
that is what they describe as "aversion."
Among these, there is permanent [elimination].
That which occurs prior to the stages (bhūmi) is called "subduing" (vāhana). Why is there no permanent [elimination] therein?
Furthermore, if on the stages prior to the bhūmis there were only suppression and no permanent abandonment,
then there would be no untainted [wisdom].
If there were no untainted [wisdom],...
By what means does the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta undergo the death and rebirth of transformation?
By this single proof,
the principle is sufficiently established.
If it is said that the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) teaches that the various fetters of views are severed at the time of the first stage (*bhūmi*) and not prior to the stages,
the sūtras also state that the "ground of ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is severed only by a Buddha.
Even in their final bodies, they remain shrouded by obscurations;
from the first stage up to the tenth stage,
there would be no sense of severance.
He says that the Buddha has severed [the afflictions];
from the tenth stage downward,
there is indeed actual severance.
Although the *Dilun* school asserts that the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*) are severed at the time of the first stage (*bhūmi*),
why would bodhisattvas prior to the stages not sever them?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"First, while abiding in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), one perceives such dharmas;
in this way, the fetters are severed."
The fetters of views are still obstacles to the selfhood of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Since that treatise states they are severed during the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
why does it say that from the first bhūmi onward they are removed without obstruction?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that there are three types of faults regarding the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
First, the fault of afflictions within the superior [category] of the miserable destinies (*apāya*).
Having transcended the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Having transcended the second subtle affliction (*sūkṣma-kleśa*),
one enters the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*) and the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Third is the fault of the activity of subtle habitual tendencies.
Having transcended these, one dwells without obstruction and enters the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmiḥ*).
Within that state of excellence, there remain the afflictions pertaining to the evil destinies (*apāya-kleśa*).
This corresponds to the second of the two types of delusion in the first bhūmi.
It shares the same obstacle as that [delusion regarding] self and phenomena, which obstructs the first bhūmi;
it is the affliction of the evil destinies from which one emerges upon reaching the first bhūmi.
Since it is not something that is first severed,
the self-conception of ordinary beings should likewise be so; why then do you say it is first severed at the first stage?
If it is said that the point at which the first stage (*bhūmi*) is abandoned is what constitutes "transcendence" (*atikrama*), rather than the point at which one emerges from it,
then this refers to the second category of subtle afflictions,
which are gradually eliminated from the second stage upward.
The eighth stage is when [the obstacles] are exhausted.
It should be stated that the two stages are considered faults because they do not reach the eighth stage.
This is the third [type of] habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
From the eighth stage onward, these are gradually eliminated until they are exhausted at the tenth stage.
It should be said that the eighth stage takes this as a fault and does not proceed to the tenth stage.
However, that point of severance is not called a transgression;
it is only upon reaching the point of emergence that it is designated as a transgression.
It is clearly known that the afflictions of the first evil destiny are transcended upon the first stage.
It is not that [the afflictions] are severed for the first time.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) relies upon mundane dhyāna."
They cultivate all factors conducive to enlightenment,
give rise to the great vows,
and sever the retribution of the evil realms.
One enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
However, that which is abandoned therein is still the second of the two types of delusion belonging to the first stage: the fruit of the afflictions of the miserable destinies.
Since that fruit is already severed from its cause within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
why would practice through understanding not eliminate it?
Furthermore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
The stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) possesses five fears and other obstacles to the first bhūmi.
Regarding this, it is said: "When practicing the highest patience (adhimātra-kṣānti) within the stage of practice through understanding..."
Having severed these marks of fault,
one enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi),
because of attaining joy.
All these signs of faults no longer exist at all;
if the obstacles of the first stage were not severed through the practice of understanding and conduct.
Why is it said that through the practice of understanding and superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one abandons these marks of fault and enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)?
If it is only upon reaching the first stage that one begins to gradually abandon them,
why is it said that at the time of attaining the Stage of Joy, all faults are entirely absent?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The bodhisattva at the stage of practice through understanding possesses inferior, middling, and superior skillful means, through which their liberation becomes progressively purified;
it is not a purification free from fault."
Within the state of joyful abiding,
there is liberation from obstacles and freedom from fault, which is pure. If,
in the first stage, the obstacles to the stage of practice through understanding are not severed, [one does not attain this].
How is it that they are said to be "successively purified"?
If [defilements] were only severed beginning from the first bhūmi,
how could they be called "liberated from obstructions," "faultless purity," yet not "unimpeded"?
Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" of the seven-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*,
bodhisattvas prior to the stages [of the path of seeing] hear the Dharma, contemplate it, and practice with diligence.
First, one overcomes the obstacle of laziness;
next, one overcomes the obstacle of transgressions;
and next, one overcomes the obstacle of lack of respect.
Subsequently, one destroys the mental obstacle of regret.
Having destroyed these four obstacles,
one enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Relying on the Stage of Joy,
one uproots the obstacles to benefit and has already entered the Second Stage.
Relying on the second stage,
one destroys the obstacle of affliction and enters the third stage.
Finally, relying upon the tenth bhūmi,
one destroys all obscurations regarding the knowable and eradicates all fundamental mental obscurations.
Entering the stage of the Tathāgata;
by this standard and verification,
one knows with certainty.
The initial obstacles are not the unimpeded right abandonments of the first stage.

If one were to say that because the obstacles to the vision of the truths in the Hīnayāna are only eliminated from the stage of "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*) onward, the same should apply to the Mahāyāna as well; [this is not so].
This will be explained later.
Furthermore, if the thirteen stages of the unimpeded path of the first bhūmi are categorized as belonging to the first bhūmi, [then...]
They do not abide in the stage of practice through understanding.
Among those of the Lesser Vehicle who have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna,
they further sever the six grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Regarding the four distinct fruits of that path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it should belong to the *sakṛdāgāmin* fruit and not to the first fruit.
The *sakṛdāgāmin* advances by abandoning seven, eight, or nine grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm.
The four fruits are distinguished according to that path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
They should belong to the Anāgāmin and not to the Sakṛdāgāmin;
for the Anāgāmin further abandons the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the two upper realms.
That path of non-obstruction should belong to an Arhat and not to an Anāgāmin; yet,
he proceeds to sever the higher fetters.
The four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are divided such that they all belong to the lower fruits.
Why then can the unhindered knowledge of the first stage (*bhūmi*) not be classified as belonging to the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryā*)?
Thus, it is made to follow later;
the abandonments of the first stage are explained [first].
Furthermore, if the obstacles of the first stage were abandoned by the first stage itself, [it would be illogical].

Among the four types of mental states— those consisting of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization— to which category does that path of non-obstruction belong? If it functions through realization to effect abandonment, [to which category does it belong?]
This would merely constitute realization and elimination;
it could not be termed "unimpeded. If one were to employ cultivation for its abandonment, [it would likewise fail to be unimpeded].
Is this cultivation worldly or is it supramundane?
If it is supramundane, [then...]
The *Dilun* school proclaims that hearing,
reflection, and cultivation are merely causes for wisdom.
Although it can give rise to that which transcends the world, its essence cannot fully fulfill the supramundane;
how, then, can it be judged as supramundane?
Furthermore, the *Dilun* states:

"The wisdom cultivated through practice that does not manifest the conceptual discrimination of the minds and mental factors of the three realms is called the wisdom of the mundane path of cultivation."
If it is not supramundane, how can it be classified as belonging to the first bhūmi? If,
on the other hand, it were mundane...
This would then belong to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*). How could it be taught that the first stage involves the correct abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*)?
Since the initial obstacle is not the correct abandonment of the first stage, [the objection stands].
Even down to the very last subtle hindrance, it is likewise so;
this is one [point] that is not [correct].
If one says that from the first stage up to the Buddha stage, all rely on unimpeded right abandonment to eliminate all hindrances.
This interpretation is incorrect.
That the Bodhisattva is unimpeded has already been refuted as previously explained.
If it were the case that the Buddha-ground constitutes the unimpeded severance,
then one would simply designate Buddha-wisdom as the "vajra.
For what reason, then, is the final mind of the tenth ground proclaimed to be the vajra?
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"One is called a bodhisattva during the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*); during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*," [one is called an arhat].)
He is named "Buddha.
Why, then, is it said that the Buddha has unimpeded right abandonment of ignorance?
The Sūtra states:
Regarding the "ground of abiding ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) which Bodhisattvas sever, that is said to be eliminated through realization.
How does this relate to the unimpeded [wisdom]? This concludes the two gates.
Next, regarding the establishment of the correct principle, there are general and specific obstacles. As for the general,
the obstacle of the self-conception of ordinary beings constitutes one category.
Up to and including the subtle cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) that hinder the Buddha’s wisdom,
each constitutes a distinct category.
As for what is meant by "distinct":
Directly within the obstacles of the ordinary person's notion of self,
there are hundreds of thousands of distinct categories;
this remains the case even up to the tenth category.
Only the eleventh category, that of the subtle obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is necessarily established as one;
it is not divided into many,
because it represents the ultimate limit.
Such are the characteristics of the hindrances.
To clarify the point of abandonment by contrasting them with the general hindrances:

the hindrances pertaining to the first stage are those [obstacles] to the various practices cultivated throughout the stage of fulfillment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
It serves as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and correctly severs those fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Thus, the *Bhūmisaṃgraha* states:
Regarding the fetters of views, they are abandoned during the stage of practice through understanding.
That same text further states:
While practicing the stage of conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), when one cultivates the lower degree of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*),
the characteristics of the five fears and other such faults increase; when one cultivates the middle degree of patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), [the same occurs].
At the stage of medium-superior patience,
and at the stage of superior patience regarding lower-level conduct,
one severs these signs of transgression and enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Furthermore, they further state:

"It is known that within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), there are soft, medium, and superior levels of skillful means (*upāya*) that progressively purify liberation; therefore, one knows that in the stage of practice through understanding, there is unimpeded right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*)."
Because the mind of the first stage gives rise to liberation through realization and elimination,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The five fears and all other marks of faults."
When joy is attained,
all [defilements] cease to exist.
That text further states:
One dwells in joy, free from obstacles, liberated, and pure of transgression;
this is known because one is liberated from the various higher fetters of affliction.
Thus, the burdens of the first stage are eliminated through external realization.
The manner in which the obstacles of the self (*ātman*) are severed for ordinary beings is thus;
this continues until the most subtle obstacles of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
which are unimpededly and correctly severed at the final moment of mind in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
It is realized and eliminated at the stage of Buddhahood;
however, regarding that initial path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*),
its specific designation is not fixed in meaning.
If one distinguishes according to the specific causes,
the result is determined to belong to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*). If,
however, one subsumes the causes under the result, [the stage] follows from that result.
It can be said that this path serves as the preparatory means (*upāya*) for that first stage (*bhūmi*);
therefore, it is judged to belong to the first stage.
This same principle applies to all stages where there is no obstruction.
If one clarifies the severance of various obstacles,
within the obstacle of the mark of a self among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
there are immeasurable distinct categories.
Regarding that first category:
at the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), there is unimpeded right abandonment;
at the initial moment of the first bhūmi, there is the realization of liberation and the removal [of obstacles].
As for the second category,
it refers to the aforementioned realization of the limit;
furthermore, there arises a mind that takes up illumination as its object and functions as an antidote.
It serves as the path of non-obstruction;
having severed those fetters,
once the non-obstruction has passed away, [the fruit is attained].
In the second moment of thought, the mind of true realization and the mind of actualization manifest as the path of liberation;
they realize and eliminate those fetters.
As for the third stage:
At the very moment that second realization-mind arises,
there further arises a counteractive mind characterized by objective illumination,
which serves as the path of non-obstruction.
Having treated the third category,
once that mind has passed away,
the mind of true realization arises within the fourth moment of mindfulness.
Liberation is realized through abandonment.
In this sequence, up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the remedies and the abandonments proceed in tandem.
Therefore, the ten stages are called "gradual purification."
Unlike the Buddha-ground, which attains purification instantaneously,
the eleventh stage’s subtle cognitive obstruction is restricted to only a single category.
The adamantine mind gives rise to unimpeded right abandonment;
as the knowledge of all modes first arises, liberation is realized and obstacles are eliminated,
such that no further distinct categories remain.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"The Tathāgata-abode is attained instantaneously as pure."
It is not as good as abiding in other ways.
Such is the gradual purification of the true meaning; thus concludes this section on the three gates.
Next follows the refutation of the true meaning.
If it is said that the initial obstacle is severed without hindrance at the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
why is the stage prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) not called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?
It is not called "transcending the world," nor is it called "rejoicing.
Furthermore, if there were unimpeded and permanent severance prior to the stages (bhūmi), [this would be untenable].
For what reason does the Benevolent King Sūtra proclaim that the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi constitute the "patience of subduing" (vītarāga-kṣānti)?
Furthermore, if those prior to the bhūmi possess unimpeded [wisdom] and have eternally severed [afflictions],
why does the sūtra state that a bodhisattva who relies on the first stage and still possesses afflictions is called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and not a noble one (ārya)?
Furthermore, if the first obstacle were severed during the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
why does the *Dichilun* (Daśabhūmika-śāstra) state that the bonds of various views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*) are extinguished at the time of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*)?
Moreover, if the first obstacle were severed without hindrance at the final moment of mind during the stage of practice through understanding, [why would this not be the case]?

Among those of the Hīnayāna, the afflictions that obstruct the vision of the truths should likewise be severed by means of that very "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) acting as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*);
however, within the Hīnayāna...
The afflictions that obstruct the vision of the truths must be severed by the mind of the path of seeing, such as the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and so forth;
it is the same in the Mahāyāna.
Having concluded the resolution of these four gates regarding the various interpretations,
next we shall resolve the erroneous objections in order to clarify the correct meaning.
Why is it that one correctly abandons the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*)?
Yet it cannot be called the Path of Seeing.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are two kinds of seeing:
first, the seeing of understanding (adhimukti-darśana).
First, by taking the principle of the truths as an object of contemplation, one severs the afflictions. Second, through realization and vision,
by taking the cessation of the mind as an object of contemplation, true illumination manifests before one.
If discussed generally, at the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding,
one contemplates the principles of the truths and eliminates the afflictions of views.
It may also be termed "view.
Therefore, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
it is said that the various fetters of view are severed at the time of practicing liberation.
However, within the Mahāyāna,
it is only when one extinguishes contemplation and realizes true vision that one truly transcends the world;
this pertains to the stage of transcending the world.
Since it explains the path of seeing,
although one can take that seeing as an object during the stage of practice through understanding, [it is not yet the actual path of seeing].
It is not given that name;
just as in the seventh stage one cultivates effortlessness yet does not receive the designation "effortless," for what reason is this stage not called "transcending the world"?
This is because the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha-vipaśyanā*) takes true virtue as its object and is therefore supramundane;
whereas that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*) takes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) perceiving the three realms as its substance,
and is thus not supramundane.
Why is it not called "joyful"? Because one is directly confronted with the afflictions and has not yet attained liberation, the mind lacks tranquility; therefore, it is not called joy.
Just as in the case of future-dhyāna, although the fetters of desire have been severed, because one has not yet emerged from it, the factor of joy (prīti) is absent;
this is likewise the case here,
even though [the defilements] have already been permanently severed.
For what reason is it called "Patience in Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*) in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*?
The explanation states that the stage prior to the [ten] grounds possesses three meanings.
First is the meaning of abandonment:
that is, by gradually eliminating the predominant ignorance of the four abodes, as well as the intermediate and coarse [ignorance],
one enters into joy.
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu*, it is stated that in the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the two obstacles are purified;
and in the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), all characteristics of faults are severed.
One enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Second, there is the sense of "subduing":
regarding the subtle four abidings (*catvāraḥ nivāsāḥ*) and the middling ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because it can only suppress and subdue [the afflictions] but cannot yet permanently sever them,
the *Ratnarājasamādhi-sūtra* refers to this as "patience through subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*).
This signifies that the three realms of existence have not yet been severed or subdued.
Because the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those four abodes, as well as the wholesome afflictions (*kuśala-kleśa*) and subtle ignorance (*avidyā*),
have not yet been severed or suppressed,
the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra* states:
For bodhisattvas prior to the stages,
both afflictions and wholesome dharmas are active.
Therefore, it is not called the "Supreme Pāramitā.
In that *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*,
five types of patience (*kṣānti*) are distinguished.
Because it reveals inferiority in comparison to what follows,
it is described as "patience through subduing" from the perspective of its capacity to suppress [defilements].
One must not, however, insist that this definitively implies the non-abandonment [of those defilements].
If one takes the *Ratnarājasūtra* to mean that "subduing patience" (*vītarati*) refers to those who have not yet attained any degree of abandonment,
then the *Ratnarājasūtra* also states that all stages from the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) downward are termed "subduing."
Only the Buddha alone is able to sever them forever;
those from the tenth stage downward must all still sever them.

That [position] is stated as being for the purpose of subduing those who hold the view that there is an interruption in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); the same applies to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Why then take the trouble to harbor doubts?
Furthermore, if a Benevolent King proclaims that the stage prior to the grounds is called "Patience through Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*),
then within that stage there would be no permanent abandonment whatsoever.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* proclaims that the first, second, and third stages are termed "faith-patience" (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
How could it be that within these there is faith alone without realization?
That sūtra states that within the stage of faith there is realization.
Regarding what he says about the state of subduing [the afflictions],
why is there no abandonment? For what reason does the Sūtra state that a bodhisattva who initially relies on a nature possessed of afflictions is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Although bodhisattvas prior to the stages have severed the afflictions of the five dwellings,
there is not a single dwelling among them where outflows are universally exhausted.
This is called "possessing the nature of afflictions";
it does not mean being entirely without abandonment,
as is the case in the Lesser Vehicle.
Although greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and views are partially eliminated during the Path of Seeing the Truths (*satyadarśanamārga*),
because they are not completely severed, they are not designated as "severed.
This case is likewise.
Furthermore, although those prior to the stages of the Path (bhūmi) have eliminated the segmented birth-and-death of the six realms,
residual karmic traces still persist within those six realms;
because they have not yet reached the state where outflows are exhausted, they are called ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
It is not that they lack noble virtue.
The treatise states:
"The fetters of views are abandoned at the first stage."
That teaching states that realization and elimination are unrelated to the unimpeded [knowledges].
For example, it is said that ignorance is severed by the Buddha’s bodhi;
how could this be the unimpeded [knowledge]?
This case is likewise the same.
To categorize the Hīnayāna as being identical to the Mahāyāna is improper.
There are three differences when the Hīnayāna is compared with the Mahāyāna.
Regarding these three points:
In the Hīnayāna, there is no untainted [wisdom] at all prior to the path of vision;
in the Mahāyāna, it exists.
Because it is absent in the Hīnayāna, one does not sever the afflictions.
Because the Mahāyāna exists, it is able to act without obstruction and correctly sever the first hindrance;
second, within the Hīnayāna, there is only one kind [of wisdom] that contemplates and illuminates the untainted (anāsrava).
There is no further true witness.
Therefore, all untainted states (*anāsrava*) that sever the fetters are judged to belong to the supramundane; within the Mahāyāna, there are two types of the untainted.
First, the untainted essence that severs fetters through the contemplation of objects is mundane;
second, the untainted essence that is free from fetters through the contemplation of cessation is supramundane.
This is because the former involves mundane objects as its antidotes.
It is able to act without obstruction;
it correctly eliminates the delusions of views.
Its essence, which consists of the merit of observing reality and attaining cessation, is supramundane.
Therefore, it is said that the realization of liberation is attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Among the three vehicles of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), wisdom and understanding are subtle and shallow; because they are subtle and shallow, [they do not constitute full realization].
That which has not yet been seen and not yet severed is called the mundane;
that which has been seen and severed is called the supramundane.
The wisdom of the Mahāyāna is profound.
To have views and to have abandonment is judged as mundane;
to still views and to still abandonment— having no views and no abandonment—
is precisely what is supramundane.
Because of these three distinctions,
the Great and Small Vehicles cannot be considered analogous;
this is in comparison to that first stage.
Since the explanation of the remedies is thus,
it extends even to the remedies taught in relation to the Buddha;
such is the meaning of the ten obstacles.
A brief exposition of this is as follows. 56.
The Meaning of the Fourteen Difficulties (6). Regarding the meaning of the fourteen difficulties: the meaning of the fourteen difficulties appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This is also fully analyzed in the "Buddhamātṛ" chapter of that *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As for what is called "difficult":
To hold onto what is false while seeking what is correct is termed a "difficulty";
it may also be said that false attachments obstruct the Noble Path.
Because they can create obstacles for the transcendence of the world,
they are called "obstacles" (*antarāya*).
These obstacles are distinguished as being of different types, and fourteen are taught.
Among these fourteen [views],
there are four types of views regarding permanence and impermanence.
The views of finitude and infinitude also consist of four types: [the world] is finite, infinite, both, or neither.
These are likewise [the views of] whether one goes to [rebirth] or does not go to [rebirth].
Furthermore, there are four kinds.
Regarding the identity or difference between the body and the spirit (ātman), there are two types.
Thus, taken together, there are fourteen difficult questions (caturdaśa-durvacana).
Regarding the four types of views concerning the permanent and the impermanent:
first, both the self and the world are eternal;
second, both the self and the world are impermanent.
The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal;
the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Now, first, we shall distinguish their characteristics regarding the self.
Subsequently, regarding the world,
that which is called "self" refers to the inverted conceptualizations of ordinary beings.
To falsely conceptualize a self and persons,
calling it a "spirit" (ātman),
and to say that this spirit is eternal— this is what is meant.
There are certain non-Buddhists who assert that the self (ātman) is eternal;
among them, there are two types.
First, the dull-witted; second, the sharp-witted.
As for those of dull faculties, it is because they regard this as a spirit.
One practices what is to be performed so as to receive the retribution in the future;
furthermore, one undergoes ascetic practices to enable the spirit to attain liberation.
Those of sharp faculties who claim that the self is permanent and that pleasure and pain do not change will conclude that there is neither sin nor merit,
thereby frequently giving rise to false views.
Regarding the statement on impermanence:
there are certain non-Buddhists who assert that the self (ātman) is impermanent.
Because they calculate [only] for impermanence,
they give rise to much negligence for the sake of the pleasures of this life.
Regarding the statement that [the self] is both permanent and impermanent:
there are certain non-Buddhists who assert that the soul (ātman) is twofold.
There are two types: the subtle and the coarse.
The subtle is eternal;
when the body dies, the spirit remains.
The coarse is impermanent;
when the body dies, the spirit perishes, as Sāṇavāsin says.
Regarding what is called "neither permanent nor impermanent":
some people perceive that both permanence and impermanence possess faults.
In what way do they possess faults?
If the self were eternal,
then there would be no retribution for demerit or merit, nor for suffering or pleasure,
just as space remains unchanged by wind or rain.
If the self were impermanent,
it would be subject to change by pleasure and pain,
just as a cowhide becomes cracked and ruined when exposed to wind and rain.
Because of these faults,
it is taught that the self is neither eternal nor impermanent; yet,
although it is proclaimed to be neither eternal nor impermanent, [it is so described].
On account of my own mind, I must necessarily assert that there is a self (*ātman*).
Having established the self in this manner,
I shall next clarify, with respect to the world, its permanence and impermanence.
Regarding what is called the "world," the treatises explain that there are three types:
first, the world of sentient beings;
second, the world of the five aggregates.
There are three types of world-realms;
among these three, they are distinguished according to the perspective of sentient beings.
There are also four kinds of divergent views, such as the view of permanence.
Regarding the claim that "the world is eternal," some say:
Those three kinds of worlds exist spontaneously;
they do not arise from causes.
This is called "permanence.
As for those who speak of "impermanence," there are people who proclaim it thus.
All worlds ultimately end in cessation and extinction,
with nothing further to follow;
therefore, they are called impermanent.
Regarding that which is said to be both eternal and non-eternal:
some say that among the things in the world, those which are coarse [are eternal].
It is impermanent;
yet the subtle atoms are permanent.
Therefore, it is called both permanent and impermanent.
Regarding what is called "neither permanent nor impermanent":
some people perceive faults in both permanence and impermanence;
therefore, it is proclaimed as neither permanent nor impermanent.
These four types are called "perverse" because they are grasped with fixed determination and not relinquished.
Question: The self (*ātman*) is originally without any inherent nature (*dharma*).
To falsely grasp at it therein may be called "perverse" (*mithyā*).
The world exists; even if one were to grasp it,
how could that be called wrong?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"It merely refutes the world's fixed attachment to permanence and so forth;
it does not refute the world."
It is like a person who, seeing a snake, falsely calls it a necklace.
A person with clear vision tells them, "This is a snake; it is not a necklace."
The Buddha is also like this:
he refutes such views as eternalism,
yet he does not refute the world.
We see directly in the world that things are impermanent, arising and ceasing;
how then can they be fixed and eternal?
Karmic retribution is never lost;
why then do you say that it is definitely impermanent?
Since the former two cases are not so, [how can this be?]
How could there be a third state that is both permanent and impermanent?
Conditioned phenomena arise and perish, yet the fruits of karma are never lost;
how then could it be definitively stated that they are neither permanent nor impermanent?
For this reason,
the four types beginning with permanence are all entirely erroneous. This concludes the first section.
Regarding the four views of finite, infinite, and intermediate [existence]:
first, both the self and the world are finite;
second, both the self and the world are infinite.
The self and the world are both finite and infinite;
the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.
Now, first, we shall distinguish these four types with respect to the self.
Regarding those who subsequently hold that the worldly deity is finite,
some proclaim that the sentient being’s self-deity (ātman) is like a minute atom.
Some are like mustard seeds, sesame, wheat, millet, or beans;
some are like dates and the like, or like a one-inch lamp, a one-foot snake, or a thread within a spider's web. Some even say:
The spirit of the small man is small;
the spirit of the great man is great. Some say:
In this way, all things are called finite;
as for the self being infinite:
Some say that the self (ātman) pervades empty space and exists everywhere;
wherever the body goes, it is able to perceive suffering and pleasure.
If there were no locus for the body, then one could not be conscious.
Although consciousness does not pervade [the entire body], the spirit (*ātman*) is indeed omnipresent.
To say that the spirit is both finite and infinite—
Some say that the spirit (ātman) has both coarse and subtle aspects;
the coarse aspect creates the body.
The subtle is the eternal body.
The created body is finite, while the eternal body is infinite.
As for the statement that it is neither finite nor infinite:
There are those who, seeing that both the finite and the infinite possess faults,
declare it to be neither finite nor infinite.
Although they thus proclaim it to be neither finite nor infinite, [it remains unestablished].
Yet it is not separate from the self (*ātman*).
Having thus proceeded with respect to the self,
one next proceeds with respect to the world to clarify whether it is finite or infinite.
Within this, first regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings, one clarifies whether they are finite or infinite.
As for what is called "finite," various explanations are given.

because they are numerous rather than singular,
they are called "various" (anekavidha).
There are those with limited perceptions;
these constitute three views,
because their objective spheres are narrow.
To call it "small" and to have the perception of the immeasurable—
these constitute four views.
Because the objects of focus are vast, they are said to be immeasurable. This concludes that section.
Regarding the eight [attainments] of non-perception:
Regarding form, there are four [types]:
the finite, the infinite,
and further, another four kinds.
Thus, there are eight [attainments].
Regarding the four involving form:
"After my passing, may I have form but no perception."
This is the first view.
That there is neither form nor perception is the second view.
Furthermore, there is form, there is the formless, and there is non-perception;
these constitute three views.
There is neither form nor the formless, nor is there non-perception.
These are the four views. Regarding the four [views] concerning finitude:
"After my death, I shall exist as finite and without perception."
This is the first view.
That there is neither limit nor ideation—
this is the second view.
There is also the view that there is both an end and no end, and that there is no perception;
these constitute three views.
There is also the view that there is neither an end nor no end, and that there is no perception.
These are the four views.
Because they are without conceptualization (*animitta*),
they cannot be described as the four [feelings] such as suffering or pleasure.
The four, such as suffering and pleasure,
exist within mental factors;
furthermore, there is no non-conception.
Therefore, it cannot be said to be either one or many, or small or immeasurable; this concludes the two gates.
Regarding the eight [factors] within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are four in contrast to form.
Regarding the finite and the infinite,
there are further four types;
thus, there are eight in total.
Regarding the four [views] concerning form:
"After my death, I shall possess form that is neither-perceptual-nor-non-perceptual.
This is the first view.
Formlessness that is neither with perception nor without perception—
these are two views. Furthermore,
there is both form and formlessness that is neither with perception nor without perception.
These are the three views.
That which is neither with form nor without form, neither with perception nor without perception—
this is the fourth view.
Regarding the four positions concerning the finite and the middle: "After my death,
there is a finite state that is neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
This is the first view.
That there is neither perception nor non-perception, which is infinite—
this is the second view.
"Both finite and infinite, neither percipient nor non-percipient"—
this constitutes three views.
"Neither finite nor infinite, neither percipient nor non-percipient."
These are the four views.
Because they are neither with perception nor without perception,
they cannot be described as the four [feelings] such as suffering or pleasure.
Furthermore, because it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it cannot be described as being one or many, small or immeasurable. Question:
Why is it not stated that there is both perception and non-perception?
In principle, this should indeed exist;
if it were further explained, [it would be so].
It is not different from the previous two;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Even if it were mentioned, it would likewise not differ from the first gate.
If one says that [the third] is also non-existent, it is no different from the second;
therefore, these three approaches are not further discussed.
As for the seventh, annihilationism:
Some say: "This body of mine,
composed of the four great elements and the six sense bases,
was born of my parents."
Nourished by milk and food,
sustained by clothing and shelter,
and protected by being rubbed and embraced.
However, this is impermanent and ultimately ends in annihilation;
this is the first view.
Furthermore, some say:
This present body of mine shall not undergo extinction;
it shall reach the heavens of the desire realm and there be extinguished without remainder.
These constitute two views.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "The bodies of the devas in the desire realm [are eternal]."
They do not undergo extinction;
their bodies remain in the realms of the form realm,
with all faculties complete.
When that retribution is exhausted,
it is extinguished without remainder;
these constitute the three views.
Furthermore, some say that within the stages of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
one cannot attain the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti).
When the retribution in the sphere of infinite space is exhausted, it is annihilated without remainder;
these are the four views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In the stage of the sphere of infinite space,
one cannot attain cessation; it is only when the retribution of the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted that [cessation occurs].
They are severed and extinguished without remainder; these are the five views.
Furthermore, some say:
Within the sphere of consciousness,
there can be no annihilation;
nowhere does there exist a complete and total cessation without remainder.
These are the six views.
Furthermore, some people say that the sphere of nothingness cannot attain cessation.
The retribution of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is completely extinguished and annihilated without remainder;
these are the seven views. Having concluded these four gates, [we now address] the five kinds of views regarding *nirvāṇa* in the present.
Some say: "This very body of mine is now nirvana. Why is this so?"
"In the present, I indulge freely in the five desires and experience happiness;
therefore, this very body is itself Nirvana."
Beyond this there is nothing more;
this constitutes the first vision.
Furthermore, some say:
This present body is not nirvāṇa;
there is yet another nirvāṇa.
It is subtle, supreme,
and peerless; I alone know it,
while others do not comprehend it.
Just as when I have abandoned desire, evil, and unwholesome states,
and having applied thought and sustained thought, enter the first dhyāna born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness—
this is called present nirvāṇa.
Beyond this, there is nothing more.
These constitute the two views.
Furthermore, some say:
There is furthermore Nirvana,
subtle and supreme; I alone know it.
Other people do not attain it,
as I do now, having extinguished and departed from applied and sustained thought.
With internal purity and one-pointed mind,
free from applied thought and sustained thought,
he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.
To equate this with what is called "present nirvāṇa," and to hold that there is nothing beyond it—
these constitute the three views.
Furthermore, some say that there is yet another nirvana,
which is subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
I alone know this;
others do not comprehend it.
Just as I have abandoned joy and dwell in equanimity.
Recalling the practice of entering the third dhyāna while experiencing bliss with settled wisdom—
this is termed "present nirvāṇa.
Beyond this, there is nothing further.
These are the four views.
Furthermore, some say that there is yet another nirvana.
It is the foremost and most subtle;
only I alone know it,
while other people do not comprehend it.
Just as I now have abandoned both suffering and pleasure,
and having previously extinguished sorrow and joy,
dwell in equanimity and mindfulness purified, which is neither painful nor pleasant.
Entering the fourth dhyāna—
up to this point it is called "nirvāṇa in the present";
beyond this, there is nothing further.
These are the five views. Question:
For what reason are the four emptinesses not taught as *nirvāṇa*?
The principle should also be explained,
but it is not discussed here in brief. [This concludes the discussion on] the sixty-two views.
This analysis is merely rough.
(59) The Meaning of the Eighty-Four Thousand Afflictions (6): Regarding the meaning of the eighty-four thousand afflictions—what are these eighty-four thousand afflictions?
The sutras merely list the numbers but do not enumerate their names;
by what means can they be identified?
One should understand that those eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the perfections correspond to eighty-four thousand afflictions;
it is just as the six defilements correspond to the six perfections, such that the six defilements are the counterparts to the six perfections.
This case is likewise.
The eighty-four thousand gates of liberation (pāramitāmukha) that correspond to these shall be discussed separately later.
The section on the afflictions (*kleśa*) is concluded. *Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Six;
*Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Seven.

Huiyuan’s Exposition: 2. The Meaning of Various Karmas (Sixteen Sections) The meaning of various karmas within the collection of defiled dharmas consists of sixteen sections: 1. The three types of karma, such as bodily karma; 2. Karma of the three natures; 3. Karma resulting in the three types of sensation; 4. Karma bound to the three realms; 5. Karma of the three periods of time;

6. The three types of karma: crooked, corrupt, and turbid; 7. The four types of karma: black, white, etc.; 8. The five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); 9. The six types of karma; 10. The seven unwholesome restraints (*asaṃvara*); 11. The eight kinds of speech; 12. The nine types of karma; 13. The ten unwholesome paths of action; 14. The fourteen defiled karmas; 15. The sixteen evil restraints (*duḥśīla*); 16. The thirty-five faults of drinking alcohol.

60. The Meaning of the Three Kinds of Action, such as Bodily Action (7). A fivefold analytical explanation of the three kinds of action, such as bodily action: 1. Defining the names; 2. Distinguishing their nature; 3. Opening and closing, expansion and abbreviation; 4. Lightness and heaviness; 5. Superiority and inferiority. First, defining the names.
To distinguish its essential nature:
the aggregation of color and form is termed the "body."
The gateway of arising discourse is the mouth;
that which observes conditions for names is the mind.
Because it arises and functions based on this,
it is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*) up to mental action (*manaskarman*);
such are their names.
What is its essential nature?
There are two types of bodily action:
first, the action of performance (karmasamutthāna).
Second is non-active karma (*akarmika*).
Regarding what is called "karma," the commentaries provide different explanations.
According to the Abhidharma,
among the three categories of phenomena (triskandha-dharma), it is subsumed under the category of form-phenomena (rūpa-dharma).
Among the twelve bases (āyatana),
it is subsumed under the base of form (rūpāyatana);
that is said to be bodily action (kāyakarman).
Because it has the nature of resistance,
it is included within the collection of matter (*rūpa-skandha*);
because it is a substantial dharma of matter, it is the object of the eye.
It is subsumed within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), namely: high and low, level and uneven, and so forth.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra):
Among the three aggregates of phenomena,
it is subsumed within the aggregate of form;
among the twelve bases, it is subsumed within the base of form.
It is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
The meaning of "form" (rūpa) is the same as before. For what reason?
Among the twelve bases (āyatana), it is subsumed under the base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
In that school’s tenet,
substantial form (rūpa) is not karma.
Whatever constitutes a conditioned phenomenon is,
in its continuity, merely a provisional form.
Only that which possesses both detriment and benefit is designated as "karma.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
When it arises in other places,
that which is capable of causing benefit or harm is called "karma."
Within the continuum,
that which arises later and differs from what preceded it is called "arising in another place."
In the Mahāyāna Dharma,
there truly exists the performance of action;
it is through continuity that this is established.
The meaning encompasses both aspects;
one must not take only one side.
Such is the nature of karmic action.
Regarding non-informative action (avijñapti):
according to the Abhidharma,
it is subsumed under the category of form (rūpa) among the three aggregates of phenomena (dharmas).
Among the twelve bases (āyatana), it is subsumed under the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Because it has the nature of resistance (sapratigha),
it is categorized as a form-dharma (rūpadharma).
This unmanifest form is not within the range of the eye;
it is known only by the mental consciousness.
Therefore, it is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among the three aggregates of phenomena:
This is neither subsumed under matter nor under mind;
among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
According to that school's tenet, there is no such thing as unmanifest matter (*avijñaptirūpa*).
It is because the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) does not share the nature of physical obstruction that it is called non-form (arūpa);
it does not share the nature of emotional or intellectual deliberation.
Therefore, it is said that it is not the mind (*citta*),
because it functions as mental activity (*manas-karma*); it is subsumed within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
In the Mahāyāna Dharma,
the meaning encompasses both aspects;
for it is a bodily action (kāyakarman).
That which is given the name "form" (rūpa) is the characteristic of formless mind; that which is named "non-form mind" (arūpacitta) is the characteristic of non-form mind.
Physical action is thus.
Verbal action is likewise twofold.
The first is the action of performance.
Second is non-action.
Regarding the term "action," the commentaries offer differing explanations.
According to the Abhidharma,
it is subsumed under the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*) among the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*),
and is included within the sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*) among the twelve bases (*dvādaśa-āyatana*).
Because it has the nature of resistance, it is subsumed under the category of form-dharmas (*rūpadharma*).
Because it is a real dharma that is the object of the ear, it is sound (*śabda*).
It is subsumed under the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
According to that school’s tenet, they do not assert that there is a conventionally designated sound which serves as the action (*karman*).
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra):
Among the three aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is included within the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
because its nature is that of resistance (*sapratigha*).
Since it is comprised within the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*) and is an object of the mental faculty (*manas*) as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*),
it is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*).
It is only within the continuity [of the stream of consciousness] that there can be loss or gain; therefore,
it is called "provisional."
Regarding "non-action" (avijñapti),
the commentaries also differ;
according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā):
Among the three aggregates of phenomena, it is subsumed under the aggregate of form;
among the twelve bases, it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
because its nature is that of form.
Being comprised within the aggregate of form,
it is included in the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), because it is an unmanifest action that is the object of mental consciousness.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among the three categories of phenomena (*trayaḥ rāśayaḥ*),
it is not subsumed under either matter (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*).
Among the twelve bases (āyatana),
it is subsumed under the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and does not possess the quality of physical form or resistance.
Therefore, it is called non-form (*arūpa*). Because it does not involve emotional deliberation,
it is called non-mind (*acitta*).
Because it is the domain of the mental faculty, it is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Within the Mahāyāna teachings,
such is the characteristic of vocal action (*vākkarman*).
The [classification of] bodily actions may be understood by analogy. Regarding mental actions,
however, various treatises differ.
According to the Abhidharma,
there is only active karma;
there is no non-active karma.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Because of three reasons,
the mind has no non-manifestation (avijñapti)."
Regarding the "three kinds," this refers to phenomena of the three natures, namely the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth.
Among material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),...
Because the three natures coexist,
