there may be unmanifest (avijñapti) evil within the sphere of wholesome bodily and vocal actions,
and there may be unmanifest good within the sphere of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions.
The mental factors are not like this;
good and evil do not coexist.
Within a wholesome mind, [they are not present].
There is neither evil nor the performance of evil; within an evil mind,
there is neither good nor the performance of good.
For this reason, there is only the performance of action;
yet that performance of action—

Among the three aggregates (triskandha), it is subsumed under the aggregate of mental factors (dharmaskandha). Among the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana), it is included within the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Among the mental concomitants (caittasika), its essence is the mental factor of volition (cetanā).
Therefore, it is subsumed under mental factors (*caitasika*). Since it is that which is traversed by the mind, it is included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The mental level possesses both informative and non-informative action;
therefore, that treatise states:
"There is no cause or condition that would prevent the mental level from possessing non-informative action."
His explanation of the performance of action is the same as that of the Abhidharma;
the point of difference is that he does not assert that there exists a separate entity of volition (cetanā) external to the mind.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"If volition (*cetanā*) were not the mind (*manas*),
what else could be said to constitute mental action (*manas-karman*)?"
Mental formations (*cetanā*) that take objects as their condition are designated as "volition" (*cetanā*).
As for "non-action," it is not subsumed under either matter (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*) among the three aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*).
Among the twelve bases (āyatana), it is subsumed under the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
It does not possess physical form or spatial obstruction,
nor is it a sentient deliberation.
It is said that it is neither form nor mind;
because it is the domain of the mental faculty, it is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are both the performed (*kṛta*) and the unperformed (*akṛta*).
Among these, karma consists essentially of volition (*cetanā*).
It is subsumed under the mental factors (*caitasika*) within the three aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*).
Among the twelve bases (āyatana), it is subsumed under the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
It is non-active because it is a mental action (citta-karma).
It can be called "mind" because it is not the characteristic of mind;
it can be called "not mind."
Among the twelve bases (āyatana), it is subsumed under the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Thus concludes this first section on the nature of mental action (manaskarman).
Next, its characteristics will be analyzed.
Within bodily action there are three types:
wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
Within the wholesome, there are two.
There are two types: cessation and activity.
To be free from the three physical misdeeds is called cessation;
acts such as prostration are called activity.
Within non-virtue, there are also two types:
first, abstention, and second, commission.
This refers to the intentional resolve not to perform acts such as prostrations and so forth.
This is called cessation.
To commit the three physical evils— killing, stealing,
and sexual misconduct— is called action.
The indeterminate is also twofold:
first, cessation; second, activity.
It refers to bodily action arising from an indeterminate mind of equanimity.
This is called cessation;
the arising [of thought] is called activity.
It is asked:
Good and evil reside within karma;
abandon those evil actions and thereby establish good restraint.
Abandoning those wholesome deeds,
one regards them as having ceased;
this occurs within the state of the indeterminate.
Why not abandon those two types of action— wholesome and unwholesome— and take that as cessation?
Instead, why abandon the karma of initiating neutral action and take that as cessation?
If, within the indeterminate,
one abandons the karma performed in the indeterminate state as the cessation,
this is the cessation within the wholesome.
One should further cease those actions that are good yet improperly performed, without abandoning the performance of evil;
the same applies to evil as well.
Thus it is explained.
This is unlike the two gates of good and evil;
they are directly contradictory,
and because they are directly contradictory.
There are two aspects that are inversely related:
first, the general; second, the specific.
To discuss them generally:
To respond to evil with good,
and to respond to good with evil;
these are distinguished and discussed separately.
Cessation within goodness must necessarily overturn what was poorly done;
cessation within evil [likewise].
It must be translated as "wholesome.
Since the indeterminate is not directly opposed to either of the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome, it does not constitute a direct contradiction.
Because it is not a direct contradiction—
There is only a reversal of the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), but no reversal of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Because it is a reversal of the general characteristic...
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is the opposite of those two categories of good and evil;
because it is not distinguished [from them],
it is the cessation of the indeterminate.
The non-inversion of the two gates of good and evil in action;
the non-inversion of the two gates of good and evil in cessation.
Within their respective categories,
the characteristics of cessation and activity are mutually inverted;
the karmas of speech are likewise threefold.
There are the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. Within the wholesome, there are two types:
first, restraint; second, active engagement.
To abstain from the four faults of speech is called "cessation. To recite,
chant, and praise sounds that accord with the Dharma is [the practice of cultivation].
This is called "active" (kriyā).
The unwholesome also has two types:
first, cessation (vairamaṇī), and second, activity (kriyā).
Not reciting and so forth—
this is called cessation (śamatha).
[It refers to] committing the four verbal transgressions.
This is called "active" (kriyā).
The indeterminate (avyākṛta) also has two types:
first, "cessation" (sthiti), and second, "activity" (kriyā).
The verbal karma arising from a mind that has abandoned the indeterminate is called "stopping" (śamatha);
its arising is called "activity" (pravṛtti).
Mental karma is also of three types:
wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
The wholesome is of two kinds.
There are two aspects: cessation and activity.
Cessation refers to the relinquishing of all unwholesome karmic volitions;
this is called cessation.
The volition that initiates wholesome karma is called "action" (*kṛta*).
Within unwholesome [karma], there are likewise two [types].
First cessation and second activity;
this is the mind of formal resolve.
Cessation is the wholesome thought of detachment.
Cessation is termed "stopping";
the arising of volition for unwholesome karma is termed "action."
The indeterminate is also twofold:
first, cessation; second, activity.
Cessation refers to the mind that is free from the mental states of deportment, craftsmanship, and so forth.
This is termed "cessation.
To give rise to this [term] is called "action" (*nāman*). Question:
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are actions performed by the body.
As for verbal instruction to kill,
there was the case where an enraged seer (ṛṣi) killed the people of an entire Gandhāra kingdom.
What is this karma? The commentaries provide different explanations.
If one follows the Abhidharma:
This is subsumed under bodily action;
it constitutes the completion of killing because it must depend upon the body.
Regarding killing through verbal instruction:
the person so instructed must actually sever the life-force with their own body before the karmic action is completed.
When a rishi kills people out of anger,
the nearby spirits and deities, knowing the rishi’s intention,
harm the people of that country.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
if one kills by means of verbal instruction,
that constitutes a verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Regarding "killing through mental anger," this refers to mental action (*manas-karman*). Thus,
the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun), in the chapter on the "Threefold Wrongness" (*Tri-vidha-mithyātva*), states:
The mouth can also teach,
and the mind can also act; however,
it is because the body is predominant.
This is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
In the remaining paths of action (*karmapatha*),
the principle of mutual engagement is likewise the same.
The single type of sexual misconduct is performed solely by the body,
because the completion of that karma necessarily depends upon the body.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
among these three types of action, that which is mental is called "right action" (*samyak-karmānta*),
while the two types consisting of body and speech are [the other two].
This is called "karma of appointment.
"Appointment" refers to a scheduled meeting;
it arises from the volition of that karma.
The convergence of the timing [of action] resides in body and speech; therefore,
it is called "timed karma" (kāla-karman).
Furthermore, that sutra states:
"Rectitude of mind is called karma;
so too are the two karmas of body and speech."
This is called the fruit of karma.
Since it is from the volition of karma that body and speech are produced, these two sections are concluded.
Next, the meaning of opening and closing, as well as expansion and abbreviation, will be explained.
The classification is indeterminate;
sometimes they are combined into one,
collectively termed "karma."
Alternatively, it may be divided into two:
first, active karma;
second, inactive karma.
This has been explained above.
Alternatively, it is said to be threefold;
within that, there are three [categories].
First, classification by way of their possession, which refers to the three types of karma: those of body, speech, and mind.
Second, classification according to their meaning.
First is action, which refers to the two types of action: those of body and speech.
Second is non-action.
These are the non-manifesting actions of body and speech.
The third is the action that is neither manifesting nor non-manifesting,
which refers to mental action.
Third, the classification according to nature:
namely, karma that is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Alternatively, it is explained as fourfold.
This refers to the four types of karma, such as black and so forth;
or it is explained as five,
as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Bodily action is twofold:
manifest and non-manifest.
Verbal action is likewise.
Thus, they are considered four;
when intention (cetanā) alone is added,
they are said to be five in accordance with the previous explanation.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
there is also both manifest and non-manifest karma on the mental level;
if this is the meaning [of your position].
Karma is said to be of six types,
or it may be divided into nine; that is,
the actions of body, speech, and mind each have three varieties.
When categorized as wholesome, unwholesome,
and indeterminate, they constitute nine.
Furthermore, this is as stated in the "Chapter on the Nine Karmas" of the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Furthermore, it is explained as ninefold. What are they?
It is said that the desire realm consists of three types.
First is action; second is non-action;
third is that which is neither action nor non-action.
This has been explained above.
It is the same for the form realm (rūpadhātu); thus, there are six.
The formless has two types:
first, that which does not perform action;
second, that which neither performs action nor does not perform action.
Including the preceding, there are eight;
including untainted (anāsrava) karma as well, there are nine.
Alternatively, they may be divided into thirteen,
as explained in the Abhidharma:
there are five [factors] of body and speech.
First, wholesome action;
second, unwholesome action;
third, indeterminate action.
There are two types of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). Together with the preceding [two], they constitute five.
Regarding these two types of non-manifest action:
First, the non-manifestation (avijñapti) of wholesome [karma];
second, the non-manifestation of unwholesome [karma].
The non-manifestation is not produced by neutral (avyākṛta) states, as they are weak and inferior.
As it is with bodily action,
so it is with verbal action;
thus, they constitute ten.
The mental stage has only three types of activity;
when combined with the preceding thirteen, [there are sixteen].
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The mental ground also possesses wholesome, unwholesome, and non-informative [karma].
Based on this, it is argued that there are fifteen types of karma.
Alternatively, it is also explained as twenty-three types of karma.
There are ten types of wholesome karma, namely: non-killing and so forth.
The unwholesome [actions] are also ten,
namely killing, stealing, and so forth;
they comprise the three types of non-defined [actions] pertaining to body, speech, and mind.
These constitute the twenty-three types of karma.
To analyze them in detail, their specific enumerations are difficult to exhaust. This concludes the three gateways.
Next, we shall distinguish the meaning of the lightness and heaviness of the three types of karma.
Among these three types of karma,
which is the most grave?
Within this, first the two types of action— bodily and vocal—
are distinguished in terms of their relative gravity compared to mental action;
subsequently, they will be discussed individually.
Regarding the statement that among body, speech, and mind, the mind is distinguished as the most significant:
mental karma is the heaviest of all bodily and verbal actions.
Because it is produced by the mind,
and furthermore, among evil karmas, false view is the most grave,
as it is capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Among all wholesome karmas, the path leading out of the world via the Three Vehicles is the most preeminent. Even for those who have become icchantikas, this remains the supreme.
Within the world, the karma of non-perception is supreme;
all things are created by the mind.
Thus, one should know that the mind is paramount.
Next, regarding the three types of action, their relative gravity will be explained individually;
among them, bodily action is the most grave.
Among the [five] most serious offenses, shedding the blood of a Buddha is the heaviest; specifically,
it refers to causing a schism in the Sangha and slandering the Vaipulya sutras.
Among all mental states, the most grave is what is called the evil karma of wrong view.
Likewise, among virtuous karmas:
The karma of awakening is considered the most weighty.
Among these three types, that of the body is light, while those of speech and mind are the most weighty. These four gates are concluded.
Next, the differences in the retribution obtained by those in the higher and lower realms are distinguished. As Nāgārjuna said:
there are three types of unwholesome [karma].
That is to say, there are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. Those of inferior [karma] are born as hungry ghosts;
those of middling [karma] are born as animals.
Above, one is born in the hells.
Within the wholesome, there are likewise three grades:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
Those of inferior birth are reborn as asuras;
those of middling birth are reborn among humans;
those of superior birth are reborn in the heavens.
Furthermore, there is another classification:
evil is of four grades,
namely, inferior, middling, superior, and supreme.
Those born in the lower grade become asuras;
those born in the middle grade become hungry ghosts;
and those born in the upper grade become animals.
The highest of the high are born in hell;
among the middling good there are likewise four [levels];
the lowest are born as humans.
Those of middling capacity are reborn in the heavens;
those of superior capacity attain the fruits of the Two Vehicles.
Those of the highest of the high attain the unsurpassed fruit.
Furthermore, within *nirvāṇa*, the wholesome is divided into four categories.
The lowest are born in Uttarakuru;
the middle in Pūrvavideha;
the highest in Aparagoyānī.
Those of the highest grade are born in Jambudvīpa;
this is because the distinction between superior and inferior is made in relation to the Path.
Those in Uttarakuru are not fit to receive the Way;
they are born there due to inferior goodness.
The middle and superior grades are difficult to understand in terms of their place of rebirth;
if one considers them in relation to the Dharma of the Path.
With middling-grade wholesome karma,
one should be born in Aparagoyānī;
with superior-grade, one is born in Pūrvavideha.
However, in that sutra, the middle and upper grades are distinguished merely according to their karmic retribution.
This refers to Jambudvīpa in the south.
It is the most excellent among those received on the path;
it gives rise to supreme goodness.
If contrasted with karmic retribution, [it is superior].
They are divided into four classes:
those born below in Jambudvīpa,
and those born in the middle in Pūrvavideha.
Those who are reborn above go to Godānīya;
those who are of the highest grade are reborn in Uttarakuru.
The meaning of the three types of karma has been briefly explained in this manner.

61. The Meaning of Karma According to the Three Natures (7). The Meaning of Karma According to the Three Natures is explained through a threefold analysis: first, defining the names and identifying the essence; second, distinguishing their characteristics; third, classifying them according to persons. Within the first section, the names are defined and the essence is identified.
Regarding the three natures of action:
they are namely the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
That which accords with [the goal] is called wholesome.
To transgress is called evil.
This transgression and its opposite, compliance,
are explained below in the section on the ten wholesome actions of the five grades.
That which is neither contrary nor compliant is explained as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
There are two senses to this interpretation:
first, the distinction based on its fruit.
The karma of neutral capacity cannot be remembered as resulting in either the retribution of suffering or pleasure; therefore,
it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Second, regarding the explanation of the indeterminate karma:
the Tathāgata does not declare such karma to be either wholesome or unwholesome.
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Such is the meaning of the name.
What, then, is its essential nature?
There are two kinds of goodness:
first, that which is acquired at birth through the maturation of past habituation;
second, that which is newly produced through skillful means in response to conditions.
The unwholesome is of only one kind;
it does not distinguish between that which is acquired at birth and that which is produced through effort. Why is this so?
All unwholesome dharmas are formed through long-standing habitual tendencies from the past;
they do not depend upon the present.
They are cultivated through skillful means;
thus they are not differentiated.
There are four types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
What are called retribution-born, deportment, craftsmanship, and transformation.
The two types of retribution, suffering and pleasure,
are termed "retribution-born."
Advancing and halting, coming and going—
these constitute his dignified deportment;
he attends to the worldly affairs of life.
These are called "crafts" (*śilpa*).
The fourteen types, such as transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and so forth, are termed "transformations. This concludes this section.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished.
There are five distinct types of characteristics.
First, the three natures are established in relation to worldly phenomena.
When all ordinary beings and sages cease from both evil and engage in both good through body, speech, and mind,
this is called "good. When they cease from both good and engage in both evil, it is likewise so.
Those associated with the unwholesome are collectively termed "unwholesome. Those born of retribution, as well as deportment, craftsmanship, and transformations,
are collectively termed "indeterminate."
Second, distinguishing according to the dharma of the renunciant path:
all wholesome acts of cessation and engagement performed by the body, speech, and mind of all ordinary and noble beings are termed "wholesome."
The two evils of abstaining from and committing [unwholesome acts] are both designated as unwholesome (akuśala).
The retributive, the non-defined (avyākṛta), the deportment, the craftsmanship, and the transformative [minds] are likewise [non-defined].
There are three distinct meanings,
as explained in the Vinaya:
that which is performed in accordance with the Dharma.
That which accords with the Dharma is called "wholesome";
that which contravenes the Dharma is generally termed "unwholesome."
That which is neither contrary nor compliant is described as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is the third distinction regarding results.
That which gives rise to pleasure is called wholesome;
that which gives rise to suffering is unwholesome;
that which cannot give rise [to either]—[is neutral].
It is described as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Within this framework,
ordinary persons and those in training (*śaikṣa*) engage in both the performance and the cessation of wholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind.
It is called "wholesome" because it is able to produce happiness; it brings to rest both types of evil:
those of commission and those of omission.
Because they are not associated with the unwholesome and are capable of producing suffering,
those born of retribution, deportment, craftsmanship, and transformation are declared to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it cannot arise;
for all that is done by an Arhat who has nothing more to learn.
It is generally termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) because it cannot bring about a future fruit; thus,
in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichizhong):
The offenses committed by Arhats are termed *avyākṛta* (indeterminate) *duṣkṛta* transgressions.
Since these offenses are indeterminate,
the same applies to wholesome states and so forth.
Fourth is the analysis according to principle.
"Principle" refers to the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which accords with this principle is called "wholesome."
That which contradicts reason is unwholesome;
that which neither contradicts nor accords with it is said to be indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Within this gate, all wholesome,
unwholesome, and indeterminate actions performed by ordinary persons are collectively termed "unwholesome."
The mind arises by grasping at intrinsic nature;
this contradicts the principle of emptiness.
The practice of the noble ones of the three vehicles accords with that principle.
It is designated as "wholesome.
The actions performed by the noble ones of the three vehicles according to their circumstances are described as "indeterminate."
The fifth is the discrimination regarding reality.
"Reality" refers to the non-empty nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
With respect to this real nature:
That which is concordant is called wholesome;
that which is discordant is called unwholesome;
that which is neither discordant nor concordant is described as indeterminate.
Within this gateway, the true realization,
practice, and virtue of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are designated as "wholesome."
All that is performed by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is entirely termed unwholesome;
within the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, one practices the cultivation of the untainted through conditions.
They are also wholesome and unwholesome.
That which accords with [the nature of reality] is called wholesome; because its nature is contrary [to that], it is unwholesome.
These are said to be unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Other non-sentient phenomena (*asattvākhya-dharma*) are said to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These two sections are concluded.
Next, we shall discuss persons.
"Persons" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas...
They possess three types of karma;
as for the Tathāgata alone,
there is a difference between the great and the small.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
it is proclaimed that the Tathāgata possesses wholesome and indeterminate karma, but no unwholesome karma;
as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Furthermore, as in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the Buddha’s responses to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are neutral,
while his other virtues are wholesome (*kuśala*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
it is proclaimed that the Tathāgata is exclusively wholesome, without being either unwholesome or neutral.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
Only the Tathāgata is entirely virtuous.
As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
The same applies here. Therefore,
he declares that the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are exclusively virtuous (*kuśala*), regardless of whether they are actions of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
This is a brief summary. 62.

The Meaning of Karma Resulting in the Three Types of Feeling (7). The Meaning of Karma Resulting in the Three Types of Feeling is explained through a threefold analysis: I. Defining the Names; II. Distinguishing by Way of Locus; III. [The Main Exposition]. First, the Definition of the Names.
Regarding the three types of sensation:
they are suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
That which is oppressive is called suffering.
That which is pleasant and delightful is called pleasure (*sukha*).
The sensation of neutral contentment abandons these two preceding types.
Therefore, it is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant; it is also called the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
As for what is called "action" (*karman*):
Because wholesome and unwholesome causes give rise to the three types of sensation,
they are called "karma. Question:
Good and evil can give rise to the five aggregates.
For what reason is it said specifically that they "receive karma," rather than being described as "karma of form" or "karma of perception" and so forth?
As stated in the "Chapter on the Three Feelings" of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
feeling is the actual retribution;
therefore, it is called "feeling-karma."
The remainder is called "retribution" (vipāka);
therefore, it is omitted here and not discussed.
As for the statement regarding "actual feeling" (vedanā):
The retributions of suffering, pleasure,
and so forth are the direct recompense for past causes of good and evil; therefore,
they are called the "actual retribution" (sabhāga-vipāka).
The remaining factors, such as form and so forth,
do not directly confront the two causes of good and evil;
therefore, they are not termed "real."
However, it is spoken of as a "retribution" by way of conventional designation;
therefore, it is called a "named retribution.
That treatise further states:
Feeling is the most excellent;
therefore, it is called "feeling-action.
The others are not like it.
This is why it is not mentioned.
As for what is called "superior," it refers to the clear manifestation of the response to causes, which gives rise to joy and revulsion.
Because its power and merit are strong,
it is called "victorious.
Others are not like this.
Therefore, it is called "not as [it appears].
That treatise further states:
"Within the conditions of sensation, distinct characteristics can be apprehended."
Therefore, it is called "receiving karma.
Other [types of karma] are not like this;
they are set aside and not discussed.
How can it be understood that feeling is conditioned by the mind?
It is as when people say, "fire is suffering" or "fire is pleasure";
all such cases are like this.
Because distinctions arise within the conditions of sensation (*vedanā*), the meaning of retribution (*vipāka*) is revealed;
therefore, it is called "karma of sensation. This concludes this section.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished. Question:
What karma can produce the sensation of suffering, and so forth, up to what karma can produce the sensation of equanimity?
The commentary states:
Evil karma can produce the sensation of suffering;
wholesome karma can produce both the sensations of pleasure and equanimity.
That evil karma results in suffering is a principle that can be understood.
Regarding good karma:
Regarding who attains pleasure and who attains equanimity,
two masters offer differing explanations in the *Vibhāṣā*.
One master explains:
goodness has three grades,
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
From the fourth dhyāna upward, there is the most excellent and sublime goodness,
which is able to attain the feeling of equanimity;
therefore, that treatise says:
Attaining neither-pain-nor-pleasure is called the supreme good;
the middle and lower [levels of] goodness follow.
All obtain pleasant sensations.
Question: For what reason do those in the lower stages lack the retribution of neutral sensation?
The Abhidharma commentary states:
"The lower stages are coarse;
equanimity is subtle."
The lower stages are not tranquil;
equanimity is tranquility.
Furthermore, when performing wholesome deeds in the lower stages, [the mind is not tranquil].
However, it is for the sake of experiencing pleasure and not for the sake of equanimity;
therefore, there is no retribution of the sensation of equanimity in the lower stages.
This is what is meant by that statement.
From the third dhyāna downward, there is no mind of retribution for one who passes away; thus,
there is no relinquishment of retribution.
Therefore, according to the system established by a certain master,
among the three grades of wholesome states, there are two wholesome states, namely the superior and the inferior.
One is able to attain equanimity;
in the intermediate state, one well attains pleasure. Thus it is said.
From the third dhyāna downward,
there is also the equanimity of retribution;
because there is the equanimity of retribution.
From the third dhyāna downwards,
one may also pass away within a resultant mind.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
this will be explained later,
among the three grades of wholesome [dharmas].
There are two types of wholesome states,
superior and inferior, which can produce the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). The inferior type can produce the retribution of the feeling of equanimity from the third dhyāna downward.
The superior [practitioner] is able to attain the retribution of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) from the fourth dhyāna upward.
This is truly because the arising of wholesome dharmas is not achieved instantaneously;
beginning subtly, they gradually become manifest, until finally they are subtle and wondrous, free from signs, and tranquil.
Therefore, those above and below equally obtain the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
while those in the middle obtain the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). Question:
Since equanimity arises from the wholesome and serves as the retribution for wholesome causes, it ought to be called "pleasure.
For what reason, then, is it called "equanimity"? There is a valid explanation for this:
it is that which is obtained by lower-order wholesome states.
It should properly be called pleasure;
however, because it is so subtle,
the perceiving mind does not discern it.
Therefore, it is called "equanimity.
That which is attained through supreme goodness is indeed a superior bliss,
because it is characterized by tranquility.
Because one abandons coarse discursive thought,
it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Question:
Regarding the statement that "the two types of pleasure, superior and inferior,
which are experienced are called equanimity," the wholesome karma capable of producing them should be termed neutral (*avyākṛta*).
To explain this:
This is incorrect.
For one who lacks mindfulness is unable to remember the karmic retribution of future lives.
Only then is it called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
This is because the meaning of "determinable" (vyākṛta) is the production of a fruit by a dharma; [an indeterminate dharma] merely causes a fruit to arise.
This is called "recording.
"Pleasure" has the meaning of being aware and cognizant.
There are two types of pleasure: superior and inferior.
Because the awakening of the mind is slight,
it is not called "joy";
it is designated as "equanimity."
Question: Regarding the pleasant fruit obtained from lower wholesome states,
it is called "equanimity" (upekṣā) because the mind's perception is subtle.
The slight suffering obtained from inferior unwholesome karma is also minimal in its perception by the mind. For what reason?
This is not called relinquishment.
The commentary states:
"It is not of the same category."
The nature of suffering is heavy and coarse;
its meaning of being contrary to the mind is powerful,
and all possess cognition.
Therefore, it is not called "equanimity.
The nature of pleasure is light and frivolous;
its arising does not conflict with the mind.
Because the meaning of the arising of cognition is subtle, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Question:
Suffering and pleasure both arise from karma.
For what reason is suffering coarse and pleasure subtle?
The explanation states:
it refers to all conditioned phenomena within the three realms.
Its essence is impermanence, characterized by arising and ceasing,
and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). That which is the sensation of suffering takes that subtle suffering of conditioned formations as its essence.
Suffering arises upon suffering;
because suffering increases, it is coarse.
As for those who experience pleasant feeling:
It also takes the subtle suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) as its essence;
because pleasure arises upon suffering and is merely superficial, it is termed "subtle."
Because suffering is coarse,
all sufferings, whether light or heavy,
are termed painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
Because pleasure is subtle, what is coarse is experienced as the feeling of pleasure (sukha-vedanā),
and what is subtle is experienced as the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā). This concludes the two sections.
In the third section, it is discussed in terms of the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the distinctions among the three worlds and the five destinies (*gati*).
First, their characteristics will be distinguished according to the three realms.
Regarding the karma of painful sensation,
it is as stated in the Abhidharma.
Its arising occurs in the desire realm,
and the retribution obtained from it likewise occurs in the desire realm.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the karma of painful sensation arises throughout the three realms.
It is bound to the desire realm;
it arises properly within the desire realm,
while the retribution obtained arises as a provisional occurrence in the higher realms.
It arises throughout the three realms,
is bound to the desire realm,
and the desire realm is its primary locus for receiving retribution.
The higher realms are the places where one temporarily dwells and experiences [existence].
It is asked:
how does suffering arise in the higher realms?
The commentary states:
When the retribution of the higher realms is about to end, one gives rise to a mind of distress;
this distress is subsumed under the category of painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*).
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Suffering and pleasure follow the body up to the fourth dhyāna;
grief and joy follow the mind up to the Peak of Existence."
Since both sorrow and suffering are subsumed under the category of painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*).
Regarding the karma of pleasant feeling (*sukhā-vedanīya-karman*),
according to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*):
The retribution received for [actions] up to and including the third dhyāna within the desire and form realms likewise exists up to and including the third dhyāna within the desire and form realms.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
karma that results in the retribution of pleasant feeling arises throughout all three realms.
It is bound to and situated within the third dhyāna and below;
the third dhyāna and below is its point of origination.
From the third dhyāna upward,
these are the places where [the state] arises;
they are the retributions obtained.
It also extends throughout the three realms;
it is bound to and belongs to the stages from the third dhyāna downwards.
From the third dhyāna downwards.
This is the locus of direct experience (*sākṣātkriyā*). From the third dhyāna upward,
these are loci of metaphorical experience (*upacāra*).
Regarding the karma of neutral feeling:
it arises throughout the three realms,
and its retribution is indeterminate.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is experienced within the three realms.
Question: [Why is this so?]
Since the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) pervades all three realms,
why does the Sūtra state that there is the sensation of equanimity above the fourth dhyāna?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
"Above the fourth dhyāna,
there are no further sensations."
Therefore, it is spoken of as "equanimity" (upekṣā) in a partial sense; however, in reality, this feeling of equanimity is not restricted to that level alone,
as it also extends to the lower stages.
According to the Abhidharma,
the retribution of the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) occurs only in the four dhyānas;
it does not exist in the lower stages.
If there is feeling in the lower stages,
it is a relinquishing by means of skillful methods;
the three realms are likewise.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished according to the five destinies.
Regarding karma that results in painful feeling:
it arises throughout all five realms of existence.
The same applies to the experience of retribution.
Within the three lower realms,
one experiences the collective retribution.
Regarding the two realms of humans and devas,
those who experience the karma of pleasant sensations undergo the suffering of individual retribution.
According to the Abhidharma,
the five destinies arise universally; thus,
one obtains the fruit of happiness.
There are both general and specific [results].
As for the result of general retribution,
it occurs only among humans and devas.
Regarding the pleasant sensation of individual retribution (vipāka),
it exists throughout the other four destinies, excluding only the hells. How is this known?
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
wholesome karma is of four types. The first is karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
Second, karma with retribution in the next life;
third, karma with retribution in subsequent lives;
fourth, karma with indefinite retribution.
Among these four types [of karma],
beings in the hells perform three,
excluding karma that ripens in the present life.
Because there is no retribution for wholesome karma within the hells,
the other four realms of existence fully give rise to all four types of karma.
It is clearly known that other realms of existence can all possess wholesome retribution;
this is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Karma that results in actual feeling arises throughout the five destinies;
it is the pleasant feeling thus obtained.
It also pervades the five destinies;
therefore, that treatise states:
"Wholesome karma has great benefit."
One obtains the rewards of humans and devas, up to and including nirvana.

Even with minor benefits from wholesome karma, one may obtain a small measure of happiness even within the three miserable realms. This refers to those who perform actions resulting in neutral feelings.
According to the Abhidharma,
it arises universally among humans and devas;
its retribution resides in the form realm heavens.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the karma of equanimity arises throughout all five destinies.
The same applies to the experiencing of the fruits.
This is a brief exposition of the three types of karma that yield retribution.

63. The Meaning of Karma Bound to the Three Realms (7). The Meaning of Karma Bound to the Three Realms: An Exposition by Way of Fivefold Analysis. 1. The Binder; 2. The Bound; 3. Analysis of the Locus; 4. Abandonment through Antidotes; 5. [Summary]. First, the Explanation of Names.
"Bound to the three realms" refers to karma bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
"Desire" refers to the desire realm.
Attachment to and craving for sensory objects is called "desire" (*kāma*); this term distinguishes [the realm of desire] from the higher realms.
This is called the desire realm;
however, within the desire realm,
one is also attached to one's own body.
They desire only the five sense objects;
since these exist below but not above,
this serves to distinguish them from the higher realms.
This refers to the name "desire" (kāmadhātu).
"Form" (rūpa) refers to the form realm (rūpadhātu),
so named in contrast to what lies below it.
It should be called "desireless.
Because within this realm one is attached to internal forms and shapes,
it is called "form" (rūpa) by virtue of that attachment.
The realm distinguished by form, categorized as superior and inferior, is called the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
That which is said to be "formless" refers to the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
From the perspective of what is grasped therein,
it should be called the mind-element (*manodhātu*); for within this element, the retribution of form is severed.
Because its name is manifested by way of excluding what is below,
it is called "formless" (ārūpya).
It is for this reason that it is distinguished from the lower realms and named the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Regarding the statement on "karmic fetters" (*bandhana-karman*),
there are four interpretations.
First, the meaning of "fettering" is distinguished by way of the essential nature of karma.
The substance of contaminated karma belongs to the three realms;
therefore, it is called "karma bound to the three realms.
Second, the meaning of "bondage" is distinguished by way of the attainment of results.
The place where karma with outflows receives its retribution is fixed within the three realms; therefore,
it is called "karma bound to the three realms."
Third, the bondage of the relative correspondence between karma and its fruit is distinguished:
within the three realms, there is the mutual binding of karma and its fruit.
Therefore, it is called "karma bound to the three realms.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"Beginning from the hells up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*)."
Among these, that which is experienced is called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
From the Brahma-world up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
that which is experienced therein is called "bound to the form realm" (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
From the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception,
the designation "formless" (ārūpya) refers to the experience of sensation within those realms.
The bondage [to these realms] is distinguished by four pairs of afflictions.
Because they are bound by the afflictions and conditions of their respective realms,
they are called "bound karma. Question:
Regarding the statement that they are called "bonds" because karma and its fruit are bound together by their common characteristics:
for what reason are they not called "fruition-bonds," but instead specifically termed "karma-bonds"?
The commentary states:
It is also possible to speak of "bondage" (saṃyojana) with reference to the fruit.
However, since this is based on the category of karma, it is called "karma that binds."
Furthermore, because karma is the root, it is specifically mentioned.
Again, it is asked:
"Afflictions (*kleśa*) are also able to bind the fruit."
For what reason are afflictions not described as "bonds," but rather is it specifically stated that karma is the bond?
To explain:
The principle of afflictions (*kleśa*) is also a bond;
however, because this discussion currently proceeds by way of the category of karma, it is called the "bond of karma.
Furthermore, because karma is the primary seed [of cyclic existence], it is specifically mentioned here.
Question: To which realm are the indeterminate and non-fixed retribution karmas bound?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains, saying:
This belongs to the realm of desire. Why is this?
Because it is the karmic retribution of the realm of desire.
He asked again:
"What is the distinction between bound karma and bound dharmas?
He explained, saying:
The fetters of karma are restricted to the three types of action and do not extend to other phenomena.
If one discusses the phenomena that are bound [by these fetters]:
The pervasive afflictions (*kleśa*), their associated mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and so forth, are all termed "bound phenomena" (*bandhana-dharma*).
Such is the meaning of the term; this concludes the first section.
Next, the fetters are analyzed;
therein are four points.
First, the distinction between the outflowing (*āsava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsava*).
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is bound;
that which is without outflows (anāsrava) is not fixed.
This is according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
It is exclusively unconditioned.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma,
there are two types of untainted [phenomena].
The first is true realization,
which is exclusively unconditioned;
the second is illuminating through conditions.
They are both bound and unbound;
with respect to the fruit of the limited portion,
they neither accumulate nor summon it.
Therefore, it is called "unbound.
In relation to the fruit of transformation,
cause and effect are mutually bound.
It is also called "bondage," because one undergoes the ripening of karmic results within the world of transformation.
Second, regarding the classification by way of the wholesome, unwholesome,

and indeterminate: if it is said that the essence of karma definitely belongs to the three realms and is called "bound karma" (saṃyojana-karma) because it is bound by the afflictions of its respective realm;
All contaminated (sāsrava) actions— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—
are termed "bound karma" (bandhana-karma).
If one says that the attainment of their fruits necessarily belongs to the three realms, [it is so].
Furthermore, that which is bound by the mutual constraints of cause and effect within the three realms is called "bondage.
Conditioned wholesome and unwholesome actions are termed "binding karma."
It is neutral and unconditioned,
because it lacks karmic retribution.
Within those two types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome— [it is neither].
Unwholesome karma is invariably bound to the desire realm.
Wholesome karma is of two types:
one is fixed, and the other is distracted.
The "disturbed" refers to wholesome states such as generosity and ethical discipline that are bound to the desire realm.
The "concentrated" refers to the karmic activities of the eight dhyāna concentrations.
Among these eight, the four dhyānas belong to the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
while the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) constitute their karma.
They are bound to the formless realm.
Thirdly, they are distinguished according to the actions of body, speech, and mind;
the two actions of body and speech are bound to the realms of desire and form.
The single category of mental karma (manas-karma) pervades all three realms.
These four are distinguished according to demerit, merit, and immovability.
"Sin" refers to unwholesome karma;
"merit" refers to scattered wholesome karma.
As for what is called "immovability":
The eighth is the karma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Among these three types,
there are the two karmas of demerit and merit.
Karma bound to the desire realm and immovable karma are bound to the two higher realms; this concludes these two sections.
Next, the objects of bondage are distinguished.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the correlation with the karma that binds.
Clarifying that which is bound.
Second, the factors associated with bondage;
clarifying that which is bound.
Within the classification of those bound by karma, there are four distinctions.
First, the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
according to the Abhidharma.
Contaminated resultant dharmas arise from karma and are bound by that karma;
uncontaminated [dharmas] do not arise from contaminated karma.
They are not bound by karma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all contaminated phenomena arise from past contaminated karma.
These are bound by karma.
Furthermore, untainted dharmas also arise from past acts such as giving and ethical discipline.
However, these are the fruits of karma rather than being bound by karma.
Why is this so? Because the sūtras speak of the existence of "unbound" sensations (*asaṃprayukta-vedanā*).
Furthermore, the arising of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) necessarily relies upon causes,
and their production necessarily depends upon conditions.
This refers to the wholesome roots previously cultivated, such as generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Taking this as a condition,
the skillful means of the untainted [path] takes it as its cause;
because the power of the cause is great.
Therefore, they are not bound.
The commentary explains it thus:
if one says that cause and effect are mutually connected and designated as such, this is called "bondage."
This principle is also unassailable;
within the Mahāyāna teachings,
there is the true realization of the untainted (anāsrava).
That which is not bound by karma is subject to transformation; that which is untainted (anāsrava) is bound by karma.
The second and third natures are conceptualized;
according to the Abhidharma,
among the indeterminate dharmas, there are those that are indeterminate by way of retribution.
This is the fruit of karma;
it is bound by karma, whereas the remainder are not bound by karma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, those of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) all arise from past contaminated karma.
Because one is bound by this karma,
that treatise states:
"I say that there are three kinds of karmic retribution."
Regarding the categories of wholesome,
unwholesome, and indeterminate:
as for what is called a "wholesome retribution," it refers to those who, because they cultivated wholesome dharmas in the past, now receive a purely wholesome retribution.
As for the retribution of unwholesome karma:
being a eunuch and the like is the retribution for lust;
venomous snakes, scorpions, and the like are the retribution for hatred.
In this way, all such results of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) are to be understood according to their meaning.
This is because of the retribution of karma;
one is bound by this karma.
Furthermore, that treatise states:
All phenomena that arise have karma as their root.
If there were no root of karma, how could they arise?
Therefore, it is known.
All phenomena are bound by karma.
There are three internal-external distinctions according to the Abhidharma system.
The internal retribution of sentient beings arises from karma;
they are bound by this karma.
As for external objects such as mountains, rivers, and all other realms, [they likewise arise from karma].
It is not born from karma;
it is not bound by karma.
Question: Why is this so?
All mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the fruits of the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of sentient beings.
How can it be said that they are not bound by karma?
Furthermore, when a person performs wholesome deeds, they are reborn in a favorable realm.
If a person commits evil and is consequently born in an evil realm,
how can it be said that they are not bound by karma?
The Abhidharma explains:
External things such as mountains and rivers take the four great elements of external phenomena as their cause;
because they do not arise from karma, they are not bound by karma.
Regarding the statement that performing virtuous karma leads to birth in a favorable realm, while performing non-virtuous karma leads to birth in an unfavorable realm:
the power of karma is like the wind; it is because of the wind of virtuous karma [that one is born in a favorable realm].
They blow upon all sentient beings;
because of the winds of evil karma, they experience pleasure in favorable realms.
They blow upon all sentient beings,
causing them to suffer in evil realms; yet,
as for their own dwelling place, [they remain there].
Since it does not arise from karma,
it is not bound by karma.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
All things, both internal and external, are the fruits of karma;
they are all that which is bound. Question:
External phenomena do not belong to the category of sentient beings;
they exist inherently from the outset and do not arise through karma.
Why, then, is it said that this is bound by karma?
Furthermore, external phenomena arise from their own kind,
just as beans produce beans and wheat produces wheat.
Why is it that, regarding karma, one speaks of "the fruit of karma" and "being bound by karma"?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
although external phenomena do not belong to the category of sentient beings, [they are still affected].
However, because these are the fruits of the collective karma of sentient beings,
they likewise arise from karma.
If one were to say that external phenomena arise through the mutual production of similar types and do not depend on karma, [it would be incorrect].
This meaning is not so.
Why is it not so? It is like those sentient beings.
Although born from the union of father and mother,
it also depends upon karma;
external phenomena are likewise so.
Although they are of the same class and arise mutually as causes for one another,
it is due to karma.
What harm is there?
Furthermore, not all things arise solely from causes of their own kind.
It is clearly known that,
as at the beginning of a kalpa, all things arise without cause.
By virtue of karma;
because they arise from karma, they are bound by karma.
There is a fourfold and threefold classification [of these].
Regarding the "three aggregates," they are namely:
form, mind, and that which is neither form nor mind.
This is according to the Abhidharma.
Among material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
only the five sense faculties as retribution (*vipāka*) and their corresponding objective supports— the matter of color, odor, taste,
and tangibility that sustain them— are the fruits of karma.
That which is bound by karma— namely,
all other expedient means that nourish the five sense organs such as the eye and the five external objects—
is entirely not the fruit of karma.
They are not bound by karma.
Among mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*),
there are only those minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) born of retribution (*vipāka*).
This is the fruit of that karma;
it is bound by karma.
As for all other mental factors of the three natures, they are likewise so.
None of these are the fruit of karma;
they are not bound by karma,
nor are they among the mental factors.
Only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the retribution of the non-percipient heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*), the category of sentient beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and their associated arising, abiding,
and ceasing are the dharmas of retribution bound by karma.
All others are not retribution;
they are not bound by karma.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Among the phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*),
there are all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and all mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
Furthermore, that which is neither form nor mind is universally both the fruit of karma and bound by karma.
The preceding four sections have distinguished [the factors] in relation to karma; next,
they clarify what is bound by distinguishing them in relation to the bound phenomena (*saṃyojana-dharma*).
According to the Abhidharma,
all contaminated phenomena within the stages of the desire realm are bound by the afflictions of the desire realm as their conditions.
They are termed "bound to the desire realm.
All contaminated phenomena within the stages of the form realm are bound by the afflictions of the form realm as their conditions.
They are bound to the realm of name-and-form;
the same applies to the formless realm.
This point is not maintained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. These three gates are concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish the characteristics of bondage according to the spheres of existence.
Based on the Abhidharma,
this concerns karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It arises only in the desire realm;
at the time it receives its retribution,
it is likewise in the desire realm.
Karma bound to the realm of form arises in the realms of desire and form;
it is at that time that its retribution is experienced.
It exists only in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and does not extend to other places;
this applies to karma of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as well.
The arising [of these states] extends throughout the three realms;
however, at the time of receiving retribution,
it must necessarily be in the formless realm.
Question: Why is it that within the lower realms one can give rise to karma of the higher realms,
yet while the body is in the higher realms one does not give rise to karma of the lower realms?
The commentary states:
Because the afflictions of that realm and stage have been severed,
the body is born in a higher realm.
The dharmas of the lower stages have been abandoned;
therefore, one who is in a higher stage does not give rise to karma of the lower stages. Question:
If karma bound to the desire realm were to be experienced only in the desire realm and not in other places,
then it would contradict what is said in the sūtras regarding the merit of washing the feet of the Saṃgha.
Attaining birth in the Brahma-world and the scattered wholesome karma of washing for the Sangha are both karmas of the desire realm.
How does one obtain the experience of the higher realms?
The explanation says:
through the causal conditions of the merit of washing the Sangha, one is led to give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, one is born in the Brahma-world.
It is not that the merit of washing the Sangha can directly produce birth there;
rather, the sutra speaks of it in terms of remote conditions.
It is said that by bathing monks, one may be reborn in the Brahma world.
Furthermore, it was asked:
"Meditative concentration (dhyāna) is the karma for the higher realms."
Regarding the fact that feeling belongs only to the higher realms and not the lower ones,
the Sūtra states:
"One who cultivates loving-kindness is reborn in the Brahma-world as its direct retribution."
In subsequent births within the desire realm, body and mind are free from affliction;
how then can it be said that this is not an experience of the lower realms?
The commentary explains:
The essence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is karma of the higher realms;
it is experienced only in the higher realms,
as stated in the Sūtras.
Regarding those who are subsequently born with bodies in the desire realm that are free from affliction:
when they cultivate loving-kindness, this refers to the preliminary and subsequent preparatory stages.
With body and speech made supple, one does not afflict sentient beings.
Because this skillful means is wholesome within the desire realm, one is born in the desire realm with body and mind free from affliction.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
karma bound to the three realms arises in its own respective stage,
yet it may also arise by way of being deposited within another realm.
For example, if one cultivates and gives rise to the eight dhyānas while in the desire realm,
this constitutes the lower realm temporarily giving rise to the karma of the higher realms;
furthermore, it is like giving rise to wrong views and so forth while in the higher realms.
This is like the arousal of unwholesome states belonging to the lower realms;
it is also like when the Bhagavan King of the First Dhyāna said to the Brahmā assembly,
"You should simply remain here."
I can lead you to the end of old age and death;
you need not go to where Gautama is.
This is also merely an arising of unwholesome desire pertaining to the realm of desire.
Furthermore, when the various Brahmās and others see the Buddha, prostrate before him, and speak words of praise,
they thereby give rise to wholesome karma of the desire realm.
Question: Since mental states such as wrong view in the higher realms are indeterminate (avyākṛta),
why is it said that those in the lower realms are unwholesome (akuśala)?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains, saying:
"The Sūtra states that wrong view is a causal condition for suffering."
It is just as all four great elements (mahābhūta) associated with painful retribution are entirely suffering;
such is the case with wrong view.
How, then, could it be indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
Because it is unwholesome,
it is bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun):
The fruits of the three realms may likewise be received through provisional reliance,
as in the case of the two aforementioned realms.
When the retribution for one's desires is about to end,
the mind gives rise to anxiety and distress;
such is the suffering of this affliction.
It is bound to the desire realm;
it is experienced provisionally in the higher realms.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
The merit of washing the monks enables one to be born in the Brahma world;
this too is the reception of the fruits of desire within the upper realms as a provisional dwelling.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras: "By means of the causal conditions of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
one is born directly in the Brahma-world."
In a future life, one will have no affliction of body or mind within the desire realm;
this is also the reception of superior retribution while temporarily residing in the desire realm.
According to the Mahāyāna teachings:
This is consistent with the explanation in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
all karmas are able to arise by depending [upon it].
All are received as provisional entrustments;
even the primary retribution is likewise received as a provisional entrustment.
This concludes the four gates concerning the remaining traces of defilements.
Next, the methods for their treatment and eradication are distinguished; therein are two parts.
First, a general clarification of the cessation of afflictions;
second, a specific discussion according to the stages.
Regarding what is called "general":
In the Abhidharma system,
unwholesome volitional karma is associated with the afflictions.
The essence of right abandonment is such that,
by virtue of this essence of abandonment,
it is the point at which this karma is exhausted.
This is called analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
As for all other remaining evil actions of body and speech,
as well as all wholesome actions:
It is only the meaning of the binding of volitional karma that is severed,
not the substance of karma; it is not the substance of karma that is severed.
Therefore, it is not called "cessation through calculation. In the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it is because of the abandonment of the afflictions.
To cause karma not to arise is called "the severing of karma.
However, within that school...
By abandoning the afflictions,
one causes karma not to arise;
all such instances constitute analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This differs from the Abhidharma,
which contains both what is correct and what is incorrect;
therefore, that treatise states:
Dharmas to be abandoned through seeing refer to the conceit of manifesting characteristics and all other dharmas arising therefrom.
Dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation refer to...
It does not indicate the pride of manifesting characteristics (*nimittamāna*) nor the other various dharmas arising from it.
The pride of manifesting characteristics is an affliction abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*).
As for the "dharmas arising from it":
This refers to the karma and the fruit of suffering produced thereby;
the pride that does not manifest its characteristics is an affliction of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
As for the phenomena that arise:
This refers to the karma produced by this [ignorance] and its resulting fruit of suffering;
therefore, one knows that the locus of cessation is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, [this is so].
One also severs the substance of karma,
because one knows that all karmas arise from the deluded mind and are fundamentally non-existent.
Such is the general characteristic.
Next, let us discuss this by way of the various stages individually.
According to the Abhidharma,
the evil karma of the three miserable realms [is as follows].
Some are abandoned through seeing;
some are abandoned through cultivation.
This has been so for ordinary beings from time immemorial.
Karma arising from afflictions abandoned through seeing the truths is severed at the time of the path of seeing.
Ordinary persons who have previously arisen [in this state] are those whose [defilements] have been produced based on the defilements of the path of cultivation.

The abandonment of the nine unimpeded paths (*anantarya-mārga*) through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is explained in detail in the subsequent chapter on the four types of karma.
This refers to the distinct retributions for evil karma experienced by humans and devas within the stages of the desire realm.
At the time of attaining the stage of anāgāmin, all [karmic results] are severed.
This includes the wholesome karma of humans and devas;
at the time of attaining the stage of anāgāmin, [it is all cut off].
Having eternally severed their fetters,
when one is born into a higher stage,
they never again manifest.
Regarding wholesome karma of the higher realms,
its fetters are severed by nine distinct paths of non-obstruction according to each respective level; thus,
one is born into the higher levels.
At the time of entering nirvana,
they never again function.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
The evil karma of the three miserable realms is exclusively severed within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Question: [Why is this so?]
In the Abhidharma, among the karmas of the three miserable realms, they are divided into two categories:
those abandoned through insight (darśana-heya) and those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Why is it established as such?
[The treatise] explains that the evil karma of the three miserable realms is abandoned only by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The commentary states:
The two schools differ in their discernment of delusions.
Within the Abhidharma system,
ordinary beings give rise to both the afflictions of the wheel of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*) and the wheel of cultivating the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Those arising from delusion regarding principles are the afflictions of the vision of the truths; those arising from attachment to phenomena are [the afflictions of the path of cultivation].
These are the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
These two types of afflictions both give rise to unwholesome mental karma that leads to the three miserable realms.
When the creation of karma is completed,
there is always that which can obtain the dharma;
it obtains those past karmas.
It is bound to the practitioner.
At the time of entering the path of seeing,
it is the unwholesome category arising from the delusions of seeing.
All are attained as being severed.
At the time of the nine unimpeded paths of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm,
the unwholesome categories arising from the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) [are abandoned].
Because all [defilements] are severed [thereby],
they are divided into two locations:
the two types of karma, namely bodily and vocal action.
Only the afflictions of the desire realm arise;
because they are abandoned through worldly [paths] and abandoned moment by moment,
there is no acquisition of their acquisition.
It is merely the volition of karma belonging to the desire realm that binds;
when that karmic volition is severed, [one is liberated].
Those fetters are also severed;
therefore, it is called "severance. This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (The Establishment of Reality).
During the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), only the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) arise;
although the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are present, they do not manifest. Why is this so?
Within that school,
all afflictions possess the nature of grasping; for ordinary beings,
when they give rise to delusion, this nature of grasping is particularly heavy.
They are abandoned at the time of the path of seeing;
therefore, all afflictions arising in ordinary persons are termed "delusions of view."
When sages give rise to delusion,
its nature is subtle and slight;
when ordinary beings give rise to delusion, it is gross.
It cannot be so; therefore,
while one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) do not arise.
This is because, according to that school, afflictions pertaining only to the time of seeing [the truths] arise;
therefore, the evil karma of the three miserable realms all arises from the delusions of seeing.
Therefore, all [such karma] is abandoned solely by the Path of Seeing.
This includes the distinct retributive evil karma of humans and devas in the desire realm,
as well as all wholesome karma of the desire realm.
When one attains the state of an Anāgāmin,
one no longer engages in any [unwholesome] actions;
although there may be wholesome acts such as prostration within that state, [they do not constitute the "path"].
It is called arising through the application of the mind;
it is untainted (anāsrava) and wholesome,
and is not karma of the desire realm.
Wholesome karma of the upper realms does not arise at all, depending on the point where the fetters are severed.
Although one practices such activities as meditative concentration within that state,
it is called "arising through the application of mind" and is not a bound activity.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma,
for those who have not yet committed the evil karma of the three miserable realms,
this occurs at the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Ultimately, they do not arise.
As for those that have already arisen,
they are either heavy or light.
That which is heavy is fixed;
that which is light is unfixed.
As for what is called "fixed":
There are three kinds of determinate karma:
first, determinate in time, because its retribution is to be experienced at a fixed time— either in the present life, the next life, or a subsequent life.
Second is the certainty of retribution,
because the fruit is definitely attained.
Third is the certainty of location.
Because they are fixed upon receiving retribution within the three miserable realms (triyapatha),
those that are "unfixed" (aniyata) are likewise of three kinds.
First, the timing is indeterminate,
because there is no fixed time for its manifestation— whether in the present life or in a future life.
Second, the retribution is indeterminate.
When encountering conditions, it undergoes [rebirth]; when lacking conditions, it does not.
Its three locations are indeterminate within the six realms of existence.
When they receive [an offering], they accept it immediately,
for there is no fixed place [for them].
As for those whose karma is fixed:
The lineage is severed at that time;
it is no longer utilized,
and one undergoes evil retribution.
Because of the mastery of being reborn in higher lineages,
those indeterminate karmas are severed at the time of the first bhūmi.
Therefore, it is proclaimed in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* that on the first bhūmi one is free from the fear of the evil realms.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The Bodhisattva of the stage of practice through understanding transforms the retribution of the evil realms and enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi),
clearly knowing [this].
In the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), evil karma is forever exhausted;
from the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*) and below, one takes birth by means of the power of compassion and vows.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Those in the stages of lineage (*gotra*) and conduct (*caryā*) may be reborn in the evil realms."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Regarding the bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*),
their past karma, which is as vast as atoms..."

The explanation states:
the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are consistently weary of and detached from saṃsāra.
Because one neither desires nor falls [into them],
at the time of seeing the Path (darśanamārga),
one will ultimately never again undergo the karma of the three evil destinies.
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages,
out of compassion and their vows,
undergo evil retributions within the three miserable realms for the sake of sentient beings.
If that is so, why is the ground not experienced [as suffering]?
Because karma has been exhausted;
it is due to the specific retributive evil karma of humans and devas in the desire realm.
These are also completely and eternally exhausted upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Such is the case with unwholesome karma;
as for the wholesome karma of humans and devas that has not yet arisen, [it is likewise].
Upon reaching the first stage,
one perceives that all phenomena are empty and quiescent,
thereby relinquishing grasping and attachment.
It does not arise again.
If one discusses this more broadly,
it refers to those above the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Seeing the suchness of all phenomena,
one no longer gives rise to them;
as for those already arisen—
There are also two kinds:
first, that which arises from a mind characterized by the nature of being bound to meditative concentration;

The mind of conventional designation arises;
within that meditative absorption,

The same applies to the indeterminate. Regarding those who are correct within meditative concentration,

One no longer uses it to undergo rebirth within the three realms of existence,

From the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward,

Therefore, that *Upadeśa* on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* proclaims that the first stage (*bhūmi*) is the departure from the fragmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
A Bodhisattva of the first stage attains twenty-five samādhis and transcends the twenty-five states of existence.
It is clearly known that,
within the indeterminate [karma], all right action belonging to the first stage, where the retribution of the three realms of existence is exhausted, [is such].
From the first bhūmi upward,
one still receives a physical body;
although within those from the first bhūmi onward there exists the dharma-nature body, it remains internal.
Because they are still mixed with those retributions,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) proclaims that those in the seventh stage possess a physical body (*māṃsa-kāya*).
The excellence lies precisely here;

it is brought to ultimate completion and exhaustion.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those from the eighth stage upward are called Anāgāmins;

Furthermore, within the indeterminate state, there are no longer any foul bodies or insect-like bodies,
yet subtle habitual tendencies remain.
It is only upon reaching Buddhahood that [the seeds] are fully exhausted; because they are not yet fully exhausted even at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*),

Only the Buddha has exhausted them;
