Regarding the three types of retributive karma,
these are the karma of retribution in the present life, the next life, and subsequent lives.
It is that which yields its fruit in the present.
This is termed "manifestation.
Next, when the retribution of the present arises,
it is designated as "birth."
That which arises in a future life and is subsequently experienced is called "the later"; this refers to the arising of wholesome or unwholesome states in the present.
The performance of those retributions is called the "threefold karma of retribution.
Such is the meaning of the names.
What are their characteristics?
Their opening and closing are not fixed;
they may sometimes divide into two.
This refers to the determinate and the indeterminate.
That which is to be experienced at three specific times is called determinate.
Those with indeterminate feeling are called "indeterminate," or they may be divided into three types.
Because it is governed by time,
there is no such thing as karma that manifests in a later life after one has already been born.
This is because there is no time for the manifestation of retribution once one has already been born.

Karma that is determinate or indeterminate and which yields retribution in the present life is collectively termed "present karma" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*); the same applies to [karma] yielding retribution in the next life or subsequent lives.
Alternatively, they are divided into four,
as stated in the sūtras:
the three aforementioned types plus one more.
Furthermore, adding one type of indeterminate retribution karma makes four;
these include karma created in the present life.
If one experiences [the result] while still living, one receives it in the present. If one does not experience it while still living,
then that which is not experienced in the present is called karma with immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
If karma is performed in the present life and its retribution is to be experienced in the immediately following birth,
yet it is not experienced there, then it is called "karma whose retribution is experienced in the next life" (upapadyavedanīya-karma).
If karma performed in the present is to be experienced in a subsequent life,
yet is not experienced in that subsequent life,
it is termed "karma with a later retribution" (aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman) because it is not experienced at all.
If one performs an action in the present,
it will be experienced upon encountering the necessary conditions within any of the three periods of time.
That which is neither encountered nor received is called "indeterminate retribution" (aniyata-vipāka). Alternatively,
when classified separately, there are eight types.
Regarding the four preceding karmas,
each has both determinate and indeterminate results;
thus, there are eight.
What are their characteristics?
There is karma that belongs to the present and whose fruit is definitely experienced in the present;
this is considered as one type.
There is karma that belongs to the present but whose fruition in the present is indeterminate;
it is experienced when conditions are encountered and not experienced when they are not.
Thus, these are considered two types.
There is karma pertaining to birth that definitely receives its retribution at the time of birth;
this is considered threefold.
There is also karma pertaining to birth whose retribution at the time of birth is not fixed.
When conditions meet, one receives [the result]; when they do not meet, one does not.
Thus, there are four [types].
There is karma that belongs to a future life and whose retribution is fixed to be received at a later time, being irreversible.
Thus, there are five types.
There are actions that belong to a future life, yet the timing of their retribution is indefinite;
they are experienced when conditions converge, and not experienced when they do not.
Thus, they consider there to be six [categories].
There are actions that are not fixed as belonging to any of the three time periods,
yet which will certainly yield their retribution within those three periods without fail.
Thus, they consider there to be seven [types of karma]:
there is karma that is not fixed as belonging to any of the three time periods, yet its retribution across the three time periods is also indeterminate;
it is received when conditions converge, and not received when they do not.
Thus, they are considered to be eight.
Within these eight types,
there are four distinct categories of meaning.
As it is said in the sutras:
first, that which is fixed in time but indefinite in its retribution;
second, that which is fixed in retribution but indefinite in its time.
In three time periods, both are determinate;
in four time periods, both are indeterminate.
What are their characteristics?
Within those three types of determinate karma,
they are divided into two categories:
that which is certain to yield its retribution.
This is considered a single phrase.
The time and the attainment are both fixed;
for those who have not yet attained it, they are not fixed.
Furthermore, this constitutes one phrase.
At that time, the timing is fixed while the retribution is unfixed;
within those three types of unfixed karma regarding timing, they are further divided into two phrases.
Regarding those whose retribution is fixed:
this constitutes one category.
In this case, the retribution is certain, but the timing is not.
The phrase "indeterminate attainment" constitutes another single clause.
Both the time and the retribution are indeterminate; this concludes the present section.
Next, the nature of karma is distinguished.
If one determines that karma in relation to the three types of retribution,
its characteristics are easily differentiated.

Among all karmas, that which is experienced in the present life is called "present karma" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma). That which is to be experienced in the immediately following birth is [called "next-life karma"].

That which is experienced in the subsequent lifetime is called "subsequent karma. That which is experienced in the intermediate lifetime is called "intermediate karma. That which is experienced in the present life is called "present-life karma. These are what are taught as the karmic activities that produce birth. As for those experienced in the subsequent lifetime, they are taught as "subsequent karma."
If one determines their characteristics based on the four types of karma, there are two distinctions.
First, the distinction according to the mind:
those who seek retribution in the present life.
That which is said to produce results in the present life is called "karma of the present. That which is said to produce results upon rebirth is called "karma of rebirth."
That which seeks a future retribution is called "subsequent karma";
that which has no expectation or intention is [not so].
Furthermore, those who perform actions are said to be indeterminate.
Second, regarding the characteristics of action, they are distinguished according to their respective meanings.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
that which is beneficial yet not heavy is karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
That is to say, repeatedly giving rise to thoughts of both good and evil toward the Buddha, the various noble ones and sages, one's parents,
and so forth; and repeatedly giving rise to thoughts of fame and profit.
Arising without earnestness is termed "lack of respect.
Because one repeatedly gives rise to both good and evil in pursuit of superior realms,
one consequently obtains retribution in the present life.
If one performs an action with intense mental focus toward a superior object,
the retribution thereof will be vast and extensive,
such that it cannot be experienced in the present life.
Therefore, those actions that are exclusively simple and not grave constitute karma for retribution in the present life.
A question is asked:
If it is said that what is beneficial yet not grave results in retribution in the present life, [how is this so?]
Lady Mallikā bestowed a single meal upon the Buddha and immediately attained its manifest fruit;
why wait for future benefit?
The Buddha replied: "There is a reason for this.
There are those who, through their merit, obtain immediate retribution that is both beneficial and not insignificant."
This refers to karma that is experienced in the present life and yields results in the present life;
it is discussed in terms of its cause and does not depend upon its conditions.
As for Lady Mallikā attaining the fruit [of enlightenment] by offering a single meal to the Buddha,
this is categorized according to her intention;
it is karma that yields its retribution in the present life.
Because it seeks immediate retribution.
If one distinguishes four types of karma based on their functional characteristics (*karmalakṣaṇa*),
this is indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*).
One may obtain a present retribution for karma that does not have its retribution in the present;
because it is not sharp,
it can only serve as a condition to assist past indeterminate karma with retribution to cause one to receive the fruit in the present.
Not related to external conditions,
it is grave yet not beneficial;
this is karma to be experienced in the next life.
This means that regarding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and so forth, within a single objective sphere,

Regarding the aforementioned objects,
this opposition and harm arises,
yet it is not with an extremely heavy mind.
Because it cannot be accomplished or resolved,
it is said to be grave; since this retribution is grave, [it is so called].
One may not receive it in the present life. Why is this so?
Because the body is small.
Then there will be no great suffering;
because life is brief,
there will be no long-lasting affliction.
Therefore, one does not undergo the heavy retribution for the karma of the five heinous crimes in the present life;
because the drawing forth of that retribution is so urgent.
Because it does not reach the subsequent middle,
one experiences its arising;
it is both beneficial and grave.
These are karmas of subsequent retribution,
namely the karma of a Wheel-Turning King, a Bodhisattva, and so forth;
such karma is difficult to accomplish.
Without calculation, one cannot attain it; therefore, Sūri,
that retribution is difficult to ascend.
Only through the utmost sincerity can it be achieved;
therefore, it must be treated with gravity,
for it is difficult to accomplish.
If it is experienced later in the intermediate state,
it is neither harmful nor heavy;
this is an indeterminate karma.
Within this category of karma,
both manifest and non-manifest [karma] are discussed collectively in terms of both wholesome and unwholesome [actions].
Among the karmas to be experienced in the present life,
its evil aspects are specifically emphasized;
as for the karmas to be experienced in future lives...
This merely emphasizes their virtues;
it is simply a matter of being hidden or manifest. This concludes the two gates.
Next, we shall distinguish their characteristics according to the realms (*dhātu*) and destinies (*gati*).
The realms refer to the three realms;
the destinies refer to the six destinies.
First, their karma will be analyzed with respect to the three realms.
Within the three realms,
each and every one is capable of fully giving rise to the four types of karma;
such is the general characteristic.
If one were to discuss them by distinguishing between persons and lands,
they would be immeasurable.
"Persons" refers to both ordinary beings and sages.
"Grounds" refers to the nine grounds,
beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Within these nine grounds, ordinary worldlings—
Wherever one may be, as long as the afflictions of one's own stage have not been exhausted,
[one remains] within that very stage.
One fully gives rise to the four types of karma.
If one has exhausted the fetters, while remaining within the desire realm, [one does not give rise to them].
A person who has regressed from their spiritual lineage (gotra) fully generates the four types of karma within their own stage (bhūmi).
Because they can fall back and be reborn in their own stage, there is karma for birth;
the other three [types of karma] may be understood accordingly. If one does not fall back...
Within its own stage,
it performs only three types of karma,
excluding those that result in rebirth in the next life.
The other three types arise because those who are non-retrogressive will necessarily be born in a higher stage in their next life; thus,
they exist within the eight higher stages.
When the fetters of one's own stage are exhausted,
regardless of whether one is subject to regression or not,
within that very stage.
All [beings] perform the three types of karma,
with the exception of karma that results in retribution in the next life; they exhaust the fetters of their own respective stages.
Furthermore, because one's subsequent body will necessarily be born in a higher realm,
and because there is no falling back from any of the higher realms.
Without discriminating against those who have regressed,
it is thus within their own stage;
as for the higher stages:
In cases where the fetters have not been exhausted,
one fully engages in the three types of karma, with the exception of karma that yields retribution in the present life.
Because the body is situated below;
that is, the body is in the desire realm while [the object] is in a higher stage.
Even those who have fallen from their spiritual lineage (gotra) give rise to the three types of karma at the point where their fetters (saṃyojana) have been exhausted.
Excluding those with karma to be experienced in the present life,
because their bodies are in a lower state; this refers to those who have regressed from their spiritual lineage (gotra).
Since it is possible to regress from that state and be reborn in those [higher] stages,
there exists karma for rebirth;
the subsequent points regarding the meaning of "subsequent" (*paścāt*) and "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) may be understood accordingly.
If one does not regress,
one creates only two types of karma,
excluding karma for the present life.
There are two other types.
Because the body is in a lower realm,
karma with immediate retribution is excluded.
Because those who do not regress have exhausted the fetters of that stage,
they will certainly be reborn in a higher stage in their next body; therefore,
karma that results in rebirth [in that same stage] is excluded.
If the body is situated from the first dhyāna upwards,
reaching as far as the sphere of nothingness,
it reaches the point where afflictions are exhausted within those higher stages.
One need not inquire whether they are subject to regression or non-regression;
in all higher stages,
both types of karma arise.
These are what are called karma with subsequent retribution and karma with indefinite retribution;
because their bodies are in the lower realms,
they do not create karma of the present life.
Because there is no falling away from the heavens,
the body subsequently arises wherever there is a locus for the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore, it is at the locus where the fetters are exhausted [that liberation occurs].
Not performing the karma that leads to rebirth,
while his body resides in a higher realm,
he acts within a lower realm.
Nothing arises at all because the lower fetters have been severed;
such is the Abhidharma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the body of an ordinary person exists within all stages,
yet it belongs to its own specific stage.
Whether fetters are exhausted or not,
all give rise to the four types of karma within the higher stages.
In the meditative states one has attained, the three types of karma are fully produced;
with the exception of karma to be experienced in the present life,
the other three kinds are produced.
Within the lower stages,
three types [of karma] also arise,
excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.
Because, in that school’s doctrine, the karma of the three realms can arise through dependence [on them],
such is the case for ordinary beings.
Next, we shall discuss the noble ones (*ārya*).
As for the noble ones (ārya),
even if their bodies reside in the desire realm, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna,
as long as the afflictions (kleśa) of their respective stages have not been exhausted.
In each of these stages, all four types of karma arise;
this is because beings are frequently reborn in these four stages. Thus, while the body resides in the first dhyāna, [the mind may be in other stages].
Within their own realm, as long as the afflictions have not been exhausted,
they perform only the three types of karma.
Excluding their subsequent retribution,
for what reason is it so?
It is because of the devas within the First Dhyāna.
Although there are three locations, there are only two [realms]:
the Brahmakāyika is one location,
comprising both the Brahmapurohita and the Mahābrahma.
They exist in the same location;
because a Sage does not take rebirth in that same place,
there is no karma resulting in a subsequent retribution.
The Abhidharma is thus. However,
according to the Avataṃsaka, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra,
and other sources, the first dhyāna consists of four heavens and three abodes.
Thus, even while abiding in the first dhyāna, a noble one (ārya) also gives rise to the four types of karma.
Although the bodies of all noble ones reside within the four formless attainments (ārūpya),
their afflictions (kleśa) have not yet been exhausted within their own respective stages.
All give rise to two types of karma:
namely, karma with immediate retribution and karma with indefinite retribution.
Regarding karma with immediate retribution:
One receives them according to the body;
thus there are present karma and indeterminate karma.
Because it is received in the present,
there is indeterminacy;
for there is no multiplicity of locations.
For all those in training, there is no karma that results in rebirth in this life or in subsequent lives, regardless of where they may be.
When the fetters of one's own level are exhausted, within that same level,
one performs only two types of karma.
This refers to karma that yields results in the present life or whose timing is indefinite;
because such karma does not produce rebirth within its own level.
They do not create karma that leads to rebirth or karma that results in retribution in a future life.
Question: What is meant by an ordinary person who has regressed from their spiritual lineage?
Within their own realm,
although afflictions have been exhausted,
they still give rise to the four types of karma.
Even noble ones may regress from their spiritual lineage (gotra).
Why, then, would they be unable to fully initiate the four types of karma?
The explanation is as follows:
Although a noble one (ārya) may undergo regression,
they never again pass through [further] births;
therefore, they cannot fully initiate the four types of karma.
It is thus for one's own stage;
all noble ones, wherever they may reside, [are likewise].
Regarding the places attained within the higher stages,
those whose fetters have not yet been exhausted.
All three types arise;
excluding karma to be experienced in the present life,
one's body resides in the desire realm.
In the higher stages,
regarding those who have exhausted their fetters but have regressed from their spiritual lineage.
They also give rise to three types [of karma],
excluding karma to be experienced in the present life; this applies to those who have fallen away from their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
It is possible to regress from that state and be reborn in those higher stages;
therefore, for one who does not regress,
regarding those higher stages...
At the point where all fetters are exhausted,
one merely performs a single type of karma with indeterminate retribution.
Because the body does not exist there, there is no karma of the present life;
because one is not reborn there again, there is no karma of rebirth in the next life or subsequent lives.
This applies to all noble ones (*ārya*).
Abiding from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
in the higher stages where fetters are exhausted,
one creates only a single type of indeterminate karmic retribution.
This is because those born in the heavens do not undergo retrogression.
Why is it that noble ones (ārya) born in the heavens do not regress?
It is because in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are no conditions for retrogression above that level.
In the lower stages, one never performs [such actions].
This is the case for those in training (śaikṣa);

The commentary states:

One who has attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) can perform two kinds of wholesome karma—namely, karma that yields results in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and indeterminate karma (aniyata-karma).
Although there is no textual evidence for this, it is so.
Based on that Anāgāmin,

Regarding the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), interpretations among its adherents differ.

an arhat, a sage beyond training,

Although noble ones may commit evil deeds, [they do not produce the latter].
However, he only gives rise to mental karma without manifesting it through body or speech;
furthermore, among mental karmas, it is light rather than heavy.
Therefore, he creates only karma of the present life and indeterminate karma.
The other two [types of karma] are entirely absent there.
Regarding those states where [afflictions] have been suppressed but not yet abandoned, or where they have been partially abandoned,
one only performs wholesome [karma] that is either manifest or indeterminate.
All others do not arise;
regarding that which has already been subdued and abandoned,
one performs no further actions whatsoever.
Even if they were to arise, these would be habitual tendencies that are not correct;
they cannot draw forth karmic retribution.
Next, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
according to that school’s tenets,
when a noble being (ārya) dwells in the desire realm or in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, [the following applies].
If afflictions have not been exhausted, one can give rise to the four types of karma; if they have been exhausted,
one will never again create them.
If one has not yet exhausted the afflictions in the first dhyāna,
one may still create the three types of karma, with the exception of those that result in retribution in a subsequent life.
If [the karma] has already been exhausted,
one will never again create it within the higher stages.
At the point where the fetters have not yet been exhausted,
one can perform the three types of karma,
with the exception of karma that yields retribution in the present life.
In the state where fetters have been exhausted,
one exclusively refrains from creating [karma] within the lower stages.
It is never done at all;
it is thus according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, however—
Regarding the karma of the stage of segmented birth (*pariccheda-karma*): those above the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) never perform it.
If categorized separately:
Regarding the four unwholesome karmas,
from the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, one never commits them.
The wholesome karma of humans and devas is never performed by those from the first bhūmi upward.
Even if Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) receive a physical body,
they do so solely through their compassionate vows as a result of their fundamental karma.
From the first bhūmi upward,
one attains the dharma-nature body;
even if there remains a subtle karmic body of humans or devas, it is [transcended].
This is indeed due to past karma and not newly created,
for those above the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra) no longer create karma.
There is no need to discuss this in terms of specific realms or stages;
prior to the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the constituent factors have not yet been established, and thus it is described as being identical to that of ordinary beings.
To speak according to the truth:
those from the stage of the Ten Faiths upward are also able to refrain from creating karma that leads to birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence.
Such are the distinctions in the karma created by noble beings. Question:
Is it possible for one to create karma belonging to a higher stage while the afflictions of one’s own stage have not yet been completely exhausted?
The commentary states:
It is possible;
that is to say, when the afflictions within the desire realm have not yet been exhausted.
The cultivation and accomplishment of future meditative concentration (anāgāmya-dhyāna) is precisely this.
This future meditative concentration and that first dhyāna—
Since both equally invite the fruit of Brahmā,
they are called superior karma. Question:
Among these four types of karma, how many kinds of karma does this [present] karma possess?
This matter is not fixed;
according to the Abhidharma:
When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) cultivates and attains [this], it possesses three meanings;
however, for a noble one (ārya), this excludes karma that ripens in the present life.
Thus, one possesses two types of karma:
namely, karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and indeterminate karma (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
What are their characteristics?
There may be ordinary persons whose craving for sensual desire is not yet exhausted,
who cultivate and attain [the meditative states] of the future.
Having attained the future [state] and further severed the remaining fetters,
he attains the first dhyāna concentration.
When this person’s life comes to an end, [he passes away].
By means of this future [karma] and the first dhyāna concentration,
one is born in the Brahma realm;
this is what is called karma that results in rebirth (upapadya-vedanīya-karma).
Furthermore, there are ordinary persons whose craving for the desire realm has not yet been exhausted;
having cultivated and attained [the state] of the future,
they will, after passing through births within the desire realm, [attain it].
Furthermore, having severed the remaining fetters,
by means of this future [attainment] and the first dhyāna,
one is born in the Brahma realm.
This is what is called karma that results in a subsequent birth or a subsequent retribution;
it is indeterminate.
Such is the case for ordinary worldlings.
For what reason do the noble ones (ārya) perform only two types of karma?
Among the noble ones, there are those who have attained the first two fruits.
If sensual desire has not yet been exhausted and one attains the future dhyāna,
this person will later sever sensual desire.
Exhaustively employing this future [state] and the first dhyāna-concentration,
one is born in the Brahma realm;
this is precisely the karma of retributive birth.
It is indeterminate and can be known.
For what reason is it not karma to be experienced in a subsequent life for a noble one in the desire realm?
Those who undergo rebirth never ascend [to higher realms],
for they differ from ordinary beings who pass through rebirths and proceed [toward liberation].
Therefore, it is not a subsequent karma.
Furthermore, among the dhyānas of the future, it is of an inferior grade;
even if one were born in the Brahma realm, [it would be so].
One receives only the retributive fruit of a single body in the first heaven,
and does not reach a second body; therefore,
it is not a subsequent retribution.
According to the Aśokarājāvadāna,
noble ones (ārya) who have undergone rebirth within the stages of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) may also attain rebirth in the higher realms.
According to what has been stated,
noble ones (ārya) likewise employ future meditative concentrations as karma for the three types of retribution,
being the same as ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
The distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*) are thus.
Next, we shall discuss them with respect to the destinies (*gati*),
according to the *Abhidharma*.
The four unwholesome karmas give rise to all five destinies;
among the wholesome, there are four karmas.
The four realms of existence— humans, devas, pretas,
and animals— are fully present within the hells.
There are only three types [of karma],
excluding karma to be experienced in the present life;
this is because within the hells, [such karma cannot exist].
Because there is no karmic reward for goodness,
although the three types exist,
they are established but not practiced.
This meaning is difficult to understand.
For example, King Ruciraketu killed a brahmin and was reborn in hell,
yet by giving rise to faith, he was reborn in the Land of Ambrosia (Amṛtāvatī).
Just as the maiden Maitrī, while in the hells, gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and cast off her hellish body—
as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—
so too did the Māra-king instruct those sentient beings in the hells.
They focused their minds exclusively on the Tathāgata and rejoiced in acts of giving;
all of these gave rise to wholesome states of mind even while within the hells.
What is meant by "non-practice"?
The commentary explains that when the treatise speaks of the non-practice of the wholesome, it refers to this.
One should respond to that by speaking in terms of skillful means (*upāya*):
because there is no hearing, reflection, or cultivation within the hells,
it is called the non-practice of the wholesome.
The roots of goodness acquired at birth are not such that they can be made not to function;
this refers to what was previously mentioned.
These should all be understood as innate wholesome states (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however,
the four types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome— and the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) all arise from them.
He states that there are virtuous retributions within the three miserable realms; thus concludes this section on the three gates.
Next, the causes and conditions are distinguished. Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*):
If a result were obtained from a single action alone,
it could only be called a condition (*pratyaya*) and not a cause (*hetu*).
This refers to present conditions assisting past karma whose retribution is not yet fixed.
Because one obtains the present fruit.
If it were to obtain the fruit by being repeatedly performed,
it could be called a cause.
Because it is that which is produced most frequently,
it is designated as the "cause";
thus it is proclaimed in the treatises.
Beneficial yet not heavy—
this is karma that yields retribution in the present life. One attains the fruit of present karma in the present life.
Because this is extremely difficult,
only those who practice it extensively can truly establish it as a cause.
Regarding karmic actions that yield indeterminate retribution after birth,
whether performed once or many times, they can both serve as causes and as conditions.
Because the karma of past lives has matured and the attainment of the fruit is easy,
one is born there through direct birth.
That which is said to be the cause is explained as that which directly assists;
that which is said to be the condition is explained as that which indirectly assists. These four gates are now concluded.
Next, to clarify the number of fruits attained and the speed of their realization, a question is asked:
"How many karmas result in a single-body retribution (*ekajātipratibaddha*)?
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* explains:
After birth, one does not necessarily obtain the fruit of a single lifetime.
Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*), one only obtains the distinct retribution of feelings such as suffering or pleasure.
It is not permitted for a single person alone;
it must be this way regardless of how many there are.
As for what is meant by "slow" or "fast":
Question: Is it possible for karma to be performed by a preceding thought-moment and its retribution to be received within a subsequent thought-moment?
The treatise says:
It cannot. Because the karma has not yet matured,
it must pass through a long period of time before its retribution is received.
The karma of the three periods of time has been briefly explained in this manner. 65.
The Meaning of Crooked, Defiled, and Turbid Karma (7). Regarding the meaning of crooked, defiled, and turbid karma: [it refers to] crooked, defiled, and turbid karma.
As stated in the Abhidharma,
that treatise proclaims:
"Crookedness arises from deceit."
Defilement arises from hatred;
what is born of desire is called turbidity—
so it was taught by the World-Honored One.
With a crooked mind of flattery,
it is difficult to transcend birth and death;
it is difficult to enter nirvana.

Just as crooked wood is difficult to extract from a dense forest and is therefore called "crooked," so too the three types of action (karma) arising from these crooked dharmas are all called "crooked."
Because their cause and effect are analogous in nature,
a mind of malice can defile both oneself and others.
Therefore, it is called "defilement.
The bodily, verbal, and mental karma arising from defiled phenomena is termed "defilement."
Because the fruit resembles its cause,
a mind of greed is turbid and agitated,
just like murky water.
Therefore, it is called turbidity.
The bodily, verbal, and mental karma produced by these turbid phenomena is also termed turbidity.
Question: Other fetters (*saṃyojana*) are also capable of giving rise to karma;
why are they not mentioned?
The commentary states:
For now, this discussion is based on one gate;
other fetters give rise to karma.
All enter into this; therefore,
the crooked, defiled, and turbid karmas are not mentioned.
This is a brief and rough summary. 66.

The Meaning of the Four Karmas of Black and White (7). The Meaning of the Four Karmas of Black and White is explained through a twofold analysis: first, the definition of the names; second, the discernment of their characteristics. Regarding the first, the definition of the names, there is the meaning of the four karmas.
The various sūtras explain this in general terms. What are these names?
First, black-black karma.
Second, white-white karma;
third, black-and-white karma;
fourth, neither-black-nor-white karma.
That which is called "black-black" refers to unwholesome karma;
it is unwholesome, base, and defiled.
It is called "black" because both cause and effect are black;
this is termed "black-black karma."
As for the term "white-white," it refers to wholesome karma;
wholesome dharmas are fresh and pure.
It is called "white";
because both cause and effect are white,
it is termed "whitely-white karma."
What is called "black and white" refers to mixed karma,
wherein good and evil are intermingled.
This is called black-and-white karma.
That which is called neither-black-nor-white karma is untainted (anāsrava) karma.
As it is said in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra:
"The outflow-free (anāsrava) state is quiescent and free from the characteristics of black and white;
therefore, it is called neither black nor white."
Question: Among the untainted (anāsrava) white [dharmas], this is the most supreme.
For what reason is it called "non-white" (aśukla)?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
"All worldly people value contaminated wholesome states;
therefore, those wholesome states are designated as 'white'."
Because one abandons those [defilements] through the untainted [state], it is called "non-white.
Furthermore, one attains the fruit of the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
It is free from the characteristic of white;
because it arises from what has been attained, it is called "not white.
Furthermore, this refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
It is the most excellent among all that is white;
because it surpasses other forms of white,
it is called "non-white."
Just as a wheel-turning monarch,
though his substance is truly that of a human being,
is so designated because of his preeminence.
The world universally says that a Wheel-Turning Sage King is pure beyond ordinary men;
the untainted (anāsrava) is likewise so.
Therefore, it is said to be "not white."
Nāgārjuna’s commentary states:
"This is untainted karma (anāsrava-karma),
which is associated with emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita)."
It is free from the marks of conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is called neither black nor white.
Furthermore, there is karma with outflows (*sāsrava-karma*).
Black and white are mutually dependent;
the untainted (anāsrava) is free from such dependence,
and is therefore called "neither black nor white karma."
The explanation of the names concludes this first section.
Next, its characteristics will be analyzed;
there are differing interpretations in the commentaries.
According to the Abhidharma,
wholesome karma of the form realm is called "white-white," while all unwholesome karma experienced in the three miserable realms is [called black-black].
It is called "black-black.
Among the hungry ghosts and animals, there are distinct retributions for wholesome karma;
likewise, all the wholesome and unwholesome karma experienced by humans and devas in the desire realm.
These are called black-and-white karma,
and they are also called mixed karma.
These are the three preceding types.
The antidote to the outflows (anāsrava) is the fourth karma; thus,
the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
Wholesome karma within the realm of form is white with a white retribution;
that which is both black and white exists within the realm of desire.
Both black [actions] are said to be impure;
if there is a volition capable of severing these various karmas, they will be eliminated without remainder.
It should be known that this is the fourth karma. Question:
For what reason is wholesome karma of the form realm specifically designated as "white"?
Because its white characteristics are manifest,
and because it is free from shamelessness, lack of dread, and ill-will.
Why is wholesome karma of the desire realm not white?
Because it is mixed with unwholesome [karma].
As for the wholesome karma of the formless realm, why is it not "white"? It is indeed white.
The white characteristic is not manifest;
for this reason, it is not mentioned.
Why is it not manifest?
At the time of creating the causes,
the characteristics of the three karmas and the ten paths of wholesome action were not fully present; yet,
at the time of receiving the retribution, [they appear].
There is only the rebirth-aggregate (upapatti-skandha) and no intermediate state (antarābhava).
Furthermore, within this rebirth-aggregate,
there are only four aggregates and no form-aggregate (rūpa-skandha).
Because they lack such white characteristics as these, they are not called "white.
Why are all evil karmas of the three miserable realms termed "black-black"?
It is because their causes and effects are exclusively black.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* refutes the Abhidharma, stating:
"Some proclaim that wholesome karma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is 'white-white' (*avadāta-avadāta*)."
The karma of the three miserable realms is considered "black-black," as is the karma experienced by humans and devas in the desire realm.
They are considered black and white.
Seventeenth, the training in thought is neither black nor white.
This interpretation is not correct.
Judging by that standard,
we know that according to the Abhidharma, the evil karma of the three miserable realms is considered "black-black."
For what reason is it taught that among the hungry ghosts and animals, the distinct retribution for wholesome karma is considered "mixed karma"?
At the time of its causal formation:
Being mixed with evil,
when the retribution is received,
one experiences it together with suffering.
Therefore, it is said to be "mixed.
A question is asked:
Why is it that karma resulting in distinct retributions for wholesome deeds occurs exclusively among ghosts and animals, and does not extend to the hells?
The suffering of the hells is heavy because its inducing cause is exclusively unwholesome;
the retribution of hungry ghosts and animals is light because their inducing causes may be mixed with the wholesome. How is this known?

As clarified in the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, there are four types of wholesome karma— namely, karma with immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma with retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), karma with retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and karma with indefinite retribution (*aniyatavedanīya*).
Among these, three exist within the hells.
Excluding karma that ripens in the present life,
because there are no virtuous fruits within the hells;
this applies to the remaining four destinies.
One who possesses the four types of karma clearly knows that ghosts and animals also have the fruits of wholesome karma.
This is because they have attained the wholesome karma that yields results in the present life.
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtras:
"The āsuras and others receive retribution similar to that of the devas."
It clarifies that there is wholesome karma.
A question is asked:
"If it is said that there are fruits of wholesome karma among ghosts and animals," [how is this so?]
Why does the *Tattvasiddhi* refute the *Abhidharma*?
It asks: "Some people proclaim that the karma of the three miserable realms is 'black-black' (kṛṣṇa-kṛṣṇa).
How can they maintain this when they acknowledge that evil karma does not preclude the presence of good?"
If there were any [position] that was correct, it would be identical to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
What, then, would the proponents of the *Tattvasiddhi* have ultimately refuted? To explain:
That which is identical is established as real and not sublated;
therein, that which is different is sublated by the establishment of reality, as proclaimed by the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Within the hells, upon first emerging from the blazing flames,
one obtains the pleasure of cold ice touching the body.
Furthermore, the pleasure of pigs, dogs, and other such creatures eating excrement—
all such things as these are virtuous fruits;
yet the Abhidharma explains them as retributions for unwholesome karma.
This contradicts the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The *Tattvasiddhi* refutes it.
One does not destroy wholesome fruits.
Why? Because all wholesome and unwholesome actions of humans and devas constitute mixed karma;
since the causes are mixed with evil, the results are mixed with suffering.
Regarding the fourth type of action,
as stated in that treatise,
there are seventeen types of untainted (anāsrava) volitions of training (śaikṣa-cetanā).
It constitutes the fourth type of karma.
Volition (cetanā) is a mental factor;
this is the essential nature of karma.
Therefore, it is explained partially.
What are the seventeen?
As stated in that treatise:
It is taught that there are twelve volitions (*cetanā*) that sever karma with black retribution,
while four volitions can sever white karma.
The first is volition, and the second is that which is free from both;
thus, there are seventeen volitions in total when combined.
As for what is called the "twelve types of karma that abandon black [actions]," [it refers to the following]:
Within the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
there are four thoughts;
within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)...
There are eight [types of] volition;
thus, in total, there are twelve. Regarding the four [moments] of the path of seeing:
This refers to the volition associated with the four types of patient acceptance (dharmakṣānti).
Because these four right efforts eliminate the evil karma of the three miserable realms within the stages of the desire realm,
they are called "severing black [karma]."
Question: Since the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) also abandons unwholesome dharmas,
for what reason is volition (*cetanā*) alone specifically mentioned?
The commentary states:
The mind of patience does not consist merely in the non-cessation of evil;
rather, it is simply the contemplation of this karma.
Now, for the purpose of distinguishing karma, this is explained specifically;
it is discussed in conjunction with its associated factors.
Patience (*kṣānti*) and so forth are the attendants of that volitional karma (*cetanākarma*).
It may also be termed "volition" (*cetanā*).
Question: Is it the volition associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Why is it not mentioned? The explanation states:
because the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is removed by external realization beyond the stages of accumulation.
Because they are not right abandonments, they are not discussed.
Again, he asked:
Why is the volition associated with this patience not mentioned? To explain:
Regarding volition associated with the patience of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-kṣānti*),
it only severs the indeterminate and defiled volitions of the upper realms,
but does not sever the unwholesome.
This is why it is not mentioned.
Regarding the eightfold path of cultivation:
within the stages of the desire realm, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation that serve as the antidotes for the path of cultivation.
Among the nine unimpeded [knowledges], the first eight are volitions associated with the unimpeded;
these eight right abandonments eliminate the black karma of the desire realm.
Therefore, it is said that "black is severed.
A question is asked:
The Abhidharma explains the karma of the three miserable realms as being "black-black."
It is severed within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Since there is no further black karma (*kṛṣṇakarma*) therein,
why is it said that the eight volitions (*cetana*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) sever black [karma]?
This is explained as above.
Ordinary beings, relying upon both the afflictions of views and those abandoned through cultivation, generate karma leading to the three miserable realms.
As for the afflictions of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*):
Because they arise from delusion regarding the principles,
they give rise only to mental karma;
these are the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
Because they arise conditioned by objects,
they fully give rise to the three types of karma and the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Once the mental karma that has been produced has ceased and passed away,
it is acquired through attainment; this occurs at the time of entering the Noble Path.
To sever those karmas so that they no longer belong to oneself is called "severance.
This arises from the afflictions of the views.
It is abandoned during the path of seeing.
That which arises from the afflictions of the path of cultivation is abandoned by the nine uninterrupted paths of the desire realm's path of cultivation.
The ninth chapter will be discussed separately later; therefore,
it is said here that the first eight [chapters] concern the abandonment of black-retribution karma—
the bodily and vocal actions arising from the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because it is severed by way of the world and severed by way of moments,
there is no attainment of attainment;
rather, it is simply that the karma is bound by those afflictions which serve as its conditions.
When the afflictions of the path of cultivation are abandoned, one is freed from the bondage of karmic actions;
this is termed "abandonment."
The categories of these abandonments are similar in meaning to the mental karma produced by the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the statement that "the four types of volition can sever the white," this refers to the defiled volitions associated with the afflictions of the path of cultivation within the stages of the four dhyānas;
these are all capable of binding the wholesome karma of their respective stages.
Within each and every stage,
there are nine grades of unhindered liberation that sever their fetters.
From among those four dhyānas and nine unhindered concentrations,
one selects the volitional karma associated with the ninth [concentration] and divides it into four types of volition.
These four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and the four dhyānas have the meaning of being superior bonds for the wholesome;
they are called "cutting off the white," yet they do not cut off the essence of the wholesome.
Question: Since the four dhyānas and the nine unhindered thoughts are all capable of severing the wholesome fetters of the higher realms,
for what reason is it specifically said that only the ninth thought can sever the "white" [fetters]?
The commentary states:
It is not that the first eight [liberations] are incapable of severing [defilements];
however, within each stage of those four dhyānas, there are nine grades of afflicted volitions.
They collectively bind all wholesome dharmas of their own level;
although the first eight layers of binding have already been severed, [they remain bound].
The ninth is the single-layered fetter;
because it still causes all wholesome dharmas within its own stage to remain unable to escape,
it is not called "abandoned."
When that ninth grade of unimpeded [wisdom] arises,
it severs those subtle grades of defiled karmic volition,
thereby causing all wholesome dharmas within its own stage to attain liberation.
To explain the abandonment of the white [karma] by means of this alone:

that which is called "a single volition associated with both abandonments" refers to the volitional karma associated with the ninth category at the limit of the nine unimpeded paths during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Taking these as one,
this is the ninth subtle category within the right abandonment of black-black karma;
it also abandons all miscellaneous karma of the desire realm.
It is called "separation from both.
Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The abandonment of purely black karma and of black-and-white karma is called separation from both."
Among those black karmas and mixed karmas,
the acquisition of the substance of unwholesome mental karma is severed,
as are all other unwholesome physical and vocal [karmas].
And all wholesome dharmas within mixed karma;
one merely severs the fetters, not the essence of their attainment. Question:
The first eight unimpeded paths of the desire realm not only sever black karma, but also sever mixed karma.
For what reason are they not called "severing both"?
The explanation states:
When the first eight [paths of action] sever black karma,
the evil karma within the mixed category is also severed accordingly.
However, because the fetters associated with the superior [levels] among the mixed wholesome [karmas] have not yet been exhausted,
one cannot say that the mixed karma has been severed;
for those mixed wholesome karmas are still bound by the minor grades of black karma and mixed unwholesome karma belonging to their own level.
Question: If it is said that one cannot be called "one who has severed mixed karma" as long as the fetters remain unexhausted despite being above the mixed wholesome [states],
then since the first eight stages of non-obstruction have not yet exhausted the black [karma].
Furthermore, one should not say that black karma is abandoned.
The commentary states:
the very essence of the abandonment of evil karma is what is called "abandonment."
Because it has the nature of abandonment,
it receives the name "abandonment" according to the extent to which its cessation is achieved;
it thoroughly abandons the fetters without abandoning their substance.
Because they have skillfully severed their bonds:
the nine grades of unwholesome states within the stages of the desire realm bind all wholesome dharmas of the desire realm.
Although the first eight unimpeded [knowledges] sever the upper eight grades of fetters that obstruct the roots of goodness,
they do not sever the ninth and final grade of fetter.
It still remains; because it is bound,
there is no place for any wholesome dharmas to be liberated.
Therefore, it is not said that they are abandoned. Question:
If abandonment is designated by name according to the degree of exhaustion based on the essential nature of the abandonment of evil, [then...]
The first eight unimpeded [knowledges] also sever the eight grades of mixed evil karma.
For what reason is it not said that they sever the mixed?
The explanation states:
That evil, combined with the wholesome karma of the desire realm, constitutes mixed karma.
Although one has severed the mixed evil,
because the mixed wholesome [karma] has not yet been transcended, it is not said to be severed.
It is just as the head, hands, feet, and other parts together constitute a human body;
although one may sever the hands and feet, this is not called "killing a person.
This case is also like that.
Question: If it is said that during the first eight moments of reflection, because the mixed wholesome states have not yet emerged,
one does not count as having abandoned [the defilements] even though mixed unwholesome states have been severed.
Among black karmas,
although mental karma may be severed,
the two karmas of body and speech [remain].
One cannot yet escape the bonds of conditions.
For what reason is it called "severing the black"?
The commentary states: There is a reason for this;
among those black karmas, mental action is considered the primary karma.
Body and speech follow karma because the mind is the primary factor;
this occurs during the first eight moments of volition.
Although the karma of body and speech has not yet escaped the bonds of conditions,
because right action has already been eliminated, it is said that "black" is severed;
this is like a person whose head is cut off or whose waist is severed.
Although the hands and feet remain, one is said to have been "killed"; likewise,
although unwholesome mental karma may be severed within the category of the miscellaneous,
wholesome mental karma [remains].
While still bound and not yet released,
one’s body and speech— whether virtuous or non-virtuous—
are likewise not exempt from bondage.
Therefore, it is not said that [these] are abandoned. Question:
What about formless and untainted (anāsrava) volitional action (karma-cetanā)?
Why is it not described as untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*)?
In principle, this would also apply;
however, it is not one of the three aforementioned methods of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).
Therefore, it is not discussed [in this context].
In the Abhidharma, it is thus;
in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, there are four types of karma.
Furthermore, it differs from that explanation:
karma belonging to the form realm and the formless realm is exclusively white.
Furthermore, wholesome karma within the desire realm is also termed "white," as is the karma of the Avīci hell.
That which is exclusively black refers to the karma of pure suffering in the remaining hells, as well as among the hungry ghosts and animals.
This too is called "black."
The humans and devas of the desire realm do not possess karma that is purely pleasant,
nor do those in the lower three realms of existence possess karma that is purely painful.
Collectively termed "mixed," all untainted (anāsrava) actions are collectively termed "neither-black-nor-white karma."
To discuss this specifically within the context of the untainted (*anāsrava*):
it is exclusively the volition (*cetanā*) of the mind that is taken as the essence of karma.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, in its ninth chapter on "Karma," states:
Volition is called karma;
generally speaking, both are included within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as the karma of the hells.
A small portion of the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) constitutes black karma (*kṛṣṇa-karma*).
The treatise itself explains this, saying:
The sentient beings therein are called "black" because they experience extreme and great anguish;
this refers to all karmic actions of the devas.
This is the result of white karma.
The treatise itself explains:
"It refers to the retributive pleasure experienced by the various devas of the three realms."
Because it is sovereign and clearly manifest, it is called "white.
The karma experienced by humans, asuras, and the eight classes of deities is called "mixed black-and-white."
Because within these karmas there is both good and evil, at the time of receiving retribution, suffering and pleasure are intermingled.
All untainted (anāsrava) states are able to destroy both the unwholesome and the tainted wholesome.
Furthermore, it uproots the fruits of both good and evil for sentient beings;
this is called "neither black nor white.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
The karma of the three miserable realms is called black;
the karma of the two upper realms is described as white.
The karma of humans and devas within the stages of the desire realm is mixed;
all [karma] that is untainted (anāsrava) is likewise [mixed].
It is neither black nor white; such are the four types of karma. 67.

The Meaning of the Five Heinous Crimes (VII): An Exposition through Seven Gates. 1. Distinguishing the Names and Defining the Characteristics; 2. Distinction by the Three Karmas and Three Poisons; 3. Distinction by Lightness and Heaviness; 4. Distinction by Degree and Order; 5. Distinction by Person and Location; 6. Distinction by the Duration of Receiving Retribution; 7. Distinction by Whether Retribution Can Be Exhausted or Not. Within the first gate:
Explaining the names and distinguishing their characteristics:
as for the "five heinous crimes" (pañcānantarya),
they refer to killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
These five types are called "reversals" (ānantarya) in the sūtras,
and they are also called "immediate" (ānantarya).
Why are these five specifically termed "rebellious" (*ānantarya*)?
It is because they involve turning one's back on kindness and violating the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Killing one's father or mother is rebellious because it constitutes a betrayal of kindness.
The other three are "contrary" because they oppose the field of merit:
killing an Arhat and causing a schism in the Saṃgha oppose the Saṃgha as a field of merit.
To draw blood from the body of a Buddha is to violate the field of merit of the Buddha.
A question is asked:
"Are not all Three Jewels fields of merit?"
For what reason is it said that violating the Dharma is not mentioned?
The explanation states:
slandering the Dharma is more grave than the five heinous crimes.
Therefore, one does not fall into the five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
It is just as the five heinous crimes do not include the four grave offenses (catur-guru-dharma).
Why are these five called "immediate" (ānantarya) karmas?
The term "release" (vimokṣa) has four meanings.
First, because it proceeds toward the fruit without interval, it is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
Because one receives the subsequent body immediately after casting off this body,
it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
Second, there is the uninterruptedness of the experience of suffering.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes will be reborn in the Avīci Hell,
where they will experience a continuous succession of suffering for the duration of one kalpa, with no interval of pleasure.
Because they are named after their results, they are called "immediate" (ānantarya) karmas;
these are the three immediate offenses regarding life and the five immediate transgressions.
One is born in the Avīci Hell,
where one's lifespan lasts for an entire kalpa without interruption.
Because the result follows directly from the cause, it is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
The four types of physical forms arise without interval;
through the five heinous crimes,
one is born in the Avīci Hell.
The Avīci Hell extends eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth;
when a single person enters within it, [it remains so].
The body also pervades;
when all people enter,
the body also pervades.
They do not obstruct one another;
because they arise from the cause as the fruit, they are called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Such is the meaning of the name.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished.
Of the four preceding types,
the characteristics are manifest and thus easily known.
The schism of the Saṃgha is difficult to identify;
it is now appropriate to provide a detailed analysis of the meaning of "schism.
Generally speaking, there are two ways of explaining it.
First is the schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) Saṃgha;
second is the schism of the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by means of six propositions.
First, clarifying the refutation of the Dharma;
second, clarifying the refutation of the person;
third, clarifying the refutation of the time.
The fourth clarifies the locus of refutation;
the fifth clarifies the refutation of characteristics;
the sixth clarifies the refutation of intrinsic nature.
Regarding what is called "destroying the Dharma," there are two kinds of Dharma:
first, the false; second, the correct.
The false is that which destroys;
the correct is that which is destroyed.
Within the context of the True Dharma, there are generally three ways of explaining this.
First is the dharma for the community of those who have gone forth,
namely the one hundred and one formal acts (karmavācanā) for those who have left the household life.
Only when one’s detailed reverence does not deviate from the proper standard can one truly become a monk;
if it is otherwise, one cannot.
They are not called the Saṃgha;
therefore, they are called the dharma of the community of those who have gone forth.
Second, the dharma of the practices of those who have gone forth.
These are the so-called four reliances:
first, to remain constantly seated under a tree for as long as one lives;
second, to wear rag-robes discarded in refuse heaps for as long as one lives.
Third, begging for food for as long as one's life lasts;
fourth, having illness for as long as one's life lasts,
taking old and discarded medicines while practicing this dharma together.
Only then can one be called a renunciant;
only then can one be called a monk.
If one does not practice this, [one is neither].
They are not called the Saṃgha;
therefore, this is called the dharma of the practice of going forth.
Third, the specific dharmas of following the practice.
That is to say: prostration, study, recitation of sutras, seated meditation, and mindfulness of concentration;
up to and including the cultivation of untainted noble wisdom—all such things vary according to the different practices of individuals.
It is not the dharma shared by those who have left the household life; therefore,
it is called the "dharma of following distinct practices."
Of these three, the first two constitute the Dharma of the Saṃgha;
they are the practices of those who have gone forth.
The latter kind is practiced by both monastics and laypeople alike;
it is not restricted to those who have left the household life.
It is not called the "monastic dharma.
Within the monastic dharma,
the first is the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) of the Saṃgha.
The second is the Dharma of the Wheel-Turning Sangha.
This Sangha is that which is to be broken.
That which is not the Dharma of the Saṃgha is not what is to be refuted;
such is that which is to be refuted.
What is it that can cause a schism?
Within the schism of the *karmavācanā*, there is no other distinct factor;
the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-saṃghabheda*) employs the five types of wrong views.
First, begging for food;
second, wearing rag-robes from refuse heaps;
third, sitting at the foot of a tree.
Fourth, one does not consume ghee or salt;
fifth, one does not consume fish or meat.
The first three are similar [to the preceding].
The latter two are false speech.
Because these five types contradict the True Dharma,
they are called "destructions."
The refutation of the dharma is thus.
Next, the refutation of the person is distinguished;
therein are three parts.
First, the object of refutation is clarified;
second, the means of refutation is clarified;
third, the number of the means and objects of refutation is determined.
Regarding those to be refuted, there are two kinds:
first, the *saṃgha* of ritual action (*karmavācanā*) among those who have gone forth.
Bhikṣus endowed with the precepts,
numbering four or more, without distinction between ordinary persons and sages.
Within a single boundary,
they collectively observe and do not deviate from those one hundred and one methods of formal ecclesiastical acts (*karmavācanā*).
The first is called the *karmavācanā* saṃgha;
the second is the Dharma-wheel saṃgha,
consisting of those who have left the household life.
Making no distinction between ordinary beings and sages,
they practice together the Tathāgata’s four reliances of the True Dharma,
harmonious and without discord.
They are called the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma.
Some say that the Four Noble Truths are [the wheel].
This is the Wheel of Dharma.
Those who have realized the Truths are called the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma.
However, those Four Noble Truths represent the meaning of the Wheel of Dharma within the context of the distinct practices of individuals;
they do not constitute the Wheel of Dharma of the Sangha regarding the precepts within the monastic community.
If the Four Noble Truths were the Wheel of Dharma,
then when Devadatta split the Saṃgha,
he should have taught five truths as a reversal of the Four Noble Truths.
Because the five perversions are taught as the opposites of the four reliances,
it is clearly known that the four reliances constitute the Wheel of Dharma.
If it is said that those noble ones who have realized the truths constitute the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha,
then lay noble ones should also be called the Saṃgha.
Since they are not the Saṃgha,
it is clearly known that those who have realized the Truths are not designated as the Wheel-Turning Saṃgha.
This is because the interpretations adopted by worldly people are erroneous and confused;
I shall now distinguish them by means of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) so that their distinct characteristics may be clarified.
What is it? First, there is the Wheel of Dharma that is not untainted (*anāsrava*),
namely, when ordinary worldlings who have gone forth practice the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
Therefore it is called the Wheel of Dharma; however,
because the noble path has not yet been realized,
it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).
Second, there are those who are untainted but do not turn the wheel of Dharma;
these refer to noble persons living as householders who possess internal noble realization.
Therefore, it is called "untainted" (anāsrava).
Because it does not practice the four reliances (pratisaraṇa),
it is not the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
Third, that which is untainted is also the Wheel of Dharma;
this refers to noble ones who have left the household life and possess internal, noble realization.
Therefore, it is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).
Because one practices the four reliances (catur-pratisaraṇa),
it is named the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
The fourth is neither untainted nor a wheel of Dharma;
it refers to the ordinary person living at home.
Since there is no noble realization within,
it is not untainted (anāsrava).
It does not practice the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni).
Therefore, it is not the Wheel of Dharma.
By means of this analysis, their distinct characteristics can be known.
Within these two types of Saṃgha:
The schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Saṃgha applies universally to both ordinary and noble monks;
it is when ordinary monks diverge from the noble ones.
It is also called "breaking" because it breaks the Wheel of Dharma; this breaking of the Saṃgha occurs among ordinary persons, not among noble ones.
The noble faith is accomplished because it is indestructible;
such is that which is to be destroyed.
Next, the schism is distinguished:
it divides the *saṃgha* through formal acts (*karmabheda*).
Both wrong views and craving can cause such a division.
The Dharma-wheel Sangha depends upon both view and practice;
for only those of sharp faculties are able to break [the cycle].
Furthermore, it breaks the *karmavācanā*.
It penetrates even those who practice pure conduct but violate the prohibitions;
with the exception of those who have committed the gravest offenses, it is able to destroy them all.
The schism of the wheel-turning Sangha is restricted to those who are pure,
because people do not trust those who have violated the prohibitions.
One cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"Only one who has long been pure can cause a schism in the Saṃgha."
It can be destroyed in this manner.

Next, regarding the person who destroys and the person who is destroyed, one shall determine their respective numbers. This refers to the destruction of the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) of the Saṃgha.
Within a single boundary (sīmā), at least eight persons must be present for the schism of the Saṃgha to be established;
this is because both parties constitute a formal assembly (saṃgha) by performing separate ritual acts (karmas).
Regarding the schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha (cakrabheda):
within a single boundary (sīmā), a minimum of nine persons is required for it to be established as a schism.
Why must there be nine?
A formal assembly consists of four members;
these are those who constitute the schism.
The heterodox group consists of five people who are capable of causing schism;
therefore, nine are required.
Within the assembly of the heterodox,
why must there be five?
Devadatta alone claimed for himself to be a Buddha.
The other four constitute the assembly;
therefore, five are required. Question:
Because there are Buddhas and assemblies within the heterodox,
five must be required;
for within the orthodox as well, there are likewise Buddhas and assemblies.
"Why do you not speak of ten, but rather of nine?
He explained:
"Although there is indeed a Buddha within the Middle Way,"
The Buddha is not included within the Saṃgha;
therefore, he is not discussed [in this context].
Among those who are heterodox, although Devadatta claimed for himself to be a Buddha, [he is likewise excluded].
In reality, they are the Saṃgha;
therefore, it is said that there are five [factors].
Furthermore, at the time of the formal schism, the Buddha was not present in the assembly.
If the Buddha is present among the assembly,
the bhikṣu Devadatta possesses no majestic power or virtue.
Because they cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha,
the Buddha is not considered [in this context]. Question:
When one is to disrupt the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha,
the two assemblies must perform their respective *karmavācanās* in separate locations;
therefore, both sides must each constitute a valid assembly.
One who destroys the Wheel of Dharma merely destroys the practice of the Dharma and has no concern for communal affairs;
why must both parties necessarily constitute a formal assembly?
The Buddha replied:
"There is a reason why those who destroy the Wheel of Dharma [are so]."
Since one must perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) with a harmonious assembly that accepts the false doctrine before proceeding,
it is necessary for both parties to constitute a complete assembly.
Such is the case regarding those who cause schism.
Next, the time of refutation is explained.
This section contains two parts:
first, clarifying the time of refutation.
Second, clarifying the duration—whether long or short—of the schism once it has been accomplished.
As for the time of the actual schism:
it is the schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).
The period is vast and long;
from the time the Buddha was in the world until the end of the Dharma,
one may break through [the obstacles] at any time.
The schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha occurs during a brief period;
it does not take place when the Buddha is in the world, nor in the final age.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
"Before or after the boundary was established,
the Muni entered parinirvāṇa."
When the polyp has not yet emerged,
and when the first pair is absent—
during these six periods.
Thus, there is no breaking of the Wheel of Dharma;
there is one [case] of not establishing the boundary,
and two [cases] prior to the schism of the Saṃgha.
The third [offense] occurs after the schism of the Saṃgha;
the fourth, during the Nirvāṇa of the Muni;
and the fifth, before the excision of the polyp.
There is no first pair among these six;
during these six periods,
there is no breaking of the Wheel of Dharma.
Regarding those who have not established a boundary:
at the time of the schism of the Wheel of Dharma,
one must necessarily rely upon the *karmavācanā*.
Since formal acts (karmavācanā) depend upon a defined boundary (sīmā), if no boundary has been established,
it is impossible to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Regarding the terms "before" and "after":
these refer to the two periods— the time prior to the schism of the Saṃgha and the time following the schism of the Saṃgha.
The community of monks is of one flavor and cannot be destroyed; therefore,
there is no schism in the Saṃgha.
Regarding those who have already entered parinirvāṇa:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
because there is no true teacher, [the Dharma] is not heard.
Furthermore, there are no false teachers;
therefore, there is no schism in the Saṃgha.
As for what was said regarding the time before the excrescence has been removed:
The wicked person Devadatta gives rise to the afflictions of evil precepts and evil views,
like a festering sore or a malignant tumor.
While this [Dharma] has not yet emerged,
there is likewise no schism in the Saṃgha,
nor is there a "foremost pair."
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—
these two individuals are designated as the foremost pair among my disciples.
When this [time] has not yet arrived,
there is no schism in the Saṃgha. Why is this so?
Devadatta saw that the Buddha had excellent disciples;
because he wished to emulate the Buddha by separately maintaining his own superior disciples,
and furthermore, because these two men were capable of bringing the Saṃgha into harmony.
Therefore, this pair has arisen to bring about the schism in the Sangha;
it is indeed due to the power of that Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings that this has come to pass.
Question: Before the World-Honored One appeared in the world, there was likewise no schism in the Saṃgha.
Why, then, is this not discussed?
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "not causing a schism in the Saṃgha during the six periods," this is spoken with reference to times when there is a Saṃgha present.
Before the Buddha had appeared in the world,
there was originally no Sangha known to exist; therefore,
in what sense could it be said that [the precepts] were not violated?
For this reason, it is not discussed;
because the Saṃgha cannot be split during these six periods,
they are termed "short."
Question: Regarding the two periods before and after the schism of the Saṃgha,
first was the case of the bhikṣu Devadatta in Rājagṛha.
He proclaimed the five kinds of heterodoxy;
by casting lots, the assembly was harmonized,
and there were five hundred newly ordained practitioners.
At the time of casting lots,
and at the time when the two groups— the heterodox and the orthodox— were performing separate rites in Gayā;
during these two occasions.
When is it precisely that there is schism?
The explanation states:
in both instances, there is the sense of schism.
The King prohibited the casting of voting tallies;
when the practice of breaking [the rules] was being abolished,
there was the Poṣadha at Gayā.
When the various dharmas are destroyed,
for this reason both occasions are called "schism in the Saṃgha. Question:
If Gayā separately performed the *poṣadha*,
this would merely constitute a violation of the communal rules (*saṃgha-dharma*) and would not concern the ritual procedures (*caryā-vidhi*).
For what reason, then, is it called "breaking the Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra-pravartana*)?
Because they perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) with a resolute and fixed intent toward what is false,
it is also called "breaking the wheel of the Dharma" (dharmacakra-pravartana).
This is the time of actual destruction.
Once the destruction is complete, after a certain period of time, they once again become reconciled,
as stated in the Sūtra.
They did not remain apart for even one night;
the Saṃgha was reconciled.
For what reason was it reconciled?
It was because of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
by means of his supernormal powers,
Maudgalyāyana caused Devadatta to fall asleep and remain unaware.
Furthermore, he manifested superior supernormal powers,
transforming those five hundred newly ordained bhikṣus and causing them to give rise to faith.
Śāriputra explained the Dharma,
causing them to give rise to understanding and return to the orthodox path;
thus, they attained harmony and union.
The manner of its destruction is thus.
Next, the location of its destruction is distinguished,
as stated in the treatise.
The schism of the *karmavācanā* occurs in three continents,
excluding Uttarakuru.
Because they lack a Saṃgha,
the schism of the Wheel-turning Saṃgha occurs only in Jambudvīpa and not in other regions.
Why is this so? The treatise itself explains:
"Because this right path exists, there is a false path."
Because there are true teachers here, there are also false teachers;
thus they exist in Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, they disrupt the *karmavācanā*.
The location is within the boundary;
the place where the damage occurred is likewise within the boundary.
As for the destroyer of the Wheel of Dharma:
the location where it is destroyed is restricted to within a single world-system,
yet the damage wrought pervades the entirety of the trichiliocosm.
Therefore, the Vinaya Sūtra states:
"Within a single moment, one should learn throughout the trichiliocosm;
that which has not been learned should be recited."
Without reciting [the scriptures], one should practice meditative concentration;
yet one does not practice meditative concentration,
until finally one should enter the untainted noble path.
One must not enter it.
Such is the case for a breach.
Next, the characteristics of a breach are distinguished.
To split the *saṃgha* by means of formal ritual (*karmabheda*), it must be within the boundary of a single great *saṃgha*,
with a minimum of eight persons divided into two factions.
Only when both parties each perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) according to the Dharma can it be called "schism in the Saṃgha.
If one group performs it in one place while the other does not, it is not so.
This is merely termed a separate-assembly *karmavācanā*;
it does not constitute a schism in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, even if *karmas* were performed simultaneously in two locations, [it would still not be a schism].
If one were to perform an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) when a legal *karmavācanā* should be performed, all such acts would fail and be considered a schism,
because what has been done is not the Dharma of the Saṃgha. This is what constitutes a schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*cakrabheda*).
Furthermore, these are persons who have left the household life and are fully ordained;
they must reside within a single boundary,
with a minimum of nine individuals.
The orthodox assembly consists of four;
the heterodox assembly consists of five.
