First, various mental factors (caitta-dharma) mutually borrow each other’s names.
For example, although the essence of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is actually wisdom (prajñā),
it is called "mindfulness" (smṛti).
This is also like that.
The two are designated according to their companions;
this Vajra-wisdom is accompanied by meditative concentration.
Therefore, it is spoken of as "samādhi" by way of its accompaniment.
This is because wisdom that is distracted accomplishes nothing;
whereas wisdom within concentration is capable of effective action.
This "Vajra" is named according to its associates;
it is named according to its capacity.
This Vajra-wisdom can cause all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be correctly settled and immovable.
Therefore, it is named "samādhi" based on its functional capacity, receiving this designation according to four meanings.
This essence of vajra-wisdom contains many meanings;
among them, it includes the sense of being correctly concentrated, stable, and immovable.
Therefore, it is called samādhi.
The nature of the mental phenomena is thus.
Next, we shall discuss its essential nature with respect to the substance of the mind.
The mind is further divided into three types.
The first is the consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*),
which refers to the six consciousnesses that take phenomena as their objects.
The second is the deluded consciousness (*mṛṣā-vijñāna*).
It is also called the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*). This refers to the seventh, false mind.
Third is true consciousness,
which refers to the eighth consciousness, the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
In the Hīnayāna, the diamond-like [wisdom] takes that discriminative consciousness of phenomena as its substance.
Within the consciousness of phenomena, the sixth mental consciousness (manovijñāna) discerns,
contemplates, and understands, thereby being able to sever the four abodes [of ignorance] and not being destroyed by the afflictions of those four abodes.
Therefore, it is called "Vajra.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are two types of Vajra: first, the Vajra of the object-condition and its antidote; second, the Vajra of the subject-condition and its antidote.
The second is true realization (*bhūtārthaprativedha*).
Its essence consists of the antidote that takes the diamond-like deluded consciousness as its object;
it is the understanding that contemplates emptiness within that deluded consciousness.
Because it can eliminate the obstructions of darkness and cannot be destroyed by the delusions of darkness,
it is called "Vajra.
Its essence is the true consciousness that realizes the true Vajra.
The nature of the true consciousness is inherently pure;
when the meaning of emptiness is obscured, it subsequently becomes defiled.
By extinguishing false defilements, the mind becomes pure and luminously clear.
Illuminating pure wisdom realizes the suchness of the fundamental nature of dharmas;
one does not perceive a single dharma that can give rise to delusive conceptualization.
Because delusive conceptualization does not arise, one is able to eliminate darkness and confusion.
It is called "vajra" because it cannot be destroyed by the obstacles of delusion;
this is because its vajra-nature is truly real.
Therefore, it is said in the sūtras that [the Buddha-nature] is the Wisdom-Seal Samādhi, the Śūraṅgama, and so forth.
Such is the essential nature; this concludes the two gates.
Next, its characteristics will be distinguished.
First, we shall distinguish the characteristics by means of opening and closing according to the Abhidharma.
Within the system of the Abhidharma, there are two distinct categories of meaning.

The first concerns only the unimpeded path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) within the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The first is taken to be the diamond-like [samādhi] (*vajropama*).

The second takes both the antidotes for the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as the diamond-like [samādhi].
First, regarding the initial meaning, the characteristics are distinguished through their opening and closing;
in total, there is only the single unimpeded path of cultivation,
which may alternatively be divided into two.
First is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna);
second is inferential knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Regarding what is called the knowledge of phenomena:
This refers to the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the dharma-knowledge of the path within the desire realm;
these are able to counteract the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and for this reason they are called "vajra."
Why are only the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path taken, while those of suffering and origin are not?
The explanation states:
the two objects of cessation and the path in the desire realm are subtler than the objects experienced in the Peak of Existence (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
By contemplating the subtle, one becomes detached from the coarse;
therefore, by contemplating the cessation and the path within that desire realm,
one is able to eliminate the fetters associated with the path of cultivation that pertain to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The suffering and origin of the desire realm are coarse compared to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
because one cannot abandon the subtle by contemplating what is coarse,
the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering and origin is not taken as the diamond-like concentration.
As for "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna),
it refers to the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Within this subsequent knowledge, the specific portion that takes the non-perception [realm] as its object of counteraction and is unimpeded is designated as the "diamond-like [samādhi]" (vajropama).
Alternatively, they may be divided into thirteen:
the dharma-knowledge of the cessation and the path are each counted as two;
and the three subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path are counted as three.
Including the previous ones, there are eight instances of observing cessation within existence;
that is, by observing cessation within the eight stages from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these are combined to form eight.
When these are added to the preceding, they total thirteen.
Question: Why is the path not divided into eight types,
while only the cessation is divided into eight?
The commentary states:
The paths of the eight stages of the upper realms are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because they arise in mutual dependence upon one another, they are collectively observed as a single path of comparison (*upamāna-mārga*).
The cessation of the upper eight stages is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
It is distinguished according to what has been ceased;
because they do not arise in dependence upon one another, they are observed individually.
Alternatively, it may be further divided into fifty-two types,
as stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
Of these, the first thirteen knowledges contemplate only the principles of the Truths (*satya*).
Within each individual wisdom, there are four modes of contemplation.
Therefore, when categorized separately, there are fifty-two.
What are these four modes?
This has been explained in detail in the previous chapter on the Four Noble Truths.
Below the truth of suffering, there are four aspects:
namely, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
Up to the path of the lower path and the vehicle of the tracks— these are the four.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eighty,
as explained in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
What are these eighty fundamental [knowledges] and twenty?
They consist of the knowledge of the path and subsequent knowledge, which are derived from the aforementioned thirteen knowledges.
These constitute eight [paths],
because they consist of observing the paths of the eight stages of the higher realms.
When combined with the others, there are twenty in total.
These twenty knowledges each involve four modes of contemplation;
thus, there are eighty. This is one sense [of the term].
Next, regarding the non-perception realm (*asaṃjñin*), we shall distinguish its characteristics by analyzing the combination and separation of the two types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
In brief, there is only one antidote for the non-perception realm;
however, it may also be divided into two.
First, the antidote for the path of seeing regarding the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
second, the antidote for the path of cultivation regarding the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Alternatively, it may be divided into three.
First is subsequent patience;
second is dharma-knowledge;
third is subsequent knowledge.
The first [of these three] counteracts the afflictions of view in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception;
the latter two counteract the afflictions of cultivation in that same sphere.
Alternatively, they may be divided into thirteen.
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
within the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñī-bhūmi*), there are four types of subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) as antidotes for the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*),
and nine types of uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) as antidotes for the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Therefore, when combined, there are thirteen;
alternatively, when further divided, there are forty-five. What are they?
In the stage of non-perception (asaṃjñī-bhūmi), there are four types of patience (kṣānti) as antidotes for the path of seeing (darśana-mārga),
and forty-one as antidotes for the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga);
combining these with the former, there are forty-five in total.
What are the forty-one [knowledges] within the path of cultivation?
The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the dharma-knowledge of the path constitute two.
The three types of subsequent knowledge—concerning suffering, origin, and the path—together with the preceding [two], constitute five.
Within the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*), there are thirty-six [aspects].
Together with the preceding, these total forty-one.
What are these thirty-six distinct contemplations within the subsequent knowledge of cessation? There are eight knowledges that contemplate the cessation of the eight stages of the upper realms.
This refers to contemplating the cessation that serves as the antidote to the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are seven knowledges when two and two are combined in contemplation,
and six knowledges when three and three are combined in contemplation.
The combined contemplation of four and four possesses five wisdoms;
the combined contemplation of five and five possesses four wisdoms;
the combined contemplation of six and six possesses three wisdoms.
The combined contemplations of the seventh and seventh stages possess two types of wisdom;
the combined contemplation of the eighth stage possesses one type of wisdom.
From the eighth stage to the first, there are thirty-six combined contemplations in total.
Alternatively, they may be further divided into one thousand four hundred and ninety-two types of vajra-samādhis,
as stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. What are these?
Next, among the preceding forty-five vajras,
the first four correspond to each of the four stages of patience; as there are four contemplations for each,
they constitute sixteen.
These sixteen names and numbers are fixed and are not further subdivided.
The latter forty-one paths of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) each have four modes of contemplation as their antidotes,
totaling one hundred and sixty-four types.
However, these one hundred and sixty-four types each counteract the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception;
when each is further divided into nine, they total one thousand four hundred and seventy-six.
Including the preceding sixteen *kṣāntis* and *jñānas* of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are a total of one thousand four hundred and ninety-two. Question:
For what reason are the sixteen *kṣāntis* within the path of seeing not divided into nine grades?
Each of the paths of solitary cultivation consists of nine grades.
The commentary states:
all afflictions of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) are abandoned through the common characteristic of their antidotes.
A single grade of the antidote treats nine grades of afflictions;
therefore, no separate division into nine grades is made.
As for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, they are treated according to their respective nine grades of abandonment.
Therefore, the path of cultivation is divided into nine grades.
These one thousand four hundred and ninety-two types can all be fully aroused, from the future dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
In the sphere of empty space, only four hundred and sixty-eight arise.
Which ones are they?
Among the previous forty-five vajras, only thirteen kinds of wisdom can arise.
This refers to the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
Within the subsequent knowledge of cessation, there are ten [moments] through the combination and separation [of objects],
specifically when observing the cessation of the four formless stages individually.
There are four wisdoms.
There are three wisdoms when two and two are combined in contemplation.
There are two wisdoms when three and three are combined in contemplation.
In the fourth stage, there is one further wisdom that combines [the previous two].
Therefore, the wisdom of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has ten types when categorized by combination and separation.
Including the three preceding analogies (anvaya), they total thirteen.
Each of these consists of four types of contemplative practice, totaling fifty-two;
each serves as an antidote to the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, acting as the nine unhindered paths.
Thus, there would be four hundred and sixty-eight [categories].
Why does he not posit the four patiences (*kṣānti*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)?
Because in that school, there is no perception of the truths (*satyadarśana*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why is it that the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path does not arise?
Because the formless realm does not take the out-flowing phenomena of lower stages as its object,
it likewise does not take the antidotes to those lower stages as its object.
Why is it that one does not take the cessation within the four dhyānas as the object of the subsequent knowledge of cessation?
It is because the formless realms do not take the contaminated phenomena of lower stages as their objects;
therefore, they do not take as their object the cessation that is the antidote to those contaminants.
Question: Can those in the formless realm take the untainted path of a lower stage as an object? Answer: It is explained that there are cases where they can.
There is a point that does not accord with the intended meaning: among the paths of the lower stages that counteract the lower stages, there is no formless [attainment];
yet those that do not take the lower or upper stages as their objects do take the formless [attainments] as their objects.
It is thus with the sphere of infinite space.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness, all things gradually diminish until nothing remains;
one may understand this by analogy with the Abhidharma, which is likewise.
Next, regarding the *Tattvasiddhi*, the distinctions between the opening and closing [of categories] are analyzed.
In the texts of the *Tattvasiddhi*, there is no fixed determination; rather, they are discussed according to their meaning, such that the opening and closing are not fixed.
In brief, it consists solely of the single uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation of emptiness.
Alternatively, they may be divided into nine,
namely the nine grades of the non-obstructive [attainments] of the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
if further subdivided according to their specific distinctions, the number of grades is immeasurable.
Because they sever afflictions through immeasurable minds,
the opening and closing [of categories] in the Mahāyāna teachings are not fixed;
in sum, however, there is only one.
That is to say, it is knowledge in accordance with reality.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
first, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Second is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Knowing all things as empty is called "knowledge of all" (*sarvajña*);
knowing the distinctions among the characteristics and modes of all phenomena is called "all modes" (*sarvākāra*).
Alternatively, it is divided into three,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
first, pure wisdom (*viśuddhajñāna*).
The first refers to the wisdom of ultimate truth;
the second refers to all-encompassing wisdom,
which is the wisdom of conventional truth.
The three types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Mastery in knowing within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called unimpeded knowledge.
Furthermore, these are divided into three.
First, the knowledge of conventional truth;
second, the knowledge of ultimate truth;
third, the knowledge of reality as it is.
Alternatively, it is divided into four:
first, conventional truth wisdom,
which knows the characteristics of worldly phenomena.
2. The wisdom of the ultimate truth, which knows that all phenomena are empty;
3. The wisdom of true reality.
Knowing that it is neither existent nor non-existent is the wisdom of the four dharma-realms; that is,
knowing the distinct categories of the dharma-realm within the true *tathāgatagarbha*.
These have been distinguished according to their various gateways;
their vast differences are difficult to exhaust.
Such is the opening and closing [of these categories]. These three gateways are now concluded.
Next, we shall discuss the meaning of "vajra" according to its respective positions.
There are both general and specific aspects;
within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there are five such general and specific categories.
First, it distinguishes the noble from the ordinary:
the untainted noble wisdom from the stage of the path of vision (darśanamārga) and above is capable of destroying that which is difficult to break, and is thus generally termed "vajra.
Second, it distinguishes cultivation from vision.
Only that which takes the unimpeded antidote of the path of cultivation as its diamond is so; all others are not.
Third, distinguishing the superior from the inferior,
as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:

"Only the uninterrupted path of both insight (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama*)."
All others are not [the case].
The fourth [point] distinguishes the superior from the inferior,
as stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
Only the unimpeded path of the bhāvanāmārga of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is considered the diamond-like [samādhi]; all others are not.
This fifth point distinguishes the end from the beginning.

Only the very last of the antidotes within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the "diamond-like" (*vajropama*); all others are not.
It is by means of this that one reaches the ultimate end and completely destroys the hindrances.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are five distinct types of faith.
The first distinguishes true faith from slanderous views.
From the stage of the Ten Faiths upward, when the mind of faith is perfected, one is forever free from slandering the Dharma; all such individuals are equally termed "Vajra.
This second point distinguishes those who abide [in the fruit] from those who regress.
From the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) upward, the accomplishment of understanding and conduct is firm and difficult to destroy; thus it is collectively termed "vajra.
The third point distinguishes these as supramundane and different from the mundane.
From the first bhūmi upward, one realizes true non-outflow (anāsrava);
because it can destroy delusive afflictions and cannot itself be destroyed, it is termed "vajra.
The fourth [point] distinguishes what is above from what is below.
In the tenth stage, all forms of wisdom are termed "vajra. Therefore,
in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, it is stated that when a bodhisattva first enters the tenth stage,
they attain the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*).
The "Stainless Samādhi" (vimala-samādhi) likewise carries the meaning of the diamond (*vajra*) that shatters obstructions.
While the fifth [stage] marks the end as distinct from the beginning,
it is only the final, ultimate single thought-moment that constitutes the diamond.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"In his final body, beneath the Bodhi tree, he attains the samādhi of being free from all stains of the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*),
which is subsumed under what is called the Vajra-samādhi."
Based on this corroboration, [the analysis] is restricted to the ultimate limit.
Such is the division of positions; these four gates are now concluded.
Next, we shall clarify the Vajra [nature] regarding the presence or absence of delusion.
Regarding this, let us first discuss it from the perspective of ultimate exhaustion.
According to the Abhidharma,
even within the diamond-like mind (vajra-citta), there can still be afflictions.
One also attains freedom from delusion;
because afflictions do not function within the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta),
it is said to be "without delusion."
The acquisition (prāpti) of the defilements to be abandoned exists only on the periphery of the mind;
therefore, it is said that "defilements exist. Question: [Why is this so?]
If one says that the acquisition (prāpti) of afflictions still exists at the edge of the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), one should not say they are abandoned.
If one says they are abandoned, there should be no acquisition.
How then can it be said that the acquisition of the abandoned afflictions still exists at the edge of the mind?
The commentary states:
The vajra is its mental dharma (cittadharma).
The attainment of the abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa) is neither matter (rūpa) nor mind (citta).
This is because that which is not of the mind cannot coexist with the mind;
therefore, regarding that vajra-mind, there may be the acquisition of delusion.
Although this vajra-mind is accompanied by such acquisition, the acquisition of delusion can no longer draw forth future [delusions].
Therefore, it is called "abandonment.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the defilements thus abandoned is an impermanent phenomenon;
it ceases simultaneously with the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) and is never again continued thereafter.
Because there is no continuity, one no longer acquires those past and future afflictions to make them one's own;
this is called attaining liberation.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), [dharmas] both exist and do not exist.
In that school, the vajra must necessarily exist within the continuum.
Since, in reality, there is no severing of fetters within a single moment,
when it first arises within that continuum, the realization of the principle is not yet clear.
As long as subtle darkness still persists, one may say that delusion exists;
when the ultimate realization is achieved and the principle is seen with clarity,
grasping and attachment are entirely exhausted, and one may say that there is no delusion.
Furthermore, this is not the same as in the Abhidharma system, where the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the abandoned afflictions (*kleśa*) resides in the same location as their antidote (*pratipakṣa*);
therefore, it is said that there are no afflictions.
[The opponent] asks:
If, at the end, there were no delusion, what would distinguish it from the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The commentary states:
"The diamond [samādhi] is the wisdom of further progress."
One should exert effort to contemplate the principle and exert effort to be free from delusion;
the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is wisdom that accords with what was previously established.
There is a difference in that one may leisurely contemplate the principle and remain free from confusion; such is the distinction.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, the explanations given by people differ.
First, the divergent views are set forth;
next, their errors are examined;
finally, the correct meaning is revealed.
Regarding what is called "different explanations," it has been traditionally transmitted since ancient times that there have always been two theories.
One theory asserts that [the self] definitely exists.
How is it known that this "Vajra-mind" belongs to those in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If they were entirely free from delusion, they should be called those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras that the Buddha’s bodhi severs the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
If there were no afflictions whatsoever within the vajra-like [samādhi],
what would the Buddha have severed?
Furthermore, some people proclaim that there is an absolute absence of delusion.
How is it known that this refers to the vajra-mind?

The clarification of ignorance through the understanding that treats it as an affliction: since the understanding that dispels ignorance and the ignorance itself do not coexist, how could there be ignorance?
Furthermore, if there were ignorance, this ignorance would necessarily have to be abandoned.
After the Vajra [shoulder], another Vajra is established;
because it is not established again, it is clearly known that there is no delusion.
Such is the divergent explanation.
Next, we shall refute that [position]. First, we shall dismantle the claim that it definitely exists.
If afflictions definitely exist at the moment of the diamond-like mind, then they could not be severed.
If one cannot sever [these], it is not called "vajra" and is not called "unimpeded"; only when one can so sever it does it receive the name "vajra."
It is called "unimpeded" because it is known with certainty to be capable of severing [afflictions].
Because it is capable of severing them, one cannot say that they exist.
If one says that [the lamp] can destroy [darkness] and yet claims that darkness exists,
then within that lamp there ought to be the very darkness it destroys.
That [state] cannot exist;
this case should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that the ground of ignorance within the *vajra-hṛdaya* is what causes the Buddha to sever [defilements], [that is also untenable].
One should name the Buddha-wisdom "Vajra," and one should name the Buddha-wisdom the "Unobstructed Path";
yet that Buddha-wisdom is not so named.
Because it is not unobstructed,
one should not say that residual ignorance remains within the vajra-like mind to be severed by the Buddha’s perfect wisdom.
Furthermore, if the Buddha’s wisdom were unobstructed and yet failed to sever it, this would contradict the sūtras.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"In the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is called a bodhisattva;
in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one is called a buddha."
Why is it said that the Buddha possesses unimpeded abandonment?
Furthermore, if the Buddha’s wisdom acts as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) to correctly abandon ignorance,

then according to the Hīnayāna teachings, one should employ the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) as the path of non-obstruction to abandon the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Since that is not the case,
this is likewise not so. Next, the absolute non-existence [of the self] is refuted.
If this concentration were entirely free from delusion, it should be called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Since it is not [yet] beyond training, it cannot be entirely devoid of delusion.
Furthermore, if the diamond-like [samādhi] were consistently free from delusion...
The principle realized should be equal to that of the Buddha,
and the wisdom accomplished should be equal to that of the Buddha,
as stated in the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-sūtra*.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages fill all realms like rice, hemp, and reeds;
yet even a hundred thousand million times the wisdom of a Tathāgata, or even any calculation whatsoever, cannot equal it.
One knows with certainty that the vajra-obstructions of delusion have not yet been exhausted.
Furthermore, the reason the Buddhas are eternal is because their delusions are exhausted and their realization of principle is ultimate.
If the diamond-like mind is consistently free from delusion and its vision of principle reaches its ultimate limit—
when delusions are exhausted and principle is fully realized— why would it not be eternal?
To argue otherwise is incorrect.
Next, the correct meaning is revealed:
within the vajra-mind, there can be both delusion and the absence of delusion.
What is the meaning of this?
Ignorance is twofold: first, ignorance of distinct characteristics.
Among all phenomena, one perceives them through conditions yet fails to understand them;
conversely, one clearly understands them.
Therefore, they are called "dissimilar characteristics."
Second is the ignorance of self-nature (*svabhāva-avidyā*).
This refers to the diamond-like characteristic (*vajra-lakṣaṇa*) which is the antidote to that [ignorance] through its illuminating condition;
although its nature is luminous clarity, it is called "ignorance of self-nature" because it is characterized by darkness and delusion.
These two are difficult to distinguish;
they should be clarified through analogy.
The ignorance of distinct characteristics (visabhāga-avidyā), which fails to comprehend its object, is like seeing in the dark.
Intrinsic ignorance is like seeing things in a dream;
although there is something perceived, its nature is one of obscurity.
Such is the characteristic of delusion.
Within the *vajra-citta*, there are distinct characteristics:
because all ignorance has been completely exhausted, it can be said that there is no delusion;
yet because innate ignorance (*prakṛti-avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, it can be said that there is still delusion.
Because he is free from delusion, he perceives and knows the realm of the Buddha in its entirety, being no different from a Buddha.
For this reason, it is said in the sutras that he is "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambuddha). Question:
If one asks how these can be distinguished as belonging to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
the explanation is that they are so called because the power of the vajra exerts itself to eliminate darkness.
The Buddha-mind is relaxed and at ease;
furthermore, the diamond-like mind illuminates its objects without delusion,
yet the Buddha-mind has no object of perception.
There is this discrepancy.
A question is asked:
If it is said that the diamond-like [samādhi] is free from delusion, why does the sūtra state that the Buddha abandons ignorance?
The commentary states:
That explanation concerns the realization and elimination of liberation;
it does not pertain to the unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, because there is still delusion within the vajra-like state, it is subsumed under the category of the "factors of training" (*śaikṣa*).
Moreover, the essence of the delusions present within the vajra-like mind is the mind of false consciousness that clings to objects.
Because the conditioned mind has not yet ceased,
the emotions remain distinct from the dharmas and cannot be fused with the mind so that it becomes as vast as the dharmas.
For this reason, the virtues of the ten stages are inferior to those of the Buddha.
When one reaches the point where the Buddha abandons them, there remains only the true mind.
This true mind is free from conditions and makes no distinction between self and other;
therefore, it can integrate the mind so that it becomes as vast as the Dharma.
Furthermore, within the True Dharma, the infinite Buddha-minds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are subsumed within the Dharma-realm.
According to the discourse on the Dharma, the mind is vast enough to encompass the entire Dharma-realm;
there is not a single gateway that does not contain the Buddha-mind.
Therefore, the Buddha’s virtues are vast and immeasurable, surpassing those of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas of the ten stages fill all worlds throughout the ten directions, as densely as rice, hemp, or reeds."
Compared to the Buddha’s merit, these ultimately fall far short; this is precisely why.
Furthermore, the essence of all delusions within the diamond-like [mind] is impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it has not yet attained the Buddha’s virtues of permanence and immovability. Question:
By whom are the delusions severed?
The commentary states:
Through the adamantine, unimpeded, and correct abandonment,
the mind of all-encompassing wisdom arises, realizing liberation and eliminating [afflictions].
Question: Since the diamond-like samādhi and the afflictions are of the same substance,
how can it rightly sever them?
If it can be correctly severed, it should not be of the same substance.
The commentary states:
"It severs ignorance that possesses distinct characteristics."
When light arises, darkness is extinguished; when understanding is born, delusion perishes.
These two are mutually incompatible and cannot constitute a single essence.
The nature of severance is such that ignorance and the resolution of delusion are of the same substance, yet they are mutually severed.
What is the meaning of this?
There are two kinds of severance.
First, by means of adamantine observation of the characteristic of ultimate truth alone, devoid of delusion,
one is able to ensure that the self-substance no longer draws forth subsequent existence,
thereby severing the meaning of its acting as a cause that draws forth subsequent existence.
Therefore, it is called "severance.
Second, by means of the power of the diamond-like condition that accords with reality, subsequent instances of the same kind are prevented from arising to meet the preceding;
this constitutes the meaning of severing the principle of the fruit repaying the cause.
Therefore, it is called "abandonment.
Question:
Does this refer specifically to the aspect of abandoning the darkness of delusion?
It also carries the sense of severing that which can be remedied by the vajra.
The explanation has both general and specific aspects;
when divided specifically, it refers solely to the sense of severing the darkness of delusion and ignorance.
Because the substance of darkness is exhausted, illumination also perishes accordingly;
just as when the oil of a lamp is exhausted, the light also perishes accordingly.
Speaking in general terms, both delusion and awakening are entirely exhausted.
It is precisely because the Vajra Contemplation of Reality is a great luminosity that it extinguishes ignorance;
because the contemplation of true quiescence is non-conceptual, it is able to still the conditions for affliction.
Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra:
Non-contemplation is bodhi, because it is free from all conditions.
Within the path of bodhi, all meanings are complete;
according to what one contemplates, there is that which is abandoned.
Therefore, in the Vajra [wisdom], both delusion and awakening are severed together.
It is asked:
Are both delusion and awakening not impermanent?
They naturally cease and pass away;
why rely on the diamond-like contemplation for true severance?
The commentary states:
Although this is impermanent and perishes of its own accord, its inherent power can draw forth a subsequent continuity so that it does not cease.
Therefore, it must be severed by the vajra so that it does not continue. Question:
Both delusion and awakening are extinguished and pass away.
Who composed this commentary on the Knowledge of All Modes?
It states that within the diamond-like mind of a bodhisattva, there is not only delusive cognition but also true virtue.
Although delusion is utterly extinguished, true virtue still remains.
"True illumination shining alone is said to be the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
A question is asked:
"The meaning of 'vajra' contains both the true and the false."
Regarding whether both the real and the false sever afflictions,
or whether only the false eliminates delusions,
there are two interpretations.
First, it distinguishes cause from effect:
the single delusion can be eliminated because the causal condition is the antidote and the result is the truth.
Because the true virtue within the *vajra* has not yet been manifested, it is not said that [the afflictions] are severed.
Second, discussing this according to its general meaning, both the real and the delusive are severed;
the delusive wisdom takes the real as its object.
Thus, one is able to extinguish delusions;
as the true nature gradually manifests, one is able to eliminate hindrances.
Such is a rough exposition of the meaning of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*).

93. The Meaning of Severing the Fetters (IX): An Exposition through Nine Gateways for the Analysis of the Meaning of Severing the Fetters. I. Distinguishing the Names and Defining the Characteristics; II. The Differences in the Paths of Treatment; III. The General and Specific Nature of the Objects of Cognition; IV. Gradual and Sudden [Severance]; V. The Conventional and the Real; VI. The Meaning of the Number of Categories and the Superiority or Inferiority of the Higher and Lower [Stages]; VII. Based on the Meditative Grounds (*dhyāna-bhūmi*); VIII. Classified by Way of the Spiritual Stages (*avasthā*); IX. Classified by Way of Consciousness (*vijñāna*). Within the first gateway: [The following sections follow].
First I shall explain its name, and afterwards I shall discern its characteristics.
As for the term "severing the fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*):
afflictions (*kleśa*), which are dark delusions, bind and accumulate birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is called a "fetter" (saṃyojana).
Furthermore, because afflictions fetter and bind sentient beings,
they are also called "fetters."
The understanding that fetters have arisen and been exhausted is termed "abandonment.
Because their doctrinal tenets differ,
their explanations of abandonment also vary.
First, I shall provide a detailed explanation based on the Abhidharma.
Within this, I will first clarify the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned,
and subsequently explain their abandonment.
There are two kinds of fetters:
first, those that are currently active;
second, those acquired through possession.
The active manifestation of greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth in relation to their objects is called the arising of afflictions.
Once these afflictions have arisen and ceased, they enter the past;
however, those of the same category are destined to arise.
Regarding those in the future:
within that interval, there is an acquisition of a defilement that is neither form nor mind;
situated at the edge of the mind, it acquires those past and future defilements.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) that follows along with the person is called "attainment" (*lābha*).
This acquisition maintains continuity like a rope binding an object;
therefore, people in the world speak of it as the "rope of attainment" (*prāpti-rajjū*).
The characteristics of delusion are thus.
Next, the methods for their treatment and abandonment are distinguished.
There are four such paths of treatment.
First, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
wherein the cultivation of insight is not yet perfected;
second, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
When the contemplation of the mind first reaches maturity,
one proceeds through the three paths of liberation,
becoming thoroughly proficient in accordance with the traditional method.
The fourth is the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), which initiates the cultivation of further advancement.
Among these four, the first suppresses and subdues what has arisen in the present.
The latter three are acquisitions through abandonment (*prahāṇa*). The first path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) correctly abandons the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) used here:
It is called "abandonment" because it causes [the acquisition of defilements] not to arise again after the moment they are attained;
it does not mean that the acquisition of defilements is called abandonment simply because it does not coexist with the Path.
That path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) simultaneously passes away into the past at the same moment as the acquisition [of the fruit].
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) arises and realizes the unconditioned state (asaṃskṛta-dharma) wherein the acquisition of those afflictions is exhausted.
The third, the path of excellence (viśeṣa-mārga), ensures that the previously acquired [afflictions] shall never arise again.
One maintains the aforementioned unconditioned state so as not to lose it;
whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), the severance of fetters is identical in this regard.
Next, one proceeds to distinguish the cultivation and severance according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun).
Within this, one first clarifies the fetters to be abandoned and subsequently clarifies their abandonment.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, afflictions likewise consist of two types.
First is manifestation;
second is attainment through accomplishment.
Manifestation of the afflictions is the same as in the Abhidharma.
The attainment of accomplishment differs from that of the Abhidharma.
The *Tattvasiddhi* does not assert that there is a separate dharma, neither form nor mind, called "attainment";
rather, it maintains that the conventional person attains past and future afflictions, causes, and effects.
It is called "accomplishment" and also called "attainment.
Such are the characteristics of the afflictions. Next, the methods for their treatment and abandonment will be explained.
First, one cultivates the eight dhyānas to subdue their manifest arising;
just as cultivating the first dhyāna subdues the fetters of the desire realm,
cultivating the second dhyāna subdues the fetters of the first dhyāna while simultaneously subduing those of the desire realm.
One proceeds until practicing the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
which suppresses the sphere of nothingness as well as the lower stages;
subsequently, one cultivates the contemplation of reality to sever what has been attained through that suppression.
This is a general and rough classification.
Within this, when discussing the subtle principles of contemplation, there are both temporary suppression and permanent eradication.
What is the meaning of this?
The Noble Path is threefold.
First is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
wherein one studies and contemplates the principles of the Truths but has not yet attained direct vision.
Second is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*),
which observes and attains right vision;
within this vision, one progresses through the three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), wherein one accords with what was previously established.
Of these three, the first is identical to the preceding meditative concentration (dhyāna) in that it suppresses the manifest [defilements];
the latter two are the unimpeded right abandonments (*anantarya-samyak-prahāṇa*) which result from the permanent eradication of the acquired defilements.
Through liberation, realization, and elimination,
and through unimpeded increase and clarity,
one is thus able to effect correct abandonment.
Liberation accords with the ancient tradition;
therefore, it merely realizes abandonment.
What are the characteristics of this abandonment?
The cause of the afflictions arises in the past;
the resulting fruit of delusion brings about the path of the future.
Arising in the intervening period, it prevents that which has passed away from acting as a cause for those causes and effects.
It prevents future [defilements] from becoming results;
therefore, it is called "severance.
According to the ultimate truth, it correctly obstructs subsequent delusions.
To cause them not to arise is what is termed "abandonment.
This occurs simply when future afflictions do not arise;
at that time, the causal status of past afflictions is rendered non-existent.
This explains the cause for abandonment;
it does not mean that an existing present cause of fault can be abandoned.
If one were to say that an existing past cause can be eliminated through its power, [it would be illogical].
This would mean that there is a past within the past.
How can there be a past within the past?
It is because the afflictions of the past have already arisen and have passed away.
This is the force from past lives that flows on until the present;
it is severed by the Path, and thus these two types of the past are eliminated once their substantial reality has been destroyed.
It is clearly known that there is no causal power present that can sever [the afflictions].
A question is asked:
"If there is no causal power present, what draws forth subsequent delusions so that they arise in the future?"
The commentary states:
When the causes of afflictions that arose in the past were about to arise, they had already completed their function of projecting and attracting [results] before they subsequently passed away.
Afflictions in the future are able to arise because they are distantly dependent upon the power of those [past causes].
It is not that present power pulls the subsequent [defilement] forth to cause it to arise. Question:
Is the defilement that arose in the past severed by a single path?
"Many paths are governed together.
This is the explanation of the term "many paths."
Why is this so? A single affliction of the past can produce many varieties of afflictions as its future fruits;
among these many varieties of fruits, there are coarse, subtle, and intermediate ones.
When the Noble Path first arises, it first severs many categories of future delusions.
At the time when coarse delusions are severed, the logical status of past delusions as "proximate causes" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those coarse delusions is not established.
Although the causes of the coarse [afflictions] have been severed, the principle that they serve as causes for the intermediate and subtle afflictions still persists;
since these can only be completely exhausted when the subsequent path arises, one must rely upon multiple paths.
Next, the characteristics of abandonment are distinguished according to the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, first the delusions are clarified and subsequently their treatment and abandonment are distinguished.
There are two kinds of delusions:
the first is the four abidings (catuḥ-vāsa).
The second is ignorance (*avidyā*).
All forms of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute the four abodes;
the darkness of delusion and lack of knowledge constitutes that ignorance.
Among the four abidings, there are both coarse and subtle [aspects].
The coarse arises manifestly through mental attention directed toward conditions;
the subtle is of the same substance as that ignorance, accomplished spontaneously according to its own nature.
Within ignorance there are both coarse and subtle aspects.
The coarse is the ignorance of divergent characteristics;
the subtle is the ignorance of intrinsic nature.
Among all phenomena, to perceive them without clear understanding and to instead possess clear comprehension is called "distinctive characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The essential nature of the seven consciousnesses is delusion and darkness.
Even if one’s perception of all phenomena is clear and distinct, it is still termed "dark delusion" and is called the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is like a person in a dream who, despite having cognition, is by nature in a state of昏睡 (deep slumber).
Furthermore, just as the nature of pleasant feeling is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
such is the characteristic of delusion.
Next, the methods for its treatment and abandonment are explained.
Regarding the abandonment of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*),
those that arise coarsely are abandoned in common with the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra); however,
as for the subtle ones, they must be extinguished through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), whereby the four abidings perish accordingly.
Among these, the treatment and abandonment are as explained regarding ignorance.
Within the abandonment of ignorance,
there are two types of treatment and abandonment for the characteristic of difference.

First, the cultivation of the mind through the contemplation of entering and emerging from meditative absorption prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) in order to clarify the process of remediation and abandonment;
second, the cultivation of the mind through the continuous contemplation on the stages themselves in order to clarify the process of remediation and abandonment.
Regarding the former, how does one first cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) prior to the stages as the causal basis for remediation?
Subsequently, one cultivates the untainted (anāsrava) as the correct remedy (samyak-pratipakṣa).
There are three types of correct remedies:
first, the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
Regarding whichever phenomenon one contemplates but has not yet seen,
it is through the two paths of non-obstruction that,
upon contemplation, one finally sees it.
The three paths of liberation follow what was previously seen; first,
the path of preparation subdues ignorance so that it does not obstruct the subsequent [paths].
This is because ignorance has already been established within the mind and cannot be forcibly suppressed to prevent its arising;
therefore, one merely suppresses it so that it does not obstruct subsequent unimpeded right abandonment.
It is like the world where light arises and darkness ceases;
liberation is realized through abandonment.
Such is the case prior to the stages.
Regarding the stages on the ground (*bhūmi*):
from the first stage upward, the untainted contemplative understanding (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*) proceeds in continuous succession;
within every moment of thought, there is no interruption of the obstacles.
Within that continuum of clear understanding, one discriminates according to the meaning;
in relation to the ignorance to be eliminated within its own respective sphere, it is called "unimpeded.
Furthermore, this very unimpeded state, arising external to the accumulation of ignorance severed by the preceding moment, is called "liberation."
Anticipating the ignorance that is to be extinguished by subsequent thought,
that which is capable of suppressing it so as not to obstruct the subsequent [thought],
thereby enabling the continuity of subsequent understanding to arise, is termed "skillful means" (upāya).
In this way, all such things are severed; this is the unimpeded illumination of objects,
the liberation through the illumination of objects.
The nature of severance takes the understanding derived from the preceding general contemplation of objects as its remedial cause;
subsequently, one cultivates the true contemplation as the primary remedy. This remedy is threefold.
First, the path of expedient means (*upāyamārga*),
wherein one contemplates that reality is without delusion yet has not yet attained direct vision.
Second, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*).
The three paths of liberation wherein one perceives the truth and is free from delusion, yet has not yet abandoned delusion;
and the path of liberation wherein one perceives the truth, is free from delusion, and is able to abandon delusion.
Among these three, in the first,
the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), gradually awakening to the emptiness of the essence is called "subduing and abandoning" (*vinirdhāvana*).
In the second, the unimpeded [path] (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is truly able to abandon it forever.

It is precisely because unimpeded right view is truly free from deluded conceptualization that it can cause the self-substance not to further attract subsequent states, and prevent the prior state from arising again; thus,
it is able to correctly sever [the cycle].
Because the self-nature of ignorance has been severed, its remedy also perishes accordingly,
just as when oil is exhausted, the light also extinguishes.
This third liberation is externally verified through the removal of burdens.
Because one realizes that the fundamental nature of phenomena is devoid of delusion,
within this gate, the conditions and the illumination are unimpeded;
this is the true realization of liberation.
The treatment and severance are thus.
Second, the distinctions within the path of treatment are clarified;
herein there are four parts.

First, the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); second, the distinction between the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);
third, the distinction between patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The fourfold analysis by way of analogy:
regarding the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), according to the Abhidharma, there are two paths of cultivation (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
First, the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*).

This refers to the severing of fetters through the six modes of practice that involve the eight worldly dhyānas, which grasp at higher levels while feeling aversion toward lower ones. What are these six modes?
They consist of observing the lower stages as suffering, coarse, and obstructive.
Observing the higher stages as peaceful, sublime,
and transcendent completes the six [contemplations].
This is like observing the desire realm as coarse, painful, and obstructive, thereby giving rise to weary detachment and severing the fetters of the lower realm.
One contemplates the stage of the first dhyāna as the sublime cessation that transcends the longing for higher tranquility;
by means of these six modes of practice, one severs the fetters of the desire realm,
continuing in this manner until one observes the sphere of nothingness as suffering, coarse, and an obstacle.
Observing the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) as the sublime cessation brings about deliverance;
one severs the fetters of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
In this single stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no higher state to be grasped, and thus equalizing wisdom (samatājñāna) remains uninterrupted.
However, these six modes of practice are generally explained collectively;
yet when discussed individually,
one should contemplate whichever single mode is appropriate among the latter three.
The same applies to the higher [realms].
One does not fully observe the six;
rather, there are two untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This refers to the contemplation of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths.
By means of this rational contemplation, one severs all afflictions.
What are these sixteen?
There are four contemplations on suffering:
namely, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
There are four contemplations on the origin [of suffering].
With the origination of clinging as condition,
there are four contemplations on cessation:
cessation, stilling, excellence, and renunciation.
The contemplation of the path has four aspects;
the path is like a vehicle following a track.
This meaning is as explained previously in the section on the Four Noble Truths.
However, these sixteen [aspects] are explained collectively for the majority of practitioners;
if discussed individually for each person, under each Truth (satya), one contemplates a single aspect.
Within the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, these are merely impure (*sāsrava*) and can only suppress [the afflictions], but cannot sever them permanently.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Because there is no severance of fetters within the mundane path (laukikamārga),
one cannot be said to be practicing for the three fruits within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga)."
Regarding the essential point of their permanent abandonment, it must be by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, the abandonment of the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsika-kleśa*) must likewise be by means of the untainted, because these are abandoned through the delusion regarding principles being severed by the vision of those principles; thus, the abandonment of ignorance regarding phenomena may also be untainted.
Training in the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) to sever ignorance regarding affairs constitutes that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
To sever the stage of ignorance so that such ignorance does not arise regarding those affairs must be without outflows (*anāsrava*). This concludes this section.
Next, regarding the distinction between the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) as remedies,
according to the Abhidharma, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms are subsumed into three categories,
beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The afflictions of seeing the truths constitute the first portion;
the afflictions of seeing the truths within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception constitute the second portion;
and the afflictions of cultivation within the three realms constitute the third portion.
Within these three realms, the afflictions of view regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are abandoned solely through the vision of the truths;
the afflictions of cultivation within the three realms are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation;
and the afflictions of the vision of the truths from the sphere of nothingness downward are not fixed as to whether they are abandoned by their antidotes.
If an ordinary person abandons [afflictions], they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because the eight worldly dhyānas are subsumed within the path of cultivation.
If a noble one (*ārya*) abandons them, they are abandoned through insight (*darśana*).
Question: Since ordinary beings lack insight and understanding,
how can they manage to sever the afflictions of the truths?
The commentary states:
Although ordinary beings lack insight, they employ the eight dhyānas;
collectively they loathe the faults of the lower realms, without distinguishing between the paths of seeing and cultivation.

Therefore, when one has severed those three emptinesses and returns to sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) are simultaneously extinguished. Question:
When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) severs the afflictions of the path of cultivation below the three emptinesses, why do the afflictions of the path of seeing also follow and cease?

When the Noble One abandons the afflictions of the three realms through the vision of the truths (*darśana-mārga*), why do the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) not depart along with them?
Why must they be abandoned separately by means of the path of cultivation? To explain:
Ordinary beings sever delusions without fixed limits;
they cultivate weary detachment based on general characteristics. Therefore, they sever them universally.
What is meant by "universal revulsion"?
It is because one universally contemplates all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) of the lower stages as suffering and so forth.
When a noble one (*ārya*) abandons afflictions, there must necessarily be a specific limit.
At the time of seeing the principle (dharma), although the delusion regarding the principle is eliminated, defiled phenomena still remain;
therefore, they must be severed separately.
In the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, all afflictions of view (*darśana-heya*) are severed solely by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
All afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are severed solely by the path of cultivation;
this is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi* within the Mahāyāna teachings.
This concludes the two sections on unmixed antidotes.
Next, regarding the path of cultivation, it is distinguished by means of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
Settling the mind in the Dharma through wisdom is called patience;
it involves making a definitive judgment regarding the object.
It is explained as "knowledge" (jñāna).
According to the Abhidharma, the patience (kṣānti) that abandons the delusions of the truths is the unimpeded [path],
while knowledge is liberation.
The knowledge that abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation is called "unimpeded" (ānantarya),
and that knowledge is called "liberation" (vimukti).
For what reason is the patience (kṣānti) regarding the afflictions of the path of seeing considered "unimpeded" but not given the name "knowledge"?
The commentary states:
Seeing and understanding established in principle is called patience (*kṣānti*).
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that have been abandoned still accompanies the mind.
Regarding the attainment of [knowledge] together with the mind, there is the case of "attainment accompanied by doubt," where one remains indecisive due to doubt;
therefore, it is not called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Why, then, is it said that wisdom serves as liberation from the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*)?
Because doubt has already been abandoned and the mind is resolute,
why is it that the knowledge of the cultivation of afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*) is termed "unimpeded knowledge" (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*) and its wisdom is termed "liberation" (*vimukti*)?
It is because doubt only obstructs the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and does not obstruct the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) treats its respective objects with absolute certainty;
therefore, all [factors therein] are termed "knowledge" (jñāna).
Why is it that doubt (vicikitsā) obstructs only the vision of the truths (darśanamārga) and does not obstruct the path of cultivation?
The commentary states:
Since doubt is an affliction that deludes one regarding the principles [of reality],
it obstructs only insight (*darśana*).
Because one is not deluded regarding phenomena, it does not obstruct the cultivation of the path.
Question: If it is said that doubt obstructs only the vision [of the truth] because it is delusion regarding the principle, [then...]
The Sage also contemplates the principles of the Truths when practicing the Path;
why, then, does this not constitute an obstruction? To explain:
When the Noble One has clearly perceived the principle within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), they have already abandoned doubt and attained certainty.
Although they repeatedly contemplate the principle within the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), there is nothing that is not fully understood due to those conditions;
therefore, they are not obstructed by the fetter of doubt.
Question: If it is said that doubt does not delude one regarding the object and thus does not obstruct cultivation,
yet we currently observe people who give rise to doubt because they are deluded about an object.
It is like seeing a stump at night and suspecting it might be a tree trunk or a person;
how can one say that [cognition] does not arise in dependence upon an object? To explain:
This doubt concerns a non-defiled dharma that cannot obstruct the path;
therefore, it is not discussed. Question:
When a sage cultivates the path, his mind is consistently free from doubt;
both non-obstruction and liberation are termed "wisdom.
This interpretation is indeed plausible.

The eight dhyānas cultivated on the path of cultivation by ordinary persons also sever doubt; these attainments arise simultaneously with the mind. For what reason are they designated as "knowledge" (jñāna) when they are without obstruction?

To explain: *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist Abhidharma commentary discussing the nature of knowledge (jñāna) versus attainment (prāpti) in the context of the dhyānas.*
Although the eight dhyānas cultivated by ordinary persons sever doubt and sever the fetters through the objects they take as conditions, these objects are coarse and easy to comprehend;
because the mind that takes them as conditions is decisive, they are designated as "knowledge.
What objects do they take as conditions? They are the observation of all contaminated phenomena of the lower stages as suffering, coarse, and so forth.

Question: When a noble one contemplates the lower realm as suffering, they are said to be "contemplating principle" (緣理). Since ordinary people also contemplate suffering, why is theirs called "contemplating phenomena" (緣事)?
The commentary states:
The Sage contemplates that every moment contains subtle *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering inherent in conditioned formations).
Because the principle of *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* is universally pervasive, it is termed "principle" (*li*).
Ordinary worldlings merely contemplate the afflictions of the eight types of suffering, such as birth, old age, sickness, death, and separation from what is loved;
therefore, this is called "contemplating objects. It is asked:
How can one settle a matter and thereby sever doubts concerning the delusion regarding principles?
The commentary states:
although one does not observe the principles with clarity, such doubts can nonetheless be severed.
By observing the lower realms as suffering, coarse, and so forth,
one is thus able to cultivate revulsion and abandon them;
such is the Abhidharma position.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, all paths of cultivation are collectively termed "patience" (*kṣānti*) and collectively termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Because the mind is settled in accordance with the Dharma, they are collectively termed "patience."
Because it is decisive and unattached, it is generally termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "knowledge" are also used interchangeably,
as in the teaching of the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*).
This applies from beginning to end.
The wisdom of the two truths and so forth extends to both the initial and subsequent stages;
according to their respective meanings, they are fully present, and there is no difference in their essential significance.
The initial observation is called patience (*kṣānti*);
its final completion is called wisdom (*jñāna*). These three gates are concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish the path of cultivation through the methods of inference and analogy.
What is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) is also termed "present knowledge.
As stated in the treatise:
because one first knows the phenomena, it is called "knowledge of phenomena."
Because it cognizes the present dharma, it is also called "present knowledge" (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
Regarding "inferential knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*): at the time of correct cognition, one also cognizes the dharma as a distinct dharma;
because it takes this [subsequent] stage as its primary object, it is called inferential knowledge.
This is because one must rely on direct knowledge to infer [the truth].
These two will be fully and extensively analyzed later in the chapter on the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
How are they remedied and abandoned?
In the Abhidharma system, prior to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), the cultivation of insight is not yet perfected;
[afflictions] are merely suppressed and not permanently severed.
Only from the stage of the Dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti) onwards, when the subsequent insight (anvayajñāna) is perfected, can they be permanently severed.
Regarding the dharma-patience, dharma-knowledge, and liberation pertaining to the afflictions to be abandoned through vision in the desire realm,
why is inferential patience not employed as their antidote?
Because their objects are distinct.
Furthermore, subsequent patience arises based on the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
At the moment dharma-knowledge arises, the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through seeing have already been eliminated;
therefore, one does not proceed to subsequent patience.
Regarding the subsequent patiences (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) that counteract the afflictions to be abandoned through vision in the higher realms:
why are the dharma-patiences (*dharma-kṣānti*) not used as their antidotes?
Because their objects (*ālambana*) are distinct; even though one has seen the lower truths, one remains deluded regarding the higher realms.
Therefore, they are not treated [by it].

Regarding the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), the unimpeded knowledge (ānantarya-jñāna), and the liberation-knowledge (vimukti-jñāna) that counteract the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
why is inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) not employed as their antidote?
Since the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation have already been eliminated when subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises,

the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*), as well as the four subsequent knowledges, serve as the unimpeded [knowledges] for the afflictions of the higher realms to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, this very [knowledge] is used as liberation.
Why is the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin not employed as the superior antidote,
but rather specifically the two types of dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path?
This meaning has already been fully explained previously in the section on the Vajra Mind.
Within the desire realm, cessation and the path are subtler than the higher objects;
one contemplates the subtle and abandons the coarse.
Therefore, it is able to cure [the afflictions].
The suffering and origin of the desire realm are coarse compared to the objects of the higher realms;
even if one contemplates them, the afflictions of the higher realms will not be eliminated.

Question: If it is said that the cessation and the path within the desire realm are subtler than the objects of the higher realms and serve as antidotes for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms,
why do they not also serve as antidotes for the afflictions to be abandoned through vision in the higher realms?
The commentary states:
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation arise by taking objects as their conditions;
by contemplating the subtle and feeling aversion toward the coarse, one is able to abandon them.
Therefore, while contemplating the two truths of cessation and the path within the desire realm eliminates the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms,
the afflictions of the higher realms that directly delude one regarding the principles of the truths must be abandoned only by seeing those very truths.
Therefore, it cannot eliminate the delusions of the higher realms.
Such is the Abhidharma position.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), however, if one discusses the suppression of delusions, even subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is capable of doing so.

If one discusses the definitive abandonment [of afflictions], it must rely solely on the manifestation of wisdom that realizes the principle (*tattva*), because this manifest wisdom perceives the principle with clarity.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, the delusions regarding the principle are abandoned by the manifest wisdom capable of such realization.
Inferential wisdom can subdue them;
it severs the delusions regarding phenomena, severing both manifest and latent afflictions.
Such is the nature of the remedial path.
Third, the clarification of the general and specific objects of focus.
"Objects" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
Within the Abhidharma system, there are two ways of contemplating these truths.
First, the general;
second, the specific.
Within the general foundations of mindfulness, one contemplates the Four Noble Truths collectively as empty and selfless.
This is termed "general.
From the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan) upward, one contemplates the Four Truths individually; this is termed "specific."
Within that, through general observation, one merely suppresses [the afflictions] but does not sever them,
because vision is not yet clear.
Within the specific [observation], when first practicing, one suppresses them but does not yet sever them.

From the stage of patience with suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanakṣānti*) upward, the cultivation of insight becomes capable of severing [the afflictions]. Within the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are also both general and specific [categories]:
in the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), and patience (*kṣānti*), they are specific rather than general.
From the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) upward, there is a general observation without differentiation.
Within the Supreme Mundane Dharmas, one generally contemplates the Four Truths as being nominally existent and conventionally designated.
From the Stage of No-Mark (*animitta*) upward, one generally contemplates the emptiness of the Truths.
Within this context, if one confronts the eight dhyānas of the conventional truth, both collectively and individually, they are severed;
thus the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"From the stage of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) onwards, afflictions are gradually severed until they are exhausted upon the realization of cessation (*nirodha*)."

This means that because one perceives the principle of cessation within the signless (*animitta*), if one observes according to the principle by distinguishing the various aspects, such observation merely suppresses [the afflictions].
Within the comprehensive observation, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has not yet achieved comprehensive observation; it merely suppresses them but does not permanently sever them.
Only when the general contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) and those above it is accomplished can [the afflictions] be permanently severed. Question:
For what reason, within the Abhidharma system, are they suppressed collectively but severed individually?
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is explained that specific [defilements] are suppressed while those common to all are severed,
because the faults established by the two schools differ.
In the Abhidharma teachings, ignorance is the root of affliction;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In the past, I and you did not see the Four Truths."
Therefore, one has long drifted in the ocean of suffering of birth and death;
this is truly because delusion and ignorance constitute the root of affliction,
and thus one’s general observation remains unclear.
However, because one can suppress the afflictions and achieve clear discernment through specific contemplation,
one is able to eradicate them forever.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, grasping is taken as the root of affliction;
yet when observing separately, the grasping at signs has not yet been extinguished,
and thus one merely suppresses the delusions.
By observing them collectively to dissolve their characteristics, one is able to sever them forever.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are likewise both collective and individual approaches.
One enters into the equality of phenomena by contemplating the emptiness of the truths collectively;
one contemplates the existence of the truths individually according to their specific distinctions.
Both the collective and individual contemplations sever the afflictions.
The affliction of attachment to existence is the darkness of delusion regarding emptiness;
it is removed by general observation (*samantad-darśana*).
The affliction of attachment to emptiness is the ignorance that deludes one regarding phenomena.
They are eliminated through distinct contemplations.
Such are the general and specific [contemplations].
Within the fourth gate, there is a distinction between the sudden and the gradual.
In the Abhidharma system, the afflictions of the truths are abandoned through the noble truths, which are gradual,
while the categories [of abandonment] are simultaneous.
The afflictions beneath the Four Truths are eliminated sequentially;
this is termed "gradual.
Within each Truth, the nine grades of affliction are abandoned all at once by a single antidote.
This is termed "sudden.
It is because the delusions of view that obscure the mind are easily eliminated;
therefore, a single treatment can destroy all nine grades.
Therefore, the treatise describes it as a skillful means for breaking stones.
Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in relation to the principle of the truths (*satya*), it is neither gradual nor sudden;
yet, in terms of the categories and numbers of those afflictions, it is termed "gradual."
By following any single truth according to conditions, one is able to sever [the afflictions] without necessarily contemplating all four;
therefore, it cannot be described as either sudden or gradual.
From the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
because the nine grades of afflictions within each stage are abandoned one by one, it is called "gradual.
This is truly because the defiled phenomena of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation arise as persistent entanglements that are difficult to relinquish.
Therefore, they are eliminated gradually.
For this reason, it is said in the treatises that the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is like severing lotus fibers.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the abandonment of the afflictions of the truths to be abandoned through seeing is considered instantaneous with respect to those truths.
The categories [of the truths] are gradual;
however, because one observes the Four Truths as a whole to sever the delusions regarding those truths,
it is called "sudden."
Because the afflictions are severed gradually according to their coarse or subtle categories and numerical distinctions,
it is called "gradual.
In severing the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one contemplates the emptiness of the truths as a whole.
It can also eliminate them;
this is the sudden approach.
Through individual contemplation, they are likewise eliminated.
It is neither gradual nor sudden.
Because it takes a single truth as its object, with respect to the categories of delusions, it is only gradual and not sudden.
