Within the Mahāyāna teachings, the severance of delusions regarding the nature of reality is sudden with respect to that truth.
The categories of the teachings are gradual;
however, by comprehensively contemplating the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) to sever that delusion,
they are termed "sudden" with respect to the Truths (*satya*).
Because the coarse and the subtle are gradually eliminated,
it is termed "gradual" in terms of its categories;
the severance of delusions regarding phenomena is gradual with respect to their objects.
The categories are also gradual;
one gradually studies all dharmas and successively eliminates them.
For this reason, they are called "gradual" with respect to their objects.
Because the coarse and the subtle are abandoned gradually,
they are also called "gradual" in terms of their categories;
such are the modes of sudden and gradual abandonment.
In the fifth section, the abandonment of the provisional and the real is explained.
In the Abhidharma system, real dharmas are subject to abandonment,
whereas this is not discussed regarding the provisional.
The Noble Path is able to sever the fetters in every moment of thought;
therefore, there is actual abandonment within it.
In that school’s system, there is no separate conventional dharma.
Therefore, it is conventionally said that [the afflictions] are not severed, because they are actually severed.
In the Path of Seeing, each of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) severs the afflictions of the truths individually in a single momentary thought.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*);
each, in a single moment of thought, abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, this abandonment occurs within a provisional intermediate state.
In reality, there is no cessation.
Thus, the "Chapter on Conventional Designations" in the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"All things attained through cessation are merely conventional designations."
It is simply because the principle is not clearly perceived in a single thought-moment that it is truly uninterrupted;
only when there is continuity does clarity arise, and thus one speaks of "intermittent cessation" as a conventional designation.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, at the time of initial cultivation, the continuity [of afflictions] can be severed;
this is because a single moment of insight into reality is not yet clear.
At the time of final accomplishment, a single moment can sever it.
The continuity [of afflictions] is thereby exhausted.
Because one perceives the principle clearly in every thought-moment, one is able to sever [the afflictions] in a single thought.
Thus, it is said in the *Bhūmi-sūtra* regarding the seventh stage (*saptamī bhūmi*).
In every thought-moment, the bodhisattva is fully endowed with all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Since these accompanying dharmas are all capable of counteracting obstacles,
a single thought-moment is thus able to effect what is to be severed.
Because they are exhausted only when obstacles and difficulties are completely eliminated and the continuum is brought to an end,
the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"It is not only severed at the beginning, nor in the middle or at the end."
One must grasp [the object] in its prior, middle, and subsequent phases in order to exhaustively sever it;
the same applies to the provisional and the real.
Sixth, this clarifies the meaning of the number of categories and their relative superiority or inferiority.
First, let us distinguish their quantity.
In the Abhidharma system, there are eight moments of non-obstruction (*anantarya*) for severing the afflictions of the truths (*satyakleśa*);
that is to say, the four dharmakṣāntis and the four anvayakṣāntis.
Each is a single moment of thought.
If one includes the paths of liberation, there are sixteen moments of mind.
Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions of the path of cultivation, there are eighty-one grades of unimpeded [paths].
Each category consists of nine grades;
there are nine uninterrupted paths for severing the afflictions of the desire realm,
and likewise nine grades for each stage up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, there are eighty-one grades of unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇa*).
If one includes both the penetrations (*abhisamaya*) and the liberations (*vimukti*), there are one hundred and sixty-two minds.
When the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are combined, there are one hundred and seventy-eight grades.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) are categorized as a single class by way of their general characteristics,
though they are immeasurable when distinguished in detail.
Not only the eight patiences and eight liberations, etc.,
which sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation,
but within each stage (bhūmi), there are generally nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation as coarse divisions.
When subdivided, they are immeasurable.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi*, in the chapter on "Eliminating Faults," states:
"One eliminates all afflictions by means of immeasurable minds."
It is neither eight nor nine.
Regarding the statement that it is not eight:
this differs from the Abhidharma, which asserts that one abandons the delusions of the truths of vision solely by means of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*).
Regarding the statement that it is "not nine":

this differs from the Abhidharma, which asserts that within each stage (*bhūmi*) one employs the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In the Mahayana Dharma as well, immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*) sever all afflictions.
It does not stop at eight or nine;
from the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra) up to the Vajra stage,
in every moment of thought, all fetters are severed.
The categories are thus.
Next, we shall discuss their degrees:
although the afflictions are numerous, they are essentially comprised of three grades.
This refers to the inferior, middling, and superior.
The interpretation of their meaning is not fixed;
however, in terms of their faults, coarse afflictions are classified as superior.
Because their faults are heavy,
gross afflictions are classified as superior; because their faults are subtle, fine afflictions are classified as inferior.
Regarding the space between the two pillars, Yue considered it to be the center;
he applied his strength to divide it, yet his coarse delusion was powerful and his subtle discernment weak.
Coarse afflictions are easily eliminated and are thus described as "lower";
subtle afflictions possess powerful force.
It is difficult to suppress and sever;
therefore, it is described as supreme.
Thus, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says:
The power of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is supreme;
the middle [part] is explained as before.
Its analysis also has three [aspects].
That is to say, there are the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior. A coarse understanding is termed inferior;
a subtle understanding is called superior.
Regarding the space between the two pillars, Yue considers it to be the center;
this is used to resolve doubts concerning the uncertainty of the upper and lower [realms].
It is directed toward the delusions of the three grades at the initial gate.
It can be said that the lower level of understanding counteracts the higher-level afflictions,
the middle level counteracts the middle-level afflictions,
and the superior level of understanding counteracts the lower-level afflictions.
This one point is as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra). Thus, that text says:
"When a Bodhisattva practicing through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) practices the lower degree of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), various signs of faults increase."
During the stage of medium patience, it is superior; during the stage of high patience, it is inferior.
This is in relation to the three grades of delusions in the subsequent section.
It can be said that the lower degree of understanding treats the lower degree of afflictions;
the middle degree treats the middle;
and the upper degree of understanding treats the upper.
Because the resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) of the Buddhas can counteract the greatest affliction, which is ignorance (*avidyā*),
the number of categories is as such.
In the seventh gate, they are distinguished according to the dhyānas.
In the Abhidharma system, the abandonment of the delusions of the truths (satyadarśana-heya) relies upon six stages of dhyāna:
the preliminary stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas; these constitute the six stages.
For those who follow the gradual path (anupūrvika), they rely upon the preliminary stage of dhyāna.
Regarding the person who has transcended, within the dhyānas of the six stages, they may rely on whichever stage is appropriate. Question:
For what reason can only the dhyānas of the six stages sever the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), and not the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
The commentary states:

The first six mental states are coarse and powerful; they take the contaminated phenomena of the lower stages as their objects for the contemplations of suffering and its origin, and they also take their antidotes as objects for the contemplations of cessation and the path.
Therefore, having abandoned the afflictions of the views,
because the mind in the formless realm is subtle, it cannot take the contaminated phenomena of the lower realms as its object for the contemplations of suffering and origin;
nor can it take their antidotes— cessation and the path— as its object for the contemplations of cessation and the path.
Therefore, it is unable to sever the afflictions of the truths (darśana-heya).
The basis for severing the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) is not fixed;
if one were to sever the fetters by means of tainted knowledge (sāsrava-jñāna), etc., [the result would be uncertain].
By means of the path of skillful means consisting of those eight dhyānas, one eliminates the fetters of the lower realms,
yet does not eliminate the fetters of one’s own level or of higher levels.
For what reason does one not eliminate the fetters of one’s own level?
Because the power of the outflows (*sāsrava*) is weak, it cannot sever the fetters belonging to its own level;
it is like a person who has been bound and cannot free himself.
For what reason does it not sever the fetters of the higher realms?
Because the outflowing [states] (sāsrava) toward higher levels only give rise to delight and cannot produce weariness,
for what reason is the future not mentioned?
The future is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the first dhyāna.
For what reason is the intermediate [dhyāna] not mentioned?
These are the attendants of the first dhyāna and cannot sever the fetters belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
therefore, they are not discussed here.
If one uses the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) to sever the fetters, [then they are relevant].
Based on the dhyānas of the six stages and the three formless attainments— excluding the desire realm and the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
the untainted Great King does not abide in the extremes.
Within those nine stages of dhyāna that serve as his basis, he relies upon the dhyāna of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage to produce the untainted [wisdom] that severs all fetters.

The untainted [attainments] (*anāsrava*) produced in the remaining eight stages sever only the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of their own stage and those of the higher stages, but do not sever those of the lower stages.
Why is this so? Because the power of the untainted is great; thus, it severs the fetters of its own stage.
Because one is able to grow weary of the faults of the higher realms, one abandons the upper stages.
Untainted (anāsrava) states necessarily arise based on pure dhyāna (śuddha-dhyāna).
When pure dhyāna arises, the fetters (saṃyojana) of the lower stages have already been abandoned.
Therefore, the untainted [path] does not sever the lower fetters.
For this reason, the untainted [path] produced by relying on the future dhyāna is able to sever all afflictions of the three realms.

The untainted [wisdom] arising from the stage of the first dhyāna is able to sever the fetters of the first dhyāna up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, but it does not sever those of the desire realm;
this continues until the untainted [wisdom] arising from that concentration of nothingness.
One can sever the fetters of one’s own stage as well as those of the non-percipient realm, but not those of the lower stages.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
the abandonment of the delusions of the two wheels relies upon the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments.
Furthermore, while it relies on the lightning-flash samādhi of the desire realm,
how is it known that it also relies on the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments?
This is because the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) states that there are seven bases of concentration (*niśraya-samādhi*).
How is it known that this relies upon the "lightning-flash" concentration?
The *Tattvasiddhi* states that beyond the seven stages of reliance, there is additionally the "lightning-like samādhi" (*vidyut-sama-samādhi*) belonging to the desire realm which serves as its basis.
Question: Why does the Abhidharma not mention relying on the "lightning-flash" (vidyut-pradīpa)? Answer:
Because the Abhidharma teaches that this meditative concentration does not exist within the stages of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
He asked again:
"For what reason does the *Tattvasiddhi* not rely on the future or the intermediate state in its explanation? He replied: "Because..."
The *Tattvasiddhi* consistently asserts that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) distinct from the level of the first dhyāna;
therefore, it does not rely upon it.
Nevertheless, that treatise also states that the Brahmā King can reach the intermediate state.
It should properly be subsumed under the first dhyāna according to its characteristics;
therefore, it is not discussed separately.
For what reason is it not based on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)?
Because in the state of non-perception, the subtle mind does not arise, and thus there is no outflow-free [wisdom] to sever the afflictions.
Question: The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims:
One enters the attainment of cessation after the non-perceptual, untainted mind.
Why, then, is it said that the untainted [mind] is not produced?
The explanation is as follows:
There is a reason for this: first, one relies on a lower stage to give rise to untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*),
and by contemplating the suffering, impermanence, and so forth of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one abandons the afflictions of that sphere.
Thereafter, one uses that mind of the non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) to take as its object the previously contemplated suffering, impermanence, and so forth;
this is termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
In reality, however, there is no untainted state of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) that severs the fetters.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
the severing of the afflictions of the two wheels primarily relies upon the four dhyānas,
because the power of the fourth dhyāna is particularly strong.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he relied upon the fourth dhyāna;
yet, in principle, it is universally explained that from the realm of desire up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is able to sever the fetters.
Question: Since the distracted stages of the desire realm lack meditative concentration,
how can it be said that one relies on the concentration of the desire realm?
The commentary states:
Because there is meditative concentration (samādhi) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) according to the Mahāyāna, Nāgārjuna said:
There is a concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) upon which the Buddha constantly relies.
How does this differ from the lightning-flash concentration of the desire realm?
The lightening-flash should be understood as the sign of that concentration;
because it is attained only momentarily, it is called "lightening-flash" by the śrāvakas.
He asked again:
The non-percipient realm does not give rise to outflow-free [states].
Why, then, is it said "up to the non-percipient realm"?
The explanation is as follows:
Śrāvakas do not give rise to untainted [wisdom] based on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
whereas Bodhisattvas can.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
What is the bodhisattva’s concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Correspondence with the true mark is the bodhisattva’s concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because it is conjoined with the true mark, it is called untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is conjoined with the true nature (dharmatā), it is able to sever the afflictions (kleśa).
It is thus according to the dhyānas.
This is found in the eighth section.
Regarding the classification by locus:
in the Abhidharma system, all afflictions are subsumed into four categories,
with the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constituting one category.
The afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception constitute the second part;
the afflictions of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) pertaining to the sphere of nothingness and below constitute the third part;
and the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) pertaining to the sphere of nothingness and below constitute the fourth part.
Among these, the first part is abandoned solely by the Path of Seeing;
the second part is abandoned solely by the Vajra-like Mind of the Diamond-like Samādhi;
and the third part is abandoned either by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Alternatively, it is abandoned by a noble one during the path of seeing.
As for the fourth part, it is abandoned either by an ordinary person or by a noble one practicing the stage of once-returner through the path of cultivation.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the stage at which the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) are severed is not fixed.
If one discusses what is severed by the wisdom of signless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā-prajñā*), it must necessarily occur in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
However, if one considers what is severed by both the vision free from signs and the vision of emptiness, then everything from the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage upward severs the delusions of the truths.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"From the stage of 'Heat' (uṣmagata) onwards, one gradually abandons the afflictions until they are exhausted upon the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana).

If one universally practices the contemplation of conceptualization (vikalpa-saṃjñā), those [afflictions] to be abandoned are eliminated; from the stages of hearing (śruta) and reflection (cintā) upwards, all afflictions of vision (darśana-heya-kleśa) are severed."
Therefore, that treatise states:
"By means of the conditions of extensive learning and the conditions of reflection, the mind of conventional designation ceases;
by means of the conditions of 'Heat' and so forth, the mind that perceives the cessation of real dharmas arises."
To apprehend and establish a fixed characteristic within the combination of causes is called the mind of conventional designation (*prajñapti-citta*).
To apprehend and establish a fixed characteristic within the combination of phenomena (*dharma*) is called the mind of real phenomena (*dharma-citta*).
These two have been extensively analyzed as previously explained in the section on the meaning of conventional designation.
Question: Hearing and so forth are not the understanding that realizes the truths.
How can one attain the severance of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing the truths?
Since that is the expedient means for the path of seeing,
the afflictions to be severed therein are collectively termed "afflictions of seeing."
In the path of cultivation, the afflictions of the once-returner stage are abandoned sequentially.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, however,
the point at which the afflictions of those who have seen the truth are abandoned is not fixed.
If one discusses the essential point of realizing liberation through true insight and severing [afflictions], it occurs primarily at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Thus, the *Dilun* states:
"Those bound by various views are first severed during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the first stage."
If one discusses the stage of unhindered vision (*darśana-mārga*), the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) is also capable of severing them;
thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"In the prior stage of practice through understanding, the bonds of all views are severed."
Furthermore, if one discusses this generally, those from the stage of the Ten Faiths upward all sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*),
as that stage serves as the preparatory means for the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). However,
the point at which the afflictions of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are severed is not fixed.
The great stages are divided such that [afflictions] are gradually eliminated from the second bhūmi upward;
furthermore, if discussed comprehensively, they can all be eliminated from the final moment of mind within the first bhūmi onward.
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu*, the fulfillment of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) is called the practice of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
Such is the division of the stages.
Regarding the ninth [stage], there are three types based on the mind and consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
The first is the consciousness of phenomena,
which refers to the six consciousnesses.
The second is the deluded consciousness.
This refers to the seven consciousnesses and the mind.
The third is the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
These three are explained in detail as in the chapter on the eight consciousnesses.
How is it treated and severed?
Within the consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*),
the severance of cause and effect is termed "severance" (*chada*).
The essence of the mind does not perish;
within the midst of deluded consciousness,
when understanding first arises and darkness is extinguished, this is called "severance."
In the end, the deluded mind is completely extinguished, which constitutes cessation;
this is because one knows that the deluded mind fundamentally has no inherent existence within true consciousness.
To dissolve delusion is called the severing of names;
it does not extinguish the substance of the mind.

This is because the true mind is the cessation of delusion; when one reaches the ultimate limit, it is reality itself and there is nothing further to be removed, and thus the mind is not extinguished.
The interruption of the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) is like cutting a rope with a knife;
it is merely a separation.
The interruption of the deluded consciousness (*mṛṣā-vijñāna*) is like burning a rope with fire.
The entire body is completely exhausted;
within true consciousness it is severed like the untying of a rope knot,
with nothing further to be removed.
The meaning of "severing the fetters" has been analyzed as such.

94. Definition of Cessation (9): The Definition of Cessation Explained through Nine Gates. I. Explaining the Name and Discerning the Essence. 1. The Characteristics of Entry and Exit; 2. The Limits of Time; 3. Analysis by Way of Realm; 4. Analysis by Way of Ground; 5. Analysis of the Tainted and Untainted; 6. Analysis by Way of Person; 7. Distinguishing its Similarities and Differences in Relation to the Eighth Liberation; 8. Explanation of the Text. Regarding the first gate:
First, the names will be explained, and subsequently, their essential natures (svabhāva) will be discerned.
As for the names, they differ from one another;
there are four such types.
First is called the concentration of mindlessness;
second is called the concentration of the cessation of feeling; third is called the concentration of the cessation of perception and feeling.
The four names for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) provide a general explanation that is one and the same; yet,
within this, there are no lack of distinctions when analyzed specifically.
As for the "mindless concentration" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti),
its name is established specifically in contrast to the mind-king (citta-rāja);
it is the state wherein mental consciousness has completely ceased.
Therefore, it is called "mindlessness.
To be free from the conceptualization and mental agitation of the mind that possesses thought is termed the "concentration of mindlessness.
As for the "concentration of the cessation of sensation":
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is called "severing the experience of pleasure.
This name is established in contrast to the category of feeling (*vedanā*);
it signifies that all five types of feeling have ceased.
Therefore, it is said that one cuts off feeling (*vedanā*). The meditative concentration in which one is free from the distraction of feeling is called the "concentration that cuts off feeling.
This is because all sufferings reside within feeling; thus, cutting off this feeling is called the "bliss of cutting off feeling."
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Whatever sensation there is, that is true suffering;
abiding in the cessation of fixed sensations is called the abandonment of pleasant sensation."
The "extinction of feeling and perception" is a designation specifically applied to the two aggregates of feeling and perception.
When perception ceases and feeling vanishes, it is called the extinction of feeling and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
The term "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is a designation applied universally to characterize all mental states and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
The simultaneous cessation of all mind and mental factors is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).
Furthermore, the total exhaustion of the mind that takes the three realms as its object is also called "extinction," as is the case within the first dhyāna.
Although sensual desires and evil thoughts have been extinguished, discursive examination (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra) still remain;
even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), although the faults of the lower stages have been extinguished, the mind of its own level still persists.
For this reason, it is not called "extinction" (nirodha).
In this meditative absorption, all [phenomena] are extinguished;
hence it is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).
"Absorption" (*samādhi*) is as explained previously.
Such are the names.
As for their essential nature,
the proponents of various treatises disagree, each presenting a different explanation.
As that Buddhadeva has stated, the mind is the essence of a sentient being.
For what reason did he speak thus? Because one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation is still called a "sentient being."
If one were entirely without mind, they would not be called a sentient being;
since they are a sentient being, it is clear that they possess a mind.
Although its essence is mind, it is utterly free from coarse conceptualization.
Therefore, it is said that [all things] are extinguished.
As for the Abhidharma teaching that non-material and non-mental dharmas constitute the essence of the meditative attainment of cessation—
what is the meaning of this?
That treatise proclaims that one attains a dharma that is neither form nor mind by severing all mental deliberations;
this must be cultivated within the body to fill the locus of the mind.
Therefore, it is said that its essence is neither form nor mind.
Question: Within this state, mental deliberations are extinguished.
"Is the mind extinguished?
He replied, "It is not extinguished."
Why is it not extinguished?
Because the extinguisher and the extinguished are dharmas belonging to the same level (*bhūmi*).
For example, although wholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) may extinguish the unwholesome states of the desire realm, they do not extinguish their acquisition (*prāpti*).
This case is also like that.
It is asked:
If this [attainment] cannot destroy the acquisition because it is a dharma belonging to the same stage as the dharma to be destroyed, then...
When the roots of goodness are severed, one severs the wholesome states of the desire realm by means of the unwholesome states of the desire realm.
For what reason is the acquisition [of these states] severed? To explain:
When an icchantika severs the roots of goodness, they sever those roots through the three paths of skillful means, unhindered knowledge, and liberation;
because this is in extreme opposition to goodness, it universally severs their acquisition (*prāpti*).
In contrast, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) extinguishes the mind solely by means of skillful means.
Therefore, there is no relinquishing or acquiring [of the precepts]. Such is the Abhidharma;
the *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims it thus.

The unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) consisting of the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the point where consciousness (*vijñāna*) is exhausted, constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Question:
If it is said that the point where consciousness is exhausted constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation, then there would be no consciousness within that absorption.
It should not be a sentient being.
Furthermore, if it were without mind, how would it differ from grass and trees?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
Because the mind persists within, it is still called "possessing mind.
Because it possesses mind, it is also called a "sentient being," and is thus not the same as grasses and trees.
What is meant by "the mind attains entry into the meditative absorption of cessation"?
It refers to the fact that one accomplishes the minds of the past and future worlds;
therefore, it is called "the mind attains."
This differs from the Abhidharma, which establishes a separate category for that which is neither form nor mind.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
one investigates names to grasp their meanings.

The state where consciousness is exhausted constitutes the essence of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). To speak according to the actual situation, within the attainment of cessation there can be both mind and no-mind.
As for what is called "no-mind":
In the śrāvaka’s meditative absorption of cessation, the six consciousnesses and the mind are absent;
in the bodhisattva’s meditative absorption of cessation, the six consciousnesses are entirely absent,
though a portion of deluded consciousness remains.
In the cessation samādhi of the Buddhas, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are entirely absent.
As for the statement that there is "mind," it means that within the cessation samādhi of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) still persists.
Because the union of the true and the false constitutes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna),
the true mind still exists within the Buddha’s state of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
If there were mental consciousness present, how could it be said that all [consciousness] has been extinguished?
Because it extinguishes the coarse mind, its essential nature is thus; this concludes the first section.
Next, the characteristics of the meditative attainments of entering and emerging from cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are distinguished.
First, let us distinguish the process of entering and emerging according to the Abhidharma.
As for the manner of entry:
according to that treatise, one first attains the eight dhyānas and brings them to complete mastery.
Next, one trains the mind by entering the six types of meditative absorption within the eight dhyānas.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One who wishes to enter the attainment of cessation must first train the mind."
What are the six kinds?
First is sequential entry:
ascending in successive order from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Second is entry in reverse order:
entering from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and descending sequentially through the stages down to emerging from the first dhyāna.
Third is entry in both reverse and forward order.
From the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
then returning to the first dhyāna, he ascends in sequence to the third dhyāna;
then entering the second dhyāna, he ascends in sequence to the fourth dhyāna.
In this manner, one descends and then ascends again, even unto the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
Fourth is the progressive leap (*anuloma-vyutkrānta*):
from the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna and leaps into the third dhyāna.
Transcending the fourth dhyāna, one enters the sphere of infinite space;
thus, by successive transcendence, one proceeds even unto the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is asked:
Why does one leap over only a single stage?
Because a śrāvaka, when leaping through the dhyānas, does not exceed one stage.
Fifth is the reverse leap.
From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he transcends the sphere of nothingness and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;
transcending the sphere of infinite space, he enters the fourth dhyāna.
Leaping from the third dhyāna into the second dhyāna,
and leaping from the first dhyāna to give rise to a mind of the desire realm—
these are the six modes of forward and reverse leaping.
From the stage of the first dhyāna, he leaps into the third dhyāna;
then, returning to the second dhyāna, he leaps into the fourth dhyāna;
then, returning to the third dhyāna, he leaps into the sphere of infinite space.
In this manner, one descends and then ascends again, even unto the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
However, these six types all involve sequential entry and transition within the contaminated fundamental dhyānas (*sāsrava-maula-dhyāna*).
It does not enter into the outflow-free state, nor does it proceed by means of skillful means.
Question: [Why is this so?]
If one enters the Peak of Existence (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and immediately emerges from meditative absorption, can one then enter a state of distracted mind?
The commentary states:
No, one cannot.
Why is it not possible?
If one were to emerge from that state and enter the distracted mind of the desire realm, one would immediately transcend the eight stages;
such a principle does not apply to the meditative concentration of the śrāvakas.
Just as a person who has attained an exceedingly superior state of wholesome mind does not subsequently give rise to grave evil,
so it is with this as well.
It is asked:
If it is claimed that one who has reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cannot immediately emerge from it and give rise to a scattered mind,
then how could one emerge from the third and sixth of the aforementioned six [attainments] when reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
The commentary states:
He descends through the stages in reverse order until he reaches the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna;
thereafter, emerging from meditative absorption, he gives rise to a mind belonging to the desire realm.
If that were so, there would be eight ways of disciplining the mind;
how then can one speak of six?
Those who enter in reverse order are identical to the second category.
Because they are subsumed in reverse order, six are taught together.
Thus, these six ways of taming the mind are completed.
Next, he forms the resolve to enter the cessation of mind and mental factors,
and further resolves that he shall emerge at a specific time;
having formed this thought, he then enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
First, one enters the fundamental concentration of the first dhyāna and extinguishes the mind of the desire realm;
next, one enters the second dhyāna and extinguishes the mind of the first dhyāna;
continuing in this manner until one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and extinguishes the mind of nothingness.
After the mind of non-perception, by virtue of its original vow, the mind and mental factors suddenly cease.
Question: There are those who enter the meditative attainment of cessation repeatedly within a single lifetime.
Should one enter meditative absorption and train the mind separately for each of the six types,
or can a single training enable entry into many absorptions?
According to that school, after the Tathāgata has undergone a single training, he is able to enter many absorptions.
Śrāvakas must be trained individually according to their specific needs.
Such is the case when entering;
how is it when emerging?
Within the meditative attainment of cessation, after a certain duration has passed,
when the time arrives for emerging according to one's original commitment,
the mental states and mental factors suddenly arise through the power of that original commitment to emerge.
The Abhidharma is thus.
Next, we shall distinguish the entry and exit [into meditative absorption] according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Within the system of the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are two sequences for entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In one type of sequential progression, one first attains the eight dhyānas;
subsequently, one cultivates the Noble Path to sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation within the desire realm,
continuing upward until the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are either exhausted or not yet exhausted.
Having severed these afflictions, one next forms the resolve to extinguish the mind and simultaneously forms the resolve that at that time one shall emerge from it;
only after generating this resolve does one then extinguish the mind.
First, one enters the fundamental concentration of the first dhyāna and extinguishes the mind of the desire realm;
continuing in this manner until one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and extinguishes the mind of nothingness.
Following the mind of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, by the power of one's original vow, all mental conceptions suddenly cease.
Question: Having accomplished the attainment of the eight dhyānas, one separately cultivates the untainted path to sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation,
and only thereafter does one cease the mind.
Why is it not so in the Abhidharma system?
The explanation says:
In the Abhidharma, one severs the fetters through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
When one attains the eight dhyānas, the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward have already been exhausted;
there is no need to further cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) path to sever fetters before ceasing the mind.
Even if one were to cultivate the untainted path, it would only sever the afflictions of a single stage, namely the perception of sorrow (*duḥkhasaṃjñā*).
Therefore, it differs from the *Tattvasiddhi*.
This single sequence of the *Tattvasiddhi* proceeds as follows:

first, one relies on the "lightning-flash" (*vidyut-pradīpa*) to cultivate the Noble Path, thereby severing the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) within the desire realm, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Next, one cultivates the eight dhyānas and attains them.
Having done so, one next forms the resolve to extinguish the mind and its mental factors,
while simultaneously forming the resolve that at a specific time one shall emerge from them.
Thereafter, one extinguishes the mind and enters from the first dhyāna up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
A question is asked:
"In the Abhidharma as well, can one likewise first sever the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and subsequently attain the dhyānas?"
The commentary states:
This differs from the method in the Abhidharma,
which maintains that one gives rise to untainted contemplation based on the future dhyāna.
When one eliminates the afflictions of the path of cultivation within the three realms, one simultaneously attains the eight dhyānas;
this is because they are cultivated as a common antidote.
Nevertheless, although these eight dhyānas are attained, they cannot be manifested.
By further applying skillful means, cultivation then manifests before one.
A question is asked:
"In the Abhidharma teachings previously mentioned, it was said that those wishing to enter the meditative absorption of cessation must first perform six kinds of mental adjustments for entry."
In the *Tattvasiddhi* as well, it is not so.
The commentary explains:
"It is unnecessary; one need only attain the eight dhyānas to be able to extinguish the mind."
Why is this so? That treatise declares:
"Having attained this dhyāna, one separately employs the untainted [wisdom] to sever all afflictions."
Because the untainted (anāsrava) mind is already disciplined, it does not require further effort;
thus, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Six Samādhis," states:
"Having attained the eight dhyānas, one is then able to extinguish the mind."
It does not depend on the six types [of consciousness]. Question:
When entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), is it through mental attention (*manasikāra*) that it ceases, or without mental attention?
Regarding the two commentaries on the *Tattvasiddhi*,
one interpretation states:
"When attention (*manasikāra*) ceases, the mind then ceases."
If one does not apply attention and further takes other phenomena as objects,
it is not called the cessation of the mind.
This is because the practitioner, having severed the afflictions, has constantly restrained the mind.
Because the mind is thus controlled, when desire is to be extinguished, it is immediately extinguished.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* quotes a sutra as saying:
"One who wishes to enter the meditative absorption of cessation must first discipline the mind."
The second explanation states:
"Without forming the intention to extinguish it, the mind extinguishes itself;
it is like when a person sleeps, [images] appear without being thought of."
Because of constant cultivation,
entry is thus; emergence is the same as in the Abhidharma.
Question: At the time of emergence, the mental faculty (manas) does not yet exist;
upon what, then, can the subsequent mind-consciousness (citta-vijñāna) depend to arise?
The commentary states:
Because the final mind preceding meditative concentration is established as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), the subsequent mind is able to arise.
Question: [Why is this so?]
The preceding mind has already ceased and passed away long ago;
how could it give rise to the subsequent one? It is for this reason that it is designated as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
Because the meaning of "cause" is established,
even though [the cause] has ceased before the subsequent arising.
Just as karma, though having ceased, can produce a subsequent fruit,
so it is established in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Next, the process of entering and emerging [into meditative absorption] is distinguished according to the Mahāyāna.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are four distinct interpretations.
The first, based on the commencement of cultivation,
is identical to that of the Abhidharma.
First, one attains the eight dhyānas and six methods for disciplining the mind;
through these required skillful means, one subsequently enters and emerges from them.
Second, based on the culmination of cultivation,
it is identical to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* in that one directly attains the eight dhyānas.
By means of the expedient of making a formal commitment, one is able to enter and emerge from concentration without relying on the six types [of preparatory practices];
thus one enters meditative absorption to harmonize the mind.
Third, regarding the purity of cultivation:
beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one enters whichever level of mind one wishes to enter.
When one wishes to emerge, one emerges immediately,
without needing to employ preliminary preparatory methods or formal vows.
Furthermore, it is not necessary to enter from the first dhyāna through to the meditative attainment of cessation in a sequential manner to extinguish the mind.
Fourth, it is established by virtue;
there is no time when it does not enter [the world],
because it is eternally quiescent.
There is no time when it does not arise,
because it is constantly active;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"To manifest dignified deportment without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation is what constitutes 'sitting in repose. He asked:
"For what causes and conditions is a bodhisattva uniquely able both to constantly enter and constantly emerge [from this concentration]?"
The commentary states:
Because a bodhisattva ultimately does not grasp at any mental characteristics,
they are able to enter [meditative absorption] constantly.
Because they do not grasp at the mark of cessation,
they are able to constantly emerge.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas skillfully enter the dharma-gate of the distinctions within the dharma-realm.
Within the gateways of the Dharma-realm, there is the gateway of the dharma of quiescent cessation of the mind.
The Bodhisattva dwells therein and never abandons it;
thus, while the mind is constantly ceased, there is further the gateway of non-cessation through discernment.
The Bodhisattva dwells therein, never abandoning it for even a moment;
therefore, it is eternally non-extinguished.
This brief analysis of the characteristics of entering and emerging from meditative concentration concludes these two gates.
Next, we shall distinguish the duration and limits of the time for entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). According to the Abhidharma system,
although sentient beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are able to remain in this attainment for a long time, they do not enter it frequently.
Among them, the maximum duration does not exceed seven days;
if they emerge from meditative absorption after seven days have passed, they die immediately. Why is this so?
Sentient beings of the desire realm sustain their bodies with edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
The potency of such edible food does not last beyond seven days;
therefore, if they emerge from meditative absorption after seven days have passed, they die immediately.
Because the sentient beings of the upper realms are free from edible food,
those who enter the meditative attainment of cessation can remain for a long duration;
yet, even after remaining for such a long time, they cannot exceed the limit of their karmic retribution.
If one remains beyond that period, one dies. According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
the Vaibhāṣika school maintains that sentient beings in the desire realm who subsist on edible food must emerge [from their meditative absorption] within seven days.

Regarding those who teach that one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) maintains the body through right application such that they do not die even after many eons have passed,
there may be among them some who emerge from that state and then die.
He enters the meditative attainment of cessation at the time when his life-faculty is about to be exhausted;
therefore, he passes away immediately upon emerging from it.
His death does not result from remaining in the meditative state for a long duration.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
there is no limit or fixed duration for the time when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
A question is asked:
The Sūtra states that Mahākāśyapa remained on Mount Kukkuṭapāda awaiting the emergence of Maitreya;
he rose from the mountain to pay his respects to Maitreya, who manifested eighteen transformations, after which Kāśyapa extinguished his body.
"He is currently on the mountain either for the sake of parinirvāṇa or for entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
There are two interpretations of this.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, he has entered the meditative absorption of cessation and maintains his body through that attainment."
Therefore, he was subsequently able to emerge from it to perform the manifestation of prostrating to the Buddha.
According to the Abhidharma, his entry into Nirvana was not the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
If one were to die immediately upon emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
how could one proceed to the Buddha to pay homage, make offerings, and extensively manifest supernatural transformations?
Furthermore, this is also declared in accordance with the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*.
When Kāśyapa was about to enter nirvāṇa, he went to take leave of King Bimbisāra and announced that he was entering nirvāṇa;
one can know with certainty that what he entered was not the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Furthermore, within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (the *Fu-fa-zang*), the World-Honored One stated:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa upheld the Dharma for twenty years.
After Mahākāśyapa entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda upheld the Dharma for another twenty years."
Thus, in this sequence,
it is known that he has now entered parinirvāṇa. Question:
If he has entered nirvana,
how could he later go to visit the Buddha and manifest such extensive supernatural transformations?
Śāriputra replied:
It is because he possesses the power of transformative mastery that he is able to act in this way.
For example, when the World-Honored Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Mahāmāyā came to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha rose from his seat for her sake.
It is also like Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others who transformed fire to burn their own bodies;
all such instances are the power of retained transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*).
Such are the temporal divisions; this concludes the three gates.
Next, we shall discuss the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
Within these, they are distinguished by means of three gates.
First, clarifying the place of attainment;
second, clarifying the place of entry;
third, clarifying the place of accomplishment.
Regarding the term "attainment-sphere" (prāptisthāna):
that which is attained through cultivation is called an attainment-sphere.
Within the teachings of the Hīnayāna:
Initial cultivation and attainment must occur in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*),
not in the two higher realms,
because they arise by means of verbal instruction.
In the stages of the desire realm, there are Buddhas who proclaim the dharma of the cessation of the mind;
therefore, it can be cultivated and brought forth.
In the two higher realms, there are no Buddhas to proclaim it.
Therefore, they do not cultivate or give rise to them. Question:
In the higher realms, where there is no Buddha preaching the Dharma, one can still cultivate the various dhyānas.
Why is it that they cannot cultivate and arise from the meditative attainment of cessation?
The explanation states:
ordinary persons have, since the distant past, already attained the various dhyānas.
Because this is a dharma that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) constantly obtain, they cultivate and give rise to it above;
ordinary persons originally do not obtain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Because this is a dharma that non-ordinary persons constantly obtain, they do not cultivate or give rise to it above.
If one falls back and practices again, it can also be attained in the higher realms. Question:
When attaining it through practice in the higher realms, is it the attainment of what has already been attained, or the attainment of what has not yet been attained?
The commentary states:
This refers to attaining what has not yet been attained and non-attaining what has already been attained. Why is this so?
Since that is not a mental dharma, it cannot be attained through the hidden penetration of the three periods of time.
Just as when a person attains the precepts, they attain both what has already been attained and what has not yet been attained within every moment of thought,
so too is it with this.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
at the beginning it is the same as the Śrāvakas in that [the meditative attainments] are cultivated and attained within the desire realm;
however, in the end, it is not so.
It is attained throughout the three realms,
because the dharma-gate of the cessation of mental phenomena is constantly manifest in all places.
As for the term "entrance" (praveśa):
That which is capable of entering wherever one happens to be is called an "entry-point" (*praveśasthāna*).
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
one is capable of manifesting entry into both the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
It is not the formless realm.
Why is this so? Because one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation has severed all mental activity.
In the desire and form realms, although the mind and form have ceased, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) still persists;
therefore, one can enter [the meditative attainments] while remaining manifest. This is not the case in the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).
Furthermore, because mental deliberation is severed and the life-faculty does not persist,
one does not enter [nirvana].
This is according to the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can manifest their entry [into the world] wherever their bodies may be.
A question is asked:
"In the formless realm, the mind ceases and one dies immediately."
What is meant by "the Mahāyāna entering all places"?
The explanation states that the Mahāyāna teaches that even the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) still possesses form.
Therefore, although the mind is extinguished, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) still persists.
Furthermore, it is taught in the Mahāyāna that there is a true mind (tathatā-citta) which is eternal and does not perish.

Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), when one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), although the functioning of the mind is stilled, the essence of the mind still persists.
Therefore, one does not pass away.
Regarding what is called "the place of accomplishment" (*siddhasthāna*): wherever the body resides, that which is accomplished and not lost is termed the "place of accomplishment."
After it has been cultivated and attained, one achieves accomplishment wherever the body may be within the three realms.
According to the Abhidharma, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is a state of non-conceptualization;
therefore, it is established throughout all three realms.
The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims that because the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is not bound by any [realm], all three realms are established.
Such is the distinction of the locations; this concludes the four gates.
Next, regarding the treatise on the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Stages" refers to the realm of desire up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is with reference to these various stages that the meditative attainment of cessation is explained.
First, the essential nature of meditative concentration is clarified;
next, the mind entering [concentration] is discussed;
finally, the mind emerging [from concentration] is distinguished.
The essential nature and doctrinal classification of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) differ according to various schools. Within the *Abhidharma* tradition,

it is taught that because the attainment of cessation is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), it is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It yields the same fruit as the meditative attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains it as an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma);
therefore, it does not belong to the three realms.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
the meaning is not fixed.

If one explains that the cessation of the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), [then it is as follows].
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it does not belong to the three realms.

If one says that the essence of the eighth true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is quiescent and constitutes the substance of the cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it likewise does not belong to the three realms.
If one says that the quiescence of the seventh deluded consciousness constitutes the substance of the cessation-concentration, it is bound to the three realms.
The general characteristics of their mutual connection do not differentiate between the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Next, we discuss the entry into the mind:
the Śrāvaka enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with a mind of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Because other states of mind are coarse and forceful, they are difficult to extinguish;
thus, while a bodhisattva’s practice initially accords with that of a śrāvaka,
their realization is ultimately different.
How are they not the same? Because the mind can enter [these states] from every stage, beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Next, we shall discuss the mind that emerges [from these states].
In the Abhidharma system, there is either emergence from the perception of nothingness, or emergence from the state of non-existence;
it is the mind of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" that emerges from the successive meditative attainments.
The transcendental meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) emerge from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Because the śrāvaka’s transcendence of dhyāna does not exceed the first [dhyāna], he does not emerge from the higher stages. Question:
The attainment of cessation is subsumed under the sphere of non-perception.
Upon emerging from the attainment of cessation, the mind of nothingness should logically follow as the immediate successor.
For what reason, then, is it said to be a "leap-over"?
The commentary states:
"In terms of the actual sequence, it should not be considered a leap;
the author of the treatise speaks of it in relation to the nine successive stages."
Because it is separated by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
although there is no textual evidence for this in the *Tattvasiddhi*, when inferred through its meaning, it is the same as the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā).
Since what is established in the Abhidharma is not refuted [by us],
in the Mahāyāna teachings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess mastery over dhyāna and are able to emerge from the mental states of all stages.
The distinctions of the stages are thus; this concludes the five gates.

Next, there is the analysis according to whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). First, we shall discuss the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Next, the mind that enters [the attainment] is distinguished; subsequently, the mind that emerges from it is clarified.
Regarding the essential nature of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), various treatises differ in their explanations.
In the Abhidharma system, it is exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava);
its essence is non-perception (asaṃjñika),
because it is a dharma characterized by outflows.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
because its essence is the unconditioned dharma of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, however...
When discussed in terms of its general characteristics, its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*);
therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* describes it as the "abode of the noble ones" (*āryavihāra*).
Within this, when analyzed in detail, there are also meanings pertaining to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

If it is said that the extinction of the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
If it is said that the quiescence of the essence of the eighth true consciousness constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation, it is likewise untainted.
If it is asserted that the seventh deluded consciousness (manas) being stilled constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
then its nature— which resembles the untainted (*anāsrava*)— would nonetheless be tainted (*sāsrava*).
Next, we shall discuss the mind that enters [this state].
In the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) system, the entry into the mind is with outflows (sāsrava),

because it enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), the entry into the mind is exclusively without outflows (anāsrava).
Question: The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is entered by means of the mind of non-perception (asaṃjñika).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the untainted (anāsrava) [path] relies solely upon the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).
The lightning-flash of the desire realm does not rely upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
How, then, can it be said that the mind enters the outflow-free state? To explain:
In the realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there is also untainted (anāsrava) [attainment]. What kind of untainted [attainment] is it?
It refers to the untainted [state] that accords with the former habitual practice of contemplation.
What is this? First, relying on the lower dhyāna, one gives rise to untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*), contemplating the suffering,
impermanence, and so forth of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Having severed the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one then uses that mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to contemplate the suffering,
impermanence, and so forth of that sphere; this is called the untainted contemplative observation (*anupassanā*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Based on this untainted state, one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, both tainted and untainted states can serve as the basis for entry.
Next, the mind of emergence is explained.
In the Abhidharma system,
the mind that emerges from meditative absorption may be either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
The mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The sphere of nothingness may be either with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*),
because within the sphere of nothingness both minds with outflows and without outflows are present.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is stated that [the mind] arising from this state is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
How is this known? As it is said in the "Chapter on the Cessation Attainment" (*nirodhasamāpatti-varga*) of that same work:
The *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Some proclaim that [the mind] enters with outflows (*sāsrava*)."
The mind that arises is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
It is not an outflow (*āsrava*),
because the practitioner who wishes to enter the meditative absorption of cessation first destroys all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) before entering it; thus,
one enters into the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Emerging from the conditions of *nirvāṇa*,
one thus emerges into the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is within the Mahāyāna Dharma.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge from both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) states through these six gates.
Having completed this discussion, we shall next consider them in terms of persons. Generally speaking, they are attained only by the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles.
Among the Hinayana followers of the *Prakaraṇapāda* school, only those who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* or *arhat* can obtain it.
Regarding these *anāgāmins* and *arhats*, there are differing explanations;
according to the *Vibhāṣā*, ten types of persons obtain it.

This refers to the nine grades of afflictions within the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). From the abandonment of one grade up to all nine grades, there are nine types of persons.
Within this stage, those who are bound by all fetters constitute one type.
Let it be for ten persons.
Among these ten, starting from those still bound by all fetters up to those who have eliminated eight grades of afflictions, they are *anāgāmins*.
Those who eliminate the ninth grade are *arhats*.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, there is no mention of one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) yet capable of attainment;
it must be through partial severance that one attains it. As for how many categories (*prakāra*) are severed, the treatise does not distinguish this.

Some commentators explain that among the nine grades of afflictions in the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, one enters the attainment of cessation because only the ninth grade remains after the first eight have been abandoned,
and one is weary of the mental toil and anxiety [associated with it].
It may be so; or, even by abandoning one,
two, three, or four grades [of afflictions], one is able to extinguish the mind,
though the abandonment is not yet complete.
This is the exhaustion of the anāgāmin;
this is the arhat.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, [it is thus].
All [stages] above the lineage (gotra) attain this.
Furthermore, if discussed comprehensively, those from the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā) upward also gradually attain it. This concludes the seven gates.
Next, we shall distinguish the similarities and differences by correlating this with the eighth liberation (vimokṣa) mentioned in the sūtras.
In the Abhidharma system, the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is correctly employed as the eighth liberation;
in the Satyasiddhiśāstra system, the attainment of cessation and that eighth liberation are entirely distinct entities.
The eighth liberation exists exclusively within the fruit [of cultivation],
whereas the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) pertains to both cause and fruit;
therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
The attainment of cessation is also attained by those in training (*śaikṣa*);
the eighth liberation is attained only by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, that treatise states:
The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) extinguishes the mind and mental factors;
the eighth liberation extinguishes all afflictions.
That treatise further states:
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) extinguishes perception and feeling;
the eighth liberation extinguishes ignorance and craving.
Thus, one should know that they are entirely distinct.
What is taught in the Mahāyāna is the same as in the Abhidharma;

thus, it is proclaimed in the "Chapter on the Subsumption of the Six Perfections" in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that the eighth liberation of a bodhisattva has the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as its essence.
Nirvāṇa is also like this. This concludes the eight sections.
Next, the text will be explained as it is taught in the Sūtra.
Transcending all stages up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the bodily realization of the cessation of perception and feeling is called the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Regarding the phrase "transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception":
The commentaries differ in their explanations.
The *Abhidharma* commentary states:
"To 'pass over' means to 'arrive.'"
Upon reaching the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), one is able to extinguish the mind;
therefore, it is called "transcending.
This does not mean that transcending refers specifically to surpassing [the realm] by severing the afflictions of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
The *Tattvasiddhi* commentary states:
"To transcend is called 'to pass beyond' (*atikrānta*).
Thus, that treatise says:
When a practitioner is able to see that all conditioned phenomena within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are empty and thereby severs the fetters of that sphere,
this is called "transcending. However,
because they have not yet severed them completely, it is not final.
Because they cannot fail to give rise [to further realization], they are called "those in training" (śaikṣa).
It is not that the very first arrival [at this stage] is described as a fault.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, there is no fixed textual determination; it is determined solely by the meaning, which is the same as in the Abhidharma.

Although a bodhisattva has not yet severed the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they nonetheless attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) according to their respective capacity.
As for the "extinction of perception and feeling," according to the principles of the Abhidharma, it actually refers to the cessation of all mental factors.
However, because the two categories of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are particularly strong, their cessation is specifically taught.
Why are they so strong?
As it is said in the treatise:
Among the phenomena of affliction (*kleśa*), feeling (*vedanā*) is the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
and perception (*saṃjñā*) is the basis of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Among pure phenomena, feeling cultivates the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Because one cultivates the formless attainments through perception,
they are said to be "strong";
this is not the case for the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
If it is argued that because the two aggregates of perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) are predominant, they alone are specifically said to cease,
then since the mind-king (citta-rāja) is the most powerful,
why does the Sūtra not state that the mind ceases?
Furthermore, since both perception and feeling both depend upon the mind-king (citta-rāja),
why not speak of the mind?
If one wishes to provide an explanation by referring to the primary factor, [one should speak of the mind].
One should say that it is the mind that ceases;
however, in that meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), it is the mind of the eight dhyānas that ceases,
while within those eight dhyāna concentrations, one cultivates the various meditations.
Because one cultivates the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) is manifested in contrast to them.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, within the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as it is established therein, all mind is ceased;
"all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*) are collectively termed "feeling" (*vedita*).
There are two kinds of feeling:
first, the feeling of perception;
second, the feeling of wisdom.

The mind that takes conditioned phenomena as its object is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā). The mind that takes unconditioned phenomena as its object is called the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā) and feeling.
As for the phrase "the cessation of perception":
This clarifies that the extinction of perception and feeling has conditioned phenomena as its object.
Because feeling is subsumed within perception,
it is said that "perception is extinguished."
The phrase "the cessation of feeling" clarifies that feeling ceases through wisdom that takes the unconditioned as its object;
it conceals wisdom and highlights feeling.
Therefore, it is said that "feeling ceases. Question:
Does the cessation of the mind encompass both the empty and the existent?
Why not simply explain the cessation of the mind through general principles?
It is in order to clarify the cessation of both the two minds of emptiness and existence that other sūtras and śāstras largely agree with the Abhidharma.
Regarding "realizing with the body":
herein there is no mind, but only the physical body;
because meditative concentration is conjoined with the body, it is called "realizing with the body."
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"The eight liberations and so forth are all realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
Why, then, is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) alone specifically described as being realized through the body?
The answer is:
Within this, there is no further mind;
there is only the body.

The meditative absorption of cessation is likewise. 95. The Meaning of the One Vehicle (9). The Meaning of the One Vehicle is explained through a twofold classification: first, the analysis of its name and meaning; second, the discernment of its essence and characteristics. Within the first section, the name and meaning are explained.
What is called a "vehicle" (yāna) is so named in relation to persons.
Because its practice can transport people and because it is mounted by people, it is termed a "vehicle."
Regarding the term "one" (*eka*), there are four interpretations:
first, it is called "one" by way of exclusion;
second, it is called "one" by way of destroying differentiation.
The three assemblies have distinct names,
while the four have no distinct names;
this is what is meant by "distinguishing."
To speak according to reality, there is only the single Mahāyāna; it is divided into three according to the needs of those to be converted.
It is in order to distinguish these three that the term "one" is used.
Regarding the "refutation of distinctions":
the Buddha provisionally established the three vehicles in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
having heard this, sentient beings grasped them as being fixed and real.
The Buddha spoke of "one" in order to shatter their attachment to the three provisional [categories].
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, neither two nor three.
Furthermore, the sutra also says:
"This alone is the one reality."
The other two are not real.
Regarding the statement "there are no two":
first, outside of the Mahāyāna there are no separate vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the statement that there are not three vehicles:
first, there is no vehicle of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas distinct from the Mahāyāna;
second, there is no Mahāyāna bestowed as a provisional transformation.
Question: Since it has already been established by directly stating that when there is no three, there is no two,
why is it necessary to separately state that there is neither two nor three?
The commentary states:
"Those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles are the counterparts to the Mahāyāna."
However, there are two kinds of greatness:
first, substantial greatness;
second, provisional greatness.
One should know that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not only the counterparts of the true great masters,
but are also the counterparts of the provisional great masters.
As for the statement "there is no duality":
The absence of the substantial Great One is the second object of contrast.
Regarding the "absence of three":
this refers to the absence of both the two vehicles as objects of contrast for the expedient Great One, as well as the absence of the expedient Great One itself.
Therefore, it is said that there are no three [vehicles]. What is the true Mahāyāna?
It is that which is taught in such works as the *Avataṃsaka*.
That teaching states that a bodhisattva truly cultivates all the untainted, genuine virtues within the thirteen stages (*bhūmi*).
By extinguishing false conceptualization and realizing the nature of reality, one attains Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called "real."
What is the greatness of the provisional?
It is that which is taught within the distinct teachings of the three vehicles.
That [teaching] says:
During the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the bodhisattva cultivates only the six outflow-tainted (sāsrava) pāramitās;
he does not practice the untainted (anāsrava) true virtues of the various stages until he has passed through these three asaṃkhyeyas.
Subsequently, during one hundred kalpas, he cultivates the karma for the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana).
In his final body, he cultivated the eight worldly dhyānas;
having become weary of and detached from them, he severed the afflictions and subsequently contemplated the Four Noble Truths to attain Buddhahood at the Bodhi tree.
Because his words did not accord with reality, it is called the greatness of expedient means (upāya).
This refutes both this provisional "great" [vehicle] and the other "small" [vehicles];
therefore, it is called "one.
As for the term "reconciling the distinct":
In total, there is only one Great [Vehicle];
the Buddha, according to the capacities of sentient beings, divided it into three.
Now, we again subsume these three to return to the single Great [Vehicle].
Because there is no difference in the cause,
there is no distinction in the resulting fruit;
therefore, it is said to be "one."
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"The exposition of the great majestic deportment is called the Prātimokṣa-vinaya and so forth.
The Prātimokṣa-vinaya is precisely the training of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are themselves the Mahāyāna.
The Lotus Sutra also says:
"What you all practice is the bodhisattva path.
This is because, fundamentally, there is no duality of dharmas. He asked:
Previously, the three were analyzed to reveal the one;
why, then, are the three now reconciled into the one? To explain:
[the answer follows].
To refute the attachment to distinctions,
it is said that the three are refuted;
setting aside the emotional [perspective] and adhering to the dharmas, there is nothing outside these three.
Therefore, meeting and parting are themselves one. Question:
A vehicle is that which is traveled; since there are three distinct types of persons who ride the vehicles, one speaks of vehicles according to those persons.
The vehicles themselves ought to be definitively distinct.
What is this "one"? The explanation says:
it is so because they are one in principle.
