Therefore, it is said in the sūtras that although the three vehicles differ, they share the same Buddha-nature.
It is just as the colors of various cows may be diverse, yet the color of their milk is no different;
such is the case with the three vehicles.
The Buddha-nature has no differentiation.
Because the nature is without differentiation,
that which realizes it before being perfected is solely the cause of a single Buddha.
Realization culminates solely in the single fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, in terms of ultimate reality, there is only the One Mahāyāna.
Thus, a sutra says:
Even if there were no Buddhas in the world, it would not be that those of the two vehicles do not realize the two types of nirvāṇa.
Since all worlds consist solely of the single Buddha-vehicle and there is nothing else,
there are no separate followers of the two vehicles who attain the two types of nirvāṇa.
The distinction between the vehicles is thus.
As for the statement that there is no distinction:
from the perspective of ultimate reality, the vehicles have been without distinction from the very beginning.
There are no three distinct entities that can be joined or broken;
it is like space, equal and non-dual.
Therefore, it is called "one."
Question: The One Vehicle takes practice as its essence;
yet these practices differ in a thousand ways.
What is meant by "riding on one"?
The explanation states that there are two kinds of dharma-gates.
First, the gate of specific characteristics;
second, the gate of common characteristics.
If one proceeds according to the specific characteristics, there are immeasurable vehicles.
Now, with respect to their shared characteristics,
they are said to be "one," just as many pieces of wood together constitute a single chariot.
This is likewise the case here.
Furthermore, within the sūtras and śāstras of this Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), it is also termed the Mahāyāna.
There are two senses in which this is understood.
First, according to the interpretation of others:
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are great beings (mahāpuruṣa);
because it is the vehicle mounted by these great beings, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Second, it is called "Great" because its analytical exposition is comprehensive and its scope is vast.
The definitions of the names are thus.
It is asked: what is the distinction between the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*) and the meaning of "path" (*mārga*)?
Explaining it by way of its general characteristics:
that which enables one to pass through is called the Path (mārga); that which enables one to transport [beings] is called the Vehicle (yāna).
Within this, there are three distinct classifications.
First, the distinction is established by contrasting the practice with the dharma:
"vehicle" (yāna) refers to the practice.
The Way is this Dharma;
because its practice can transport people,
it is called a vehicle (yāna).
The Dharma serves as the practice by which one is able to traverse the mind;
therefore, it is called the "Path.
Nevertheless, within the context of the vehicles (yāna), it is not that the Dharma does not exist.
Now, in contrast to the Path (mārga), it is specifically designated as "practice" (caryā).
The Path also possesses practice;
however, in contrast to the practices of those other vehicles, it is specifically designated as "Dharma."
Second, regarding the distinctions made according to their meanings within the context of practice:
all qualities of practice that can lead [to liberation] are termed "path" (mārga), and those that can convey [one there] are termed "vehicle" (yāna).
Furthermore, the essence of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is collectively termed the "path" (mārga),
and their function is collectively termed the "vehicle" (yāna).
In what way is their essence common?
Because its activity is unobstructed. How does it function?
It is able to transport people.
Third, within the context of the dharmas, they are differentiated according to their respective meanings:
that which enables thorough penetration is called the "Path" (mārga), and that which enables transport is called the "Vehicle" (yāna).
Furthermore, the essence of all dharmas is collectively termed the "Path" (mārga),
and their function is collectively termed the "Vehicle" (yāna). It is asked:
What is the distinction between the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*) and the meaning of "gate" (*mukha*)? Generally speaking, that which is categorized as a comprehensive entry point is called a "gate";
that which is capable of transporting [one] is called a "vehicle."
Within this, there are also three types of analysis:
first, distinguishing differences by correlating the practice with the phenomena; second, [distinguishing them] solely by way of the phenomena.
Because it is that which people traverse,
the vehicle (yāna) refers exclusively to its function;
for it is that which can transport people.
Second, regarding the differentiation according to the meaning within the context of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
all doors of conditioned phenomena are termed "doors. That which is capable of transporting [beings] is termed a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) universally enter through what is called a "gate" (*mukha*); because they transport [beings], they are called "vehicles" (*yāna*).
These three are differentiated according to their respective meanings within the Dharma.
All dharmas are gates; their specific designations are called "gates. That which conveys and transports is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Furthermore, that into which all dharmas universally enter is called a "gate" (*mukha*).
"Vehicular conveyance" (yāna) is defined as the "functioning of transport. Question:
What is the distinction between the meaning of "path" (mārga) and the meaning of "gate" (dvāra)?
The commentary states:
"The substance is one, yet names differ according to their meanings;
they universally enter through the gates of nomenclature."
The section on "penetration leading to the name 'path'" concludes here.
Next, the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*) is analyzed, briefly categorized through five gates.
The differentiation of the One Vehicle Dharma:
there are two kinds of vehicles.
The first is the vehicle of the teachings (dharma-yāna).
Second is the practice of the vehicle (*yāna-pratipatti*).
There are three kinds of dharmas:
first, the dharma of teaching (*deśanā-dharma*).
The so-called Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras;
second is the Dharma of Principle,
namely, Buddha-nature.
Within this, the principle is that the two truths are distinguished as one reality, which is the dharma-realm of dependent origination.
Third is the practice of the Dharma, consisting of the ritual procedures of the six perfections and so forth.
It is said that the practices of the vehicles are essentially of three kinds:
first, hearing;
second, reflection.
Third is the cultivation of practice:
based on the teachings, one gives rise to hearing;
based on the principles, one accomplishes reflection.
One practices the cultivation of conduct based on the dharma of conduct.
A question is asked:
The Sūtra speaks of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.
Why is it that realization is not mentioned within these two practices?
Because it is subsumed under cultivation.
These two practices eliminate conceptual discrimination.
Although the virtues of practice are numerous, they do not exceed three types:
first, wisdom;
second, merit.
The third is retribution;
*prajñā* is wisdom;
the five perfections are merit.
Furthermore, prajñā is exclusively wisdom;
generosity, ethical discipline, and patience are exclusively merit;
while diligence and meditative concentration are both merit and wisdom.
The eight kinds, such as longevity and so forth, are its retribution.
Within these three types, merit arises based on wisdom,
and retribution arises based on merit.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"If the retributive cause and the retributive fruit both arise based on merit,
that merit arises based on wisdom."
When these three reach the fruit, they are renamed as prajñā, liberation, and the dharma-body.
Wisdom is prajñā; merit is liberation.
Recompense constitutes the Dharma-body;
such are the virtues of practice.
As for what is called the virtue of cessation:
It consists essentially of three aspects:
first, the severance of afflictions;
and second, the disappearance of the fetters of the five abodes.
This is what was previously severed and extinguished by wisdom.
Second is the severance of karma:
the two types of causes—fragmentary birth and transformation—are extinguished.
This is because it has been distanced by prior merit.
Third is the cessation of suffering:
the exhaustion of both types of retribution, those of分段 (segmented birth) and 變易 (transformation).
This refers to the renunciation resulting from pure retribution mentioned previously.
Among these three types, because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, various karmas do not arise.
Because karma does not arise, the retribution of suffering does not manifest.
Because suffering does not arise, one attains Great Nirvana.
Taking this practice of severance as the essence of the One Vehicle,
there is a threefold distinction between the two practices of self-benefit and benefiting others.
Self-practice is twofold:
first, the practice of renunciation that arises from wearying of the conditioned;
second, the practice of accumulating merit that arises from seeking the Buddha’s wisdom.
Benefiting others also has two aspects:
first, through the skillful means of great compassion,
one uproots them and causes them to emerge from suffering.
Second is the skillful means of great compassion,
which transforms beings so that they may attain happiness.
These two practices together constitute the essence of the One Vehicle.
The vehicle for one's own practice comes to rest upon reaching its fruition;
the vehicle for transforming others is ultimately inexhaustible,
because the sentient beings to be transformed can never be exhausted.
Fourth is the analysis of the teaching of realization.
The manifestation and perfection of primordial dharmatā as present virtue is termed "realized practice."
The cultivation of the virtues of skillful means based upon the teachings is called "practice according to the teachings.
These two types of practice encompass both the beginning and the end.
Fifth, the distinction between cause and effect:
although causes are numerous, they do not transcend the Path of Cessation;
although effects are immeasurable, they do not transcend the virtues of Bodhi and Nirvana.
Question: One may call that which carries one from the causal practice to the fruition a "vehicle" (yāna).
However, once the merit of the fruition is fully perfected, there is no further progress to be made. How can it be called a vehicle?
What is meant by "vehicle" (*yāna*)?
The explanation has three meanings:
first, it is that which carries one from the cause to the fruit.
First, because the fruit still retains the name of its cause, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
Second, regarding reaching the fruit:
although there is no place to go, it is not the case that the qualities of the fruit cannot transport one there.
Just as the fire at the end of an eon has nothing further to burn, yet there is nothing that fire cannot consume,
so it is with this. Because it can transport [beings], it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
Although one has personally completed the practice within the fruits of the three [vehicles], one does not cease transforming others;
by means of the Great Nirvāṇa, one circulates to deliver all sentient beings equally,
and is therefore called a "Vehicle."
The essence of the vehicle varies according to specific cases and is difficult to discuss in full detail;
however, briefly stated, these five practices encompass it all without exception.
Such is the One Vehicle.

96. The Meaning of the Two Kinds of Adornments (9): An Explanation by Way of Four Gates Regarding the Meaning of the Two Kinds of Adornments. I. Analysis according to stages; II. Discernment of essence; III. Analysis according to persons; IV. Regarding the two kinds of adornments: 1. Analysis according to stages; 2. Discernment of essence; 3. Analysis according to persons; 4. As for the two kinds of adornments: [they are]...
First is the adornment of merit,
which is also called virtue;
second is the adornment of wisdom.
Regarding the term "merit" (puṇya):
it is so called because it is well able to provide sustenance and nourishment, thereby benefiting the practitioner.
Thus, it is named "merit."
Welfare (*śreyas*) is the specific quality (*guṇa*) belonging to the category of the virtuous.
It is like coolness and so forth being the specific qualities belonging to the category of water.
As for the term "merit" (*guṇa*):
"Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to the efficacy of being wholesome, providing sustenance, moisture, and beneficial fortune;
thus it is called "merit.
This merit constitutes the virtuous qualities of one who practices goodness, and is therefore termed "meritorious virtue" (*guṇa-dharma*).
Regarding the term "wisdom" (prajñā):
illuminating and seeing is called knowledge (jñāna);
thorough understanding is termed wisdom (prajñā).
These two are distinct:

that which knows conventional truth is called "knowledge" (jñāna), while that which illuminates the ultimate truth is called "wisdom" (prajñā); yet, when considered comprehensively, their meaning is identical.
In the sūtras, this merit and wisdom are sometimes called "ornaments," sometimes described as "requisites for enlightenment," and sometimes termed "aids to the path."
Alternatively, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
Regarding what is termed "adornment," it is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
There are four types of discernment:
first, that which can adorn the person;
second, that which can adorn the mind.
The third is the adornment of the fruit;
the fourth is the common characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their adornment.
Therefore, they are called "adornments."
That which can serve as the cause for Buddhahood is also called an "attribute of enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa).
That which provides the resources and conforms to enlightenment is called an "aid to the path" (mārgasādhana).
Regarding what is called "restraint" (saṃvara):
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"Internal regulation is called discipline (*vinaya*);
when one's practice accords with the true principle, it is so named."
Therefore, it is called *vinaya* (discipline).
Furthermore, that which can be regulated is termed *vinaya*; when one's conduct accords with the precepts, it is called *vinaya*.
Therefore, it is called "restraint" (vinaya);
because it can adorn the practitioner,
it is called "adornment" (vyūha).
The explanation of the names and meanings is thus concluded for this first section.
Next, the essential nature (svabhāva) is analyzed,
which is further distinguished by means of three specific sections.
First, the classification according to practice;
second, the classification according to essence and qualities;
third, the classification according to essence and function.
Regarding practice: "practice" refers to the six perfections.
These six types are subsumed as merit and wisdom.
As for their characteristics,
the sūtras and śāstras differ,
presenting four distinct variations.
First, according to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*,
generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence constitute the category of merit;
patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom constitute the category of knowledge.
Why is this so? Because giving and ethical discipline assist the practitioner by being cultivated according to their respective objects;
since their meaning as beneficial merit is manifest, they are called "merit" (puṇya).
Because it cannot illuminate and perceive,
it is not called wisdom.
Although diligence can universally stimulate all formations, the nature of that diligence is merely incitement.
Because the characteristic of diligence becomes manifest through the practice of specific activities,
it is subsumed under merit along with ethical discipline and generosity.
Among the remaining three [perfections],...
Prajñā is precisely the nature of illuminating vision;
therefore, it is called "wisdom" (jñāna).
When that same prajñā is established as a dharma, it is termed "patience" (kṣānti).
The essence of patience (kṣānti) is wisdom (prajñā);
therefore, it is subsumed within the category of knowledge,
as in the case of the five patiences (pañca-kṣānti) and so forth.
However, within the category of patience (*kṣānti*), there are three distinct types of meaning.
The first is patience toward harm from others (*parāpakāra-marṣaṇa-kṣānti*),
which is the ability to endure injury and loss inflicted by others.
Second is the patience of enduring suffering,
which is the ability to withstand encountering hardship.
Third is the patience of reflecting on the Dharma.
One is able to abide securely in the Dharma.
Among these three types, the first two are not wisdom;
the last one is wisdom.
That sutra specifically teaches that the contemplation of dharmas through patient acceptance constitutes the perfection of patience;
therefore, it is subsumed within wisdom.
That very prajñā abiding in its object is termed concentration (samādhi).
The essential nature of meditative concentration (samādhi) is wisdom (prajñā); therefore, it is subsumed within the category of knowledge.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of its internal meaning, there are two distinct types within concentration.
First is concentration on phenomena, wherein the mind is bound to and dwells upon an object;
second is concentration on principle, wherein the wisdom-mind is unmoving.
That sutra specifically refers to concentration on principle as dhyāna.
Therefore, the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) is subsumed within wisdom (prajñā).
According to both the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, generosity, ethical discipline,
and patience are collectively categorized as the portion of merit (puṇyabhāga).
The wisdom of *prajñā* is categorized as wisdom (*jñāna*).
Diligence (*vīrya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom.
Generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and patience (*kṣānti*) can only serve as provisions and nourishment.
Therefore, it is called "merit";
its essence is not the nature of wisdom,
and thus it cannot illuminate and perceive.
Therefore, it is not called "knowledge" (jñāna);
because its nature is the wisdom of prajñā,
it is spoken of as "knowledge."
To distinguish it from the preceding category,
it is not termed "merit" (puṇya).
Rather, the essential nature of diligence (vīrya) and meditative concentration (dhyāna) is merit.
Because they arise from those [roots],
merit and wisdom are divided into two types;
thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
Based on diligence, one practices generosity, ethical discipline, the four immeasurables, and so forth;
these constitute the portion of merit.
The arising of hearing, reflection, and cultivation constitutes the portion of wisdom.
Cultivating the four immeasurables and so forth by means of dhyāna constitutes the portion of merit;
cultivating skillful contemplations of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases constitutes the portion of wisdom. Question:
As previously stated, based on diligence, one practices generosity, ethical discipline, the four immeasurables, and so forth as branches of merit. Why is it that,
based on meditative concentration, one cultivates only the immeasurables as branches of merit?
The commentary states:
Diligence universally exerts all conditioned phenomena;
therefore, it universally gives rise to wholesome states such as generosity and ethical discipline to constitute the portion of merit.
Generosity, ethical discipline, and miscellaneous wholesome deeds do not arise based on meditative concentration;
therefore, one generates only the four immeasurables and so forth as the portion of merit.
Furthermore, he asked:
Vigor gives rise to the wisdom-constituent through the combined application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Why is it that, based on dhyāna, only the skillful contemplation arising from the wisdom of cultivation is taken as the wisdom-constituent?
It is precisely because vigor universally stimulates all practices.
Therefore, the combined arising of hearing, reflection, and cultivation constitutes the category of wisdom.
Since the two types of wisdom— those of hearing and reflection— are causes of dhyāna rather than its fruits,
one relies upon dhyāna to give rise exclusively to the wisdom of cultivation as the category of wisdom.
Third, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other scriptures,
the first five perfections constitute the category of merit (*puṇya*),
as their essence is not the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) because they do not illuminate the dharmas.
Therefore, that sūtra describes it as "blind.
Prajñā is the essence of knowledge,
for its nature is wisdom, which illuminates all phenomena.
Therefore, it is described as "the eye" in the treatises.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
the first five perfections and the *prajñā* pertaining to conventional activities are collectively categorized as the "merit portion."
Because they are unable to perceive the true meaning,
the Prajñā that illuminates principles is called "wisdom" (jñāna);
because it perceives the true meaning, it is so designated.
Therefore, that sutra states:
"The adornment of merit consists of everything from the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), excluding the perfection of wisdom itself;
the adornment of wisdom is the perfection of wisdom."
What is wisdom that is not the perfection of wisdom?
What is wisdom that is the perfection of wisdom?
He explains that each of the six perfections has two types:
first, those from generosity up to wisdom that are not yet *pāramitās*.
Second, the perfections (pāramitās) ranging from generosity to wisdom are merely perfections when practiced according to specific phenomena without reaching the ultimate reality;
because they do not constitute the transcendence through intrinsic purity, they are not [true] pāramitās.
That which is established through reasoning is a *pāramitā* because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is purity;
among these, the first five do not have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence, but consist exclusively of merit (*puṇya*).
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, that portion which is not the perfection (pāramitā) is taken as an aid to accomplish the preceding five perfections and is likewise judged to be merit;
that portion which is the perfection itself is wisdom.
The preceding section was the first, which distinguished [the two accumulations] according to their practice.
Next, they are divided into merit and wisdom according to their essence and qualities.
True Mind is their essence.
The cultivation of various practices based on conditions is taken as virtue;
the essence of the mind is inherently pure, yet it is said to be defiled due to conditions.
Once subsequent delusory defilements are stilled, the true mind finally becomes pure.
When the true mind is first purified and internally illuminates the dharma-realm,
this is termed wisdom (*jñāna*). From conditions,
one cultivates and gives rise to the virtues of skillful means (*upāya*) through practice.
In terms of its capacity to accord with the meaning [of merit], it is strongly established as "merit" (puṇya) in general discourse;
such is the nature of its substance and virtue.
Although the substance of practice is manifold, it does not transcend realization and teaching.
The beginningless *dharmatā* manifests as present virtue;
this is the practice of realization.
Cultivation arising from skillful means is the practice of instruction (*śāsana-caryā*).
Because the cultivation of the practice of instruction gives rise to conditions that are supportive and compliant,
it is generally described as merit (*puṇya*).
The essence of realized practice is luminous illumination that penetrates the entire dharma-realm;
this is described as wisdom.
Such is the nature of its essential virtue.
Next, they are divided into two types according to their essence and function.
Essence refers to the practice of realizing suchness and attaining nirvana;
function refers to the practice that accords with conditions within the mundane world.
To employ [merit] in accordance with the world and share in worldly blessings and goodness is what is called "merit";
its essence, however, accords with the illumination of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is called wisdom.
Within the course of worldly conduct, it is not that wisdom does not exist;
rather, it remains concealed and is not manifest.
It is as if there were no merit within the course of practice,
yet it remains hidden and unspoken;
therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
As for the adornment of merit:
it is conditioned, tainted, possesses retribution, is obstructive, and impermanent;
it is the dharma of ordinary worldlings.
The adornment of wisdom is unconditioned,
untainted, and without karmic retribution;
it is unimpeded and eternally abiding.
These are the dharmas of the noble ones;
these are the dharmas of ordinary beings.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly remain in the world, acting in common with ordinary beings.
Because they are identical to the mundane, they are conditioned, tainted, obstructive, and impermanent.
As for that which is the noble Dharma,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have abandoned the worldly and act in accordance with reality.
Because they accord with suchness, they are unconditioned, untainted, unimpeded, and eternally abiding.
These two are precisely the two kinds of fruits of craving—the permanent and the impermanent—within the *Dharaṇī-sūtra*.
Merit is the fruit of impermanent love;
wisdom is the fruit of permanence.
Nevertheless, these two natures are not mutually exclusive.
Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"The impermanent is co-existent with the permanent, and the permanent is co-existent with the impermanent.
Such is the essential nature of these two kinds of adornment; thus concludes this section on the two gates.
Next is the discussion on the stages (*avasthā*).
There are two distinct categories of stages:
first, the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane (*lokottara*) in contrast to one another.
That which precedes the stages is mundane;
that which is upon the stages is supramundane.
Nevertheless, the meanings of "merit" (puṇya) and "wisdom" (jñāna) have both common and specific applications.
Discussing them in general, both the mundane and the supramundane are included;
as for what is meant by "specifically," it is as stated in the *Dharmadundubhi-sūtra*:
"The practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are called merit."
That which is practiced on the stages is called wisdom.
This is because, prior to the stages, one practices within the realm of signs (*nimitta*) and remains moistened by various activities; therefore, it is called merit (*puṇya*).
One has not yet been able to realize or see the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is not called "wisdom.
From the first bhūmi upward, because one realizes and perceives the profound nature of phenomena with clarity,
it is called "wisdom."
It is not called "merit" because it distinguishes itself from the preceding category.
Second, it is distinguished according to what is seen by the eye and what is seen through hearing,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
From the first stage up to the ninth stage, although one hears and perceives the Buddha-nature, one is not yet able to see it with the eyes;
for this reason, it is termed "merit.
At the tenth stage, if one is able to see it with the eyes just as a Buddha does, it is termed "wisdom."
The distinctions among these stages are thus concluded; this concludes the three gates.
Next, we shall discuss the persons involved:
namely, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
To distinguish merit and wisdom with reference to this person,
there are briefly two approaches:
first, the analytical approach based on principle.
The conduct of ordinary persons, which accords with and is nourished by mundane phenomena, is called merit;
because they have not yet seen the principle, it is not called wisdom.
Because that which is practiced by the three vehicles is accomplished through the vision of principle,
it is collectively termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
To distinguish it from the preceding category, it is not termed "merit" (*puṇya*).
Second, the distinction with respect to reality.
Reality refers to the non-empty nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles have not yet seen this reality.
All practices are collectively termed "merit" because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive the true nature [of reality].
All practices are collectively termed "wisdom" for the same reason.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are not without wisdom,
yet it remains hidden and does not manifest.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not without merit.
It is hidden and not explained. Thus, the two kinds of adornment have been briefly distinguished.

97. The Meaning of the Two Kinds of Lineage (IX). The meaning of the two kinds of lineage is analyzed through three gates. First, determining their sequence by correlating the stages of practice; second, analyzing them directly; third, analyzing them according to practice. Regarding the first gate: [The text continues with the analysis of the two lineages.]
To determine the sequence [of the two natures] based on their practice and stages:
as for the two types of nature, the first is the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*).
Second, the two types of lineage (*gotra*).
Regarding these two types of lineage, if distinguished by their stages, the cultivated lineage (*bhāvanā-gotra*) comes first and the innate lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) comes later;
however, if discussed in terms of their actual functioning, the innate and the cultivated are simultaneous.
Because they are simultaneous, the sequence of before and after is not fixed.
When explaining the arising of function based on the substance, one first clarifies the innate seeds (*prakṛtisthagotra*) and subsequently clarifies the acquired seeds (*samudānītagotra*).
When seeking the substance by means of its function, one first clarifies the acquired seeds and subsequently clarifies the innate seeds.
This is similar to the relationship between the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of realization (*darśanamārga*).
In terms of their respective stages, the path of cultivation is prior and the path of realization is subsequent;
for worldly conduct constitutes the path of cultivation.
Therefore, it is placed first because the conduct on the ground serves as the proof of the Way;
therefore, it is placed last.
According to the evidence of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, teaching and realization are simultaneous;
because they are simultaneous, their sequence is not fixed. This is determined by taking the essence as the basis for the function.
First realization, then teaching;
seeking to grasp the essence through practice, first teaching, then realization.
Such is the sequence of priority and posteriority.
In the second section, the analysis is conducted according to the stages;
it is discussed in order to distinguish the lineages as they pertain generally to the stage of practice through understanding and the ten bhūmis.
Within this, there are four distinct sections regarding its meaning:
first, the explanation of its name;
second, the classification according to understanding.
Third, they are distinguished according to their practice;
fourth, they are differentiated by way of their understanding and conduct.
What are their names?
What is called "spiritual lineage" (gotra) is also termed the "ten abodes" (daśavihāra).
If one speaks of the ten abodes, they should be distinguished by their respective names:
when understanding, contemplation, and accomplishment are achieved and there is no regression, it is called an "abode."
If it is said that the name "cultivated nature" (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*) is established in contrast to what follows,
this refers to the qualities of practice accomplished by the innate nature (*prakṛti-gotra*) based on prior contemplation and understanding;
these have been cultivated but are not yet perfected.
To speak of it as "cultivation" (śikṣā):
that which is capable of producing the fruit of Buddhahood in the future is called a "seed" (bīja).
The second, the innate seed-nature, is also termed the "ten practices" (daśa-caryā).
If one says that the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) should be distinguished as being fully endowed with the nature of all practices within the *dharmadhātu*,
they are therefore called "practices.
As for the term "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*), its name is established by looking back from what precedes it and forward toward what follows it.
The virtues practiced during the preceding stage of the "nature of cultivation" (gotrabhūmi) become unshakable upon reaching this stage;
therefore, it is called "nature" (prakṛti).
In relation to the subsequent fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "lineage" (gotra) because it is capable of producing it.
The stages of the position of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) have four distinct names:
first, the stage of practice through understanding;
second, the stage of generating the resolve (cittotpāda).
Third is dedication;
fourth is the lineage of the path.
As for what is called "practice through understanding":
This name is established in reference to the supramundane path.
Because one understands and practices within the supramundane path,
it is called "practice through understanding" (adhimukti-caryā).
Regarding the term "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*):
it is named in reference to its fruit.
Because one directs the intention toward and seeks great enlightenment, it is called "arousing the mind."
It is also called "arousing the mind" because it gives rise to the aspiration for transcendence;
as for "dedication," this name is likewise established in relation to the fruit.
To turn one's own wholesome dharmas toward enlightenment is called "dedication" (pariṇāmanā).
As for the term "path-seeds":
Its name is established by way of its own specific category in relation to what follows.
Within its own category, it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it is established as being like the path of vision;
it is called a "seed" (*bīja*) because it is capable of producing the fruit of Buddhahood in relation to what follows.
The stage of the ten grounds also has four names:
first, the Ten Grounds;
second, the Expedient Means of Practice.
Third are the factors of enlightenment;
fourth are the noble lineages.
Regarding what are called the ten stages:
They are designated by their respective names.
A "ground" (bhūmi) is so called because it is the dwelling place where the accomplishment of conduct and virtues resides;
alternatively, it may be called a "ground" because it can produce [subsequent stages].
Regarding the practice of skillful means:
it is designated by its name.
Skillfully initiating the various perfections is called the practice of skillful means.
Regarding the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa):
they are so named because they constitute the path that transcends the world, which is called bodhi.
The distinctions in the practice of the Path are called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Furthermore, this term may be applied by way of its result:
the path to the fruit of Buddhahood is called *bodhi*.
Those practices on the stages that serve as causes for that [enlightenment] are called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
As for the term "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa),
their names are established by looking forward from each respective stage to what follows.
Within its own category, it is correctly designated as "noble" (ārya);
because it is capable of producing [subsequent results] when viewed in relation to what follows, it is called a "seed.
Such is the name; this concludes the first section.
Next, we shall distinguish the stages according to the perspective of contemplative understanding.
There are four distinct types of understanding.
The first is knowing the teachings.
First, knowing the various teaching gates, whether provisional or ultimate;
second, knowing the dharmas of meaning,
knowing the various gates of meaning, whether general or specific.
Third, knowing the principle-dharma:
knowing that characteristics are empty and quiescent.
Fourth, knowing the reality-dharma.
Knowing that all phenomena arise from the Buddha-nature, the true mind, their essence is thus real.
Generally speaking, at every stage one understands these four aspects;
however, when distinguished specifically, it is during the stage of the seeds of practice (*śikṣā-bīja*) that one primarily understands the teachings.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes understand the teachings they hear for themselves as soon as they hear them;
their awakening does not depend on others."
In the stage of the nature-seed (*prakṛtisthagotra*), one seeks the expressions to reach their intended meaning,
thereby understanding the dharmas of the teachings.
In the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), one shatters appearances to return to quiescence, thereby understanding the dharmas of the principle.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one awakens to reality and exhausts its source, thereby understanding and knowing the true dharma.
Because there are such distinctions in this understanding, four stages are established.
Furthermore, it is further distinguished that within the stage of the cultivated lineage (*śikṣā-bīja*),

one seeks out and apprehends phenomena through designations, knowing the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); whereas within the stage of the innate lineage (*prakṛti-bīja*), [one knows the ultimate truth].
Abandoning the conventional expression to seek the principle, one knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one destroys and departs from existence and non-existence, enters the Middle Way, and knows the single true meaning.
From the first bhūmi upward, one awakens to reality and, in accordance with conditions, realizes the inexhaustible dharma-realm of dependent origination;
because there is this distinction in understanding,
four stages are differentiated.
First, understanding and knowing the characteristics of birth-and-death, nirvana, defilement, and purity;
second, understanding and knowing the principle of signlessness and emptiness;
third, understanding and knowing the meaning of the single reality that is neither existent nor non-existent.
The fourth is the gate of understanding the true *dharmadhātu* dependent origination within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
While the explanation is distinct for each [stage],
in reality, when discussed generally, all individual stages possess these four.

To discuss them individually: within the stage of the acquired seeds (*samudānīta-bīja*), contemplative practice first arises, whereby one understands and discerns the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) regarding the distinctions between the defiled and the pure.
Within the stage of the innate seeds (*prakṛti-stha-bīja*), contemplation and understanding become increasingly superior.
Abandoning signs and tending toward quiescence, one understands and realizes the signless ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), contemplative realization becomes increasingly profound;
by utterly destroying signs, one understands and realizes the dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent.

From the first bhūmi upward, there is a distinction in understanding: one observes and realizes through contemplation, while the other realizes through ultimate liberation, knowing the true dharma-realm of dependent origination.
Because there is this difference in realization, four stages are distinguished. This concludes the two gates.
Next, their stages are distinguished by means of the various formations (*saṃskāra*).
There are two levels of formations:
first, the types of formations.
Second is the virtue of practice (*caryā-guṇa*).
Within these two, each has its own beginning and end.
Regarding the types of practice, the lineage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-gotra*) is the beginning.
The seeds of habitual nature are ultimately perfected.
Among the practices and virtues, the stage of practice through understanding begins with cultivation and reaches ultimate perfection in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Because there are these distinctions in practice, four stages are thus divided. This concludes the three gates [of the preceding section].
Next, the four stages are distinguished according to the stage of understanding and practice (adhimukti-caryā).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the discussion on understanding and practice;
second, the exposition of understanding and practice together.
Regarding the term "discussion" (saṃlun):
within these four stages, they are divided into two pairs.
The first pair consists of understanding first and practice later.
Regarding the latter two pairs, first the understanding and then the practice are explained.
What are their characteristics?
In the stage of the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*), one achieves understanding through the teachings.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes attain spontaneous understanding and liberation according to the Dharma they hear, without relying on the awakening of others.
Within the stage of the Innate Lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*), they initiate teaching and practice accordingly."
Therefore, it is taught as the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) in the *Avataṃsaka*.
The first pair is as described above.
In the second pair, the initial stage involves the practice of understanding through cultivation and comprehension.
Therefore, it is called "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*) in the sūtras,
because understanding serves as the practice.
Furthermore, the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states that for such a person, the practice through understanding is characterized by clear observation (*vipaśyanā*).
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means "understanding.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one accomplishes the practice of principle;
therefore, the treatise calls it the "retention of the skillful means of practice" (*caryā-upāya-dhāraṇī*).

Based on this, one may discuss the accomplishment of the practice-lineage (śikṣā-bīja), the stage of understanding and practice (adhimukti-caryā), and the realization through contemplation (vipaśyanā-siddhi).

It is said that the qualities of the practice and the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are accomplished through the nature-lineage (prakṛti-bīja). As for the phrase "and is explained together": [it refers to the fact that these are taught in conjunction].
Among the four stages of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization,
hearing and reflection constitute understanding,
while cultivation and realization constitute practice.
In the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*), one generates understanding based on the teachings and accomplishes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
In the stage of the lineage of nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*), one generates understanding based on the meaning and accomplishes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
In the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*), one initiates practice based on the teachings and accomplishes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
From the first bhūmi upward, practice is established based on principle, resulting in the accomplishment of actual realization.
Such is the distinction between the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) and the stage of realization.
The preceding four sections together constitute the second [major division]: the analysis according to the stages (*avasthā*).
Within the third section, there is an analysis according to practice (*caryā*).
Now, within the context of practice, there are four distinct points of meaning.
First, the explanation of its name.
Second, the elucidation of the essential nature and characteristics; third, the clarification of the meaning of true and false as arising and ceasing;
fourth, the differentiation according to time.
What is the meaning of these names?
As for the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛtisthagotra*), it is named after its essence;
the beginningless *dharmatā* is what is referred to as "nature."
This dharmatā is originally obscured by delusion;
it is described as defiled. Through the cultivation of remedies, one becomes free from defilement, and it is only then that it is revealed.
It is taught that this constitutes purity;
thus, the pure qualities are first revealed as the basis for the fruit and are designated as the "seed."
This indicates that because the nature (prakṛti) constitutes the seed, it is called the "nature-seed" (prakṛti-bīja).
Since the meaning of "seed" is not sublated,
it is further termed "nature."
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The nature-lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*) is the natural state of phenomena from beginningless time;
the cultivated lineage (*samudānītagotra*) is named after its cause."
The roots of virtue of skillful means were originally non-existent but now exist;
they arise from cultivation,
and are therefore called "cultivation."
Because the cultivation of conduct and virtue can produce the true fruit,
it is called the "cultivated seed" (*śikṣā-bīja*).
The meaning of its nature is the same as previously explained.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"That which has been obtained through the cultivation of virtue from the outset is called the nature of the cultivated seed (*abhyāsa-gotra*).
Such is the meaning of the term; this concludes the first section.
Next, the essential nature and characteristics are distinguished.
These two types of nature both take the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) as their essence; within this true consciousness, there are three distinct aspects:
essence, characteristic, and function.
The essence refers to the dharmatā of equality as it truly is;
eternally and profoundly tranquil throughout past and present, it is neither hidden nor manifest, neither cause nor fruit.
Thus, a sutra says:
That which is neither cause nor effect is called Buddha-nature;
this is what is meant.
To speak of its characteristics:
The true dependent origination is the integration of mental activities;
that is to say, all the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are integrated within the mind of true awakening.
When this mind is obscured by delusion, it is conventionally described as defiled.
The meaning of emerging from entanglements and being free from defilement is explained as "purity" (*viśuddhi*).
Since it is the beginning within purity that can serve as the basis for the fruit and give rise to subsequent fruits,
it is called the "nature-seed" (*prakṛti-bīja*).
Regarding its function:
when true consciousness is in a state of defilement, it harmonizes with delusion to give rise to birth and death;
when it is in a state of purity, it accords with the remedies to accumulate and give rise to the virtues of practice.
When the practice of virtue is first established and is capable of producing subsequent fruits, it is called the "cultivated seed" (*xi zhong*).
Its essential nature and characteristics are roughly as described; this concludes the two preceding sections.
Next, we shall examine the meaning of the arising and ceasing of the true and the delusory.
Within this, first it clarifies that the two minds—the true and the deluded—have respectively the capacity for activity and the lack thereof;
subsequently, it clarifies that the true and the deluded have respectively the capacity for cessation and the lack thereof. It is asked:
Within the two minds of reality and delusion,
which mind is able to produce the seeds of habituation and the virtues of practice, and which mind does not?
The commentary states:
Only that which is real is devoid of the principle of activity;
likewise, mere conceptual construction alone is also devoid of the logic of activity.
The meaning of "activity" exists only when the real and the false are mutually dependent. What does this mean?
If there were only the real and no falsehood, the real would be merely uniform.
Therefore, there is no cultivation or activity.
If there were only deluded thought and no reality,
then the phenomena of deluded thought would vanish of their own accord as they arise, and since their substance would not be established, [delusion itself could not persist].
Because there is the activity of the multitude [of dharmas], the Sūtra states:
"If the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) did not exist, these seven dharmas would not abide."
One must not weary of suffering nor seek nirvana with longing.
Because the false relies upon the true and the true follows the movement of the false,
there is the activity of cultivation.
Question: By what conditions can the deluded mind produce [its effects]?
Explanation:
The deluded mind has three causes and conditions by which it is able to function:
first, it is able to function through the power of the present condition of virtuous friends.
This means that because sentient beings are taught and transformed by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and virtuous friends in the present life,
they are able to cultivate all the practices and virtues of their spiritual lineage within their deluded minds.
Second, it is by the power of the causes of past virtuous conduct that one is able to act;
that is to say, all sentient beings, through the cultivation of various virtues in the past, have caused these latencies to manifest within their present minds.
Therefore, one is able to cultivate various practices within the deluded mind.
Third, it is produced by the true power of the object of focus;
that is to say, within the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is its basis.
The nature of all dharmas endowed with merit perfumes and awakens the deluded mind;
therefore, various virtues arise within that deluded mind. Question:
For what reason can the true mind act?
The explanation states:
the true mind is also able to act by means of three conditions.
First, it is through the power of conditions provided by present spiritual friends that one is able to act;
that is to say, sentient beings in the present world are transformed and guided by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends.
Therefore, all conditioned phenomena arise from the true mind.
Second, they are produced through the power of the熏 (xūn, perfuming) of deluded cultivation;
that is to say, when sentient beings cultivate and accumulate various virtues within their deluded minds, those virtues perfume the mind.
Therefore, various wholesome dharmas arise from within the true mind.
Third, they are produced through the power of perfuming by its own essence.
What is the meaning of this?
The essence of the true mind is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fully present.
Because those dharmas permeate the mind, various virtues arise within the true mind.

If the essence of the mind did not inherently possess all the dharmas of the nature of reality as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, then even with the application of effort, wholesome states could not arise.
Such is the case regarding the performance of good deeds. Next, we shall distinguish between that which is true and that which is delusive, and whether they are subject to extinction or not.
In the distinct discussion of the true and the false:
deluded thoughts, being cultivated through conditions, are invariably extinguished;
true cultivation is not extinguished.
Why is this so? Because the characteristics of dharmas born of false conceptualization have no substantial reality;
when investigated to their ultimate limit, they are exhausted.
Therefore, they are utterly extinguished.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"It is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)."
The wisdom of nirvāṇa extinguishes my [concept of] nirvāṇa;
the true nature of dharmas is hidden within their reality,
yet it becomes manifest when investigated.
The manifest true nature is described as having the quality of activity;
therefore, it is not extinguished.
According to the meaning, when discussed in full, both the true and the false possess the sense of being both extinguished and non-extinguished.
What is the meaning of this?
The essence of false phenomena is empty; they ultimately return to ashes and extinction, which is why they are completely extinguished.
The false defiles the true; thus,
the practices and virtues of reality arise through the defilement of the false,
and for this reason they are said not to perish.
When delusion is exhausted, the truth subsides along with it and does not arise again; therefore,
it is said that "truth ceases."
The true essence exists eternally;
therefore, it is said not to perish.
This brief analysis of the meaning of "perishing" concludes these three sections.
Next, the fourth section distinguishes [the two] by way of time.
During the stage of the external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana), these two types of nature are merely termed "Buddha-nature" and are not yet termed "practices and virtues."
There are two kinds of Buddha-nature:
first, the Buddha-nature of Dharma;
second, the Buddha-nature of retribution.
The Buddha-nature of the Dharma is the nature-seed cause;
the Buddha-nature of the retribution is the practice-seed cause.
What is the distinction between these two natures?
The Buddha-nature of the Dharma is the originally existing essence of phenomena;
its substance remains without increase or decrease from the causal stage to the resultant stage,
differing only in its concealment or manifestation.
The distinction lies in purity and impurity.
As for the Buddha-nature of retribution, it originally has no substantial essence;
there is only the principle that it can be produced through skillful means.
These two have been fully and extensively analyzed as previously presented in the "Chapter on Buddha-nature.
These two types of Buddha-nature, based upon the Stage of Reaching the Ground (*pratilambha-bhūmi*), are termed the "two kinds of nature.
The nature of the Dharma-Buddha is further designated as the "nature-seed" (*prakṛti-gotra*).
The qualities of practice produced by the nature that is the fruition of Buddhahood are called the "seed of cultivation" (*śikṣā-bīja*).
These two natures, when they reach the stage of "understanding and practice," are termed "attainment of skillful means" and "orientation toward purification."
That which is the stage of the nature of cultivation (śikṣāgotra) up to the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukticaryā) is called "attaining skillful means" (upāyaprāpti).
That which is the stage of the nature of the lineage (gotragotra) up to the stage of practice through understanding is called "tending toward purity" (viśuddhyabhimukha).
When that attainment of skillful means and tending toward purity reach the first bhūmi and above, they are further designated as the "two paths" (dvimārga).
That which is the skillful means of attainment is termed the path of teaching (*śāsanamārga*).
That which is the purification of the tendency toward it is termed the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*).
When the path of teaching reaches its fruition, it is termed the Buddha of Retribution (*vipākabuddha*), the skillful means of enlightenment (*bodhiprayoga*), and the skillful means of nirvāṇa.
When the realization of the Way reaches its fruition, it is renamed the Dharma-Buddha, the Pure Nature of Buddha-nature, and the Pure Nirvana of Bodhi-nature.
Although these terms change according to the occasion, their essential meaning does not differ.
The two types of lineage have been briefly distinguished above. 98.

The Meaning of the Twofold Practice of Realization and Teaching (IX). The meaning of the twofold practice of realization and teaching is explained through a threefold analysis: 1. Explaining the Names; 2. Distinguishing the Characteristics; 3. Examining the Meaning of What Can and Cannot Be Spoken. First, explaining the names.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the two modes of practice—realization (*adhigama*) and scripture (*āgama*).
What is termed "realization" is a specific designation for the act of knowing and attaining.
It is called realization because one truly contemplates equality and accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding what is called "teaching," there are seven distinct meanings.
First is the virtue of skillful means and practice,
which arises through cultivation based upon the teaching and proceeds from its basis.
Therefore, it is called "practice through teaching.
Second is the practice of differentiation;
this practice can be distinguished by means of teaching, as it follows from the designations used for expression.
Therefore, it is called the practice of teaching.
Third, knowing the teachings spoken by all Buddhas;
because one acts according to what is known, it is called the practice of teaching.
Fourth is the practice of the knowledge of teaching the Dharma (*dharmajñāna-pratipatti*). Because it is able to give rise to verbal discourse to instruct and benefit the world,
it is called the practice of instruction (*deśanā-pratipatti*).
The five modes of practice for realizing equality are distinguished by their verbal expressions;
these differences arise from the distinctions among the teachings.
Therefore, it is called "teaching and practice.
The six practices are able to manifest the true meaning and are thus termed "teaching";
for example, based on the practice of the causal stage, it is called "expounding the Great [Vehicle]."
The meaning of "teaching" (*jiao*) is that the superior virtue of the seven [buddhas] is bestowed upon those below;
as the *Laṅkāvatāra* states:
"the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, the teaching, and so forth."
However, these two practices rely upon the teachings to manifest their correspondence; thus, they should generally be termed "Teaching" (jiao).
When the practice is perfected and accords with the Dharma, it should generally be termed "Realization" (zheng).
These distinct names for the two practices are used to differentiate between their hidden and manifest aspects.
Because the realization of the equality of reality reveals the meaning of the Dharma,
it is specifically termed "realization" (*pratyakṣa*).
The virtues of skillful means and practice are easily accessible through the expression of the title.
Therefore, it is uniquely termed "name-and-teaching" (nāma-dharma). This proof—that name and teaching arise together as "activity" (saṃskāra)—is the meaning of the term; thus concludes this section.
Next, the characteristics of the essence are distinguished;
there are nine distinct meanings.
First, the distinction between cultivation and realization is used to differentiate the realized from the taught.
The practice of cultivation through expedient means prior to all stages is called "instructional practice" (*śrutamaya-caryā*),
because it initially relies upon words for its commencement.
The virtues accomplished within all stages are called "realized practice" (*adhigama-caryā*).
Because one realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by means of this perfected virtue,
these two are precisely the realization of the stage of accomplishing the Buddha-dharmas, which is the first practice within the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
The commentary states:
That which is first practiced is the *āgama*;
the practice that accomplishes the Buddha-dharma is the practice of realization (*adhigama*).
This is what is meant by that.
Furthermore, this teaching refers to the practice of the "Great Cause" (mahāhetu) division of that [path],
while the realization therein refers to the practice of the "Great Fruit" (mahāphala) division of its meaning.
Second, the classification according to the stages:
that which is practiced prior to the [ten] stages is called "practice based on instruction," because worldly practice arises in dependence upon words.
From the first bhūmi upward, all virtues collectively constitute the practice of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-pratipatti*),
because as practice matures, one abandons verbal expression to realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
These two are precisely what the *Bhūmi-sūtra* praises as the two purities of the assembly.

He explains that for those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*) constitute the purity of the scriptural transmission (*āgama-viśuddhi*). Just as these teachings and practices are so,
the qualities of the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) collectively constitute the purity of realization (*adhigama-viśuddhi*).
This is like the practice of realization.
The threefold distinction between the true and the false—
wherein all false cultivation occurs— is what is termed "doctrinal practice."
All genuine cultivation is uniformly the practice for realization.
Therefore, the *Dichilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and that which is born of retribution."
This can indeed be explained;
because it can be explained, it is termed "teaching.
True wisdom is not like this.
Because it is free from words;
because it is free from words, it is said to be realized.
Fourth, directly engaging with false cultivation and making distinctions according to the meaning.
There are two types of false cultivation:
first, the practice of cultivating merit according to specific phenomena;
second, the practice of cultivating wisdom based on principle.
Merit relies on phenomena and is easily manifested through words;
therefore, it is called "teaching" (śāsana).
Wisdom relies on principle to achieve its realization, illuminating that principle with clarity.
Therefore, it is said that [false cultivation] serves as proof.
A question is asked:
"False cultivation cannot realize the Truth."
What is meant by "realization"?
The explanation states:
although one may practice erroneously and fail to embody the correspondence within conditions, [it is still termed realization].
Therefore, it is termed "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Fifth, within the context of the ultimate truth, the relative aspect is contrasted with the real aspect;
within the causal stage, that supramundane realization of the ultimate truth which is signless (*animitta*) is designated as "teaching and practice."
Because those signs appear within the practice of the teachings, one seeks the signs and attains reality; this is explained as the practice of realization.
These two are precisely the Dharma-gate of the Light of the Supreme Sublime Dharma within the *Dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds).
That supreme dharma (adhipati-dharma) is the practice of realization (adhigama-pratipatti);
that luminous dharma (āloka-dharma) is the practice of instruction (deśanā-pratipatti).
As for what is called "luminosity":
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"Because this Mahāyāna Dharma illuminates all other dharma-gates;
that is to say, it reveals [them] within the minds of mundane practitioners."
Sixth, regarding the distinction between essence and attributes within the perspective of ultimate truth:
the manifestation and perfection of the beginningless *dharmatā* as present attributes constitutes its essence.
To cultivate the practice of skillful means through conditions is its virtue;
when the essence is realized,
the practice first becomes manifest.
Because the quality of the realization of the self-nature through pure wisdom serves as the basis for the practice of the teaching,
and because the quality of the practice of skillful means arises from cultivation based on verbal instruction,
these two are precisely the dharmas illustrated by the analogy of golden ornaments in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
The pure golden substance is a metaphor for realized practice (*adhigama-caryā*);
the characteristics of the bracelets and so forth are metaphors for scriptural practice (*deśanā-caryā*).
This seventh [point] distinguishes between essence and function within the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The preceding [section] established that both realization and teaching are identical in their essence (*tattva*).
Based upon this essence, the manifestation of teaching and wisdom externally is designated as their function (*vṛtti*).
The essence constitutes the practice of realization.
Because it realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it serves as the practice of the teaching;
because it correctly expounds the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it illuminates the world.
These two are precisely what the *Bhūmi-sūtra* illustrates through the metaphor of the light of a mani-jewel.
The purity of the jewel's substance is a metaphor for realized practice (adhigama-caryā),
while its light shining outward is a metaphor for teaching practice (deśanā-caryā).
Therefore, the *Dilun* says:
The light of the Āgamas is emitted from within the maṇi-jewel of the dharma-illumination of realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
Regarding the eight [categories], they are analyzed according to the ultimate reality by way of linguistic expression, and according to the provisional reality by way of meaning.
The realization of the equal essence is termed "realized practice" (*sākṣātkāra-caryā*).
This very essence of realization, when categorized by its verbal expressions, is taught as the tenfold path of instruction.
These two are precisely the dharmas illustrated in the *Bhūmi-sūtra* by the analogies of the tracks of birds in the sky and drawings in the sky.
The analogy of the equality of space refers to the realization of practice.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The locus of bird tracks is the locus of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; it is subsumed under the realized wisdom of the Bodhisattva stages."
The tracks of birds in the sky and the patterns drawn by the wind serve as metaphors for the teachings and practices;
thus, the treatise states:
"It is not that these verbal expressions concerning the distinctions of the ten stages do not exist therein."
Briefly stated, there are ten divisions;
thus, they are called "discourse" (*vyavahāra*) because they are expressed through designations.
Ninth, within the context of reality (*tattva*), there is a distinction made between the internal state (*svabhāva*) and progressive advancement (*viśeṣa*).
All the qualities of practice accomplished by oneself, whether in terms of their essence or their function, constitute "practice through realization" (*sākṣātkriyā-pratipatti*),
because one has personally realized these dharmas. Within the stage of further progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*),
receiving the Buddha's teachings in a superior manner is called "practice through instruction" (*anuśāsana-pratipatti*).
These two are likewise found within the *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra*,
where it is proclaimed that the realization of Vajragarbha and the power of the *āgama* are both present therein.

The sublime, stainless wisdom, the immeasurable meaning, the eloquent exposition, the beautiful words, and the correspondence with reality act together as the power of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-bala*).
Just as through this practice of realization,
the firm and pure wisdom that attends to the teachings of the Buddha constitutes the power of scripture (*āgama-bala*).
The practice of this teaching is such that its essence and characteristics are as described; these two sections are concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish between the meanings of the teaching regarding realization that are expressible and those that are inexpressible.
Among these, let us first discuss the initial pair;
the others may be understood by analogy.
Within the first pair, concerning the gateway of cultivation and accomplishment, there are three distinct meanings.
First, by correlating realization and teaching through the two aspects of practice,
one distinguishes the meanings of what can be expressed and what cannot be expressed;
second, by relying solely on realization.
How is it that these three are distinguished solely in terms of the contrast between teaching and realization?
The practice of teaching can be explained;
the practice of realization is beyond discussion.
This refers to the discourse given at the time of cultivation and realization; at the very beginning of initial practice, one has not yet transcended names and forms.
Outside of practice, there are still names and forms that can be apprehended, which are employed to manifest cultivation.
Therefore, it can be said that at the time of realization, one realizes the suchness of all phenomena;
beyond this realization, no further names or characteristics can be apprehended.
Knowing this, by what means could one further manifest or substantiate it?
Therefore, the realization of practice is never spoken of;
for that which can be spoken resides exclusively within the teachings.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it speaks only of one part;
what is called "one part" refers to the causal portion (*hetu-bhāga*).
This is called the causal stage (*hetubhāga*) of the conduct of one who has newly begun to practice the path of instruction.
Because this cultivation is inexpressible,
the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states:
The ten stages are likewise.
They cannot be described or heard;
the two modes of practice—realization and teaching—are related in this same way.
Next, we shall distinguish the meanings of the expressible and the inexpressible solely from the perspective of realization (*adhigama*).
However, while realization is entirely inexpressible when contrasted with the teaching (*deśanā*),
there are also specific instances within it that possess both expressible and inexpressible aspects.
What are the characteristics of its meaning?
There are five aspects of differentiation.
First, it may be generally indicated by its profound name as "that which can be spoken."
Therefore, in the *Dharmadhātustava*, five verses are proclaimed to reveal the greatness of the meaning (*artha-mahattva*).
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras as proof that it cannot be pointed out by means of signs (*nimitta*) to show to others; it is "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*).
Therefore, the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states:
"Words cannot reach it;
this meaning is like the tracks of birds in the sky or drawings of wind in space."
That which can be expressed through profound discourse is called "the expressible.
That which cannot be pointed out by means of characteristics to show others is called "the inexpressible.
Second, that which can be revealed by brushing away characteristics is called "the expressible."
That which cannot be discussed through characteristics is called "ineffable.
Why is this so? Because realization is free from names and characteristics, and thus it cannot be described or heard.
Now, returning to the path, the realization is inexpressible and cannot be heard.
To speak of that Dharma is called "explaining the realization.
Therefore, Vajragarbha reveals that the difficulty of explaining the stages is the manifestation of the greatness of their meaning.
If one says that the realized Dharma can be spoken or heard,
yet one’s words deviate from that Dharma, then it cannot be called "spoken.
Thirdly, when the means of expression can metaphorically illustrate and reveal [the Dharma], it is termed "speaking."

Therefore, in the *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds), the practices cultivated through those causal factors are used to illustrate the distinct characteristics and true virtues of the resultant stage; this is called "correspondence by analogy.
"Yù" (analogy) means "to illustrate by comparison."
That which cannot be directly explained or manifested as such phenomena is called "ineffable.
Fourth, that which can mutually manifest through its own essential nature as true phenomena is called "effable."
Among these, in some cases cause and effect are mutually manifest;
thus, in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, those qualities of the Buddha-dharma are cited to illustrate the qualities of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Alternatively, essence and function may be mutually illustrated.
As stated in the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-asambhedanirdeśa-sūtra*, in that sūtra, the phenomena illustrated by the ornaments of gold manifest the essence through their function,
while the phenomena illustrated by the light of mani-jewels and so forth manifest the function through their essence.
Alternatively, the dharmas of the stages may be mutually revealed through the practice of the path;
thus, in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, those true knowledges (*tattvajñāna*) are employed to reveal the dharmas of the stages.
All such instances where these intrinsic, true dharmas mutually manifest one another are termed "discourseable" (*vaktavya*).
One cannot use that conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) to manifest the true name as being "inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*).

Rather, it is explained by comparing the fifth [category] of conventional reality with ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); based on this comparison of the conventional to the ultimate, there is an ultimate reality that exists beyond the conventional.
That which can be discussed is called "discourseable.
From the perspective of reality, apart from the mind there is no objective reality;
once this is known, by what means could one further apply names to discourse about reality?
Therefore, it cannot be spoken of.
Such is the distinction between the meanings of what can be spoken of and what cannot be spoken of regarding the realization of the Middle Way.
Next, the meanings of what can be spoken of and what cannot be spoken of shall be distinguished with respect to the practice of the teaching.
Within the teachings, according to their meaning, there are also aspects that can be explained and aspects that cannot be explained.
Within the practice of the teachings, meanings may contain both the true and the false;
that which is falsely cultivated and can be described is termed "explicable."
Because true cultivation is difficult to manifest and its name is ineffable, the *Bhūmi-sūtra* clarifies the virtues of the causal stage of contemplative cultivation, stating:
"It is difficult to explain; it is known by one's own mind."
This concludes the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-arthaviniścaya-śāstra* (Dacheng yizhang),
which has thus distinguished [the teachings] through both realization (*adhigama*) and scripture (*āgama*). [Fascicle Ten begins.]

In the *Jingfa ju yinfa* (The Causes of the Collection of Pure Dharmas) compiled by Dharma Master Yuan, this fascicle contains twelve sections: the meaning of the Three Refuges; the meaning of the Three Studies; the meaning of the Threefold Aggregate of Precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*); the meaning of the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*);

the meaning of tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); the meaning of the three kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*); the meaning of the three types of *prajñā*; the meaning of the three types of knowledge (*jñāna*); the meaning of the three measures of cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*); the meaning of the three paths of identical characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); the meaning of the three paths of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); and the meaning of the three types of abiding (*vihāra*).

99. The Meaning of the Three Refuges (10). The Meaning of the Three Refuges explained through a threefold classification: I. The Name Explained. 1. That which is taken as refuge; 2. That which takes refuge; 3. First, the explanation of the name.
Regarding the term "three refuges" (triśaraṇa):
it means to seek refuge, to surrender, and to rely upon;
therefore, it is called "taking refuge."
The aspect of seeking refuge is like a son returning to his father;
the meaning of relying and submitting is like subjects relying on their king,
or as nature relies upon courage.
Taking refuge is differentiated according to its objects into three:
namely, taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
One relies upon the Buddha as one's teacher.
Therefore, it is said that one takes refuge in the Buddha.
Relying on the Dharma as medicine,
one is thus called to take refuge in the Dharma.
Relying on the Saṃgha as one's friend is called "taking refuge in the Saṃgha. Question:
Why are these three specifically singled out?
It is because these three ultimate destinations enable sentient beings to transcend birth and death and are designated as "nirvāṇa";
such is the meaning of their names.
In the second section,
the objective realms of the Three Jewels to which one takes refuge are specifically elucidated.
Within the meaning of the Three Jewels, they are analyzed through three gates.
First, explaining its name;
second, discerning its essential nature and characteristics;
third, clarifying its sequential order.
First, I shall explain its name.
That which is called "Buddha" is,
in the correct foreign pronunciation, named *Buddha*.
This is called the "Awakened One" (Buddha).
Because he has perfected his awakening through practice,
he is named the Awakened One.
Furthermore, there are those who possess awareness and are also called "the aware.
Awareness has two meanings:
first, the act of discerning is called awareness.
The second is awakening, which is called "bodhi" (awakening).
As for the term "discernment," it refers to [the overcoming of] the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The afflictions and their harmful activities are like thieves;
only the noble ones perceive them and thus are not harmed by them.
It is just as when people in the world become aware of a thief, the thief can do them no harm.
It is also like this;
therefore, it is called "awakening.
To speak of "awakening" (bodha) is in contrast to the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa).
The state of being obscured by ignorance and slumbering over phenomena is like sleep;
only the Noble One alone awakens, unobstructed,
just as one who has slept attains waking.
Therefore, it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
The ignorance (avidyā) that stands in opposition to it is of two kinds:
first, ignorance regarding the principle (tattva).
Because one awakens to the true nature of phenomena by eliminating those [afflictions],
it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
Second is ignorance regarding objects (vastu-moha-avidyā).
Because one realizes all phenomena of the three categories— wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral— in order to eliminate those [afflictions],
it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
This latter meaning is the same as that found in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
That which is called "Dharma" is,
in the correct foreign pronunciation, named *dharma*;
it is also named *dharmma*.
This is merely a different transmission of what was originally a single sound.
Here it is translated as "Dharma.
The meanings of "Dharma" vary.
There are two general explanations.
First, "dharma" refers to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
That which is called the three categories of phenomena— wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—
is termed "Dharma" (dharmas). It defines and clarifies the rules for conduct and ritual propriety.
