Because it can serve as a guide for the mind, it is called "Dharma.
Now, regarding the Dharma discussed within the context of the Three Jewels,
that which functions as a rule or standard is termed "Dharma."
Regarding what is called "Saṅgha":
in the original foreign pronunciation it is named *saṃgha*;
in this land, it is translated as "the harmonious assembly."
When one's conduct and virtue do not conflict,
it is called harmony.
Harmony is not a single thing.
These are called the "multitude.
Why are these three types called "treasures"?
In the world, jade and precious stones are what people prize.
These three types are respected by the world like rare worldly treasures;
therefore, they are described as "jewels" (ratna) by way of analogy.
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, it is explained that there are six meanings [of a jewel].
It is likened to a treasure in the sense of being rare;
just as worldly treasures cannot be obtained by those who are impoverished.
The Three Jewels are thus.
Sentient beings of meager merit may not encounter them for thousands of millions of lifetimes;
for this reason, they are called "jewels."
Second is the meaning of being free from defilement:
just as the substance of a genuine worldly jewel is without flaw or impurity,
so it is with the Three Jewels.
Because it is utterly free from all outflows (*āsrava*), it is called a "jewel.
Third is the meaning of power (*bala*).
Just as worldly treasures eliminate poverty, remove poison, and possess great power,
so too are the Three Jewels;
they are endowed with the inconceivable power of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Therefore, they are called "jewels.
Regarding the meaning of the four adornments:
just as worldly precious jewels can adorn the body and head, making the person exceptionally beautiful.
The Three Jewels are thus.
Because they can adorn the practitioner’s pure *dharmakāya*,
they are called "jewels."
The fifth is the sense of being most excellent:
just as a precious gem is superior among all things in the world,
so too are the Three Jewels.
It is the most preeminent among all worlds;
therefore, it is called a "jewel" (ratna).
Sixth is the meaning of being unchanging.
Just as genuine gold cannot be altered by burning, grinding, or polishing,
so it is with the Three Jewels;
they are not changed by the eight worldly concerns.
Therefore, it is called a "jewel.
Such is the meaning of the name; this concludes the two preceding sections.
Next, the essential nature and characteristics are distinguished.
Within this, I shall briefly distinguish it by means of three points:
first, clarifying their distinct characteristics;
second, clarifying their single essence.
Third, the abiding and maintaining [of the Three Jewels].
First, regarding their distinct characteristics:
in the sūtras, they are also called the "staircase Three Jewels."
The Three Jewels differ in their characteristics; therefore, they are called "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
According to the stages of transformation and descent, among the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha is the lowest.
Therefore, it is called a "staircase.
Within this staircase,
the Jewel of the Buddha is first elucidated.
Within the Jewel of the Buddha, there is a fourfold analysis:
first, determining its essential nature; second, distinguishing its characteristics through the classification of its expansion and contraction.
Third, the Buddha’s virtues are elucidated;
fourth, the cultivation and realization are discussed:
what is their essential nature?
The sūtras and śāstras differ;
what they teach varies.
Within the Abhidharma system, it is proclaimed as follows:
Apart from the Tathāgata’s five aggregates (skandhas), there is no separate conventional person;
it is merely upon the aggregates that the name "person" is conventionally applied,
just as a poor and lowly person might be given the name "wealthy and noble."
It is the same in this case:
because there is no person, one does not speak of a conventional person as the Buddha Jewel.
Rather, within the five aggregates, one takes only those aggregates of goodness accomplished through skillful cultivation as the Buddha Jewel.
That which is indeterminate (avyākṛta) is not the Buddha-jewel,
because indeterminate dharmas are not worthy of veneration.
Among the virtues accomplished through cultivation, untainted (anāsrava) merit constitutes the Buddha-jewel.
If it were with outflows (*sāsrava*), it would not be so; for even if there were meritorious qualities associated with outflows, they would not be worthy of veneration.

Therefore, according to that school, the physical forms of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas with their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the virtues of their knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are not the Buddha-jewel.
According to their tradition, they also maintain that the Buddha attains the untainted (anāsrava).
In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), only the conventional person is designated as the Jewel of the Buddha;
the actual qualities of the five aggregates are subsumed under the Jewel of the Dharma within that school.
Therefore, it is not the Buddha-jewel.
Why is that? Because their school asserts only a conventionally designated person (*prajñapti-pudgala*) as the Buddha-dharma;
that school maintains that there exists a person who is a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*).
The essential point for a master to benefit others lies in the provisional;
therefore, he speaks of the provisional person as the Buddha Jewel,
which is subsumed under the category of the Buddha Jewel within the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The provisional person and the real virtues are both entirely the Buddha-treasure;
such is their essential nature. Next, the characteristics are distinguished through the method of opening and closing.
The opening and closing [of the categories] are not fixed;
in total there is only one Buddha,
though sometimes they are divided into two.
The second [category] has two gates:
first, the birth-body and the dharma-body,
which are distinguished and divided into these two types.
The physical form endowed with the marks and signs produced by one's parents is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).
The fivefold merit consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth, which is cultivated through skillful means, is called the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
The second [category], the True and the Responsive, is divided into two or three;
the third has two gates.
First, the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body are distinguished into three types,
as explained in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
Second, the Transformation-body, the Response-body, and the True-body are distinguished into three types.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*,
it may also be divided into four.
These four consist of two gates.
The opening of the one truth and the merging with the response should be discussed in four ways.
What is the meaning of this?
As it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
First, the Buddha of Transformation;
second, the Buddha of Merit;
third, the Buddha of Wisdom.
Regarding the four *tathatā*-buddhas:
among these four, the first is equivalent to the aforementioned *nirmāṇakāya* (response body),
while the middle two are the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body).
The retribution [body] is divided into two types according to its correspondence with merit and wisdom;
the latter is the Dharma-body.
When both the True and the Responsive [bodies] are expanded, they are discussed as four types.
What is the meaning of this?
Within the True [Dharmakāya] there are two,
namely the Dharma-body and the Retribution-body.
The intermediate [birth] likewise has two aspects:
namely, being born from a miraculous manifestation (*upapāduka*) and being born from a royal palace to demonstrate the process of attaining Buddhahood through practice.
This is called the "Responsive Body" (nirmāṇakāya); based upon this responsive body, other emanation Buddhas arise, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni manifested immeasurable Buddhas to receive the offerings and honors presented by the great assemblies."
Alternatively, they may be divided into ten,
as explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
if expanded, they are immeasurable.
These points will be analyzed in detail later in the chapter on the three Buddhas.
Having thus clarified their characteristics,
we shall next explain the Buddha’s virtues.
Although the virtues of a Buddha are manifold, they are essentially of two kinds:
first, the virtue of the practice of enlightenment (bodhicaryā-guṇa);
second, the virtue of the cessation of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-prahāṇa-guṇa).
The practices and virtues differ;
within a single gate, three are taught:
namely, prajñā, liberation, and the dharma-body.
Based on prajñā, liberation arises;
based on liberation, the dharma-body is perfected.
These three are simultaneous.
The distinctions in meaning follow a sequence of priority.
The virtue of cessation in *nirvāṇa* also has three kinds:
first, the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second is the severance of karma;
third is the severance of the retribution of suffering.
One first severs the afflictions.
Because afflictions are severed, the fetters of karma do not arise.
Because karma does not arise, the retribution of suffering does not follow one.
It is by means of the aforementioned prajñā that afflictions are severed.
Because it is endowed with the aforementioned liberation, it is able to bring about detachment from karma;
because it is endowed with the aforementioned dharmakāya, it is able to extinguish suffering.
Such are the virtues of the Buddha.
Next, the cultivation and realization [of the path] are explained. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
it is clarified that the stages of cultivation and realization as taught by Kātyāyanīputra consist briefly of four levels.
First, during the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one cultivates the six impure pāramitās;
one does not yet cultivate the pure [pāramitās] and does not sever the various fetters.
Because they do not cultivate the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),

there are no distinctions among the stages of the noble ones, ranging from the lineage of the habituated (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
This constitutes the second crossing of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Next, for one hundred kalpas, he cultivates the karma for the primary and secondary marks;
even during this time, he has not yet cultivated the untainted [wisdom] to sever all fetters and bonds.
In the third period, during his final existence, he cultivates the eight worldly dhyānas.
By means of the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), one takes the higher realms as an object of focus while feeling aversion toward the lower;
thereby, one eliminates all afflictions (*kleśa*) from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
One cultivates the first dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna*) to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm.
By cultivating the second dhyāna, one abandons the fetters of the first dhyāna;
continuing in this manner up to the cultivation of the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one abandons the fetters of the sphere of nothingness.
Within the single stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no further state above it to be reached.
The conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) is not excluded.
Within the fourth stage, one cultivates the contemplation of the truths (*satya-darśana*),

observing the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths to sever both the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
There are sixteen moments of mind that eliminate the afflictions of the views,
namely the eight patiences and eight knowledges within the path of seeing.
There are eighteen moments of mind that eliminate the afflictions of cultivation.
This refers to the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Taken together, these comprise thirty-four moments of mind.
Among these, the first thirty-three moments of mind are untainted within the causal stage.
That which is not the essence of the Buddha-jewel is the untainted [state] within the thirty-four fruits;
this is the essence of the Buddha-jewel.
Within the Abhidharma school, this meaning is relied upon.
The *Tattvasiddhi* is largely the same as the former, with only slight differences.
As for what is said to be the same:
The practice cultivated in the fourth quarter is similar to the preceding ones. As for what differs:
the eight dhyānas cultivated in the third quarter are only able to suppress the fetters (saṃyojana).
They cannot be permanently severed.
The Noble Path cultivated during the fourth stage contemplates the emptiness of the Truths as a whole,
universally severing both the afflictions of view and the afflictions of cultivation within the three realms.

This differs from the previous school’s position, which holds that the contemplation of the truths is distinct and limited, thereby excluding the cessation of the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Furthermore, according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the severance of fetters occurs through multiple moments of mind,
rather than being restricted solely to thirty-four moments of mind.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are fifteen stages of practice and cultivation.
Briefly stated, they are as follows:
first, cultivating pure faith while in the stage of the ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*) within the realm of fortunate rebirths.
The second is the cultivation of correct understanding within the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*).
The third is the cultivation and arising of various practices within the stage of the lineage of nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*).
The fourth is the training in contemplation as it truly is within the stage of conduct through understanding (*adhimukticaryā*).
For the fifth time, he made the great vows within the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
For the sixth time, he cultivated pure ethical discipline within the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
For the seventh time, he refined pure meditative concentration within the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*).
In the eighth stage, one cultivates the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment within the Ground of Blazing Wisdom;
in the ninth stage, one practices the contemplation of the truths within the Ground Difficult to Conquer;
and in the tenth stage, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination within the Ground of Manifestation.
In the eleventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūramgamā), one cultivates all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In the twelfth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), one cultivates the purification of Buddha-fields.
In the thirteenth stage, the Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī), one cultivates the practice of the wisdom that expounds all teachings.
In the fourteenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one cultivates all supreme practices of wisdom.
Upon reaching the culmination of the tenth and fiftieth stages, one gives rise to the Vajra-like Samādhi, severing even the subtlest obscurations and entering the realm of the Buddha.
It should be understood that within each and every one of these stages, the qualities of practicing the dharmadhātu are fully cultivated.
These have been divided in this manner merely according to their described characteristics.
This concludes the section on the Jewel of the Buddha.
Next, the Dharma Jewel is distinguished.
Within it, there are briefly five distinct categories of meaning.
The first is the teaching (śāsana).
Second, the dharma of principle;
third, the dharma of the aids to the path;
fourth, the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Fifth is the method of transformation through teaching.
As for what is called "teaching," it refers to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
This meaning has been explained in detail within the preceding collection of teachings on the Dharma.
As for what is called the "Dharma of Principle," it is proclaimed within the Abhidharma.
The Four Truths and the sixteen noble practices constitute the Dharma Jewel.
The sixteen noble practices are explained in detail in the chapter on the Four Truths,
as set forth in the *Tattvasiddhi* (The Establishment of Reality).
The names and functions of the Four Noble Truths are conventionally existent as the principle of the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
while the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
There are three distinct meanings discussed in the Mahāyāna.
First, elucidating the principle by means of characteristics;
second, the mutual correspondence between characteristics and reality;
third, speaking solely in terms of reality.
Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one establishes the principles of reasoning by means of those phenomena arising from deluded mental states.

The principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) consists of conditioned existence that is devoid of characteristics; the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) consists of emptiness that is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and without characteristics (*animitta*).
Regarding what is called "discerning characteristics through their true counterparts":
this refers to using the characteristics arising from deluded mental states to discern the principle by contrasting them with the true Tathāgatagarbha.
The dharmas of nature and characteristics have a substantial body and are unconditioned; this is the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The nature, characteristics, realm, and substance of the *tathāgatagarbha* are conditioned; this is the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This meaning is as explained in that *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
To contemplate the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination as having substance but lacking names is the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
To observe the true mind is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As for the statement "to accord with reality":
The dharma-gate of activity within the true *tathāgatagarbha* constitutes the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
while the gate of quiescent extinction constitutes the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Such is the nature of these principles.
The factors that assist the path (bodhipakṣadharma) refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
In the Abhidharma, their explanation contains two meanings.
First, the disintegrating conditions;
second, the non-disintegrating conditions.
As for what are called "disintegrating conditions":
Because it does not distinguish between the different realms of the Three Jewels,
it is called "corrupting conditions.
Within this gateway, all the untainted merits of the three vehicles are entirely the Jewel of the Dharma that aids the path.
Regarding "unbreakable conditions":
the distinct establishment of the spheres of the Three Jewels is called unbreakable conditions.
Within this gateway, one takes only the untainted merits of bodhisattvas and the untainted causes and effects of pratyekabuddhas as the factors that assist the path.
The remaining untainted merits of the śrāvakas are designated as the Saṃgha Jewel,
while the untainted qualities of the Tathāgata are designated as the Buddha Jewel;
therefore, they are not described as factors conducive to the Path.
Question: The aids to the path are subsumed under the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
The truth of the path has already been explained within the preceding section on the principles of the Dharma.
"Why is it necessary to further explain the factors conducive to the path? He replied:
"Within the path, there is both principle and practice."
"Penetration" refers to principle, while "distinction" refers to phenomena.
The numerical classifications of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the categories of ethical discipline, meditative concentration,
and wisdom constitute the path of phenomena.
The principle that the four meanings of the "vehicle of tracks" are broad and pervasive constitutes the path of principle.
That which was elucidated as the Truth of the Path within the preceding section on the Dharma of Principle is this path of principle.
As for the factors conducive to the path discussed here:
Regarding the practice of the Path:
because the practice and the principle differ, this is further clarified as it is proclaimed within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
Since one provisionally takes persons as the Buddha and the Sangha,
all the untainted merits of the three vehicles are auxiliary dharmas;
this is also taught in the Mahāyāna.
All the untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of the three vehicles serve as factors conducive to the path (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Regarding the dharma of nirvāṇa:

according to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), it is taught that the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*)—the place where afflictions, karma, and volition are completely extinguished—is the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Question: The essence of nirvāṇa is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
This has already been explained as "cessation" within the preceding section on the principles of the Dharma.
"Why trouble yourself further by speaking of the Dharma-jewel of Nirvana?
He replied: "Within cessation (nirodha), there is also both principle and phenomena."
Specifically termed "phenomena" (vastu),
it is generally termed "principle" (nyāya).
Its cessation is discussed in terms of the relative magnitude of the categories of afflictions, karma, and so forth, which are to be eliminated.
When cessation involves gradations and inequalities of superiority and inferiority,
it is termed "cessation as a phenomenon" (*vastu-nirodha*).

When it encompasses the four broad and pervasive meanings of exhaustion (*kṣaya*), tranquility (*śānti*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*), it is its "cessation as principle" (*tattva-nirodha*).
The truth of cessation discussed in the preceding section on the Principle (li) is the cessation of principle;
the present Dharma of Nirvana is the cessation of phenomena (shi).
Phenomena and principle are not the same.
Therefore, it must be discussed further.
In the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, nirvāṇa is defined as the state where afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*) have all been exhausted.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, however, there are two types of nirvāṇa.
First, the unconditioned state of cessation through analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Second, the perfect stillness of the myriad virtues of the wholesome conditioned state is the dharma of nirvāṇa.
These are the dharmas employed for transformation.
As it is said in the sutra:
"To practice what is not the path and yet penetrate the Buddha-way— such is the Dharma."
The Dharma Jewel is thus.
Next, the Sangha Jewel is distinguished;
herein there are three sections.
First, the essential nature;
second, the virtues of the Saṃgha;
third, the analysis of its characteristics through opening and closing.
What is its essential nature?
In the Abhidharma system, there are two kinds of Saṃgha:
first, the Saṃgha worthy of offerings (arhat-saṃgha).
From all the Buddhas down to the most lowly ordinary person and novice monk,
everyone is equally the Sangha.
Therefore, when a donor invites individuals according to the order of the Sangha, they receive the merit of making offerings to the Sangha regardless of whether the invitees are high or low.
The second and third refuges— the Sangha—
are restricted solely to the four fruits and four stages of the path among the śrāvakas as the Sangha Jewel;
ordinary bhikṣus possess no virtue worthy of refuge.
For this reason, it is not accepted;
for when a Pratyekabuddha appears in the world, there is no harmonious assembly,
and thus the Saṃgha is not established.
Therefore, it is not discussed;
for within that treatise, the noble Bodhisattva dwells alone without a companion,
and thus does not constitute a Saṃgha.
Therefore it is not mentioned;
for the Buddha is the Buddha Jewel and is not the Sangha.
Therefore it is not discussed.
Furthermore, among the Śrāvakas, only the real dharmas of the five aggregates are taken as the essence of the Saṃgha Jewel;
they do not say that a conventional person constitutes the Saṃgha Jewel,
because in their school there is no separate person apart from the aggregates.
Furthermore, among actual virtues, those that are untainted (anāsrava) constitute the Jewel of the Sangha;
those that are tainted (sāsrava) do not.
This is because tainted virtues cannot be measured.
Within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), the Sangha is also twofold.
The first is the Saṃgha of Worthy Recipients (*arhat-saṃgha*),
which is similar to what was described previously.
Two or three take refuge in the Saṃgha;
the general circumstances are the same as before,
with the sole exception that one takes refuge in the Śrāvakas and not in other assemblies.
Regarding what is called "difference":
among the śrāvakas, those on the four paths and the four fruits are designated by conventional names as the practitioners who constitute the substance of the Saṃgha Jewel;
their actual virtues are not grasped.
Because the merit arising from receiving offerings belongs solely to the conventional person (pudgala),
when discussed according to the Mahāyāna dharma,
the noble assemblies of all three vehicles are all the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Briefly stated, the great differs from the small; here, we take only the Bodhisattvas.
Within this, by means of the category of the Saṃgha, both provisional persons and actual virtues are subsumed as the Saṃgha Jewel.
This is a rough analysis of their essential nature.
Next, the virtues of the Saṃgha are distinguished.
There are two kinds of virtue: first, conduct;
second, realization.
Second, the practices for abandonment.
Although virtues are manifold, they are essentially of only three types:
first, merit (*puṇya*).
The two wisdoms;
thirdly, the pure retribution.
Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience constitute its portion of merit.
The category of prajñā-wisdom;
diligence and meditative concentration are both merit and wisdom.
Relying upon diligence, the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, the four immeasurables, and so forth constitutes their meritorious aspect.
Arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation constitutes the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Cultivating the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) constitutes the aspect of merit (*puṇya*).
Cultivating skillful observations (*upāya-kauśalya-darśana*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) constitutes the aspect of wisdom.
The bodhisattva accomplishes eight kinds of supreme rewards; these are his retributions.
These are fully explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
Such are the virtues of his practice.
The virtue of abandonment is also threefold, namely: the abandonment of afflictions, karma, and suffering.
By means of the aforementioned wisdom, one is able to abandon the afflictions.
By virtue of former merit, one is able to sever all karmic actions;
by virtue of former pure retribution, one is able to be free from all suffering.
Such is the virtue of the Sangha.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished;
therein, the opening and closing, as well as the expansion and abbreviation, are not fixed,
though in total there is only one *saṃgha*.
Alternatively, it may be divided into two.
These two have three gates.
First, the division into two based on their status.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"The first, the 'nominal Saṃgha,' exists prior to the path of vision and has not yet attained the virtues of a Saṃgha."
The "provisional Sangha" refers to those designated by the name "Sangha.
The "true Sangha" consists of those whose stage is at or above the realization of the truths (dṛṣṭasatya).
Those who possess actual virtues within are called the "Sangha of Reality.
Second, there is a division based on the object [of harmony],
which consists of the Sangha of concord in practice (*samvṛti-saṃgha*) and the Sangha of concord in principle (*paramārtha-saṃgha*).
The concord of the Saṃgha through practice according to existence is termed concord through matters;
the concord of the Saṃgha through practice according to principle is termed concord through principle.
Regarding the third, concord through the Dharma, it is divided into two.
These refer to the *karmavācanā* (ritual) Sangha and the Dharma-wheel Sangha.
Regarding the distinctions between their respective dharmas, there are generally three types:
first, the dharma of the monastic community (*pravrajita-saṃgha*).
This refers to the matters of the one hundred and one *karmavācanās*.
When four or more ordained *bhikṣus* collectively uphold this dharma, it is called the Dharma of the Community of the Homeless.
Second is the Dharma of the Practices of the Homeless.
These are known as the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*). They are the practices of those who have gone forth, commonly observed by all who leave the household life.
What are these four?
That is to say, a bhikṣu begs for food as long as he lives,
wears rag-robes from refuse heaps,
and sits beneath a tree.
To take old or discarded medicine when ill—this is the fourth reliance.
Question: [What is this?]
The precepts received by a bhikṣu are likewise the dharma practiced by those who have gone forth;

why then are they not called the "dharma of the practices of one who has gone forth," while only the four reliances (catur-yāni) are specifically termed the "dharma of the practices of one who has gone forth"?
The commentary states:
The precepts constitute the very essence of a bhikṣu;
therefore, they are set aside and not discussed here.
The four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) are the practice of bhikṣus;
therefore, they are explained specifically for them.
The three paths, however, are dharmas common to both the laity and the ordained.
What is called "sitting in meditation and studying the contemplation of emptiness to sever the fetters"—
all such practices shared by both monastics and laypeople are termed "universal dharmas" (*tongfa*).
Among these three categories, the first two are the specific dharmas of the Sangha.
To distinguish the types of *saṃgha* by way of their numerical composition:

within the legal framework for the community of renunciants, when four or more persons are gathered within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the rules, it is designated as a *karmasaṃgha*.

Within that practice of the Dharma for renunciation, those who are universally followed by the ten directions and act in harmony without discord are called the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra-saṃgha).
Some say that the principle of the Four Noble Truths is the Wheel of Dharma.
The understanding of the realization of the truths is the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha.
However, those four truths are the Dharma-wheel traversed by both the laity and the clergy; they are not the Dharma-wheel traversed exclusively by the monastic Saṃgha.
If it is said that the Four Truths are the Wheel of Dharma of the Saṃgha, and that Devadatta, when breaking the Saṃgha, spoke words resembling them,
then one should speak of Five Truths.
For what reason is it proclaimed that there are five perversions?
Since it is taught that the five perversions are "similar" [to the Dharma],
it is clearly understood that the principle of the Four Noble Truths does not constitute the Wheel of the Sangha.
Furthermore, if one were to consider the understanding that accords with the Truths as the Wheel of the Sangha, [it would follow that...]
Among those living at home, the noble ones who have attained the three fruits all realize the principles of the truths and should thus be called the Saṃgha; however,
they are not [considered] the Saṃgha.
Knowing full well that those who do not possess the realization of the Truths are not considered members of the *dharmacakra-saṃgha*,

one may infer from this that one should simply allow them to leave the household life; regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or sages, they should equally observe the Four Reliances without any divergence in their disposition.
All these are called the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-saṃgha*).
Because the wheel of dharma is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is difficult to distinguish between its similarities and differences;
therefore, I shall now analyze this fully by means of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What are the four? First, those who are members of the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha but are not untainted (anāsrava);
that is to say, ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) who have gone forth.
Because they equally follow the four reliances, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

Because they do not yet possess noble virtues, it is not untainted (*anāsrava*). Second, these two [the Sangha of the Noble Ones and the Sangha of Learners] are untainted, but they are not the Wheel of Dharma. The Sangha is [the community].
This refers to noble ones who dwell at home;
because they possess internal noble virtues, they are called "untainted" (anāsrava).
However, because they do not practice the four reliances, it is not the Dharma-wheel.
The third is both the Wheel of Dharma and also untainted (*anāsrava*);
that is, the noble ones who have left the household life are the Wheel of Dharma because they follow the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
Because it possesses noble virtues within, it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
The four non-Dharmic wheels are likewise not untainted;
that is to say, they belong to ordinary householders.
Because it does not practice the four reliances, it is not the Wheel of Dharma;
because it does not possess noble virtues, it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).
By inferring from this, the similarities and differences between the Wheel of Dharma and the untainted state can be understood.
One must not consider only those who are undefiled noble ones (anāsrava-ārya) as the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra-saṃgha).
Thus far, the three gates have divided the Saṃgha into two;
alternatively, it is explained as three.
Within this, there are also three distinct categories.
First, distinguished according to their status, there are three:
first, the status of the nominal Saṃgha, which belongs to those at the stage of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Those who do not yet possess monastic virtue but are provisionally granted the name "monk" are called the "provisional-name monks.
The two types of pure monks belong to the stage of ordinary persons within the mundane realm.
The third, the Saṃgha of the True [Dharma], resides at the stage of the Path of Vision (darśanamārga) and above;
because they internally possess true virtues, they are called the Saṃgha of the True [Dharma].
Second, regarding the Saṃgha of Practice, it is divided into three types.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"The first is 'impurity through breaking the precepts.
Although one maintains the precepts and is careful not to commit transgressions, one dwells together with those who break the precepts during the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the *śīla*."
Second, the deluded monk:
although he personally maintains the precepts, when he sees his own disciples commit transgressions, he causes them to repent and eliminate them;
yet, when he sees others commit transgressions, he remains silent and fails to censure them.
The three kinds of pure monks:
they personally uphold the precepts and, seeing others commit transgressions, are able to instruct them in repentance and purification.
Third, the three [categories of] major and minor divisions.
These are what are called the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
therefore, the sutra says:
"The Sangha refers to the assembly of the three vehicles."
Alternatively, they are divided into four types,
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
first, the "mute sheep" monk.
Ignorant bhikṣus do not distinguish between good and evil, nor between the gravity of transgressions and their observance;
they fail to recognize and repent for the offenses they commit,
remaining like mute sheep until death, without a sound.
These are called "dumb-sheep monks.
Second are "shameless monks," who,
although they know the distinction between good and evil and the gravity of upholding or violating the precepts, lack any sense of shame within.
Therefore, this constitutes a transgression.
Third, the conscientious Sangha recognizes what is wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the gravity of observance and violation, and harbors a sense of shame within.
He is cautious regarding transgressions and does not commit them.
The fourth is the Sangha of the True Realities,
who internally possess noble virtues.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five,
as stated in the Vinaya-vibhāṣā:
"a group of monks."
They are similar to the "mute sheep" among the four types mentioned previously.
The second type, the shameless monks,
is similar to the "shameless" among the four types mentioned previously.
Third, the separate community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha-vibhakta*):
although they personally do not commit offenses, they do not perform the *poṣadha* or recite the precepts together.
Fourth, the pure community of monks (*pariśuddha-saṃgha*).
The fifth resembles the former four in its differences;
the fifth is the *bhūtasamgha* (real community),
which resembles the reality of the former four.
Furthermore, if one were to expand the classification of the Saṃgha, it would be immeasurable;
as stated in the Abhidharma, there are the fourteen noble ones (āryapudgala),
while the *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims twenty-seven noble ones.
The Mahāyāna proclaims forty-one noble stages (*ariya*):
namely, the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*).
These together constitute forty.
Adding the stage of Equal Enlightenment makes forty-one;
if the ten stages of faith are included, there are fifty-one.
These are fully and extensively analyzed later in the chapter on the Worthies and Sages.
The distinction between the Three Jewels as separate entities has been explained in brief.
How are they one essence?
Within this, there are three points of differentiation.
First, regarding the matter itself:
based on the essence of the Buddha, it is divided into three according to its respective meanings.
From the perspective of the meaning of awakening and illumination, it is designated as the Buddha Jewel.
The virtues of that Buddha possess the quality of being a standard for emulation, and are thus called the Jewel of the Dharma;
the exhaustion of all faults of contention is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Although these three meanings are distinct, the essence of their virtues is not different.
Therefore, it is called "one essence.
This single principle is fully present in equal measure within the Abhidharma, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, and the Mahāyāna;
it does not belong exclusively to the Mahāyāna alone.
Second, regarding the Three Jewels from the perspective of the principle of emptiness through the deconstruction of characteristics:
although their specific phenomena differ, their essence is equally empty;
therefore, they are called the "one essence."
It is also called "identical substance.
This meaning exists only in the Mahāyāna;
it is not found in the *Tattvasiddhi* or the *Abhidharma*, because those schools do not teach that the substance of dharmas is empty.
Third, regarding the discussion of oneness in terms of reality:
although the Three Jewels are distinct, none of them fail to take true nature (*dharmatā*) as their essence.
Within this, the elucidation of oneness varies according to the specific dharma.
If one proceeds from *nirvāṇa* to distinguish the Three Jewels, these Three Jewels are, within the single great *nirvāṇa*, termed a "single essence.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"I show that these three things are themselves *nirvāṇa*."
If one distinguishes the Three Jewels by way of their intrinsic nature (*dhātu*),
the Three Jewels are identical with that nature and are thus termed a single essence.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
These three refuges are precisely my own nature.
If one distinguishes the Three Jewels according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
the Three Jewels are truly of one essence.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one can contemplate that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to ultimate truth,
such that my own nature and the Buddha-nature are neither two nor distinct."
If one distinguishes the Three Jewels according to the meaning of permanence,
the Three Jewels are permanent and are thus termed a single essence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
I have never said that there are distinct characteristics among the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha;
I have only taught that they are eternal, constant, unchanging, and without distinction.
If one distinguishes these three from the perspective of the gate of non-duality:
The three are non-dual and are thus called a single essence.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The Buddha is the Dharma."
The Dharma is itself the Sangha.
These Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are equal to space.
All phenomena are likewise so.
This means that within the gateway of the entire dharma-realm, whichever phenomenon one examines, the explanation of its oneness is always thus.
Since this has been established regarding the single essence of the Triple Gem, it applies accordingly to all.
All phenomena are of one essence and category, all of which conform to this pattern.
This single principle is restricted to the Mahāyāna;
it does not exist within the Hīnayāna.
The distinction between the three jewels as one entity is thus briefly explained.
What is meant by "sustaining" them?
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, clay shrines and wooden images constitute the sustaining Buddha.
Cotton, silk, bamboo, and silk are the dharma for maintaining [the teachings];
ordinary bhikṣus are the saṃgha for maintaining [the community].
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are two types of maintenance.
First, abiding through transformative function;
second, abiding through actual virtue.
Regarding "transformative function":
The great compassionate activity of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Their manifestation through the eight stages of enlightenment constitutes the Buddha as the Sustainer;
the dissemination of all verbal teachings spoken according to the needs of those to be converted for the benefit of the world constitutes the Dharma as the Sustainer.
In accordance with the Dharma, they transform and bring forth the multitudes of the three vehicles as the Sangha of maintenance.
Furthermore, although all Buddhas have attained nirvana, they ultimately never abandon the practices of a bodhisattva.
They are constantly able to manifest as bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth;
this is also called the "monastic community that sustains" (sthiti-dhāraka-saṃgha).
Such is the function of their transformative power.
What are the actual virtues?
The eternal abiding of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constitutes the Buddha as the sustainer;
the permanence of the dharmatā constitutes the Dharma as the sustainer.
The Sangha of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, whose practice is never extinguished, constitutes the Sangha of Sustenance.
This brief explanation of the three jewels as the Sangha of Sustenance concludes these two sections.
Next, the meaning of the sequence of the three jewels will be clarified.
The sequence differs,
and briefly there are three meanings:
first, the sequence of arising and transformation.
First the Jewel of the Buddha is clarified,
followed by the Dharma and then the Sangha;
for the Buddha is the fundamental basis of transformation.
Therefore, the Buddha is clarified first;
since it is from the Buddha that the teaching arises,
the Dharma is clarified next.
Because they are transformed according to the Dharma into the various assemblies of the Three Vehicles,
the Sangha is explained last. Second,
this is the sequence of the order of transformative benefit.
Furthermore, one first clarifies the Buddha, then the Dharma, and finally the Sangha.
First, the Jewel of the Buddha is clarified to inspire faith in sentient beings;
next, the Jewel of the Dharma is clarified to transform sentient beings and engender understanding.
Next, the Jewel of the Sangha is elucidated.
This is because people engage in practices of transformation so that they may make offerings and cultivate meritorious deeds;
furthermore, it is because one desires to cause people to learn and practice these deeds.
Third, the sequence of accomplishment through cultivation:
either the Dharma is clarified first, followed by the Saṃgha and then the Buddha;
or the Saṃgha is clarified first, followed by the Dharma and then the Buddha.
Within this, since the Jewel of the Dharma is first elucidated by taking its practice and conduct as the Dharma—
because the practices and virtues of the Jewel of the Saṃgha arise based upon that Dharma—
the Jewel of the Saṃgha is elucidated next.
Because when a monk’s practice is perfected, he immediately attains Buddhahood,
the Buddha is explained last.
However, if one takes the principle-nature (*li-xing*) as the Dharma Jewel, then the Sangha is explained first.
Because when the practice of the Sangha is perfected, one realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Next, the Dharma is explained;
because when the realization of the Dharma is brought to ultimate fulfillment, one attains Buddhahood.
The subsequent section clarifies the Buddha as the object of refuge. Thus concludes the general explanation;
within the third gate, the subject of refuge is explained in detail.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the characteristics of taking refuge;
second, distinguishing the intent of taking refuge.
There are three types of refuge. First is the refuge of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Taking refuge with a devoted mind within the external Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is called the refuge of distinct characteristics.
Second is taking refuge in one's own excellence (*svaguṇa-śaraṇa*):
this refers to generating a mind that takes refuge in and turns toward the qualities of the Three Jewels within oneself in the future.
Third is taking refuge in one's own reality (*svabhāva-śaraṇa*).
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the Three Refuges is one's own inherent reality.
To abandon those external, divergent pursuits and take refuge in the true nature of the Three Jewels as one's own inherent reality is called "refuge in one's own inherent reality."
The characteristics of taking refuge are thus concluded in this first section.
Next, the intent of taking refuge is distinguished;
there are three purposes for taking refuge in the distinct [refuges].
First, it is for the sake of renunciation;
that is, for the sake of renouncing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and evil, unwholesome states.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
All sentient beings, out of fear of the evil hunter of birth and death, seek the three refuges.
Śrīmālādevī also said:
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas rely upon the Tathāgata because of their fear."
Second, one takes refuge for the sake of attainment;
that is, for the sake of attaining pleasant fruits and wholesome dharmas.
Third, one takes refuge for the sake of benefit.
Because one relies upon the Three Jewels for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
there are likewise three aspects to the refuge of one's own virtues.
First, taking refuge for the purpose of separation.
First, it is for the sake of becoming free from the evil and unwholesome states of birth and death;
second, it is for the sake of attaining [them] by taking refuge;
and third, it is for the sake of attaining the supramundane path to nirvāṇa.
Third, they take refuge for the sake of benefit:
that is, seeking the benefit of future fruits and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, the actual objects of refuge are also threefold.
First, one takes refuge for the sake of detachment;
that is, for the sake of detaching from the phenomena of delusive conceptualization and falsehood.
Second, one takes refuge for the sake of attainment.
First, it is for the sake of realizing the dharma of suchness as it truly is;
second, it is for the sake of benefiting others by returning [to them];
and third, it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings by realizing one's own true reality.
The meaning of the Three Refuges is roughly as explained above.

100. The Meaning of the Three Trainings (10): A Fivefold Analysis of the Meaning of the Three Trainings. First, the explanation of the names; second, the discernment of their characteristics; third, the analysis according to stages; fourth, the inclusion of characteristics; fifth, the application of antidotes. First, the explanation of the names.
Regarding the three trainings:
first, the training in higher ethical discipline;
second, the training in higher concentration.
It is also called the increase of intention (*cetanā*) and the increase of mind (*citta*).
Third is the increase of wisdom (*prajñā*).
That which restrains and prohibits is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Clarity and stillness are called *samādhi*.
Because the spirit is stilled within through *samādhi*, it is further termed "mind" (*manas*) and also termed "heart" (*citta*).
Penetrating observation is designated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Among these three, the practice of progress is called "training" (śikṣā).
The advancement of training is termed "increase.
Such is the meaning of the terms.
Question: What is the essential nature (svabhāva) of this training?
Explanation: [As follows:]
One is able to learn by taking the mind as the essence.
If one discusses the practice being learned, it takes the three practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom as its essence. Question:
Do the three trainings apply exclusively to the cause,
or do they also extend to the fruit?
The explanation states:
The mind of training is restricted exclusively to the cause;
when the qualities of the fruit are fully perfected, the mind of training ceases.
Therefore, it is described in the sūtras as "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
If one discusses what is studied as pertaining to both cause and fruit,
a question is raised:
Why is it called "beyond-learning" (*aśaikṣa*) within the state of the fruit?
How does the practice of training result in the attainment of the fruit?
It is explained that within the fruit, the factors such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom are accomplished through training.
This concludes the exposition of this single gateway, which is also called "Training.
Next, its characteristics will be distinguished. There are three aspects of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
First, the precept of restraint;
second, the precept of gathering wholesome qualities;
third, the precept of gathering sentient beings.
This meaning is analyzed in detail later in the section on the three clusters of precepts (*śīla-skandha*).
The training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is also threefold: first, that which is with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*).
This refers to the meditative concentrations from the desire realm up to the first dhyāna. Question:
How can there be meditative concentration in the desire realm?
The commentary states:
The Abhidharma does not teach that meditative concentration exists,
whereas the Mahāyāna *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims that it does.
The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims that the lightning-like samādhi (*vidyut-sama-samādhi*) constitutes the meditative concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Nāgārjuna, however, proclaims that the meditative concentrations of the desire realm are those in which the Buddha dwells eternally;
they are not merely like a flash of lightning that appears for a moment.
Second is that which is without vitarka (applied thought) but with vicāra (sustained thought),

namely the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). It is called "intermediate" because it exists above the first dhyāna and below the concentration of the second dhyāna, having removed both vitarka and vicāra.
The third category consists of those states without vitarka and without vicāra,
namely from the third dhyāna upwards through to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This meaning will be fully and extensively analyzed later in the chapter on the eight dhyānas.
The training in wisdom is threefold:
namely, that consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed in the subsequent chapter on the three types of wisdom; thus, these two sections are concluded.
Next is the discussion on the stages.
The practice of the three trainings pervades the beginning and the end;
yet, according to the specific stages, there are indeed distinctions in their true manifestation.
What are these distinct characteristics?
Within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there are two distinct meanings.
The first is the analytical exposition of the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-citta*).
The general and specific foundations of mindfulness have not yet attained the water of concentration;
by cultivating the category of ethical discipline,
one attains the four mental states beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), which have already attained the water of concentration.
One cultivates the category of meditative concentration;
having realized the truths, one subsequently cultivates the category of wisdom.
According to the second interpretation, one gradually trains in ethical conduct starting from the stage of the inner ordinary person (ābhyantarapṛthagjana).
Upon reaching the stage of the first fruit, one achieves perfection in ethical conduct (*śīla*),
because one has attained the noble precepts that are indestructible. Thereafter,
in the practice of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), one gradually trains in the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Upon reaching the fruit of anāgāmin, one achieves the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As an anāgāmin, one gradually studies the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).
Upon the ultimate attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), one achieves the practice of wisdom.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are likewise two meanings.

One meaning is that the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin cultivates the category of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) through the practice of pure conduct; the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta cultivates the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) through the stages of lineage and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
From the first bhūmi upward, one practices together with the category of wisdom.
Regarding the second meaning: beginning from the mundane level, one gradually studies ethical conduct until it is perfected upon reaching the Stainless Bhūmi (vimalā-bhūmi).
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu*, the Vimalā-bhūmi is designated as the stage of superior morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
During the preparatory practices of the third bhūmi, one gradually trains in the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
Upon abiding in the third bhūmi, the practice of concentration is perfected.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* proclaims that the three stages constitute the dwelling in superior intention (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*);
the *Saṃdhinirmocana* describes them as the purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śuddhi*);
and from the fourth stage upward, one gradually trains in the category of wisdom (*prajñā-pakṣa*).
Upon reaching the tenth stage, the practice of wisdom is perfected;
therefore, in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, it is taught that the four stages are considered the purification of wisdom.
Such is the division of the stages. This concludes the three gates.
Next, the characteristics of inclusion are distinguished; therein are four parts.
First, [the inclusion] is established by correlating [these factors] with the fivefold dharmakāya as their common characteristic.
Second, the mutual inclusion of the six pāramitās;
third, the mutual inclusion in relation to the seven purifications;
fourth, the mutual inclusion in relation to the eightfold noble path.
The five aggregates of the body are as follows:

namely, the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; these are the five.
Among these five aggregates, the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha) is morality;
the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-skandha) is concentration;
and knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) constitute the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā).
Regarding the different treatises on the nature of liberation,
according to those who maintain that it is a substantial entity, liberation is the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*),
because in their school the essential nature of liberation is wisdom.
According to the Abhidharma, this is a factor of liberation (vimukti-skandha) and is not of the nature of wisdom (prajñā);
it is not included within the three trainings (tri-śikṣā).
In terms of their mutual inclusion within the categories of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*),
they are largely accompanied by and follow after these two.
Next, they are mutually subsumed according to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the first four perfections constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
Thus, that treatise states:
"The requisites, the essential nature, the retinue, and the inexhaustibility—these are the training in ethical discipline."
Generosity serves as the cause for ethical discipline;
therefore, it is called an "accessory.
The perfection of ethical discipline is the very essence of the training in ethical discipline.
Therefore, it is called the essential nature (svabhāva).
Patience and conduct that assist morality are called its retinue (parivāra).
Because of diligence, one maintains the precepts without interruption;
therefore, it is called inexhaustible.
Dhyāna is the training in concentration (samādhi-śikṣā).
Prajñā is the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā). Question:
Diligence governs all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Why, then, is it specifically subsumed within ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
To explain:
In truth, they are all-pervasive; however, for now, they are specifically subsumed under the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) based on three reasons.
First, the training in ethical discipline comes first.
Therefore, within the inclusion of the precepts,
two of the three trainings in morality encompass the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*),
because extensive and manifold practices are accomplished through diligence.
It is included within the precepts.
Why is it extensive?
Because the precepts fully contain the three clusters of dharmas.
Furthermore, because it fully encompasses generosity, ethical discipline,
and patience; third, because practicing with a distracted mind through the training in ethical discipline does not accord with the Dharma,
making accomplishment difficult and failure easy.
It must be established through diligent assistance; therefore,
within the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*),
one follows the first three precepts according to the *Saṃgīti-sūtra*.
Dhyāna is the training in concentration;
Prajñā is the training in wisdom;
and the practice of diligence serves as the general support for all three trainings.
Question: For what reason is the factor of wisdom more numerous within the five aggregates than the aggregate of form,
and why are the factors of ethical discipline more numerous among the six perfections than the perfection of giving?
The commentary states:
The various formations (saṃskāra) differ in their opening and closing,
each according to a particular meaning.
At times, precepts are relaxed,
as in the case of the Six Perfections and so forth;
or again, meditative concentration is relaxed.
One should understand that there are principles not yet seen,
or else one should open up wisdom,
such as the five aggregates of dharma, the seven purities, and so forth.
At times they are both opened, as in the case of the Eightfold Noble Path;
at other times they are both closed, as in the case of the Three Trainings.
Thus, the dharma-gates differ.
It would be better to categorize them into a single group by subsuming them within the seven purifications (sattavidha-visuddhi).
What are these seven purifications?
First, purity of ethical discipline;
second, purity of concentration;
third, purity of view.
Fourth is purity regarding doubt;
fifth is purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path;
sixth is purity regarding practice.
The purification through knowledge of the abandonment of the seven [types of] conduct. This meaning is fully and extensively analyzed in the subsequent chapter on the Seven Purifications.
Among these seven, the first is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
The second is the training in concentration;
the latter five are the training in wisdom.
Next, these are subsumed under the common characteristics of the Eightfold Noble Path.
As for the "Eightfold Path," it consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right concentration, right thought, right view, and right effort.
Among these eight, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*);
right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*);
and right thought and right view constitute the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
The single factor of diligence serves as a comprehensive strategy for the three trainings.
Question: Within the training of ethical discipline (*śīla*), what is the distinction between right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*)?
The term "right" (*samyak*) has three meanings.
First, verbal action arising from the absence of hatred and delusion is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
Bodily action arising from the absence of hatred and delusion is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
The two types of action, bodily and vocal, arising from freedom from greed are called right livelihood.
According to the second interpretation,
the vocal action arising from freedom from greed, hatred, and delusion is called right speech.
Bodily action that is free from greed, hatred, and delusion is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Freedom from the four types of wrong livelihood is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). As for what are called the "four wrong [livelihoods]":
As Nāgārjuna said:
first is eating with the mouth,
namely, cultivation.
1. Compounding decoctions and medicinal drugs, or engaging in agriculture and trade to sustain one's life;
2. Sustaining oneself by gleaning food from the fields (āyuktabhaktika).
This refers to seeking a livelihood by means of divining the signs of the sun, moon, and constellations, performing rituals for the veneration of deities,
and engaging in the "three ways of verbal sustenance":
namely, flattery toward those of power and high status, acting as a messenger to facilitate connections, and seeking profit through clever speech to sustain one's life.
The fourth is "subsisting through the mouth.
This refers to supporting oneself by practicing various incantations, divining good and bad fortune, and performing various arts and crafts.
To be free from such activities is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
The third meaning is as Nāgārjuna has said:
to be free from the four verbal transgressions by means of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) is called right speech (samyag-vāc).
To abandon the three evils of the body by means of this noble wisdom is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
To abandon the five wrong modes of livelihood is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). As for what are called the "five wrong [modes of livelihood]":
First, for the sake of gain and support, they falsely manifest the appearance of being someone extraordinary and unique;
second, they speak of their own merits;
and third, they practice divination of signs and fortune to proclaim them to others.
Fourth, they raise their voices to manifest an air of majesty, causing others to feel awe and respect so as to secure their own profit.
Fifth, they speak of the gains and offerings they themselves have received in order to stir the hearts of others.
Among these five, the first is wrong bodily action,
and the latter four are wrong verbal action.
To be free from these five forms of wrong livelihood is called right livelihood.
Question: What is the difference between right mindfulness and right concentration within meditative absorption?
Explanation:
These two differ from beginning to end.
Seeking the skillful means for concentration and maintaining the mind upon its object is called right mindfulness;
when it ultimately achieves immovability, it is termed right concentration.
He asked again:
"What is the difference between right reflection and right view within wisdom? He replied:
This also differs in its beginning and end:
the initial mind of discrimination is called right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*),
while its final completion and thorough realization is termed right view (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*).
The summary of characteristics is thus; this concludes the four gates.
Next, the remedies are distinguished.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, regarding the cultivation of the antidotes by way of karma, afflictions, and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
ethical discipline (*śīla*) prevents non-virtuous karma;
meditative concentration (*samādhi*) eliminates the arising of delusions; and wisdom (*prajñā*) severs the underlying tendencies.
Second, the treatment [of the hindrances] is distinguished by pairing them with the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
The two hindrances of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) can give rise to evil karma and obstruct the category of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*).
Precepts can remedy it;
agitation and remorse obstruct concentration,
and concentration can remedy them.
Excitement and sleep obstruct wisdom;
wisdom is able to remedy them.
Doubt, conversely, obstructs all three categories.
The three trainings serve as remedies.
Three [trainings] are paired with six vices to distinguish their respective antidotes.
Stinginess, greed, breaking the precepts, anger, and laziness are able to obstruct ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Precepts can remedy this;
distracted thoughts obstruct concentration,
and concentration can remedy them.
Ignorance obstructs wisdom;
wisdom is able to remedy it.
This is a brief exposition on the meaning of the three trainings.

101. The Meaning of the Threefold Aggregate of Precepts (10): A Seven-Gate Analysis and Explanation of the Names of the Threefold Aggregate of Precepts. I. Explaining the Substance; II. Distinguishing the Characteristics; III. Establishing the Formulations; IV. Differences between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; V. Distinctions between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; VI. The General and the Particular. First: Explaining the Names.

The three clusters of precepts (tri-saṃvara-śīla) refer to the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla).
Regarding the morality of restraint:
It is also called the "precept of detachment" and the "precept of right reception.
Regarding the term "restraint" (*saṃvara*):
the method that restrains evil is called "restraint" (*vinaya*).
Because its practice relies upon the precepts of the Vinaya,
it is termed "Vinaya-restraint" (*vinaya-saṃvara*). Furthermore,
internal self-discipline is also called "Vinaya," while external conformity to truth is designated as "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
Restraint through prevention is called *śīla*.
Since this very discipline (*saṃvara*) involves abstaining from the faults of killing and so forth,
it is therefore called the "precept of abstention" (*virati-śīla*).
This is precisely the practice of being separated from what is loved;
therefore, it is also called "rightly receiving the precepts. Regarding the "precept for gathering wholesome qualities," that which accords with and benefits [the path] is termed "wholesome."
It is called "gathering" (saṃgraha) because it involves the commitment to undertake virtue;
being free from the fault of non-gathering, it is termed the "precept of gathering virtue.
As for the "precept of gathering sentient beings":
In the treatise, this is also called the "precept of gathering sentient beings.
The multitude of births and deaths is termed "sentient beings" (sattva).
Because one makes a formal vow to gather and transform them, it is called "gathering" (saṃgraha).
The precept of gathering sentient beings is so called because it avoids the fault of non-inclusion;
it benefits others through the Path,
and for this reason, it is also termed the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
Because these three are accumulations, they are called the "three aggregates" (triskandha).
Such is the meaning of the term.
In the second section, their essential nature is analyzed.
Among these, there are five [distinctions]:
first, the distinction between undertaking and maintaining;
second, the distinction between manifest action and non-manifest action.
Third, the distinction between cessation and activity;
fourth, the distinction between the two practices of self-benefit and benefiting others;
fifth, the distinction between the three aggregates of form, mind, and so forth.
Regarding the term "upholding" (dhāraṇā):
although the precepts and practices are numerous, they are essentially comprised within upholding.
The initial mind that receives the Dharma is termed "receiving" (samādāna).
Guarding in accordance with the Dharma is explained as "upholding" (dhāraṇa).
Receiving, however, is the Abhidharma;
it is accomplished through formal commitment.
When maintained, it confronts conditions;
through protection, it is perfected.
This "reception" (vedanā) and "maintenance" (dhāraṇā) are distinguished by their respective types.
When expanded, it consists of four types.
Regarding these four, there are two within "receiving":
first, receiving correctly from another; [the second is receiving by oneself].
Second, receiving with a well-purified mind.
Within this, there are also two aspects:
first, guarding and maintaining it with single-minded diligence.
Second, being able to repent after having committed an offense.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains these four virtues as the nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*). This concludes the first section.
Next, there is a distinction between the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
First, "manifest" (*vijñapti*) and "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) are explained with respect to the practice of undertaking;
subsequently, they are explained with respect to the practice of maintaining.
What is the practice of undertaking?
Regarding the performance within the category of "receiving" (prāpti), there are generally two types:
first, performance within the cause,
which refers to the preparatory means for seeking the precepts.
This refers to such acts as prostrating before a teacher and requesting the precepts.
Regarding the second fruit,
it consists of the final momentary duration of bodily and other actions that are associated with the Dharma.
The "action" within the cause is the cause of the *kriyā-śīla* (precept of action), not the essence of the *kriyā-śīla*.
The "action" within the result is the essence of the *kriyā-śīla*.
Such is the nature of the *kriyā-śīla*.
Next, the non-informative (avijñapti) is analyzed.
According to the Abhidharma,
the non-informative in this text consists briefly of three parts.
First, non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) at the time of the cause:
this means that within the preceding cause, when there is a manifestation of wholesome action, non-manifestation arises concomitantly.
Second, non-manifestation at the time of the fruit.
This means that at the very last moment of that [action], there arises a non-informative action (avijñapti) concomitant with the informative action (vijñapti) on the side of virtue;
herein, two kinds of non-informative action arise simultaneously together.
The first refers to non-manifest action (avijñapti) that arises simultaneously with manifest action (vijñapti). The second refers to non-manifest action arising from a formal commitment.
That which is called "arising simultaneously with manifest action" (karmasaha-jāta) is so named because wholesome non-manifest action arises in accordance with that manifest action.
Because the arising of an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) based on a prior commitment is called a "vow" (*samādāna*). Question:
These two [the vow and the unmanifest action] exist simultaneously.
Why is it that one alone is specifically designated as "arising together with action" (*kṛta-sahaja*)?
The explanation states:
"Arising together with action" refers to that which arises directly from action itself.

Therefore, it is called "concomitant with action" (*kriyā-sahabhū*). However, because the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arises through the power of the prior commitment made during the preliminary effort (*pūrvaprayoga*),
for this reason it is not called "concomitant with action."
This is the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) at the time of the second fruit.
Regarding the non-informative [action] after the three fruits:
it is called "after the fruit" because the non-informative [action] continues to arise following the informative action (vijñapti).
Among these three periods,
during the causal period there is no action, and it is categorically not the non-informative (avijñapti) essence of the precept.
During the resultant period and the subsequent period, it may or may not exist.
If performed simultaneously, it is not [an undertaking]; if there is a formal commitment, it is indeed so.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, it likewise consists of three parts.
First, the time of the cause;
second, the time of the fruit;
third, the time after the fruit.
At the time of the cause, the result is similar to what precedes it;
at the time of the result, there is no activity, and the great comparison remains the same as before.
As for that which is said to be different:
In the Abhidharma system, both the "simultaneous with action" (*kriyā-sahabhū*) and the "having made a commitment" (*samādāna*) arise together.
In this school [the Sautrāntika], at the time of the fruit, there is only that which is "simultaneous with action," while the "having made a commitment" does not yet exist.
Because it does not yet exist, it is designated solely as "simultaneous with action."
How is this known? As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, that treatise asks:
Regarding what should be called "unmanifest" (avijñapti),
the treatise itself explains:
that which occurs at the moment of the second thought-moment is named unmanifest.
That which is called "vocal action" (*vijñapti*) constitutes the first moment;
therefore, "non-vocal action" (*avijñapti*) is designated as the second moment.
During these three periods—the causal period and the resultant period—it is exclusively not the case that the substance of non-vocal action exists.
The non-manifesting (avijñapti) vow that is subsequently generated after the fruit is the non-manifesting precept (*avijñapti-śīla*).
Within the Mahāyāna precepts, there are likewise three parts:
the first is the causal stage.
The second is the time of fruition;
the third is after fruition.
The causes and that which follows fruition are the same as those in the Hīnayāna.
At the time of fruition, there is no fixed determination regarding the composition [of the treatise];
it may accord with the *Abhidharma* or it may accord with the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Among these three periods,
during the causal period there is neither the non-active nor the non-non-active precept;
during the resultant period, it is indeterminate.
If it is said that at the time of the fruition there exists only the active [karma] and not the non-active precept, then [the position is maintained];
however, if it is said that both types arise simultaneously at the time of the fruition, then one must separately take the formal undertaking as the non-active precept.
If it were simultaneous with the action, it would not be [the result]; the same applies after the result has arisen. If it were simultaneous with the action, it would not be [the result].
The formal commitment is thus;
the reception of the precepts is likewise.
Next, regarding the observance of the precepts, there are the manifest and the unmanifest actions.
There are four exegeses regarding its meaning.
First, the distinction between manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is clarified by way of activity:
guarding against conditions is termed "manifest observance" (*vijñapti-dhāraṇa*).
Based on performance, there is non-performance (avijñapti); when wholesome [non-performance] arises, it is called "possession through non-performance" (avijñapti-samvara).
Second, according to the distinction between the beginning and end of practice and cultivation:
the initial mental application (*manasikāra*) of guarding the precepts of training is called "possession through performance" (vijñapti-samvara).
When the cultivation of the mind has reached maturity, one spontaneously transcends faults without relying on deliberate mental effort; this is called "effortless retention" (anābhoga-dhāraṇī),
like a wheel turning by means of a staff.
That which is associated with a staff is called "active transformation" (kriyā-vartana).
That which moves spontaneously when the staff is removed is called "non-active transformation" (akriyā-vartana).
This case is also like that.
Third, regarding the stages of practice, there are the categories of manifest and non-manifest [observance].
All ordinary persons whose cultivation of the precepts is not yet perfected are collectively termed "observers of manifest observance" (zuochi).
The accomplishment of the ethical conduct of all noble ones and sages is called "unconditioned upholding" (anabhisaṃskāra-dhāraṇa).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"One who is not complete in ethical discipline..."
