Within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, those who abide in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) can give rise to these precepts in both male and female bodies;
they can be accomplished within all physical forms.
Since the sūtras and śāstras never state that those with dual sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) and the like lose this precept,
those in the higher realms who are neither male nor female bodies are unable to produce or accomplish it.
A Bodhisattva is born and fully realized within all forms;
such are the distinctions among these forms. This concludes the six gates.
Next, we shall discuss this in terms of persons.
People are either heterodox or orthodox;
those outside the Way are called heterodox, while those within the Way are called orthodox.
According to the Abhidharma, the Pratimokṣa precepts are received by the disciples of the Buddha.
It is not attained by non-Buddhists.
Within the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is also attained by non-Buddhists;
therefore, that treatise states: "Non-Buddhists also, with a profound mind, abandon evil."
Therefore, one receives the precepts through formal undertaking.
As for the dhyāna restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), it is obtained both internally and externally,
because even non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cultivate the eight dhyāna concentrations.
The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) is obtained only by the disciples of the Buddha and not by non-Buddhists, because they abide in wrong views and lack the Eightfold Noble Path.
Such is the distinction between persons; this concludes the seven gates.
Next, the meaning of acquisition, relinquishment, and accomplishment will be discussed.
First, their acquisition will be examined;
next, their relinquishment will be clarified.
The subsequent section explains accomplishment (*siddhi*). As for what is called "attainment" (*prāpti*):
that which did not previously exist but now arises is termed "attainment."
The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained solely through formal undertaking and has no other meaning;
the distinctions within its undertaking are analyzed in detail within the section on the three clusters (triskandhaka).
As for the dhyāna restraint:
According to the Abhidharma, there are two kinds of attainment (*prāpti*):
first, the attainment through abandonment (*prahāṇa-prāpti*). When one abandons lower faults, one attains the dhyāna-precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*) of the higher stages.
The second is that obtained by birth (*upapatti-labdha*):
when one falls from a higher stage and has not yet been born into a lower stage, one obtains the lower dhyāna-precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, there is only that which is obtained through abandonment (*prahāṇa-labdha*).
It does not say that it is acquired by birth.
That [text] states that when one is born in a higher realm, it is not said to be acquired by birth;
for it says that when one is born in a higher realm, one does not lose what was acquired in the lower realm.
When one falls back and is born [into a lower realm], it is not called "newly acquired.
Regarding the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), according to the Abhidharma, there are three kinds of acquisition:
first, acquisition through abandonment (*prahāṇa-lābha*).
One obtains the precepts of the noble path (*āryamārga-śīla*) by severing the lower [fetters] at the appropriate time;

secondly, one obtains them through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), because at the moment of the transformation of the faculties, one relinquishes the precepts of dull faculties and acquires the precepts of sharp faculties.
Third is "regaining after falling back":
when one realizes the fruit of sainthood, one relinquishes that untainted precept from the causal stage;
later, when one falls back from that fruit, one regains the original precept.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is held that in the Mahāyāna there is only the attainment of abandonment, while other matters are not discussed.

That treatise states that when one transforms the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) or attains a fruit, the previously existing dharmas become more manifest; it is not that one abandons the former dharmas, for there is no separate attainment [of them].
The characteristics of acquisition are thus.
Next, the meaning of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*) is discussed.
That which previously existed but is now lost is termed "relinquishment."
Within the Dharma of the Hīnayāna, there are four ways in which the prātimokṣa precepts are relinquished:
first, relinquishment through not employing the path;
second, relinquishment at the end of life.
Third, abandonment through the severance of the roots of goodness;
fourth, abandonment through the arising of both sexual organs,
meaning that when both male and female sexual organs arise, one loses the vows of discipline (*śīla*).
Some people proclaim that by committing the first category of offenses, one also loses the restraint of the precepts; this is not so.
This merely defiles the precepts;
it is not called "abandoning" them.
All the sūtras and śāstras agree with this explanation.
There are two ways in which the bodhisattva vow may be relinquished,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
first, the regression from the bodhicitta.

Second, there is the offense of a *pārājika* due to predominant afflictions (*kleśa*), the reasons for which differ from [the previous case]; these are fully and extensively analyzed in the chapter on the three clusters (*triskandhaka*).
Regarding the precepts of the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara-śīla*), there are two ways of relinquishing them.
First is abandonment through regression:
when one regresses from a higher dhyāna or precept by giving rise to a lower fault.
Second is abandonment at the time of being born into a higher realm.
Because when one with outflows is born into a higher realm, one loses what belongs to the lower;
thus, according to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, there is only the loss through retrogression (*parihāṇi*). They state:
Because one who is born into a higher realm does not lose the lower ones, it is called the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
In the Abhidharma system, there are three kinds of relinquishment:
first, relinquishment through falling back (*parihāṇi-parityāga*).
When one falls back from the Noble Path, one loses the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Second, there is abandonment through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*); at the time of transforming the faculties, one abandons the precepts associated with dull faculties.

Third is abandonment through the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*). At the time of attaining a noble fruit (*ārya-phala*), one abandons that untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*) belonging to the causal stage.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, all three types of abandonment are entirely absent.
It is abandoned only at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, that which is associated with both the object and its antidote is abandoned at the time of realizing the truth;
that which is associated with true realization is ultimately never abandoned.
The three types of discipline have been distinguished in this brief manner.

103. The Meaning of *Śamatha*, *Vipaśyanā*, and *Upekṣā* (10). The Meaning of *Śamatha*, *Vipaśyanā*, and *Upekṣā*: An Exposition through Eightfold Analysis. I. Definition of Terms; II. Distinguishing Characteristics; III. Establishment; IV. Successive Order of Cultivation; V. Analysis According to Objects; VI. Analysis According to Stages; VII. Analysis According to Persons. First, the Definition of Terms.
Regarding "calm abiding, insight,
and equanimity," these are also termed "concentration, wisdom,
and relinquishment" in the sūtras; this represents the distinctions within cultivation.
The meanings of "cultivation" differ;
one gate explains three [aspects].
As for *śamatha*, it is called *śamatha* in foreign lands.
This translation is called "stopping" (śamatha).
Because one guards the mind, abides in its object, and remains free from distraction and agitation,
it is termed "stopping."
Because the mind is stilled and not distracted, it is further called "concentration" (samādhi).
As for "contemplation" (vipaśyanā)— the foreign term for which is *vipaśyanā*—
this is translated here as "contemplation."
Investigating and discerning phenomena is called *vipaśyanā* (contemplation).
The penetration of contemplation is termed *prajñā* (wisdom).
As for "equanimity" (*upekṣā*), it is called *u-pi-xia* (憂畢叉) in foreign lands.
This is translated as "equanimity" (upekṣā).
Because the mind practices impartiality and abandons biased habits, it is called equanimity. This concludes this section.
Next, the essential nature is distinguished.
According to the interpretation based solely on the Abhidharma doctrine, there are two [positions].
The first is discussed in terms of mental factors that arise simultaneously with the mind.
Calm abiding (śamatha) takes the aggregate of concentration as its essence;
insight (vipaśyanā) takes either the aggregate of discernment or the aggregate of wisdom as its essence.
The contemplation that investigates and seeks has the mental factor of *vitarka* (applied thought) as its essence;
the contemplation that illuminates phenomena has the mental factor of *prajñā* (wisdom) as its essence;
and equanimity (*upekṣā*) has, alternatively, the mental factor of *upekṣā* itself as its essence.
Alternatively, it takes the two—concentration and wisdom—as its essence.
The equanimity that abandons faults takes the abandonment of counting as its essence;
through the equality of concentration and wisdom, it relinquishes partiality and habitual tendencies.
It is named "equanimity" (upekṣā).
It takes that very same concentration and wisdom as its essence.
Second, it is distinguished according to the meaning of its cultivation in the preceding and succeeding stages.
Calm abiding (*śamatha*) takes the correct practice of concentration as its essence,
with concentration being the primary factor.
All minds and mental factors that abide in mutual conformity with their objects are collectively termed calm abiding.
Those who practice contemplation may take the act of contemplating as its essence,
with the counting of breaths as its primary focus.
All mental states and mental factors that follow along, observing and seeking, are collectively termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
Alternatively, it takes that mental factor of wisdom (prajñā) as its essence,
with wisdom being predominant;
all mind and mental factors that follow along and illuminate objects are collectively termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
Equanimity (upekṣā) either takes the mental factor of equanimity as its essence,
or it is primarily the numerical category of equanimity;
because all minds and mental factors follow along with and abandon faults, they are collectively termed "equanimity."
Alternatively, it takes the two practices of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence,
with these two factors serving as its primary subjects;
all mental states and mental concomitants that follow this concentration and wisdom are collectively termed equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If one explains according to the meaning of the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are likewise two [aspects].
First, regarding phenomena that are of the same substance and simultaneous, they are distinguished according to their respective meanings:
within the single substance of the mind, the sense of abiding is called *śamatha*.
Illuminating the meaning is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā);
balancing [the mind] is called "equanimity" (upekṣā).
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma, which posits these as distinct entities.
Second, distinguishing according to the meaning of cultivation in terms of sequence:
mental attention that abides upon an object is called *śamatha* (calm abiding);
mental attention that illuminates the object through cessation is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
It is only when one attends to the sign of equanimity that it is called "equanimity.
This is entirely a function of the mind;
there is no separate primary or secondary factor.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are three distinct meanings:
first, cultivation within the *vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of things); second, cultivation within the *mṛṣā-vijñāna* (the deluded consciousness).
Cultivation occurs within the three true consciousnesses.
Cultivation within the phenomenal consciousness (samsveda-vijnana) is the same as in the Abhidharma,
because the mental factors (caitta) are distinct.
Cultivating the coarse within false consciousness is the same as in the Abhidharma;
cultivating the subtle is the same as in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. How is this known?
As Aśvaghoṣa stated:
within the seventh consciousness, there are six layers of coarse and subtle [states];
regarding the fundamental four mental factors, their numerical categories are not distinct.
Therefore, they are equally established as real.
In the final two [categories], mind and number are distinct,
yet both are associated with the mind.
Therefore, it is the same as the Abhidharma.
Within the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), there are three distinct meanings regarding cultivation.
First, within the dharmas that are simultaneous and of the same substance, they are differentiated according to their respective meanings.
The meaning of stillness is called *śamatha*;
the meaning of illumination is termed *vipaśyanā*;
and being free from characteristics is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Second, regarding the mutual inclusion of different categories within phenomena that are simultaneous and identical in essence:
taking the meaning of *śamatha* (calm abiding) as the gateway,
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that accord with it are collectively termed *śamatha*.
The meaning of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) serves as the gateway;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that follow it are collectively termed "contemplation.
The meaning of relinquishment (*upekṣā*) serves as the gateway.
All virtues that follow these are likewise termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the meaning of cultivation, they are distinguished sequentially:
the initial mind abiding in the Dharma and departing from delusion is called "calm abiding" (*śamatha*).
Right view is called contemplation;
because it ultimately realizes the characteristic of equanimity, it is termed equanimity.
Such is its essential nature.
By means of these and other such formations, these two gateways are concluded.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished;
therein are two gateways.
First, the general classification of the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through their opening and closing;
second, the specific classification of the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena through their opening and closing.
Regarding the first, the general classification of the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena through their opening and closing:
These three practices may be expanded or condensed without fixed limit;
in total, they constitute one, namely,
that which is subsumed under the practice within the triad of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Alternatively, it is divided into two,
namely *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight),
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
To not give rise to conceptual constructions regarding any phenomena is called *śamatha*.

To know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as having an ineffable intrinsic nature, and to know the immeasurable phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) in their various aspects, is called *vipaśyanā*.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three:
namely, tranquility (śamatha), insight (vipaśyanā), and equanimity (upekṣā). These three are likewise subsumed within the aforementioned tranquility and insight.
Cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā separately constitutes the first two [categories],
while cultivating them together constitutes the latter one;
thus, there are three types.
Alternatively, it may be divided into four,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
first, the cultivation of śamatha (calm abiding).
Second is the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā).
Third is the cultivation of both tranquility (śamatha) and insight.
Fourth is the delight in abiding in tranquility and insight.
These four are likewise subsumed under the three practices of prior śamatha, vipaśyanā, and upekṣā.
Within upekṣā, two aspects are distinguished:
the former for the sake of cultivation, and the latter for the sake of abiding in bliss.
There is no other practice besides this.
What is called "stopping" (śamatha) refers to the settling of the mind by binding it to an object or its meaning.
To remain far removed from all hypocrisy, frivolity, and conceptual constructions is called *śamatha*.
"Matter" refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Meaning" (artha) refers to the ultimate truth for one who has abandoned frivolity;
it means to pacify and eliminate the distracted mind regarding worldly affairs.
"Free from conceptualization" (saṃjñā-vigata) means—
It is to remain far removed from conceptualizations that deviate from reason.
What is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to the recollection and discernment of both phenomena and their meanings.
This is called "contemplation.
One who cultivates cessation and contemplation constantly and suddenly practices the aforementioned cessation and contemplation.
For one who delights in śamatha and vipaśyanā,
because they have long practiced these previously, they do not exert effort in skillful means; rather,
they blaze forth with unwavering intensity.
If categorized extensively according to their meanings, the cultivations are immeasurable;
such is the opening and closing [of categories] regarding all formations (*saṃskāra*) in general.
Next, we shall discuss them in terms of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each formation.
First, regarding the characteristics of the practice of *śamatha*, they are distinguished according to their opening and closing as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
in total there is only one concentration,
or it may be divided into two non-dual aspects.
First, the worldly meditative concentrations on the eight dhyānas;
second, the supramundane tranquility that accords with principle.
Alternatively, these may be divided into three.
This refers to the superior, the middling, and the inferior. The inferior refers to the meditative concentration of ordinary persons.
The middling refers to the stillness of the two vehicles that accords with principle.
The superior [type] refers to the true concentration of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which is free from delusion.
This may be divided into four parts:
first, the regressive portion (*hānabhāgīya*).
Second is the stage of abiding;
third is the stage of superior progress;
fourth is the stage of certainty.
This decisive stage of nirvāṇa is called "that which performs great benefit.
The meaning will be explained below.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five parts.
These are the samādhis attained by ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. Furthermore,
within nirvāṇa, five types are further distinguished,
the first of which is the "foodless" (anāhāra) samādhi.
This refers to the first dhyāna.
Because it is free from solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it is called "foodless.
It is the second, the samādhi without fault.
This is also the first dhyāna.
Because one is free from sensual desires and evil, it is called "faultless.
It consists of the purity of the three bodies and mind, and single-minded samādhi.
This refers to the Second Dhyāna.
Being free from the faults of vitarka and vicāra within the six consciousnesses is called purity of body and mind.
Because it is a single locus of internal clarity, it is termed "one-pointedness of mind."
Fourth, the simultaneous presence of cause and fruit,
which refers to the third dhyāna;
this is because the bliss therein is preeminent.
The Samādhi of Constantly Contemplating the Five Constants refers to the four dhyānas up to birth in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
Those [beings] there escape the three calamities and are severed from the four types of sensation.
Because the mind remains unmoving through the meditative concentration that is free from inhalation and exhalation,
it is called "constant mindfulness.
Alternatively, it may be divided into six parts.
This refers to the five methods of settling the mind (*pañca-vastūni*) and the contemplation of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). The five methods of settling the mind are as follows.
Alternatively, they may be divided into seven.
This refers to the samādhis attained by the srotāpanna,
as well as those attained by the sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and Buddha;
these may be divided into eight types.
To the aforementioned seven, add all that is attained;
furthermore, the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and the eight dhyānas may also be categorized as eightfold,
as explained below.
There are also nine attainments to be distinguished,
namely: the nine successive meditative concentrations (*anupūrva-samāpatti*),
consisting of the eight fundamental dhyānas and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The successive entry into one another is called the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihāra).
Alternatively, they may be divided into ten,
namely by including the "all-encompassing bases" (kṛtsnāyatana).
This is also as explained below;
in detail, it is immeasurable.
Next, the characteristics are distinguished by means of the expansion and contraction of the practice of wisdom (prajñā-caryā).
In total, there is only one wisdom;
alternatively, it may be divided into two:
the first is mundane conventional knowledge (*lokasaṃvṛtijñāna*).
The second is supramundane.
This refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which can likewise be divided into three: first, *prajñā*.
This is translated as "wisdom" (prajñā).
Second is vipaśyanā, which is translated as "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
The third is *jñāna*, which is translated here as "wisdom.
Regarding these three, what is their difference? There are two explanations in the sūtras.
First, distinguishing by way of persons:
those called "prajñā" are all sentient beings.
All ordinary beings equally possess the mental factor of wisdom;
therefore, it is called *prajñā*.
*Vipaśyanā*, however, belongs exclusively to all noble ones (*ārya*).
These are called the noble ones among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
because they are able to contemplate suffering, impermanence, and so forth,
it is termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
As for the term *jñāna*,
it refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who know the distinctions among all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Therefore, it is called "wisdom" (jñāna).
Second, regarding the distinction according to the object:
that which is termed *prajñā*—
This is the contemplation of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*), which specifically discerns conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
*vipaśyanā* [in its general sense] is the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*).
To know the ultimate truth in its entirety:
that which is called *jñāna* (wisdom) is the contemplation that shatters appearances.
By breaking away from the knowledge of existence and non-existence, one realizes the single ultimate truth (ekasatyatā).
This can also be divided into four aspects, namely: the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and the contemplation of the four noble truths (caturāryasatyadhyāna), and so forth.
Furthermore, five types [of knowledge] may be distinguished:

namely, knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), knowledge of nirvāṇa, knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhi-jñāna), knowledge of non-contention (araṇā-jñāna), and knowledge of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-jñāna).
These are explained in detail as follows.
Furthermore, the five kinds of immeasurable wisdom are likewise fivefold,
as explained below;
they may also be divided into six.
This refers to knowing that birth and death are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure, and that *nirvāṇa* is tranquil extinction.
This can also be divided into seven types:

namely, knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), knowledge of meaning (*artha*), knowledge of time (*kāla*), knowledge of moderation (*mātrā*), knowledge of oneself, knowledge of the assembly, and knowledge of the honorable and the humble; these are also explained as below.
Alternatively, it is divided into eight:
knowing that the phenomena of birth and death are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
and knowing that the phenomena of nirvana are permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
One may also attain nine:
knowing the preceding eight kinds as well as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
One may also attain ten.
The meaning of what are called the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) is explained below.
Furthermore, the ten powers (*daśabala*) are likewise ten.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eleven,
namely the ten knowledges plus "knowing as it truly is," which is also explained below.
If expanded, it is immeasurable.
Regarding renunciation, there are two aspects:
first, the simultaneous cultivation of concentration and wisdom.
To be free from biased habitual tendencies is what is meant by the meaning of equanimity (*upekṣā*), as in the two preceding cases;
there is no separate practice.
This is the characteristic of abiding in the equanimity of emptiness.
It is named "equanimity" (upekṣā),
but its meaning is not fixed;
in total, it is simply one equanimity.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
first, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, which is equal toward all beings.
Second is the contemplation on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which is equal toward all phenomena;
alternatively, it may be divided into three.
This refers to the three contemplations on emptiness;
alternatively, they may be divided into four,
namely the four contemplations on emptiness.

There are four [types of emptiness]: the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existing phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of other-nature (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*). These are the four.
They are explained in detail as above.
Alternatively, they may be divided into five.

This refers to the contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*), as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Within the principle of emptiness, there is no sign to be grasped; this is termed "signlessness."
A mind that lacks aspiration and delight is called "wishless" (apraṇihita).
That for which there is no fruit to be produced is named "non-action" (anabhisaṃskāra).
Because there is no cause from which it can arise, it is said to be "unoriginated" (anutpāda).
Alternatively, it is divided into seven,
namely the seven contemplations on emptiness (*saptavidha-śūnyatā*), which are also explained as above.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eleven;
one contemplates these eleven emptinesses as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eighteen,
as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
if expanded, they are immeasurable.
The analysis of the characteristics is thus concluded; these three gates are finished.
Next, the establishment [of the system] is analyzed:
for what reason are these three types of conduct established as neither more nor less?
There are eight meanings of "understanding" (jñāna).
First, the nature of their practice differs:
fixed numerical categories constitute *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The factor of wisdom is discernment;
the factor of equanimity is relinquishment.
These two differ in their modes of activity.
Abiding in conditions is śamatha;
knowing phenomena is vipaśyanā;
balancing them is upekṣā.
Third, their functions differ:
*śamatha* (calm abiding) can still the distractions,
while *vipaśyanā* (insight) can sever the afflictions.
Abandonment is that which opposes and counteracts [the afflictions].
Fourth, the timing of their cultivation differs,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
If the mind is arrogant while practicing śamatha,
the afflictions will increase, the precepts will weaken, and the sense faculties will become unbalanced; in such a case,
one should practice vipaśyanā regarding wholesome states, doubt, and regret.
If concentration and wisdom are unequal, one must cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, the sūtras declare that when concentration and wisdom are equal, it is appropriate to cultivate equanimity.
The gates of the five elements differ,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Therein, that samādhi of emptiness is termed "cessation" (*śamatha*).
Because the mind abides in emptiness and is free from conceptual discrimination,
the samādhi of wishlessness is described as contemplation;
for through the contemplation of wisdom, one is able to sever and relinquish birth and death.
The signless samādhi is described as the practice of relinquishment,
for upon entering the realization of nirvāṇa, one relinquishes all signs.
The six sense faculties depend upon their respective objects, which are not the same.
There are many approaches, as will be explained later;
for now, we shall discuss this based on a single aspect.
One cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding) by relying on a concrete object.
Just as with the eight worldly dhyānas,
because one abides in conditioned phenomena,
one cultivates contemplation in reliance upon the Dharma.
To observe that all phenomena are suffering, impermanent, and so forth is called "contemplation.
Therefore, one cultivates equanimity based on this principle;
by realizing the equality of emptiness, one abandons all conceptual signs.
Seventh, these vary according to different individuals;
there are many approaches as will be shown later.
For now, they shall be explained based on a single characteristic.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess much concentration and little wisdom;
bodhisattvas possess much wisdom and little concentration."
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the equality of meditative concentration and wisdom;
this they describe as equanimity (*upekṣā*).
There are eight aspects in which these differ.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
one cultivates śamatha for three reasons.
First, to depart from afflictions, one relies on dhyāna to subdue the fetters;
second, to adorn great wisdom, one relies on dhyāna to give rise to insight;
third, to attain mastery, one relies on dhyāna to develop supernormal powers.
It is for three reasons that one cultivates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). First,
in order to contemplate the faults of the retribution of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one relies on wisdom (*prajñā*) to extinguish suffering.
Second, for the sake of increasing wholesome dharmas, one relies on wisdom to abandon karma;
third, for the sake of destroying afflictions, one relies on wisdom to eliminate delusion.
It is for these three reasons.
The reason for cultivating equanimity is twofold:
first, to harmonize concentration and wisdom so that they become equal;
second, to realize emptiness and thereby relinquish attachment to signs of existence.
Third, in order to attain the Middle Way, one departs from both existence and non-existence.
Having thus completed the establishment of these four gates,
the meaning of the sequence for cultivating and arising [realization] will next be explained.
Within this, there are briefly four successive stages:
first, the abandonment through restraint, arousal, and relinquishment; second, the abandonment through tranquility, exertion, and relinquishment.
Third is the equanimity of cessation and contemplation;
fourth is the equanimity of concentration and wisdom.
These four gates provide a general explanation that is one and the same.
Within this, the preceding two stages are distinguished as the practice of the preparatory means (*upāya*),
while the latter two constitute the attainment of the dharma through perfected cultivation.
Within these preliminary means, there is both a beginning and an end.
The attainment of the Dharma is likewise;
thus, there are four stages:
its establishment, its arousal, its relinquishment, and its abandonment.
The beginning of skillful means is the antidote to torpor and discursive thought.
"Torpor" refers to drowsiness;
"discursive thought" refers to the afflictions of the eight types of unwholesome thoughts.
Regarding the eight perceptions:
they are the perception of sensual desire, ill will, cruelty, kinship, country, immortality, lineage, and contempt.
If any unwholesome perceptions arise, one should immediately restrain them, and by restraining the mind, cause it to abide in the gateway of mindfulness of breathing and so forth.
If one is deluded, one should arouse the thought that the body is impermanent,
that there is suffering in the three evil realms,
and that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
By using this whip to drive away sleep and mental fog, one becomes free from both drowsiness and agitation; thus the mind is cultivated to attain the Middle Way.
This state is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding "stopping, uplifting, and equanimity":
these are the final skillful means for counteracting lethargy and agitation.
Lethargy refers to sinking.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) refers to agitation.
A turbid and stifled state of mind is termed depression (*laya*).
When the mental factors (*caitta*) attend to various objects, it is described as excitement.
If the mind is agitated, one should cultivate tranquility by focusing the mind on the tip of the nose, the space between the eyebrows, or the toes—
whichever location is appropriate. If the mind is sunken,
one should cultivate upliftment by reflecting on the body’s impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and so forth.
When one is free from both sinking and agitation, the mind is cultivated to attain the middle way;
at that time, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). This refers to the equanimity of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
At the beginning of attaining the Dharma, there are three objects of cultivation.
First, the cultivation is clarified by means of confronting craving and views;
the afflictions of the four abodes are divided into craving and views.
The first is *darśana* (viewing);
the latter three are *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
Within this framework, the cultivation of *śamatha* as an antidote to craving consists of the mundane eight dhyānas and their preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Cultivating contemplation as an antidote to views refers to the supramundane, untainted skillful means;
practicing both tranquility and insight together while remaining free from partiality is at that time termed "equanimity."
Second, cultivation and purification are explained by way of delusion (*moha*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The afflictions of the five abodes are divided into delusion and craving;
ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed delusion.
The remaining four are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Within this framework, the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) remedies craving,
while the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) remedies delusion (*moha*).
When both delusion and craving are abandoned,
and both tranquility and insight are cultivated together,
this state is called equanimity.
Third, the cultivation and remediation are distinguished in relation to delusion and falsehood.
Within the ground of the abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) itself, there is both darkness and falsehood.
That which obscures and covers all phenomena is termed "darkness."
To falsely grasp at things and declare them to be false is as described in the *Bhūmivastu*:
"That suchness which fools do not know as it truly is— that is darkness."
The arising of the eight types of false conceptualization is what constitutes delusion.
Within this gate, one cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding) as an antidote to delusion,
as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The Buddha taught this to Śāṇakavāsin Mahākātyāyana:
that one should practice meditative concentration without relying on the conceptualizations of all dharmas, such as earth and so forth.
The *Treatise by Aśvaghoṣa* (*Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra-śāstra*) also states this in the same way.
To be free from all conceptualizations is called the cultivation of *śamatha*.
The cultivation of *vipaśyanā* serves as the antidote to the mind of deluded darkness;
thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
Not giving rise to conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Knowing the ineffable nature [of phenomena] and knowing the immeasurable skillful means of conventional truth is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Cultivating both together while remaining free from partiality is at that time called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the equanimity of concentration and wisdom:
once this state of the Dharma is attained, there is no further need for other remedies.

The qualities of practice accomplished at the point where the afflictions eliminated by the preceding calm abiding and insight are ultimately exhausted constitute concentration, wisdom, and equanimity.
Having thus completed the cultivation of these five gates.
Next, the three types of conduct are distinguished according to their objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
Within this, there are briefly three stages of differentiation in meaning.
First, the three types of conduct are defined by correlating them with the three dharmas.
Second, the three modes of practice are distinguished by correlating two pairs of dharmas;
third, they are distinguished by applying them sequentially to each individual dharma.
Within the first section, which correlates three dharmas, there are further two distinct gates.
First, the three types of practice are distinguished based on phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).
Phenomena refer to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*);
one practices *śamatha* (calm abiding) by relying upon these.
Just as there are the eight worldly dhyānas,
"dharmas" refers to [truths] such as suffering and impermanence;
one practices contemplation based upon these.
Principle refers to what is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Relying upon this, one cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*),
thereby relinquishing all marks (*nimitta*).
Second, the three types of practice are distinguished by means of the three truths.
Regarding the three truths:
the first is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which refers to the appearance of phenomena as existing.
Second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which refers to the signlessness (*animitta*) of phenomena.
Third is the single reality truth (*eka-bhūta-satya*), which refers to the characteristic of phenomena being neither existent nor non-existent.
Within these three gateways, the arising of cultivation is indeterminate.
One who engages with reality relies on the mundane to cultivate *śamatha*,
such as the eight worldly dhyānas;
therefore, relying on the ultimate truth, one cultivates *vipaśyanā* to contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena.
Arising from tranquility to manifest activity, one relies on the truth to cultivate cessation (*śamatha*),
because it is free from conceptual discrimination;
relying on the world, one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*) by observing all phenomena.
By practicing the cultivation of equanimity based on the single ultimate truth, one abandons both existence and non-existence. Therefore,
in the *Bhūmivastu*, that which accords with the grasping of phenomena is called "equanimous contemplation" (*samatā-vipaśyanā*),
while that which accords with the grasping of suchness is called "equanimous mind" (*samacitta*).
"Equality" (*samatā*) is synonymous with "stopping.
To relinquish both existence and non-existence is called the "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Thus far, the practice has been explained in relation to the three objects.
Therefore, it is summarized by way of two objects. As for these two objects:
first, the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the two true dharmas:
generally speaking, not giving rise to deluded thoughts within these two is collectively termed *śamatha* (calm abiding);
clearly perceiving both truths is collectively termed *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Therefore, in the *Bhūmivastu*, the non-arising of conceptual constructions is called "calming" (*śamatha*);
thoroughly understanding the two truths is likewise termed "insight" (*vipaśyanā*);
and the balanced cultivation of both calming and insight is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Within this, the distinct divisions of their arising and functioning differ:
if one approaches it from the perspective of contemplative entry, one cultivates *śamatha* based on the conventional and *vipaśyanā* based on the ultimate;
if one discusses the manifestation of function, one cultivates *śamatha* based on the ultimate and *vipaśyanā* based on the conventional.
The balanced cultivation and harmonization of both śamatha and vipaśyanā is called equanimity (upekṣā).
Next, one distinguishes the three modes of conduct based on a single dharma:
whatever dharma or object one collects through śamatha and dwells peacefully within is termed śamatha.
Thoroughly examining is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
The balancing of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is called *upekṣā* (equanimity).
Thus concludes these six gates according to their objects.
Next is the discussion of the stages (*bhūmi*).
There are five distinct stages:
first, the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Second, the stage of the inner ordinary person;
third, the stage of the path of seeing; fourth, the stage of the path of cultivation;
and fifth, the stage of no-more-learning.
Discussing them comprehensively, each stage possesses all three types of practice.
Within these, there are three distinct variations regarding progress and regression.
First, as for the analytical classification of meaning: in the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), one cultivates the eight worldly dhyānas.
This is termed "calming" (śamatha).
Within the stage of the ordinary person, training in the contemplation of the principles of the truths is termed "insight" (vipaśyanā).
From the stage of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) upward, because the realization of the principle is equal and uniform, it is termed "equanimity" (upekṣā).
According to the second meaning, within the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala), one settles the mind upon the principles of the truths but has not yet attained direct vision.
This is explained as "cessation.
Therefore, prior to the vision of the truths, it is termed "purity through concentration" (*samādhi-pariśuddhi*).
Within the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), one first perceives the principle of the truths.
This is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Once the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) has been attained and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced, it is termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the third meaning: prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), these are likewise termed "calming" (*śamatha*).
The two paths of seeing and cultivation are called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) because they illuminate the principle;
in the stage of no-more-learning, one attains the fruit of nirvana and relinquishes the ten signs,
and is therefore called "relinquishment" (prahāṇa).
The distinctions among the stages are thus; this concludes the seven gates.
Next, we shall discuss persons.
There are five kinds of persons.
First are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
second are śrāvakas;
third are pratyekabuddhas.
The fourth is the bodhisattva;
the fifth is the Tathāgata.
Discussing them comprehensively, every person possesses both śamatha and vipaśyanā, as well as equanimity (upekṣā).
Within this, there are briefly three distinct meanings.
First, when ordinary persons cultivate the eight worldly dhyānas,
they possess only the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have contemplative practices that consist of observing the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth; however,
bodhisattvas and buddhas realize the equality of all phenomena.
There is its practice of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Second, ordinary persons possess tranquility (*śamatha*);
the meaning is as explained previously.
Bodhisattvas and followers of the two vehicles alike contemplate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
they possess such contemplative practice,
yet it is the Buddha who realizes nirvana.
There is the practice of relinquishment.
Third, setting aside ordinary beings, we speak directly of the noble ones:
for a śrāvaka, abiding in tranquility is called *śamatha*.
When a Bodhisattva thoroughly understands the differentiated realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
this is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
When a Buddha attains nirvāṇa, [this is called "cessation"].
There is the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*). This brief explanation of the meaning of equanimity within the context of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is thus concluded.

104. The Meaning of the Threefold Wisdom (10). The meaning of the threefold wisdom is explained through a fivefold analysis: 1. Definition of terms (*nirukti*); 2. Analysis by way of essence (*svabhāva*); 3. Analysis by way of stages (*avasthā*); 4. Analysis by way of realms (*dhātu*); 5. Analysis by way of persons (*pudgala*). First, the definition of terms.
Regarding the three types of wisdom:
in the sūtras, they are sometimes called hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
and at other times described as the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The general explanation is one and the same;
however, within it, there are distinctions in meaning regarding its breadth and narrowness.
If one were to speak directly of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta*, *cintā*, *bhāvanā*):
The meaning of this is broad and encompasses everything.
Within that universal scope, the initial undertaking and practice of the Dharma is generally termed "hearing" (śruta).
The analytical discernment of the teachings thus heard is generally termed "wisdom" (prajñā).
According to the Dharma, correct practice is generally described as "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
However, if one were to categorize it specifically as the wisdoms of hearing,
reflection, and cultivation, its meaning would be narrowly restricted to *prajñā* (wisdom) alone.
It does not pertain to other practices.
Within the context of *prajñā*, receiving the teachings is called "hearing" (*śruta*);
the arising of understanding is termed "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Simple meaning" refers to reflection (*cintā*).
Attaining understanding through reflection is called "wisdom born of reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Progressing in practice is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
The wisdom obtained through cultivation is called "cultivated wisdom" (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Such are the names and meanings; this concludes the first section.
Next, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) shall be analyzed.
The three types of wisdom all take the mental factor of wisdom as their essence.
Wisdom is established in dependence upon dharmas,
and these dharmas are of three kinds.
First, the teaching;
second, the meaning;
third, the method of practice.
The Tripitaka refers to the numerical categories of its teaching;
the principle of the Three Truths refers to its doctrinal meaning;
and the practices and protocols of the Three Vehicles refer to its methods of cultivation.
Within this, they are distinguished as follows: based on the teaching, one gives rise to hearing;
based on the meaning, one enters into reflection;
and based on practice, one gives rise to cultivation.
Discussing this comprehensively, each and every phenomenon possesses the three types of wisdom.
Within the teachings, one first receives the name and hears them;
then, by discerning right from wrong, one explains them as reflection.
The practice of accomplishing the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining is explained as cultivation.
Within the meaning of the Dharma, there are three kinds:
first, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Second is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
third is the single true reality (eka-bhūta-satya).
Discussing these three truths in general, it is here that one first receives the names and teachings.
Discernment is called "reflection" (cintā);
the accomplishment of right knowledge is said to be "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
According to their distinct characteristics, they are established based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā).
Worldly dharmas may be practiced through verbal instruction and reliance on the conventional; however, the wisdom born of reflection is accomplished by relying on the ultimate truth,
for its principle transcends words.

Because it can be reached only through the deliberation of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), one accomplishes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) by relying on the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyatattva*);
because it can be seen only through the practice of direct realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkāra*) that is singular, subtle, and authentic.
Within the practice of the Dharma, first one receives renown;
then one discriminates and reflects upon it; finally, the performance of the practice is called cultivation (bhāvanā).
Furthermore, the first three—practicing in accordance with the teachings—are collectively termed "hearing" (śruta).
Abandoning words to proceed toward realization is called "reflection" (cintā).
Attaining realization and its correspondence is termed "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
Furthermore, when the characteristics of realization first appear within the mind, this is explained as "hearing" (śruta).
This is indeed the hearing of what was previously unheard. When one correctly attains this, it is called "reflection" (cintā).
Having attained [this], to advance further is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Such is the nature of these two gates; this concludes the section on them.
Next, we shall discuss them according to their stages (*avasthā*).
In general, all stages possess everything;
yet, when distinguished specifically within them, there is no lack of difference.
What are these differing characteristics?

According to the Abhidharma, within the stage of the ordinary person (bālapṛthagjana), the initial reception of the teacher’s instruction is designated as "wisdom derived from hearing" (śrutamayī-prajñā).

This is because the practices of the five meditations for settling the mind (pañca-viṣkambhana-bhāvanā), the general and specific applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), and the contemplations of perception and mind have not yet attained the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) through meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).

That which is categorized as the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) pertains to the stages prior to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). That which is practiced based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from "Heat" onwards is categorized as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Furthermore, the initial stage of practicing the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-bhāvanā*) according to the teachings is classified as the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).
Once one has distanced oneself from the teachings through the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the observation of the mind becomes increasingly powerful.

That which is categorized as the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) pertains to the stages prior to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). That which is categorized as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) pertains to the practices based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from "Heat" onwards.

In the *Tattvasiddhi*, prior to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the initial reception of the teacher’s instruction and the attainment of understanding according to what was heard is judged to be the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Within the stage of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the capacity to conceptually analyze and discern one's own mind is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
From the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and above, the direct realization of the principle of emptiness is called wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Question: The *Tattvasiddhi* explains the three types of wisdom in this way.
Among these three types of wisdom, what phenomena are understood and known?

Some commentators explain that on the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one attains the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) by analyzing the aggregates (*skandha*).

On the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one contemplates the five aggregates individually as being subject to the suffering of disintegration and impermanence, thereby fulfilling the previously mentioned emptiness of sentient beings.

Furthermore, they pursue the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). From the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) upward, one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as suffering in its conditioned nature (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) and impermanent, thereby attaining the emptiness of all phenomena.
This is merely human opinion and has no basis in the sūtras or śāstras.
If the wisdom of hearing were to understand only the emptiness of persons,
where would the emptiness of phenomena and the tranquility of hearing reside?
If the wisdom of reflection were to dismantle phenomena to establish the emptiness of persons, [where would the emptiness of phenomena be?]
If the mind of the emptiness of phenomena is already quiescent, where does thought abide?
If one cultivates the stage of wisdom and understands only the emptiness of phenomena,
where does the cultivation of the emptiness of persons abide?
The principles of both types of emptiness must first be heard,
followed by reflection and then cultivation before one can realize them;

yet it is said that regarding the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), there is only the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) and no wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā).
If one practices the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) without having heard or reflected upon it,
is this not a deluded and futile error?
One should know that the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) fully encompasses the hearing of both types of emptiness.
Within the stage of wisdom derived from reflection, one fully perceives the two kinds of emptiness;
within the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation, one fully perceives the two kinds of emptiness.
One must not grasp them in a partial manner.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, the stages are not fixed;
speaking from the perspective of the beginning,
within the stage of the "cultivated seeds" (śrutavāsanā-bīja), one attains realization through the teachings and accomplishes the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā).
Therefore, it is proclaimed in the *Avataṃsaka*:
"In the stage of the Ten Abodes, one immediately attains self-understanding according to whatever Dharma is heard;
within the stage of the Innate Lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*), one abandons the conventional expression to grasp the meaning, thereby accomplishing the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)."
In the stages above the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), one cultivates the path of transcendence and achieves the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Regarding the subsequent superior stages,
within the stage of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), one can only hear of and know the supramundane path.
They have not yet been able to engage in reflection;

they are alike in being wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Within the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one is able to contemplate the path of transcendence, which is classified as wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
From the first bhūmi upward, right practice gradually increases;
this is categorized as the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). This is established by subsequent treatises.
The nature of the stage of the lineage of practice (śikṣāgotra) directly accomplishes the supramundane seeds,
yet one is not yet able to enter the path of transcendence through skillful means;
both [the wisdoms of] hearing and reflection are absent.
In the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one is able to give rise to skillful means and enter the path of transcendence;
regarding supramundane dharmas, one is able to hear and reflect upon them, thereby possessing the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*).
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that the stage of practice through understanding is fully endowed with the contemplation of the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of reflection.
From the first bhūmi upward, the initiation of correct practice is termed "wisdom arising from cultivation" (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā).
According to the ultimate treatises,
all practices based on the teachings prior to all the bhūmis are collectively termed "wisdom arising from hearing" (śruta-mayī-prajñā).
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one begins to contemplate persons; this is classified as the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
From the second stage upward, the realization of the mind increases further; this is classified as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Such are the distinctions of the stages; thus concludes this section on the three gates.
Next, we shall discuss the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and so forth,
as explained in the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
The wisdom derived from hearing is restricted to the desire and form realms and does not extend to the formless realm;
because the formless realm lacks physical form, it is incapable of listening or receiving [teachings],
and for this reason, there is no hearing there.
Wisdom derived from reflection is restricted to the stages of the desire realm and does not exist in the higher realms.
Why is this so? Because the retribution in the higher realms is quiescent.
When mental application (*vitarka*) is withdrawn, it corresponds with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);
therefore, there is no wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Question:
If there were no wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) in the higher realms, there would be no applied thought (vitarka) or sustained thought (vicāra).
The commentary states:
"All applied and sustained thought existing in the higher realms are subsumed under wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā)."
Therefore, there is concentration;
the cultivation of wisdom is restricted to the form and formless realms and does not extend to the desire realm.
Because all meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) are subsumed under cultivated wisdom (bhāvanā-prajñā),
there is cultivation in the higher realms; however, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is no meditative concentration.
Therefore, there is no wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). According to Ghoṣaka’s explanation, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are as previously stated;
the wisdom of cultivation alone pervades all three realms.
That [text] states that because meditative concentration exists in the desire realm,
the wisdom derived from hearing established in the *Tattvasiddhi* is as described above,
whereas the wisdom derived from reflection is not fixed.
Contemplation that follows the teachings is restricted to the realms of desire and form;
contemplation that investigates the meaning pervades all three realms. How is this known?
The treatise explains *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought): coarse thinking is called *vitarka*,
while subtle thinking is called *vicāra*.
He asserts that vitarka and vicāra exist in all three realms;
thus it is clearly understood that they are pervasive and universally present throughout the cultivation of all three realms.
He further asserts that the "lightning-flash samādhi" exists within the desire realm.
Regarding the clarification that the cultivation of the three types of wisdom in the Mahāyāna extends throughout the three realms:
for what reason is this so?
Although a bodhisattva may reside in the formless realm, they are able to come to the presence of the Buddha to hear and receive the true Dharma;
furthermore, because they have attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining,
they fully receive all the Buddha’s teachings.
Therefore, there is the supernormal power of hearing;
the bodhisattva constantly contemplates,
and therefore there is the supernormal power of thought.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* proclaims that there is meditative concentration within the desire realm; therefore,
one cultivates the supernormal powers.
The classification of the realms is thus; these four gates are concluded.
Next, we shall discuss them in terms of persons.
"Persons" refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
To discuss this in general terms, everyone possesses these qualities.
Within this context, however, there is a specific distinction for those of the śrāvaka type who, upon hearing the teaching, awaken to the Way and achieve the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
For this reason, they are designated as "śrāvakas" based on their characteristics.
The Pratyekabuddha deeply contemplates the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby achieves the wisdom of reflection;
for this reason, he is designated as a "Pratyekabuddha" (One Awakened to Conditions).
Here, "condition" (pratyaya) is the meaning.
Awakening refers to volition.
The Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the path that benefits both self and others,
thereby accomplishing the cultivation of wisdom.
Therefore, you should be addressed as a bodhisattva.
This term "bodhisattva" translates as "one who seeks the path for sentient beings," because they cultivate the path that benefits both themselves and others.
The three types of wisdom are thus. 105.
The Meaning of the Three Kinds of Prajñā (10): Regarding the meaning of the three kinds of *prajñā*, these three kinds of *prajñā* appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
That which is called *prajñā* is a foreign term; here it is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*).
To observe and penetrate the nature of phenomena is what is designated as wisdom.
The meanings of "wisdom" (prajñā) differ.
One gate explains three [types].
What are these three names?
First, the Prajñā of a Single Syllable;
second, the Prajñā of Contemplative Illumination;
third, the Prajñā of Ultimate Reality.
Among these three types, the single type of contemplative observation is the essence of prajñā;
the true reality of words and letters is the dharma of prajñā.
Because the essence of the dharma is explained in combination with these, there are three types.
As for what is called "words and letters," it refers to the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; this is not itself prajñā.
It is named "prajñā" because it can express prajñā.
Just as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is called "nirvāṇa" because it elucidates nirvāṇa,
so too is this the case here.
Furthermore, these syllables can give rise to prajñā, and thus they are also called "prajñā."
Just as one speaks of "eating life" when referring to the act of eating,
so too, that which is called "contemplative observation" (vipaśyanā) refers to the discerning penetration of the wisdom-mind; this is what is meant by contemplative observation.
This very essence of contemplative observation is termed "contemplative wisdom" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*).
It is like how the eye itself is called the "eye-organ.
Within this, the distinctions between its inclusion and exclusion are analyzed as being indeterminate.
In total, there is but a single wisdom;
alternatively, it may be divided into two,
and these two have many categories.
First, there are two divisions based on the object:
namely, conventional wisdom and ultimate wisdom.
The knowledge of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is called "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākāra-jñatā),
because it is the knowledge of the specific distinctions among worldly phenomena.
The knowledge of ultimate truth (paramārtha-jñāna) is called "omniscience" (sarvajña).
This is because one knows that all phenomena are as they truly are (*tathatā*).
Second, regarding the distinction between the real and the delusory:
within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, the discerning reflection upon objects is their delusory cognition.
The wisdom that illuminates the essence within the eighth consciousness is its true gnosis.
What is the meaning of this?
It is the integration of the mind and phenomena, comprising the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, within the Tathāgatagarbha.
The nature of this mind is pure, yet it appears impure because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions.
Later, when the delusive defilements cease, the aspect of purity first manifests.
This manifestation of the pure consciousness, which universally illumines the dharma-realm, is called true wisdom.
The third [stage] is divided into two parts: the Great and the Small.
In the preliminary practice (*upāya*), the contemplative understanding differentiates between this and that regarding conditions;
it cannot extinguish perceptions yet universally illumines all things.
It is therefore termed "small.
Thus Nāgārjuna said:
"The contemplation of the eighteen emptinesses is called small wisdom."
When the contemplation of cessation and prajñā sever all conceptualizations of objects, they are able to universally illuminate the entire dharma-realm;
this is termed "Great.
Thus, Nāgārjuna said:
The Prajñāpāramitā is great wisdom.
It may be divided into three [categories],
and these three have many gateways.
First, regarding the stages of entry, there are three:
namely, hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Second, regarding the objects, there are three.
That is to say, the knowledge of conventional truth, the knowledge of the ultimate meaning, and the knowledge of the single true reality.
These three are further divided according to their meanings into three:
namely, pure knowledge, omniscience, and unimpeded knowledge.
The meaning is as explained later.
Fourth, according to persons, it is divided into three:
first, that which is attained by the Omniscient Ones (sarvajña) and the two vehicles; [the other two categories follow].
Second is the knowledge of the aspects of the path, which is attained by bodhisattvas;
third is the knowledge of all aspects, which is attained by Tathāgatas.
These are also as explained below.
The five [consciousnesses] follow the three divisions of consciousness:
first, the discerning wisdom within the consciousness of phenomena;
second, the discerning wisdom within the deluded consciousness.
Within the three true consciousnesses, there is the wisdom of discernment;
this may further be divided into four, namely:
that arising from hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.
Alternatively, it is divided into five:
first, hearing;
second, reflection.
Third, cultivation;
fourth, the knowledge of consciousness born of retribution.
When the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of a transformed saint (*parivṛtti-ārya*) arises and one perceives phenomena, it is called the knowledge born of retribution.
These four are false;
the fifth is realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*),
namely, non-conceptual discernment within the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
Alternatively, they may be divided into eleven:
namely, the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) together with the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
This meaning will be analyzed in detail later in the section on the eleven knowledges.
When expanded, it is immeasurable. Question:
What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*)?
As Nāgārjuna has analyzed,
there are six different types of human explanations.
The first school asserts that only tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) constitutes the essence of *prajñā*.
Why is this so? Because, according to the Hīnayāna, one only severs the afflictions (*kleśa*) beneath the Bodhi tree.
All wisdom cultivated prior to this is termed *prajñā*; therefore, it should be known as being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is the second school’s explanation.
Untainted noble wisdom (anāsrava-ārya-prajñā) is the essence of prajñā;
that which is tainted (sāsrava) is not.
This is because the mind that perceives reality is designated as prajñā.
According to this explanation, within the Hīnayāna teachings, the untainted skillful means (*anāsrava-upāya*) cultivated during the Buddha’s final existence is *prajñā*;
everything prior to that is not.
This is the position of the third school.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until sitting beneath the tree of awakening, all wisdom cultivated therein—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—is entirely *prajñā*.
Upon reaching Buddhahood, it changes its name to *sarvajñājñāna* (all-knowing wisdom).
According to this explanation, prajñā exists only in the causal stage and does not extend to the fruit.
The fourth school asserts that all wisdom cultivated by a bodhisattva is collectively termed "with outflows" (sāsrava) and collectively termed "without outflows" (anāsrava), and is entirely prajñā.
The commentary’s own explanation states:
Because one practices the Buddha-way by contemplating nirvāṇa, it is collectively termed "outflow-free" (anāsrava);
because the fetters have not yet been completely severed, it is collectively termed "with-outflows" (sāsrava).
The fifth school asserts that within the wisdom of a bodhisattva, the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be perceived; rather,
the essence of *prajñā* is non-conceptual, eternal wisdom.
The sixth school asserts that all knowledge of the conditions of impermanence is entirely non-existent,
and that the essence of prajñā cannot be apprehended.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither permanent nor impermanent;
it is neither empty nor substantial, and is not comprised of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, without arising or ceasing, and without grasping or relinquishing.
Just as a flame cannot be tasted or touched, for if one touches it, it burns the person;
so it is with prajñā—
it cannot be grasped or clung to.
All that was grasped is now refuted and discarded.
Everything previously grasped is entirely incorrect.
It is asked:
What is the difference between this section and the previous fifth section?
The explanation states:
the previous fifth section proceeds from the cultivation of skillful means based on conditions.
The arising of true wisdom constitutes the essence of *prajñā*.
This teaching states that the Buddha-nature, the true mind which is beginningless, is manifested through cultivation based on conditions;
yet, once realization is attained, looking back toward its original essence, it ultimately has no conditions external to that essence.
Since conditions do not exist, the truth also lacks a counterpart.
This absolute, ultimate true mind is called the essential substance of a bodhisattva’s prajñā;
everything else is not.
Question: Among these six, which ones are correct?
The treatise provides two different judgments.
Every single word is thus, just as the bhikṣus each explained the meaning of this, that, and what lies between them.
The Buddha said,
"All are correct."
This is also like that.
One word: that which was spoken by the Sixth is it.
The first five are all not the true essence of prajñā;
therefore, they are said to be "not [prajñā].
Contemplative observation is thus.
Regarding the term "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa):
it refers to the objective realm known through the preceding contemplative observation.
Because the essence of all phenomena is real, it is termed "real."
The essential nature and characteristics of reality are termed "marks" (lakṣaṇa).
What are they? They are the indeterminate states of opening and closing.
In total, it constitutes a single reality;
alternatively, it may be divided into two,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
First, the dharma-nature of phenomena is real according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Second, the true dharma-nature is real according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Alternatively, it may be divided into three.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
first, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
second, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The single reality of the three truths may also be divided into four: first,
the reality of phenomena, such as the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).
Second, the reality of phenomena as suffering, impermanence, and so forth;
third, the principle of emptiness and non-self;
fourth, the nature of reality as the true dharma of Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains that the four types of true meaning (*tattvārtha*) are also four kinds of reality:
first, that which is known by the world;
second, that which is known through training (*śaikṣa*).
Third, the phenomena that are the objects of practice for the purification of the afflictive hindrances;
fourth, the phenomena that are the objects of practice for the purification of the cognitive hindrances,
as extensively distinguished above.
When these dharmas are discussed in general terms, they are all the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Within this, when distinguished specifically, only the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called the true nature.
This true nature, in its essence, is not prajñā.
It is called "prajñā" because it is able to produce prajñā.
Just as form, fragrance, and so forth are not themselves desire,
yet they are called the "five desires" because they can produce a desirous mind.
Question: Noble wisdom not only knows the real but also knows the false.
For what reason is that which is known referred to solely as the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa)?
The commentary states:
The sage knows in accordance with the Dharma;
whether knowing the real or knowing the unreal, all conform to the preceding Dharma.
Therefore, it is called "real" in a comprehensive sense.
Furthermore, when one knows the real, one realizes that the fundamental is devoid of delusion;
thus, it is spoken of as merely "the real."
Question: Contemplative observation is itself prajñā.
These three types are all designated as prajñā.
Why can it not be given the general name "contemplative observation" (*vipaśyanā*)?
The explanation states:
It may indeed be so called; however, within that treatise, it is distinguished from the contemplative observation of the *prajñā* of words and letters by means of the true reality (*tattva*).
Therefore, this single type is specifically named "contemplative observation" (vipaśyanā).
Furthermore, if one were to distinguish its meaning within the framework of that door of contemplative observation,
it may also be described as three types of contemplative observation.
First, contemplation through a single syllable;
second, contemplation through prajñā;
third, contemplation of the true mark (dharmatā).
Since their meanings are equal and balanced,
one may not take [only] one side;
such is the brief analysis of the three kinds of prajñā.
106. The Meaning of the Three Knowledges (10). Section One: Distinguishing the Characteristics through Two Gates. A. Distinguishing by way of persons. First, the distinction of characteristics.
As for the three types of knowledge:
first, the knowledge of the aspects of the path; second, all-knowledge.
Third is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
These three types [of knowledge] are extracted from the *Mahājñāna-śāstra*.
Regarding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*):
The knowledge that discerns and names all the various paths is called the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
Furthermore, the knowledge that knows all the paths for transforming sentient beings is called the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
What is it that is known?
As extensively analyzed with increasing numbers in that treatise,
it is sometimes said to be a single path—
namely, the path leading toward nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, they may be divided into two;
these two have many categories, namely:
the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The mundane and supramundane;
the tainted and untainted; insight and cultivation; those in training and those beyond training;
the unhindered knowledges and liberations; the paths toward the fruits and the attainment of the fruits.
Such immeasurable [classifications] cannot be fully detailed;
they may be divided into three,
and these three also have many further categories.
That is to say: the three evil realms; the three wholesome paths of humans, devas, and *nirvāṇa*; the paths of the three vehicles;
and morality, concentration, wisdom, vision, cultivation, the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Thus they are immeasurable;
alternatively, they may be divided into four,
and these four have many categories.
That which is called the path of ordinary beings and the three vehicles—
the paths of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas;
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and so forth.
Thus they are immeasurable;
alternatively, they may be divided into five,
and these five also have many gateways.
This refers to the five destinies and the five gates of contemplation on the perfections (pāramitās).
These include the paths of ordinary beings, the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and buddhas;
thus they are immeasurable.
Whether there be six, seven, or even eighty-four thousand paths and dharmas—
to know such distinctions among these paths and dharmas is called the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgajñatā).
What is the difference between that omniscience (sarvajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)?
The general explanation is one;
within it, there are specifically six types of distinctions.
First, the distinction between the general and the particular.

Knowledge of phenomena through their general characteristics is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā); knowledge of phenomena through their specific characteristics is called "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
For example, knowing the Truth of Suffering is all-knowledge.
Discrimination (vikalpa) refers to the immeasurable varieties of suffering, which constitute "all modes" (sarvākāra).
All such [categories] are distinguished through both general and specific classifications.
To know the universal characteristics of all phenomena—such as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self—is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā).
