To know the specific characteristics of all phenomena, such as the five sciences, is called "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā).
The three emptinesses involve conceptual differentiation.
To know that all phenomena are empty is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā).
To know their various conventional phenomena is called "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā).
Fourth, the distinction between the concise and the detailed:
knowing all phenomena concisely is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā);
knowing all phenomena in detail is called "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā).
The knowledge that counteracts the causes and effects of the *paricchinna* (segmented) realm is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
The knowledge that counteracts even a portion of the causes and effects of both the *paricchinna* and *pariṇāmika* (transformative) realms is called "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is also like this: just as one who knows the affairs of a single world is called "all-knowing" (sarvajña), one who knows the affairs within all worlds is called "omniscient" (sarvākārajñatā).
It is just like this.
Fifth, the distinction between the great and the small:
the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā),
while the wisdom of the Mahāyāna is called "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā).
Question: Since the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgajñatā) previously discussed has already encompassed the full knowledge of all phenomena,
why is it necessary to separately explain the knowledge of all things (sarvajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)?
The commentary states:
The aforementioned knowledge of the modes of practice (*mārgajñatā*) directly knows only the dharmas of the path;
all other things, such as the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), emptiness, selflessness, and the ultimate truth (*paramārthadharma*), are not within its scope of knowledge.
Therefore, having further clarified this single gate,
we shall next discuss it in terms of persons.
"Persons" refers to śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Regarding this person, there are four ways of explaining the meaning.
First, the classification according to the specific individual,
as explained in the treatise.
Śrāvakas possess omniscience because they are able to know all phenomena through their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, while śrāvakas are only able to know phenomena through their general characteristics, they cannot know them through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because they can only know all phenomena in brief and cannot know them extensively,
it is said that they possess "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā).
Bodhisattvas, however, possess the "knowledge of the modes of the path" (mārgajñatā).
Because they are able to know all distinct paths and dharmas in order to transform sentient beings,
all Buddhas possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
for they are able to extensively know dharmas through their discernment of specific characteristics.
Second, the distinction between the superior and the inferior:
within this framework, the lower does not encompass the higher,
whereas the higher may encompass the lower.
For this reason, śrāvakas possess only a partial wisdom and lack the other two types;
whereas bodhisattvas possess the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) together with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), yet they do not possess the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
All Buddhas and Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the three types of knowledge.
These three distinguish the Great [Vehicle] from the Small;
the Buddha and Bodhisattvas belong to the Great.
The Śrāvaka is small; among the small,
there is only a single direct [attainment] of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
whereas it is not so in the great.
Both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the three types of knowledge (*trividya*).
Fourthly, when discussed in terms of actual reality, although Śrāvakas partially possess these three, Bodhisattvas gradually surpass them,
and Buddhas reach the ultimate perfection.
The three types of knowledge are thus. 107.

The Meaning of the Knowledge of the Three Valid Cognitions (10): An Exposition through Three Gates. I. Explaining the Names; II. Distinguishing the Characteristics; III. Distinguishing by Way of Stages. First, the explanation of the names.
The meaning of the three measures (*pramāṇa*) originates from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
Because the wisdom-mind apprehends phenomena each with its own specific limit,
they are called "measures."
The types of valid cognition differ;
one gate explains three kinds,
the first of which is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The second is inference (anumāna);
the third is scriptural authority (āgama).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Tattvasiddhi* also present these same characteristics.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Direct knowledge, inferential knowledge, and that which is heard from a teacher.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* says:
Seeing, hearing, and inference are likewise three such [means of knowledge].
Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
the direct cognition of phenomena is called direct perception.
Furthermore, one knows that the present dharma is also termed "present.
Within this, there are two kinds of discernment: the first is the knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*).
Second is knowing the principle.
Regarding "knowing phenomena," it means that at whatever time or in whatever context one encounters a phenomenon, one does not rely on inference.
That which can be known without relying on the words of others is likewise termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because its objective characteristics are coarse and proximate, it can be directly perceived at any time and in any place.
Regarding the statement "knowing the principle," according to the method of the *Abhidharma*, it is distinguished by way of location (*sthāna*).
To know the dharmas of the desire realm is called "the present. For what reason?
It is known that the dharmas of the desire realm alone are designated as "manifest.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The attainment of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) necessarily occurs within the desire realm."
One must first perceive the suffering and so forth of the desire realm, and subsequently perceive those of the higher realms.
This is because the phenomena of the desire realm are coarse and easy to perceive, and thus they are perceived first;
having perceived them first, one understands them clearly.
Therefore, it is specifically designated as "manifest" (pratyakṣa).
This is not the case for the higher realms;
thus, one should know that the higher realms are not termed "manifest."
Furthermore, the practitioner has two types of direct perception regarding the suffering of the desire realm:
first, direct perception through detachment,
because one directly illuminates and knows it by means of the path of detachment.
Second is direct perception by oneself;
because the suffering of the body in the desire realm is directly experienced,
whereas in the higher realms, there is only one kind of suffering.
Detachment from desire is directly perceived;
yet the body does not exist therein,
because it is not cognized.
It is like two loads of goods:
one is carried by oneself, while the other is carried by employing another person.
Regarding what one carries, there are two types of direct perception:
first, knowing that it is an object;
second, knowing its weight.
One knows that the suffering of the desire realm is of this nature;
regarding what another carries, one only perceives a single kind of object,
for its lightness or heaviness cannot be known through direct observation.
The higher realms are likewise.
Because two [types of] manifestation are known to exist in the desire realm, it alone is specifically designated as "manifest.
In the higher realms, there is only one.
Therefore, it is not called "manifest.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the analysis is made according to time;
therein, the manifest has two types.
First, according to the beginning of cultivation:
prior to the realization of the truths (satyadarśana), during the present time, one contemplates that which is conventionally designated as lacking intrinsic nature;
this is termed "present."
Second, according to its accomplishment through cultivation:
having already seen the truths, one directly perceives the principle of emptiness within the dharmas of the three periods of time;
this is likewise termed "present."
The Mahāyāna generally distinguishes [the stages] according to time and place;
there are four explanations of their meaning.
First, based on the commencement of cultivation.
To perceive the suchness of all phenomena solely within the present phenomena of the desire realm is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because the present phenomena of the desire realm are easy to observe.
Second is the sequence of cultivation:
either one perceives the suchness of the three periods of time within the desire realm,
or one perceives the suchness of the present within the three realms.
This is called "direct perception by the same name.
Third is that accomplished through cultivation,
wherein one directly perceives the suchness of all phenomena throughout the three times within one's own continuum.
All are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Fourth, based on meditative cultivation,
upon reaching the time of awakening, one directly perceives all phenomena of the three periods of time.
All are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
without distinguishing between one's own portion and another's portion.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, directly know, see, and awaken to all phenomena;
such is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for inference (*anumāna*):
For example, the knowledge that measures and understands phenomena is called inference (anumāna).
Within this, there are also two types of discrimination.
The first is knowledge of phenomena;
the second is knowledge of principles.
Regarding "knowledge of phenomena":
In whatever time or place, knowing through inference within the Dharma is entirely termed *anumāna* (inference).
Regarding the phrase "knowing the principle," in the *Abhidharma* system, it is distinguished according to the bases (*āyatana*).
Knowing the principles of the Four Truths of the two higher realms is called inference (*anumāna*).
Within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), there is a temporal distinction:
prior to the vision of the truths, observing that past and future phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) through conventional designations is called inference.
The Mahāyāna generally distinguishes [the stages] by way of time and place;
there are three interpretations of their meaning.
The first is based on the commencement of cultivation.
Inferring the nature of phenomena in other realms and other lifetimes based on the nature of phenomena currently present in the desire realm is called inference (*anumāna*).
This is based on the sequence of cultivation;
alternatively, one may infer the two higher realms based on the nature of phenomena throughout the three times in the desire realm.
Alternatively, one may infer the past and future by means of the present phenomena within the three realms; this is called inference (*anumāna*).
This is based on cultivation, wherein one relies upon the nature of the phenomena of the three times within the three realms as they are known within one's own continuum.
The suchness of all phenomena throughout the three realms and three times, which has not been seen by others through inference,
is called *anumāna* (inference).
For what reason is the cultivation of breath (*ānāpāna*) not mentioned?
Because at the time of attaining bodhi, there is nothing further with which to compare it;
nevertheless, this *anumāna* (inference) is also called *aupamya-pramāṇa* (analogy as a means of valid cognition) in the sūtras.
In its general explanation, they are one and the same.
Among these, the discernment of similar classes through comparison is called inference (*anumāna*).
Comparison of dissimilar classes is called analogy (*upamāna*).
As for authoritative testimony (*āgama*):

There are dharmas that are profound and remote, which cannot be known through one's own power but are understood by relying on the teachings; these are termed "teachings as valid cognition" (*āgama-pramāṇa*).
Within this, there are also two kinds of discernment: the first is the knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*).
Second is the knowledge of principle (*tattva*).
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), that which is known by relying on the teachings is called the knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*);
within the principles of the two truths, that which is known by relying on the teachings is called the knowledge of principle.
Within this category of scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*), it is also termed "authoritative speech" (*āptavāda*).
Generally explained, they are one and the same;
however, when distinguished within that context, those teachings which are proximate to the Dharma itself and through which one enters by means of words are called authoritative speech.
The Dharma is vast, profound, and transcendent; that which is known by relying upon the teachings is termed "scriptural authority" (*āgama-pramāṇa*).
Some divide this authority into four categories, with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) being the first.
Inference is the second;
scriptural authority is the third;
and authoritative testimony is the fourth.
This also does not constitute a fault;
it is simply that such terminology is not found in the sūtras or śāstras. Thus concludes this section on names and meanings.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished.
It is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There are three types of inference (*anumāna*).
By comparing one member of a class with another, similar phenomena are used to infer others,
as explained in the *Śata-śāstra*.
There are three distinct meanings.
The first is like a remnant:
just as when a person takes a single drop of water from the ocean and tastes it to know its saltiness, they thereby know that all the rest is likewise salty.
It is also like a person who, within a single dharma, perceives suffering, impermanence, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, and knows that all others are likewise.
In this way, everything is as it was originally.
Second, it is as in the original text.
Just as when a person has previously seen that fire is accompanied by smoke, they will certainly know that there is fire upon seeing smoke elsewhere;

likewise, just as when a person has previously perceived that all phenomena are suffering because they are impermanent, they will certainly know that phenomena are impermanent upon perceiving their suffering.
All such cases are known through common analogy. For example,
when a person sees a man moving from east to west, one infers that the sun in the heavens, which likewise moves from east to west, must also be in motion.

It is also like a person who, seeing that the nature of form (rūpa) is impermanent because it arises and ceases, subsequently sees that the other aggregates—perception (saṃjñā), feeling (vedanā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna)—also have the nature of impermanence because they likewise arise and cease.
It is thus for all of them.
These three together constitute the analogy of the similar class (*sādharmya-upamāna*).
Second is the comparison of the inferior with the superior,
such as when a country lacks gold and uses brass to represent it.
Furthermore, as in the sutras, the Buddha-nature is illustrated by means of worldly space, which is neither born nor extinguished;
all such cases are like this.
Third, the superior is compared to the inferior.
It is like a country that lacks brass and compares gold to it;
it is also like the sūtras using the analogy of the Great Nirvāṇa being neither existent nor non-existent to illustrate the king’s crime of murder.
All such cases are like this.
The subsequent two sections provide a general explanation;
they are also analogous, as they share partial similarities.
Inference is thus. Next, the authority of scripture (āgama-pramāṇa) is distinguished;
its meanings are threefold.
Regarding phenomena that exist at different times:
they are known by relying on the teachings.
For example, because past and future phenomena are not directly perceived, they are known only through verbal explanation.
Second, phenomena in other locations are known by relying on the teachings;
for instance, because matters in other realms are not directly perceived, they are known through verbal explanation.
Third is the principle of simultaneity and co-location,
which is known by relying on the teachings,
such as the explanation that the Tathāgata-nature exists within the body.
Such is the authority of scripture (*āgama*).
Within this scriptural authority, that which is known is not fixed;
for instance, profound and sublime dharmas such as the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), nirvāṇa, and the Path can only be known by relying upon scripture.
Alternatively, there are intermediate phenomena that can only be known by relying on the teachings, such as suffering and its origin;
or there are coarse and superficial phenomena that can only be known by relying on the teachings, such as matters difficult to discern within the world. These two categories are concluded.
Next is the distinction of the stages (*avasthā*).

This refers to the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣamāṇagotra*), the stage of the lineage of understanding and practice (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).
Within these stages, there are three ways of analyzing their meaning.
Beginning with the union and ending with it:
the lineage of practice (śikṣā-bīja) constitutes the first,
and the lineage of nature (prakṛti-bīja) constitutes the second.
The stages of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) and above are combined as the third [category],
because they equally contemplate suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this section, one may distinguish the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by regarding three positions collectively in relation to a single dharma.
That is to say, regarding the dharmas observed at levels above the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*),
the lineage of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣā-bīja*) is the authoritative measure (*pramāṇa*) for them;
yet they remain profound and remote from that [stage].
Because one knows through the teachings,
the nature-seed (prakṛtisthagotra) is known of that [nature] by means of inference (anumāna),
for its stages and divisions are adjacent and can thus be known by comparison.
For those above the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), their respective attainments are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are known through manifest realization.
Alternatively, one may distinguish the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by considering each single stage in relation to the three factors.
The stage of the lineage of practice (śikṣāgotra) regards the dharmas realized by itself as direct perception (pratyakṣa),
because they are known through manifest realization;
it regards the dharmas realized at the stage of the lineage of nature (prakṛtisthagotra) as inference (anumāna).
Because their respective stages are adjacent, they can be known by comparison;
however, in relation to the dharmas realized in the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā), these are the measure of scripture (āgama-pramāṇa),
for those dharmas are profound and transcendent.
In the preceding section, the shallow was taught to reveal the profound;
in this section, the shallow is revealed to clarify the profound.
Alternatively, one may consider three distinct stages in relation to three dharmas.
Looking back at the preceding three stages from one's own perspective, all that is attained is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus, direct perception encompasses both the profound and the shallow;
it opens up the middle stage to unify it with the first and the last.
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
the nature of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) and the nature of the seeds (*bījagotra*) are combined into one,
because their seeds are identical.
The practice of understanding constitutes two stages;
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are combined as the third,
because they equally realize suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this gate, one also attains three stages which collectively refer to a single dharma.
In relation to the dharma realized from the first bhūmi onward,
the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi) constitutes the measure of scripture (āgama).

The inferential cognition of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and the direct perception of the stages (*bhūmi*) also each obtain one stage when viewed individually in relation to the three dharmas,
and they also obtain three stages when viewed individually in relation to the three dharmas.
The preceding categories may be understood accordingly.
Third, the beginning of union and the end of opening:
the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) are combined into one.
Because the stage of faith is the same [as the preceding],
the ten stages constitute two [categories],
and the Buddha stage constitutes the third.
Within this gate, one may also obtain three stages that collectively refer to a single dharma;
when compared to the stage realized by the Buddha, they are named "teachings" (śāsana) prior to the grounds,
being separated from it by an abyss of profundity.
Because it is known through faith in the teaching,
that which exists on the stages (bhūmi) is called "inference" (anumāna), for one infers the Buddha based on what one has personally attained.
The stage of the Buddha is called "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*), because its nature is directly realized; it also constitutes a distinct level when compared to the three dharmas.
Furthermore, that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) when compared to the dharmas preceding those stages.
Regarding the dharmas on the ground, it is an inference (*anumāna*);
regarding what the Buddha has attained, it is scriptural authority (*āgama*).
Because it is profound and transcendent, it also possesses three stages.
The three dharmas of distinct expectation are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because they are equally perceived by direct observation.
Such are the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

108. The Meaning of the Three Paths of Identical Characteristics (10). The Meaning of the Three Paths of Identical Characteristics is explained through a twofold classification: first, the analysis of the names; second, the discernment of the essence. First, the explanation of the names.
Regarding the *Tongxiang Sandao Chudi Jinglun* (The Sūtra and Treatise on the Three Paths of Identical Characteristics), what are their names?
The first is the Path of Realization (*darśanamārga*).
Second is the path of assistance;
third is the non-abiding path.
As for what is called the path of realization:
"Realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) signifies the meaning of attaining through intimate union.
When the mind merges with true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), ceasing all discrimination and entering into union with equality,
it is called "realization."
Regarding the term "aids to the path" (*bodhipakṣa*):
"aid" carries the meaning of supporting, assisting, providing resources for, and conforming to.
The various practices, such as the perfections (*pāramitā*), mutually support one another and provide resources that conform to *bodhi*.
Therefore, it is called "assistance.
To say "not abiding" means the sense of being free from attachment.
Skillful means and wisdom proceed in tandem without partiality;
therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
These three [perfections] are all established based upon the Dharma.
Both should be termed "realization," as they equally serve to support the fruit;
both should be termed "aid," as they act together.
Transcending the mundane and distinct from the sages,
their fame is equal yet they do not abide therein;
thus, three gates are distinguished.
The three distinct sections on the different names for concealment and manifestation follow the terminology used for what is manifest;
they provide evidence for the essence of the mind.
Because the mind is pure and luminous, the meaning of the Dharma becomes manifest;
therefore, it is specifically termed "realization.
Within the suchness that is realized, there is no fruit to be obtained.
Therefore, it is not called "assistance," for the characteristics of defilement and purity have merged and the meaning of non-abiding is obscured;
thus, it is not called "non-abiding."
Because "aid" (*zhu*) carries the strong sense of being a supportive resource that accords with the practice,
it is specifically termed "aid.
As for "viewing the fruit," since the fruit can be sought and realized, its meaning is implicit.
Therefore, it is not called "realization.
Is there a seeking of emergence from what is turned away from?
The meaning of non-abiding is subtle.
Therefore, it is not called "non-abiding" [in the ordinary sense].
Because the meaning of skillful wisdom that is free from attachment is revealed,
it is specifically termed "non-abiding."
Because they wander through both defilement and purity while realizing the meaning of the hidden suchness (*tathatā*),
it is not called "realization.
They follow both defilement and purity simultaneously, rather than seeking exclusively for liberation.
Because they do not exclusively tend toward the fruit,
they are not called "aids.
These three types exist throughout all the stages (bhūmi).
This is termed "identity. The mode of being and characteristics of that identical activity are designated as "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, these are the essential characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), not the defining characteristics (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*).
His companion, Xutong, identified him as Tong.
He asked: "These three names share the same character."
The fact that seeing and cultivation are without effort is called their distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Do the realization, the aids, and so forth have distinct characteristics?
Within seeing, cultivation, and so forth, are there not common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)?
Śāriputra replied:
"There are indeed some. Which ones are they?"
As stated in the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sutra), those at or below the third stage are termed "worldly" (*laukika*).
Because they have not yet realized the Dharma,
the various practices they cultivate are judged to be aids to the Path (*mārga-sahāya*), as they provide distant support for the supramundane.
In the fourth bhūmi, one first enters the supramundane;
the internal realization of the light of the Dharma is designated as the Path of Realization (bodhimārga).
From the fifth bhūmi upward, having attained the supramundane, one is subsequently able to conform to the mundane, which is termed the Path of Non-abiding (apratisthita-mārga).
Therefore, in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is only from the fifth bhūmi onward that the excellence of the non-abiding path (*apratiṣṭhita-mārga*) is first proclaimed.
This is precisely the proof for the distinct characteristics [of the stages].
For the bodhisattva’s vision and understanding exist on every stage.
The same applies to the practice of cultivation.
The meaning of "effortlessness" (anābhoga) also encompasses both the beginning and the end.
Thus, the *Dilun* says:
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, because one abandons effort (*prayoga*) according to one's respective capacity, it is not called "defiled conduct.
This is precisely what constitutes the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of their views and so forth.
If this is so, then they are equal in both respects.
Why is it that realization and so forth are exclusively termed "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
while the paths of seeing and cultivation, despite being effortless, are exclusively termed "distinct characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)?
The commentary states:
These statements are thus because of the concealment and manifestation [of the meaning].
Since all are equally concealed and manifested, why is it that the realization and so forth are specifically termed "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
This is based on the accomplishment of virtue.
Since they all generally possess the meaning of "manifestation," they are collectively termed "identical. Why,
then, are "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and the others specifically termed "distinct"?
This is based on the characteristics of cultivation:
from the arising of cultivation through understanding, to its maturation and the relinquishing of effort,
the distinctions between the stages become manifest.
Therefore, they are designated separately.
Why is it that *sākṣātkriyā* (realization) and so forth are exclusively based on perfected qualities (*guṇa*)?
Why is it that *darśana* (vision) and so forth are exclusively characteristics of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
The commentary states:
Among the three paths of the same characteristic (*sādharmya*), the path of realization (*darśanamārga*) is primary.
The auxiliary [factors] and non-abiding are explained in reliance upon this realization.
Therefore, this constitutes the perfection of virtue.
Among the three distinct characteristics, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is primary;
from seeing, cultivation (bhāvanā) arises.
One cultivates beyond the previous views;
when the cultivation of the mind has long been pure, it then becomes effortless.
Effortlessness transcends cultivation.
Because they arise in successive stages, they are called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Since the characteristics of this cultivation proceed through gradual steps, they are termed "distinctive characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Since their accomplishment and their virtue occur simultaneously, they are called "identical characteristics.
Such are the names and meanings; this first section is concluded.
Next, the essential nature and characteristics are distinguished.
Generally speaking, all take the true mind as their essence;
yet, when differentiated within this context, there are indeed no differences.
What is the nature of these distinct characteristics?
That which realizes the essence of the Way is the true-consciousness mind (*tathatā-vijñāna-citta*).
Within the essence of this mind, all the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are fully present.
That which is called the Dharma-realm consists of such dharmas as permanence, bliss, self, purity, wisdom, samādhi, and liberation.
When one gathers these dharmas with the mind, they do not transcend the single mind;
yet, according to the differentiation of these dharmas, the mind is divided into as many distinct parts as there are atoms within the Dharma-realm.
The mind illuminates those phenomena as being of the same essence, pure and free from the obscuration of darkness.
Although its nature is eternally pure, it appears impure due to delusory defilements;
subsequently, one cultivates remedies to extinguish and eliminate these taints.
The originally hidden pure mind becomes manifest, thereby perfecting its virtues.
First, the pure virtue is revealed; like the nature of sweet-tasting ginseng, it internally illuminates the dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is called "realization."
This is indeed spontaneous, non-discriminative illumination, not illumination dependent on conditions.
As for the essence of the auxiliary path,
it refers to the six *pāramitās* involving effortful cultivation.
What is the meaning of this?
When one practices the antidotes and manifests realization as previously described, one fully cultivates all practices of the dharma-realm.
Because these practices permeate the true mind, the true virtues within the mind gather and arise; thus, they are called "auxiliaries to the path."
Regarding the essence of non-abiding,
there are briefly three types.
The first clarifies non-abiding from the perspective of contemplative understanding.
Second, based on practice and cultivation;
third, regarding the qualities of the fruition.
As for what is called "contemplative understanding":
The Bodhisattva contemplates that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
Because he perceives them as not existent, he does not cling to the extreme of existence; because he perceives them as not non-existent, he does not cling to the extreme of non-existence.
Because one does not abide with partiality or attachment toward either existence or non-existence,
it is called "non-abiding.
As for the practice of conduct:
There are three distinct meanings.
First, by contrasting realization with its auxiliaries, it clarifies that the practice of realization does not abide and that auxiliary practices involve active engagement.
It assists while constantly realizing, yet does not abide exclusively in activity;
it realizes while constantly assisting, yet does not abide exclusively in quiescence.
Because it moves freely between both quiescence and activity without abiding in attachment, it is called "non-abiding."
Second, it clarifies non-abiding by focusing specifically on realization.
Because one realizes the equality of reality such that there is no dharma in which to abide,
it is called "non-abiding."
Therefore, in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), that which is called the "path like walking" is termed the "non-abiding path.
The third [section] clarifies non-abiding specifically by way of its auxiliaries;
herein there are three parts.
The first is the classification of the two practices of benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
Because a bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the practice of benefiting oneself, they do not abide among ordinary worldlings;
because they cultivate the practice of benefiting others, they do not abide among those of the two vehicles.
Therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
Second, it is explained in terms of one's own practice of merit and wisdom;
merit follows along with the arising of existence.
Wisdom relies on non-existence,
yet because one cultivates merit, one does not abide in non-existence;
because one cultivates wisdom, one does not cling to existence.
Therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
Third, one should clarify non-abiding with reference to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
as in a single act of giving, one does not perceive the giver, the recipient, the material gift, or the karmic fruit, and thus remains unattached to existence.
One always practices giving by relying on three things and does not abide in non-existence;
therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
As it is with giving, so it is with all else.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise.
These latter three gates are combined to form the meaning of "aiding non-abiding.
The preceding section clarified non-abiding by way of the aids to realization.
Next, [the text] treats the realization exclusively and then treats the aids exclusively;
these together constitute the second section on the practice of non-abiding.
Within the third section, it speaks of clarifying non-abiding by way of the qualities of the fruit.
This means that the Buddha-Tathāgata has attained Great Nirvāṇa while not abandoning the world.
Because he has attained Nirvāṇa, he does not abide within the conditioned phenomena of saṃsāra;
because he does not abandon the world, he does not abide within the unconditioned phenomenon of quiescent extinction.
Therefore, it is called "non-abiding.
This concludes the rough explanation of the three paths according to their common characteristics.

109. The Meaning of the Three Paths According to Their Distinct Characteristics (10): An Exposition through Three Gates. I. Defining the Stages; II. Discerning the Characteristics; III. The Three Paths According to Their Distinct Characteristics as they appear in the *Sūtra* and the *Śāstra*.
It may also be termed the three paths distinguished by their stages.
What are these names? First, the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
Second is cultivation;
third is effortlessness.
Regarding the first, it says "seeing."
The discerning mind that investigates and clarifies is called "view" (darśana).
Progressing in practice is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
When the cultivated mind becomes long-term, pure, and spontaneously ascendant, resting from its engagement with objects, it is called "effortlessness" (anābhoga).
These three types differ according to their respective stages;
this is termed "distinction.
The specific modes of activity and essential characteristics are designated as "marks" (lakṣaṇa).
These three modes of practice, being universally pervasive, are called the "Path.
Because these three are differentiated,
they are also termed the "Three Paths of Distinct Stages."
The section on names is thus concluded. Next is the section on the determination of stages (*avasthā-viniścaya*).
According to the actual state, this is discussed in general terms.
All stages possess these three; however, according to their specific characteristics, they are categorized as being situated in the supramundane.
There are two types of the supramundane.
First, from the first bhūmi upward, it is called "supramundane.
Second, according to the characteristics of the stages, it is only from the fourth bhūmi upward that it is called "supramundane.
Within the first of these two approaches, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the first bhūmi is further divided into its major sections.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
"Those bound by views abandon them at the time of the path of seeing within the first stage (*bhūmi*);
from the second stage upward through the seventh stage constitutes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)."
From the eighth stage upward, it is called "effortless" (*anābhoga*).
When analyzed in detail according to reality, vision is of two kinds:
first, vision as an object-condition (*ālambana-dṛṣṭi*).
At the final moment of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Those bound by views are severed during the stage of practice through understanding."
The second is realization through vision,
occurring at the initial moment of the first bhūmi.
The path of cultivation also has two [aspects].
The first is the practice of cultivation (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*), which occurs at the fulfillment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* (Stages of Yogic Practice) proclaims the first stage as the "pure mind" (*viśuddha-citta*) and the "initial practice of wisdom" (*prathama-prajñā-caryā*).
The second is correct cultivation,
which occurs from the second bhūmi upward;
within this state of effortlessness, there are likewise two kinds.
The practice of effortlessness occurs within the seventh stage;
thus, it is proclaimed in the *Bhūmi-sūtra* that one cultivates effortlessness in the seventh stage.
The second is the accomplishment of effortlessness;
from the eighth stage upward, it is similar in meaning to the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The initial practice of non-arising occurs within the seventh bhūmi;
the perfection of non-arising is achieved from the eighth bhūmi onward.
Such is the first gate.
In the second section on the broad classification of stages,
the initial entry into the supramundane within the fourth stage is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, in the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā Sūtra* (Renwang jing), the fourth stage is designated as *srotāpanna*.
Furthermore, the *Dìjīng* (Śrāvakabhūmi) states:
"With the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as the foremost,

all matters such as the arising and ceasing of the conceit of 'I,' 'person,' 'sentient being,' the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are completely abandoned in the fourth stage."
From the fifth stage upward, it is categorized as the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga);
from the eighth stage upward, it is termed effortless (anābhoga).
When strictly subdivided according to reality, there are two types of vision (darśana).
First, the cultivation of insight occurs at the final moment of mind in the third stage,
wherein one contemplates that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, but exist through causes and conditions.
Second, the perfection of insight occurs within the fourth stage.
One correctly views all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing.
There are also two types of cultivation:
the first is the cultivation of practice, which occurs at the final moment of mind in the fourth stage.
First, one exerts diligent effort within the practice of skillful means;
second, correct cultivation occurs on the five stages [of the path],
wherein the two types [of cultivation] within the state of non-effort are as described above.
However, within the sūtras and śāstras, the classification and synthesis of the stages (bhūmi), as well as their progression and regression, are not uniform.
Sometimes the former are expanded while the latter are condensed; sometimes the latter are expanded while the former are condensed.
Alternatively, one may open up the middle [category] to merge it with the preceding and following ones.
For now, based on a single approach, these three have been divided.
Such are the distinctions between the stages; this concludes the two gates.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished.
There are two kinds of seeing:
first, habitual seeing.
The first is the study and contemplation of reality within the stage of practice through understanding;
the second is the perfection of vision,
which refers to the manifestation of true contemplation within the first bhūmi.
There are two aspects to this accomplishment.
First is the internal realization:
upon first entering the first stage (bhūmi), one clearly realizes and illuminates the dharma of selflessness within one's own sphere of realization.
Second is superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

This refers to the practice of ascending through the stages above the first stage, wherein one clearly discerns the attainment and loss of cultivation, just as in the first stage, such as the fruit of setting forth (*prasthāna-phala*) and so forth.
The cultivation of the path also has two aspects. The first is the cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*),
which refers to the generation of various great vows and the practice of ethical discipline and so forth within the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Second is correct cultivation,
which refers to the practice of the precepts and so forth on the second bhūmi and above.
Within "correct" there are two [aspects].
First is gradual cultivation;
second is sudden cultivation.
Regarding gradual cultivation:
This refers to the five modes of superior progress from the second bhūmi up to the sixth bhūmi.
Regarding these "five modes," they are as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Grounds of Bodhisattva Practice).
On the second stage, one cultivates ethical discipline;
on the third stage, one practices meditative concentration;
and on the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one cultivates wisdom.
Wisdom is of three kinds.
First is the wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment,
which is cultivated throughout the four stages.
Second, the wisdom associated with the two truths,
which is practiced in the five stages;
third, the wisdom associated with dependent origination.
These are the trainings of the sixth stage.
When combined with the preceding [stages], they constitute five practices.
Because these five arise progressively, they are called "gradual cultivation."
Regarding "simultaneous cultivation," this refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), wherein all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) arise instantaneously in every moment of thought.
Within this state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), there are likewise two kinds.
First is the practice of effortlessness,
which occurs within the seventh stage;
therefore, the treatise states:
On the seventh stage, one cultivates effortlessness.
Second is maturation,
which occurs from the eighth stage upward.
Within the stage of completion, there are also two aspects.
The first is the "natural" (svabhāva),
which refers to the maturation of the fruition and practice within the eighth stage.
Second is superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).
This refers to the spontaneous orientation toward unsurpassed enlightenment through the encouragement of all Buddhas within the stream of the Dharma on the stages from the eighth upward.
Within this superior progress, all practices arise in their entirety.
Now, according to the characteristics of the stages, they are briefly divided into three types:
first, in the eight stages, one achieves the bodily karma of being born through transformation in a pure land;
second, in the ninth stage, one achieves the verbal karma of benefiting beings through eloquence.
Within the thirty stages (*triṃśad-bhūmi*), one attains the accomplishment of mental action through the practice of profound wisdom.
The specific characteristics of the three paths have been explained in brief.

110. The Meaning of the Three Kinds of Abiding (10). Regarding the meaning of the three kinds of abiding, there is an analysis and explanation according to two gates: first, the definition of the names; second, the discernment of their characteristics. The meaning of the three kinds of abiding is derived from the *Śrīghana-bhūmi-śāstra* (*Chizhidi-lun*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also provides a detailed analysis of this.
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) is named according to its locus;
however, the meanings of "abiding" differ.
Three are taught within a single category.
What are these three?
The first is the noble abiding.
The second is the Brahma-abode;
the third is the Deva-abode.
As for what is called the Noble Abode:
The realization that accords with reality is called "sagehood" (ārya).
Because the sage serves as a refuge for others,
it is termed the "abode of the sage" (āryavihāra).
Furthermore, the "Noble Ones" (ārya) are those who are sages (arhat).
That which is the basis for the noble ones is called the "noble abode" (āryavihāra).
As for what are called the "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra):
Pure conduct is called "Brahma.
Since Brahma is the refuge for humans,
it is termed a "Brahma-abode" (brahmavihāra).
Furthermore, the noble ones who are free from desire are called "Brahmā.
The dwelling place of Brahmā is termed the "Brahma-abode.
As for what is called the "divine abode":
Because they possess the dharmas of the eight dhyāna heavens, they are called "devas.
The devas are the support for humans.
It is called the "abode of devas" (*devasthāna*).
Alternatively, the noble ones (*ārya*) themselves are the pure devas;
the dwelling place of these devas is therefore called the "abode of devas."
Question: Why are the abodes of humans, ghosts, animals, and so forth not mentioned?
Explanation:
There is no harm in explaining this in general terms, as it is not superior and thus is not discussed here.
Such is the meaning of the name; this concludes this section.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished;
though their opening and closing are indeterminate,
they are summarized as one.
That is to say, among the seven kinds of unsurpassedness, there is the unsurpassedness of abiding;
this may be divided into two:
the first is mundane.
Second is the supramundane.
The Brahma-abodes and the Heavenly abodes are mundane;
the Noble abode is exclusively supramundane.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three;
the names of these three are as mentioned above.
Within this, there are briefly three points of explanation and interpretation.
First, distinguishing by way of the fruit:
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
the six heavens of the desire realm are called the "abodes of devas."
The gods of the form and formless realms are called the Brahma-abodes because they are free from sensual desire.
The noble dharmas of nirvāṇa are called the Noble Abodes.
Second, the classification according to causes is also as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
wholesome acts such as giving, observing precepts, and prostrating are called the "abodes of devas."
Because they can attain the fruits of the six heavens of the desire realm;
the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the four immeasurables are called the Brahma-abodes because they enable one to attain the Brahma-worlds of the higher realms.
These form and formless realms are collectively termed "Brahma.
The three types of samādhi and so forth are termed "noble abodes" (āryavihāra).
These three are distinguished according to their practice.
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*,
the meditative concentrations of the eight dhyāna stages are called "divine abodes" (*devasthāna*),
because they serve as their basis.
The four immeasurable minds are called the Brahma-abodes,
because by means of these four practices, one is free from faults and purified throughout all births.
Those three samādhis and the attainment of cessation are called the Noble Abodes.
Because these are the bases upon which the noble ones rely,
the latter three abodes of nirvāṇa are called the "dwellings of the three practices.
This carries the same meaning as "places of residence."
Alternatively, they may be divided into four,
as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is by adding one further stage to the previous three, making four in total.
As that treatise states:
"The immeasurable samādhis such as Śūraṅgama,
as well as the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, unique qualities, and so forth."
All Buddha-dharmas are collectively termed the "abodes of the Buddha" (buddhavihāra).
Alternatively, they may be divided into sixteen;
among those, the divine abodes (devavihāra) include eight meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi).
These are thus counted as eight.
Including the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) within the Brahma realm, they total twelve.
There are four noble abodes,
namely the three samādhis and the attainment of cessation;
together with the preceding sixteen, they constitute twenty.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,

among these sixteen [abodes], the Tathāgata dwells most frequently in the fourth dhyāna within the celestial abodes (*devasthāna*), which are four of the unsurpassed abodes (*anuttaravihāra*). This is because in the three lower dhyānas,
wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is deficient.
In the four formless attainments of the higher realms, wisdom is generally deficient while concentration is predominant;
because concentration and wisdom are uneven,
their functioning does not accord with one's intention, and therefore one does not dwell in them for long.
Only in the fourth dhyāna are concentration and wisdom equal in their function, which accords with the mind;
therefore, one dwells in it frequently.
For this reason, the Tathāgata attained initial enlightenment and entered parinirvāṇa therein.
They all dwell extensively within the four dhyānas and the divine abodes (brahmavihāras).
The Tathāgata of Great Compassion constantly keeps in mind sentient beings who suffer;
with great compassion, he is able to uproot their afflictions.
Therefore, he dwells much therein;
among the noble ones, he dwells much in the gate of the emptiness samādhi and in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This is because the emptiness samādhi is supreme among those characterized by detachment, and the attainment of cessation is the ultimate limit of tranquility.
Therefore, one dwells in these extensively;
according to their meaning, the classifications of dwelling are immeasurable.
For now, based on a single approach, we shall discuss three types.
The third dwelling is thus.
*Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Ten ends;
*Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Eleven begins.

In the *Jingfa ju yinfa* (The Collection of Pure Dharmas: Causes and Conditions) compiled by Master Daoyuan, this fascicle contains nineteen sections: 1. The meaning of the four stages of the mind, beginning with *uṣmagata* (Heat); 2. The meaning of the four reliances for persons; 3. The meaning of the four reliances regarding the Dharma;

4. The meaning of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*); 5. The meaning of the four types of reverent practice; 6. The meaning of the four practices for transforming karma; 7. The meaning of the four meditative cultivations (*dhyāna*); 8. The meaning of the four kinds of indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*); 9. The meaning of the four firmnesses (*thāma*); 10. The meaning of the fourfold path; 11. The meaning of the four kinds of wholesome dharmas; 12. The meaning of the four kinds of flavors (*rasa*); 13. The meaning of the four bases of virtue (*guṇasthāna*); 14. The meaning of the four kinds of seeking knowledge; 15. The meaning of the four *dhāraṇīs*; 16. The meaning of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); 17. The meaning of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); 18. The meaning of the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva; 19. The meaning of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
111. The Meaning of the Four Minds, such as *ūṣmagata* (Heat), etc. (1-1) Regarding these four minds, such as *ūṣmagata*, there is a detailed analysis in six sections:

1. Explanation of their names; 2. Determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); 3. Discernment of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); 4. Analysis of their combinations and expansions or contractions; 5. Distinction based on duration; 6. Distinction according to the realms (*dhātu*). First, the explanation of their names.
"Heat," "Summits," "Patience," and "the Supreme Mundane Dharmas" are their names.
As for what is called "Heat," it is named after a metaphor.
The untainted [state] is like fire.
These roots of goodness, when cultivated through the contemplation of principles,
attain the characteristic of that fire and are called "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
That which is called "summit" (mūrdhan) is also designated by way of a metaphor;
it is like the peaks of worldly mountains, which are referred to as "summits."
Because this wholesome state exists above the level of "Heat" (uṣmagata), it is called "Summit" (mūrdhan). Question:
Among the four grades of wholesome roots, such as Heat and so forth, the Dharma-Summit is a sequential dharma; it is not the ultimate.
Why is it called "Summit"?
The explanation states:
among the roots of goodness, there are those that are subject to regression and those that are not.
The first two are mobile because they are subject to regression;
the latter two are immobile.
Because it is irreversible.
The "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is the ultimate point within movement,
like a mountain peak from which rivers diverge.
Therefore, it is called "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). Question:
Why is the ultimate state of immovability not itself designated as the Summit?
Because that which he received was the foremost among them.
It is asked:
how can those of great and small virtue and rank stand side by side?
As Nāgārjuna said:
"The first stage of a bodhisattva is called the 'Summit' (mūrdhan).
The final moment of mind in the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā) is called 'Falling from the Summit' (mūrdha-pāta)."
If those minor degrees of patience regarding suffering were to be abandoned before they could be called "Summits," why is it now said that the worldly roots of goodness are the Summits?
The explanation is as follows:
The meaning of "summit" (mūrdhan) is not restricted to the upper or lower [stages].
All practices that, according to their respective degrees, surpass what preceded them may be termed "summits.
This is because the term is not restricted.
The categories of "great" and "small" are analogous; the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) possesses the sense of being "at the summit" within the mundane realm,
and the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) likewise possesses the sense of being "at the summit" regarding the supramundane,
because both possess these qualities.
According to Nāgārjuna’s treatise, the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) is spoken of in terms of the supramundane stage of non-retrogression;
whereas in the Hīnayāna, it is defined as the ultimate limit of mundane virtue from which one may still fall back.
What is called "patience" (kṣānti) is named according to its characteristic:
the mind of wisdom abides in the Dharma.
Therefore, it is called "patience" (kṣānti).
Generally speaking, all four [stages] are indeed patience;
however, this specifically clarifies the meaning of being established in the beginning of immovability.
Therefore, it is specifically termed "patience" (*kṣānti*).
As for "the supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*):
it is a designation highlighting its excellence; because this wholesome state is the most superior within the world, it is called "supreme."
However, within these four types of *Vibhāṣā*, there are four distinct names:
first, "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
second, "contemplation of the truths" (*satyadarśana*).
The third is called cultivation and purification;
the fourth is called roots of goodness,
as explained in that treatise.
Regarding the term "factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): the supramundane noble wisdom that penetrates and thoroughly perceives the principles of the truths is called "penetration."
These four roots of goodness are of the same nature as that [nirvedha-bhāgīya];
therefore, they are called "parts leading to penetration" (nirvedha-bhāgīya). As for the phrase "contemplating the truths":
Prior to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one has not yet contemplated the principles of the truths (satya).

From this stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and above, one contemplates the four truths by means of the sixteen aspects (ākāra) such as impermanence; therefore, it is called "contemplation of the truths" (satyālambana-vipaśyanā).
Regarding "cultivation and purification":
it refers to cultivating and purifying the vessel of the body in order to seek the noble path and the fruit of the noble path,
just as a worldly farmer cultivates and cleanses a field in order to seek the grain of seed.
Therefore, it is called "cultivation and purification.
As for the term "roots of goodness," the Noble Path is what is meant by "good."
Nirvana is the wholesome fruit;
the four stages beginning with "heat" (ūṣmagata) are its initial foundation,
and are therefore called "wholesome roots" (kuśalamūla).
Furthermore, these four kinds of pliancy are called "wholesome" (kuśala).
Because they can give rise to the Noble Path (āryamārga),
they are termed "faculties" (indriya).
The names and meanings are thus.
In the second section, its essential nature is analyzed;
therein are two parts.
The Dharma of the One-Minded Differentiation:
According to the Abhidharma, these four roots of goodness are defined by their essence as wisdom (*prajñā*).
They consist of the wisdom directed toward the Four Noble Truths that are being investigated.
If one discusses its retinue, it has the nature of the five aggregates:
this wisdom is associated with feeling, which constitutes the category of feeling; it is associated with perception, which constitutes the category of perception.
The mind-king constitutes consciousness;
the remaining factors constitute formations;
and the precepts associated with meditative concentration constitute the aggregate of form.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, these four are also of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*);
their preceding and succeeding attendants are subsumed solely within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
If one speaks of remote conditions, they are of the nature of all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Second, the distinction between that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). According to the Abhidharma, it is exclusively with outflows,
because it can only suppress the fetters (*saṃyojana*) but cannot permanently sever them.
Furthermore, because they are the path of skillful means for noble wisdom,
within the *Tattvasiddhi*, these four roots of goodness are seen as directly perceiving the principle of emptiness;
their nature is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because they possess mixed characteristics,
they are also called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
Such is their essential nature.
Third, the differentiation of characteristics.
This contains four parts.
First, the distinction based on the object.
Second, there is a distinction in the contemplation of the mind;
third, there is inequality in the arising of understanding;
fourth, there is a difference in the remediation of hindrances.
Regarding the summary of the objects of focus: as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*,
one contemplates the five aggregates as suffering, impermanent, and so forth.
It is called "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Contemplating the virtues of the Triple Gem is called "Summit" (mūrdhan).
Contemplating the Four Noble Truths is called "Patience" (kṣānti).
To observe only the suffering of the body is called the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
In reality, these four [preparatory stages] all contemplate the Four Noble Truths;
they are merely designated as such for the sake of distinguishing their respective differences. This concludes this section.
Regarding the "distinctions in contemplation":
although these four types equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths, there are differences in the degree of their mental observation;
therefore, there are four distinct varieties.
What is the meaning of this?
According to the Abhidharma, there are thirty-two categories when classifying the elements (*dhātu*) of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
"Elements" refers here to the three realms.
The practitioner's so-called sixteen noble practices consist of suffering, impermanence, and so forth.
Within the stages of the desire realm there are these sixteen practices;
it is the same for the higher realms.
When explained comprehensively according to the higher and lower stages, there are thirty-two;
the correct observation within each individual stage is termed "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
When the contemplation is not yet clear, it is called the "aid to warmth" (*uṣmagata-prayoga*);
when the mind of contemplation becomes distinct, it is called the "attainment of warmth.
Such is the nature of the dharma of warmth.
Contemplating the coming and going within each individual mental state and gradually abbreviating it until one reaches contemplation with a single mind is called the "Summit" (mūrdhan).
That which precedes this single-minded contemplation is called the "Preparatory Means" (prayoga).
Contemplating with a single mind at the end is called "accomplishment.
Although this contemplation within the heart of the summit gradually becomes abbreviated, it is still considered a complete observation when compared to the Four Noble Truths and the sixteen aspects.
It is not called "abbreviated.
However, this established state is each a single-mind observation that resembles the initial observation within the subsequent stage of Patience (*kṣānti*),
just as the Supreme Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) resembles the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: It would be better for the roots of goodness to increase gradually;
why is it necessary to be concise?
The commentary states:
When first observing many minds, even with repeated application of the conditions, it is still not clear;
however, when observing the mind subsequently with purely few conditions, one sees it immediately.
Therefore, it is diminished. Such is the nature of the Peak Dharma (*mūrdha*).
Next, the Dharma of Patience (*kṣānti*) is distinguished.
One contemplates each of the thirty-two lines of those upper and lower realms with single-minded attention;
even down to the contemplation of the single line of suffering in the lowest part of the desire realm, this is described as "patience" (kṣānti).
Within this stage of patience, there are thirty-two cycles of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the first cycle, one contemplates each individual practice with single-minded focus; first, one contemplates the four lower modes of suffering within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Next, one contemplates the suffering of the higher realms;
subsequently, one contemplates the origin of the desire realm through the four aspects of the lower [realms],
followed by the origin of the higher realms, and so on, until one contemplates the path.
The same applies to the other categories;
each involves four modes of contemplation.
This is the second round.
In the third round, one omits two lines from below the path of the upper realm and observes the remainder.
Proceeding in this manner by degrees until finally one contemplates only two aspects of the suffering of the desire realm—
either suffering and impermanence, or emptiness and non-self—
from the beginning until this point of contemplating only these two aspects of the suffering of the desire realm is called the "preparatory stage of patience" (*kṣānti-upāya*).
Observing only a single aspect is called the accomplishment of patience (*kṣānti*).
Previously, one observed the mind directly and briefly within the crown of the head;
now, in this stage of patience, both object and subject are briefly withdrawn.
Question: Since it would be better to contemplate the dharmas of the truths extensively, why is it necessary to provide a brief *vibhāṣā*? It says:
For example, it is like a wealthy man who wishes to travel to another land;
because his wealth and goods are so vast that he cannot carry them away, he exchanges his wealth for money, yet still finding the amount of money excessive, he further exchanges it for gold.
It is like one who, fearing that his gold is excessive, uses the gold to purchase a precious gem of great value and carries it away, leaving the earth and dust behind.
The practitioner is just like this:
desiring to enter the supramundane path from the mundane world.
First, one abandons the many successions of outflow-tainted minds and gives rise to the higher patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Because it takes only a single aspect as its object, it is easy to enter the Noble Path;
therefore, this is summarized.
The Dharma of Patience is thus.
Next, the first stage is distinguished.
Following the Supreme Patience, one again gives rise to a single moment of mind that takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object.
Only that which takes a single aspect as its object is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma).
Because it consists of a single moment of mind, there is no further distinction in the means by which it is accomplished.
In the Abhidharma it is thus; in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is stated directly:
When the practitioner observes the five aggregates through the practice of impermanence and gives rise to the knowledge of nirvāṇa,
the inferior stage is called "Heat" (uṣmagata) and the middling stage is called "Summit" (mūrdhan).
The superior stage is called "patience" (kṣānti);
the superior-of-the-superior stage is called the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma).
This does not clarify the distinctions between the four types of observed characteristics.
Now, let us explain this according to its meaning.

Within the initial stage of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma, one first uses the wisdom that observes the present five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of karmic retribution as being impermanent and lacking a fixed nature;
by means of this, one analogically knows that the same is true for the past and the future.
Next, one contemplates that the present collection likewise arises and ceases, lacking any intrinsic nature;
the past and future are the same.
Next, one contemplates that the present cessation is established through dependence and relativity, lacking any fixed nature.
The same applies to the past and the future.
Later, one contemplates that the present path is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and devoid of intrinsic nature;
the past and future are likewise identical.
In the second summit, one first contemplates that the truths of suffering and its causes are provisional and lack intrinsic nature.
By means of this, one infers that the past and future are likewise so.
The contemplations of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path are similarly applied.

Previously, one observed that phenomena arise from suffering and impermanence as processes of birth and cessation, analyzing the nature of dharmas through their numerical divisions and modes of disintegration.
Now, observation becomes even more superior, for by clarifying the principle that causes and conditions are provisional and false, one realizes that dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
Within the third stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one first contemplates in general that all phenomena of the three periods of time are provisional and devoid of intrinsic nature;
the same applies to the contemplations of origination, cessation, and the path.
Previously, at the beginning of the contemplation, one contemplated the three periods of time individually.
Now, the "superior observation of the turning" is the collective observation of the three periods of time.
Within the "Supreme Mundane Dharma," one collectively observes the four truths across the three periods as being merely provisional.
This is because this collective observation serves as the skillful means for the collective vision of the emptiness of phenomena within the signless state.
The detailed examination of these two gates is thus concluded.
Regarding the distinction in the arising of understanding,
it is as stated in the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*.
In the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one first takes the Truths as an object and is able to produce lower clarity;
in the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), middle clarity is produced; and in the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), superior clarity is produced.
Because the illumination of the truths (satya) serves as the object within this body, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) arises; thus concludes the section on these three gates.
Next, the treatment of the obstacles is explained, as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*.
The stage of Heat first takes the Truths as its object and is able to suppress the delusions of the higher realms;
the stage of Summits suppresses the delusions of the middle realms;
and the stage of Patience suppresses the delusions of the lower realms. Because these delusions within the body have been suppressed, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas arise.
The manifestation of these characteristics is thus; this concludes the four gates.
Fourth, the explanation of their opening and closing, as well as their expansion and abbreviation:
these four roots of goodness, taken collectively, constitute the single root of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Alternatively, they are divided into two,
as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*:
first, the movement of the roots of goodness.
The second is immovable.
The former two are movable because they are subject to regression.
Furthermore, because mixed wholesome states of the desire realm arise,
the latter two are immovable,
as they cannot be lost.
Furthermore, because it does not arise mixed with the wholesome states of the desire realm,
it is sometimes divided into three types,
as explained in the *Vibhāṣā*.
That is to say: inferior, intermediate, and superior.
"Heat" (ūṣmagata) is called inferior;
"Summits" (mūrdhan) is called intermediate.
Patience (*kṣānti*) and the first [dharma] are taught as the higher levels (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Alternatively, they are divided into four;
"Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is designated as the lower level.
The "Summit" is called the middle;
"Patience" is called the superior;
and the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" are called the most superior.
Alternatively, they are divided into nine types,
as explained in the *Vibhāṣā*.
There are three levels of the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
These are the lower-lower, the lower-middle, and the lower-upper.
The Dharma of the Summit (mūrdha-dharma) has three grades:
namely, the middle-lower, the middle-middle, and the middle-upper.
The Dharma of Patience has two types:
namely, the lower-upper and the upper-middle.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma has only one type.
This is what is called "the most excellent.
Furthermore, in that same treatise, there is another statement:
"The stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) is of two kinds."
These are the lower-lower and the lower-middle.
There are three types of the Peak Dharma (mūrdha):
namely, the lower-upper, the middle-lower, and the middle-middle.
The Dharma of Patience (kṣānti) is of three types:
namely, medium-superior, superior-inferior, and superior-medium.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is of only one type.
What is called "the highest of the high" may be divided into ten;
the first three each have their own distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior.
Among the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), its single category is common to the preceding ten.
Regarding the three [levels] within "Heat" (*uṣmagata*):
one begins to contemplate the thirty-two aspects of the Four Truths, yet has not yet seen them.
To name them: dull perception is the inferior;
obscured perception is the middling;
and clear perception is the superior.
Regarding the three levels within the "summit" (*mūrdhan*):
among those various meditations on formations with multiple mental states, the first, which is a brief single observation,
is called the "lower" (*mṛdu*).
Briefly omitting those from the second onwards, up to the thirty-two modes of practice, each with three moments of contemplation is explained as the middling;
each with two moments of contemplation is explained as the superior.
Regarding the three levels within patience (*kṣānti*):
first, to contemplate each of the thirty-two practices with single-minded focus is termed "inferior" (*mṛdu*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Contemplating the practice of suffering in the desire realm up to the practice of the path in the higher realms through thirty-two moments of mind is called 'lower patience' (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
Within these thirty-two practices, after omitting one..."
Even down to the lower stage of suffering within that desire realm,
observing only two aspects of practice is called medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*).
Within this medium patience, there are at most thirty-one moments of mind.
When there are at least two moments of mind, and the lower [aspect] of the suffering of the desire realm takes only one category as its object,
this is called "higher patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* says:
Furthermore, contemplating the suffering of the desire realm with a single mind is called "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti).
Within the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma), there is only this single moment of mind;
there are no further varieties.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eighteen, as Ghoṣaka says;
the first two roots of goodness are termed "shaking."
Within this movement, there are nine distinct grades,
beginning from the lowest-lowest up to the highest-highest.
Among these nine grades, the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) consists of three grades.
Within the stage of the summit (mūrdhan), there are six;
the latter two roots of goodness are called "immovable" (akampya).
Within these immovable states, there are likewise nine grades.
Beginning from the lowest-of-the-low up to the highest-of-the-high,
within these nine grades, there are eight grades of patience (*kṣānti*),
while the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is only the highest-of-the-high.
When explained by combining the preceding and following [categories], there are eighteen;
yet when subdivided according to their specific meanings, they are infinite.
The opening and closing are as described above.
Regarding the distinction between long and short within the fifth gate,
it is as explained in the *Vibhāṣā*.
The roots of goodness of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* are exclusively continuous;
within the stage of *kṣānti*, they are either continuous or consist of a single moment.
The middle and lower levels of patience consist of a succession of many moments,
whereas the superior level of patience is restricted to a single moment.
The supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is likewise restricted to a single moment.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the four stages beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) all continue in succession,
because a single moment of mind cannot fully contemplate the Four Noble Truths.
The length and brevity are as such.
Within the sixth section, there is an analysis according to the realms (*dhātu*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
The proponents of various treatises differ, their explanations being each distinct.
According to the Venerable Dharmatrāta, the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth are subsumed solely within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possesses the wisdom that universally conditions all objects and can contemplate the Four Noble Truths of both the higher and lower realms,

the wholesome intermediate states of the form realm are categorized as either "mobile" (*iñjita*) or "immobile" (*aniñjita*). Among those that are mobile, the inferior grade is designated as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
The superior [level] is called "Summit" (mūrdhan).
Among the intermediate and inferior [levels], that which is explained is called "Patience" (kṣānti).
The superior [level] is called "First" (prathama).
For what reason is it not included within the desire realm?
Because, according to that school, there is absolutely no meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm;
since [the path] cannot arise through cultivation based upon it, it is not so included.
For what reason is it not included within the formless realm?
Because within the formless realm there is no wisdom that universally conditions [all objects],
and thus one cannot contemplate the four noble truths of the lower realms.
That mind is weak; therefore, it is not pervasive.
Thus says the Venerable Ghoṣaka.
These [levels of] heat and so forth are comprised within the desire realm and the form realm,
not the formless realm;
thus it is said.
The desire realm also possesses the six dhyāna concentrations;
because they can be cultivated and arise therein,
they are included within the desire realm.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) can be known.
That which is subsumed under the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) is called "movement" (cala).
Among these movements, the lowest is designated as "warmth" (uṣmagata).
The highest is called the Peak (mūrdhan).
That which is subsumed under the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is called the Imperturbable (āniñjya).
Within the Imperturbable, the lower grade is termed Patience (kṣānti).
The "upper" is called the first.
For what reason is it not included within the formless realm (*ārūpya*)?
This is as explained previously.
The Saṃmitīya school asserts that it is subsumed within the three realms;
this is what they say.
The desire realm possesses meditative concentrations;
because they are cultivated and arise in dependence upon them, they are subsumed within the desire realm.
The form realm may be understood in the same way.
In the formless realm (*ārūpya*), one is able to fully contemplate the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is included within the formless [attainments].
