The name is not an object of the world.
As for what is called "supremely wholesome," its conduct and virtue are as profound and vast as the dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is called "superior.
Regarding the phrase "due to being wholesome":
wholesome conduct of aspiration can serve as the cause for both permanent fruits and impermanent fruits.
Therefore, it is said that they are caused by the wholesome.
As for the term "constant fruit," it refers to Great Nirvāṇa.
Regarding "impermanent results":
this refers to the compassionate activity of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
because it arises and ceases in accordance with the world, it is called impermanent.
These two are none other than the two kinds of adornment found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
"Constant" corresponds to the adornment of wisdom;
thus, that sūtra says:
The adornment of wisdom is unimpeded and eternally abiding;
impermanence is the adornment of its merits.
Therefore, that sutra says:
The adornment of merit is obstructed and impermanent.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are impermanent together with the permanent, and permanent together with the impermanent."
This is a permanent fruit that is eternally coexistent with the impermanent;
this is what is called the impermanent fruit of craving.
May one’s virtuous aspirations likewise be able to give rise to that same [fruit].
Therefore, it is called the cause.
As for what is termed "great goodness," it refers to the aforementioned self-benefit.
This is the benefit of others;
because the practice of benefiting others is as vast as the realm of sentient beings,
it is called "great."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"He protects and shelters the entire realm of sentient beings;
he is not one who is timid or weak."
Because the Bodhisattvas have partially realized the wisdom and virtue of all Buddhas and are able to enter the profound with hearts free from fear or retreat,
it is said they are "not timid.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
It is said that these six kinds of definitive explanations enable one to enter the ground of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. 149.
The Meaning of the Six Sublime Practices (12): Regarding the meaning of the six sublime practices, the six sublime practices are as follows:
The noble one beyond training (aśaikṣa) practices free from faults.
This sūtra is also called the "Six Sublime Dharmas.
Generally, the term "action" (saṃskāra) explains all that arises and is produced.
The intrinsic nature of this practice is explained as being the Dharma.
Because this practice is far removed from all unwholesome and coarse faults,
it is called "sublime."
When distinguished according to their specific characteristics, there is indeed a difference between "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*) and "sublime phenomena" (*saddharma*).
How do these characteristics differ?
That which is free from fault within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is called sublime conduct.
The remaining aggregates (skandhas), when free from defilement, are said to be the sublime Dharma.
What is the meaning of this?
According to the Abhidharma, consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations arise simultaneously.
When visual consciousness arises, it is already endowed with four aggregates:
visual consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness;
that which is simultaneously experienced and designated as feeling is the aggregate of feeling.

Simultaneously, that which is conceptualized and enumerated is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), while the remaining volitions, desires, and so forth are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
This remains the case even when mental consciousness arises.
Among those six types of conduct, that which is free from transgression and fault is called the six sublime conducts (ṣaḍ-ārya-vihāra).
The remaining three aggregates, being free from faults and untainted, are called the six sublime dharmas (*ṣad-ārya-dharmāḥ*).
It is the same for the Mahāyāna.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) arise in a temporal sequence.
Following visual consciousness, there are four types of mind:
first consciousness itself, followed by perception, feeling, and finally mental formations;
this is likewise true up to and including mental consciousness.
Because there is no fault in the subsequent activity of those six consciousnesses, they are called the "six sublime practices.

Although the nature of consciousness, perception, and feeling within those six consciousnesses is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they do not give rise to the faults of the outflows (*āsrava*) of afflictions within their subsequent activity.
Furthermore, they are called the six sublime dharmas because they do not arise from the outflows of affliction (*āsrava*).
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the six sublime practices. 150.
The Meaning of the Six Kinds of Wholesome Dharmas (12): Regarding the meaning of the six kinds of wholesome dharmas, it is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
What are these names?
They are the five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) and unconditioned cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these constitute the six.
Within the five wholesome aggregates, there are four kinds.
First, the aggregate of goodness acquired in this life,
which is now perfected through past habituation;
second, the aggregate of goodness resulting from skillful means.
Now, one cultivates and gives rise to the three untainted aggregates of goodness (anāsrava-kuśala-skandha); that is,
persons of the Three Vehicles take the Dharma-body as their object of cultivation.
The four are the eternally abiding five aggregates,
which refer to the true *dharmakāya* of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
One abandons impermanent form and attains permanent form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
These points have been fully and extensively analyzed as previously detailed in the chapter on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The unconditioned state of cessation through analytical knowledge is briefly of three kinds.
The first is the cessation of afflictions,
which refers to the extinction of all afflictions of the five stages.
Second is the cessation of karma,
which refers to the cessation of both contaminated and uncontaminated karma.
Third is the cessation of suffering.
This refers to the cessation of the fruits of both *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative) [rebirth].
These have been extensively analyzed and explained as in the previous section on the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
All of these are distinguished according to the Mahāyāna.
The six virtues are thus. 151.
The Meaning of the Six Bases of Concord (12). Regarding the meaning of the six bases of concord (*ṣaḍ-samrañjanīya-dharma*):
they are the practices that bring about peaceful dwelling together and freedom from affliction.
To act in a manner that does not conflict with one's name is called harmony;
because of this harmony in conduct, their hearts become mutually affectionate and valued, which is termed respect.
Harmony and respect are distinct.
One gate explains six [categories].
What are the names of these six?
First, the sameness of bodily action;
second, the sameness of verbal action;
third, the sameness of mental action.
Fourth is commonality of precepts;
fifth is commonality of giving;
sixth is commonality of views.
Among these six, the first three demonstrate their commonality with respect to the body,
while the latter three explain their commonality with respect to conduct.
Regarding the commonality of bodily action:
Briefly, there are two kinds.
First, equality in the avoidance of faults:
being equally free from such acts as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Second, the commonality of performing wholesome deeds.
This refers to the commonality of performing all wholesome acts such as prostrations and so forth.
Regarding the commonality of verbal karma:
There are also two kinds.
First, equality in the avoidance of faults:
they are alike in that they all remain far removed from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Second, they are equal in performing wholesome deeds.
This refers to being equal in performing wholesome acts such as reciting, chanting, and praising.
Regarding equality in mental action:
There are also two kinds.
First, equality in the abandonment of faults:
being equally free from all afflictions, karma, and volitional thoughts.
Second, they are equal in performing wholesome deeds.
This means they equally cultivate all wholesome dharmas, such as faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Regarding their equality in precepts:
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, equality in receiving the precepts;
second, equality in upholding the precepts.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts:
first, the commonality of manifest precepts;
second, the commonality of non-manifest precepts.
It can also be divided into three types:
first, the commonality of the restraint of ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara-śīla); second, the commonality of the restraint of gathering wholesome qualities (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla).
The precept of gathering sentient beings is the same.
Regarding what is called "giving equally," there are briefly two types.
First, the commonality of internal giving:
personally relinquishing one's own body to serve and honor [the Teacher].
Second, the commonality of external giving.
The relinquishing of other requisites for life can likewise be divided into three types;
the first is identical to the giving of material wealth.
Second, they are identical in the giving of the Dharma;
third, they are identical in the giving of fearlessness.
Regarding what is meant by "identical views":
"View" refers to a perspective or understanding.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), views and understandings are not distinct.
In the two truths, there is no distinction between seeing and understanding.
Question: Is there not anything that is not subsumed within the first three practices?
For what reason are the latter three further explained?
The explanation states:
the former three are its "efficient causes" (kāraṇa-hetu).
The latter three are what is produced;
therefore, they are explained again.
Furthermore, within the former three, the inclusion of practices cannot be fully exhausted.
It is not yet known what was done in the three preceding instances;
therefore, they are explained again. He asks:
The specific practices to be performed are immeasurable;
why, then, are only ethical discipline, generosity, and right view specifically mentioned?
It is because these are presented in brief.
Among the six perfections, ethical discipline and generosity come first,
while wisdom and vision come last;
by referring to the beginning and the end, their commonality is demonstrated.
The intermediate sections may be understood;
therefore, they are omitted here without further discussion.
This concludes the brief exposition on the meaning of the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ābhiprasannāni*).

152. The Definition of the Sixfold Cultivation (12): The Sevenfold Analysis of the Definition of the Sixfold Cultivation. I. Distinguishing the Characteristics; II. Differentiation of the Meaning of Practice; III. Analysis by Way of Stages; IV. Analysis by Way of Bases; V. Analysis by Way of Realms; VI. Analysis by Way of Wisdom; VII. Analysis by Way of Feeling. First: Distinguishing the Characteristics.
Regarding the six modes of cultivating concentration:
first, counting;
second, following.
Third is cessation;
fourth is contemplation;
fifth is called returning.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, this is termed "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*);
the sixth is termed "purity" (*viśuddhi*).
Regarding the first term, "counting" (*gaṇanā*):
To counteract discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), one binds the mind to the counting of breaths;
this is called "counting" (*gaṇanā*).
Within this counting, there are four [stages].
First, increase;
second, decrease;
third, disorder.
The four immeasurables are analyzed in detail within the context of the five perfections.
This number constitutes the skillful means for the cultivation of śamatha.
As for what is called "following":
the mind, without any other activity, dwells following the movement of the breath,
whether it is long or short.
Is it near or far?
Does it pervade the entire body or abide in a single location?
To what place does it go?
By means of what does one turn the mind back and follow along with awareness?
This is called "following.
This following is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the practitioner of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
As for what is called "stopping" (śamatha):
one fixes the mind as appropriate upon a part of one's own body—such as the space between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, the navel, or the toes—and causes it to remain there;
therefore, it is called stopping.
As for what is called "contemplation," it begins by observing the breath within one's own body to determine whether it is harmful or beneficial, cold or warm.
Examine and observe thoroughly.
This breath is, in fact, the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
As the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Because of the wind element, one contemplates the four great elements as equal.
Having contemplated the four great elements, one next contemplates the derived matter produced by them, namely:
visible form, sound, odor, taste, and so forth.
Upon what phenomena can form (rūpa) exercise its formative activity?
It is upon mental phenomena (citta-dharma).
Therefore, one next examines feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).
To observe these is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
What is called "returning" (pratyāgama) refers to the capacity of the practice of "calming" (śamatha).
Because the practice of tranquility has been accomplished, when thoughts or perceptions regarding sensual desires or unwholesome states arise,
one is able to restrain them and cause the mind to return to abide within the perception of renunciation;
this is called "returning."
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The thought of desire is practiced little;
the thought of renunciation is practiced much."
In the *Vibhāṣā*, for what reason is this termed "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*)?
It is because one transforms away from unwholesome thoughts and abides in wholesome thoughts.
Furthermore, within wholesome thoughts, transforming from a lower level to arise at a higher level is also called "transformation."
What is called "purity" refers to the capacity for contemplation.
Because the practice of contemplation is perfected, one is able to extinguish all evils.
Therefore, it is called "pure.
These six characteristics conclude this first section.
Next, the distinctions in the meanings of the practices such as *śamatha* (calm abiding) will be explained.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*,
counting has two aspects:
first, counting the inhalations and exhalations.
Second, the ability to abandon unwholesome thoughts also has two aspects:
first, following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
Second, it can eliminate unwholesome thoughts.
*Śamatha* also has two aspects:
first, it can cause the mind to abide at the tip of the nose, between the eyebrows, or on the toes.
Second is the samādhi of non-abandonment.
Contemplation also has two aspects:
first, the contemplation of inhalation and exhalation.
Matters such as loss and gain have been analyzed above.
Second, being able to properly apprehend the characteristics of the mind and mental factors;
this transformation also has two aspects.
First, one is able to know the five aggregates;
second, one is able to enter the noble path.
Purity also has two aspects.
First, it can sever the fetters;
second, it can bring about purity in the knowledge and vision regarding the truths.
Such are the distinct practices for these two gateways. Thus concludes [the section on] the two gateways.
Next is the discussion of the stages (*sthāna*).
Generally speaking according to their meaning, these stages exist throughout all levels.

Within this, when specifically categorized by number, they correspond to the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-citta-sthiti*) within the stage of the five preliminary practices (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*).
This continues from the foundations of mindfulness up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) arises as one turns toward and enters the inhalation and exhalation."
In this sequence, up until the transformation of patience and the arising of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
it is called "transformation.
That which is "pure" (*śuddha*) pertains to the stage above the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The pure [factors] refer to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and so forth. This concludes the three gates.
Next, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Grounds" refers to the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, these six— the preliminary stage (*anāgāmya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) of the first, second, and third dhyānas— are included within the desire realm.
Among these, the specific categories of the two types of practice are subsumed under the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) of the desire realm, the *anāgāmya*, and the second and third dhyānas.
Calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and purification (*pariśuddhi*) are subsumed under the preparatory path of all stages (*bhūmi*).
Since each of the stages (bhūmi) possesses the fourfold meaning of tranquility (śamatha), insight (vipaśyanā), returning (pratyāgamana), and purification (viśuddhi), these four gates are concluded.
Next, we discuss this in terms of the realms (dhātu).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, these six first arise in the desire realm;
subsequently, they may also arise in the form realm based on that. This concludes the discussion of the five doors.
Next, we shall discuss them in terms of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Wisdom refers to the ten wisdoms.
These six are subsumed solely within conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
because they are cultivated through worldly meditation.

If, according to the classification by stage, purification (*viśuddhi*) occurs from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards, then within that purification the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) is fully present. This concludes the six gates.
Next, we shall discuss it in terms of feeling (*vedanā*).
Feeling refers to suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
These six are associated exclusively with the faculty of equanimity,
because they are not subsumed within the levels of the fundamental dhyānas.
If one speaks in terms of the meaning of the various dhyānas, śamatha and vipaśyanā, as well as the restoration of purity,
may be associated with joy, or associated with bliss, or associated with equanimity.
In the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*);
in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*);
in all other instances, it is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The six types are thus. 153.
The Meaning of the Six Samādhis (12): The meaning of the six samādhis is as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
What are these names?
Cultivating each individual characteristic constitutes one characteristic;
cultivating both characteristics together constitutes various characteristics.
1. Cultivating the single characteristic as both the single characteristic and manifold characteristics; 2.
Cultivating the fourfold manifold characteristics as manifold characteristics;
3. Cultivating the manifold characteristics as the single characteristic.

Regarding the six kinds of cultivation of various characteristics (*nānātva-lakṣaṇa*) as being both various characteristics and a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), how are these characteristics defined?
The commentaries provide differing explanations.

Certain masters of the Abhidharma say that the cultivation of the fourth dhyāna is called "cultivation of a single characteristic," whereas the cultivation of the fivefold noble concentration is called "cultivation of various characteristics."
The five factors of noble concentration are explained in detail as above.
Regarding the statement that "cultivating a single characteristic results in a single characteristic":
it refers to cultivating the fourth dhyāna in order to attain the fruit of arhatship.
To say that practicing with a single characteristic leads to various results means that one practices the fourth dhyāna in order to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
To say that practicing with a single characteristic leads to both a single characteristic and various results [means that...].
One cultivates the fourth dhyāna to attain arhatship and the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
Cultivating various characteristics for various purposes means that one cultivates the five noble factors (pañcāryāṅga) to attain the five supernormal powers.
Cultivating various characteristics to become a single characteristic means cultivating the five noble factors to attain arhatship.
Cultivating various characteristics to become both various characteristics and a single characteristic [means...]
The cultivation of the five noble factors for the sake of attaining the five supernormal powers and the fruit of arhatship—
this single point is not established in the *Tattvasiddhi*; therefore,
it is not their [the Sarvāstivādins'] teaching.
Among the five factors of enlightenment (*pañca-sambodhyaṅga*), the first three are still the mundane four dhyānas.
When one attains arhatship, one relies upon whichever one of the four dhyānas is appropriate.
Why, then, is it said that cultivating the five factors of enlightenment to attain the fruit of arhatship is called "one characteristic" (*eka-lakṣaṇa*)?

Furthermore, within the two branches of clear observation (*vipaśyanā*), one attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the branch of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not by relying on the branch of clear observation.
Thus, it is known that the attainment of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) is not achieved through the practice of the five branches of the noble ones (*pañcāryāṅga*).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, that which is established as concentration maintaining a single object is called "cultivation of a single characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇabhāvanā*).
That which is the wisdom-mind perceiving the various distinctions among phenomena is called "cultivation of diversity" (*nānālakṣaṇabhāvanā*).
To say that cultivation of a single characteristic is "of a single characteristic" [means]:
The treatise states:
Based on meditative concentration, one further gives rise to the supernormal power of the mind (ṛddhi-samādhi),
just as one arises from the first dhyāna into the second dhyāna, and so forth.
To say that practicing with a single characteristic results in various characteristics means that wisdom arises based on meditative concentration.
To say that practicing with a single characteristic results in both a single characteristic and various characteristics [means...]
Based on concentration, concentration arises and wisdom arises;
as for the statement that "various cultivations result in various [results]," it means that based on wisdom, wisdom arises.
Just as hearing gives rise to reflection, and reflection gives rise to cultivation,
the statement that various modes of cultivation constitute a single characteristic refers to the arising of meditative concentration based upon wisdom.
Regarding the statement that various cultivations constitute various characteristics as well as a single characteristic:
it is based on wisdom that all concentrations and wisdoms can be produced.
Question: [What is this?]
Regarding the arising of concentration and wisdom within this context,
it is not definitively determined in the treatises whether they are with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
There are three expositions of the meaning.
First, from a general perspective:
all meditative concentrations and wisdoms, whether generative or generated, encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Second, regarding the mutual discussion of the concealment and manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*):
concentration is exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*), while wisdom is exclusively without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Third, regarding the mutual discussion of the concealment and manifestation of meditative concentration and wisdom in terms of that which produces and that which is produced:

The meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that can produce both concentration and wisdom are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the concentration and wisdom produced [by them] are exclusively without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Such is the explanation of the meaning of the six types of *samādhi*. 154.
The Meaning of the Sixfold Compendium (12): The meaning of the sixfold compendium is derived from the *Bhūmivastu* (Treatise on the Stages of Yogic Practice).
Categorizing phenomena according to the Path is termed "comprehension" (saṃgraha).
Since the loci of comprehension differ,
six types are explained within this single section.
What are these six names?
First, instantaneous inclusion;
second, predominant inclusion.
Third is grasping by taking;
fourth is long-term grasping;
fifth is short-term grasping.
Sixth is the subsequent gathering (*paścād-āvarjana*).
Among these six, the first three distinguish the transformative deeds (*nirmāṇa-karman*);
among these three, the first concerns those to be transformed (*vineya*) instantaneously.
In the second section on the first gate, regarding the body of the emanator, the third section on the first gate concerns the complete perfection of the emanated implements.
The latter three types are distinguished according to their faculties:
the first is for those of inferior faculties.
Next is one of medium capacity,
and finally one of superior capacity;
thus, there are six types.
Regarding "sudden inclusion":
one regards all living beings as one's own parents and,
according to one's capacity, provides for them with every kind of peace and benefit.
This is called "simultaneous inclusion.
Regarding "superior inclusion," it means that when a bodhisattva dwells in a position of authority, their gathering of sentient beings is termed "superior inclusion."
According to the treatise, there are three [applications]:
first, for a king to skillfully govern the people;
second, for a head of a household to skillfully benefit his kin.
Third, regarding the father’s equal benefit toward his children,
his feelings are free from partiality;
as for what is meant by "gathering through speech":
One is able to gather in sentient beings through both material wealth and the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "gathering for a long time":
sentient beings with dull faculties require a long period of transformation before they reach maturity.
"Those gathered before long" refers to sentient beings of middling faculties who are easily transformed and quickly purified.
"Those gathered later" refers to...
Sentient beings of superior faculties are capable of attaining purification within the present life;
because the benefits of their transformation reach their ultimate limit, it is called "subsequent inclusion.
A question is asked:
Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), by which characteristics are these six subsumed?
The explanation states:
the four means of integration are common to all six.
They do not correspond individually; the sixfold inclusion is thus. 155. Section 155:

The Meaning of the Sevenfold Wholesome Restraint (12). The meaning of the sevenfold wholesome restraint is analyzed through four gates: first, defining its characteristics; second, opening and closing [the categories] regarding their breadth and brevity; third, analysis according to the objects; fourth, the discussion of the branches, causes, and the presence or absence of the unmanifested wholesome as restraint.
The vows of discipline differ;
they are explained as seven under a single heading, namely:

abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech.
Regarding what is called "non-killing," the treatise states that there are three types.
The first is "abstinence from the cause."
Second is separation through the practice of the fruit;
third is separation through the antidote.
There are two types of separation from causes.
First is the common cause,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion;
all karmas take these as their causes.
Therefore, it is called "common.
Second is the uncommon cause,
which refers to keeping weapons, branches, and so forth while free from the intent to kill.
Because this is solely the cause of killing, it is called "unshared.
A question is asked:
If it is said that being free from the intention to kill is the cause of being free [from the offense], [then...]
Why is it stated in the treatise that the fruit is "separated"?
The explanation says:
the intention of the one who kills is not fixed.
If one considers covetousness and so forth, they constitute its fruit-action;
if one considers the actual act of killing, they constitute its cause-action.
Here, according to the latter perspective, they are described as "separation from the cause."
Regarding "abstention from the result," this refers to the actual abstention from the karmic act of killing.
Regarding "abstention as an antidote," it refers to...
That which is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the mind of peace (*kṣema*), and so forth.
Loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness;
peace is able to grant what is wholesome (*kuśala*).
Because these two types can counteract the karma of killing, they are called "antidotes.
Regarding what is called "not stealing," there are likewise three kinds.
First, separation from causes;
second, separation from the practice of results;
third, separation through antidotes.
There are two kinds of causes for detachment.
First is detachment from common causes,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Second is the separation from uncommon causes,
namely, the intent to steal and the lack of the necessities of life; therefore,
in the *Kṣetrasamudgama-sūtra*, the fulfillment of the necessities of life is termed "separation from causes."
Regarding "fulfillment":
it refers to constantly cultivating a mind of few desires and contentment, having no further cravings or needs;
therefore, it is called fulfillment.
Regarding "abstention through the fruit of action," this refers to the actual abstention from the karma of stealing.
Regarding "abstention through its antidote":
Regarding what is called generosity,
that which is termed non-lustfulness likewise has three kinds.
First, separation by cause;
second, separation by antidote;
third, separation by the practice of the fruit.
There are two kinds of causes for detachment:
first, detachment from common causes,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Question: The treatise declares that sexual misconduct is accomplished solely through a mind of greed.
Now, how can it be said that being free from greed, hatred, and delusion constitutes the cause for such freedom?
The explanation is:
in the end, it is established that this depends solely upon greed.
In the distant sense, they arise from greed, hatred, and delusion;
therefore, their separation is collectively termed "separation as cause.
Second is "separation from the uncommon cause."
This refers to the lustful mind and the absence of one's own wife.
Thus, in the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, being content with one's own wife is called the cause for renunciation.
What does "being content" mean?
In the present life, his holy life remains incomplete;
yet, being free from desire for the mind, he is said to be "satisfied with the form of a wife.
Because he is self-sufficient, his mind is devoid of longing or craving.
Therefore, one who abandons the cause of sexual desire and whose conduct is free from it is truly one who has abandoned the karma of sexual misconduct.
As for the antidote to detachment,
it consists of constantly practicing the pure life (brahmacarya),
the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), and so forth.
Regarding "not speaking falsely," there are two explanations in the treatise: first,
[the explanation of] abandonment through its antidote.
That which is called truthful speech is the antidote to a deceitful mind;
it is the practice of the two fruits that constitutes the correct abandonment of false speech.
To discuss this according to its actual nature, there are also three kinds:
first, separation from causes;
second, separation from the practice of results.
Third is separation through antidotes.
There are two types of separation from causes:
first, separation from common causes.
These are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Second, there is the uncommon cause of dissociation,
which is the intention to deceive others.
"Abandonment through the fruit of practice" refers to the actual abstention from false speech.
"Abandonment through its antidote" refers to...
One should constantly practice truthful speech.
It is asked:
In this context, truthfulness fully possesses the three abstentions.
Why does the treatise speak only of two?
The explanation states:
it is to demonstrate that verbal speech is easily produced and does not depend on remote causes.
Therefore, it is not stated that they are separated by being free from greed, hatred, and delusion as their cause.

Although being free from the intention to deceive others is indeed a cause for separation, it is not discussed separately because it is included within the discussion of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) that counteract the mind of deception.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
"The antidote to a deceitful mind is precisely 'separation from [others],' which constitutes not engaging in divisive speech."
There are also three kinds:
first, separation by cause;
second, separation by antidote.
The three fruits are separated from their practice.
There are two types of separation from causes:
first, separation from common causes.
That is to say: greed, hatred, and delusion.
Second, it is free from uncommon causes;
it is free from a mind of malice.
As for "fruition-abandonment," it refers to the actual abandonment of divisive speech.
As for "antidote-abandonment," it refers to...
Cultivating harmonious speech and refraining from harsh speech also consists of three types.
First, separation from causes;
second, separation from the practice of results;
third, separation through antidotes.
There are two kinds of causes for separation.
The first is separation from common causes,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Second is the abandonment of the non-common cause,
namely, the mind of malice.
Regarding the abandonment of the resultant conduct:
One correctly abandons harsh speech.
As for the antidote to such abandonment,
one constantly cultivates gentle speech.
Regarding those who do not engage in frivolous speech,
there are also three kinds.
The first is due to detachment.
Second, separation through the practice of the fruit;
third, separation through the antidote.
There is separation by way of the cause.
First, it is free from common causes,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion;
second, it is free from uncommon causes.
This refers to the mind of frivolous speech.
As for "abstaining from its fruit and practice," it means correctly abstaining from frivolous speech.
Regarding the antidote for distancing:
one constantly cultivates right speech. This concludes this section.
Next, the meaning of opening and closing, as well as expansion and abbreviation, will be explained.
The classification is not fixed; in brief,
it is subsumed within the single category of wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*),
or it may be divided into two.
First is bodily action;
second is verbal action.
The first three are bodily actions.
The latter four are vocal actions;
alternatively, they may be divided into seven,
as fully explained above.
Alternatively, they may be divided into twenty-one;
since each of these seven types of restraint arises from superior, middling, and inferior grades of mind,
there are twenty-one in total when considered collectively.
Alternatively, they may be further divided into sixty-three.
Since each of the preceding twenty-one arises from the three wholesome roots of non-greed, non-hatred,
and non-delusion, there are thus said to be sixty-three in total.
Question: Since the three wholesome [roots] always follow one another and are never separated,
why are they separately divided into sixty-three?
The commentary states:
Although the three wholesome natures exist simultaneously, they are not without a sequence of priority based on the relative strength of their respective functions.

For instance, the contemplation of impurity has non-attachment as its nature; the contemplations of loving-kindness and compassion have non-hatred as their nature; and the contemplations of causes and conditions have non-delusion as their nature.
Since the three types of wholesome [action] possess the sense of arising separately,
why would the resulting restraints not arise separately?
Therefore, they can be divided into sixty-three kinds.
If one follows the distinctions in the realms of the various stages of dhyāna for ordinary beings and sages, these two gates are immeasurable. This concludes the discussion.
Next is the discourse on the objects [of the precepts]:
these seven types of restraint arise universally toward all sentient beings.
If it were not thus, the restraint one has received would be subject to increase or decrease.
It is asked:
Does the restraint arise with respect to sentient beings of the present?
Regarding its arising in relation to sentient beings of the three periods of time,
the commentaries offer differing explanations.
According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it arises universally in relation to sentient beings of all three periods.
Because by means of these conditions, one can give rise to wholesome states of mind.
According to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), [unwholesome actions] arise only with respect to sentient beings in the present.
This is because it is impossible to kill, steal, or even engage in frivolous speech toward sentient beings of the past or future.
Because of these conditions, the restraint (saṃvara) does not arise.
A question is asked:
If one obtains the restraint with respect to present sentient beings, then when those present sentient beings die and perish, one should lose that restraint.
The commentary states:
It is not lost,
because one constantly attains restraint with respect to present sentient beings in every moment of thought.
Question: Is the restraint not obtained by those who are not sentient beings?
Explanation:
It is also obtained;
therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"It is not a wholesome restraint obtained by sentient beings."
Question: Can one obtain the wholesome restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*) by taking as its object those things that do not belong to the category of sentient beings?
Explanation: Yes.
This is not possible;
therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states that one must rely upon sentient beings to obtain the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*).
Why is this so? Because they distance themselves from natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) toward sentient beings,
and distance themselves from proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) toward non-sentient things.
Abstention from [unwholesome] nature is the basis.
Therefore, it must be obtained with respect to sentient beings;
one does not generate the restraint by merely taking grass and such as the object. This concludes the three gates.
Next, the presence or absence of the constituent factors of the cause is explained.
"Factors" refers to the seven factors,
beginning with non-killing and ending with non-frivolous speech.
The causes are what are called the superior, middling, and inferior minds.
It is asked:
"Must all seven branches be complete in order to attain [the result]?"
It may also be attained without being complete.
The commentary states that this is not fixed.
The great bhikṣu precepts must be fully possessed to be obtained;
śrāmaṇeras and laypeople may obtain them even without full possession.
Therefore, the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the ten precepts all lack seven [of the factors].
Question: Regarding those three types of causes— superior, middling, and inferior— is it necessary for them all to be present for the arising of precepts,
or can they be obtained even when not all are present?
The commentary states:
It is not fixed.
There may be those who, possessing superior, middling, or inferior faculties, receive the lay precepts, the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, or the full bhikṣu precepts.
This is called "possessing the causes.
Alternatively, if one receives the three types of precepts with a predominantly superior state of mind,
or with a middling or inferior state of mind, it is called "not possessing [the causes]."
Because these factors (aṅga) and causes (hetu) may be either complete or incomplete,
there is a fourfold analysis within the mixed mind. What are these four?
First, all causes but not all factors:
this refers to receiving the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts with minds of superior, middling, or inferior capacity.
When one relies upon the possession of these three causes, it is termed "all causes."
That which is undertaken consists only of abstaining from the transgressions of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
therefore, it does not include all factors.
Second, there are cases where all factors are present, yet not all causes are present.
There are those who receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) with a mind of the highest grade,
or of the middle or lower grades; yet the precepts they receive are complete in their seven branches,
and are therefore called "all branches."
Not possessing the three minds is called "not being a cause for all [precepts].
These three universal causes are also the universal branches.
One receives the lay precepts, the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, and the full bhikṣu precepts by means of superior, middling, and inferior grades of mind.
The fourth case consists of those that are neither universal causes nor universal factors:
namely, when one receives the lay precepts or the śrāmaṇera precepts with a weak mind;
the same applies to middling and superior minds.
The seven virtuous restraints (*śīla-saṃvara*) are summarized thus.

156. The Sevenfold Meaning of Purity (12): The Sevenfold Meaning of Purity analyzed by way of two gates—first, the discernment of characteristics; second, the analysis according to stages. [These consist of] conduct, virtue, and stainlessness.
This is termed "purity.
The meanings of purity differ;
seven aspects are explained through a single gateway.
What are these seven names?
First is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).
Second is the purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), which is also called the purity of mind (*citta-viśuddhi*).
Third is purity of vision;
fourth is purity through the overcoming of doubt;
fifth is purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
Of these, the first five are identical in name for both the large and small [vehicles],
while the latter two differ in name.
According to the Small Vehicle, these six are called the "purities of practice" (*caryā-śuddhi*).
The seventh is called the purity of the knowledge that abandons practice.
According to the Mahāyāna, the sixth is called the abandonment of practice,
and the seventh is called the progressively superior purity of reflecting upon the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The latter two names are as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*.
Regarding "purity of ethical discipline" (*śīla-viśuddhi*): it refers to maintaining the precepts and remaining free from transgressions at the outset of one's practice and cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that the precepts are pure.
Because the precepts are pure, one is able to give rise to pure concentration, which is called the purity of concentration.
Because concentration is pure, true wisdom is produced.
Having been born [in the higher realms], being able to eliminate the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is called purity of vision (*dṛṣṭiviśuddhi*).
Being able to sever doubt is called purity of overcoming doubt (*kāṅkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhi*).

Being able to abandon attachment to precepts and rituals and knowing that untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) is the true path, while precepts and the like are not the path, is called purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*mārgāmārgajñānaviśuddhi*).

Within the latter two types, if one relies on the Hīnayāna, the progressive cultivation of practice by taking the principles of the truths as a primary object is called the purity of practice (*caryā-viśuddhi*).
When that practice exhausts all obstacles, it is called the purity of the knowledge of the abandonment of practice (*caryā-prahāṇa-jñāna-viśuddhi*).
If, according to the Mahāyāna, the removal of obstacles in accordance with the path is termed the abandonment of practice,
then entering the realm of the Buddha by means of this abandonment of practice is termed the supreme purity of thought-enlightenment (*cittabodhi*).
Among the seven [categories], the first is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*);
the next is the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*);
and the final five are the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). This concludes this section.
Next is the discussion on their respective positions.
While their practice is truly uniform and universal,
there are no fewer than distinct stages of difference according to the concealment or manifestation of their characteristics.
As for their distinct characteristics:
according to the Hīnayāna, the first two are situated prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
while the subsequent three are situated within the path of seeing.
Next is one [path] of cultivation;
finally is one of no-more-learning.
For what reason are the precepts and meditative concentration explained before the [paths of] vision?
The coarse transgressions of external worldlings cannot be prevented without the precepts;
therefore, the precepts are explained first.
The supramundane noble path does not arise without meditative concentration (samādhi).
Therefore, concentration is explained next.
Why are the [next] three specifically situated within the Path of Seeing?
Because within the Path of Seeing, one abandons the three fetters and accomplishes the three purities; thus, they are specifically placed therein.
What are the three fetters?
They are namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt.
By abandoning the view of a self-identity, one attains purity of vision.
Because one has severed doubt, one attains the purity of crossing over doubt.
Because one has severed attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*), one attains the purity of the path and what is not the path.
It is asked:
When a noble one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the ten fetters (*daśasaṃyojana*) are abandoned simultaneously.
Why, then, is it said that only the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) are abandoned?
This is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Because these three are layered,
they are explained specifically;
it is just as people in the world say, "the king comes" or "the king goes."
Because they are heavy, they are discussed separately.
Furthermore, among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), the five views and doubt only obstruct the vision of the truths;
they are abandoned at their ultimate point upon entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Greed, hatred, delusion, and pride generally obstruct both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
they are not fully abandoned upon entering the path of seeing.
The five views and doubt are exhausted within the path of seeing.
Therefore, because greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and views have not been exhausted, they are designated by their names; because they have not been severed,
they are not given the designation of "severed."
Among the five views and doubt that are abandoned therein, three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are the root and three are the secondary;
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root.
Extreme views are the secondary factors;
attachment to precepts and observances is the root;
and attachment to views is the secondary factor.
Doubt is the root;
wrong view is the derivative.
It is the same when speaking of the removal of the three roots and their three derivatives.
Therefore, in the sūtras and śāstras, it is specifically taught that the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Why is the purification of conduct (*caryāviśuddhi*) specifically situated in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
It is because in this stage, one repeatedly contemplates the principle of the truths (*satyārtha*) and proceeds toward the practice of cultivation.
Why is it that the abandonment of conduct (*caryā-prahāṇa*) pertains exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Because the path of those beyond training has completely abandoned all obstructions.
In the Mahāyāna teaching, the first five [aspects] are the same as before.
The latter two exist within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Within the path of cultivation, there are both general and specific aspects.
Generally speaking, they pertain to all stages (*bhūmi*).
That which has the sense of eliminating hindrances is all termed "abandonment through practice" (*caryā-prahāṇa*);
that which has the sense of seeking what is superior is all designated as "deliberation" (*tarka*).

Within this, when distinguished specifically, the abandonment of hindrances during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) from the second stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage is called "abandonment through practice."
From the eighth stage upward, within the flow of the Dharma, one enters the realm of the Buddha;
this is called the supreme purity of deliberation (*uttara-uttara-vicāra*).
Such are the seven purities.
157. The Meaning of the Seven Riches (12). Regarding the meaning of the seven riches:
they are called "riches" because they are excellent provisions.
The categories of wealth differ;
one gate explains seven.
What are the names of these seven?
First, faith;
second, precepts;
third, generosity.
Fourth is hearing;
fifth is wisdom;
sixth is shame.
The seven types of shame (*hrī*).
This meaning is fully and extensively analyzed later in the chapter on the ten treasuries (*daśa-kośa*).
Such are the seven riches.

158. Seventeen Kinds of Mahāyāna Meanings (12): Seven Kinds of Mahāyāna Meanings. The seven kinds of Mahāyāna appear in the *Bhūmivastu* (*Dizhi lun*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) is so named because it conveys and transports [beings].
Do not add anything to the vehicle;
it is called "Great" because the Great Vehicle is peerless.
Seven [qualities] are explained under a single heading.
What are these seven names?
The first is the greatness of the Dharma (*dharmamahattva*).
Second is the greatness of mind;
third is the greatness of understanding;
fourth is the greatness of the pure mind.
Fifth is the greatness of the assembly;
sixth is the greatness of the time;
seventh is the greatness of attainment.
Among the seven, the first six are described as "great" in terms of their causes,
while the final one is discussed as "great" in terms of its fruit.
Within the causes, the first is the causal dharma itself.
Regarding the subsequent five causes of practice,
what is called the "Great Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna twelvefold canon, specifically the Vaipulya Piṭaka.
It is called "Great Dharma" because it surpasses other sūtras.
Question: Within the Dharma, both the principles and the teachings are explained.
Why is it that the teaching is explained exclusively here?
The commentary states:
In reality, it is universal.
Since the essential meaning is subsumed within its verbal expression, it is not discussed separately.
As for "the greatness of the mind," it refers to the arousal of the mind set upon unsurpassed bodhi.
It is called "great mind" because it transcends all other vows.
As for "great understanding," it refers to the understanding of the Bodhisattva’s Vaipulya-piṭaka.
That which excels other forms of understanding is called "great understanding.
This mind and its understanding exist prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
As for "great pure mind":
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), having transcended the dwelling of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), one enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Therein,
one realizes the mind's liberation from defilements, which is termed the "great pure mind" (*viśuddha-citta-mahat*).
The greatness of the equipment refers to the stages from the second to the seventh bhūmi.
Cultivating the equipment of merit and wisdom and proceeding toward bodhi is called the greatness of the equipment.
Regarding "greatness in terms of time":
from the eighth stage up to the tenth stage, one traverses the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and fulfills all practices;
this is called greatness in terms of time.
Regarding the statement "attaining greatness," this refers to the attainment of the fruit of bodhi at the stage of the Tathāgata, which is without equal,
let alone surpassed by anything above it.
Therefore, it is called "attaining greatness.
The sevenfold Mahāyāna has been briefly explained in this manner.

159. The Meaning of the Seven Grounds (12): The Meaning of the Seven Grounds is analyzed through three gates: first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of their essence; third, the differentiation of their characteristics. First, the explanation of names.
The meaning of the seven stages is derived from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*. That which can give rise [to cultivation] is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*).
The opening and closing, as well as the expansion and contraction of these stages, are difficult to definitively establish.
Now, based on one gate, we shall briefly discuss seven stages:
first, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
3. The stage of the pure mind-ground;
4. The stage of the tracks of practice;
5. The stage of certainty.
Sixth, the stage of definitive practice;
seventh, the ultimate stage.
Regarding the stage of the lineage:
The "nature of the stage of practice" (śikṣā-bīja-gotra) and the "nature of the lineage" (gotra-gotra) are both termed *gotra*.
Because they are established as the fundamental basis for practice and are capable of producing cause and effect,
they are called "seeds" (*bīja*).
The meaning of "lineage" (gotra) is not destroyed;
it is designated as "nature" (prakṛti).
Because this nature distinguishes the stages, it is called the "stage of the lineage" (gotrabhūmi).

Regarding the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*): based on the aforementioned spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one initiates the skillful means of cultivation and enters the supramundane state;
because one understands and practices within the supramundane path, it is called "practice through understanding."

The stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) is so called because it involves the understanding of the distinctions between the stages. As for the stage of the pure mind (*śuddhi-citta-bhūmi*),
it is situated within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
Having transcended the stage of practice through understanding and entered the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one realizes that the mind is free from defilement;
this is called the "pure mind.
Furthermore, pure faith and aspiration toward bodhi are also called the "pure mind."
Because of this specific name, it is called the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*). Regarding the Stage of the Path of Practice (*pratipadabhūmi*):
from the second stage up to the seventh stage, the arising of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is termed the "path of practice."
The stage of practicing distinct paths is called the stage of tracks because it involves specific modes of practice.
Regarding the stage of certainty:
within the eighth stage, one abides in the stream of the Dharma and proceeds with certainty toward unexcelled enlightenment; thus, it is named the stage of certainty.

The stage of definitive practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*) refers to the ninth stage, which is called the stage of definitive practice because one relies on the aforementioned definitiveness to progress further toward the highest degree.
As for the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*):
This refers to the tenth stage and the stage of the Tathāgata.
In the tenth stage, the practice of the cause is brought to ultimate fulfillment;
in the stage of the Tathāgata, the merit of the fruit is perfected to its highest degree.
For this reason, they are given the same name, "ultimate.
This discussion is based merely on one approach;
if one enters through other approaches, the causes and effects differ.
The explanation of the names and meanings of this single section is thus concluded.
Next, its essence is determined:
all the stages (bhūmi) take practice and virtue as their essence.
The opening and closing, as well as the expansion and contraction, of the gate of practice are not fixed;
in total there is only one practice,
though it may be divided into two.
First is the practice of realization;
second is the practice of the Āgamas,
as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, with respect to merit and wisdom, they may also be divided into two,
or separated into three; that is to say,
realization, assistance, and non-abiding, as explained above.
Furthermore, morality, concentration, and wisdom may also be divided into three,
or expanded into four:
hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.
Some explain them as six,
namely the six pāramitās;
others divide them into ten.
This refers to the ten pāramitās.
Furthermore, faith and the other [faculties] may also be divided into ten.
Alternatively, they may be further categorized as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
If expanded, it is immeasurable.
Such is the essential nature [of these two gates]. Having concluded these two gates, next we shall distinguish their characteristics.
The opening and closing, as well as the expansion and brevity, of these stages are not fixed;
however, when summarized, they are essentially only two:
the first is the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
Second is the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-bhūmi*).
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages who have faith, compliance, and orientation toward the supramundane path are called those on the stage of faith (*adhimukti-bhūmi*).
From the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, those who are in accord with the realization of reality are called those on the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-bhūmi*).
Alternatively, it is divided into three,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
the first type, the lineage-holding (*gotra-dhara*), resides in the stage of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).

Second, the maintenance of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is situated on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). Third, the maintenance of the application of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is situated from the first bhūmi upward.
Alternatively, these may be divided into four.
First, the path of expedient means (upāyamārga) exists prior to the stages (bhūmi).
Second, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) exists in the first stage.
Third, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) exists from the second stage upward.
The four paths of no-more-learning exist within the stage of Buddhahood;
alternatively, they may be expanded into five,
by distinguishing the path of skillful means from the preceding four as the separate stages of lineage, understanding, and practice.
Thus, there are five types;
alternatively, they may be divided into six,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichichi).
1. The stage of the nature of a single type;
2. The stage of practice through understanding;
3. The stage of the pure mind.
The fourth is the stage of the four tracks;
the fifth is the stage of certainty,
namely the eighth and ninth stages.
The sixth is the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), which refers to the tenth stage.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is stated that this is for those bodhisattvas who abide in the six stages.
Speaking on this basis,
some further explain seven [stages],
as extensively distinguished above.
Within the first six, the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*) is divided into certainty itself and the practice of certainty (*niyata-caryā*);
thus, there are seven types.
Furthermore, they can also be divided into eight.
Within the first seven [stages], the lineage-nature (*gotrabhūmi*) is divided into the categories of the cultivated lineage-nature (*śikṣā-gotra*) and the seed-lineage-nature (*bīja-gotra*);
thus, there are eight. Furthermore, they can also be divided into nine.
Within the first eight [stages], the stage of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) is divided into the stage of ultimate perfection and the stage of the Tathāgata;
thus, there are nine types.
Alternatively, they may be divided into thirteen.
As stated in the "Chapter on Abiding" of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*,

by adding the stages of the lineage-abiding (*gotra-vihāra*), the practice-through-understanding-abiding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), and the Tathāgata-abiding (*tathāgata-vihāra*) to those ten stages, there are thirteen.
It can also be divided into fourteen.

What are called these are: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, not drinking intoxicants, not dancing, singing, or performing as entertainers, not wearing garments scented with perfumes, not using high or wide beds, and not eating past midday; such are their names.
Because these serve as prohibitions and restraints, they are called *śīla* (precepts).
To be pure and clean is called *śuci*. Question: [What is this purity?]
Regarding the phrase "abstaining from sexual misconduct" within those five precepts,
why is it now stated simply as "abstaining from sexual intercourse"? To explain:
The five precepts are the lay precepts observed by householders;
they prohibit only sexual misconduct and do not forbid [intercourse with] one's own wife.
For this reason, it is simply stated as "no sexual misconduct."
The treatise states that while those who observe the eight precepts are householders, they are able to maintain the precepts of one who has left the home life;
for these precepts do not merely prohibit misconduct with others, but also guard against even one's own wife.
Therefore, it is said: "one abstains from sexual misconduct."
Question: Within this, there are nine items that are abstained from; for what reason is it called merely the "eight precepts"?
Explanation:
There is a reason for this.
According to the Abhidharma, one does not wear perfumed clothing nor sit upon high beds;
these two [prohibitions] arise from the same basis: the impulse toward adornment.
Combining these into one,
they are thus said to be eight.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the first eight constitute the precepts (*śīla*).
The last one is the *upavāsa* (fasting observance).
Since the precepts and the fasting observance are explained together, it is called the "Eightfold Fasting Observance. This concludes this section.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished.
Among these, there are five. First, the essential nature:
the discernment that one does not exceed the midday meal is the *niyama* (the rule), and it is also a branch of the *niyama*.
The remainder are factors of the wings of concentration but are not concentration itself;
for example, right view within the Eightfold Noble Path is both the path and a factor of the path,
whereas the remaining [factors] are factors of the path but are not the path itself.
This is also like that.
By means of non-killing and so forth, one prevents evil and restrains transgressions, thereby assisting in the accomplishment of the *śīla* (precept) dharma.
Within this assistance to the *śīla* dharma, there are various distinctions.
Therefore it is called "equal-interval" (śīla).
It is not a method of fasting;
thus it is not called "fasting."
However, because abstaining from midday meals is a method of fasting, it is called *naiṣpeṣika* (the fast).
Because it is distinct from the preceding seven types, it is termed a "limb of the fast" (*upavāsāṅga*).
Second is the analysis according to the nature of the prohibitions.
The first four types involve abstaining from natural misdeeds (*prakṛti-sāvadya*),
while [the remaining] abstaining from drinking alcohol and so forth involves abstaining from proscribed misdeeds (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Question:
There are seven types of natural evil,
beginning with killing and extending to frivolous speech.
Why is it that one does not abandon all of them, but only abandons the first four?
Because frivolous speech and the like are difficult to guard against, and because those living as householders are unable to abandon them,
the treatise states:
"Even those who have gone forth are not yet able to abandon them."
How much more so for those living at home?
Furthermore, because frivolous speech and the like are contrary to the Dharma, they are collectively termed "false speech";
however, apart from abstaining from false speech, one should follow the same principle for the others.
Therefore, they are not discussed separately.
Furthermore, the first four types are explained in detail because they are grave,
whereas the others are omitted because they are light.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
[The opponent] asks:
"The distinctions among prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are immeasurable."
Why not speak of "abandoning" rather than "staying far away from" drinking alcohol and so forth?
It is because other faults are difficult for laypeople to guard against;
furthermore, since drinking alcohol and the like give rise to grave transgressions, they are specifically mentioned as things to be abandoned.
The remaining transgressions are not discussed because they are minor.
This concludes the analysis of merit according to the three paths.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
being free from the first five faults constitutes the causal conditions for merit (*puṇya*),
while being free from the latter three transgressions constitutes the causal conditions for the Path (*mārga*).
Because those who live as householders have not yet attained the Way,
he has therefore only spoken of the causes and conditions for the Way.
When one attains penetration, all are equal.
Fourth, the analysis according to the complete sets.
"Complete sets" refers to the three types of action:

abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from drinking intoxicants, abstaining from wearing perfumed garments, abstaining from using high or luxurious beds, and abstaining from eating past midday.
This is the action of body.
Not speaking falsely is the action of speech.
"Not dancing or singing" refers generally to the actions of body and speech;
it is distinguished by five things that are to be guarded against.
According to the Abhidharma, the first four factors of the precepts consist in the nature of abstaining from evil;
as for not drinking alcohol,
this is the factor of non-negligence, which distances one from the causes and conditions of negligence.
The remainder consists of the *dhāraṇī-śākhā* (branches of retention) and the remaining prohibitions against faults.
In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* as well, these are divided into three;
their names do not differ.
He says that the first four [precepts] involve the actual abandonment of evil,
whereas not drinking alcohol does not.
One departs from all gates of evil.
As for the others, they are far removed from the causes and conditions of negligence. These two sections are concluded.
Next, the distinctions among the causes and conditions for attaining the precepts are explained.
According to the Abhidharma, there are eight causes and conditions.
Thus, that verse says:

namely, the upavāsa, the undertaking [of the vow], the time, another person, the two declarations, the completeness [of the precepts], one day and night, and the avoidance of adornment and [ordinary] deportment.
Upavāsa is one such cause and condition;
it clarifies that these eight precepts are for upāsakas who have not gone forth.
This is because those who have gone forth are capable of undertaking and maintaining the lifelong precepts.

Regarding what is called "receiving," these two conditions clarify that one must formally undertake these eight precepts to distinguish them from dhyāna-precepts, untainted (anāsrava) precepts, and so forth.
Regarding the term "time," these are the three reasons [for specifying it];
they clarify that these eight precepts must be received at the time of dawn and cannot be received at any other time.
Because one wishes to fulfill [the precepts] for a full day and night,
one may receive them at any time within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi) system.
As for what is called "another":
These are the four causes and conditions.
This clarifies that these eight precepts must be received from another; they cannot be undertaken through a self-vow.
The *Tattvasiddhi* differs from this.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"If no person is present, one may receive [the precepts] through mental recollection and verbal declaration.
As for the phrase "two declarations": [it refers to the following].
These are the five causes and conditions.
It is only through these two modes of instruction that the eight precepts are properly received:
first, the preceptor teaches the recipient, and subsequently, the recipient follows along.
The preceptor asks first and the recipient answers later;
this constitutes two distinct utterances.
The *Tattvasiddhi* differs from this.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Because one does not understand it oneself, one requires the instruction of a teacher;
if one understood it oneself, what need would there be for a teacher's instruction?"
For this reason, it is unnecessary to state both;
that which is called "complete" refers to these six causal conditions.
It is understood that these eight precepts must be received in their entirety to be validly received; they cannot be received partially.
However, in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is held that they may be received even if not complete.
Thus, that treatise states:
The amount— whether much or little— is indefinite according to one's capacity and strength.
As for the duration of one day and night,
these are the seven causal conditions.
It clarifies that the duration of these eight precepts is strictly one day and one night, neither more nor less;
thus, their establishment differs [from other systems].
Therefore, that treatise states:
If it is said that the eight precepts are fixed for one day and night,
this is not so; they vary according to the duration of time.
Whether it be for half a day or even up to a month,
what fault could there possibly be?
To depart from formal decorum constitutes these eight causes and conditions.
One should clearly understand that the essentials of these eight precepts involve the skillful undertaking of them by remaining free from various ornaments for the body;
this is because those living at home practice and train in the precepts of one who has gone forth according to their capacity.
Although the treatises differ,
the recipient should receive [the precepts] according to the Abhidharma,
as it largely accords with what is taught in the various sūtras. Thus ends this section on the three gates.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished according to the realms and destinies.
"Realms" refers to the three realms;
[feeling] is acquired in the desire realm.
It does not belong to the two upper realms.
"Destinies" refers to the five destinies,
according to the Abhidharma.
The inhabitants of the three continents are able to receive the eight precepts because they possess the power of swift and alert mental awareness;
this does not extend to other realms of existence nor to Uttarakuru.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
humans, devas, pretas, and animals are all able to receive it;
thus that treatise states:
Just as the Lord of Devas frequently observes the eight precepts, so too do the nāgas and others observe them;
they are not restricted to humans alone. This concludes the four gates.
Next, we shall distinguish their characteristics according to their physical retribution.
According to the Abhidharma,
those of male or female form may receive [the precepts],
while others with different forms cannot.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, even eunuchs, those with dual sexual organs, and impotent persons may receive [the precepts];
it is not restricted solely to men and women. This concludes the five gates.
Next, we shall distinguish their commonality and exclusivity by correlating them with the realms (*dhātu*).
One should know that the eight precepts are obtained in relation to all sentient beings universally;
they cannot be obtained through specific conditions. Question:
Is it attained in relation to all sentient beings of the present,
or is it attained in relation to sentient beings of the three periods of time?
The commentaries offer differing explanations.
According to the Abhidharma,
it is acquired only in relation to present sentient beings;
according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is acquired universally in relation to sentient beings across all three periods of time.
Although sentient beings of the past and future cannot be killed, stolen from, and so forth, wholesome or unwholesome states can still arise by taking them as objects; thus ends this sixth section.
Next, the ritual for receiving and upholding the eight precepts is explained.
Those who wish to receive the precepts should first give rise to a mind of revulsion toward birth and death and seek the aspiration for nirvana;
only then should they receive them.
This is because the precepts thus received are supramundane.
What is the method for receiving the precepts?
On the six fast days, at the time of early dawn,
one should go to the place of the preceptor.
First, pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Next, pay homage to the Precept Master.
Standing before the Precept Master:
Kneeling with palms joined,
first repent of all transgressions,
and then receive the precepts.
The preceptor instructs them in the three refuges in the Triple Gem;
this is completed after the refuges have been recited three times.
Administer the five precepts,
which are the same as those for a śrāmaṇera;
thereafter, perform the dharmas listed above.
He asks about their capacity:
"To refrain from killing one creature is the precept of an upāsaka.
If a woman receives it..."
It should be said that this is the Upāsikā precept;
it is received for one day and one night, from the present moment until the dawn of the following morning.
"Can you uphold [the precepts] as the Buddhas have done?
The recipient should answer, "I can.
In this manner, it continues until the prohibition against eating past midday.
The question and answer were the same as before;
one round was sufficient.
Having finished, he prostrated and departed.
The method for maintaining [the precepts] is the same as that for the monastic precepts.
All items used for adorning the body should be discarded.
Men and women must not sleep in the same room.
The eight precepts are thus concluded.

First, the discernment of its name.
The names differ;
briefly, there are seven kinds.
The first is called dhyāna (meditative concentration).
The second is called concentration (*samādhi*);
the third is called samādhi;
the fourth is called right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*).
The fifth is called samādhi;
the sixth is called śamatha;
the seventh is called liberation.
It is also called "back-turning liberation" (prātimokṣa).
"Dhyāna" is the term used in the Middle Kingdom (China).
This is translated as "cultivation through reflection" (*manasikāra-bhāvanā*).
It is also called the "Forest of Merits.
Regarding "cultivation through reflection":
The designation is established based on its cause:
the careful mental deliberation regarding the object of concentration is called *vitarka* (reflection);
the progressive advancement of that mental state is termed *bhāvanā* (cultivation).
From the perspective of defining it by its function, it is called "cultivation through contemplation" (*manasikāra-bhāvanā*).
Alternatively, this term may be used as a designation based on its essential nature:
the mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) that correctly apprehends its object of focus is termed "contemplation."
The advancement of the mind through reflection is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"Forest of merit" is a name derived from its fruit.
Wisdom, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth are its merits.
Because it is said that a "grove" (*vana*) is an accumulation of manifold virtues,
meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is able to produce it.
Because the cause is designated by the name of its fruit, it is therefore called a "grove of merit.
As for what is termed "concentration" (samādhi):
The essence itself constitutes the name.
Because the mind abides upon a single object and is free from distraction and movement, it is called "concentration" (samādhi).
As for the term "samādhi":
This is a term from a foreign language; here it is called *samyaksamādhi* (right concentration).
Concentration is explained as before; because it is free from error and distraction, it is called "right. As for the term "right reception" (*samyaksamāpatti*), [it refers to this].
This is explained in the same manner as before.
"Dharma" refers to what is received;
"samādhi" refers to meditative concentration.
These are foreign terms.
*Samādhi* and *samāpatti* were originally one and the same name;
it is only that their phonetic transmissions differ.
This is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
When the function of concentration manifests, it is termed *samāpatti*. As for *śamatha*:
It is also a foreign term;
here it is translated as "stopping" (śamatha). It refers to the mind’s gathering and abiding upon an object.
To "cease" refers to the eye;
that which is called "liberation" is a designation for the severing of bonds.
Regarding the term "relinquishment" (*prahāṇa*):
it is called "relinquishment" because one turns away from and abandons lower faults.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna says: [text follows].
