Because the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object arise by taking the untainted as their condition, there is an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because they do not obstruct the savoring [of the object], there is a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Because they are not of the same category (na svabhāga), there is no cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya).
Because they are not born from a proximate cause (*samanantarapratyaya*), there is no sequential condition.
Second, regarding the analysis by way of the stages (*bhūmi*):
with respect to the flavors of one's own stage and the flavors of other stages, they are said to lead toward two conditions.
Because one can give rise to fetters by taking as objects those [dharmas] belonging to another stage, a higher stage, a lower stage, or the untainted (anāsrava),
there exists an object-of-the-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya).
Because the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad in scope, it exists [in all cases].
Regarding the numerical classification of the three grades:
in the context of functioning as a condition, no distinction between superior, middling, or inferior grades is made. This concludes the section on the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Next, the meditative absorption of relishing (*āsvādanasamādhi*) is explained. Regarding the relationship between one instance of relishing and another instance of relishing, it is also explained by way of three propositions.
First, the extent of the presence of conditions.
This possesses four conditions;
as in the case of the pure [factors] mentioned above,
the similar types may be understood accordingly.
Second, the classification according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
In relation to its own stage, it possesses all four conditions;
in relation to a higher stage looking down upon a lower stage, it possesses the remaining three conditions, excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The afflictions are bound to their respective stages;
since they are not of the same category when compared across different stages, their causal conditions are excluded.
At the time of retrogression, a superior flavor gives rise to an inferior one.
Therefore, there are sequential and predominant conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya* and *adhipati-pratyaya*).
However, regarding this superior flavor within all flavors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the lower stages,
it possesses the full sense of both sequential and predominant conditions.
Without distinction as to whether it is near or far—
meaning that within the higher stages,
a defiled mind arises.
Because defiled minds arise in all lower stages, those [minds] of the higher stages take them as objects;
thus, they cause [the defilements] to arise by taking the higher [stages] as objects.
Therefore, there is an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
When looking down from a lower level toward all higher levels,
none are present. When there is a lower flavor,
the flavor of the higher levels can only be accomplished [through cultivation].
Because they do not manifest [as actual entities],
they are distinguished by way of three grades.
All afflictions— whether superior, middling, or inferior grades— act as the four conditions for one another when compared reciprocally.
Question: For what reason, within the context of the pure and untainted [states],
are the causes and conditions explained in relation to those that are equal and superior?
One does not expect the lower grade within this concentration of taste.
Is it then by referring generally to the lower grade that the causal conditions are explained?
The commentary states:
"Wholesome dharmas originally non-existent now exist;
they arise through the cultivation of skillful means."
The phenomena that arise through conditioning proceed from the subtle to the manifest;
therefore, an inferior cause does not produce a superior effect, nor does a superior cause produce an inferior effect.
Descending from the superior to the inferior constitutes the order of retrogression,
not the order of birth.
Therefore, they are not causes [in the strict sense].
Nevertheless, because all afflictions have long been habituated until they become innate and mutually stimulate one another,
that which is superior may also serve as a cause for that which is inferior.
Furthermore, when descending from a higher stage to give rise to the fetters of a lower stage,
all nine grades of afflictions are acquired simultaneously;
whichever may arise first serves as the cause.
Therefore, when the higher [dhyāna] is viewed in relation to the lower, there is the sense of being a cause; this concludes the first section.
When the "flavoring" (āsvādana) is viewed in relation to the pure dhyāna, it is also explained by way of three propositions:
first, the extent of the conditions possessed.
Excluding those with specific causes and conditions, there are three remaining types.
Second, regarding the classification by stage:
within its own stage, it possesses all three conditions in their entirety.
The same applies to the lower levels.
After a mind of superior taste, one may give rise to a pure concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*) of a lower level to prevent falling back from one's own stage.
Therefore, looking toward the lower pure [attainments], there is the sense of successive superior conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Based on the lower pure meditative concentration, one trains in contemplating the higher "flavor" (*āsvāda*) as suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Thus, the flavor of the higher stage serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the lower stage.
One may expect that the higher pure concentration possesses the status of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
What is the meaning of this?
It is that another person, perceiving me as an inferior and tainted object, gives rise to a mind of revulsion toward me.
Therefore, there is an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Since my enjoyment does not obstruct the superior purity of others,
there is a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The numerical classification into three grades:
regarding the state of being a condition, there is no distinction between superior, middling, and inferior grades. These two sections are concluded.
With respect to the flavor [of the outflows] in relation to the untainted (anāsrava), it is also explained by way of three propositions.
First, regarding the number of conditions:
there is only the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
the meaning of the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is not its own portion.
Therefore, it lacks those causes and conditions.
Because it does not arise from a proximate cause, it lacks the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Second, the analysis according to the stages.
Regarding those [dharmas] belonging to the same level,
there are both object-conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) and predominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya).
The same applies to those belonging to lower levels.

Because the higher stages take the taste of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rasa*) as their objects of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), they possess the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since the higher does not obstruct the lower, they possess the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In relation to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the higher and lower stages, both of these [conditions] are likewise present.
My own attachment (āsvādana) takes the untainted (anāsrava) states of other higher stages as its objects of suffering and origin;
therefore, it possesses an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
My own attachment does not obstruct the untainted states of others in the higher stages.
Therefore, there is predominance.
Although the three grades are distinguished numerically,
no distinction between superior, middling, or inferior grades is made in their capacity to serve as conditions.
The distinctions among these conditions are thus.
Within the eighth section,
there are briefly thirteen variations regarding the differences between the Great and Small [Vehicles].
The nature of their unity differs:
the meditative concentration (dhyāna) of the Hīnayāna takes the phenomenal consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) as its essence;
the Great [Vehicle] likewise initially takes the phenomenal consciousness as its essence during the stage of cultivation.
Next, the conventional consciousness (*saviṣayavijñāna*) is eliminated, taking deluded consciousness as its essence;
finally, the deluded consciousness is eliminated, taking true consciousness (*tathatāvijñāna*) as its essence.
These two differ in being eternal and non-eternal, respectively.
That which is attained by the Hīnayāna is exclusively impermanent;
within the Mahāyāna teachings, one begins by cultivating the realization of impermanence,
yet ultimately achieves that which is permanent.
Because the Truth (satya) is the essence,
there is a distinction between the three outflows (āsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava).
In the Śrāvaka vehicle, from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), both the outflowing and the outflow-free are present.
The single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, although it exists, it only accords with the traditional contemplations and is not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
In the Mahāyāna, the eight dhyānas all pertain to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"What is the bodhisattva’s concentration on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
That which is conjoined with the true nature (dharmatā) is called the bodhisattva’s concentration on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Fourth, regarding the differences in the cessation of hindrances:
the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the Hīnayāna can only eliminate the coarse disturbances of the four abodes (*catur-vāsana*),
whereas the meditative concentrations of the Mahāyāna can eliminate all [hindrances].
Fifth, there are differences in depth and shallowness.
The meditative concentration of the Hīnayāna is shallow;
it can be moved by conditions.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"When the great Kinnara king played the lapis lazuli lute,
Kāśyapa rose to dance."
Ānanda’s chanting was shallow because his meditative concentration was not yet deep;
it was unlike the profound stillness of the dhyāna-concentration of the various bodhisattvas.
It is such that even celestial thunder cannot disturb it.
Sixth, the conditions for the mind differ:
the meditative concentration (dhyāna) of the Hīnayāna possesses both mental objects and conditions.
In the Mahāyāna, at the initial stage of practice, there is conceptualization and objective conditions;
at the final stage of accomplishment, one becomes free from conditions.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
As the Buddha previously taught to Kātyāyana:
"A bhikṣu does not rely on anything when practicing dhyāna.
How is it that he does not rely?
If one eliminates [notions] stage by stage,
up until the elimination of all and every notion,
there are seven ways in which the objects of focus differ.
Ordinary beings take the phenomena of meditative concentration as their object;
those of the Two Vehicles take the characteristics of dharmas such as suffering and impermanence as their object;
and Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take true nature as their object.
Eighth, the difference regarding emergence and entry:
in what is attained by the Hīnayāna, there is both emergence and entry;
in the Mahāyāna Dharma, there is emergence and entry from the very beginning.
In the case of the perfected ones, it is not so;
for at all times, there is no lack of concentration.
Ninth, they differ in their transcendence.
The Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna cannot transcend more than one stage within the dhyānas;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, however, are able to transcend all stages according to their respective capacities, whether few or many.
There are ten different modes of taking birth.
The followers of the Two Vehicles, having attained dhyāna, are unable to return to take birth in the desire realm;
Bodhisattvas, however, are fully able to remain free from fetters while within meditative concentration.
Thus, there are eleven points in which their practices differ.
The practitioners of the Hīnayāna cultivate dhyāna solely for their own benefit, whereas those of the Mahāyāna benefit both themselves and others; thus,
the virtues produced over twelve lifetimes differ accordingly.
The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the Hīnayāna can produce only a small portion of merit,
whereas the meditative concentrations of a Bodhisattva produce everything.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration gives rise to meritorious qualities;
even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know their names,
much less can they give rise to them.
Thirteenth, the attainment of the fruits differs:
the meditative concentrations of the two vehicles result only in small fruits,
whereas that which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas results in great enlightenment.
It is not so. Above, the first section provided a general explanation of the eight dhyānas;
below, the second section provides a specific explanation of the eight dhyānas.
First, one understands the four dhyānas;
subsequently, one understands the four formless attainments.
Within the understanding of the four dhyānas:
There are another six gates:
first, identifying and determining what is being explained; second, analyzing the characteristics through the method of opening and closing [the categories].
1. The establishment or rejection of the three types of causes based on their similarities and differences, their sequence, their essential nature, and their degree of completeness;
2. The demonstration of their general and specific characteristics in relation to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa); 3. The characteristics of their cultivation and accomplishment.
Sixth, the explanation of the meaning according to the text.
First, we shall determine the subject to be explained:
there are three kinds of dhyāna.
The first is flavor, the second is purity, and the third is the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Flavor refers to afflictions;
it is not a meritorious dharma.
I shall now set this aside without further discussion.
As for the fruits of untainted dhyāna,
I shall likewise not explain them here.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of pure dhyāna (*śuddha-dhyāna*): there are four divisions.
The first is the regressive division (*hāna-bhāgīya*).
Second is the stage of abiding;
third is the stage of superior progress;
fourth is the stage of certainty.
Regarding the term "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*),
there are two interpretations.
First, it refers to a state of pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) of inferior grade that is adjacent to inferior afflictions (*kleśa*).
Joy is called the "part conducive to decline" because it is defeated by the afflictions of the lower stages;
since this can be lost, it is termed "decline."
It is not that [the practitioner] has already fallen away.
Second, it is called the "part conducive to decline" (hānabhāgīya) because it is mixed with the afflictions of its own level;
that is to say, one enters the afflictions of the realm of desire from a pure meditative absorption (śuddha-samādhi).
From the defiled state of attachment, one returns to enter pure concentration.
Just as a weak and inferior wholesome mind within the desire realm is again mixed with the unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm,
so it is in this case as well.
Even though it is mixed with those afflictions,
it is not called "losing concentration," because the factors belong to the same stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the term "stationary part" (*sthiti-bhāga*),
there are two interpretations. First,
it refers to firmly maintaining one's own stage (*sva-bhūmi*).
Because one is not defeated by the afflictions of the lower stages,
it is called "abiding. This distinguishes it from the initial retreat of the higher stages.
Second, one firmly maintains a pure mind,
untainted by the afflictions of one's own level;
therefore, it is called "abiding."
After the stage of "simplification" (prāntakoṭika),

there is the stage of "progression" (viśeṣabhāgīya). This refers to the state of wearying oneself of the defects of one's own level and proceeding toward the higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that accord with them.
The stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) refers to the training in contemplating all phenomena as suffering, impermanent, and so forth,
thereby proceeding in accordance with the Noble Path.
Yet they have not yet attained the state of an Ārya.
Within the second gate,
the classification and synthesis of their characteristics are presented through various modes of opening and closing that are not fixed.
In total, there is only one dhyāna;
that is to say, among the three trainings, it is exclusively the training in concentration,
and among the six perfections, it is exclusively the perfection of dhyāna.
Alternatively, they may be divided into two: first, remoteness;
second, cessation.
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
"In the first dhyāna, being far removed from desires, evils, and unwholesome states is called 'separation' (*viveka*).
From the second dhyāna upward, the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and so forth is called 'tranquility' (*upaśama*)."
Alternatively, they may be divided into three.
Regarding these three, there are two approaches:
first, dividing them into three based on the types of sensation (*vedanā*).
The first and second dhyānas are called dhyānas accompanied by joy;
the third is accompanied by bliss;
the fourth is accompanied by equanimity.
Second, regarding the presence or absence of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), there are three divisions:
the first dhyāna is called "with vitarka and with vicāra";
the intermediate dhyāna is called "without vitarka and with vicāra."
From the second dhyāna upward, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Alternatively, they may be divided into four,
namely the four dhyānas, which differ according to six meanings.
Therefore, they are divided into four.
First, the obstacles eliminated differ:
in the first dhyāna, one distances oneself from desires and unwholesome, evil states.
In the stage of the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are eliminated;
in the third dhyāna, joy (prīti) is eliminated;
and in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (sukha) is eliminated.
Second, the cessation of feeling differs.
As it is said in the sūtras:
"In the first dhyāna, sorrow is ceased."
In the second dhyāna, suffering is extinguished;
in the third dhyāna, joy is extinguished;
in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure is extinguished.
Question: In the first dhyāna, both sorrow and suffering are extinguished.
Why, then, is it said that sorrow is extinguished in the first dhyāna and suffering is extinguished in the second dhyāna?
According to the Abhidharma,
within the stage of the first dhyāna, there exist the three groups of consciousness— visual, auditory, and tactile.
These three groups of consciousness are the bases for the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
Therefore, cessation is not mentioned.
If that is so, then since the mental consciousness and the faculty of grief have their basis in the first dhyāna, there would be mind in the first dhyāna.
One should not extinguish sorrow.
The commentary explains:
"The fault of the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) is coarse and heavy."
Since concentration exists within the desire realm,
it is taught that the first dhyāna eliminates sorrow. What,
then, is "coarseness" (dausthulya)?
Sorrow arises from the mind of craving within the desire realm;
because one becomes attached to the five sensory objects of the desire realm,
sorrow is produced only when one perceives their disintegration and ruin.
Suffering is not like this;
therefore, its cessation is not mentioned.
Furthermore, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) arises only after one has fallen away from meditative concentration.
Suffering is not like this;
it arises immediately upon emerging from meditative absorption.
Therefore, these two cases are not analogous.
What is discussed in the *Tattvasiddhi* is that suffering is not extinguished because the three bodies of consciousness still exist due to desire in the first dhyāna; rather,
it is because that first dhyāna is close to the ground of the desire realm and possesses an unstable mind.
Because painful sensation can arise within an undetermined state of mind,
suffering is not extinguished;
this is the case when one is near the desire realm.
One should also experience sorrow;
why, then, is it said to be extinguished?
The commentary explains:
Sorrow arises from a mind of greedy joy;
it is only when one withdraws from meditative concentration that it is produced. If one does not cling to desire, [it does not arise].
One ultimately does not give rise to sorrow;
suffering is not like this.
Therefore, although there is the sensation of suffering, the root of sorrow is extinguished.
Third, the factors specific to each stage differ:
in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra differ from those in the other dhyānas;
in the second dhyāna, there is internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
In the third dhyāna there is tranquility and wisdom;
in the stage of the fourth dhyāna there is neither suffering nor pleasure;
these are each distinct from one another.
Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish four [stages];
because the concentrated mind varies in its coarseness and subtlety, the four dhyānas are distinguished.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The mind in the first dhyāna-concentration is like finely kneaded dough;
the nature of the mind is otherwise scattered and restless."
Because it is sustained by the Dharma,
it is able to abide upon its object;
the mind of the second dhyāna is like a spring on a mountain peak.
The water flows forth from within;
it does not come from without.
The mind in the third dhyāna is like a lotus flower in a pond.
Internally and externally overflowing,
his mind in the fourth dhyāna was like a lamp in a sealed chamber,
serene and unmoving.
The four dhyānas are distinguished because the fruits of the five types of sensation differ.
The first dhyāna can attain the fruits of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā heavens.
The second dhyāna can attain the fruits of the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara heavens.
The third dhyāna can attain the fruits of Parīttābha (Limited Radiance), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Radiance), and Ābhāsvara (Utmost Purity).
The fourth dhyāna can attain the fruits from Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born) and Brhatphala (Vast Fruit) up to Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Peak) Heaven.
The fourth dhyāna is divided into four abodes because their breadth and narrowness differ,
as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*. Regarding this,
there are two treatises.
One school of thought states that the abode of the first dhyāna is equal in extent to a single four-continent world system (cāturdvīpaka),
while the abode of the second dhyāna is equal to a small thousandfold world system (sāhasracūḍika).
The dwelling places of the third dhyāna are like a two-thousandfold world system;
the dwelling places of the fourth dhyāna are like a three-thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, there is another explanation.
The abodes of the first dhyāna are like a thousandfold world system;
the abodes of the second dhyāna are like a two-thousandfold world system;
the abodes of the third dhyāna are like a three-thousandfold world system.
The abodes of the four dhyānas are immeasurable and boundless;
it is because of these differences that they are divided into four.

It can also be analyzed into five factors, namely:

vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), adhyātmasaṃprasāda (internal serenity), upekṣāsmṛtisamprajanya (equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension), and aduḥkhāsukha (neither-pain-nor-pleasure).
Furthermore, according to the distinctions between the stages, it can also be analyzed into six factors.
This refers to the preparatory, intermediate, and fundamental stages of the four dhyānas;
as their mental factors differ, they can also be divided into nine.
The five factors of the first dhyāna constitute five distinct counts.
Awakening is a factor of awakening;
contemplation is a factor of awakening;
joy is a factor of feeling.
Pleasure (*sukha*) is the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*). One-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) is the factor of concentration (*samādhi*).
In the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is added as one [additional factor].
Including the preceding [factors], there are six in total.
This factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is based on the Abhidharma;
it is a member of the category of faith (*śraddhā*).
One believes that the lower stage is characterized by much fault due to the agitation of vitarka and vicāra;
one believes that the dharmas of the second dhyāna are tranquil and secure. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also speaks of this as "faith.
Joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind are the same as in the first dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, three additional factors— equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), and clear comprehension (samprajanya)—
are added, making nine in total.
As for equanimity:
These are the mental factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*) among the universal wholesome factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) and discernment (*samprajanya*) are the two factors of mindfulness and wisdom (*mati*) common to all stages (*sarvatraga-bhūmika*).
Pleasure (*sukha*) is the same as the previously mentioned joy (*prīti*), both being factors of feeling (*vedanā*).
One-pointedness of mind is identical to the factor of one-pointedness in the preceding dhyāna;
therefore, it is not discussed separately.
Within the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity and mindfulness is identical to the factors of equanimity and mindfulness in the third dhyāna.
Neither-pain-nor-pleasure is the same as the preceding joy.
As for the factor of one-pointedness of mind, it is the same as the preceding one-pointedness of mind;
therefore, it is not mentioned separately.
The names of the practices differ, and when categorized separately, they become ten.
The five factors of the first dhyāna constitute five;
inner serenity constitutes the sixth.
Equanimity, mindfulness, and settled wisdom, together with the preceding factors, constitute nine.
Within the third dhyāna, the mental factor of pleasure (*sukha*) is distinguished as being the same as the preceding joy (*prīti*);
its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is distinguished as being the same as the preceding pleasure.
The state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is included within the previously mentioned ten factors.
This mental factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is the same as the previous factor of joy (*prīti*);
because it is a mental factor of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), it is not discussed separately.
The term "equanimity" (upekṣā) refers to a discernment distinct from the preceding joy and bliss;
therefore, it is explained separately.
In the fourth dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind are not different from those mentioned above.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
The meanings of their modes of activity differ, and thus they are divided into eleven categories,
as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Within the first ten,
"joyful undertaking" (pramodya-karaṇīya) is divided into two; thus, there are eleven.
As for the reason for this distinction:
the bliss of the first and second dhyānas is the bliss of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*);
the bliss within the third dhyāna is the bliss of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*).
This is how they are divided. According to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), if one distinguishes them according to their functions—
such as the elimination of hindrances and so forth— there are sixteen types.
The first dhyāna has four aspects.
The first is the cessation of hindrances,
which means the cessation of sensual desires and evil.
Second is the remedy,
namely vitarka and vicāra.
Third is the benefit.
These are what are called joy and bliss.
Fourth is the samādhi that serves as the basis for those two,
namely, one-pointedness of mind.
As it is with the first dhyāna,
so it is with the other three;
thus, there are sixteen.
When divided according to their distinct factors, there are eighteen.
Among the ten types categorized as the preliminary stages,
these include applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), internal purity, tranquility, wisdom, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is divided into one part,
which is further divided into five;
the faculties of joy (*prīti*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are each likewise divided into two.
Including the previous eleven,
there are two types of the factor of joy (*prīti-vibhāga*):
namely, the joy of the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.
The factor of equanimity and mindfulness refers to the equanimity and mindfulness of the third and fourth dhyānas.
The factor of bliss is threefold.
Including the preceding ones, there are fourteen.
Since the first, second, and third dhyānas all possess bliss (*sukha*),
they are divided into three types.
Each *citta* is divided into four;
thus, there are eighteen.
Within each of the stages of the four *dhyānas*, there is one *citta*.
Thus, they are divided into four types.
To speak according to their actual enumeration,
there are twenty-three distinct mental factors.
That is to say, ten factors pervade the universal ground (mahābhūmika):

perception (saṃjñā), desire-to-act (chanda), contact (sparśa), wisdom (prajñā), mindfulness (smṛti), volition (cetanā), liberation (vimukti), attention (manaskāra), concentration (samādhi), and feeling (vedanā).
Ten factors pertain to the wholesome universal ground (kuśalamahābhūmika).
These are non-attachment, non-hatred, shame, dread of blame, faith, pliancy, heedfulness, non-harming, diligence, and equanimity.
When the mental king (citta-rāja) is added along with initial and sustained application, they constitute twenty-three factors.
This is discussed in detail according to the specific stages (bhūmi).
There are eighty-six [factors].
Within the stage of the first dhyāna there are twenty-three;
within each of the latter three dhyānas there are twenty-one.
Excluding vitarka and vicāra,
the opening and closing are thus.
Within the third section, there are four distinct meanings.
The first member [of the syllogism] is based on identity and difference;
the second member is based on priority and posteriority;
the third consists in the determination of the essential nature.
Regarding the establishment and abolition of the various branches of causes according to the four explanations,
as for their similarities and differences,
they rely upon the *Abhidharma*.
The five factors of the first dhyāna differ in their essential natures;
this is likewise the case for the distinct factors up to the fourth dhyāna.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however:
Throughout the general discussion from beginning to end, it is established that all [phenomena] are nothing other than the mind; externally, they are not numerous.
According to their modes of activity (*ākāra*), there is no absence of similarity or difference.
As in the case of the first dhyāna,
the essence of vitarka and vicāra is the same, differing only in their sequence;
so it is said there.
The initial volition of the coarse mind is called *vitarka* (applied thought),
while the subsequent volition of the subtle mind is termed *vicāra* (sustained thought);
yet their essence is one.
In the first and second dhyānas, the essence of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) is the same.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"When that joy first arises in the body, it is called bliss."
Later, it is called "joy.
He states that the pleasure within the first and second dhyānas is also the feeling of pleasure.
Therefore, joy (*prīti*) is one [factor].
Inner purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) in the second dhyāna is identical with one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Thus, that treatise states:
The factor of internal purity is the essence of the second dhyāna;
in the third dhyāna, serenity and wisdom share the same essence as mindfulness.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"In the third dhyāna, tranquility (praśrabdhi) and discernment (samprajanya) are identical with mindfulness (smṛti).
Consequently, discernment is not established as a separate factor within the subsequent [higher] dhyānas."
The three untainted dhyānas are described as being subsequent stages relative to the tainted dhyānas.
Furthermore, within these three dhyānas, equanimity and pleasure are concurrent;
thus, that treatise states:
I do not say that there is a pleasure distinct from and separate from equanimity; rather, it is the very relinquishing [of the lower factors] that is called pleasure.
In the fourth dhyāna, the four factors are each distinct.
In the Mahayana teachings, consciousness consists of three types:
first, the consciousness of phenomena;
second, the deluded consciousness.
The third is true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
Within that object-consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*), the mind and its mental factors are distinct;
herein, dhyāna is explained.
The supporting causes and conditions are each distinct.
Within deluded consciousness, there are six levels of differentiation in meaning,
as Asvaghosa has explained.
The fundamental fourfold mental states have no distinction in their numerical count.
Among them, when discussing the dhyānas,
the factors (aṅga), causes, and essential natures are identical.
In the final two sections, the mind and its numerical factors differ;
therein, the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and their constituent factors (aṅga) are explained as being distinct from one another.
Within true consciousness, the mental factors have no distinction;
herein, dhyāna is explained.
Since the factors and the essence are one, this section on the "Single Gate" concludes.
Regarding the sequence of priority:
according to the Abhidharma,
the five factors of the first dhyāna are simultaneous in their essential nature.
There is a sequence of priority among their application;
this is likewise true even for the categories up to the fourth dhyāna.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The five factors of the first dhyāna are established in a temporal sequence;
they cannot exist simultaneously,
for it is taught that mental concomitants do not arise at the same time.
Because they do not occur simultaneously;
only after the first four have ceased does one attain single-mindedness. Question:
If it were said that one only attains one-pointedness of mind after the first four [factors] have ceased,
then the first dhyāna would not be constituted of five factors.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtra:
In the stage of the first dhyāna, five factors are present together.
What is their sequence? Furthermore, at the moment of a single mind, if there were no vitarka and vicāra, [how could it be called dhyāna]?
How does this differ from the second dhyāna?
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on the Second Dhyāna," explains and resolves this point.
As for what was said previously—that the first dhyāna is not composed of five factors—[the following is the explanation].
I do not say that all five factors constitute the first dhyāna. Rather,
because there are vitarka, vicāra, and so forth proximate to the first dhyāna,
it is said that the first dhyāna is accomplished by means of these five factors.
When the Sūtra states that the five factors of the first dhyāna are "concomitant" (saha),
although there is a slight contradiction,
they are nonetheless called concomitant.
It is like saying that a disciple and his teacher are together;
although there is a slight difference in their sequence,
they are still called "together."
As for what distinguishes this from the second dhyāna: in the first dhyāna,
there is proximity to distraction, and meditative concentration has not yet reached profound stillness.
In both entering and emerging [from concentration], there are the mental states of vitarka and vicāra;
this is not the case in the second dhyāna,
where both are absent in both entry and emergence.
Therefore, they are not the same. Question:
Since the first dhyāna is close to vitarka and vicāra, it is said that these are its factors (aṅga).
They are also close to the five sensual desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). Why, then, are the five sensual desires not taught as factors (*aṅga*)?
The treatise says:
Because the five desires turn their backs [on it], they are not called "near.
Furthermore, because the five desires do not abide as causes, they are not said to be near. Question:
If it is said that when one reaches the state of single-mindedness (ekāgratā), joy and bliss (prīti-sukha) no longer exist,
how then can joy and bliss reach the second dhyāna?
To explain this:
In that school, mental factors do not coexist;
therefore, within a single moment of mind, there is no joy or pleasure,
for they are not absent due to being severed.
Regarding the factors of the second dhyāna:
as it is with the first dhyāna,
so it is with the remaining dhyānas by analogy.
That treatise is biased in its adherence to the sequence of function and characteristics;
therefore, it contradicts the principle of simultaneity.
What is taught in the Mahāyāna is the same as that in the Abhidharma.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"For example, during the daytime the many stars do not appear;
it is not that the many stars do not exist."
The mental factors are likewise;
they receive their names according to the occasion.
It is not that these various categories do not exist. This concludes the two gates.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the essential nature," as explained in the Abhidharma,
it refers to [the factors] among the five branches of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the factor of one-pointedness of mind:
it is both dhyāna and a factor of dhyāna.
As for the statement that "it is dhyāna":
This refers to the essence of dhyāna.
To speak of its "limbs" (aṅga) refers to their specific distinctions.
The remaining four are branches but not the dhyāna itself;
they are distinct branches rather than the essence of the dhyāna. Question:
In relation to what are these five said to be "limbs"?
The explanation states:
they are called limbs because they are considered collectively in relation to the stage of the first dhyāna.
All sūtras and śāstras explain it in this same way;
only the *Ratnavali-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states that there is a sixth mind, which is the mind of silence.
If one considers dhyāna to be the essence and the five factors to be the cause,
why are they not identical?
This treatise is composed because that sutra explains the states of both ordinary persons and noble ones in common.
Of these, the first five refer to the mundane meditative mind and are described as the cause;
the sixth refers to the noble mind of silence and is described as the essential nature of concentration.
Regarding how [the person] is established,
the treatise provides no definitive judgment;
commentators explain it in various ways.
Some commentators explain that it is identical to the *mālā* (garland);
it likewise takes the sixth [mental factor], taciturnity (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*), as its essence.
The term "limb" (aṅga) refers to the equality of the single mind;
because it is the cause, it is a cause rather than the essence itself.
According to the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yingluo jing*).
If one discusses this generally for both ordinary beings and sages,
there is no logical flaw; however,
if one proceeds directly from the perspective of mundane dhyāna, [the following applies].
To say that its function is silence as its essence is incorrect.
How is it known to be so?
As that treatise explains the meaning of samādhi:
"The mind abiding on a single object is called the characteristic of samādhi.
This explains the factor of one-pointedness of mind.
To speak of dwelling in a single object of focus, free from applied and sustained thought and accompanied by joy,

its meaning is similar to that of vimokṣa-samādhi.

However, while abiding in samādhi upon a single object, it is impossible to further establish an entity of samādhi outside of that.
The same applies to dhyāna.
Since it abides in a single object, why establish silence as its essential nature?
If you argue that because the sūtras describe factors such as one-pointedness of mind as branches of dhyāna, silence must also be established as an essential nature, [we reply:]...
In this case, since the sūtras speak of the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),

since that [separate essence] does not exist elsewhere,

How can one establish it further?

this is spoken of as a limb in relation to the general stage of the first dhyāna.

Question: If that is so, then it is identical to the Abhidharma;
how can it be distinguished from it?
The commentary states:
The *Tattvasiddhi* merely maintains that the five factors [of dhyāna] do not exist simultaneously, as in the *Abhidharma*;
it does not deny that a single mind constitutes the essence of dhyāna, clearly indicating that they function in common.
Since the five factors of the first dhyāna are thus fully present, the other dhyānas are of a similar nature. This concludes the three gates.
Next, the causes for the number of factors and their establishment or exclusion will be explained.
The first dhyāna and the third dhyāna both establish five factors,
while the second dhyāna and the fourth dhyāna both establish four factors. Why is this so?
The term "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) has two meanings.
First, it is distinguished according to its counteracting of hindrances:
both the first and second dhyānas equally counteract external distraction.
The third and fourth dhyānas together subdue internal disturbances.
External disturbances are of two kinds: first, sensual desires that are evil and unwholesome; [the second being perceptions of form].
Second, regarding the body of the three consciousnesses within the first dhyāna:
because the first dhyāna is the primary antidote to external distraction and requires great effort,
it is established as having five factors (*pañcāṅga*).
The second dhyāna marks the end of the counteraction of external distractions;
because the effort required is slight, it is established as having four factors.
There are two types of internal distraction.
The first dhyāna has joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha).
Regarding the third dhyāna, which counteracts internal distraction,
five factors (aṅga) are established because it initially requires much effort.
Because the fourth dhyāna counteracts internal distraction at its conclusion,
it is established with four factors;
such is the nature of the dharmas of these two stages.
As in the case of the first dhyāna,
exactly five [factors] are established;
there cannot be any more.
That [state] turns its back on desire and evil;
because it requires applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) as its antidote, it possesses applied and sustained thought.
Because it celebrates that which has been abandoned, it possesses joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
The essential nature of single-minded concentration must necessarily be established.
Why, then, is there no factor of "internal serenity"? It is because that [factor] counteracts applied and sustained thought (*vitarka* and *vicāra*).
Because this [stage] possesses vitarka and vicāra,
there is no inner serenity (adhyātmasamprasāda).
Furthermore, within this stage, there are three groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya).
Just as a reflection does not appear on hot, turbid mud,
there is no internal clarity.
Why, then, would there be equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension?
That [state] is contrary to joy (*prīti*).
Since there is joy in this stage,
there is no equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"In the first and second dhyānas, the coarse movement of pliancy and bliss is incompatible with equanimity;
therefore, there is no factor of equanimity."
Why is neither-pain-nor-pleasure not established [as a factor]?
It is because it belongs to the category of feeling (*vedanā*).
The factor of joy (*prīti*) in the first dhyāna likewise belongs to the category of feeling.
Because the two types of feeling do not coexist, they are omitted and not established [therein].
In the second dhyāna, exactly four are established;
no others can exist.
What is the meaning of this?
Because it counteracts vitarka and vicāra as well as the three bodies of consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna,
"inner serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) must be established.
Rejoicing in what has been attained,
one establishes joy and bliss;
this is the essential nature of single-minded concentration.
Logically, it must be established.
Why is it not established? Because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are its factors (*aṅga*).
Because this internal purity is able to counteract that [defilement],
why are equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension not established [as factors]?
This is explained as before.
Because it is contrary to joy (*prīti*).
Why is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha*) not established [as a feeling]?
This is also explained as before.
Because this [feeling of] joy cannot coexist with it,
only five factors are established in the third dhyāna; there can be no others.
To remedy the fault of attachment to joy,
the three factors of equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are established;
pleasure is that which is beneficial.
It is not appropriate that it should not be established.
The essence of single-minded concentration must exist;
its principle must be maintained.
Why are vitarka and vicāra not established as factors?
Because they have already been abandoned previously.
Why is inner serenity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) not established as a factor?
Internal purity is the antidote to vitarka and vicāra.
Once vitarka and vicāra have long been absent, they are no longer required,
just as a person who has recovered from an illness no longer requires medicine.
Why is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling not established [as a separate category]?
Because it belongs to the category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and cannot coexist with this pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
In the fourth dhyāna, there are exactly four [factors].
There must be nothing else remaining;
because one seeks to eliminate the fault of attachment to pleasure,
equanimity, mindfulness, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure are established.
This benefit must logically be established:
the essential nature of single-minded concentration.
The principle is omnipresent.
Why is it that there is no "inner purity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) associated with vitarka and vicāra?
The meaning is the same as explained previously.
Why is there no joy? Because it has already been relinquished previously.
Why is "tranquillity and wisdom" not established as a factor?
According to the Abhidharma,
within the fourth dhyāna, neither-pain-nor-pleasure is concordant with the category of ignorance,
whereas the nature of wisdom (prajñā) is clarity.
These two are contradictory;
therefore, they are not established [as such].
Furthermore, within the third dhyāna, one must guard against these two faults.
First, joy belonging to other stages;
second, bliss belonging to one's own stage;
therefore, "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*) is established.
This stage merely excludes the faults of the pleasures of other stages;
for this reason, it is not established [as a separate level]. If one relies on the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra):
In the fourth dhyāna, tranquility and insight are subsumed within mindfulness;
therefore, they are not established separately.
Thus, that treatise states:
In the latter part of the third dhyāna, there is still no peaceful wisdom;
how much less so in this fourth dhyāna?
Why, then, is there no pleasure?
Because this equanimity cannot coexist with it,
the fourth section distinguishes between its general and specific aspects in relation to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
Within the practice of dhyāna, there are eleven constituent factors:

namely, vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), praśrabdhi (tranquility), ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind), adhyātmasaṃprasāda (internal clarity), upekṣā (equanimity), smṛti (mindfulness), saṃprajanya (clear comprehension), sukha (bliss), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Within the *mārga-varga*, there are ten factors constituting the essence of practice:

namely, faith (*śraddhā*), energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), reflection (*mati*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
These are to be viewed in relation to one another.
In reality, they are equally pervasive;
within this, there is no lack of distinction between the implicit and the explicit.
There are three types of such pervasive and specific distinctions.
First, there are factors of dhyāna that are not factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), namely:
investigation (vicāra), pleasure (sukha), and neither-pain-nor-pleasure (aduḥkhāsukha).
Why is there no investigation?
Because within that path, wisdom pervades from beginning to end,
and its conventional contemplation of meaning is subtle; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Why is there no pleasure?
Because that which has the nature of pleasure is not conducive to the Path;
for this reason, it is not discussed.
If that were so, joy (*prīti*) should not be established as part of the path;
for joy functions as mental exhilaration and remedies the fault of excessive sorrow.
The aspiration for the Way and its principles is firm; this is why it is established.
For what reason is there that which is neither painful nor pleasant?
Because neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] accords with the category of ignorance and is contrary to the Path,
it is not mentioned here.
Second, there are factors of the path that are not branches of dhyāna.
This refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and diligence (*vīrya*). Why is ethical discipline not included?
Because "dhyāna" is defined as meditative cultivation through contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Precepts are not mental factors;
because they lack the quality of volitional reflection, they are not mentioned here.
Furthermore, among the eightfold noble path, it is called a wheel;
precepts must serve as its hub,
whereas meditative concentration (dhyāna) is not so.
Therefore, it is omitted and not discussed.
Why is diligence (*vīrya*) not mentioned among the dhyānas?
Because diligence is that which initiates activity.
Because they are not conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are concealed and not mentioned. If that were so,
then the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) should not be established within the dhyānas.
The commentary states:
"Awakening" refers to the ability to carefully examine objects and restrain coarse faults,
thereby exerting a powerful function for the arousal of meditative concentration.
For this reason, it is established [as such].
The third [category] is both dhyāna and the path;
this refers to other dharmas.
Among these, joy (prīti), equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), and wisdom (prajñā) have identical names in both [the dhyānas and the path];
the others differ in name.
Regarding "volition (cetanā) within the path":
In the context of dhyāna, it is called "awareness" (saṃbodha). "Reflection" (vitarka) has the meaning of awareness.
In the context of the Path, it is "reliance" (praśrabdhi).
Dhyāna is called bliss because it is said to be bliss due to the subsiding of coarse suffering.
This refers to those who have faith within the Path.
Dhyāna is called "internal purity.
It is named internal purity because faith is free from the turbidity of doubt.
As for concentration within the path:
Dhyāna is called "one-pointed mind" (ekacitta). Because there is no distraction from other objects, it is termed "one-pointed mind.
This is explained by distinguishing the various types of dhyāna.
The meaning is clear. In the fifth section, the characteristics of cultivation and accomplishment are elucidated,
as taught by Nāgārjuna.
One proceeds toward the first dhyāna by distancing oneself from five factors and abandoning five factors.
One cultivates five dharmas,
accomplishes five dharmas,
and enters the stage of the first dhyāna.
To distance oneself from the five dharmas means to remain aloof from the five objects of desire: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
To sever the five dharmas means...
This refers to the severing of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
As for the cultivation of the five qualities, they are:
zeal, mindfulness, energy, skillful means, wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind.
To aspire for the higher tranquility is called desire;
to keep in mind the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances within the lower stages.
Because one maintains mindfulness of the cessation, the excellence, and the emergence of the higher stages,
it is called "mindfulness"; thus,
one diligently cultivates the concentrated mind.
What is called diligence is the discernment of lower faults and the knowledge of superior benefits above;
what is called skillful wisdom is the same.
Maintaining the mind on a single object is called "one-pointedness of mind.
This constitutes the fifth dharma.
These are vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and ekāgratā,
as explained in detail later.
One proceeds toward the second dhyāna by abandoning these two factors.
What are called vitarka and vicāra are the cultivation of five factors,
namely desire, mindfulness, and so forth.
One accomplishes four factors:
namely, internal purity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind;
these are also as explained later.
Proceeding toward the third dhyāna, one abandons the single factor of joy and cultivates five factors,
namely: desire, mindfulness, and so forth.
He accomplishes five factors—
namely, equanimity, mindfulness, tranquility, discernment, and bliss— and attains one-pointedness of mind while abandoning one kind of pleasure, thereby proceeding toward the four dhyānas.
One cultivates five factors,
namely desire, mindfulness, and so forth;
these are cultivated universally because they are the essential causes for attaining meditative concentration.
One accomplishes four factors:
namely, purity of equanimity and mindfulness, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
These are explained according to the text within the sixth section.
The Sūtra says:
"In the first dhyāna, one is detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states;
with directed thought and sustained thought, born of detachment, one enters and dwells in the joy and happiness of the first dhyāna."
The difficulty of abandoning desire, evil, and unwholesome states constitutes an obstacle to cessation.
This explanation has four meanings.
First, being free from the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm is called "abandoning desire and evil."
Second, according to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
being far removed from the five desires is called "renunciation of desire.
This is still the same as the previously mentioned "renunciation of the five dharmas."
The severance of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) is called "being free from evil and unwholesome states.
This is still the same as the previous severance of the five factors.
According to the Abhidharma, being far removed from the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) is called "freedom from desire" (*vairāgya*).
To sever the ten unwholesome actions is called "leaving evil.
To eliminate the five hindrances is called "leaving what is unwholesome.
The four reliances bring about the realization of reality.
To sever the mind of craving is called "detachment from desire.
To abandon the ten unwholesome actions, such as killing and stealing, is called "abandoning the unwholesome.
Applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) serve as their antidotes.
Gross thought is called *vitarka* (applied thought), and subtle thought is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).
It is like the ringing of a bell.
Coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka* (applied thought),
and subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained thought). Question:
The Abhidharma states that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously.
Why, then, is it said here that a coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka* (applied thought) and a subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained thought)?
Nāgārjuna explains:
Although the various minds and mental factors are simultaneous in substance,
they receive their names according to the time;
it is like how the many stars do not appear during the daytime.
It is not that there are no stars;
the mental factors are likewise.
Therefore, it can be said that coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka* (initial application) and subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained application).
The benefit thereof is the joy and happiness born of seclusion;
one rejoices in being free from sensual desires and evils, and thus joy arises.
This is also celebrated because the mind frequently experiences the joy of being free from [afflictions]; it is specifically described as such because,
through the abandonment of evil, body and mind become tranquil and at ease,
which is designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Entering the practice of the first dhyāna is the essence of the first dhyāna;
this corresponds to the factor of "one-pointedness of mind" mentioned in the sūtras.
As the sūtra says:

In the second dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are extinguished. With internal purity, the mind becomes one-pointed; free from applied and sustained thought, one enters the second dhyāna, which is characterized by the joy and bliss born of concentration.
"The extinction of applied and sustained thought" refers to the cessation of these hindrances.
Although vitarka and vicāra serve as antidotes to what precedes them,
they act as obstacles to what follows;
therefore, they must be extinguished.
Internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is its antidote.

Internal purity purifies the essence by departing from the preceding applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) as well as the body of the three consciousnesses belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna;
it is the realization of faith and purity regarding the phenomena of the second dhyāna.
Therefore, it is called "internal purity.
That the mind is in a single place refers to the characteristic of the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*).
The term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) has two meanings.
First, it is explained according to cultivation:
that which is pure and continuous within.
Because it is free from other intervals,
it is called "one place. Therefore,
the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
Cultivating the untainted (anāsrava) and uninterrupted state is called "one-pointedness of mind" (cittaikāgratā).
That [text] states that this refers to the internal purity cultivated by a bodhisattva;
therefore, it is described as untainted.
If we consider other persons,
the mere state of internal purity with a continuous succession is called "one-pointedness of mind.
Second, it is explained by way of its object.
Because the mind takes a single object as its focal point, it is said to be "one-pointed.
Thus, the *Dilun* states:
"Practicing within a single objective sphere is called 'one-pointedness of mind' (*cittaikāgratā*)."
What is the single object?
It is as explained in that *Śāriputrābhidharma*:
within the stages of the desire realm, mental activity occurs in six locations.
These are the so-called six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
In the first dhyāna, one has already abandoned the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue, as well as the mental activities associated with the four bases.
From the second dhyāna upward, one further abandons the consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body.
Therefore, it is called "one-pointedness of mind.
That is to say, it functions within the single object-field of a dharma;
its capacity for cultivation consists in being without vitarka and without vicāra.
This means that with an inwardly pure mind, one is able to be without directed thought (vitarka) and without sustained evaluation (vicāra).
The benefit thereof is the joy and happiness born of concentration (samādhi).
Because one rejoices at having attained this state, it is called "joy born of concentration."
This too is said with a particular emphasis because there is much rejoicing at being free from [suffering] and rejoicing at attaining [happiness].
"Bliss" (sukha) is explained as before.
Entering the practice of the second dhyāna constitutes its meditative essence, which is the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).
The Sūtra states that the third dhyāna is free from joy (*prīti*).
Having abandoned mindfulness and equanimity, one experiences pleasure with the body;
this is what the noble ones describe as "dwelling in the third dhyāna while experiencing pleasure through mindfulness and equanimity."
One abandons joy and extinguishes hindrances;
although joy is beneficial in the preceding stage,
it becomes an obstacle and distraction in view of the subsequent one.
Therefore, it must be extinguished.
Because the second dhyāna is coarse,
one merely extinguishes what was previously treated.
Because this dhyāna becomes increasingly subtle,
it supersedes the previous benefits;
equanimity, mindfulness, tranquility, and wisdom are its antidotes.
It is called equanimity (*upekṣā*) because it relinquishes the previous fault of joy;
it is called "equanimity of action" (*kāyikī upekṣā*) to distinguish it from the equanimity that is a feeling (*vedanā*);
and it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*) because it recollects the previous fault of joy.
Because mindfulness (smṛti) and recollection (smaraṇa) coexist, they are termed "recollection-mindfulness" (smṛty-upasthāna).
Because it knows the faults of prior joy, it is called "wisdom" (prajñā).
Because it is the wisdom that conforms to meditative concentration (samādhi), it is called "established wisdom" (samprajanya).
The benefit consists in the experience of physical pleasure and so forth.
It is called "experiencing pleasure" because the reception of the Dharma gives rise to a sense of well-being.
This pleasure is a mental satisfaction that pervades both body and mind.
Because the preceding mind was joyful,
it is said that there is bodily sensation;
this bliss is profound and weighty.
Only the noble and holy ones are able to speak of its faults and are capable of abandoning it; most others are not.
Therefore, it is said that the noble ones (ārya) are able to both speak of and relinquish [sensual pleasure].
This is cited to manifest the profundity of their bliss.
Mindfulness of the experience of bliss and so forth constitutes the essence of these dhyānas.
Mindfully reflecting upon the faults of experiencing pleasure within one's own stage,
one enters into single-minded concentration;
this is called the practice of entering the third dhyāna by being mindful of the experience of pleasure.
The Sūtra says:
"In the fourth dhyāna, suffering is abandoned and pleasure is abandoned;
previously, sorrow and joy have been extinguished."
With neither suffering nor pleasure, and with equanimity and mindfulness purified,
one enters the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
Having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and having previously extinguished sorrow and joy— this is the elimination of hindrances.
Since the suffering that was eliminated within the first two dhyānas is likewise absent in this stage,
it is said that "suffering is severed."
The bliss of the third dhyāna has been personally eliminated at this stage;
therefore, it is said that "bliss is abandoned. Question:
Suffering is abandoned by the second dhyāna;
it is not directly extinguished by this [first dhyāna]. Why, then, is it mentioned?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains that this dhyāna is cited to demonstrate that it is the "immovable dhyāna" (*aniñjya-dhyāna*), wherein both suffering and pleasure are utterly severed.
Thus it is raised as an example.
Furthermore, that which is called the bliss within the third dhyāna may itself be regarded as suffering;
when that bliss is abandoned, it is termed the abandonment of suffering.
Therefore it is said that suffering is abandoned and pleasure is abandoned.
A question is asked:
Why is that pleasure called suffering?
Nāgārjuna’s commentary states:
"In view of those with coarse minds,
that [state] is described as pleasure."
For one who harbors subtle thoughts,
this constitutes great suffering,
just as when a person strikes wood with their fingers or hands.
To be awake is happiness;
for one who delights in sleep, it is considered a great suffering.
This case is likewise so.
The sensation of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is first extinguished within the first dhyāna,
and the sensation of joy (*prīti*) is first extinguished within the third dhyāna; therefore,
it is said that they are "first extinguished."
If that is so, then suffering is also extinguished in the preceding stage;
why was it not mentioned first?
The explanation says:
They should be equal.

However, because sorrow and joy both cease prior to the cessation of the preceding ground, their prior cessation is made manifest; although suffering ceases first [of these two], [it is not so indicated].
In this stage, one first becomes free from the pleasure that arises in relation to suffering.
If it were said that suffering and pleasure are extinguished first,
it would mean that pleasure is also extinguished first.
For this reason, they are not manifested.
Question: Since sorrow and joy have already ceased in the preceding stage, why are they not manifested?

Why is this said? The *Tattvasiddhi* also states that this is to demonstrate that this dhyāna is the "unmoving dhyāna" (*aniñjya-dhyāna*), which completely eliminates the four types of sensation (*vedanā*).
This is why it is so stated.
That which is neither painful nor pleasant is its benefit.
Question: [Why is this?]
In all other dhyānas, the remedies are first made manifest;
why, then, are the benefits clarified first in this dhyāna?
It is because it follows upon the preceding context.
Because it is convenient for clarifying the meaning of "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" in contrast to the preceding [feelings of] pain and pleasure,
this is mentioned first.
This benefit is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Having abandoned former suffering and pleasure,
it is therefore called neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
If that is so, this feeling also abandons sorrow and joy.
Why are they not called "neither sorrowful nor joyful"?
There are three reasons for this explanation.
First, suffering and pleasure are present before one.
Therefore, it is first designated as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" in contrast to pleasure.
Since this pleasure, which is the opposite of pain, is directly abandoned at this stage,
it is therefore called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant."
Sorrow and joy are not directly severed at this stage;
therefore, they are not addressed here.
This third point distinguishes the general from the specific.
There are five classifications of feeling (*vedanā*),
in which sorrow and joy are situated outside of suffering and pleasure.
There are three classifications of feeling.
Sorrow and joy are collectively termed suffering and pleasure.
Because suffering and pleasure are thus subsumed,
what is here contrasted with them is termed "neither-suffering-nor-pleasure."
The purity of equanimity and mindfulness is its antidote.
Because one abandons the fault of prior pleasure and maintains mindfulness of that fault,
it is called "equanimity and mindfulness."
In the preceding stage, joy (*prīti*) was cultivated;
now, furthermore, bliss (*sukha*) is cultivated.
Because it has completely mastered and transcended [the former], it is called "pure" (*viśuddha*).
Entering the practice of the four dhyānas constitutes the essence of these four dhyānas.
Regarding the analysis of the four emptinesses, there are specifically three gates.
First is the discernment of their characteristics.

Second, explaining the distinctions between the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of space and consciousness, the two liberations (*vimokṣa*) of space and consciousness, the two meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of space and consciousness, and the sphere of totality of space and consciousness;
third, explaining the meaning according to the text.
First, the definition of the characteristics: regarding the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*),
the practitioner deeply perceives that the signs of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) within the stages of the four dhyānas are afflictive and obstructive.
Therefore, one must cultivate it.
What is the method of cultivation?
Briefly, there are four kinds.
First, the path of preparation;
second, the path of non-obstruction;
third, the path of liberation.
The fourth is the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), it is of two kinds.
First, the remote preparation:
when about to cultivate the concentration of emptiness,
one first trains in dwelling the mind.
Having attained stability of mind, one trains in the contemplation of emptiness;
beginning with the empty space within doorways and well-holes,
one returns to abide in the mind.
Having settled [the mind], one observes again;
thus, by moving back and forth, one causes the mind to see emptiness with perfect clarity and distinctness,
gradually expanding this scope.
Returning again, one dwells in the mind;
having dwelt in the mind, it expands further.
In this manner, proceeding by stages, one perceives all realms.
There is only this single emptiness, with no further marks of form.
Second is the proximate application:
likewise relying on the mind of abiding, one trains in contemplating lower phenomena as suffering, coarse, and obstructive.
He observes the superior dharmas as being supremely sublime and transcendent;
he then returns to abide in the mind,
and having so abided, he observes again.
In this way, one repeatedly cycles through these stages until they are thoroughly matured.
Since both of these involve contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) based on conceptualization and mental construction rather than the actual vision of phenomena,
they are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Regarding the path of non-obstruction:
by the power of the preparatory application cultivated through prior effort,
one enters and abides within the mind.
Below, regarding the arising of wisdom that sees things as they truly are:
it views [phenomena] as either suffering, coarse, or an obstruction;
thus, among these three, one enters into one.
It is not necessary to possess all three;
because one uses this right abandonment to sever the fetters of the four dhyānas,
it is called "unimpeded."
Regarding the path of liberation:
immediately after the unimpeded mind, one perceives the higher stage—
whether it be cessation, the sublime, or emergence.
Among these three, one may follow any single one;
it is not necessary to possess all three.
These arise externally as afflictions.
Therefore, it is called "liberation.
In this way, the nine [meditations] taking lower objects universally constitute "non-obstruction," while the nine taking upper objects universally constitute "liberation."
Regarding the essential nature of concentration (*samādhi*):
the first three are all preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the sphere of infinite space.
It is at the limit of the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that one attains the dharma of the sphere of infinite space; this is designated as the essential nature of concentration.
At that time, although it was attained,
it had not yet manifested; therefore,
one further employs skillful means.
Only when the mind is withdrawn and enters [the next stage] does it manifest before one.
As for the concentration on the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*), one suffers from the external objects of the preceding concentration on space.
Therefore, one must cultivate it.
There are four aspects to this cultivation.
First is the path of skillful means (upāyamārga).
Second, the path of non-obstruction;
third, the path of liberation;
fourth, the essential substance of meditative concentration.
Within the path of skillful means, there is also a distinction between the distant and the proximate.
As for the distant skillful means,
one first attains abiding of the mind.
Relying on this state of mind, one relinquishes external empty objects and takes internal consciousness as the object;
returning once more to abide in the state of mind,
and having so abided, one again takes it as the object.
In this manner, by moving back and forth, one causes the mind-consciousness to perceive with clarity;
gradually expanding this,
one causes all boundless consciousnesses to become fully manifest.
What is "boundless"?
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
because space is boundless, consciousness is also boundless.
This takes as its object the infinite space and consciousness within the previously mentioned base of infinite space.
The rest is as explained before.
As for the base of nothingness:
Fearing the suffering of the previous state of consciousness being broad and expansive in its objects,
one therefore cultivates it again.
This cultivation also has four aspects.
The names are the same as before.
Within the path of skillful means (upāyamārga), there are also distinctions between the distant and the proximate.
As for the distant skillful means:
First, one attains the state of abiding of the mind;
relying on that abiding of the mind, one takes as the object of focus only a single consciousness,
and returns to abide in that state of mind.
Having stabilized it, one takes it as an object again;
thus, by alternating back and forth, one makes it extremely clear,
and then relinquishes it once more.
The cultivation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception also has four types.
Their names are the same as those mentioned previously.
Within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), there is also a distinction between the distant and the proximate.
Regarding the remote preparation (*dūrasamudācāra*):
first one abides in the mind,
and subsequently, based on that abiding in the mind.
Abandoning the previous object of focus,
one performs the contemplation of non-perception and returns to dwell in the state of the mind of entry.
Having dwelt [in that state], one observes again;
thus, through repeated alternation, one brings it to complete mastery.
This is the proximate preparation (*sāmantaka-upāya*).
Relying on that state of mental abiding,
one contemplates non-existence as being a coarse obstacle to suffering.
One contemplates the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the sublime emergence of cessation;
thus one proceeds back and forth until it is thoroughly mastered.
The remainder is as explained previously.
In the second section, the distinct characteristics of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), such as those of space and consciousness,
are clarified. Among the ten spheres of totality,
the spheres of totality of space and consciousness take only space and consciousness as their two preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*).
Because it is able to take a vast range as its object,
none of the others are taken up among the eight liberations.

The "liberations of space and consciousness" refer exclusively to the two paths of liberation consisting of space and consciousness, as well as the essential nature of their respective meditative absorptions;
all else is not included. Why is this so?
Because that path of expedient means has not yet abandoned the defects of the lower stages, it is not liberation;
although the path of non-obstruction severs the defects of the lower stages,
it is still unable to transcend the burdens of existence.
Nor is it liberation. Furthermore, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The unhindered [knowledge] takes the lower realms as its object."
Therefore, they are not "turning away" (*prātikūlya-vairāgya*). Because they are not turning away, they are not called "liberations" (*vimokṣa*).
[The opponent] asks:
Are all the two paths of liberation—emptiness and consciousness—as well as the essential nature of their respective meditative absorptions, themselves liberation?
There are both those that are and those that are not. The explanation involves both general and specific distinctions.
In general, all [attainments] are included therein; yet,
when distinguished specifically within them,
those obtained by the noble ones (ārya) are what is meant here.
All that is attained is not [ultimate]. Thus Nāgārjuna said:
"The liberations from the sphere of emptiness up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are like the four formless concentrations."
As for what is meant by "difference":
that which is attained by the noble ones is called liberation;
that which is attained by ordinary worldlings is not called liberation.
Because there is regression,
liberation is thus. Within the eight dhyānas,
the meanings of the two concentrations on space and consciousness have both general and specific aspects.
Discussing them collectively,
both the unhindered liberations (*pratisaṃvid-vimokṣa*) and the essential nature of those meditative absorptions are termed "concentration" (*samādhi*).
This is just as future dhyāna is also termed "dhyāna."
Regarding the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), because one has not yet attained the superior dharmas (*agra-dharma*),
one does not grasp them. Specifically, one grasps only the essential substance of the meditative absorptions of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-samādhi*).
Taking this as concentration (*samādhi*),
the preparatory stages (*prayoga-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are the preparations for concentration rather than the actual essence of concentration;
therefore, they are not included.
If one discusses the two spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness,
all [of these] are included therein;
thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
Whether determinate or indeterminate,
whether defiled or pure,
whether cause or fruit.
Both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are entirely empty consciousness.
This shall be analyzed and explained according to the text within the third section. Regarding the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*):
The Sūtra says:
"Transcending all perceptions of form,
and extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance."
One does not give rise to thoughts of differentiation,
nor does one discriminate among objective spheres such as form;
one knows infinite space.
One immediately enters the practice of the infinite space.
Passing beyond form and so forth, not even thinking of diversity—this is the cessation of hindrances.
One ceases the perception of form as an object.
