Question: For what reason does one not extinguish the substance of form (*rūpa*), but only extinguish the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*)?
Explanation:
The mind's afflictions can be abandoned through cultivation;
therefore, one eliminates the perception of form.
Yet, the substance of form is difficult to detach from.
One must be born in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) in order to be able to abandon it;
therefore, this is not discussed here.
It is asked:
Why is it that one does not speak of the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*) and other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
but speaks specifically of the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*)? The explanation states:
"Perception" (saṃjñā) has the meaning of grasping signs.
Because one grasps those signs of form,
and because this is exclusively the fault of perception, it is said that "perception is extinguished."
Although it is said that "perception is extinguished," other minds and mental factors also follow accordingly as appropriate.
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, most feelings (*vedanā*) are extinguished.
Within the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), most perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are extinguished;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned here.
The objects of perception (*ālambana*)—namely, forms (*rūpa*)—are indeterminate as to whether they are separated or combined.
In total, it is simply one form;
alternatively, it may be divided into two:
first, visible form.
That is to say, the range of the eye;
second, invisible forms,
which are the objects of the ear, nose, and so forth.
Alternatively, it is divided into three:
first, that which is visible and resistant,
namely the domain of the eye.
Second are invisible objects with resistance (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*),
namely the objects experienced by the ears, nose, tongue,
and body; all of these possess resistance.
It is called "with resistance" (sapratigha) because it is that which is encountered by the physical sense faculties (rūpīndriya).
Three [of these] are invisible and non-resistant (anidarśana-apratigha).
This refers to that which is traversed by the mind.
Because unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is not obstructed by or confronted by the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*),
it is said to be "without resistance" (*apratigha*).
Alternatively, it is divided into six,
namely the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
That which is the substance of form (*rūpa*) as the object of the eye is called "form" (*rūpa*).
The matter that is the object-domain of the remaining sense-faculties is called "matter" (*rūpa*).
Alternatively, it is divided into eleven types:
namely, the five faculties, the five objects, and unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
These are subdivided into immeasurable categories;
for now, based on one approach, we shall discuss three types.
By correlating these, we clarify the cessation of the three kinds of perception.
"Transcending the perception of form" means that the perception of visible and resistant form ceases;
thus, the *Dilun* says:
This refers to the cessation of the perception associated with the conjunction of visual consciousness.
The "cessation of that which possesses resistance" means the cessation of the perception of visible forms that possess resistance.
Therefore, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
This means that when the perceptions associated with the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue,
and body cease, and one does not attend to perceptions of diversity,
the perception of invisible and non-obstructive form ceases as well.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:

"That which is called the extinction of the conceptualization associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) occurs precisely because the mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its object."
Within this, they are distinguished by taking the limit of form as their object;
therefore, they are said to be "distinct.
The first phrase refers to "transcending."
The second [member] is called cessation;
the third is the non-recollection of discursive speech.
Question: Do the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue cease within the body in the first dhyāna?
The bodies of the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and body—are extinguished within the second dhyāna.
Why is it that only here is it stated that the "perception of the conjunction" of eye-consciousness up to body-consciousness is extinguished?
The commentary states:
There are four kinds of antidotes. First, the antidote of destruction (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*).
This refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), which observe lower dharmas as suffering, impermanent,
and so forth; these are the two types of antidotes for abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
That is to say, the path of non-obstruction correctly abandons the lower faults;
it consists of the three types of antidotes,
with liberation as its primary feature.
Furthermore, all subsequent unimpeded liberations sustain the preceding unconditioned state,
ensuring it is not lost;
this is the fourth, the antidote through distancing.
Liberation is primary;
furthermore, through all subsequent unimpeded liberations, it can ensure that the various faults previously abandoned do not arise again.
Now, regarding the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) in comparison to the perception associated with those five consciousnesses:
Because there exists both the antidote of possession (*prāpti-pratipakṣa*) and the antidote of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*), it is said that [defilements] are abandoned and extinguished;
this principle is largely consistent across all treatises.
Only in the *Tattvasiddhi* is there a unique alternative interpretation of that [passage].
It states that "transcending the perception of form" means transcending the perceptions of those [objects]— namely, color, odor, taste, and tangibility.
As for the cessation of resistance,
it refers to the cessation of the perceptions of form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
because these involve mutual obstruction, they must be ceased.
The Way says that when one does not give rise to thoughts of differentiation,
the perception of sound ceases.
Sound arises from the striking together of various conditions.
Therefore, it is said that they are distinct.
Since that school does not establish the existence of unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), this explanation is provided.
When examining and deliberating upon the meaning of the sūtra,
it should be understood as explained previously:
that the non-differentiation of form and so forth is its specific antidote.
Knowing infinite space is its benefit;
entering the practice of infinite space is the essential nature of that concentration. As for the concentration of the sphere of consciousness:
The Sūtra states:
"Having transcended the perception of infinite space,
one perceives the faults of external mental attention and coarse discrimination."
Knowing the sphere of infinite consciousness to be secure,
he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness,
transcending the perception of infinite space.
This is the cessation of hindrances.
The treatise states:
"Because the practitioner deeply loathes form, he takes emptiness as the antidote."
Once the affliction of form has been eliminated,
even the remedy of emptiness is abandoned,
just as one who has crossed a river leaves behind both the boat and the raft.
It is also like leaving behind a thief and departing to a distance;
thus, one eliminates the perception of emptiness.
Perceiving the coarse faults of external thoughts is its antidote.
The benefit is that consciousness is established in peace;
the essence of the meditative absorption is the entry into the sphere of infinite consciousness.
As for the absorption of nothingness:
The Sūtra says:
"Having transcended the perception of infinite consciousness,
one perceives the faults of coarse thought and conceptualization."
Knowing that non-existence is peace,
one enters the practice of the placeless within the place;
transcending infinite consciousness is the cessation of its hindrances.
Because space is infinite,
the consciousness that takes space as its object is likewise infinite.
Because consciousness is infinite...
Suffering is also boundless;
therefore, it must be extinguished.
Perceiving the faults of coarse conceptualization is its antidote.
Knowing that non-existence is peace and security is its benefit;
entering into non-existence is the essential nature of this concentration.
As for the "perception of non-ideation":
The Sūtra says:
"Having transcended the perception of nothingness,
one perceives the faults and afflictions of the conceptualization of the thought of nothingness."
Knowing the peace of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one enters the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
transcending the perception of nothingness is the overcoming of its hindrance.
The discernment of the faults of perception and thought is their antidote.
Although one has abandoned manifold thoughts through the prior stage of nothingness,
there still remains a subtle degree of perception.
Seeing those few perceptions as like an abscess,
like a sore, like poison, and like an arrow,
he again abandons them and takes non-perception as his object.
Furthermore, one perceives the fault of being exclusively non-percipient,
namely, that it is a state of delusion,
conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, one may simply be envious of the fault of having perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because it is based on non-perception (*asaṃjñā*),
the Noble Ones explain it as "having perception" according to its underlying principle.
It is named "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Knowing that non-perception is secure is its benefit;
entering into the practice of non-perception is the essence of this meditative absorption.
The preceding section was the second part, the detailed explanation of the eight dhyānas.
In this third section, the requisites for meditative concentration are clarified.
The causes that give rise to concentration are termed "requisites for concentration" (samādhi-sambhāra).
The inclusion, exclusion, expansion, and abbreviation of these factors are not fixed;
sometimes they are taught as four, namely,
the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Because they are all causes of certainty, they are called the "requisites of certainty.
This shall be explained in detail later.
Alternatively, the five [requisites] may be discussed as extensively explained above.
That is to say: desire, mindfulness, diligence, skillful wisdom, and single-mindedness;
or they are said to be seven, as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
First, maintaining pure precepts;
second, guarding the doors of the sensory faculties;
third, knowing the proper measure in eating.
Fourth, eliminate drowsiness.
Fifth, associate with virtuous persons.
Sixth, recognize transgressions and refrain from committing them.
Seventh, there is the one who commits an offense but is able to repent. These seven are said to be skillful means;
it should be understood that they are also the requisites for meditative concentration.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eleven,
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:
first, maintaining pure precepts.
Second, obtaining virtuous friends;
third, guarding the doors of the sensory faculties;
fourth, knowing moderation in eating and drinking.
Fifth, the elimination of drowsiness;
sixth, possessing wholesome wakefulness;
seventh, possessing wholesome faith and understanding.
Eighth, the division of those who possess the practice;
ninth, the bases of liberation;
tenth, the absence of obstructions.
Eleventh, non-attachment.
First, regarding the observance of precepts:
one distances oneself from the seven unwholesome karmas, such as killing, stealing, and so forth.
Furthermore, if we discuss this in general terms,
the renunciation of the ten unwholesome actions necessarily arises from ethical discipline.
Therefore, one must maintain the precepts.
Second, regarding the "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra):
one who is able to bestow the methods of meditative concentration upon others is called a good spiritual friend.
Since it necessarily arises from a teacher,
one must rely on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
A virtuous friend is one who provides the complete causes and conditions for attaining the Way.
Third, guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
The eyes and so forth are the faculties (*indriya*).
Mindfulness and wisdom firmly guard these six faculties,
not allowing the thieves of sensory objects to destroy one's virtue therein.
It must necessarily be maintained through preservation;
therefore, it is essential to preserve it.
The Dharma is immeasurable.
Why is it that one guards by means of mindfulness and wisdom alone?
Mindfulness is able to draw in the object,
while wisdom is able to discern it.
Therefore, one uses it to maintain [the body].
Fourth, knowing the proper measure in eating:
the practitioner does not eat for the sake of physical strength, sexual desire, or delicious flavors.
One eats only for the sake of sustaining the body and practicing the Path;
if one eats excessively,
it increases afflictions and hinders the cultivation of meditative concentration.
Therefore, one must exercise moderation in measure.
To what extent does this moderation reach?
It is well and beneficial to consume no more than two-thirds of what one would normally eat.
Fifth, regarding the elimination of drowsiness:
the practitioner reflects to himself,
"The great task remains unfinished."
Success depends upon diligence;
if one delights in sleep,
worldly affairs will be difficult to accomplish.
How much more so for those who have entered the Way;
therefore, one must eliminate sleepiness.
What is the method for eliminating it?
Reflecting on the impermanence of the body, the suffering of the three evil realms, and the fact that sleep is of no benefit when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish—
one uses this to whip the mind and dispel [drowsiness].
This is the sixth, possessing wholesome awakening.
One should abandon the eight unwholesome thoughts, namely:
thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, affection for kinsmen, attachment to one's country, thoughts of immortality, pride in one's lineage, and thoughts of contempt.
One should cultivate the eight thoughts of a great person.
This refers to having few desires and being content, as well as detachment, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and the absence of frivolous conceptual proliferation.
Seventh, one who possesses virtuous faith:
they believe that the phenomena of birth and death are base, evil, and loathsome.
Nirvāṇa is to be rejoiced in.
Regarding the eighth [topic], the factors of one who practices fully,
there are five explanations in the treatise.
First is faith: having faith in and accepting the words of the teacher, one is able to practice in accordance with them.
Second is the absence of flattery.
Toward spiritual friends, one should be straightforward and not crooked;
thus the treatise says:
"Deceit and crookedness are difficult to rescue."
They are upright and easy to guide.
Just as a worldly patient who truthfully describes their symptoms can be easily treated,
these three have few ailments and possess sufficient physical strength to cultivate meditative concentration.
Fourth, one diligently seeks meditative concentration without weariness;
it is like drilling for fire, which is quickly attained if one does not cease.
Fifth, through wisdom, one is able to cultivate detachment from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
This causes the first four practices to attain the fruit of the noble path.
These five are called the factors of the practitioner.
Ninth is the factor of possessing the basis for liberation.
The commentary consists of five parts. First,
the Buddha and his bhikṣus preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to comprehend the meaning of the words,
to rejoice, to experience tranquility and bliss, to collect their minds, and to exhaust all outflows.
Second, reciting the sutras with excellence;
third, expounding the Dharma for others;
fourth, dwelling alone in contemplation.
The five signs for correctly grasping meditative concentration are:
tranquility (śamatha), exertion (pragraha), and equanimity (upekṣā).
Among these five, the first three constitute the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
The next one is the wisdom of reflection;
the last one is the wisdom of cultivation.
The tenth is "unobstructed."
This means that there are no afflictions, karma, or retribution;
because one has already perfected the four wheels of goodness, one is able to be free from them.
Fifth, as for what are called the "four wheels":
First, one is born in a central land;
second, one relies upon virtuous people;
third, one personally makes right vows.
Fourth, having planted roots of goodness in past lives,
one is born in a central land;
this is due to having planted roots of goodness in past lives.
One can be free from the obstacle of retribution;
by relying on virtuous persons,
one can be free from the obstacle of karma.
One spontaneously gives rise to right vows and becomes free from the hindrance of afflictions.
Regarding the eleventh, "non-attachment":
Being free from a mind of grasping and attachment,
he moves unimpeded through the world, heading directly toward nirvana,
like water in the Ganges.
Departing from eight causes and conditions, one proceeds directly toward the great ocean.
As for departing from these eight conditions:
first, not clinging to this shore.
Second, not clinging to the other shore;
third, not sinking in midstream;
fourth, not emerging onto dry land.
Fifth, it is not taken by humans;
sixth, it is not taken by non-humans;
seventh, it does not enter eddies.
Eighth, it does not rot or decay.
The practitioner is likewise:
within the six internal sense bases, they do not conceive of a self or a person.
Not clinging to this shore is called not reckoning "mine" regarding the six external sense bases;
not clinging to the other shore is called not clinging to the opposite bank.
Being free from greed, hatred,
and delusion is called not sinking in the middle of the stream;
not giving rise to pride is called not being haughty.
Its name does not extend beyond the land;
it does not associate with the fourfold assembly;
its name is not grasped by people.
Not observing the precepts while seeking rebirth as a deva is called being seized by non-humans;
not falling away from the precepts and returning home.
Not entering the whirlpools is called not being corrupted;
not violating the grave prohibitions is called not being putrid.

The requisites for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are thus. Within the fourth section, its obstacles to concentration are clarified; that which hinders concentration is termed an "obstacle" (*āntarāyika*).
Difficulties vary in their gravity;
light difficulties are immeasurable.
Briefly stated, there are fifteen types.
First, the obstacle of excessive speech:
one should remain silent and speak little.
Second, the obstacle of excessive activity.
One should desist and not act [upon it].
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Do not wander about excessively."
Third is the difficulty of excessive conceptualization in concentration;
one should rest in a single object.
Fourth is the difficulty of inverted concentration.
This means that those with excessive greed should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion,
while those with excessive anger should practice the contemplation of impurity and so forth;
they should thus engage in proper cultivation.
Fifth is the difficulty of uneven concentration:
when the practice is neither too lax nor too urgent,
one should skillfully regulate it.
Sixth is the difficulty of concentration regarding the inability to properly apprehend the signs of meditative absorption (*samādhi-nimitta*).
This refers to not skillfully cultivating the mental states of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); one should cultivate them skillfully.
Seventh is the difficulty of bodily discomfort.
It may arise from any internal or external contact that causes the body to be ill at ease.
Or, due to greed and anxiety,
one may fail to properly regulate the mind through mindfulness;
this is the eighth difficulty regarding the meditative concentration of non-delight.
If one encounters a good teacher or a place where the excellent Dharma is found,
yet the mind feels no affection or joy,
one should reproach oneself.
Since these are the causes and conditions [for distraction],
by relying on what further dharma can meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) arise?
He then reflected:
One's own nature is the dharma of suffering;
knowing this, where could there be any pleasure worth praising?
This is the ninth difficulty of fixed sorrow and anxiety.
If you seek meditative concentration but do not attain it, you will give rise to distress;
you should instead resolve this for yourself.
Meditative concentration is a supreme dharma of great merit.
"It is only after long cultivation that one attains it.
How is it that I, a person of meager merit,
have already attained meditative concentration (dhyāna) upon merely beginning my practice?"
Furthermore, as for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
it constitutes more than half of the path to attaining the Way;
if it can be easily cultivated and attained, [the goal will be reached].
The Path is not a superior dharma.
There are ten fearsome obstacles to meditative concentration within the state of dhyāna.
Upon seeing something fearsome,
fear arises in the mind; at that time, one should bring [the Buddha] to mind.
These are produced by one's own deluded and false mind;
since these dharmas are fixed as such,
one should not give rise to fear.
Eleventh is the obstacle of divergent signs within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Within the state of meditative concentration,
one may perceive images of Buddhas, female forms, and so forth.
One should reflect:
"The mind creates; there are no phenomena external to the mind.
This is the twelfth difficulty regarding the meditative absorption of loathing.
While in meditative concentration,
he perceived the sign of impurity;
his loathing and revulsion became so excessive that he was unable to eat or drink.
If one should wish to commit suicide,
one must change one's mental orientation and practice counting the breaths and so forth,
as explained in the Vinaya.
Thirteenth is the difficulty of the meditative absorption of joy (prāmodya-samādhi). Within this meditative concentration,
one perceives luminosity and other such phenomena.
When joy arises in the mind,
one should reflect:
"This is merely a coarse sign of meditative concentration, not a supreme dharma."
One should not give rise to joy.
Furthermore, even if one attains dhyāna,
it is a mundane phenomenon.
Impermanence is easily lost;
what is there to rejoice in?
The fourteen types of pride are certainly difficult to overcome.
While in meditative concentration,
if you should become self-exalting on account of whatever dharma you have attained,
you should reflect as follows:
This is a coarse, mundane phenomenon;
impermanent and easily lost,
it is not yet sufficient to rely upon.
Furthermore, one observes who it is that attains this dharma,
and thus becomes self-exalting;
this is the fifteenth difficulty regarding doubt concerning meditative concentration.
Having attained the Dharma, one may not recognize it;
unaware of what is good or evil, and what should be adopted or rejected,
one must consult an enlightened teacher.
The minor obstacles are thus.
Among the major obstacles, there are also immeasurable varieties;
however, the *Tattvasiddhi* briefly enumerates ten sets of three factors as definitive obstacles.
The first three are lack of shame, lack of dread, and heedlessness.
If a person commits evil, it is due to these.
The absence of shame within is called *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect);
the absence of dread of external reproach is termed *anapatrāpya* (lack of decorum).
Because of this lack of shame and decorum, one loses what is wholesome and follows after evil; this is termed *pramāda* (heedlessness).
The second triad refers to being disrespectful and difficult to converse with.
Associating with evil friends arises from previous lives;
failing to accept the teacher’s instruction due to negligence is called disrespect.
To violate the words of one's teacher is called being difficult to converse with.
To distance oneself from virtuous teachers and elders while associating closely with evil people is called practicing with evil friends.
The third set of three is as follows:
This refers to lack of faith, wrong precepts, and indolence.
These arise from previous lives;
specifically, because one has associated with evil friends and received false teachings, one lacks conviction in cause and effect—this is termed "lack of faith."
Because they do not believe in the true law of cause and effect,
they observe the precepts of the crow, the chicken, the deer, the dog, and so forth;
these are called "wrong precepts."
Because one has received false precepts, one considers virtue to be of no benefit;
because one is unwilling to practice with diligence, laziness arises.
In this *Tattvasiddhi*, this constitutes the fourth section;
however, following the sequence of the arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
it is now moved here to become the third.
The fourth triad refers to taking no pleasure in virtuous people and having an aversion to hearing the true Dharma.
They delight in exposing the faults of others;
this arises from previous lives,
due to which they take no pleasure in virtuous people because of their own indolence.
Because they do not delight in virtuous people, it is said that they lack those who practice with genuine sincerity.
Because they lack sincere practice, they have a distaste for hearing the true Dharma.
Because they have a distaste for hearing the Dharma, they claim that practicing the true Dharma is just like practicing false teachings, providing no benefit whatsoever.
Therefore, they delight in exposing the faults of others;
this constitutes the third section within the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Now, this [section] relies upon the sequential order of the arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The fourth is turning back.
As for the third of the fifth,
it refers to frivolity.
Not guarding the sense faculties and violating the precepts—
these arise from previous lives.
Because the mind becomes agitated by the intent to expose the faults of others, frivolity arises;
and due to this frivolity, one fails to restrain the sense faculties.
Because one does not restrain the sense faculties, one gives rise to the breaking of precepts.
The sixth set of three refers to false recollection.
One does not practice settled wisdom;
the distracted mind arises from what was produced in a previous life.
Due to the breaking of the precepts, false recollections arise;
because false recollections arise, one does not practice settled wisdom (*samprajanya*);
because there is no settled wisdom, the mind becomes distracted.
The third of the seven [factors] refers to the mind being submerged by wrong mindfulness and wrong conduct;
this arises from what preceded it.
Because the mind is distracted, perverse thoughts arise;
because of perverse thoughts, one follows a deviant path;
because one follows a deviant path, one becomes lost and submerged in wholesome dharmas.
The third group of eight consists of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*);
these arise from what preceded them.
Because the mind is submerged in what is wholesome, there arise the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), adherence to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā).
As for the third triad of the ninth [stage],
it refers to greed (rāga), hatred (dveṣa), and delusion (moha).
These three arise due to the views regarding the previous life, the clinging to precepts and rituals,
and doubt. The thirteenth refers to birth, aging, and death.
These three arise from greed, hatred, and delusion;
because these ten types arise one after another, they are extinguished by severing the preceding and succeeding moments.
Question: By what kind of person are these [defilements] severed and extinguished?
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains:
The abandonment of the first four types constitutes the purity of the householder;
the abandonment and separation from the fifth constitutes the purity of the renunciant;
and the eradication of the sixth constitutes the purity of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The seventh is the purification of the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth;
the eighth is the thorough purification of the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within the state of the non-characteristic (*animitta*);
and the ninth is the purification of the three aforementioned fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Excluding the purity of the tenth fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), the meaning of the eight dhyānas has been explained in this rough manner.

162. The Meaning of the Eight Liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). (13) The meaning of the eight liberations is explained through a sixfold analysis: I. Explaining the names and defining their characteristics; II. Analyzing their essential nature (*tattva*); III. Analysis according to their stages (*bhūmi*); IV. Analysis according to their locations (*sthāna*); V. Attainment, relinquishment, and accomplishment; VI. Determining their relative superiority and inferiority by comparing them with other categories. First: Explaining the names and defining their characteristics.
Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*),
they are also called the eight relinquishments (*aṣṭapratinihsarga*) in the sūtras,
as explained by Nāgārjuna.
It is called "reversal" (*prātikūlya*) because one turns one's back on the five desires and abandons the mind of attachment;
furthermore, it is also called "reversal" because one turns away from lower faults.
To be exempt from and sever the bonds of craving is termed "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
Liberation is not uniform; it is explained in one gate as being eightfold.
What are these eight names?
First, possessing the perception of internal forms, one observes external forms.
Second, perceiving external forms while being internally without the perception of form;
third, the liberation of pure form;
fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The fifth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The sixth is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
The seventh is the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The eighth is the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*).
Regarding the first three among these eight, they are named after their objective spheres (*viṣaya*), which are material forms (*rūpa*).
Concerning the middle four liberations, there are differing opinions among the commentators.
If one follows the Abhidharma,
names are designated based on their essential nature and locus;
for that treatise declares that the four meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) constitute liberation.
Nāgārjuna is likewise.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the name is designated according to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Because one attains liberation by contemplating the four bases of emptiness,
the eighth liberation is named after its essential nature. Furthermore,
because the dharma of cessation is described as liberation, it is so designated.
The names are thus;
as for their characteristics,
they differ according to their respective schools, and what is taught by each varies.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
regarding "one who possesses internal perceptions of form and contemplates external forms":
one's own body is termed "internal."
The bodies of others are called "external.
Regarding internal and external forms that have not yet ceased or disintegrated,
one contemplates both internal and external forms as entirely impure by means of the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
This is the first liberation.
Question: In this [state], both internal and external forms have not yet been destroyed.
Why is it that internal form alone is specifically said to exist?
The explanation states:
regarding external form, during the first three contemplations, it remains entirely undestroyed and thus exists.
Because it includes the previous three cases,
"existence" is not stated exclusively in the first instance;
internal form (*rūpa*) is not like that.
"It exists initially but does not exist subsequently.
To distinguish it from this subsequent non-existence, one says that it "exists initially.
Furthermore, he asked:
Within this [practice], one contemplates both internal and external forms as impure.
Why, then, is it said here specifically that one "contemplates the external"? To explain:
This is a case of manifesting the hidden and concealing the name.
Within [the internal], existence is manifested while the meaning of contemplation is concealed;
without [the external], contemplation is explained while the meaning of existence is concealed.
Each side cites its own position;
in truth, however, both are equally valid.
Furthermore, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is intended to produce revulsion toward one's own body.
Contemplating the internal is easy to understand;
therefore, it is omitted here.
Furthermore, as for this contemplation, one first takes the signs of another's corpse and so forth, and then applies them to one's own body.
Because it begins with the preliminary skillful means, it is said that one "contemplates the external.
Regarding "being without internal perception of form while contemplating external forms":
this refers to first taking up the signs of one's own future death, such as the signs of being devoured by worms, burned by fire, or destroyed and disintegrated.
Because one forms the perception of disintegration regarding the present,
it is said that there is "nothing within.
Furthermore, [one perceives] the present as being separated and destroyed.
Even down to the most minute atom, there is nothing at all;
this is also called "internally non-existent.
Contemplating external impurity is called "contemplating external forms."
Question: For what reason does one not contemplate the non-existence of external objects?
Explanation:
Since one's own body is impermanent, fragile, and devoid of self-perception,
it is easily brought to an end; therefore,
it is said that there is no [self] within.
External elements such as the great earth are stable and difficult to destroy;
because it is difficult to perceive them as non-existent, they are not mentioned here.
Furthermore, because one's own body is narrow and limited, it is easily exhausted; thus, one contemplates that there is no form within.
Form is vast and manifold, difficult to extinguish;
only upon reaching the sphere of infinite space can it be extinguished.
Therefore, within this contemplation, one does not contemplate the non-existence of external objects.
A question is asked: If it is said that external forms are vast and difficult to contemplate as being non-existent, why then is it possible to contemplate the impurity of external forms?
The commentary states:
Impurity is that which possesses contemplation;
it accords with the preceding object.
Because the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā) is easily accomplished, one can attain it by observing external objects as impure; however,
the cultivation of calm abiding (śamatha) is difficult to achieve.
For this reason, one cannot observe the external as being non-existent.
A question is asked:
Why, within the first gate, does one universally observe both the internal and external as impure?
This refers exclusively to observing external objects.
The treatise states:
"In the former case, the observation of the mind was not yet subtle."
Because it is difficult to collect [the mind] in a single location, one observes both the internal and external;
this mind then becomes subtler and easier to collect in a single location.
Therefore, one contemplates only the external.
Furthermore, in the previous section, because internal form had not yet ceased to exist, one contemplated both the internal and external;
now, in this section, because internal form has already ceased to exist, one contemplates exclusively the external.
Question: If there is no self within, who observes external forms?
Treatise: [Answer]...
This is a contemplation based on mental construction;
it is not that [the object] is actually non-existent.
Therefore, one is able to contemplate the external.
The preceding two gates constitute the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the liberation through purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*):
one removes the skin and flesh and contemplates only the white bones.
Furthermore, one contemplates the light of the bones, forming perceptions of them as blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth;
this is called the liberation of purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
How does one contemplate the dharmas?
First, one must take the light of gold, silver, various jewels, and so forth to illuminate the skeletal marks;
only then can they be seen. He asked:
Ordinary persons perceive purity within the impure; this is called an inversion (*viparyāsa*).
This [contemplation] likewise observes the impure as pure.
Why, then, is it not an inversion?
The treatise states:
"Female form is in truth impure;
yet ordinary beings perceive it as pure and become stained by attachment toward it."
Therefore, this is a perversion.
This practitioner of pure contemplation observes only white bones;
yet, when compared to the skin and flesh, the bones possess only a slight appearance of purity.
Therefore, it is not an inversion.
Furthermore, within this contemplation, one sets aside the skeletal form and contemplates only the radiance of the bones;
this bone-radiance is pure and clear.
Therefore, it is not an inversion.
Furthermore, at the time of this contemplation, one first takes up the color and light of gold, silver, and various jewels to compare them with the color of the bones;
the colors of these jewels taken up are actually pure.
Therefore, it is not an inversion.
Furthermore, although one contemplates purity,
no defiled attachment arises.
Therefore, it is not inverted.
Within this nirvana, it is called "liberation through bodily realization" (kāyasākṣin-vimukti).
By observing the pure body, one realizes liberation.
These are called the liberation through realization by names.
These three color-observations and the liberations from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are like the four formless attainments.
Regarding what is called "difference," Nāgārjuna’s commentary states:
those four meditative absorptions of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) are attained by both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*),
whereas these four liberations (*vimokṣa*) are attained only by noble ones.
Because that liberation does not revert; as for the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*),
in their school it has the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as its essence.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Mutual Inclusion of the Six Perfections" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The bodhisattva’s meditative absorption of cessation is the eighth liberation.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also speaks in this same way.
The essential characteristics of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) have been explained at length as previously set forth.
Question: For what reason is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) not called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*)?
The treatise states:
This is the entering and exiting of those with wrong views;
they thus regress and re-enter into wrong views.
Therefore, it is not liberation.
In the Abhidharma system,
the first three and the last one are the same as those of Nāgārjuna;
however, the textual characteristics of the four formless liberations differ slightly.
What is the distinction between their different characteristics? In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
the four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) and the four formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) are distinguished according to whether they are universal or restricted.
Concentration and supernormal powers pertain to both ordinary persons and noble ones; liberation pertains only to noble ones.
According to the Abhidharma system:
There is a distinction between the broad and the narrow senses of the term. In its broad definition,
"concentration" (samādhi) encompasses both the unhindered knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and liberation (vimukti).
The meaning of "liberation" (vimukti) is narrow;
it does not extend to the unhindered paths (ānantarya-mārga) nor to the mind at the moment of death.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* excludes the nine unhindered paths of the four formless attainments as well as the mind at the moment of death [from the category of liberation].
All other wholesome dharmas are said to be liberations (*prahāṇa*); however,
because they take lower objects as their conditions without obstruction, they are not liberations.
The mind at the moment of death neither turns toward the place of rebirth nor turns away from it.
Question: The phrasing differs;
what is its meaning?
The commentary states:
"The meaning is identical; it is only the expression that differs in being implicit or explicit."
Since Nāgārjuna relies predominantly on the meaning of the Abhidharma for his treatises, it may also be the case that,
according to the Abhidharma, liberation consists of [the attainment of] the nine unhindered knowledges and the mind at the moment of death.
Nāgārjuna agrees with this;
Nāgārjuna states that the eight liberations are exclusively for the noble ones (*ārya*),
whereas the Abhidharma differs.
What is the meaning of this?

As stated in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vyākhyā*: "Excluding the nine unhindered knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the mind at the moment of death, all other wholesome dharmas are said to be 'turning away' (*pratyāgamana*).
If that which is obtained by ordinary beings were not "turning away," [it would contradict this].
This is not called an exhaustive exposition.
The arguments presented in the *Tattvasiddhi* differ entirely from those preceding it;
in that treatise, the initial three observations regarding the emptiness of form (*rūpa*) are termed "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
One does not consider the discernment of the pure and the impure through intimacy to be liberation.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Eight Liberations" in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Some people say:"
To claim that the first two [liberations] are impure while the third liberation is a pure contemplation is incorrect.
Why is this? Because there is no liberation attained through either the contemplation of purity or the contemplation of impurity.
Furthermore, even non-Buddhists are capable of observing both the pure and the impure.
This clarity is not liberation;
it is only through the contemplation of emptiness that it is called liberation. Question:
It is asked: "Non-Buddhists also practice the contemplation of emptiness;
why is it not called liberation?
The treatise states:
The non-Buddhists merely practice contemplation based on faith and understanding, rather than true contemplation;
it is only when one truly perceives emptiness that it is called liberation.
However, in their own texts:
The textual characteristics of the first three liberations are extremely obscure.
According to traditional exegesis,
"possessing the perception of internal forms while observing external forms" means:
One's own body is called "internal," while the bodies of others are called "external.
Regarding these internal and external forms of the five sensory objects:
One has not yet seen their emptiness;
rather, one sees only that the four elements and five sense-faculties—both internal and external—are empty of the provisional designation of "form.
This is the first liberation.
Within these names, each mentions only one side;
while some apply to both the internal and external,
others specifically manifest the internal.
This contemplation applies to both the internal and external; here, it is explained specifically regarding the external.
This corresponds to what was previously analyzed as the contemplation of the impurity of external objects while maintaining the perception of internal bodily forms.
The meaning is similar.
Regarding "internally being without the perception of form while observing external forms":
one observes that the forms of the five sense objects, both internal and external, are empty.
This is the second liberation;
however, within the names,
it is stated as "non-existence" above.
The preceding discussion was on external observation;
these two [sections] merely alternate their phrasing.
Both of these observations examine the emptiness of form within the desire realm.
Regarding the liberation through the pure:
one contemplates the pure forms of the form realm as empty;
within these three gateways, one also perceives the mind as empty.
To distinguish them from those that follow, it specifically mentions "contemplating form.
Furthermore, the subsequent four liberations differ from the preceding ones:
whereas the former take the actual substance of the four *ārya-samādhis* (the four formless attainments) as the four liberations themselves.
Regarding what is now being discussed:
the Sage first attains the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti);
having done so, he then gives rise to untainted contemplation (anāsrava-vipaśyanā) based upon whichever dhyāna he relies upon.
Having contemplated the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) thus acquired as being suffering,
impermanent, empty, selfless, and so forth,
one becomes free from bondage therein; this is called liberation (vimukti).
Therefore, that treatise states:
"By virtue of attaining the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
the noble ones (*ārya*) are able to contemplate those aggregates (*skandha*) as suffering, impermanent, and so forth."
This is called liberation.
The eighth liberation differs from the preceding ones;
previously, the meditative attainment of cessation was described as the eighth liberation.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the attainment of cessation is entirely denied;
thus, the *Tattvasiddhi* states:
"When the practitioner realizes nirvāṇa..."
All afflictions are extinguished and all tasks are completed;
this is called the eighth liberation.
It does not state that the cessation of all mind and mental factors constitutes the eighth liberation;
thus, it is clearly known to be different.
Furthermore, it says:
The practitioner of the Way attains the meditative absorption of cessation but does not attain the eighth liberation;
the Ārhat "Lightning-flash" attains the eighth liberation but does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation.
It is clearly understood that they are not the same.
That treatise further states:
"The liberation through cessation extinguishes ignorance and so forth;
the meditative attainment of cessation extinguishes perception and feeling and so forth."
Although they are clearly distinct,
when discussed comprehensively,
the two kinds of nirvāṇa attained by those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) constitute the eighth liberation.
Such liberation also exists in the Mahāyāna.
Within the second section, its essential nature is analyzed through five points of distinction.
First is the distinction between the provisional and the real.
Some say that the eight liberations take only the conventional person as their essence,
precisely because afflictions bind the conventional person.
When a person attains liberation, that very liberation constitutes their essence.
Furthermore, there are those who say that only reality constitutes the essence.
All of these are extreme biases.
When discussing the person who has attained liberation,
the conventional designation (prajñapti) serves as its substance.
The qualities of liberation are explained as having true dharmas as their essence; therefore,
the sūtra speaks of liberation through wisdom and liberation of the mind.
Since the meaning encompasses both aspects,
how can one take only one side?
Second, there is the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In the Abhidharma system, there are eight co-existent conditioned factors (*sahabhū-saṃskāra*).
The first seven are the conditioned mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
and the eighth is the non-material conditioned factor (*arūpa-saṃskāra*).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the first seven [categories] are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and the eighth is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because that [system] explains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as the eighth [unconditioned],
in the Mahāyāna dharma, while the liberation according to phenomena (*suvimukta*) initially accords with the Abhidharma,
in the end it is entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Contemplating emptiness and attaining liberation initially accord with the *Tattvasiddhi*;
ultimately, one achieves all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
for they are neither born nor extinguished.
Third, regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*):
according to the *Abhidharma* system,
the first three are exclusively contaminated, while the latter two are exclusively uncontaminated.
The first three matters are with outflows (*sāsrava*) because they are objects of contemplation;
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is with outflows because the noble ones do not abide therein;
and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is also with outflows because it is bound to the state of non-perception.
The middle three types are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
whereas in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun), all are uncontaminated.
Therefore, that treatise states:
Because they are empty, all are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma,
the first seven types are tainted for those who are beginners.
Ultimately, it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*).
The eighth type is exclusively untainted;
therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichiding lun) states that the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is considered a noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*).
The four minds are distinguished by their mutual opposition to non-mind;
among them, the first seven are mental factors while the eighth is not mind.
The five [factors] are distinguished as being wholesome.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion constitute these three wholesome states.
In the Abhidharma system, the first three are the wholesome state of non-greed. Question:
If the first three [liberations] do not have non-greed as their intrinsic nature,
why does the Sūtra say they are "contemplating form"?
For contemplation has wisdom as its intrinsic nature.
What is non-attachment?
The explanation states:
this is explained by way of proximity.
The wholesome root of non-attachment must be accompanied by wisdom to be able to abandon greed;
therefore, it is described as "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) because of its powerful companion. Although it is called contemplation, [it is so designated for this reason].
Non-attachment is primary,
because it destroys craving. Question:
It may be that the first two, which are the contemplations on impurity,
can destroy greed; but how does the third, the contemplation on purity, destroy greed?
The commentary states:
Although one practices the contemplation of purity within this [state],
it is called "non-attachment" because it serves to destroy desire.
Question: Since the destruction of greed through the contemplation of impurity constitutes attainment,
why is the contemplation of purity necessary?
The treatise states:
"The practitioner, desiring to test himself, observes the impure;
if no lust arises, [he knows his mind is controlled]."
This is not yet to be considered extraordinary.
To see purity and yet remain free from craving—
that alone is truly extraordinary.
Therefore, one performs this contemplation.
Furthermore, if the practitioner does not contemplate purity,
they proceed to eliminate greed by means of it.
Furthermore, one may see pure forms that could give rise to desire;
it is to prevent this fault that [the following is taught].
First, one contemplates the pure to bring the mind into a state of composure.
A question is asked:
"Is it not the case that the contemplation of the impure can destroy lustful desire?"
Furthermore, one must employ pure contemplation (*śubhā-vipaśyanā*) to assist in destroying greed and the perception of kinship (*jñāti-saṃjñā*) to remedy hatred. Why, then,
not employ the perception of an enemy (*amitra-saṃjñā*) to assist in this?
The commentary states:
The perception of purity is not exclusively a fault;
for example, it is like contemplating the jewel-like colors and other marks of the Buddha’s body.
One does not give rise to desire-taints;
therefore, one forms the perception of purity to assist in the destruction of greed and desire.
The thought of resentment is merely a fault;
therefore, one does not engage in it.
Furthermore, craving is difficult to sever.
Therefore, one must employ pure contemplation to assist in breaking it down; thus,
hatred and anger are easily eliminated.
Therefore, only the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) is uniquely able to dispel [the notion of beauty].
Since the subsequent four liberations have wisdom (*prajñā*)— which is by nature free from delusion— as their essence,
the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the nature of the perception of superior form (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa-saṃjñā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*);
thus, the eighth [perception] is neither mind nor included among the three wholesome [roots].
The first seven are of the nature of wisdom because they consist of the contemplation of emptiness;
the eighth is unconditioned and is not subsumed under the three types of wholesome states.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, liberation according to phenomena is the same as in the Abhidharma;
liberation through the contemplation of emptiness is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Such is the nature of their essence.
Regarding the classification of positions within the third gate,
there are two interpretations of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) in the Abhidharma.
The first distinguishes the noble ones from ordinary persons.
The eight liberations are attained only by two types of persons: the *anāgāmin* and the *arhat*.
Among *anāgāmins*, at most eight are accomplished;
at least, they are not fixed.
Among Arhats, at most eight [attainments] are achieved,
and at least seven; this excludes the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Because they are only attained by those liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
It is asked:
among these eight, the first three liberations are antidotes to sensual desire (kāmacchanda).
Anāgāmins and Arhats have already transcended craving;
for what purpose, then, do they practice? To explain:
These three are practices for guarding against faults,
not practices for severing faults;
for the noble ones fear falling back and the arising of lower-level afflictions.
Therefore, one cultivates these three not for the purpose of abandoning desire.
Question: How is it known that these three types are not practices for abandoning faults?
The treatise states:
The first two are cultivated and arise based on the first and second dhyānas;
the third is cultivated and arises based on the fourth dhyāna.
Since the antidote to greed must necessarily exist in the future,
we know that these three are not practices for severing faults. Question:
Why do those who have attained *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* not [attain it]?
The explanation says:
the first three [fruits] arise based on the four *dhyānas*.
The latter five exist within the four empty spaces.
Śrotāpannas and Sakṛdāgāmins do not attain the eight dhyānas;
it is for this reason that they do not obtain them.
Question: Ordinary worldlings also attain the eight dhyānas;
why is it that they do not [attain them as such]?
Because there is regression from what has been attained,
it is not called liberation.
This is according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This meaning is certain. Regarding the general discussion of both ordinary persons and noble ones:
the first three liberations and the four formless attainments can be attained through contaminated liberation by ordinary persons.
It is attained either by those who are Non-returners (anāgāmin) or Arhats.
If one cultivates and attains the eight dhyānas while still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), then it is attained by an ordinary person.
If, however, one cultivates the eight dhyānas only after having already attained the state of a noble one (ārya), then it is attained by a Non-returner or an Arhat.
That non-returner (anāgāmin) first attains it upon becoming established;
the arhat attains it because they already possess it.

The untainted liberations (anāsrava-vimokṣa) of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, as well as the liberation of cessation (nirodha-vimokṣa), are attained only by non-returners and arhats.
Question: Why do these [beings] not attain the fruit of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin?
Answer: Because they have not attained the eight dhyānas.
In the Abhidharma, it is thus.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the eight liberations exist only among the noble ones (*ārya*) and do not extend to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Within the category of the noble ones:
It exists only on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga);
it does not extend to the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Within those paths of cultivation and no-more-learning:
The practice of contemplating emptiness is generally termed "liberation" (*vimokṣa*),
without distinguishing between the specific categories of "unhindered liberation" (*anāvaraṇa-vimokṣa*) and so forth.
Among these, the cultivation of the first two occurs from the stage of the *sakṛdāgāmin* up to the path of approach (*pratipannaka*) for the *anāgāmin*.
Because they serve as the antidotes to the afflictions within the stages of the desire realm, they are established in the stage of the Anāgāmin;
next, the four cultivations are established in the practice of the Arhat because they serve as the antidotes to the afflictions within the two upper realms.
The liberation of non-perception begins its cultivation within the practice of an arhat and is perfected in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The liberation of cessation exists only in the stage of no-more-learning.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings,
everything from the spiritual lineage (gotra) upward is fully complete;
furthermore, if one discusses this comprehensively:
It is also acquired within the states of the happy destinies (*sugati*).
Such are the distinctions between the states.
In the fourth section, they are distinguished according to their location.
Within this, there are three:
first, the basis of meditative concentration;
second, the locus of the body.
Third, regarding the locus of the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*). As for "relying on the locus of dhyāna," according to the *Abhidharma* method:
The first two liberations are cultivated based on the first and second dhyānas.
Why is this so? The treatise states:
In the desire realm, there are two kinds of desire:
first, bodily desire,
which refers to the mind of greedy attachment within the five consciousnesses.
Second is the desire of the mind,
which refers to the defiled mind within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, one relies on the first dhyāna to cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an antidote to that desire.
Within the stage of the first dhyāna, there are likewise two kinds of desire.
The first is bodily desire,
which refers to the mind of lustful attachment within the three groups of consciousness— namely, those of the eye, ear, and body.
The second is the desire of the mind,
which refers to the defiled mind within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, one relies on the second dhyāna to cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an antidote to that desire.
Because there is no desire for the body from the second dhyāna upward,
one no longer cultivates it in the third dhyāna and above. Furthermore,
within the third dhyāna, one experiences the bliss of its own stage.
One is unwilling to contemplate those impure matters.
In the fourth dhyāna, the mind and nature are tranquil;
one does not delight in contemplating those impure matters.
Therefore, it is not established for them.
Since there is only a small amount therein,
it is not mentioned.
The third liberation relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this so? Because one contemplates impure phenomena and regards them as pure.
It is difficult to accomplish;
it can only be achieved when the power of wisdom is strengthened within the fourth dhyāna,
for in other dhyānas, wisdom is inferior.
This is why they do not arise.
Furthermore, in the first two types of contemplation, one regards the forms of the desire realm as impure;
because this is a direct observation of what is truly impure, it is easily accomplished when practiced closely.
Because it is difficult to achieve when far removed [from the object],
it is found exclusively in the first and second dhyānas.
The third liberation contemplates the forms of the desire realm.
Taking this as pure constitutes the contemplation of the provisional;
it is easily accomplished when approached from afar.
Because it is difficult to achieve when near [the lower stages], it is found exclusively within the fourth dhyāna;
even if it were to exist below that, it would not be so.
Because they are subtle, they are not mentioned.
The next four liberations belong to their respective stages;
it should be understood that the liberation of cessation is associated with the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The *Tattvasiddhi* states that the eight liberations are based upon the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Just as when relying on the first dhyāna, one contemplates the internal and external forms of the desire realm as empty and quiescent; these constitute the first two liberations.
Contemplating the emptiness of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) constitutes the third liberation.
Contemplating the emptiness of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) previously acquired constitutes the four [formless] liberations.
Relying upon that first dhyāna to sever and extinguish all causes and effects of birth and death constitutes the eighth liberation.
As it is with the basis of the first dhyāna,
so it is for all stages up to the sphere of nothingness.
Based on the lightning-flash concentration, one attains only the first three [liberations] as well as the final cessation.
The middle four [factors] cannot be obtained. Why is this so?
The treatise states:
The Sage attains the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti),
and thereafter contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, and empty;
this is called liberation.
The Arhat Dianguang did not attain that samādhi;
having nothing upon which to focus his contemplation,
he failed to achieve it for this reason.

Because the mind in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is inferior, it does not give rise to the increase of insight that severs the fetters through the outflow-free path; therefore, it is not relied upon.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, the contemplation of emptiness for liberation fully relies upon all eight dhyānas.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-conceptual and untainted (anāsrava),
its liberation according to phenomena (yathābhūta-vimukti) initially accords with the Abhidharma; once the cultivation of practice has reached full maturity, it becomes distinct.
The first three liberations are based upon all four dhyānas; the next four [liberations] are based on their respective stages;
and the liberation of cessation is based on all stages and can be entered into as a present realization. This concludes this section.
Regarding their basis in terms of the realms of existence (*dhātu*): according to the Abhidharma,
the first three liberations exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The inhabitants of the three continents are capable of cultivating and establishing it,
but not those in other bodies or places;
this is because it serves as the remedy for sensual desire in the realm of desire.
It does not exist in the higher realms.
A question is asked:
"In the first dhyāna, there still exist both types of desire: those of the body and those of the mind."
Why is this antidote not cultivated in the higher realms?
The explanation is:
although the first dhyāna possesses both [types of] desire.
However, this [practice] is specifically for treating the affliction of lust;
since those in the upper realms have already abandoned it, they do not cultivate it.
Although the six heavens of the desire realm possess sensual desire,
their attachment to pleasure is so profound that they are unable to cultivate [the path].
Although the inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a thin attachment to desire, [they likewise cannot cultivate it].
The power of wisdom is weak and inferior;
for this reason, one does not cultivate it,
due to the obstacles and difficulties of other realms of existence.
Furthermore, because there is no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not arise.
Next, the four liberations (*vimokṣa*) can all be cultivated and brought forth within the bodies of the three realms.
Those that are with outflows (sāsrava) are cultivated starting from the lower stages and subsequently arise in the higher ones;
those that are without outflows (anāsrava) can be cultivated in the lower stages as well as in their own respective stage.
The liberation through cessation is cultivated and arises in the desire realm, not in the two higher realms.
Question: Why is this so?
For what reason do the formless attainments arise through cultivation,
whereas the cessation attainment does not?
The treatise states:
The three powers of meditative concentration arise as follows:
first, the power of the cause (*hetubala*),
because that which was previously cultivated serves as its own specific cause (*svabhāva-hetu*).
First, the power of manifestation, which can give rise [to rebirth] in the present; second, the power of karma,
because one has cultivated the karma for birth in the higher realms in this life.
Mutually supporting and stimulating one another, those above are able to give rise to the three powers of skillful means;
that is to say, by instilling fear of calamities such as fires, they cause [the practice] to be cultivated and arise.
Due to these three powers, it is cultivated and brought forth in the higher realms;
however, the meditative attainment of cessation arises solely from the power of instruction.
This is because the Dharma of the meditative attainment of cessation was taught by a Buddha in the desire realm.
Therefore, they are cultivated and brought forth;
since there is no one above to teach them,
they are not cultivated or brought forth.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the first two liberations are cultivated and arise only within a body of the desire realm;
thus they are called "bodies of the desire realm."
Because they are considered internal,
the third [liberation] can be cultivated and arisen in both the desire and form realms.
The latter five liberations can arise in all three realms.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, one initially accords with the Two Vehicles;
ultimately, however, one achieves the arising of all [phenomena] in all places through these two gates. Thus ends [this section].
Next, the discussion concerns the objects and spheres.
According to the Abhidharma,
the first three liberations take the phenomena of the desire realm as their objective sphere.

In the liberation from outflows (*āsravavimokṣa*) regarding the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, one takes only the dharmas of one’s own level and the higher levels as objects.
Those paths of liberation take only their own respective levels as objects.
Regarding the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), it takes a higher stage as its object. Question:
Why does it not take lower dharmas as its object?
Because it is not a liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Furthermore, that which takes a lower stage as its object is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it is not a liberation.
Among these three bases, the objects of untainted liberation regarding suffering and its origin pertain only to their own level and higher levels;
they do not take lower levels as objects.
The formless [realms] do not take the outflows of the lower realms as their object;
the Truth of Cessation is likewise.
This is precisely because they do not take the outflows of the lower realms as their object.
Nor does it take as its object the cessation that is their antidote.
Within the Truth of the Path,
everything belonging to one's own stage and all those of the stages above take the lower stages as their objects.
Thus, it is not fixed.
If one relies on a lower dhyāna to give rise to the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) to remedy the faults of a lower level,
then [the mind] does not take anything as its object.
Furthermore, because they do not take lower contaminated states as objects,
they do not take their antidotes as objects;
rather, they are able to counteract the faults of their own level and those of higher levels.

The [attainments of] mastery (abhibhvāyatana) take all [realms] as their objects. The liberation of non-perception (asaṃjñi-vimokṣa) takes only the contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena of its own level as its object.
As for the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti), it has no object; thus, there is no need to discuss it.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the objects of the first two liberations (vimokṣa) are in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the object of the third liberation is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and the objects of the four formless liberations are in the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When extinguished, there is no objective realm.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, liberation through the contemplation of emptiness is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
while liberation according to phenomena is the same as in the *Abhidharma*.
Within the fifth section, the meaning of acquisition, relinquishment, and accomplishment is clarified.
First, acquisition is explained:
that which previously did not exist and now exists is termed "acquisition."
The *Abhidharma-śāstra*’s explanation of the meaning of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) has two parts.
First, it distinguishes the noble ones from ordinary persons:
the eight liberations are exclusively the meritorious qualities of noble beings.
Among these, the impure liberations (*sāsrava-vimokṣa*) of the first three and the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc. are acquired solely through the abandonment of desire;
this is because when one abandons the desire of a lower stage, one acquires the dharmas of the higher stage.
Regarding the pure liberations (*anāsrava-vimokṣa*) of the [first] three spheres of emptiness, there are two kinds of acquisition.
First, attainment through detachment from desire,
because when one becomes detached from lower desires, one attains the higher dharmas.
Second, attainment through falling away.
That is to say, when one regresses from the faculties or regresses from the noble fruits, one obtains these fundamental dharmas.
The eighth liberation is obtained solely through skillful means;
having attained the eight dhyānas, one practices them through skillful means and subsequently attains it.
Question: Why is it that the first seven liberations are attained through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya-prāpti*),
whereas the cessation [attainment] is not so, being attained only through preparatory effort (*prayoga-prāpti*)?
The commentary states:
The first seven are dharmas for the abandonment of desire that directly oppose the lower desires;
therefore, at the time of abandoning the desires of those lower stages, [they serve as antidotes].
Thus, being without dependence,
one immediately attains it.
This liberation through cessation is the dharma that extinguishes the mind.
Although one has abandoned the desires of the lower realms,
because the higher mind has not yet ceased,
this [attainment] is not obtained.
Second, a general discussion concerning both ordinary beings and noble ones.
The liberation attained by ordinary beings is generally termed "liberation" (*vimukti*).

Within this category, the first three [formless attainments] and the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.)—being tainted liberations (*sāsrava-vimukti*)—possess two kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*).
First, that obtained through detachment from desire;
its meaning is the same as explained previously.
Second, that obtained through birth.
When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) descends from a higher realm to be born in a lower one, they obtain the dharmas of that lower realm.
This is because, while in the higher realms, they possessed the outflowing (*sāsrava*) states of those levels and thus lost those of the lower;
upon descending to be born there, they regain them once more.
The remainder is as explained previously.
There is no explicit text in the *Tattvasiddhi*;
it is analyzed here according to its underlying meaning.
The first seven liberations are acquired solely through the abandonment of desire;
that is, they are attained at the time one permanently severs the desires of the lower stages.
The eighth is not fixed.
Among these, the nirvāṇa with remainder is attained solely through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*).
The nirvāṇa without remainder is attained either through the abandonment of desire or through skillful means (*upāya*).
When the retribution of karma no longer arises, this is attainment through the abandonment of desire.
That which is called "separation" is attained precisely when one is free from the desire for perception;
it is attained through skillful means by the complete cessation of present retribution,
because one employs the supernormal power of the knowledge of the ultimate limit to extinguish the attainment of retribution.
The Arhat’s attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation is also acquired through skillful means.

In the Mahāyāna teachings, liberation according to circumstances is the same as in the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), while liberation through the contemplation of emptiness is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi). This concludes this section.
Next, the meaning of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*) is explained.
That which previously existed but is now lost is termed "relinquishment.

According to the *Abhidharma*, the first three [dhyānas] as well as the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) possess two kinds of relinquishment regarding their contaminated liberations (*sāsrava-vimokṣa*).
First is relinquishment through regression (*parihāṇi-parityāga*),
which refers to the loss of higher liberation when one regresses and gives rise to the desire of a lower stage.
Second is relinquishment through birth (*upapatti-parityāga*).
When one is born in a higher stage, one loses the dharmas of the lower stages.
Regarding the untainted liberations of the three lower formless attainments, there are three kinds of relinquishment:
first, relinquishment through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
According to that school, there is retrogression from the untainted state;
secondly, there is abandonment through the transformation of faculties, because when one transforms from dull untainted faculties to sharp faculties, the dull faculties are lost.

Third, there is relinquishment through the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*). At the time of realizing the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one relinquishes the path of learning (*śaikṣa-mārga*); thus, the seventh and eighth [faculties] are relinquished solely through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the first seven are relinquished solely at the time of entering nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The eighth is "no relinquishing.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, one relinquishes when attaining the true realization through the cultivation of conditions for liberation;
however, in ultimate, true liberation, there is ultimately no relinquishing. This concludes these two gates.
Next, the attainment [of liberation] is explained.
Wherever it occurs, that is called "attainment.
According to the Abhidharma method, regarding the first two liberations, from the second dhyāna downwards, they are all attained wherever the body is located.
One born in the higher realms does not accomplish the outflow-tainted [attainments],
because one who is born in the higher realms loses those of the lower realms.
The third liberation is accomplished by all stages from the fourth dhyāna downwards.
If one is born in a higher realm, [the lower ones] are not accomplished.
Regarding the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the outflow-free liberations (*anāsrava-vimokṣa*) of their own stage and all those of the lower stages are accomplished;
however, if one is born in a higher realm, they are not accomplished.
The untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimokṣa*) of those three spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), as well as the latter two types of universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), are accomplished.
However, within that school, one is able to enter into the first seven liberations in their actual manifestation according to the respective spheres in which they are accomplished.
The eighth liberation is accomplished and entered within the desire and form realms;
although it is accomplished in the formless realm, one cannot enter it there,
for that realm lacks material form.
Furthermore, if the mind were extinguished,
life would come to an end; therefore,
in the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, all liberations are established as being present in all places.
In the sixth section, their relative superiority and inferiority are distinguished.
Within this, their superiority and inferiority are analyzed in relation to the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
These eight bases of mastery and ten totalities shall be discussed in detail later.
The Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) distinguishes the superiority and inferiority of the first three liberations in relation to the eight stages of mastery and so forth solely on this basis:
because the first three liberations observe general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
they are considered the lowest.
The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are explained as the intermediate [level] in detail;
