because the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) involve the most extensive contemplation, they are said to be the superior [level]. According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, this is not so.
That treatise declares that because they are conceptual meditations (parikalpita-bhāvanā) on the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana),
they are considered the most inferior.
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and the latter are without outflows (*anāsrava*);
they are described as being intermediate.
As for the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), they are exclusively without outflows.
It is said that those of superior capacity are so designated; among them, those of inferior capacity belong to the stage of external ordinary persons (bāhyapṛthagjana),
while those of middling capacity have already entered the stage of internal ordinary persons (adhyātmapṛthagjana).
The "superior" refers to those who have already attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and above.
This concludes the rough explanation of the meaning of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). **163.

The Meaning of the Eight Bases of Mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*):** An explanation analyzing the meaning of the eight bases of mastery through four gates: I. Explaining the names and defining their characteristics; II. Discerning their essential nature (*tattva*); III. Analysis according to persons; IV. Analysis according to locations. **First: Explaining the Names and Defining Their Characteristics.** [The text continues with the formal definitions of each base of mastery.]
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
they are also called the eight spheres of removal (*abhibhāyatana*) in the sūtras;
this is for the sake of this meditative practice.
Because they are able to pacify greed and desire— the most formidable of afflictions—
they are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The term "entry" (*praveśa*) is also a synonym for "base."
Because they are the places for removing afflictions, they are called "bases of removal" (abhibhvāyatana).
As these bases of removal differ,
eight are taught within a single category.
What are these eight names?
First: possessing internal perception of form, one perceives external forms that are limited.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is called "perceiving external forms, whether beautiful or ugly, with superior knowledge and superior vision."
Second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many;
third, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few;
fourth, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many.
Five are blue;
six are yellow;
seven are red.
Eight white.
Among these eight, the first two correspond to the first liberation among the eight liberations.
One's own body is termed "internal."
When one's own body parts have not yet been extinguished or destroyed, it is called "having internal form.
When, among external forms, one first contemplates a single body as impure,
it is called "contemplating the small externally."
For what reason is it not many?
Nāgārjuna explains:

At the beginning of training in contemplation, the fearful mind is difficult to restrain; one does not dare to contemplate extensively. It is like a deer that has not yet been tamed—it cannot be let loose at a great distance.
Regarding "beautiful and ugly," the treatise states:
among those external forms, those that are the result of wholesome karma are called beautiful.
Evil fruits are called "ugly.
Furthermore, among external forms, that which gives rise to lust is called "beautiful," while that which gives rise to anger is described as "ugly."
Furthermore, among those thirty-six constituent parts, the skeletal form is called beautiful,
while the forms of skin, flesh, and so forth are said to be ugly.
Moreover, within external forms, to forgetfully perceive them as pure is termed beautiful.
Furthermore, one sees the impure and describes it as ugly;
yet, regarding what is beautiful and what is ugly, one gives rise to neither greed nor hatred.
One merely contemplates that the four great elements are a combination of causes and conditions, which is called superior knowledge and superior vision.
Regarding the second [stage], "internally possessing the perception of forms while externally perceiving many":
internally, it is the same as before;
through the transformative mastery of the observing mind, one is able to perform extensive observation.
When the entire great earth is filled and one perceives it all as impure,
this is called "extensive external observation.
The next two spheres of mastery correspond to the second liberation among the eight liberations.
To conceive the thought that one's own body is dead, or that it is being devoured by worms or consumed by fire until it is utterly extinguished,
is called "internal non-existence.
The details regarding its extent are the same as before.
Blue, yellow, red, and white constitute the third liberation among the eight liberations.
Within external forms, one removes the skin and flesh and forms the perception of bones;
subsequently, one contemplates these bones, forming perceptions of them as blue, yellow, red, and white.
Regarding the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
how does one contemplate phenomena? One contemplates them as blue while desiring [to see them as such].
First, one attains the four dhyānas.
Next, one takes up a small mark of blue among external forms;
returning to meditative concentration, one again contemplates that blue.
In this manner, one should alternate back and forth until it is thoroughly mastered;
this is called the "blue superior sphere" (nīla-uddeśa).
The same applies to yellow and the others.
Question: What is the difference between these four and the four *kṛtsnāyatanas*—blue, yellow, red, and white—among the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*?
Nāgārjuna explains, saying:
In the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one takes as objects everything extensively and universally, such as all things being blue and so forth;
in the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the objects are limited.
This is the distinction between them. This concludes this section.
Next, the essential nature is distinguished.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This contemplation concerns conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Second, it is distinguished according to whether it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
In the Abhidharma system, it is exclusively with outflows.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) are established;
thus, its eighth chapter on "The Eightfold Excellence" states:
"First, one contemplates the outflowing."
Ultimately, it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*).
The Mahāyāna is likewise.
It is the discrimination of the phenomena of the three minds.
In the Abhidharma system, this is of the nature of non-greed,
because it is the antidote to craving.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* system, it is of the nature of wisdom.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, those who directly contemplate phenomena are the same as the Abhidharmikas;
those who additionally perceive emptiness are the same as the Satyasiddhi school. These two approaches are concluded.
Next, we shall discuss this in terms of persons.
In the Abhidharma system, these may be cultivated and produced by non-Buddhist ordinary persons,
or they may be cultivated and produced by *anāgāmins* and *arhats*.
The *Tattvasiddhi* explains as follows:
The arising [of the path] occurs among the disciples of the Buddha; it does not extend to non-Buddhists.
Among the disciples of the Buddha, it arises through the cultivation of those who are ordinary persons within [the Buddhist fold].
Because the former is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and the latter is without outflows (*anāsrava*),
throughout the Mahāyāna teachings, from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward, one is able to fully cultivate and give rise to these three gates.
Next, we shall discuss them in terms of their locations.
There are four bases.
First is the base of dhyāna.
According to the Abhidharma, the first four [immeasurables] are cultivated by relying on the first and second dhyānas.
The latter four arise based on the fourth dhyāna.
As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, in the chapter on the "Eight Victorious States," states:
"Based on the lightning-flash concentration of the desire realm and the concentrations of the form realm, all [of these] can be cultivated and brought forth."
Second, the locus of the object;
third, the locus of cultivation and origination;
fourth, the locus of accomplishment.
These [eight liberations] possess discernment;
their meaning is similar to the first three liberations among the eight liberations.
Such are the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

164. The Meaning of the Eightfold Contemplation (13). The Meaning of the Eightfold Contemplation: An Exegesis through Two Gates—Distinguishing Names and Defining Characteristics (I); Distinguishing by Stages (II). First: Distinguishing Names and Defining Characteristics.
Regarding the "contemplation of the eight practices," as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
to engage in pursuit within the eight objects of focus is termed "practice."
"Contemplation" (guan) refers to illuminating observation.
In reality, it universally contemplates all dharmas;
for now, however, we shall discuss it with reference to a single form (rūpa).
Other categories may be understood accordingly. What are these names?
The first is the contemplation of form (*rūpa*).
Second, one contemplates the arising of form;
third, one contemplates the cessation of form,
which is also called the detachment from form.
Fourth, contemplating the path of form;
fifth, contemplating the gratification of form;
sixth, contemplating the peril of form.
It is also called the affliction of form.
Seventh is the contemplation of the emergence from form;
eighth is the contemplation of the ultimate meaning of form.
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*,
among these eight, the first seven observe the meaning of form;
that is to say, they observe the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The latter one examines the ultimate meaning of form (*rūpa*).
Among the preceding seven [examinations],
the first four correctly observe the essential nature and meaning of form.
Regarding the latter three observations of the arising of form,
among the first four, the initial observation of form is as follows:
To contemplate the nature of form as suffering, impermanent,
and so forth— this is precisely the contemplation of the Truth of Suffering.
To contemplate the origination of form...
To observe the causes of form— namely karma and afflictions—
is the contemplation of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
To observe the cessation of form is...

Because one contemplates the limit of the exhaustion of form as the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is called the "cessation of form. Because one is extinguished from and detached from the characteristics of form, it is also called the "detachment from form.
This is precisely the contemplation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Regarding the contemplation of the path concerning form:
it is the observation of the path that serves as the antidote to that form;
this is precisely the contemplation of the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
Next, regarding the contemplation of the "taste" (*āsvāda*) of form among the three contemplations:
one contemplates the arising and accumulation of form.
Because one gives rise to craving and becomes attached to the object of form, it is called the "taste of form."
Regarding the observation of the faults of form (*rūpa*): one observes that form gives rise to suffering.
Because the resulting retribution of suffering is a phenomenon characterized by fault and affliction, it is called the "fault of form."
It is also called the "affliction of form.
To contemplate the emergence from form is also called "detachment" in the sūtras.
Since "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) and "separation" (*visamyoga*) are alternative designations for cessation (*nirodha*),
among the four aspects of that Truth of Cessation,
some state them as exhaustion (*kṣaya*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Alternatively, it is further described as cessation, tranquility, and sublime detachment.
Thus, one knows that "renunciation" is a synonym for "cessation.
This contemplation of material phenomena is capable of producing cessation.
Cessation is a non-existent dharma;
how could it arise? One contemplates form and attains its cessation.
In terms of its meaning, it is explained as "arising.
However, the attainment of nirvāṇa within nirvāṇa is not called "non-arising";
their meanings are similar.
Why is it not said that the contemplation of form gives rise to the Path?
The Path is the ultimate contemplation (paramārtha-darśana) of the subsequent stage;
it is not that it is not taught at all.
The eighth [contemplation], the contemplation of the ultimate truth of form (*rūpa*), consists in contemplating that form is without self (*anātman*).
There are two kinds of selflessness.
First, there is no self among sentient beings; within form, there is no person.
Second, there is no self in phenomena; the nature of form is empty and quiescent.
Among these eight [points], the first seven are the skillful means of contemplation.

Just as one contemplates form through subsequent correct contemplation (*anvaya-samyag-darśana*), so it is with the categories of feeling, perception, mental formations, and so forth; this concludes the first section.
Next, the discussion proceeds by way of the stages (*avasthā*).
The texts do not provide a definitive judgment;
however, by inferring according to the underlying meaning,
the coarse [level] can also be understood.
In the Abhidharma system,
one gradually practices observation from the four preparatory stages, such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and above;
from "Patience regarding Suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) onward, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) becomes distinct and clear.
Next, regarding the three skillful means of the *sakṛdāgāmin* who proceeds toward the ultimate state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
the contemplation of non-self (*pudgala-nairātmya*) in the eighth gate applies to both stages.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the observation of the first seven matters belongs to the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
The latter consists of the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).
From the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) upward, one gradually studies and practices;
from the stage of "Signlessness" (*animitta*) onward, right view becomes clear and distinct.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, [the stages] truly encompass both the higher and lower levels; yet,
when differentiated according to their characteristics,
the first seven preparatory practices (prayoga) belong to the stage prior to the bhūmis.
The latter one, right contemplation, pertains to the stage beyond the world (*lokottara*).
Thus has the meaning of the eightfold contemplation been briefly explained. 165.
The Meaning of the Eight Great Persons' Awakenings (13). Regarding the meaning of the eight great persons' awakenings: the eight great persons' awakenings are as follows.
The Buddha is a Great Being.
All Buddhas, the Great Beings, have realized that this Dharma is the cause of Nirvana;
thus it is called "the realization of the Great Being."
The realizations differ.
Eight [aspects] are taught through a single gateway.
What are these eight names?
First, having few desires;
second, being content;
third, delighting in tranquility.
Fourth, diligent perseverance;
fifth, maintaining right mindfulness;
sixth, cultivating meditative concentration.
Seventh, cultivate wisdom.
Eighth, refrain from frivolous conceptual proliferation;
do not extensively pursue those dharmas of the five sensual desires that have not yet been attained.
This is called having few desires.
Having received what has been obtained within the Dharma, one accepts it with limits;
this is termed contentment.
To dwell alone in a secluded and quiet place, far removed from all bustle and clamor,
is called "delighting in tranquility.
To practice all wholesome dharmas with diligent and uninterrupted effort is called "vigor."
To observe the Dharma without failing is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
To abide in the Dharma without distraction is termed meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
To give rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation is explained as wisdom (*prajñā*).
Realizing freedom from conceptual discrimination is called "non-proliferation" (*aprapañca*).
Each of these points is explained in detail, as in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching). Among these eight [topics]:
The former seven are the preparatory practices,
while the latter one is the direct realization;
such is the brief summary of the eight awakenings of a great person.

166. The Meaning of the Mahāyāna Subsumed under Eight Dharmas (13). Regarding the "Meaning of the Mahāyāna Subsumed under Eight Dharmas": The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Treatise on the Stages of Holding) states that the Mahāyāna is subsumed under eight dharmas.
Mahāyāna is a foreign term; here it is called the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
The practice of the Great Vehicle is vast.
The eight factors encompass [all things];
because this collection is contained within them, it is called "inclusion" (saṃgraha).
What are these eight names?
First is called faith;
second is called hearing and reflection;
third is called the wisdom of contemplation.
Fourth is the purification of the mind;
fifth is the initial cultivation of the practice of wisdom;
sixth is the extensive cultivation of wisdom.
Seventh, the fruit of cultivated wisdom is accomplished;
eighth, ultimate transcendence.
These occur within the stage of practice through understanding for those of the bodhisattva lineage.
Because one achieves pure faith regarding the eight bases of liberation, it is called "faith.
What are the eight excellences?
They are the virtues of the Three Jewels.
The supernatural powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
the various causes and effects,
and the meaning of ultimate reality.
One attains the meaning and attains the skillful means;
the various causes and effects are the dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The meaning of reality is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The meaning of attainment is unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
"Attaining skillful means" refers to the path cultivated and studied by bodhisattvas;
in these eight points, bodhisattvas place their full faith.
Regarding "wisdom derived from hearing":
it refers to the initial aspiration for the path of deliverance within one who understands and practices,
and who fully hears the supramundane teachings.
Regarding what is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*): it is the culmination of understanding and practice, consisting of thorough deliberation upon the teachings one has heard.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
The Bodhisattva’s practice of understanding consists of reflecting upon the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from contemplation.
Regarding the "purified mind," it refers to the initial stage of the first bhūmi, where one perceives the principle of non-self and realizes the purity of the mind.
Therefore, it is called "purifying the mind.
For one who first practices through wisdom,
at the completion of the first stage (bhūmi), they give rise to ten great vows and practice faith and the other perfections.
This is precisely that which is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), being the beginning of the path of cultivation;
therefore, it is called "initial.
As for the breadth of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*):
From the second bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi, the path of cultivation gradually increases;
this is called the expansion of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). As for the fruition of cultivated wisdom being accomplished:
From the eighth stage upward, the retributive conduct becomes fully matured;
this is called the perfection of the fruit of cultivated wisdom.
This constitutes ultimate transcendence.
This refers to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgata is forever free from all obstacles, it is called "ultimate emergence.
This brief exposition on the Mahāyāna as subsumed within the eight categories is thus concluded.

167. The Definition of the Nine Successive Attainments (13): Regarding the definition of the nine successive attainments, they consist of the eight dhyānas and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

As Nāgārjuna stated: "These nine [attainments] refer exclusively to the essential body of the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) and do not extend to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*),
because during the time of the fundamental absorptions, they transition into one another."
The eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are explained in detail above.
Furthermore, this is also called the nine successive cessations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti).
Upon entering the first dhyāna, the mind of the desire realm is ceased.
Entering the second dhyāna, one extinguishes the mind of the first dhyāna;
continuing in this manner until entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one extinguishes the mind of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Such are the names of the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

168. The Meaning of the Nine Contemplations of Loathsomeness (13): An Analysis of the Characteristics of the Nine Contemplations of Loathsomeness through Eight Gates. I. The Essential Nature of Concentration. II. The Objects of Focus. III. Differences in the Remedy for Afflictions. IV. Distinguishing Similarities and Differences in Relation to the Ten Contemplations. V. Determining the Sequence of Concentrations in Relation to the Various Dhyānas. VI. Determining the Root and Branches of Concentration in Relation to the Factors of Enlightenment. VII. The Purpose for Cultivating and Arising [the Practice]. First: Analysis of the Characteristics.
What are the nine perceptions?
First, the practitioner of the perception of death does so with the desire to destroy the thief of sensual desire.
First, one contemplates the perception of death.
One observes that when a person dies, they speak their final words of farewell; the out-breath does not return, and suddenly they die.
One reflects: "I am subject to this very same fate; those I love are likewise so."
One uses this to revile the afflictions.
Second is the contemplation of bloating:
one sees the corpse bloated like a leather bag filled with wind, its appearance altered from its original form.
Reflecting that what is naturally dear to me is likewise so for others, one uses this to rebuke craving.
This is the third perception: the perception of a livid corpse.
Seeing that corpse, blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, its color turning bluish and mottled, its original form and appearance destroyed;
one reflects, "It is natural that what I love shall likewise become so.
This is the fourth perception: the perception of putrefaction.
Having seen that corpse turn bluish-black, it will soon thereafter become festering with pus, foul-smelling, putrid, and loathsome.
One reflects: "What is dear to me shall likewise become so.
This is the fifth, the perception of disintegration (*vibhava-saṃjñā*).
Contemplate that corpse, which grows increasingly large and disintegrated by the wind and sun as it lies upon the ground with pus and blood flowing forth.
Having reflected thus, one should realize that what is beloved is likewise so. This is the sixth visualization:
the visualization of being smeared with blood.
Having contemplated how the corpse, once decomposed, is smeared with blood and flesh,
one should likewise reflect that those who are beloved are also thus. One should cultivate the perception of being devoured by seven kinds of worms.
Contemplate that corpse— neither burned nor buried, cast away in the wilderness to be devoured by various insects and wild beasts—
and see that one's own body is likewise similar, and that what is loved is also thus.
8. The contemplation of the skeletal chain (*asthi-śaṅkalā*): When that flesh has completely vanished, one sees only the skeletal chains interconnected and supporting one another.
9. The contemplation of disintegration (*vibhāga*):
When the remaining tendons have been severed and the skeletal chains are separated, this is called the contemplation of disintegration.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the contemplation on death is supplemented by the contemplation on burning.
One observes that those remaining bones are consumed by fire until they finally become ashes;
one then reflects that this will surely be the same for oneself and for those one loves.
Question: Why does that treatise exclude death?
It is because at the very moment of initial death, the physical form has not yet changed.
Because they still grasp at pure characteristics,
this single gate has not yet been fully explained.
Next, the essential nature is distinguished.
The treatise says:
These nine are the intrinsic nature of perception (*saṃjñā*),
because they grasp signs (*nimitta*).
If judged by their ultimate accomplishment,
these are of the nature of non-greed,
as they serve as antidotes to craving; thus ends this section on the two gates.
Next, the objects of focus are distinguished:
these nine take as their objective domain only the impure forms within the level of the desire realm.
These three gates conclude the section on destroying the mind of craving for the desire realm.
Next, the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā) are explained to treat afflictions differently;
these nine perceptions are able to cure the disease of craving.
There are two kinds of greed:
first, attachment to one's own body.
As an antidote for the five kinds of impurity, [one should practice as follows].
As was extensively analyzed in the previous chapter on the five perfections:
second, regarding attachment to another's body,
nine perceptions serve as the remedy.
Regarding the bodies of others, the sūtras and śāstras differ.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it is said that there are four types of desire.
First is the desire for deportment (*īryāpatha*),
which is the craving for matters such as one's advancing, halting, and speech.
Second is the desire for physical form (*rūpa*).
One loves such things as blue, yellow, red, and white;
these are the desires of the three locations,
which may be attached to the eyes or the ears.
Some crave the nose and mouth;
some covet the waist and body;
such as these, all are alike.
Fourth are the desires for subtle touch,
which consist of craving for sensations such as smoothness, softness, and pliancy.
These four kinds of desire are individually countered by the nine perceptions.
First, the desire for deportment is treated by the perception of death;
the desire for form and color is treated by the perception of [the corpse] becoming livid, festering, and smeared with blood;
the desire for location is treated by the perception of [the corpse] bloating, decaying, being devoured by worms, and dispersing.
For those with a desire for fine tactile sensations, the "chain of bones" (asthisamkalā) serves as the remedy;
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
there are seven types of such defilement.
First, they are attached to their dignified demeanor and cherish their every movement.
Second, they are attached to their speech.
They delight in their voices, speech, and playful laughter;
these two are like the aforementioned desire for deportment.
Third is attachment to form and color.
This is like the desire for shape and form among the four previously mentioned;
it is attachment to physical appearance and love for one's own body.
This is like the desire for the four types of objects among the aforementioned four bases;
the fifth is attachment to tactile sensations such as smoothness and softness,
which is like the desire for subtle touch among the aforementioned four.
The six [types of] attachment pertain to the first five [objects]. The seventh pertains to the mark of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*),
namely, men’s desire for women and women’s desire for men, and so forth.
Among the seven [meditations], the first two serve as remedies for the sign of death.
For those attached to physical form and color, the bloated, the festering, and the blood-smeared serve as remedies.
For those attached to the physical figure, the swollen, the disintegrating, and the worm-infested and scattered serve as remedies.
For those attached to subtle tactile sensations, the visualization of the skeleton and the visualization of burning serve as their remedies.
The latter two types [of visualizations] are common remedies for all nine [aspects].
These nine destroy greed.
The various fetters, such as hatred and the rest, all likewise become attenuated. This concludes the four gates.
Next, the similarities and differences are distinguished in relation to the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*).
The ten perceptions are fully and extensively analyzed in the subsequent chapter on the ten perceptions.
The nine perceptions are compared with those [other meditations];
there are similarities and differences.
As for what is said to be different:
As Nāgārjuna said:
"The nine perceptions are for beginners;
the ten perceptions are for those at the end."
The initial practice serves as the cause,
and its ultimate fulfillment constitutes the fruit.
Furthermore, the nine contemplations (navasaṃjñā) restrain the lustful mind of those who have not yet attained meditative concentration.
The ten perceptions can extinguish [defilements],
while the nine perceptions can obstruct them like a bound thief;
the ten perceptions can extinguish them like a slain thief.
What is meant by "the same" is that both equally take the cultivation of the abandonment of desire as the cause for nirvana; however,
regarding the mutual inclusion within this, their explanations differ.
Some commentators explain that among those ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) fully subsumes the other nine perceptions.
Others, moreover, say:
Among the ten [meditations], the perception of impurity in food and the perception of the world as unsatisfactory encompass all nine perceptions.
Furthermore, some say:
Those nine contemplations of perception comprehensively encompass the ten perceptions.
Contemplating the signs of death and their gradual transformation is the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*).
If one becomes attached to these phenomena...
When impermanence brings about destruction, suffering and affliction arise;
this is the perception of suffering.
Because it is impermanent and suffering, one lacks mastery over it.
This is the notion of non-self.
One contemplates that notion of death;
through the nine notions, one observes that the body possesses not a single mark of purity.
Because it is impure,
although the food remains in the mouth,
brain-fluid and saliva flow down and combine with it to form flavor.
Once it has been swallowed and enters the abdomen, it immediately becomes impure;
there is nothing in it to crave or cling to.
This is the contemplation of revulsion toward food.
By means of these nine perceptions, one becomes weary of and detached from the world;
this is precisely the perception of the world as unattractive.
Contemplating the body through the nine perceptions as impermanent and subject to decay is the perception of death.
Knowing that these nine perceptions can sever the afflictions is called the perception of severance;
one employs these nine perceptions to obstruct all afflictions.
This is called the abandonment of perception.
By means of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), one prevents the aggregates (*skandha*) from arising;
this is precisely the exhaustion of perception.
It is also called the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*). Such are the similarities and differences; this concludes the five gates.
Next, the sequence of these [attainments] is distinguished in relation to the various dhyānas.
As stated in the treatise:
the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are the preparatory means for the various dhyānas;
one first cultivates the nine perceptions to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thereafter, one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
A question is asked:
"In the sūtras, meditation is often taught first and the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) afterwards."
Now, why is it said that the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are the skillful means for entering dhyāna? Nāgārjuna explains:
First, one praises the various dhyānas so that people may come to love and delight in them;
the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) one delights in is accomplished by means of the nine perceptions.
Therefore, having first completed these six gates,
we shall next distinguish their roots and branches in relation to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa),
as Nāgārjuna has explained.
The contemplation of the nine perceptions opens the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
the foundation of mindfulness of the body guides the three subsequent foundations of mindfulness;
and through the four foundations of mindfulness, the remaining factors of the path are opened.
By means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one opens the gate to nirvāṇa; this concludes the seven gates.
Next, the purpose for which they are practiced will be clarified, as explained in the treatise.
Those of the Hīnayāna cultivate the nine notions for the sake of entering nirvāṇa;
Bodhisattvas cultivate the nine notions out of compassion for all sentient beings, in order to gather the various Buddha-dharmas and deliver them.
The meaning of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) has been explained in its broad outlines.

169. The Meaning of the Nine Knowledges of Abandonment (*nava-prahāṇajñāna*). (13) The Meaning of the Nine Knowledges of Abandonment: An Exposition through Five Gates. I. Explaining the Names and Defining the Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) II. Analysis according to the Path (*mārga*) III. Analysis according to the Bases (*sthāna*) IV. Attainment, Relinquishment, and Accomplishment V. The Reason for their Establishment First: Explaining the Names and Defining the Characteristics.
The meaning of the nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) is as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
the point at which afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted is called "abandonment.
Abandonment is the fruit of knowledge.
Because the fruit retains the name of its cause,
it is termed "knowledge of abandonment.
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* says:
Although wisdom is itself wisdom,
since abandonment is the fruit of wisdom,
it is called "the wisdom of abandonment."
It is like how the fruit of karma is also called "karma.
[The questioner] asks:
How is that abandonment the fruit of knowledge?
The term "liberation" (vimukti) has two meanings.
First, looking at it from the perspective of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), it severs hindrances by means of wisdom;
because one attains that severance, it is called the fruit of wisdom.
If that is so, since the state in which the afflictions of those who have seen the truths are exhausted is attained through the abandonments by means of patience (*kṣānti*),
it should be called "abandonment by patience.
For what reason is it also called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*)?
The commentary states:
"Patience (kṣānti) is an attendant of wisdom;
it is collectively designated as 'wisdom'."
Because they are collectively termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*),
the fruits of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) are also called "abandonment-knowledge.
These two are considered in relation to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
It is called the "fruit of wisdom" because it is realized through wisdom.
Question: That wisdom realizes [the object] by taking it as its objective condition (ālambana).
"Is it not the case that they do not take [them] as objects?
He replied, "They do not take them as objects."
Just as when the knowledge of the origin of phenomena (samudaya-dharma-jñāna) arises, it takes the origin of the desire realm as its object;
it does not take their abandonment as its object, yet it is able to realize it.
Therefore, wisdom does not take them as its object.
This applies to all such cases;
the same holds true for names and meanings.
What are their essential characteristics?
There are nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).

Within the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one knowledge of abandonment is established at the point where the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and origin (*samudayasatya*) are exhausted.
At the point where the afflictions under the truths of cessation and the path are exhausted, one is established for each;
together with the preceding, these are said to be three.
The same applies to the higher realms.
Including the previous [three], there are six.
Since the points where the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are exhausted in each of the three realms are distinct, they each constitute one;
including the previous [six], there are nine.
Question: For what reason do the points at which the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted in the two upper realms not follow the distinctions between the realms,
whereas the points at which the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are exhausted are divided according to each realm?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
Because the antidotes for the afflictions of the higher realms are the same, they do not vary according to the distinction of the realms.
Because they are distinguished by their respective cultivation and refinement, they are categorized according to their realms.
What is the meaning of this?
The delusions of view are easily eliminated.
When the mind of the "patience regarding the knowledge of suffering" (duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) manifests for a single moment,
the afflictions that delude one regarding suffering within the two upper realms are severed all at once and instantaneously.
The same applies to the remaining patiences;
therefore, they are said to have the same objective support. The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are difficult to eliminate.
Because each realm is abandoned separately,
they are called "distinct remedies" (*pratipakṣa*).
In the second section, the analysis is made in terms of the path (*mārga*).
It possesses four meanings:
first, the distinction between the two paths of seeing and cultivation;
second, the reliance on direct perception and inference.
Third, [the classification] is based on patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Fourth, it is distinguished according to whether it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As for the terms "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*):
Regarding the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*):
the first six are the knowledges that abandon through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
because they obtain the abandonment of hindrances through the non-obstructive path of seeing.
The latter three are the knowledges that abandon through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because they attain the unimpeded abandonment of hindrances in contrast to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The first five are the knowledges that abandon through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because they realize liberation within the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*).
The subsequent three are the knowledges that abandon through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because liberation is realized within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
the latter one is the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Because liberation is realized within the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*), this concludes the section on the single gate.
Next, they are distinguished according to the two gates of Dharma and Subsequent Knowledge (*dharmanvaya*).

The first three abandonments and knowledges are exclusively the fruits of Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), in relation to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*).
This is the fruit of the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*); in relation to the path of liberation, this is the fruit of the knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
The next three [moments] are the fruits of subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
In relation to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are the fruits of subsequent patience.
The path of liberation is the fruit of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
the next one is exclusively the fruit of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
Because the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation are severed by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
the two subsequent knowledges of abandonment are either the fruit of the knowledge of phenomena or the fruit of inferential knowledge (anvayajñāna).
If one eliminates the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms by means of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path regarding the desire realm,

this is the fruit of that dharma-knowledge; if one eliminates the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms by means of the four subsequent knowledges, [this is the fruit of those subsequent knowledges].
This is the fruit of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
this constitutes the complete discussion.
As for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), it has six fruits of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
There are three [knowledges] for the path of seeing and three for the path of cultivation. Inferential knowledge has five fruits of abandonment;
there are three for the path of seeing and two for the path of cultivation. These two sections are concluded.
Next, they are distinguished by way of the two gates of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
In relation to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), the first six patiences are the fruition-patience (*phala-kṣānti*) and constitute the path of non-obstruction.
Because they are attained through the severing of hindrances,
the latter three are the wisdom of the fruit; because they are attained through the severing of hindrances, they constitute unimpededness.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The three types of abandonment are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*);
the others are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*)."
The path to liberation is likewise the fruit of wisdom;
since both are equally realized and known by wisdom, these three gates are concluded.
Next, regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*):
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is contaminated, while analytical insight (*yoniśomanasikāra*) is uncontaminated.
The untainted [knowledges] possess nine fruits of abandonment,
because they are able to sever all fetters;
the tainted [knowledges] possess only two fruits of abandonment.

This means that because the Noble Ones (ārya) sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) pertaining to the desire realm and the form realm by means of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna),
the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The fruits of the conventional path are two."
There are nine fruits of noble wisdom.
Such is the classification according to the path.
Within the third section, they are distinguished according to their locations.
Within this, there are four [categories]:
first, the realm of the three worlds;
second, the stages of dhyāna.
The locus of the three paths;
the locus of the four aggregates of clinging;
and the locus of the three realms.
In the desire realm there are four:
three are abandoned by insight and one is abandoned by cultivation.
In the higher realms there are five.
The three [knowledges] are abandoned through vision and the two through cultivation; this concludes the first section.
Next, distinguishing them according to the dhyāna stages:
the abandonment-knowledges rely on the preliminary stage (anāgamya-dhyāna) and possess all nine abandonment-knowledges.
Because it is able to sever all fetters in the future.
Regarding the four fundamental dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna, there are differing opinions among scholars;
according to the explanation of Ghoṣaka:
He possesses the eight knowledges of abandonment;
with the exception of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters within the desire realm,
he is fully endowed with all the rest.
This is because the afflictions of the path of cultivation within the desire realm are abandoned by the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya),
and not by the four fundamental dhyānas or the intermediate dhyāna;
this is explained according to the preeminence of the supporting basis.
It possesses five types of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*);
namely, three belonging to the vision of the two higher realms and two belonging to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of those same realms.
Thus it is said.
The exhaustion of all fetters of the desire realm depends solely on the future [dhyāna],
and not on the four dhyānas or the intermediate state;
therefore, these are not discussed.
Regarding this explanation:
for those who enter the noble path by relying on the four fundamental dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna,
they sever only the afflictions of the higher realms pertaining to both seeing and cultivation.
Without severing the fetter of desire,
one first removes the fetter of desire by relying on the path of skillful means pertaining to the sphere of infinite space.
One attains the single type of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) at the stage where the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) cultivated through meditation are completely exhausted;
for it is by means of this that one can sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the fourth dhyāna.
This relies upon the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), specifically the lower three spheres of emptiness.
One attains one type of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) at the point where the afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) are exhausted.
This is because that untainted [knowledge] (*anāsrava*) is capable of severing the delusions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the formless realm.
Since there is no untainted [knowledge] whatsoever in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), these two gates are concluded.
Next, the stages and positions are distinguished:
from the stage of the ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*) up until the five moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
there has been no fruit of the knowledge of abandonment at all.
When one attains the patience of subsequent knowledge regarding origination (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*), one possesses one knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
When one reaches the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), one possesses two knowledges of abandonment.
When one reaches the patience regarding subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*), one possesses three knowledges of abandonment.
Up to and including the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) within the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one possesses four knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Up to and including the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) within the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), one possesses five knowledges of abandonment.
At the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), one possesses six knowledges of abandonment.
The meaning of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* is not fixed.
If a person who has transcended [the lower stages] enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as a candidate for *sakṛdāgāmin*,
they are similar to a candidate for *srotāpanna*.
If a person following the gradual path is heading toward the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, they possess six knowledges of abandonment;
this is similar to the fruit of Srotāpanna, for the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin likewise possesses six abandonments.
The same applies to the fruit of srotāpanna.
The meaning of anāgāmin is also not fixed;
if a person who has transcended enters the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), [they may attain it].
The candidate for the stage of non-returner (anāgāmipratipannaka) is similar to the candidate for the stage of stream-enterer (srotāpattipratipannaka).
If one is a person following the gradual path (ānupūrvika), the candidate for the stage of non-returner is similar to the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala).
The fruit of anāgāmin constitutes one knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna),
namely, the knowledge of abandonment regarding the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana). Question:
An Anāgāmin has severed only two types of lower fetters— sensual desire and ill will— whereas the remaining three lower fetters,
namely the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt, have already been abandoned previously.
Now, why is it said that there is the "knowledge of abandonment" regarding the exhaustion of the five lower fetters?

The explanation is as follows: although self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth have already been abandoned previously, [they are not yet considered exhausted until their latent tendencies are eliminated].
Because they are gathered here, they are combined into a single abandonment.
Among those who are candidates for arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*), those who have not yet exhausted their craving for the form realm (*rūpārāga*) achieve only one [abandonment],
which is the same as that of the *anāgāmin*.
One who has exhausted craving for the realm of form achieves two;
within the fruit of arhatship, one achieves only one,
namely, the exhaustion of all fetters throughout the three realms.
One should accomplish nine;
however, because they are gathered and abandoned in this single location, it is simply called "one. These three sections are concluded.
Next, the locations of their gathering are explained.
Abandoning the previous [attainments] and obtaining them collectively as one is called the "knowledge of the collected abandonment" (*saṃkalanaprahāṇajñāna*).
There are two types of places where this is collected.
That is to say, the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala). Question:
For what reason are these not collected in other places?
Only in these two places does the treatise state that the knowledge of abandonment is accumulated upon attaining the fruit and crossing over the realm.
The Anāgāmin and Arhat are the ones who attain the fruits and transcend the realms;
therefore, they gather the knowledge of abandonment.
Why is it that these two attain the fruits and transcend the realms?
In that state, the Anāgāmin has exhausted the five lower fetters (saṃyojana),
while the Arhat has exhausted the five higher fetters; therefore,
in these two stages, they attain the fruit and transcend the realms.
The five higher and lower fetters (*ūrdhvādhara-saṃyojana*) have been extensively analyzed within the preceding discussion of afflictions.
The stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is the attainment of the fruit, but not the crossing of the realm;
the stage where craving for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) is exhausted is the crossing of the realm, but not the attainment of the fruit.
The others neither attain the fruit nor transcend the realm;
thus they do not accumulate [karma].
Such is the distinction of their locations.
The fourth section clarifies their acquisition, relinquishment, and accomplishment.
First, it clarifies their acquisition, which refers to that which previously did not exist but is now established; this is termed "acquisition."
The attainments are not fixed; some obtain one,
some two, or some six.
Regarding the statement "attaining one," there are nine instances;
these occur within the sixteen moments of mind that contemplate the Truths (*satya*).
The sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, fourteenth, and sixteenth moments of mind each attain one abandonment upon their respective arising;
these constitute the six locations.
When the mind of the fruit of anāgāmin (once-returner) arises in succession,
one attains one knowledge of abandonment;
together with the previous seven stages, [there are eight].
For an Arhat who has exhausted attachment to the form realm, one knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) is attained;
including the previous eight stages, this constitutes nine.
For an Arhat who has attained the fruit, one knowledge of abandonment is attained.
Including the previous nine locations,
the statement "attaining two" refers to an Arhat who falls back from the fetters of the formless realm.
One attains two kinds of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*): the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
Regarding the statement "one attains six":
this refers to when a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or Arhat falls away and gives rise to afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the desire realm.
Having attained the six kinds of knowledge of abandonment within the realization of the Truths (satyābhisamaya), this first section is concluded.
Next, the relinquishing of what was previously established and now lost is explained;
this is termed "relinquishment" (prahāṇa).
Regarding the intermediate state of relinquishment, it is indeterminate:
one may relinquish one, or two, or five.
Alternatively, one may abandon six.
Regarding the statement "abandoning one," there are three instances in which this occurs.
First, one who has regressed from the fruit of arhatship abandons one knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
Second, an anāgāmin who has exhausted desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) regresses and gives rise to those fetters (*saṃyojana*).
One abandons one knowledge of abandonment.
When an Anāgāmin who has not yet exhausted craving for the three realms falls away and gives rise to the fetter of desire,
they abandon one knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the statement "abandoning two," there are two instances:
first, at the time of attaining arhatship; [the second is at the time of entering the path of seeing].
There are two kinds of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*): the exhaustion of the five lower fetters and the exhaustion of attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*).
When an Anāgāmin who has exhausted attachment to the form realm falls away and gives rise to the fetters of the desire realm, he abandons these two knowledges of abandonment.
Regarding the statement "abandoning five":
at the time of attaining the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) by means of transcendence,
one suddenly abandons the five types of knowledge of abandonment belonging to the stage of the candidate (pratipannaka).
Regarding the statement "abandoning six":
this refers to the sequential abandonment of the six types of knowledge of abandonment previously attained at the time of realizing the fruit of anāgāmin; these two sections are now concluded.
Next, the explanation of accomplishment:
that which is attained and not lost is called accomplishment.
The number is indefinite;
some may achieve one, or two, or three, or four, or five.
Alternatively, it may be established as six.
Regarding what is said to be "established as one," there are three locations.
First, at the time of the knowledge of the dharma of the first dhyāna;
second, at the time of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala);
third, at the time of the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
All achieve one. As for the statement that they achieve two,
there are two instances.
First, at the time of the knowledge of inference (anvaya-jñāna);
second, when one is a candidate for arhatship through the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (rūpa-rāga-kṣaya)—both of these possess two.
As for the statement that they possess three: [it refers to]...

Regarding the statement that "four are established" at the time of the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), this refers to the time of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñāna*).
Regarding the statement that five are established:
at the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path, six are established;
at the time of the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
The fifth clarifies the reason for its establishment.
As stated in the treatise,
the knowledge that abandons [defilements] through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is established based on four causes and conditions.
First, the two causes are extinguished;
second, one becomes detached from both fetters;
third, one attains the acquisition of untainted liberation.
The fourth [category] lacks the first existence (bhavāgra).
As for the cessation of the dual causes:
these are the views, doubt, and ignorance pertaining to the truths of suffering and its origin.
As they look toward one another, each serves as a pervasive cause for the other;
thus they are called "mutual causes.
Both causes are simultaneously severed.
This is called the cessation of the dual causes.
Regarding the "separation from all fetters":
it refers to the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) underlying the truths of suffering and its origin.
Being mutually bound by conditions is called "simultaneous fettering. When both sides sever [the bonds] equally, it is called simultaneous liberation.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the untainted liberation": it means that when the path of liberation arises,
one realizes and attains the untainted state.
This is called attaining untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).
Regarding "deficient in the summit of existence" (*bhavāgra-vaikalya*):

the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that have been severed, extending upward through to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), are termed "deficient in the summit of existence."
At the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti), all four meanings are absent;

therefore, the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-jñāna) is not established. This is also the case at the stages of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the patience regarding the subsequent [knowledge] of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti).
Although one may attain the attainment of untainted liberation,
it is not established [as such] because other conditions are incomplete.
Because the underlying afflictions have not yet been eliminated,
both causes have not been extinguished and both fetters have not been abandoned.
In the two upper realms, delusions regarding suffering still persist;
therefore, they are not yet said to have "deficient" [attachment to] the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Question:
When the patience of subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) severs the afflictions deluded about suffering in the two upper realms,
why is it not called "breaking through the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*)?
The explanation states:
At the time when the afflictions to be abandoned are severed, one still possesses patience;
therefore, it is not yet called "deficient.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-patience regarding origin (*samudaye dharma-kṣānti*), although one attains untainted liberation and the attainment of deficiency regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because the two causes have not yet been extinguished and the simultaneous fetters have not yet been abandoned,
it likewise does not receive the name of "knowledge of abandonment."

When the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) is attained, it is only when four conditions are fulfilled that it is designated as "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*). What are these fulfilled conditions?
First, the afflictions deluded by suffering have already been eliminated.
Delusion and accumulation are now exhausted;
thus, the two causes are extinguished and both fetters are abandoned.

At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), and the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), one has already realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this is called attaining the acquisition of untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti-prāpti*).
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, one eliminates the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therefore, it is called "complete.
The subsequent knowledge regarding cessation and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path are likewise established as the knowledge of abandonment through these four causal conditions. Question:
Why is it that the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) is not mentioned at the conclusion of all patiences?
Because one has not yet attained the untainted liberation (*anāsravavimukti*).
The knowledge of abandonment for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is established based on five causes and conditions.
This means that in addition to the previous four, one further realm of permanent abandonment is added.

Within that desire realm, the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are bound to one another in succession, continuing up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the case for every stage.
In that desire realm, from the abandonment of one grade up to eight grades,
although one attains untainted liberation and has previously vacated the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
other requirements remain incomplete.
Therefore, one does not establish the simultaneous abandonment and knowledge [of the defilements],
because the ninth grade of subtle defilement still exists and the dual causes have not yet been extinguished.
When one is bound by both [fetters], has not yet abandoned them, and the realm has not been permanently severed,
it is only at the time when the nine grades [of defilements] are abandoned that the five meanings are fully present.
Thereupon, the knowledge of abandonment is established.
Within the stage of the first dhyāna, from the abandonment of one grade up to the eighth grade,
it likewise possesses two conditions.
That is to say, one who has attained the untainted liberation and the attainment of the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) possesses [the remaining] three; since these are not complete,
the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) is not established.
When the nine grades [of afflictions] are being abandoned, four causal conditions are present;
because the realm has not yet been permanently severed, it is not yet designated [as "abandoned"].
The principles for the second and third dhyānas are likewise the same.
Within the fourth dhyāna, the abandonment of the first eight grades is similar to what preceded;
however, at the time of abandoning the ninth grade, five conditions are fully perfected.
The establishment of the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) within the four stages of the dry-wisdom (*śuṣkavasthā*) can be understood by analogy with what precedes,
because the knowledge of abandonment is established within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) due to the presence of five causal conditions.
Although an ordinary person may sever all afflictions through conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
they do not attain untainted liberation (anāsrava-vimukti),
nor have they yet fully transcended the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Therefore, it is not the knowledge of abandonment.
If, while still an ordinary person,
one had previously abandoned the afflictions.
Subsequently, upon entering the noble path and being certified by untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna),
it is termed the "knowledge of abandonment" (prahāṇa-jñāna).
What is meant by "attestation"?
It refers to one who, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), has abandoned six grades of afflictions within the desire realm and subsequently enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
When the path-comparative knowledge arises,
the previously unconditioned seal immediately constitutes the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* liberation. This is the case if one was at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions within the desire realm,
one subsequently enters the path of seeing;
at the stage of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one confirms the previously attained unconditioned state.
It is called "seal of certification" because it pertains to the fruit of liberation for an Anāgāmin.

It is not a seal of certification at the point where the remaining grades of afflictions in the desire realm are exhausted, nor at the point where the afflictions of the two higher realms are exhausted.
Because it is not a place of rest where one has attained the fruit.
Question: At the time of sealing, what serves as the condition?
But is the seal not to be without an object?
The commentary says:
it is not without an object.
The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the path of cultivation takes the paths of the higher realms as its object,
yet it realizes the exhaustion of the afflictions of the desire realm; therefore,
it does not take [the desire realm] as its object.
The general outline of the meaning of the nine knowledges of abandonment (*navaprahāṇajñāna*) is thus roughly concluded.
This concludes the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dacheng yizhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna). [Fascicle Fourteen of the *Dacheng yizhang* begins.]

In this fascicle of the *Jingfa ju yinfa* (Collection of Pure Dharmas and Causes of Dharmas) compiled by Dharma Master Yuan, there are twenty-one sections: the meaning of the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*); the meaning of the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*);

the meaning of the ten noble abodes (*daśāryavihāra*); the meaning of the ten kinds of consolation; the meaning of the ten vows (*daśapraṇidhāna*); the meaning of the ten kinds of offerings; the meaning of the ten inexhaustible treasuries (*daśākṣayakośa*); the meaning of the ten practices beginning with faith (*daśaśraddhādipratipatti*); the meaning of the ten clarities (*daśavaiśāradya*); the meaning of the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*); the meaning of the ten patiences of non-arising (*daśānutpattikadharmakṣānti*); the meaning of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*); the meaning of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*); the meaning of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmana*); the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); the meaning of the ten merits (*daśaguṇa*); the meaning of the ten dharmas for realizing the nature; the meaning of the ten causes of nirvāṇa; the meaning of the ten powers of a bodhisattva (*daśabodhisattvabalāni*); the meaning of the ten fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva (*daśabodhisattvavaiśāradyāni*); and the meaning of the ten stages common to the three vehicles (*triyānasādhāraṇadaśabhūmi*).

170. The Meaning of the Ten Perceptions (14): An Exposition by Way of Five Gates on the Meaning of the Ten Perceptions. I. Definition of Terms and Analysis of Characteristics; II. Essential Nature; III. Analysis by Way of Location; IV. Analysis by Way of Person; V. Analysis by Way of Feeling. First: Definition of Terms and Analysis of Characteristics.
When observing the mind regarding phenomena, one grasps their characteristics through names and concepts (*saṃjñā*).
These conceptualizations differ from one another; they are explained in a single section as ten.
What are these ten names?
First, the perception of impermanence;
second, the perception of suffering;
third, the perception of non-self.
4. The perception of the repulsiveness of food;
5. The perception of the lack of delight in all worldly realms;
6. The perception of death.
7. The perception of impurity;
8. The perception of abandonment;
9. The perception of detachment.
The tenth is the perception of cessation,
also called the perception of exhaustion.
As for the perception of impermanence:
Observing that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subject to flux and lack permanence,
they are called "impermanent" (*anitya*).
There are three types of impermanence.
First is the impermanence of temporal segmentation;
the retributions of the six realms differ according to the divisions of the three periods of time.
Within this, there are two types.
First, there is death with remainder, wherein the body perishes but the name remains;
second, there is death without remainder, wherein both body and name cease.
These are the two aspects of momentary impermanence.
Conditioned phenomena undergo transformation through the four characteristics in every moment.
Third, their intrinsic nature is not established as real; they are impermanent.
Conditioned dharmas are a hollow gathering of causes and conditions.
There is no fixed nature;
arising is non-arising,
and ceasing is non-ceasing.
As Nāgārjuna said:
"To perceive the body as utterly extinguished is the foremost form of impermanence regarding the limited [existence]."
Arising and ceasing moment by moment—
this is the impermanence of mindfulness.
At the time of arising, there is no coming.
At the time of cessation there is no going;
this is its intrinsic nature, which is unestablished and impermanent.
By means of these three contemplations, one can extinguish the afflictions.
Question: Some people,
by seeing impermanence, further increase their afflictions,
fearing that their prime of life will not last long.
One gives rise to deep attachment.
How can it now be said that the perception of impermanence can extinguish afflictions?
Nāgārjuna explains:
One who sees in this way is said to have a partial vision and is not called one who possesses complete vision.
One who possesses complete vision destroys the afflictions.
What is meant by "being fully endowed"?
It is as the Buddha formerly told Śāriputra:
"One should cultivate the perception of impermanence thoroughly."
Because it is impermanent, it is empty;
at the time one attains emptiness, impermanence itself is also non-existent,
for such things as arising, abiding, and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
When arising, abiding, and ceasing are seen to be unattainable, this is called the ultimate impermanence of intrinsic nature.
Since nature itself is impermanent,
what pleasure could there be to crave?
Question: If it is said that when emptiness is attained, impermanence also does not exist,
why did the Buddha teach the meaning of impermanence as the reality of the Truth of Suffering?
The treatise states:
Because the Buddha addresses those with false views who claim that the world is eternal,
he teaches that impermanence is the reality of the Truth of Suffering.
It is not said that impermanence is the reality; rather,
regarding the perception of suffering, one contemplates that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are suffering because they are impermanent.

Suffering is of three kinds: namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed as previously set forth in the chapter on the Four Noble Truths.
Question: If it is said that all phenomena are suffering,
how can there be the distinctions between the three feelings of pain, pleasure, and equanimity?
As stated in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, ordinary beings falsely conceive the notion of pleasure amidst suffering;
in reality, it is indeed suffering. Question:
If phenomena are suffering because they are impermanent,
is the Noble Path, being impermanent in its essence,
also suffering? Nāgārjuna explains:
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering;
this is said with reference to the five aggregates of clinging that are subject to outflows,
not to the Noble Path.
The reason for this is that the Path is able to destroy suffering and accords with the true meaning of emptiness and non-self; therefore,
although it is impermanent, it is not suffering.
Question: The five aggregates of a noble one (ārya) are impermanent.
When the five aggregates disintegrate, does the noble one suffer?
Nāgārjuna explains:
For those with a mind of attachment, the destruction of phenomena leads to suffering;
because the Noble Ones are free from attachment, although things are impermanent, they do not give rise to suffering.
Question: If it is said that the noble ones have no suffering,
how is it that the Sūtras speak of Śāriputra’s affliction by the suffering of wind-disease?
Piliṅgavatsa suffered from the affliction of eye disease,
and the bhikṣu Rāvaṇa suffered from the affliction of hemorrhoids;
how can you say that there are none?
The treatise states:
"The noble one merely lacks mental suffering;
it is not that they lack physical suffering."
Question: If the noble ones have no mental suffering, for what reason do they attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of cessation?
Explanation:
Those who are "without [the notion of self]" merely lack the suffering of pursuit, change, and decay;
it is not that they lack the suffering of suffering or the suffering of conditioned formations.
As for those who do not have the notion of a self:
Because conditioned phenomena are impermanent and suffering, they lack autonomy;
therefore, there is no self.
Furthermore, all phenomena lack an inherent nature.
Therefore, there is no self.
There are two kinds of non-self:
first, the non-self of sentient beings.
Second is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed as previously set forth in the chapter on selflessness. Question:
Since we clearly perceive that there is purposeful activity,
how can it be said that there is no self?
The treatise states:
However, it arises through the causal conditions of the combination of the five aggregates;
in reality, there is no self. Question:
Are impermanence, suffering, and non-self one or different?
If their essence were one, it would be improper to speak of three.
If their essence were different, the Buddha should not have said that impermanence is itself suffering and suffering is itself non-self.
The treatise states:
"The entity is one, yet it is divided into three according to its meaning;
it is divided into five according to its five meanings."
First, the section on contemplation has three parts.
Regarding the practice of impermanence:
that which is observed is described as impermanent.
Those who practice the contemplation of suffering speak of it as "suffering";
those who practice the contemplation of non-self name it "non-self.
These two are divided into three parts.
One cultivates the perception of impermanence so as not to enter the triple world;
one cultivates the perception of suffering so as to know the faults of the triple world;
one cultivates the perception of non-self so as to relinquish the triple world.
Third, regarding the treatment of views, three are taught.
Cultivating the perception of impermanence serves as the antidote to the view of permanence;
cultivating the perception of suffering serves as the antidote to the view of pleasure.
Cultivating the perception of non-self serves as the antidote to the view of self.
The three [perceptions] are taught to eliminate obstacles;
cultivating the perception of impermanence severs the mind of attachment.
Cultivating the perception of suffering eliminates arrogance;
cultivating the perception of non-self eliminates all views.
The five fundamental factors are divided into three.
The Treatise states:
"The five aggregates are impermanent;
that which is impermanent is suffering."
Suffering is non-self.
For these various reasons, it is divided into three kinds.
As for the perception of revulsion toward food:
One contemplates that the food one consumes arises mostly from impure causes and conditions;
for instance, meat arises from semen and blood,
while dairy products such as milk and curd arise from blood.
The remaining food is mostly defiled by insects, rats,
and filth; various impurities enter his mouth,
where saliva flows down from the chest and mingles with it.
Once it enters the stomach, it becomes excrement;
there is nothing therein to be craved or delighted in.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that what is eaten is obtained through great effort.
Because one undergoes various sufferings for the sake of seeking this food,
one should cultivate weary detachment.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the faults and transgressions of craving for food.
Born in the hells, they swallow iron and drink molten copper;
born among the hungry ghosts, they undergo the suffering of hunger and thirst;
born among the animals, they consume various kinds of filth and excrement.
In this way, all these immeasurable sufferings arise for the most part from food;
therefore, one should cultivate revulsion toward it.
Nothing in the entire world is worth delighting in.
One contemplates that all worlds are impermanent and suffering,
and there is nothing therein to be craved or delighted in.
Within these worlds, there are two kinds.
First, the world of sentient beings;
second, the receptacle world.
The world of sentient beings consists of five types of phenomena.
One should not crave pleasure.
First, because it is endowed with the eight kinds of suffering, it is not to be enjoyed.
Second, because it is endowed with immeasurable afflictions and fetters, it is not to be enjoyed.
Third, because they are possessed of all manner of evil karma, they are not to be desired.
Fourth, because it is difficult to possess auspicious matters, they are not to be desired;
for there may be those who practice virtue yet suffer physical affliction and distress.
Some have physical well-being yet their conduct is improper;
some are fond of giving yet are poor;
others are wealthy yet are stingy.
Some may be gentle yet greedy;
others may have few desires yet be prone to much anger.
In all such cases, it is difficult for these qualities to be fully present together.
It is not to be delighted in because it is difficult to find satisfaction in five ways:
either one sees what is base and deems it sycophantic,
or one sees what is upright and deems it arrogant.
Or seeing those who are close and attached, one deems them greedy;
or seeing those who are distant, one deems them hateful.
In this way, there are these five matters in the world of sentient beings that should not be craved or delighted in.
Within the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) as well, there are many kinds of things that should not be craved or delighted in:
whether it be heat or cold, water or drought, calamity or treachery, ruggedness or the increase of unwholesome states, or manifold terrors.
Because all things are thus, they are not to be delighted in.
It is asked:
