In the second dhyāna stage, the skillful means (*upāya*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), as well as their future counterparts, the intermediate state, and untainted (*anāsrava*) merits, are collectively able to counteract and sever [defilements]; this is termed "common counteraction" (*samapratipakṣa*).
Among those untainted [knowledges], there are the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, the four subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna), and the superior knowledges (viśeṣa-jñāna).

Within these seven types, whichever single one arises toward [the goal] is called "cultivation through shared antidotes" (sabhāga-pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) for severing the fetters of the first dhyāna; the others are all likewise designated as such.
Question: When one becomes free from the fetters of desire, the future, intermediate, and untainted merits of the first dhyāna should have been attained beforehand;
why then is it said here that they are only attained once the fetters of the first dhyāna are severed?
The commentary states:
Although all untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the lower stages can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
at the time one severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the lower stage, none of these [higher-stage paths] have yet been attained.
It is only when one severs the higher fetters that this is first attained;
therefore, this statement was made.
Since this is the case for both the desire realm and the first dhyāna in terms of their common antidotes, [the same applies to the others].
The other stages are similar.
Fifth is cultivation based on the fundamental [knowledge].
Cultivating the four dharma-knowledges so that the subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna) above them become increasingly clear and luminous is called cultivation based on the fundamental.
Since dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is the basis for subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), one cultivates dharma-knowledge so that subsequent knowledge becomes increasingly clear.
This is called "superior cultivation" (*uttarottara-bhāvanā*). To cultivate superior qualities so that those on a lower level become increasingly clear is termed "superior cultivation."
The views and the practices differ;
the practices cultivated are likewise distinct.
How do these differing characteristics manifest?
Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the meaning of cultivation is distinguished in terms of the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) that serves as its basis and in relation to the lower stages,
rather than in relation to the stage where [defilements] are abandoned, as previously explained.
Relying on the future dhyāna (*anāgamyadhyāna*), one enters the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*).

One eliminates all afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) pertaining to the three realms; however, one cultivates only the conventional knowledge of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-saṃvṛtijñāna*) within the future dhyāna, and does not cultivate it in the higher stages.
This applies likewise even up to the category of the fourth dhyāna.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), cultivation is distinguished according to what is abandoned,
not according to its basis.
Just as by relying on the future [state], one gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to sever the afflictions of the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
such that the qualities below the first dhyāna become increasingly bright and clear.
Having abandoned the afflictions of the second dhyāna, the merits from the second dhyāna downward increase and become more luminous;
continuing thus until the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are abandoned, the merits of all three realms equally attain increase and luminosity.
Just as one relies on the future [stage] to cultivate the abandonment of the lower [stages],
this principle applies likewise up to the cultivation of abandonment based on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This is because, although the afflictions of delusion regarding principles (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) have been abandoned, one cannot attain the higher dhyānas.
Because this cannot be severed, cultivation cannot be distinguished.
The afflictions of the path of cultivation bind one according to their respective stages;
if one severs the fetters of the lower stages, one then attains the higher dhyānas.
Therefore, cultivation is distinguished according to the point at which [the afflictions] are severed;
this constitutes their identity or difference.
Furthermore, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one universally cultivates the knowledge of the desire realm and so forth by ascending to higher stages.
Within the path of cultivation, those of the Middle Vehicle cultivate only the wisdom of the eight dhyānas and so forth, and do not cultivate that of the desire realm.
Why is this so? It is because the mind of the desire realm is likewise capable of generating weary detachment from the faults of suffering and its origin.
Seeking with joy the cessation [of suffering], one cultivates that which accords with the path of seeing;
therefore, the insight of seeing also universally cultivates those knowledges.

However, the conventional knowledges (saṃvṛtijñāna) of the desire realm and so forth do not possess the quality of being a common antidote (pratipakṣa) toward those afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
For this reason, one does not cultivate it. Seventh, there is cultivation through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*):
a person liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) seeks to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
When a person of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) seeks what is not occasional,
it is called the transformation of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti).
A learner (śaikṣa) who transforms their faculties cultivates one path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) and one path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
One is then able to sever the roots of obstruction and ignorance,
transforming dullness into sharpness;

it is only through the cultivation of the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) that one can effect this transformation of the faculties.
Why is this so? It is because for a practitioner whose afflictions are not yet exhausted, the mind seeking gain is still intense;
thus, through a single path of non-obstruction and a single path of liberation, they are able to transform their faculties.
Because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have exhausted their fetters (*saṃyojana*), their desire for gain is remote;
therefore, it requires nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to transform the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
This involves eight types of cultivation through meditation (*dhyāna-bhāvanā*).
How is the method of perfuming [the seeds] carried out?
A noble one first attains the fourth dhyāna; having already attained it, they first perfume the fourth [dhyāna].
First, one enters into hundreds of thousands of outflow-free minds;
next, one enters into hundreds of thousands of minds with outflows;
and again, one enters into hundreds of thousands of outflow-free minds.
When there are two moments of outflow-free mind (anāsrava-citta) on both sides with an intermediate moment of outflowing mind (sāsrava-citta), it is called "perfuming dhyāna" (vāsita-dhyāna).
By gradually abbreviating this process until only the final two outflow-free moments remain,
these latter two outflow-free moments are termed the completion of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) for perfuming dhyāna.
Each of these single minds is called the accomplishment of perfumed dhyāna.
Within this accomplishment, the first two are also unimpeded,
while the last one is liberation.
Next, one perfumes [the mind] through the third dhyāna down to the first dhyāna;
the procedure is the same as before.
This constitutes the ninefold cultivation of the supernormal powers.
Cultivating the five supernormal powers based on the fundamental concentration of the four dhyānas is called the cultivation of the powers.
This is explained in detail later in the chapter on the six supernormal powers.
One cultivates the power of the body, the knowledge of others' minds, and the recollection of past lives.
Each of the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and each of the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) exist within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The cultivation of the divine eye and divine ear each constitutes one unhindered knowledge that exists within meditative concentration; however, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as a whole exist outside of meditative concentration.
The Ten Great Clouds of Illumination Manifesting Cultivation:
When an Arhat realizes the fruit of no-more-learning,
all their merits become entirely clear and pure.
Among these ten types, the "contemplation of increase within its own category" (*svabhāga-vṛddhyālambana*) occurs only on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The "contemplation of the same antidote for those free from desire" (*vairāgyasamāna-pratipakṣa*) and the "contemplation based on the fundamental [dhyānas]" (*mūlāśraya*) occur only on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The "great illumination" (*mahāvidyotana*) is found exclusively in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The first type of vehicle pertains to both the paths of seeing and cultivation;

it involves the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), the cultivation of dhyāna, and the cultivation common to both the paths of seeing and cultivation, as well as the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Such is the Abhidharma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, if all meritorious qualities are only those that manifest in the present, they are designated as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*);
others are not so designated. Therefore, the ten [types of cultivation] are not discussed.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there should next be a division;
however, this single section is not yet concluded in the text.
Next, the distinctions between the mental wisdoms cultivated are explained.
According to the Abhidharma, when the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are divided, there are two hundred and nine distinct types of mental states (*citta-viśeṣa*).
Generally speaking, there are four categories.

First, regarding the minds that sever the fetters (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa-citta*), including those of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the unhindered knowledge (*ānantarya-jñāna*), and liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*), there are one hundred and seventy-eight minds in total.
There are sixteen moments of mind for abandoning the afflictions of the Truths:
eight patiences and eight knowledges.
There are one hundred and sixty-two moments of mind for abandoning the afflictions of the Path of Cultivation.
From the abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there are nine grades of unhindered knowledge and liberation within each of the nine stages;
when combined with the preceding paths of seeing and cultivation, these constitute one hundred and seventy-eight moments of mind.
There are twenty minds for the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
For a trainee (*śaikṣa*) undergoing the transformation of the faculties, there are two minds:
namely, one path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) involves eighteen moments of mind:
namely, nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Regarding the three types of perfumed dhyāna-minds, there are three varieties.
The first is untainted (anāsrava);
the next is tainted (sāsrava);
the last is untainted.
The first two are the unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
the latter one is liberation (*vimukti*).
These four are the minds cultivated for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Among these, there are eight:
namely, the five unhindered powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*),
excluding the supernormal powers of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).
Because these two types are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are not treated as objects of cultivation.
Taken together, these constitute two hundred and nine minds.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, all afflictions are severed by means of immeasurable minds.
It is impossible to definitively determine the number of these two gates.
Next, regarding the meaning previously established, the extent of cultivation will be clarified;
herein there are four sections.
First, regarding the cultivation of the one hundred and seventy-eight moments of mind within the process of severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*), this explains the extent of that cultivation.

Within this, it clarifies the extent of cultivation according to the stages of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Within the stage of the external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana),
one cultivates either only one wisdom or two.
What is the meaning of this?
Ordinary persons cultivate the knowledge of the eight dhyānas and so forth,
severing the fetters of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
Within each stage, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.

In all cases of the unhindered knowledges (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
In all other stages, the paths of liberation cultivate both types of knowledge.
That which is called conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) serves as the antidote from the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna.
Within these three stages, the ninth liberation possesses the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) with respect to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to its own stage.
The knowledge of others' minds directed toward lower stages can be cultivated by means of higher stages;
however, for all other liberations, there is cultivation by means of higher stages only regarding the knowledge of others' minds directed toward lower stages,
and there is no principle of cultivating them by means of their own stage.
Among those in the stage of inner ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the seven types of practitioners of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) cultivate only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Logically, only the four minds beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) are termed "inner ordinary persons.
Here, however, these are designated as "inner ordinary persons" in contrast to those in the seven preparatory stages who remain perpetually submerged among the outer ordinary persons.
Up until the fifteenth moment of mind within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),

it is generally stated that one fully cultivates all seven knowledges (*jñāna*); this excludes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as these do not belong to those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds because one has not yet abandoned desire,
one simultaneously cultivates two [knowledges].
At the conclusion of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), one additionally cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The cultivation of the characteristics during the subsequent knowledge of cessation is likewise.
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path, one either cultivates six knowledges or cultivates seven.
Regarding those who practice the six [knowledges] in successive order:
they necessarily rely on the future [moments] to enter the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and simultaneously cultivate the six,
namely, the four noble truths-knowledges, dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) manifests, while the remaining knowledges (*jñāna*) are acquired through subsequent cultivation (*anvaya-bhāvanā*). Question:
Do the remaining knowledges exist within the stage of the candidate (*pratipannaka*)?
How is it that one cultivates other knowledges through the subsequent attainment of the Path?
According to the Abhidharma, when one attains the stage of Srotāpanna, one relinquishes the previously acquired individual attainments;
instead, a collective attainment arises anew, which takes all the aforementioned knowledges as its unified fruit-body.
The *Tattvasiddhi* is not so;
therefore, its "Chapter on the Nine Knowledges" states:
"The single attainment of the outflow-free [path], up to and including nirvāṇa, is never abandoned midway."
Therefore, at the time of attaining the fruit, there is no further "collective attainment" (saṃgraha-prāpti).
As for the statement that "one cultivates seven," this refers to those who transcend [the stages] and enter the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga) based on the four fundamental dhyānas.
Because the fetters of the desire realm have already been severed,
at the time of the sixteenth moment— the subsequent knowledge of the path— one fully cultivates seven knowledges:
the six previously mentioned types as well as the knowledge of others' minds.

Next, regarding the number of moments of consciousness cultivated among the one hundred and sixty-two moments of the unhindered knowledges (*abhisamaya*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) that serve as antidotes to the afflictions of the nine stages, it is explained as follows:
in the case of the antidotes for the fetters of the desire realm, although there are nine grades of unhindered knowledges and eight liberations, only seven knowledges are cultivated.
That is to say, there are the knowledges of the Four Truths, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge.
Based on the cultivation of what they share as their object of treatment, one cultivates the knowledges of the Four Truths, dharma-knowledge, and conventional knowledge;
based on the cultivation of the fundamental [object], one cultivates subsequent knowledge.
In the cultivation of the ninth liberation, one cultivates eight knowledges:
the seven aforementioned types as well as the knowledge of others' minds.
This extends from the counteractive stage of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.

At the conclusion of the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), one simultaneously cultivates seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
Because one is still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are excluded.
Because there is no room for anticipation, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

In all stages, at the conclusion of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one simultaneously cultivates eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Question:

For what reason is it that among the remedies for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), only at the limit of the ninth grade of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
whereas in all paths of liberation of the other stages, one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds uniformly?
The commentary states:
The knowledge of others' minds arises solely based on the fundamental stages of the four dhyānas.
One attains the fundamental dhyāna at the time of the ninth path of liberation within the desire realm.
One also attains the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding the first eight paths of liberation, one has not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas;
for this reason, they are not cultivated.
Within the counteractive paths of the first, second, and third dhyānas,
the first eight liberations involve "cultivation by ascending" (adhigama-bhāvanā) relative to the minds of lower stages;
the ninth liberation involves "attainment-cultivation" (pratilambha-bhāvanā) relative to the knowledge of others' minds within its own stage.
Regarding the aspiration for the minds of lower stages, there is cultivation by means of ascending;
from the antidotes of the four dhyānas up to the sphere of nothingness,
all liberations, although not cultivated through attainment within their own respective stages, involve cultivation by means of ascending with respect to the minds of lower stages.
This is because they are dissimilar.
In the nine paths of non-obstruction that serve as the antidotes to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one cultivates six knowledges:
namely, the knowledges of the four truths, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
How can one cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? The knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgadharmajñāna*) is able to sever those fetters,
because they share the same object of cultivation (*pratipakṣa*).
For what reason is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) not cultivated?
Because conventional knowledge cannot sever the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
as there is no common antidote (pratipakṣa).
The first eight liberations are cultivated through seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and conventional knowledge.
This is because the ninth liberation is cultivated as the manifestation of great illumination.
One cultivates the merit of the ten knowledges across all stages.
Above, first, the cultivation of the number of mental states was clarified in relation to the mind that severs the fetters;
second, the cultivation of the number of mental states was clarified in relation to the twenty types of minds during the transformation of the faculties.
If a practitioner transforms their faculties based on future-dhyāna,
they cultivate six knowledges equally regarding the unhindered knowledges and liberations,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds.
Because the knowledge of others' minds resides in the fundamental dhyānas,

it also excludes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Because it resembles the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it excludes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Because they are not yet beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
When a person in training (*śaikṣa*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) by relying on the four fundamental dhyānas,
they also cultivate six knowledges (*jñāna*) during that path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It is similar to the preceding [case].
For the cultivation of liberation, there are seven [knowledges],
with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds.
Because the transformation of the faculties must rely on the dhyānas of the six stages and not on the formless realms,
it is not mentioned. If an adept (aśaikṣa) transforms their faculties by relying on the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna), [it is likewise not mentioned].
One cultivates only seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds.
Since the knowledge of others' minds exists only in the fundamental dhyānas,
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is likewise excluded.

Because it resembles the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the Knowledge of Destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are excluded, as they have not yet been attained.
When one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) based on the four fundamental dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), [the same applies].
In the nine paths of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), one cultivates only seven knowledges (jñāna).
This excludes the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) because it cannot intervene [in the process], and it also excludes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
Because it is not the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is excluded.
Since it has not yet been attained, during the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one cultivates eight knowledges:
the seven previously mentioned knowledges and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Because they are cultivated while mounted [upon the vehicle], the ninth liberation fully cultivates the ten knowledges (*jñāna*),
for it brings forth and manifests the cultivation of all meritorious qualities, making them all luminous and pure. Thirdly,
regarding the three types of minds in the *vāsita-dhyāna* (perfumed meditation), the extent of their cultivation is clarified.

For a learner (śaikṣa) practicing the two paths of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) in the cultivation of dhyāna, only seven knowledges (jñāna) are cultivated, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), as it is not applicable;

the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are excluded because [the practitioner] is not yet an adept (aśaikṣa). Since they are not adepts, eight knowledges are cultivated in the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Including the knowledge of others' minds:
in the untrained (aśaikṣa) cultivation of meditation, there are nine unimpeded cultivations excluding the knowledge of others' minds;
in the cultivation of liberation, there are ten.
If one is of dull faculties, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is excluded.
Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), among the eight types of minds, the extent of their cultivation is clarified:
one cultivates five supernormal powers, each with one unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The unimpeded knowledge of others' minds consists of the cultivation of seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds because it has not yet been accomplished,
and excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising because they are not of the nature of vision (*darśana*).

Because one cannot investigate the minds of others, the remaining four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) cultivate only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This applies to the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhividhi*),
the supernormal power of the mind of others (*paracittajñāna*), and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
These three liberations are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Now, regarding the cultivation of the liberation of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavimokṣa*), one cultivates eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
As for the remaining two liberations, one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
If one wishes to provide a detailed analysis based on the treatise,
one should seek it through three gates within each verse of that *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
First, it is necessary to clarify how many of the ten cultivations are fully present among them.
Second, it must be clarified how many of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated among them,
and how many of the two hundred and nine minds are cultivated among them;
such is the Abhidharma.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the meaning of simultaneous and concurrent cultivation is not taught,
as there is no need to analyze or explain it;
this point is extensively refuted in the "Chapter on the Nine Knowledges" (*Navajñāna-varga*) of that work.

The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are thus. 192. The Meaning of the Eleven Knowledges (15). The meaning of the eleven knowledges is analyzed through two gates: first, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles regarding their commonality and particularity; second, the analysis of their characteristics. First, the analysis of their characteristics.
The meaning of the eleven knowledges is set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
What are their names? They are the ten knowledges and the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
The first ten are as explained above.
Regarding the "knowledge of things as they truly are" (*yathābhūtajñāna*), there are generally two types of explanations:
first, the unique dharma (*asādhāraṇadharma*); second, the shared dharma (*sādhāraṇadharma*).
When all forms of knowledge are subsumed under a single reality, it is called the "exclusive dharma" (kevala-dharma).
When considered in relation to other forms of knowledge, it is spoken of as eleven types, termed the "shared dharma" (sādhāraṇa-dharma).
Regarding the exclusive dharma, the thorough knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*) is broad and pervasive.
One knows that all phenomena are entirely termed "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*).
It is not merely by knowing the principle of "as-it-is" that it is called "knowledge as-it-is.
If this were not merely the knowledge of the principle of "as-it-is," [it would be so].
How is it called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*)?
According to the *Bhūmivastu-vibhāṣā*,
knowledge free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is called knowledge as it truly is.
What is the meaning of this?
Those with overweening pride do not know all phenomena yet claim to know them;
therefore, they are not in accordance with reality.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas truly know all phenomena and declare that they know them;
therefore, it is called "according to reality.
Within this, there are briefly three kinds of distinctions.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"Pure wisdom, omniscience, and unimpeded wisdom are called the wisdom that is free from pride.
Here, "pure wisdom" refers to the ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized reality and are free from defilement, they are called "pure.
Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the conventional wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is called omniscience because it knows all things—across all worlds, in all places, regarding all matters, and in all their various aspects and distinctions.
In all respects, this is equal to the explanation in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Unobstructed knowledge is also mundane knowledge;
it knows among all phenomena that are objects of omniscience.
Being sovereign, one does not rely on expedient means;
the very moment the mind is aroused, it is known as unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*).
Among the shared dharmas, the one who possesses knowledge according to reality knows that objects are not fixed.
The names and meanings also differ.
Within this, there are two sections.
First, the eleven knowledges are explained by contrasting the Great and Small Vehicles.
The wisdom and understanding of the Hīnayāna are explained as the former ten [stages];
the wisdom and understanding of the Mahāyāna are collectively termed "as-it-is" (yathābhūta).
This "as-it-is" wisdom is still the same "as-it-is" regarding the unique dharmas mentioned previously.
In relation to the Hīnayāna, they are distinct.
Second, according to the Mahāyāna meaning, they are divided into eleven.
Within this category, the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) is narrow.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know the principle of reality as it truly is; this is called "knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Knowledge of other conventional truths is categorized under the preceding ten [categories].
Such is the nature and characteristic of these; this first section is concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish their universal and limited scope by means of the Great and Small Vehicles.
This analysis consists of two parts.
First, the mutual discussion of the hidden and the manifest.
As Nāgārjuna stated:
the preceding ten types are the wisdoms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the final one, suchness (yathābhūta), is the wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
Although the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that suffering and the other truths are also subsumed under their knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*),
this [category] distinguishes the superior from the inferior;
the wisdom and understanding of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are vast and extensive, possessing eleven types of knowledge.
Because the wisdom and understanding of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are narrow, they possess only ten knowledges and lack the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna),
for they are unable to know the principle of reality as it is.
The meaning of the eleven knowledges has been briefly explained thus. 193.
The Meaning of the Eleven Purities (15). Regarding the meaning of the eleven purities: these eleven types of purity are set forth in the *Bhūmivastu* (*Dizhi lun*).
What is this "name"? It refers to the two kinds of purity of the lineage (*gotra*).
The seeds of all Buddha-dharmas exist within the person; when these are free from coarse afflictions, it is called the purity of the lineage.
Second is the purity of practice and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-viśuddhi*).
This refers to the cultivation of pure patience on the stage of practice and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), whereby all faults are eliminated.
Entering the path leading out [of saṃsāra] is called the purity of practice through understanding.
It is the three purities of mind; that is, mental purity. Namely:
On the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one attains indestructible pure faith in the Triple Gem;
the purification of the mind through seeking great enlightenment with a pure heart is called "purity of mind.
Fourth is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).
That is to say:

on the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (Vimalā-bhūmi), because one is fully endowed with natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*) and has completely abandoned even subtle transgressions, it is called "purity of morality.
Fifth is purity of mind (*manas*).
On the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), one attains worldly-truth meditation (*saṃvṛti-satya-dhyāna*) and suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the concentrated mind is pure, it is called "purity of intention" (*manas-pariśuddhi*).
Sixth is the purity of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi-pariśuddhi*).
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one contemplates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
knows the truths as they truly are, and awakens to dependent origination;
the eradication of false delusions is called the purification of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*).
Seventh is the purity of fulfilling all practices of skillful means.
This refers to the cultivation of all ten types of wisdom regarding skillful means on the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
The fulfillment of the superior practice of initiating [the path] and the satisfaction [therein],
which remedies the obstacle of abandoning the bliss of the preceding stage and the lack of volitional effort, is called the purity of the fulfillment of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Eighth is the purity of true knowledge and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
That is to say:
in the eighth stage, one achieves skillful wisdom and is endowed with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
because their functioning is inexhaustible, it is called "the purity of the supernormal power of true wisdom."
Ninth is the unimpeded purity of the inexhaustible teaching of the true meaning.
This means that in the ninth stage, one attains the perfection of wisdom and realizes the inexhaustibility of the meaning.
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) constitute the purity of mastery in speech, which is the inexhaustible and unimpeded exposition of names and meanings.
The ten [powers] constitute the purity of knowing all aspects of the knowable.
That is to say:
In the tenth stage, one accomplishes the Tathāgata’s greatness of the sevenfold wisdom.
Regarding all knowable phenomena in every respect, one possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision;
this is called the purity of the wisdom that knows all aspects of the knowable.
Eleventh, the purification of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions and cognitive obstructions;
that is to say,
in the stage of the Tathāgata, the obstructions and habitual tendencies are forever extinguished.
The fruit of virtue and liberation is termed the purification of the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Thus, the eleven meanings of purity have been briefly explained. 194. The Meaning of the Twelve Dhūtas (15).

The meaning of the twelve dhūtas is explained through two gates: first, the definition of the names and the discernment of their characteristics; second, the differentiation of their similarities and differences in relation to the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). First: The Definition of the Names and the Discernment of Their Characteristics.
*dhūta* is a word from the language of the Hu;
in this context, it is correctly translated as "shaking off.
This refers to the practice of detachment.
It is designated by way of an analogy:
just as shaking out a garment can remove dust and grime,
so too the cultivation of this practice can abandon greedy attachment.
Therefore, it is called "shaking off" (dhūta).
The dhūta practices comprise sixteen items;
however, because they are concealed or revealed according to the sūtras and śāstras, twelve are taught.
Regarding the "sixteen," there are four within clothing,
six within food, and six within locations.
This is the sixteenth.
Regarding the four types of robes:
the first is the refuse-rag robe (pāṃśukūla).
Second, the woolen robe;
third, the patched robe;
fourth, the three robes.
Regarding "rag-robes" (pāṃśukūla):
these refer to garments scorched by fire, gnawed by oxen, bitten by rats, or the clothing of the deceased, and so forth.
People in foreign lands discard such items in the streets and wilds.
Because its nature is like that of discarded refuse, it is called "refuse-rag clothing" (pāṃsukūla).
The practitioner takes it, washes, dyes, and sews it, using it to provide for the body.
It is asked:
For what reason is it that only those who receive this robe are of three grades—
namely, inferior, middling, and superior?
Those of inferior capacity acquire clothing through various wrong livelihoods, such as farming, trade,
and commerce. Those of middling capacity distance themselves from these former faults and receive robes from within the Saṃgha or as gifts from donors.
Those who practice the higher path do not accept robes from the Sangha or robes offered by donors, but accept robes of discarded rags (pāṃsukūla).
Why do they not accept robes from within the Sangha?
If they were to accept such robes, they would have to conform to the communal rules of the Sangha.
He adjudicates monastic affairs and assigns duties;
he settles disputes and banishes those with distracted minds to inspire them toward the Path.
For these reasons, he does not accept robes from within the Saṃgha.
For what reason does he not accept robes offered by donors?
Because the pursuit of robes leads mostly to wrong livelihood;
furthermore, if he were to accept robes offered by donors, it would give rise to attachment and craving, making liberation difficult to attain.
Furthermore, if one accepts robes offered by a donor,
one becomes partial toward those from whom they were obtained and creates distance and hindrance toward those from whom they were not;
this obstructs equal transformation [of others].
Furthermore, if one receives robes offered by a donor,
one should not give rise to pride, nor harbor resentment or speak ill of them,
saying that they lack wisdom, do not recognize the field of merit, and fail to give what should be given.
Or one may feel self-contempt and shame, giving rise to distress;
furthermore, if one accepts robes offered by a donor,
one must frequently visit them, which neglects the path and leads to resentment.
Furthermore, because of accepting the gift of robes from a donor, one may harbor hatred and envy toward virtuous people;
one may slander the good and wholesome, desiring that they not remain.
Seeing these many faults, [one should abandon such acceptance].
For this reason, one does not accept robes offered by donors.
Why, then, accept only rag-robes?
To simplify affairs and increase the Path.
Being free from faults and without transgression,
one accepts it alone.
As for what is called "woolen clothing," it is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The fine hair of birds is called *vāla*.
If a practitioner cannot obtain a robe made of cast-off rags (*pāṃśukūla*), they may seek this as a garment.
As for the "patchwork robe" (*nāṃgaka*), it refers to a garment made by sewing together tattered, worn-out, and dilapidated pieces for the sake of the body.
One does not wear fine clothing.
Why must this be so? If one seeks fine clothing, it gives rise to affliction and leads to transgression.
To expend effort and abandon the Way is due to being unattached to this;
furthermore, fine clothing is a point where those who have not yet attained the Way give rise to craving and attachment.
Furthermore, in the wilderness there are many dangers from bandits,
which may even lead to the loss of life.
Because there are such many faults, one accepts the patched robe (pāṃsukūla).
Regarding the "three robes," they refer to the five-strip robe,
the seven-strip robe, and the great robe (saṃghāṭī).
Those who follow the upward path accept only these three robes and do not keep any others.
Why is this so? It is because laypeople, seeking pleasure, keep various kinds of clothing.
The non-Buddhists practice together with the naked, being devoid of shame;
because the Buddha dwells in the Middle Way, abandoning the two extremes, he maintains three robes.
Furthermore, seeking many robes involves wasting effort and neglecting the Path.
Because one is not yet able to manage affairs when young, one keeps three robes;
however, these three robes are sufficient for the needs of the body.
When engaged in manual labor or coming and going for the sake of the major or minor calls of nature, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
When performing various virtuous deeds, one should wear the seven-strip robe (saptaka-cīvara).
When converting and gathering worldly people to inspire their reverence and faith,
one must wear the great robe (saṃghāṭī).
Furthermore, one should wear the five-strip robe (pañcakaṣāya) in private places;
when entering the assembly, one should wear the seven-strip robe (saptakaṣāya);
and when entering royal palaces or villages, one must wear the great robe (saṃghāṭī).
Furthermore, when the weather is temperate and warm, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṇṭhaka*);
when it is cold, one adds the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṇṭhaka*);
and when the suffering of the cold becomes severe, one adds the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
Thus, once during the middle of winter at night, when the cold was so severe it split the bamboo,
the Tathāgata put on his five-piece robe during the first watch of the night;
as the night grew long and the cold intensified, he added his seven-piece robe.
During the latter part of the night, as the cold intensified, the Buddha added his great outer robe (mahākāṣāya). He then thought:
"In future ages, there will be sons of good family who cannot endure the suffering of the cold; for them, these three robes shall be sufficient to sustain their bodies."
For these many reasons, one keeps the three robes.
Regarding the six types of food,
the first is alms-food.
2. Begging for food in successive order;
3. Not eating food that has not been made permissible through the *khalupaścādbhakti* rule;
4. Eating in a single sitting.
The fifth is eating in a single sitting, which is also called moderation in portion.
The sixth is not drinking liquids after midday.
Regarding those who beg for food, there are three types of persons.
That is to say:
inferior, middling, and superior.
Those of the inferior class, though they have gone forth as monastics, sustain themselves through wrong livelihood.
Those who cultivate fields, plant crops, and manage their livelihoods then turn to various crafts and employ all manner of wrong means of subsistence to survive.
Those of middle capacity abandon these former faults and accept meals from the Sangha or invitations to dine at the homes of donors.
Those of the highest grade do not accept food from the Saṃgha nor invitations to meals from lay donors (dānapati), but practice only alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta).
Why do they not accept food from within the Saṃgha?
Because the fault is the same as that regarding their robes; therefore, they do not accept it.
If a donor invites one to eat, it is the same as before.
For what reason does one exclusively practice begging for food?
There are two purposes for doing so.
The first is for the sake of attending to one's own affairs and practicing the Path;
the second is for the sake of the welfare and benefit of others in the world.
Those who beg in successive order are also included within the practice of begging for food.
To demonstrate that the time for begging is free from partiality and error, this is discussed separately.
Ordinary fools crave flavors; they abandon poverty to follow wealth.
The compassion of those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is narrow;

they abandon the wealthy to seek out the poor. Those of the higher practice, however, free themselves from greed and narrow-mindedness to extend equal compassion to all sentient beings, without discriminating between the rich and the poor, begging from them in successive order with impartiality.
Regarding what is called "not performing the *kṛtya-karaṇīya* (the ritual for leftover food)," it is as explained in the Vinaya:
there may be someone who, although begging for alms in regular succession, frequently obtains proper food at the places where he seeks it.
One may eat repeatedly by performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite for leftover food).
The practitioner reflects:
"Although the World-Honored One has occasionally permitted this *khalupaścādbhakti* for those who are ill..."
Since I am currently free from illness, I should not accept it;
therefore, I do not perform the ritual of *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the formal method for consuming food) when eating.
This is included within the general category, and it is likewise subsumed under the practice of eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*).
Therefore, in the sūtras and śāstras, they are generally not distinguished separately.
In the Vinaya, those who observe the rule of eating in a single sitting do not consume any other minor snacks before midday.
As for other minor meals, they differ from this category in that they involve abstaining from frequent formal meals; therefore,
they are mentioned separately.
Among those who eat at a single sitting, there may be some who, although they do not eat regularly during the formal mealtime,
nevertheless consume other cakes, fruits, gruel, and so forth before midday.
The practitioner reflects as follows:
Fools, craving the body, consume food repeatedly to increase their afflictions;
I now practice for the sake of the Path, not for the nourishment of the body,
and act to destroy afflictions, not to increase the fetters.
Therefore, he accepted only one meal.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"Seeking even a single meal has already caused many hindrances to the Path."
How much less should one seek to eat much?
Therefore, one should take only a single meal.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that food and drink arise from within much suffering.
If one consumes many meals, disturbances will be even more numerous;
therefore, one observes the practice of eating only one meal a day.
Furthermore, one contemplates that food and drink are offerings bestowed out of faith.
One meal is difficult to digest;
how much more so many meals?
Eating a single morsel is also termed "moderation in eating" in the sūtras.
Taking food only once is called "one morsel of food" (*piṇḍapāta*).
Eating frugally and sparingly is called "moderation in eating" (*bhojanamātrajñatā*).
Why are these explained in this sequence?
There are those who, although they observe the practice of eating only one meal a day,
indulge themselves in drinking and eating during that single meal until their bellies are full and distended; thus,
for half the day they remain drowsy and sluggish, failing to diminish this state and thereby obstructing the practice of the Dharma.
Therefore, one must exercise moderation in eating.
Furthermore, excessive eating increases afflictions, making them difficult to subdue;
thus, one must exercise moderation.
Furthermore, eating too much increases drowsiness, makes digestion difficult, causes illness, and leaves the body in a state of unrest;
therefore, one must moderate one's intake.
To what extent should this moderation go?
According to what one can afford, set aside one-third to give to birds and beasts,
and eat the remainder oneself;
even this small amount of benefit is virtuous.
Regarding "not drinking liquids after midday":
there are those who, although they practice moderation in their food and drink,
still crave flavors and consequently consume various liquids such as honey-syrup and the like after midday.
In seeking this beverage, one often resorts to wrong livelihood,
wasting effort and neglecting the Path;
for this reason, it is not drunk.
Furthermore, observe that this mind is difficult to let loose;
like a horse without a bridle that grazes on grass to the left and right,
it cannot swiftly follow the will of the driver.
Furthermore, it is only by adding the bridle and bit that one can advance swiftly and move according to the will of the person; therefore,
it is necessary to exercise decisive judgment.
Regarding the six abodes for staying in the middle: first, one must be in an araṇya;
second, in a cemetery;
third, at the foot of a tree.
The fourth is sitting in the open air;
the fifth is the permanent seat;
the sixth is sitting wherever one happens to be.
*Āraṇya* is translated here as "a place of empty seclusion.
Where is such a place? As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*:
Four cubits constitute one bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred bows are called one *krośa*.
One and a half *krośas* is designated as an *āraṇyaka* (forest hermitage) location.
It is approximately three *li* away.
For those practicing *dhūta* austerities, it is best to stay as close as possible;
however, it is even better to remain at a distance.
"Why am I here? The practitioner reflects:
"In the past, when I was at home, I was bound by my parents and relatives."
Therefore, one must abandon them.
Now that you have already left the household life, if you return to become attached to teachers, disciples, fellow students, and spiritual friends, you will be no different from the laity;
for this reason, you must abandon such ties and dwell in an araṇya.
Furthermore, in a village, men and women mingle, which greatly increases the defilement of desire;
it is not appropriate to dwell therein. Therefore, one must stay in an araṇya.
Furthermore, the clamor and noise near a village hinder the cultivation of a concentrated mind;
therefore, one must stay in an araṇya.
Regarding the "cemetery" (śmaśāna): in a cemetery, there are many corpses that are putrefying, bloated, and foul-smelling.
Beholding these makes it easy to enter the gateway of the meditation on impurity;
therefore, one dwells among the charnel grounds.
Furthermore, in the charnel grounds, corpses are decomposed, devoured by worms, consumed by fire, dismembered, and scattered until they vanish.
Beholding this makes it easy to enter the gateway of the contemplation of impermanence;
therefore, one dwells among the burial mounds.
Furthermore, in the burial mounds, skeletal remains are scattered about.
Beholding these things makes it easy to enter the contemplation of emptiness and non-self;
therefore, one dwells among burial mounds. As for "under a tree":
Previously, while dwelling among the tombs, I observed corpses and accomplished the task of attaining the Way;
therefore, I have left the tombs and come to the foot of this tree.
Furthermore, previously at the tombs, I took the characteristics of corpses as my object of focus.
However, because there were many sounds of weeping and the like that obstructed the cultivation of right contemplation,
he came beneath a tree to fix his mindfulness and engage in analytical reflection;
furthermore, the shade of the tree provided a shelter equivalent to half a house.
To settle the body and cultivate the Way,
one stays beneath a tree;
furthermore, most of the Buddhas and noble sages who attained the Way and realized the fruits did so by relying on trees.
Therefore, he stayed beneath a tree;
as for those who sat in the open air, they suffered from the long-term dampness and shade under the trees,
and thus he went to the open air.
Furthermore, while under a tree, the thought of the tree arises;
or else one discriminates between this as good and that as bad.
To eliminate these afflictions, one must abandon the tree and come to an open space.
Because what is manifested is clearly understood and unimpeded,
one should remain in the open air.
Furthermore, when the moonlight shines upon the open ground, the mental image becomes clear and pure, making it easy to enter the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Therefore, he remains in the open air.
Regarding those who practice "constant sitting," among the four modes of deportment,
walking and standing are too strenuous, while lying down is too indulgent.
Sitting apart from the two extremes enables one to endure for a long time;
therefore, one must practice constant sitting.
Furthermore, when walking or standing, the mind becomes agitated and is difficult to restrain.
When lying down, one falls into dullness and frequently enters sleep; thus, one must abandon both dullness and agitation and practice constant sitting.
Furthermore, for a seeker of the Way whose great task remains unaccomplished, the thieves of the afflictions constantly watch for an opportunity to strike.
It is not appropriate to lie down in sleep;
therefore, one must always sit.
Furthermore, much that is accomplished occurs while sitting.
Food is easily digested and the breath is harmonized;
therefore, one must practice constant sitting (*prahāṇa*). As for "sitting according to circumstances" (*yathāsaṃstarika*), it means sitting wherever a grass mat is available.
Therefore, it is called "following the seat.
When subdivided according to their specific distinctions, there are sixteen;
however, the sūtras and śāstras, based on this, teach twelve by means of concealing or revealing and combining or separating them.
What are their characteristics?
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, two [categories] are established for robes and four for food.
Six are established within the bases,
making twelve in total;
two are included within clothing.
First, the patched robe;
second, wearing the three robes;
all others are not discussed.
Regarding the four [faults] concerning food:
first, begging for food;
second, eating without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual.
3. Eating in one sitting;
4. Eating in a single mouthful;
"begging in sequence" is included within the category of begging for alms.
Not drinking liquids after midday is included within the single sitting;
therefore, it is not discussed separately.
Regarding the six [rules] for the intermediate period, they are fully explained as established above.
Based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, three [categories] are established among robes, three among food,
and six among dwellings.
These together constitute twelve.
Regarding the three types of robes:
the first is wearing the refuse-rag robe (*pāṃsukūla*).
Second, wearing garments of coarse wool;
third, maintaining the three robes;
all other matters are not discussed here.
Regarding the three types of food, they are:
begging for alms, eating in a single sitting, and eating a single morsel;
the others are not mentioned.
The sequential [practice] is also subsumed within alms-gathering;
since it is included within "not making extra food" and "not drinking liquids after midday" during a single sitting,
it is not discussed separately.
The six [factors] situated in the middle have been fully explained above.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, twelve [factors] are also taught,
which differ from the previous enumeration.
According to that treatise, two types of robes are established:
first, those who wear the *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe);
second, those who wear the three robes (*tricīvara*).
It is the same as in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.
Among the practices for eating, five are established.
The first is begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*).
2. Begging in sequence;
3. Eating at one sitting;
4. Moderating the amount of food.

Among these five [practices], not drinking even thin gruel after midday is subsumed under the practice of eating in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*) by means of the ritual of "no further food" (*kṛtapiṇḍapāta*);
it is not established as a separate category.
The five [precepts] are taught here as being intermediate,
excluding the practice of sitting together;
there should be further variations in other sūtras and śāstras.
All that has not been seen before is the teaching of the Sages.
Once one has completed this single gateway, all modes of practice are attained.
Next, one must distinguish their similarities and differences by correlating them with the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
As for the four noble lineages: first, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*); [and so forth].
Second is begging for food;
third is sitting at the foot of a tree;
fourth is taking old, discarded medicine when ill.
This has been explained in detail above.
Regarding the comparison between the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) and the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), there are three points of similarity and difference:
first, that which is both a noble lineage and an ascetic practice.
That is to say: wearing rag-robes, begging for food, and sitting at the foot of a tree.
These can give rise to what is called the "noble lineage" (*āryavaṃśa*);
abiding in these, one is able to overcome desire for clothing, food, and so forth.
Therefore, it is called *dhūta*.
This practice of wearing refuse-rag robes (*pāṃśukūla*) subsumes both the patched robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and the woolen robe (*vālkala*).
Within this practice of begging for food, the practice of begging sequentially (*sāvadāna-bhikṣā*) is included.
Sitting beneath a tree refers to practicing in a secluded hermitage (*araṇya*).
Second, there are those which are noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) but not ascetic practices (*dhūta*);
namely, the practice of using discarded medicine.
Those discarded medicines are what the sick require;
however, the sick are unable to practice the ascetic practices (dhūta) of austerity.
For this reason, they are not described as dhūta-dharmas.
Third are those that are dhūta practices but not noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

These are: keeping the three robes, eating at one sitting, eating a single morsel, not drinking liquids after the proper time, dwelling in cemeteries, dwelling in the open air, always sitting, and sitting wherever one happens to be.
Why are these not called the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa)?
For the noble lineages are the universal practices of all who have gone forth;
all those who have gone forth receive and practice them.
The dhūta practices are exclusively the supreme ascetic disciplines.
These supreme ascetic disciplines are what is cultivated by superior persons;
specifically, such things as possessing only the three robes and eating at a single sitting are the methods of ascetic practice.
What the superior person practices cannot be endured by those of middle or inferior capacity;
therefore, it is taught as *dhūta*, but is not called a "noble lineage" (*āryavaṃśa*).
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of *dhūta*.
195. The Meaning of the Twelve Skillful Means (15). Regarding the twelve skillful means, they are as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (*Yogācārabhūmi*).
Because they involve skillfulness in the practice of cultivation, they are called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Generally speaking, there are four types of expedient means (*upāya*) categorized according to their specific distinctions.
First is the expedient means of progression,
such as the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*) prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Second is skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*),
such as the wisdom of skillful means among the two types of wisdom; in reality,
there are no three vehicles (*triyāna*).
They are performed through skillful means.
The three types of giving constitute the application of skillful means,
as described in the *Pāramitā of Skillful Means* and other such texts.
Because all that is performed is skillfully cultivated, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
It is the expedient means of the fourfold integration:
the skillful integration of all phenomena as being of one essence.
Because the one encompasses all and all becomes the one,
it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* explains the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) as expedient means.
Furthermore, that treatise states:
"This dharma is skillfully established as the means of accomplishment (*upāya*).
What is discussed here is this third method of construction and accomplishment, and not the other three types."
Within the practice of giving, there are specifically three types.
The first is the skillful means of the path of instruction,
which consists of being adept at cultivating what is practiced in the world.
Second is the skillful means of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga-upāya*).
By being able to relinquish the marks of emotional attachment, one realizes and enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, in the eighth stage of that *Bhūmi-sūtra*:
It is appropriate to explain the path of realization as the skillful means for the perfect accumulation of wisdom.
Regarding the third, the skillful means of non-abiding,
there are three sub-divisions within it.
The relative nature of emptiness and existence is used to clarify skillful means:
while abiding in existence, one remains unstained and is constantly able to enter into emptiness.
Entering into emptiness, they do not realize it;
they are always able to accord with existence.
As explained in the context of the seventh stage, they possess this skillful means.
Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Second, regarding the relative nature of defilement and purity: not abandoning the world while constantly abiding in nirvāṇa;
attaining great nirvāṇa without abandoning the world.
Therefore, it is called "skillful means" (upāya).

Third, regarding the relationship between self and others: one does not abandon self-benefit while constantly benefiting others, nor does one abandon benefiting others while constantly benefiting oneself; thus, one practices without partiality or attachment.
Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
What is discussed here is its initial gateway, the expedient means of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
Within the practice of the path of teaching, the extent of detail is not fixed, being sometimes extensive and sometimes concise.
Now, based on one gate, we shall briefly explain twelve [categories].
What are their names?
As that treatise states:
There are six skillful means for giving rise to the internal Buddha-dharma,
and six skillful means for externally bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Regarding the six for giving rise to the internal [Buddha-dharma]:
First, regarding all sentient beings with a heart of compassion—
this is precisely what constitutes the mind that keeps sentient beings in mind.
How is it that this compassionate mindfulness of sentient beings can be called "the internal arising of the Buddha-dharma"?
Because one personally accomplishes the Buddha-dharma by means of transforming sentient beings,
one is said to "internally give rise to the Buddha-dharma" through mindfulness of sentient beings.
Second, it is the thorough and authentic understanding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are.
This is precisely the mind that grows weary of the conditioned;
that is to say, knowing the faults of the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth of the conditioned formations of birth and death, one gives rise to weariness and detachment.
Third is the wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi;
this is precisely the mind that seeks omniscience.
These are the three fundamental practices.
The latter three rely on the former to manifest skillful means.
The fourth relies on mindfulness of sentient beings to abandon birth and death,
based on the mindfulness that sentient beings ought to remain within birth and death.
Why does he abandon them?
This is because such is the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva.
What is this skillful means? It is relying on mindfulness of sentient beings with the desire to rescue and deliver them.
Since one cannot escape the suffering of birth and death by one's own power,
one must rely on vows and mindfulness to swiftly abandon them;
this explains the skillful means based on the initial resolve.
Fifth, by understanding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are,
one revolves through birth and death with an undefiled mind; yet,
by understanding conditioned formations as they truly are, one should renounce birth and death.
For what reason does he undergo cyclic existence?
It is likewise due to the skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattva.
What are these skillful means?
Because one knows that birth and death are false and devoid of reality,
one is able to remain within them forever without defilement;
this explains the skillful means based on the second [stage].
Sixth is the blazing diligence based on seeking the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because the Buddha achieves [enlightenment] through exertion, he gives rise to diligence;
this is explained as the skillful means based on the third [stage].
Regarding the six skillful means for externally accomplishing sentient beings:
first, obtaining immeasurable fruits from small roots of goodness;
that is to say, the Bodhisattva teaches inferior sentient beings.
One gives small material wealth as an offering to an inferior field of merit,
and employs this slight merit to seek the awakening of all-encompassing virtues;
by means of this dedication, that slight merit is made to attain immeasurable fruit.
As it is with giving,
so it is with all other practices:
through a small amount of skillful means, one generates immeasurable goodness.
Within this, there are two aspects:
first, teaching sentient beings to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox;
second, teaching sentient beings to abandon the Hinayana and return to the Mahayana.
Within each of these two categories, there are numerous sub-sections,
as fully detailed in the treatise;
they cannot be listed in their entirety here.
The first two of these are practices for transforming others;
the middle one is skillfulness in initiating practice;
and the third is removing the violence of sentient beings who destroy the Dharma.
This is the generation of faith in others.
Among the four bases, it causes sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma;
this is the dharma that generates understanding in others.
Fifth, causing those sentient beings who have already entered [the path] to achieve accomplishment;
this is the practice of benefiting others.
Sixth, causing those sentient beings who have already matured to attain liberation.
This transformation attains the fruit.
Among these four subsequent types of transformative activity for others, it is included within skillful means for gathering people.
Within these latter four, there are specifically six kinds of skillful expedient practices.
It enables sentient beings to embrace the Dharma, eliminate harm, and even attain liberation. First,
it is the skillful means of conformity,
which skillfully explains the meaning of the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, enabling them to awaken and enter into it.
Second, the skillful means of establishing commitments:
when sentient beings have a request, one causes them to cultivate wholesome deeds.
Third, the skillful means of repaying kindness.
A bodhisattva has previously practiced bestowing favors upon sentient beings;
when they come to seek recompense,
the bodhisattva does not accept it.
Exhorting them to cultivate goodness;
fourth, the skillful means of distinct characteristics:
if there are sentient beings who have no needs or desires.
When a bodhisattva wishes to gather others in, they first become friends with them and encourage them to cultivate virtue;
yet those people do not comply.
The Bodhisattva manifests signs such as anger and reprimand to cause others to cultivate wholesome dharmas;
this is the fifth expedient means of coercion.
When a bodhisattva acts as a king or a sovereign lord,
he compels the people and retinues under his jurisdiction to practice virtue through six methods of purification.
The attainment of enlightenment through the eight phases and the preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings—these twelve expedient means have been briefly distinguished as such.

196. The Meaning of the Thirteen Abodes (15). The Meaning of the Thirteen Abodes is analyzed according to seven gates: listing the names, distinguishing their characteristics; 1. Gradual and Sudden; 2. Analysis by way of application and cultivation; 3. Analysis by way of practice; 4. Subsumption of the abodes under the eight dharmas; 5. The limits of cultivation; 6. The limits of remedial abandonment; 7. First, listing the names and distinguishing their characteristics.
The meaning of the thirteen abodes (*trayodaśa-vihāra*) is derived from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-samvara-vinaya-sūtra* (Dizhi lun).
That which is the locus where practice is perfected is called an "abode.
Furthermore, that which achieves non-retrogression is also termed an "abode."
The meanings of "abiding" (sthiti) may be analyzed, combined, expanded, or condensed;
they are not fixed. For now, based on one approach, we shall discuss thirteen.
What are their names?
There is one stage of abiding in the single lineage,
namely the lineage of practice and the lineage of nature,
which the Buddha establishes as firm and indestructible.

The first is called the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotrasthāna*). The second is the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryāsthāna*), which refers to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
Entering into the practice of correct contemplation on the supramundane path without regression is called the Stage of Practice through Understanding (Adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi).
Third is the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
This refers to the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*),
wherein the supramundane, true realization of the bodhicitta arises;
one abides firmly without regression and rejoices in what has been attained.
The first is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
The fourth is the Stage of Higher Ethics (*adhiśīla-vihāra*),
which refers to the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Being fully endowed with pure ethical discipline and not committing even the slightest transgression is called the dwelling of superior morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
Fifth is the dwelling of superior mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*).
What is called the "Ground of Clarity" (Prabhākari-bhūmi) is the dwelling in the higher resolve (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*), characterized by the excellence of a concentrated mind;
it is the dwelling in wisdom (*prajñā-vihāra*) associated with the six factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

What is called the "Blazing Ground" (Ārciṣmatī-bhūmi) refers to the dwelling in wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣya-dharma), which are the thirty-seven factors of awakening;
and the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the seven truths.
This refers to the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā bhūmi*).
It consists of the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths through skillful observation,
and the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the eightfold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This refers to the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Because one is well able to observe the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is called the dwelling in wisdom associated with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-pratisaṃyukta-prajñā-vihāra*).
The ninth is the signless dwelling with effort and development (*sābhisaṃskāra-sābhisamskāra-nimitta-vihāra*).
This refers to the Ground of Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā-bhūmi).
Because the practice with effort (*sābhoga-prayoga*) is collectively developed, it is called "having development.
Because quiescence and activity proceed together, free from the characteristics of the interval between existence and non-existence, it is called "abiding in the signless" (*animitta-vihāra*).
The tenth is the dwelling in signlessness without practice and without effortful development;
this refers to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Because the practice of fruition has become thoroughly matured and the practice without effortful application (*anābhoga-caryā*) arises together with the common characteristics, it is called "without practice and without development."
The state in which the characteristics of effort and interval are far removed is called the "Abode of Signlessness" (animittavihāra).
Its eleventh stage is called the "Unobstructed Abode" (asaṅgavihāra), which refers to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (sādhumatībhūmi).
The ability to teach the Dharma for the benefit of others through forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence is called the "Unimpeded Abode.
Its twelfth stage is named the "Supreme Abode," which refers to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
Because the practice of learning has reached its ultimate fulfillment, it is called "supreme.
Its thirteenth stage is named the Tathāgata-abiding.
Because the fruit and virtue have reached ultimate fulfillment and there is the purity of transcendence, it is called the Tathāgata-abiding. This concludes this section.
Next, the various stages (*vihāra*) are distinguished according to the sudden and the gradual,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"The preceding bodhisattva stages become progressively purified."
Subsequently, the Tathāgata abides in the sudden attainment of purity.
Teaching and practice are called "sudden attainment" when they are perfected;
realization and practice are called "purity" when they are suddenly manifested.
Why is this so? Because within each and every stage of those bodhisattva grounds, the categories of obstacles to be remedied are innumerable;
they are only fully exhausted after being gradually severed over a long period of time.
This constitutes gradual purification;
the obstacles that hinder Buddhahood are restricted to only one category,
which is finally severed by the unimpeded path within the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).
When the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) arises, everything is purified instantaneously and no longer exists in manifold categories;
therefore, it is not purified gradually.
This concludes these two gates concerning the distinction between the stages of the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata.
Next, regarding the cultivation and realization,
as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
the stages of lineage (*gotra*) and conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) are called the expedient means of signless cultivation (*animitta-bhāvanopāya*).
Gradually training in the deconstruction of signs, one enters the supramundane state.
From that Dwelling of Joy up to the Dwelling of Wisdom Corresponding to Dependent Origination,
one attains the cultivation of signlessness and is truly able to deconstruct signs and realize entry into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Second is the dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*), which purifies the cultivation of signlessness.
By attaining the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one knows that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen;
this is the fruit of the signless cultivation, reaching unimpeded Buddhahood.
Based on the preceding [section] on the accomplishment of various virtues through the departure from marks, these three gates are concluded.
Next, the discussion proceeds according to practice,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The lineage, the stage of practice through understanding, and the cultivation of minor practices involve the abandonment of conduct and lack certainty in attainment, as there is regression;
because their application of conduct is limited and narrow, they are called "minor."
Being unable to practice constantly is called "having interruption.
Because the practicing mind is not firm, it is called "indefinite.
Because one regresses upon encountering conditions, it is called "having regression."
From the stage of joy up to the dwelling in the wisdom of dependent origination, one cultivates and extensively practices these stages.
One does not sever them, remains certain of what has been attained, and does not regress.
Within each of these dwellings, every single practice is fully present within each individual practice.
Therefore, it is called "vast.
To act constantly without ceasing is called "uninterrupted."
When the mind of practice is firm and stable, it is called "determination.
When conditions cannot cause its defeat, it is named "non-retrogression.
There is practice and opening, up to the supreme cultivation of immeasurable practices.
Because they are unceasing and certain, what has been attained is non-retrogressive.
Within each of these stages, one is able to fully possess all aspects within all those practices; thus, they are called "immeasurable practices."
The remaining points, such as "non-interruption" and so forth, are fully explained as previously set forth.
That Tathāgata-dwelling accomplishes the fruits that are immeasurable, uninterrupted, certain, and non-retrogressive; thus concludes this section on the four gates.
Next, the thirteen stages (*vihāra*) are subsumed by eight factors,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
Regarding these eight factors:

First, faith; second, hearing; third, reflection; fourth, purification of the mind; fifth, the initial practice of wisdom; sixth, the expansion of wisdom; seventh, the accomplishment of the fruit of wisdom; eighth, ultimate liberation.
What is meant by "comprehensively abiding"?

It refers to the stages of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), and the cultivation of faith; within the stage of practice through understanding, one accomplishes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and engages in contemplation.
