The initial entry into joy is called the "purified mind.
The fulfillment of the Stage of Joy is called the "practice of cultivated wisdom.
From the Stage of Freedom from Defilement upward is called the "extensiveness of cultivated wisdom."
From the stage of Immovability (*acalā*) upward, it is called the fulfillment of the fruit of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The stage of Buddhahood is termed "ultimate transcendence" (*atyantanairyāṇika*); this concludes the five gates.
Sixth, the delimitation of the components of cultivation is clarified.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
it takes three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to progress from the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) to Buddhahood;
if this duration is reduced, enlightenment will not be achieved.

In the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one passes through the stages of the spiritual lineage (gotra) and the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā), attaining the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
In the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, from the Stage of Joy up to the Stage of Manifestation (abhimukhi), one passes through them and attains the Stage Beyond Manifestation (dūraṅgamā-bhūmi).
In the third asaṃkhyeya [kalpa], having transcended the stages of Non-Obstruction and Unimpeded Abiding, one attains the Supreme Stage.
*Asaṃkhyeya* is a foreign term; it is called "innumerable."
In the Avataṃsaka, there are one hundred and twenty great numbers;
this is the first number.
Furthermore, there are three types of kalpas.
First, an immeasurable number of days, months, and years is called an asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Second, an immeasurable number of intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas), such as the Bhadrakalpa and others, is called an asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
The dimensions of this kalpa are as described by Nāgārjuna:
a city forty *li* in size is filled with mustard seeds,
which are leveled flat with a wooden measure.
If one mustard seed were removed every hundred years,
the kalpa would still not be exhausted when those forty *li* of stone were depleted.
A single *liang* and three *zhu* of celestial raiment, if brushed once every hundred years,
would exhaust the stone yet the kalpa would not yet be exhausted;
three such great kalpas constitute what is called an immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*.
As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,
those sixty-four kalpas, such as the Bhadrakalpa and others, are called a mahākalpa.
For what reason is it definitively stated that there are sixty-four?
There are three kinds of kalpas,
namely those of fire, water, and wind.
Among these three types of kalpas, the fire kalpas are most numerous, the water kalpas are next, and the wind kalpas are the fewest.
Seven fire kalpas and one water kalpa; seven water kalpas and one wind kalpa.
Thus, after a total of seven cycles of seven fire kalpas and one water kalpa, following that final water kalpa, there must again pass seven fire kalpas before a single wind kalpa occurs.
It would thus amount to sixty-four kalpas,
which is also acceptable,
similar to the case of the Bhadrakalpa and its like.
Counting up to the *asaṃkhyeya*, it is called one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
If one discusses the intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to the first bhūmi,
the time already passed amounts to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
One must not say they are one;
if one speaks of a great kalpa, it may be only one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa and must not exceed that.
The same applies to the others. These six sections are concluded.
Next, the limits for severing obstacles during the various stages (*vihāra*) are explained as taught in the *Bhūmivastu*:
there are two distinct types of obstacles.
First is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
namely the four abidings (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*).
Second is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding what is called ignorance (*avidyā*),
that afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has three points of fault,
from the beginning up to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
At that time, all the superior and middling afflictions of the evil destinies are completely transcended.
Among the afflictive obscurations, the two grades of middling and superior are capable of producing evil karma and causing one to receive a body in the evil paths.
Therefore, these are called the afflictions of the evil destinies.
From the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, they are gradually eliminated; at the time of *muditā* (joy), they are exhausted.
From *muditā* up to the abiding in non-development (*anābhoga*), all inferior-grade afflictions are completely transcended.
From the stage of "No-Opening" up until the time of the Supreme Abode, one completely transcends all afflictive habit-energies (*kleśa-vāsanā*).
Upon entering the Tathāgata-abode, there are likewise three types of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
first, the coarse category of ignorance known as the "outer-skin obstruction."
They obstruct the coarse aspect of that Bodhisattva’s dharmakāya;
because they are like the afflictions within the skin of worldly people, they are called "skin obstructions" (tvag-āvaraṇa).
Second, the "flesh obstruction" refers to middling-grade ignorance.
This obstructs the medium-grade dharmakāya of that bodhisattva;
because it is like a malady within the skin of an ordinary person, it is called the "skin obstruction" (tvag-āvaraṇa).
Third is the "bone obstruction" (asthi-āvaraṇa), which is subtle ignorance.
Because it obstructs that Bodhisattva’s subtle Dharma-body,
much like a disease within the bones of an ordinary person, it is called the "bone-obstruction" (asthi-āvaraṇa).
Upon first reaching the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), one completely severs the "skin-obstruction" (tvak-āvaraṇa).
From the stage of joy up to the stage of non-development, one eliminates and exhausts the obstruction of the skin.
From the stage of non-development up to the stage of the Tathāgata, one eliminates and exhausts the obstruction of the bone. Question:
Why is it that among the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are transcended upon the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*),
whereas among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), even the most subtle are only transcended at the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*)? To explain:
The four abodes are coarse and easily abandoned;
therefore, they are overcome first.
Ignorance is difficult to exhaust.
Therefore, there is a subsequent fault.
Furthermore, it is asked:

Why is it that within the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one must separately abandon the residual traces (*vāsanā*) beyond the three grades, whereas for the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), this is not the case?
The commentary states:
The nature of afflictions is the arising of delusion;
therefore, it is taught that the subtle [aspect] constitutes the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
The nature of ignorance is a subtle delusion.
Because "subtle" refers to its level (bhūmi), it is not termed "residue" (vāsanā).
If one speaks of the remnants remaining within the coarse [level], that is what is called residue.
Thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that the Buddha has severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is a brief exposition of the meaning of the thirteen stages (*trayodaśa-vihāra*).
197. The Meaning of Abandoning the Fourteen Defiled Actions (15). Regarding the meaning of abandoning the fourteen defiled actions, it is as explained in the *Sujāta-sūtra* of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
What is this "name"?
It is to be free from the karma of the four fetters, to refrain from committing various evil deeds in the four places,
and to be free from the six ways of wasting wealth.
These constitute the fourteen.
Regarding the abstention from the four karmas: they are the abstention from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech; these are the four.
The paths of action of body and speech comprise seven types.
For what reason are these four specifically guarded against?
It is because, among these four, covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is a grave offense that extends across [all three realms]; therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, these fourteen are the occupational activities of householders.
A householder may be able to restrain these four,
yet they cannot restrain or prohibit the remaining paths of vocal action.
Therefore, it is not said that they are free from [defilements]. Thus, the treatise states:
"Even those who have left the household life cannot yet be free from them."
How much more so for those living at home?
Furthermore, since frivolous speech and the like are contrary to the Dharma, they are all subsumed under false speech;
therefore, they are not discussed separately.
One who does not engage in unwholesome conduct regarding the four bases— namely,
the bases of attachment, aversion, delusion, and fear— does not rely on these bases to give rise to unwholesome conduct.
One who is free from the six ways of squandering wealth.
First, do not indulge in alcohol;
second, do not engage in gambling;
third, do not be dissolute.
Fourth, not being deluded by music and entertainment;
fifth, not associating with evil friends;
sixth, not being indolent or lazy.
It is said that there are six kinds of loss resulting from indulgence in alcohol;
therefore, one must abstain from it.
The first is the loss of wealth.
Second, the arising of illness;
third, mental strife and contention;
fourth, the spread of ill repute.
Fifth, anger and violence arise;
sixth, the eye of wisdom is impaired.
There are likewise six kinds of faults associated with gambling.
Therefore, one should abandon it;
for first, wealth is exhausted,
and second, even toward those born superior, enmity arises.
Third, one is reviled by the wise;
fourth, one is not respected or trusted by others;
fifth, one is alienated from people.
There are six kinds of theft born of joy,
and there are also six kinds of loss resulting from dissipation;
therefore, one must abandon them.
First, not protecting one’s own body;
second, not protecting one’s wealth and possessions;
third, not protecting one’s children and grandchildren.
Fourth, one is constantly filled with alarm and fear.
Fifth, various painful and unwholesome dharmas constantly entwine the body.
Sixth, one delights in giving rise to falsehoods.
There are also six faults in being infatuated with music and performance;
therefore, one must abandon them.
The first is the pursuit of song.
Second, seeking dance;
third, seeking the lute and zither;
fourth, *pāṇavī*.
Five tāla-padas; six śīrṣa-hastas.
These latter three types of measures are not translated [into Chinese] in the sūtras.
One does not know what it is; moreover,
there are six kinds of evil friends with whom one may associate, and for this reason,
one must distance oneself from them.
First, deceiving through expedient means;
second, taking pleasure in secluded places;
third, seducing the family members of others.
Fourth, plotting against the property of others;
fifth, seeking wealth and profit for oneself;
sixth, delighting in exposing the faults of others.
There are likewise six kinds of faults of indolence,
which one should therefore abandon.
The first is being unwilling to perform labor despite possessing wealth and pleasure.
Second, being impoverished and unwilling to practice diligently;
third, during cold weather and unwilling to practice diligently;
fourth, during hot weather and unwilling to practice diligently.
Fifth, when the time is early, one is unwilling to practice diligently;
sixth, when the time is late, one is unwilling to practice diligently.
These constitute the distancing from the fourteen defiled karmas.
The meaning explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* corresponds to this. 198.
The Meaning of Avoiding the Six Directions and Four Evil Friends and Embracing the Four Good Friends (15). This meaning also appears in the *Sujāta-sūtra* within the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
First, to clarify the avoidance of concealing the six directions:
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was the son of an elder named Sujāta.

His ancestors had maintained the tradition of constantly bathing in fragrant water and performing rites toward the six directions, so that the deities of those quarters would come to protect the family estate. Thus, his endeavors were always harmonious and successful;
he even encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
He went to the Buddha and inquired:
"Is there such a teaching within the Dharma of the Noble Ones?
The Buddha then replied:
Within the Dharma of the noble ones, there are likewise six directions,
though they differ from yours.
He then spoke a verse:
Parents are the eastern direction;
teachers and elders are the southern direction;
wives and children are the western direction.
Relatives are the north;
servants and attendants are the nadir;
and śramaṇas are the zenith.
All those sons of householders who pay homage to the various directions,
who act with reverence and propriety without missing the proper time, shall all be reborn in heaven upon death;
they benefit many people through their generous giving and their warm, kind speech.
As stated in that sutra:
among the five ways a child respects and complies with their parents, the first is to show reverence toward the east.
First, to serve and attend to them so as not to cause any transgression or failure;
second, to first inform one's parents before undertaking any action;
third, to respectfully comply with whatever the parents do and not oppose them.
Fourth, they ensure that their parents do not dare to transgress [their will].
Fifth, they do not interrupt the righteous occupations undertaken by their parents.
When a child serves their parents with such reverence, it ensures that they are secure and free from anxiety in that place.
Parents regard their children with respect through five matters:
first, they restrain their children from engaging in evil;
second, they instruct them and point out what is good and what is evil.
Third, to love with compassion that penetrates to the very marrow of one's bones;
fourth, to seek out virtuous spouses for one’s children;
and fifth, to provide whatever is required at the appropriate times.
Regarding the respect shown toward the south:
a disciple should show reverent compliance with five matters toward their teacher.
First, they shall attend to and serve them.
Second, paying homage and making offerings;
third, honoring and looking up to with reverence;
fourth, complying with and not contradicting whatever instructions the teacher gives.
Fifth, one should hear the Dharma from the teacher and retain it well without forgetting.
The teacher, in turn, should regard the disciple with respect through five kinds of matters:
first, by guiding them in accordance with the Dharma.
Second, to instruct them on what they have not yet heard;
third, to cause them to correctly understand the meaning according to what they have heard;
fourth, to point out virtuous friends to them.
Fifth, one exhausts oneself in instructing others with what one knows without parsimony;
this is to revere those in the West.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which a husband reveres his wife.
First, they treat one another with courtesy;
second, their majestic demeanor never oversteps the bounds of propriety;
third, their food and clothing are provided according to the needs of the season.
Fourth, she adorns him at the proper times.
Fifth, she entrusts the affairs of the household to him.
A wife honors her husband with these five matters.
First, rising first;
second, sitting down last;
third, speaking with gentle words.
Fourth is respectful compliance;
fifth is anticipating one's intentions and inquiring after their whereabouts.
This is the respect shown toward those in the north.
A person must respect their kinsmen through five matters:
first, by providing gifts;
second, by speaking kind words.
Third is benefiting others;
fourth is sharing benefits;
fifth is being free from deception.
Relatives must also treat others with affection and respect through five matters:
first, to protect them from negligence;
second, to protect them from the loss of wealth.
Third, to protect against fear;
fourth, to instruct and admonish one another in private;
and fifth, to constantly praise one another’s virtues.
Regarding the five matters for managing subordinates: one should follow and comply with these five points when leading servants and attendants.
First, employ them according to their abilities.
Second, providing food and drink at the appropriate times;
third, bestowing comfort and encouragement at the appropriate times;
fourth, providing medical treatment for those who are ill.
Fifth, one seeks leisure from them;
yet even a servant attends to his master in five matters:
first, he must rise early.
Second, to be comprehensive in one's duties;
third, not to give or take [what is improper];
fourth, to perform tasks in their proper order.
Fifth, praising the name of the patron.
Regarding the service of those above and those in the middle,
the donor must provide the five kinds of requisites to support śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
First, practicing loving-kindness through the body;
second, practicing loving-kindness through speech;
third, practicing loving-kindness through the mind.
Fourth, giving at the proper time.
Fifth, not obstructing when asked.
These six matters should be used by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to instruct the donor.
First, to protect them so that they do not commit evil;
second, to instruct them toward wholesome states;
third, to teach them to harbor a virtuous mind.
Fourth, to cause those who have not heard [the Dharma] to hear it;
fifth, to cause those who have already heard it to understand it;
sixth, to reveal and show the correct path.
Thus, serving with such reverence brings peace and freedom from anxiety to all directions; this concludes the first section.
Next, the avoidance of the four kinds of evil friends is explained, as stated in that sutra:
There are four enemies who should be recognized as being like friends:
first, the friend who subdues through fear, who submits out of dread.
In truth, there is no sincere heart;
this is based on their underlying intent.
Second, though their words are beautiful and their speech is compliant, their hearts are at variance.
This refers to their speech:
though they outwardly show respect and compliance toward their friends, feigning intimacy and attachment,
they harbor no sincere heart within.
This refers to their physical bodies.
Fourth, they are accompanied by evil friends and evil matters.
There are four kinds of intimidation and subjugation.
First, giving before taking back;
fearing [the recipient] at one time, one gives, but when no longer fearing, one takes it back again.
Second, giving little while hoping for much, seeking to obtain without satiety.
Third, they feign intimacy out of fear;
fourth, they falsely seek intimacy in order to escape suffering.
There are four kinds of sweet speech.
First, both good and evil follow from this.
Second, there are difficulties to be abandoned and left behind.
Third, when external goodness approaches, one should stop it with honeyed words.
Fourth, when there is a perilous matter, they immediately slander one another.
There are four ways of showing respect and compliance:
the first is to deceive beforehand.
Second is subsequent deception;
third is manifest deception;
fourth is to inflict corporal punishment upon seeing even a minor transgression.
There are four kinds of evil friends:
first, those who act as friends when drinking alcohol;
second, those who act as friends when gambling.
Third, he is a companion during times of sexual indulgence;
fourth, he is a companion during times of singing and dancing.
One must distance oneself from all such things; having concluded these two sections:
Next, clarify that these encompass the four types of virtuous friends.
As stated in that sutra:
"One should be intimate with the four kinds of kin."
First, one restrains a friend from unwholesome matters;
this refers to their speech.
Second, one feels compassion for a friend’s suffering and pities them; this refers to their mind.
This is based on their underlying intent:
third, the friend who benefits others through beneficial deeds;
and fourth, the friend who shares the same purpose and assists them in their endeavors.
These two are based on the body.
There are four types of restraint (*saṃvara*):
first, being able to restrain oneself upon seeing that others have committed evil.
Second, demonstrating integrity to others,
which means teaching the correct principles;
third, instructing and guiding them with kind words out of a compassionate heart.
Fourth, showing people the correct path and teaching them to cultivate the way out of suffering.
There are four kinds of compassion:
first, rejoicing in the benefit of others upon seeing it.
Second, one feels sorrow upon seeing the evils of the age;
third, one praises the virtues of others;
fourth, when seeing others speak ill of others, one is able to restrain them.
There are four benefits:
first, protecting people so as not to allow them to become negligent;
second, protecting people so that they do not lose their wealth.
Third, protecting people so that they do not experience fear.
Fourth, providing instruction and admonition in private. Regarding the four ways of sharing in the same purpose (*samānārthatā*): [they are as follows].
First, for their sake, one does not begrudge even body or life;
second, for their sake, one does not begrudge wealth or treasures;
third, for their sake, one rescues them from fear and terror.
Fourth, the mutual admonition in private.
These points concerning the separation from concealment have been briefly explained according to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras).

199. The Meaning of the Fourteen Transformational Minds (15): An Exposition by Way of Six Gates. I. Explaining the Names and Defining the Characteristics; II. Classification According to Locus; III. Classification According to the Three Natures; IV. Acquisition, Abandonment, and Accomplishment; V. Distinctions in Transformative Activities; VI. Differences Between the Great and the Small. In the first gate, the names are explained and the characteristics are defined.
That which arises suddenly from non-existence is called "transformation" (hua).
The intention behind this arising transformation is called the "transformative mind" (huaxin).
These transformative minds are not the same.
It is taught as fourteen,
or it is taught as twenty.
Within the Hīnayāna teachings, it is taught as fourteen.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, twenty [stages] are proclaimed;
as for the statement that there are fourteen,
there are two in the first dhyāna.
First, the transformation of the first dhyāna;
second, the transformation of the first dhyāna for the sake of the desire realm.
Regarding the second dhyāna, there are three [types].
First, the second dhyāna manifests as the second dhyāna;
second, the second dhyāna manifests as the first dhyāna;
third, the second dhyāna manifests as the desire realm.
The third dhyāna has four [types]:
one belonging to its own level and three belonging to lower levels.
The four dhyānas consist of five [factors]:
one belonging to their own level and four belonging to lower levels.
It is simply because the followers of the Hīnayāna are unable to manifest transformations in the higher stages; therefore, they possess only fourteen [superknowledges].
As for the statement that there are twenty, it refers to bodhisattvas who develop the supernormal powers based upon the four dhyānas.
Each one is able to manifest as five stages, namely from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna; thus there are twenty.
This is because the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers are sovereign, enabling such a feat.
Since the names and numbers are thus established, what are their characteristics?
There is someone who, having attained supernatural powers through the cultivation of dhyāna,
intends to manifest a transformation and first forms this thought:
"I shall manifest such things through transformation.
Following this thought, one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), where transformations spontaneously appear;
this is called the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
The section on names and characteristics is thus concluded.
Next, we shall discuss the bases (*āyatana*).
There are two distinct types of bases.
There is one basis of reliance,
which exists only in the four dhyānas and not in other stages. Why is this so?
Because there is no meditative concentration in the desire realm, one does not produce emanations.
Even if emanations were produced there, they would merely be wisdom-born.
In the four dhyānas of the formless realm (*ārūpya*), the mental resolve is weak and inferior;
furthermore, because they do not take form (*rūpa*) as an object, these [dhyānas] do not arise.
Within the stages of the form realm, other factors—such as the auxiliary members of meditative absorption (*samādhi-aṅga*)—are incomplete, and thus they lack great functional power.
Therefore, they do not arise.
For this reason, one relies solely upon the four fundamental dhyānas.
Thus, the treatise states:
The five supernormal powers reside in the four dhyānas;
they exist in the fundamental [dhyānas] and not in other concentrations.
Within the four dhyānas, according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there are two types of the first dhyāna.
The second dhyāna has three;
the third dhyāna has four;
the fourth dhyāna has five.
These are fully detailed as listed above.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, each possesses five modes of transformation,
also as explained above.
Second, regarding the places of manifestation:
according to the Hīnayāna,
both the desire realm and the first dhyāna each possess all four [meditative attainments].
That is to say, there is the transformation [body] of that fourth dhyāna stage;
there are three of the second dhyāna;
and there is one of its own stage.
The transformative mind of the higher stages is of two kinds:
there are two in the third dhyāna,
and one belonging to its own stage.
In the higher stages there is one [type of transformation]. In the fourth dhyāna, there is only the transformation belonging to its own stage;
those in higher stages can transform those in lower stages.
Therefore, those below increase in number;
since those below do not transform those above,
those above gradually decrease.
If, according to the Mahāyāna, each of the five stages (*bhūmi*) is fully equipped with the transformative power of the four dhyānas, one asks:
between the transformative mind of the second dhyāna in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the transformative mind of the first dhyāna, which is superior?
If one relies on the perspective of the Hīnayāna, where there are mutual degrees of superiority and inferiority,
within the stages of the desire realm, the emanation of the second dhyāna is superior because it can travel further;
and within the stage of the first dhyāna, the emanation of the first dhyāna is superior because it reaches higher levels.
If one relies on the Mahāyāna perspective, within the stage of the first dhyāna, the transformations produced by the first dhyāna are invariably superior because they occupy a higher level; however,
when departing from that state, their proximity or distance is similar to that of the transformations produced by the second dhyāna belonging to the desire realm.
Because they are equally able to proceed to all stages.
Just as it is when comparing the first and second dhyānas,
the same principle applies to all other stages when compared with one another.
Question: When a dhyāna of a higher stage arises as a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of a lower stage,
does it belong to the lower level or to the higher dhyāna?
The commentary states:
"It follows that,
if this were so, when one relies on the eye-faculty of a higher stage to see forms of a lower stage,"
The visual consciousness produced [therein] would then belong to a lower stage.
To this, the commentary replies:
"This is not analogous."
What does it mean to be "not analogous"?
There are two senses to this explanation.
The first sense is as follows:
Relying on a higher dhyāna, one gives rise to a transformative mind of a lower level;
because this is similar in its coarseness or subtlety to the mind that initiates activity in the lower stage,
it is categorized as belonging to that lower stage.
When the eye-faculty of a higher stage sees forms of a lower stage,
the consciousness produced does not correspond to the lower stage; therefore,
it does not belong to the lower stage.
Regarding the second meaning:
among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), only the power of the body (*kāyavikurvaṇā*) is capable of transformation and manifestation.
Manifestation possesses two capacities.
First, it can initiate an activity at a different time;
even though the creator of the transformation has passed away, the transformation remains as before.
This is like the image left behind by the Buddha after his parinirvāṇa that continued to abide at Rākṣasagiri.
The Mother descended from heaven, rose from her seat, and preached the Dharma.
As for the various Arhats, although their physical bodies had entered parinirvāṇa, they remained as transformed fire to cremate their own bodies;
thus, these two performed their functions in different locations.
Relying on a higher supernormal power,
one gives rise to a lower transformative mind;
among the other supernormal powers, there is no such transformation.
It cannot initiate the functional activity of another level.
When the eye of a higher level perceives visible forms,
the consciousness produced therein does not belong to a lower level.
The ear-consciousness is likewise so; this concludes the two gates.
Next, we shall distinguish the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
There are two kinds of transformation.
Throughout his life he transformed others through wisdom;
it was as if the Māra-king had manifested a transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha),
and all such things were likewise so.
Second is transformation through cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Based on dhyāna, one develops supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); based on these powers, one initiates transformation.
This transformation produced by wisdom is retributive and neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).
Regarding the transformation of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the explanations in the treatises differ.
According to the *Abhidharma*, the essence of the transformed mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*), whereas the essence of cultivated wisdom is wholesome (*kuśala*).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is not the case that the mind for benefiting others arises from the refutation of the *Abhidharma*;
how then could it be indeterminate?
One should know that the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) is invariably wholesome.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, the meaning encompasses two aspects.
If one discusses the arising of transformative activity through conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), it is the same as the Abhidharma;
therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* describes it as the "unspecified meditative absorption of transformation."
The wisdom that knows things as they truly are (yathābhūta-jñāna) is invariably wholesome; this concludes the three gates.
Next, the meaning of acquisition, relinquishment, and accomplishment is explained.
First, its acquisition is discussed.
That which was previously non-existent and now exists is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
There are two kinds of attainment: first, attainment through the separation from desire (*vairāgya-prāpti*).

When ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles sever the fetters of the desire realm and attain the first dhyāna, they suddenly acquire two types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the first dhyāna:
first, transformation within that same level; second, transformation of lower levels.
In this sequence, up until the time one severs the fetters of the third dhyāna,
one suddenly attains the five types of transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the fourth dhyāna:
one belonging to its own level and four belonging to the lower levels.
When a bodhisattva severs the fetters of desire and attains the first dhyāna,
they suddenly acquire five types of transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) of the first dhyāna:
one belonging to their own level and four belonging to other levels.
This applies likewise even up to the category of the fourth dhyāna.
Second is that which is acquired by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*):
through dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*), one loses what is below upon being born above.
At the time of descending and being reborn, one again attains the fundamental dharma, which is called "attained at birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika*).
When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) descends from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the fourth *dhyāna*,
they suddenly attain the five types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the fourth *dhyāna*.
When one is born into the third dhyāna from the first intermediate stage or the fourth stage,
one suddenly attains the four types of transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) of the third dhyāna.
Upon being born into that first dhyāna, one suddenly attains the two types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the first dhyāna.
For śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is no possibility of retrogression from such a birth.
For this reason, it is not discussed.
A Bodhisattva born in a higher realm does not lose the dharmas of the lower realms;
therefore, there is no attainment through birth.
Not only does one who is born in the higher realms not lose the dharmas of the lower realms,
but even until the attainment of the fruit of Great Nirvāṇa, one does not abandon worldly affairs.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Without abandoning the world, one attains great nirvana;
without severing afflictions, one enters nirvana.
If even the afflictions are not severed, how much less so other meritorious qualities?
Next, the meaning of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is discussed.
That which previously existed but is now lost is termed "relinquishment.
There are two kinds of relinquishment.
First is "receding and abandoning.
When a śrāvaka or ordinary person recedes from that first dhyāna and gives rise to afflictions of the desire realm,
they simultaneously lose the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the first dhyāna.
Even when one regresses and gives rise to the fetters of the third dhyāna,
one suddenly loses the five types of transformation-minds of the fourth dhyāna;
when a Bodhisattva regresses, they lose five [minds] in each stage.
Second is the arising of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
When śrāvakas and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are born into a higher stage, they lose the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the lower stage;
this is termed "equanimity."
When one is born into the second dhyāna, one suddenly loses the two types of transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the first dhyāna;
continuing in this manner, when one is born into the fourth dhyāna stage, one suddenly loses the five types of transformation-minds of all four dhyānas.
Next, the discussion concerns accomplishment (*siddhi*).
To possess something and not lose it is called accomplishment.
This is according to the *Abhidharma*, regarding phenomena that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The lower [levels] accomplish the upper, but the upper do not accomplish the lower.
For this reason, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, while their bodies reside in the desire realm or the stage of the first dhyāna,
each produce the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the four dhyānas.
Within the second dhyāna, one achieves the three types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the two higher dhyānas;
those of the lower stages are not achieved.
When the body is in the third dhyāna, one achieves the two types of transformative minds of the three higher dhyānas.
In the fourth dhyāna, one achieves only the single type of transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta) belonging to that level;
however, when a Bodhisattva’s body resides anywhere from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they achieve all types.
Because there is no loss, these four gates are concluded.
Next, the activities performed by the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) are explained,
as set forth in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dìchí lùn).
In brief, there are only three:
first, the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body),
which refers to manifesting the physical forms of sentient beings.
Second, the realm of transformation:
transforming external objects such as form, fragrance, taste, and so forth.
Third, the transformation of sound.
Within the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are four divisions according to form;
eight are discussed according to location, and there are likewise eight according to activity.
Regarding the fourfold division by form, it is as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra).
It is just as when the master of the transformation appears as a person,
and the transformed person resembles himself.
The forms and types of devas, nāgas, and so forth are all likewise.
Second, they do not resemble one's own body;
for instance, devas are human.
When they cease, they likewise transform into humans;
yet these do not resemble their own original selves,
and the same applies to others as well.
Third, the transformation resembling another's body:
while the other person is a human being,
the transformed person resembles them.
The same applies to the devas and others.
Fourth, they do not resemble others:
although these beings transform themselves back into human form, they do not resemble those [original] humans.
The same applies to the gods and so forth.
Regarding the eight [types] based on location, as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*:
first, one manifests a body of oneself and dwells in one's own stage.
Second, manifesting as another's body while remaining in one's own stage;
third, manifesting as one's own body and proceeding to another's stage;
fourth, manifesting as another's body and proceeding to another's stage.
What is the meaning of this?
When the master of the emanation remains within the first dhyāna and emanates both his own body and other bodies as belonging to the first dhyāna,
he abides in that first dhyāna, thereby constituting both the first and second [categories].
One transforms one's own body and the bodies of others into those of the First Dhyāna;
descending to the Desire Realm constitutes the latter two [transformations].
Since this is the case for the body in the First Dhyāna when manifesting transformations, so it is for the others.
This applies even when the body is in the fourth dhyāna;
thus ends the first set of four.
Fifth, one transforms oneself into the body of another stage and then dwells in that other stage.
Sixth, manifesting as another person in another stage and remaining in that other stage;
seventh, manifesting as one's own body in another stage and returning to one's own stage;
eighth, manifesting as another person in another stage and returning to one's own stage.
What is the meaning of this?
When the master of the transformation resides within the desire realm and gives rise to the mind of transformation based on the first dhyāna,
he designates that very first dhyāna as his own level.
The locations of the desire realm are designated as "other grounds. For this reason,
when one manifests a transformed body of oneself or another within the desire realm, it is called "abiding on other grounds."
Taking the former two as the basis, one uses these two transformations to go to the First Dhyāna; this is called "reaching one's own level.
Taking the latter two as the basis, one proceeds likewise.
Just as it is when comparing the desire realm with the first dhyāna,
so it is for all stages when compared to one another.
Regarding the eight matters, they are as Nāgārjuna has explained.
First, the ability to make things small;
second, the ability to make things large;
third, the ability to make things light.
Fourth, the power of mastery, such as making the large small and so forth;
fifth, the power of accomplishment, being a sovereign with effective agency;
sixth, the power of reaching distant places.
Seventh, the ability to move the earth;
eighth, the ability to obtain whatever one desires at will—such are the transformations of the body.
Next, the transformation of the environment is explained.
Within this, there are two types:
first, manifesting all objects within one's own stage;
second, manifesting all objects within other stages.
Next, the emanated voice is explained.
Within emanated voices, there are briefly only two types:
first, internal; second, external.
The sounds produced by sentient beings are designated as internal;
the sounds produced by all other grasses, trees, and so forth are designated as external.
Within the internal category, they are divided into four types based on human beings.
First, manifesting sounds similar to one's own;
second, manifesting those dissimilar;
third, manifesting the sounds of other sentient beings.
Fourth, there are seven characteristics of non-likeness (*asādṛśya-anuvyañjana*),
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
first, the perfection of exquisite voice (*svara-saṃpad*).
Second, the perfection of broad resonance;
third, arising from oneself;
fourth, arising from others.
Fifth, there is nothing from which they arise.
Sixth, they preach the True Dharma.
Seventh, they provide instruction according to specific circumstances.
Each of these is explained in detail as in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dizhilun).
The specific functions among external sounds are immeasurable and cannot be discussed in full. Thus concludes this fifth gate.
Next, the meaning of the differences between the Great and Small [Vehicles] is explained.
There are six points of difference.
First, the difference in the object of focus (ālambana) and the mind.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the mind that takes objects as its support undergoes transformation;
whatever is manifested arises through deliberate mental attention (*manasikāra*).
In the teachings of the Mahāyāna, one begins with deliberate mental attention and ultimately achieves non-deliberation (*amanasikāra*).
There is no mental discrimination,
for the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness causes all sentient beings to see [it] spontaneously.
Second, there is a difference in degree.
A śrāvaka can transform with a single mind only one thing and cannot do so infinitely;
a bodhisattva, with a single mind, can manifest all forms and sounds throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Third, they differ in their breadth and scope:
Śrāvakas can transform only a single world-system,
whereas Bodhisattvas do not limit themselves in this way.
They are able to manifest emanations throughout all worlds.
Fourth, there is a difference in their range of reach:
while a śrāvaka manifests emanations within a single buddha-field, they do not reach other realms.
Bodhisattvas manifest transformations that reach immeasurable realms,
such as when Vimalakīrti dispatched a manifested bodhisattva to the Fragrant Accumulation World and other such instances.
Fifth, there is the distinction between having a mind and being without a mind.
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas manifest as humans, they have no intentionality therein;
whereas Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest with intentionality.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
He transforms immeasurable people, each causing them to possess a mind.
This is because the Buddha-mind pervades all places; thus, he transforms those who have existence.
The six realms differ in their reality and emptiness.
Although the emanations of clothing and other such things produced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not yield practical utility,
the transformative acts performed by Buddhas and bodhisattvas do indeed yield practical utility.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) is likewise. *Dacheng yizhang*, Scroll Fifteen.
*Mahāyāna-artha-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle 18, Compiled by Dharma Master Yuan. Section 2:
Dharmas of the Fruit (Eighteen Sections). Within the dharmas of the fruit of the pure dharma-aggregate, there are eighteen sections. This fascicle contains two sections: [The Great Parinirvāṇa...]
The Meaning of *pāra*: The meaning of unsurpassed *bodhi*. 205. The Meaning of *nirvāṇa* (18).

The Meaning of *nirvāṇa* explained through a fivefold classification: 1. The limits of cessation; 2. The definitive essence; 3. Distinguishing characteristics through opening and closing; 4. Analysis of miscellaneous meanings; 5. [Title]. First, the explanation of the name.
"Nirvāṇa" is a term from the language of India.
According to its full expression, it is called *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
"Mahā" means "great."
There are six great meanings.
The first is the meaning of permanence.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
What is called "great" (mahat) is termed "permanent" (nitya).
For example, if a person has an immeasurable lifespan, they are called a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa).
Second, it has the meaning of "vastness."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is called 'Great' has a nature that is vast and expansive;
it is like empty space, reaching everywhere."
Nirvana is thus; therefore, it is called "vast.
Third is the sense of "many meanings."
The discerning capacities are not one;
thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"It is like a great treasury containing many rare and wondrous treasures."
Nirvāṇa is likewise;
because it contains many various kinds of exquisite dharmas and rare jewels,
it is called "Great."
Fourth is the profound meaning.
It is deep, vast, and difficult to fathom;
as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The "Great" is called inconceivable.
Because all those in the world— whether śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— cannot fathom the meaning of nirvāṇa,
it is called great.
Fifth is "exalted meaning" (*udāra-artha*).
Its status and rank are so elevated that others cannot reach them.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
For example, just as no person in the world can reach the summit of a great mountain,
it is therefore called "great.
Nirvana is likewise.
Ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and even all bodhisattvas cannot fathom its limits;
therefore, it is called "Great.
Sixth is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Just as those who are superior and preeminent in the world are called "Great Beings" (mahāpuruṣa),
so too is nirvāṇa; it is the most excellent among all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "Great.
Such is the meaning of "Great.
What, then, is this "Great"?
There are three kinds of Greatness.
First is the Greatness of Essence (*tài-dà*).
The essence of the Nirvana of Innate Purity exhausts true nature and its meaning pervades the Dharma-realm.
Second is the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*):
its skillful means and nirvāṇa are such that there is no transcendence not exhausted and no virtue not fully prepared.
Third is the greatness of its function (*karmamahātmya*).
The wondrous function of responding through transformation and entering nirvana is vast and expansive, manifesting inexhaustibly;
thus the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The Great Parinirvāṇa is able to establish great significance."
The meaning of "yi" (義) is "usage" (yòng).
As for what is called "pan" (般), this is translated as "entry" (rù).
There are three meanings of entry.
First, regarding entry according to ultimate reality:
ceasing delusion to return to the truth,
proceeding from cause toward fruition.
Second, in contrast to the true and the responsive,
one ceases transformation and returns to the true;
therefore, it is called "entering."
The third [meaning] refers exclusively to what is present:
because one abandons the faults of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and enters into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it is called "entry."
Regarding the term "nirvāṇa," some scholars of the human race explain it as follows:
others explain that the name "nirvāṇa" belongs neither to the Hu nor to the Han; it is simply the Buddha’s own word.
If we discuss the Buddha’s words, all of them are [the ultimate truth];
how could it be the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* alone?
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
Various treatises, writings, and incantations are all spoken by the Buddha.
Although they are spoken by the Buddha, they do not depart from local dialects;
if they were to depart from local dialects, the Buddha would have nothing to say.
The essence of nirvāṇa is not names;
therefore, it is not sound.
For this reason, some people further say:
"Nirvāṇa" is a foreign term that encompasses all myriad virtues;
since no single name exists in this land that can translate it,
we retain the foreign original and speak of it as "nirvāṇa."
The essence of nirvāṇa truly possesses all virtues;
however, the single name "nirvāṇa" does not exhaustively encompass all these virtues.
If the name "nirvāṇa" were to exhaustively encompass all virtues, [it would be inadequate].
This is precisely when one proclaims the myriad virtues;
one should not establish further names based on those virtues.
When one wishes to express the meaning of "permanence," one establishes the name "permanent" to designate that meaning, and so it is in all such cases.
It is clearly known that "nirvāṇa" is named after the virtue of inexhaustibility;
furthermore, the name "nirvāṇa" is established [for this purpose].
Since the ten thousand virtues are subsumed here [in this land], we likewise use the collective term "ten thousand virtues" as a translation for that *nirvāṇa*.
Why should it not be permissible to do so?
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
According to the various sounds of their species, he universally addresses all sentient beings:
"Today the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa. He speaks differently according to each species.
How can this not be translated? If it were translated according to its literal characteristics, it would be called "extinction" (nirodha).
According to their respective meanings, various alternative translations are used;
sometimes it is called "non-arising" (不生) and sometimes "non-emergence" (不出).
Some call it "unconditioned action" (anabhisamskāra), some call it "non-arising" (anutpāda),
and others name it "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta).
Some call it signless;
some say it does not burn;
others say it is non-conscious.
Some call it quiescence;
some say it is peace and security;
others name it liberation.
Or it is called "the other shore.
Such various [terms] are all as explained in the sūtras.
How is it known that this refers to cessation and not to the whole?
Now, let us examine this by means of four points.
First, we shall seek it according to what was established in the past;
for the Tathāgata previously, in other sūtras, [stated as follows].
"Ordinarily, you have taught that the extinction of afflictions, the non-existence of the body, and the loss of consciousness constitute nirvana.
Today, the name 'nirvana' is no different from before;
why then do you suddenly say it is total [extinction]?"
Second, it is verified by the final event:
as the Tathāgata was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he issued a great voice that reached everywhere,
proclaiming, "Today, the Tathāgata is about to enter nirvāṇa."
At that time, all sentient beings, hearing of the Buddha’s nirvana, were filled with grief and distress; they went before the Buddha and entreated him to remain.
If the name "nirvana" contains ten thousand virtues, then it would be fitting to proclaim those ten thousand virtues to show them to people.
Sentient beings ought to rejoice.
Why, then, do they approach the Buddha in grief and distress to entreat him to remain?
Upon hearing of the Buddha’s nirvana, they are overcome with sorrow and distress, and thus entreat him to stay.
It is clearly known that *nirvāṇa* is cessation, not total [annihilation].
The three [remaining points] are established according to the terminology of the definitive scriptures.
When people from foreign lands see someone die, they all say,
"So-and-so has entered *nirvāṇa*.
Why do people of the world, upon death, collectively refer to it as *nirvāṇa*, even though there is no virtue therein?
Ordinary people call death and extinction "nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is clearly known that nirvāṇa is cessation, not total [annihilation].
The text of the four graspings serves as proof;
as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
when the Buddha praised Cunda.
Excellent, excellent!
You are able to understand that the Tathāgata’s manifestation of entering parinirvāṇa through skillful means is identical to that of ordinary beings.
Among the sentient beings of the world, when has there ever been such a parinirvāṇa endowed with those ten thousand virtues?
The Tathāgata manifests in accordance with this teaching, appearing to undergo extinction together with the world;
this is what is meant by "entering parinirvāṇa.
This is clearly understood.
Nirvana is cessation, not totality.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states that after the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had finished preaching the Lotus Sūtra, [he entered parinirvāṇa].
In the latter part of the night, he entered *nirvāṇa*.
In the subsequent verse section, it is stated that the Buddha passed into extinction that night like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted;
in the prose (*gadya*) portion, it says he spoke of *nirvāṇa*.
The verse says "extinction" (nirvāṇa).
It is clearly understood that *nirvāṇa* is cessation, not total annihilation.
Question: If nirvāṇa is cessation, why does the sūtra state that the extinction of the fires of the fetters is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa),
and that it is termed "nirvāṇa" because it is free from applied and sustained thought?
The commentary states:
In foreign lands, there are many names for "cessation" (nirodha).
Briefly, there are three distinct types.
The first is nirvāṇa,
which is translated as "extinction.
The second is Merudhara.
This is also called cessation.
Third is the Vinaya;
this is also called cessation.

Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all Buddha-dharmas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—are fully present;
they are not separate, not severed, not detached, and not different.
Since it is said they are "not separate," this clarifies that there is no distinct nature.
Since dharmas have no distinct intrinsic nature, how could they not be empty?
Furthermore, dharmas of identical substance must necessarily establish one another;
in the case of mutually establishing dharmas, there is both the general and the particular.
When particulars are subsumed to form a whole, all phenomena can exist;
yet when the whole is divided back into its particulars, the characteristic of the whole is no longer established.
How, then, could they not be empty?
If the whole were divided into parts,
the meaning of the whole would not be empty; since it arises from the division of the five aggregates,
that arising should likewise not be empty.
The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is thus.
If one were to say that *nirvāṇa* truly exists and is not empty, this meaning would be incorrect.
As it is said in the sūtra:
Nirvana is not existent;
it is said to exist only in accordance with worldly convention. Nirvana is not existent.
What is meant by "not empty"?
Furthermore, the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra* states:
"That which is empty of its own intrinsic nature is called 'purity by nature' (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*)."
How is it that nirvāṇa of identical characteristics is not empty?
Furthermore, the sūtra states:
"Bodhi and nirvāṇa are all empty."
How can it be said that [nirvana] truly exists?
Furthermore, if nirvana truly exists and is not empty, then grasping at nirvana with right view would not be erroneous.
Why, then, did the Buddha refute this by teaching emptiness and non-self?
Furthermore, if nirvana were truly permanent and not empty,
then the view of permanence would not be a fault.
If it is said that nirvana is empty because the mind of deluded sentiment grasps at its characteristics, it is therefore called "empty."
If the essence of nirvāṇa were definitively non-empty,
this would contradict the scriptural teaching that nirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, that which is "existent" is so called because it can possess other [attributes], and is therefore designated as existent.
The substance [of the self] ought not to exist.
If the person then defends themselves by saying, "I say it does not exist," [the response is:
since you yourself lack the characteristics of another, how could there be another?
This should be further investigated:
the sūtras proclaim that it is in dependence upon the tathāgatagarbha that there is birth and death.
Relying on the Great Nirvāṇa, one can establish the great purpose and give rise to various transformations;
this is precisely what constitutes "having others.
If one says there are no others, then because one lacks others oneself, it is impossible for there to be others.
If it exists, it already possesses an "other," and thus cannot be without an other;
this is one difficulty.
Furthermore, if it does not exist, it would be entirely without an other.
Yet its essence is not non-existent; thus, while that which exists is invariably something other [than the essence], the essence itself is not that [other].
Although existence is indeed other [than the essence], this does not preclude the existence of the essence itself.
Thus, even if that which is non-existent has no other [counterpart], what prevents its essence from being non-existent?
To be either exclusively existent or exclusively non-existent is a great affliction within the Buddha-dharma;
it must be extensively refuted according to principle.
Such is its essential nature.

This nirvāṇa is the wondrous fruit of the perfect quiescence of all Buddhas.

Because its meaning fills the Dharma-realm, its virtues are complete within every atom;

This single point is as explained in the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
Thus, that text states:
Birth and death are of two kinds:
conditioned and unconditioned.
Nirvāṇa is likewise of two kinds.

Birth and death by way of fragmentation is called conditioned;
birth and death by way of transformation is called unconditioned.
These two have been extensively analyzed as before in the context of the two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The nirvāṇa attained when conditioned birth-and-death has been exhausted and no longer exists is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Because there are still further births and deaths remaining beyond that point,

The nirvana attained when the conditioned births and deaths have been completely exhausted and there is no place left for them is called "nirvana without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa).
Because there is no further birth-and-death beyond this point,
and because there is also no other nirvana. Next,

The schools differ in their tenets,
and what they teach varies accordingly. Some say:
In the Abhidharma system, the total extinction of afflictions is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).
When one is far removed from the bonds of conditions within the body that experiences retribution in the present life,
this is described as *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
This interpretation is incorrect.
The afflictions of one's own continuum bind all internal and external objects;
for a noble one beyond training (aśaikṣa), these bonds have already been severed at the very moment they first attain the fruit.
At that time, it is not called "nirvana without remainder.
Only after the present body and consciousness have ceased does one then proclaim "nirvana without remainder."
On what basis can it be said that the body’s liberation from the bonds of conditions is called "nirvana without remainder"? If this is not it, then what is?
In the Abhidharma system, the essence of nirvana is one.
Regarding the statement that "the substance is one" while designating two names based on different perspectives:
within this school, [these refer to] afflictions, karma, and volition.
By the power of the Path, that which should arise does not arise; this analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is the essence of *nirvāṇa*.
This essence is one.
Based on the body and wisdom, two designations are established.

as there remains further body and wisdom in comparison to what follows.

When body and wisdom are completely exhausted and one proceeds toward nirvana, it is renamed "nirvana without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*), because in relation to what follows, there is no further remainder of body or wisdom.
Question: At the place where body and wisdom are entirely exhausted, [what remains?]
For what reason is it not called *nirvāṇa*?
According to that school, because the body and cognition arise and then pass away, they are subject to impermanent cessation; therefore, they are not *nirvāṇa*.
Since the cause has been severed, subsequent effects do not arise.

According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the essence of nirvāṇa is twofold:

The exhaustion of the fruits of birth and death is one nirvāṇa;

Question: [Why is this?]
Why is it that in the Abhidharma system, the exhaustion of the fruits of birth and death is not called "Nirvana," whereas in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* it is so designated?
The explanation states:
[This is because] in the Abhidharma, one seeks [the truth] within the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.
That which is directly severed by the Path is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is not directly severed is not analytical cessation.

If a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) brings about the cessation of the appropriation of retribution by means of the knowledge of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*), it is termed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

These four names each have two meanings:

which perfumes and awakens the true mind so that various virtues arise.

the merit produced through cultivation is directly termed *bodhi*.

it possesses no sense of arising.

Because they are perfectly penetrating, as explained in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

cultivation that reveals bodhi is termed intrinsic purity.

for since both types enter nirvāṇa,
there must also be a distinction between them based on the names "inherently pure" and "expedient."

thus, in that sūtra, the characteristic of purity is liberation.

it is not something that was previously defiled and later becomes free from defilement.

Not arising from causes and conditions, it is intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). Question:
It can be understood that the fruit is attained through the cultivation of skillful means based on conditions;
the nirvana of intrinsic purity is the realization of the object-condition.
Is it not the case that this fruit does not manifest from conditions?
The explanation says:
it is not fixed.
It is both a fruit and not a fruit.
What is the meaning of this?
Although its essence is not a fruit, it is only upon reaching Buddhahood that it is fully realized as such.
Because it is that which the Buddha has thoroughly realized, it is called the "fruit.
It is because of this fruit that the *Dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages) proclaims:
the cessation of the Buddha’s practices and meditative concentrations is precisely *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity).
How could that which is practiced by the Buddhas not be a fruit?
Furthermore, how could the subtle essence and characteristics of the wisdom of all Buddhas not be a fruit?
At the moment of attainment, it is free from conditions and has no cause to be requited.
It may be said that it is not a fruit;
because it is not a fruit, the Sūtra extols the Buddha,
stating that he has attained the dharma that is without cause and without karmic retribution.
Furthermore, the Sūtra also states:
"The essence of Nirvāṇa is neither cause nor fruit.
Since this is the case for Nirvāṇa, all its qualities are likewise so.
Fourth, the distinction between essence and function is twofold.
All that was previously explained regarding the essence of nirvāṇa is termed "purity of nature" (prakṛti-viśuddhi);
its function is designated as "expedient means" (upāya).
Because it employs skillful means regarding signs,
it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Its essential nature is eternally quiescent.
Therefore, it is called "purity of nature.
Fifth, regarding the distinction between principle and phenomena, there are two parts.
All the previously mentioned skillful means of the practices and virtues of nirvana are termed "expedient means" (upāya).
The essence of reality is eternally quiescent;
this is described as "inherently pure.
This is precisely the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering within the Sūtras.
Question: How does this principle differ from the "innate purity" (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*) discussed previously in the third pair? Answer:
It is explained as follows.
The essence is one;
it is divided according to its meanings.
As for the previously explained nirvana of intrinsic purity:
The encompassing of phenomena—from human beings to the Buddha—is that which is exhausted by the Buddha and realized through practice.
Having realized it, the skillful means are without concealment or manifestation, and without cause or fruit.
What is now termed "principle" (li) is discussed in terms of the eternal dharma.
In all Buddhas, the single suchness is neither defiled nor pure, neither hidden nor manifest, and neither cause nor fruit; it is only through these distinctions that differences arise.
Among the five kinds of natures taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the meaning of the "neither-cause-nor-fruit" nature corresponds to this gate.
It is simply because when one investigates reality to discuss its actual nature, there are no conditions apart from reality;
thus, conditions do not exist. This is what is known.
Furthermore, based on what are defilement and purity spoken of, and cause and fruit spoken of? Therefore, it is neither defilement nor purity, neither cause nor fruit;
such is its essential nature and characteristic.
Next, we shall determine its cause.
First, we shall distinguish its causes by means of the preceding pairs.
Regarding the first pair mentioned above, the meaning of the cultivation of merit through expedient means (*upāya*) is explained as being twofold.
From the perspective of its arising, it is termed "purity of expedient means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*).
From the perspective of the meaning of its manifestation, it is termed "naturally pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*).
Now, we shall distinguish its causes by means of those very conditions—the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
There are three ways of distinguishing these causes.
First, discernment based on correct objects;
second, discernment arising from birth;
third, discernment produced by formation.
How is this so? From the perspective of its essence, it is considered the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*hetu*) from the standpoint of its functional aspect,
because within the Buddha-nature there is the sense of being capable of arising.
There is a meaning that can be relied upon to produce those virtues;
therefore, it serves as the direct cause (hetu).
The various practices such as the perfections (pāramitās) are taught to be the conditions (pratyaya).
This is similar in meaning to the principle that the Buddha-nature within nirvana serves as the direct cause,
while the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment acts as the condition,
resulting in the fruit of bodhi.
When analyzed according to the characteristics of the factors of merit produced through cultivation, these are themselves bodhi;
therefore, they are identical to it.
From the perspective of their functioning through the power of those conditions, they constitute the primary causes for the various perfections (pāramitās).
Buddha-nature acts as the condition for the generative causes of the six perfections within nirvana;
Buddha-nature is the revealing cause.
The attainment of the fruit of bodhi is similar in meaning [to this].
"Arising" (sheng) is precisely the primary cause (zheng),
while "understanding" (liao) is the condition (yuan).
Next, we discuss arising and producing.

From the perspective of the essence of that Buddha-nature, when viewed from the standpoint of its functional manifestation, the various perfections (pāramitās) are the causes for the arising of Buddha-nature, while [the essence itself] is the consummation.
This is because Buddha-nature is the cause of arising.
Nirvana is thus proclaimed.
Although buddha-nature is non-existent, it is not the same as a rabbit’s horn;
for while a rabbit’s horn cannot be produced by any measure of skillful means, [buddha-nature can be realized].
The Buddha-nature can be brought forth;
because it can be brought forth, it is called the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). The various perfections (*pāramitā*) are the revealing causes (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
Within *nirvāṇa*, there is furthermore a "revealing cause" (*viddhetu*).

The meaning of the six *pāramitās* and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is similar [to this]. If one considers them from the perspective of the sense of being activated by the power of conditions (*pratyaya*), [they function as a revealing cause].
The causes for delivering sentient beings are the nature of Buddhahood as the cause of realization;
within Nirvana, there is further the cause of production,
namely the six pāramitās and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the nature of the Buddha as the revealing cause and bodhi share a similar meaning.
Taking the nature of the Buddha as the object,
one accomplishes the virtues of a Buddha by perceiving that nature.
Therefore, it is said that [the cause] is "productive.
Next, the treatise discusses "production" (janana) and "functioning" (kāraṇa). These terms—production-cause and functioning-cause—provide a general explanation for all [causes].
According to their characteristics, they may be provisionally distinguished as having no lack of difference. How do these differing characteristics function?
That which arises through the power of conditions that differentiate a single object is termed the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The designation of "causal agent" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Buddhahood (*buddhadhātu*) is described as the "generative cause" (*janana-hetu*) because it possesses the sense of being producible, arising from conditions within itself.
The second is the quality of being able to proclaim dependent origination, which is called the "causal condition for arising" (*janana-hetu*).
The Buddha-nature becoming perfected qualities is called the "causal condition for production" (*nirmāṇa-hetu*),
just as gold is fashioned into vessels.
The initial correspondence is as described above.
Next, in correspondence with the second [point], the two types of nirvāṇa—those attained through cultivation and those manifested through cultivation—are established by determining their causes.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, discernment based on conditions;
second, discernment that gives rise to birth.
How is it that it is based on conditions?
To judge roughly between the manifest and the hidden in relation to the fruit of intrinsic purity:
the Buddha-nature is the direct cause,
while the various perfections serve as the conditions.
Regarding the primary causes for the fruits of the skillful means and the various perfections (pāramitās),
buddha-nature serves as the condition (pratyaya).
To speak with ultimate precision, these are considered in relation to the two types of nirvāṇa.
In both [traditions], the Buddha-nature is taught as the direct cause (*hetu*).
However, within the Buddha-nature there are two meanings:
first, the Dharma-Buddha-nature;...
The first is the dharma-body as it inherently exists, like gold within ore;
the second is the Buddha-nature of retributive fruition.
Within the substance of this Dharma, there is the principle that it can arise in accordance with conditions, yet there is no separate dharma-substance.
It is like gold within ore, which possesses the potential to be fashioned into ornamental objects;
even before the ornaments exist, they are already present within the gold.
That dharma-buddha-nature, in relation to the fruit of intrinsic purity, is called the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That retribution-buddha-nature, in relation to the fruit of skillful means, is called the direct cause.
The various perfections (*pāramitās*) are not fixed.
What is the indeterminate?
There are three aspects to the six perfections.
First, the cultivation of the six perfections through their objects.
That is to say:
practicing all activities within the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness;
second, truly engaging in the performance of the six perfections.
Relying on prior conditions, one cultivates and awakens the true mind, causing all merits within that mind to arise;
this is the third: the six perfections of true non-action.
The true mind is fundamentally the nature of all meritorious virtues;
when manifested through conditions,
it is called the six perfections of reality and non-action.
In relation to the fruit of expedient means (*upāya*), the six *pāramitās* of "truly having activity" (*satya-sakriyā*) are also the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*),

while the other two [the fruits of nature-purity and wisdom] serve as conditions (*pratyaya*). In relation to the fruit of nature-purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), the six *pāramitās* of "truly being without activity" (*satya-niṣkriyā*) constitute its direct cause.
The other two serve as conditions.
Next, we discuss arising and production:
in relation to those fruits of skillful means, buddha-nature is their productive cause (*janakahetu*).
The nature of aspiration and the pure fruit are its "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).
Because there is the sense of being able to produce [the fruit] within the essence of Buddha-nature, it produces the fruit of skillful means;
therefore, it is called the "producing cause" (*janaka-hetu*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Although the Buddha-nature is non-existent, it is not the same as a rabbit’s horn. Why is this?
Because a rabbit’s horn cannot be produced, whereas the Buddha-nature can be produced; therefore, it is called a "cause of production."
The Buddha-nature inherently possesses the meaning of being manifestable and realizable;
ultimately, through its manifestation and realization, it becomes the fruit of pure nature.
Therefore, in relation to that fruit, it is designated as the "cause of realization."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Although the Buddha-nature differs from empty space, why is this so?"
Although space cannot be seen despite immeasurable skillful means,
the Buddha-nature can be seen;
because it possesses the meaning of being visible and intelligible, it is called the "cause of understanding."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The cause of nirvāṇa is what is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The nature of Buddha-nature does not give rise to nirvāṇa."
Therefore, it is called the "revealing cause" (vijñapti-hetu).
The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are not fixed. Why are they not fixed?
The three types of the six perfections have already been explained as before.
In relation to the fruit of skillful means, the six pāramitās that involve actual effort are also the cause of production,
just as milk produces curd and curd produces clarified butter.
Up to the stage of *sarpis* (clarified butter), these successive stages that give rise to one another are all called "causes of production" (*janakahetu*);
the remaining two are called "causes of manifestation" (*vyañjanahetu*).
Because it is not [merely] correct arising,
everything is termed "realization" in relation to the fruit of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-phala*).
By ultimately perfecting and manifesting the six perfections through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), one accomplishes the fruit of intrinsic purity.
Because they can manifest and bring about clear understanding, they are called "causes of manifestation" (*vijñapti-hetu*).
As for the other two, they are called "causes of manifestation" because they manifest their distinct characteristics.
Why, then, are the two causes—the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) and the creative cause (*nirmāṇa-hetu*)—not mentioned?
Regarding the fruit of expedient means (*upāya*), there is arising and activity,
as has already been distinguished above.
Regarding the fruit of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), there is neither arising nor activity.
Therefore, we shall not discuss it further.
Next, with respect to the third [category], we shall determine its cause by examining both cultivation and realization in relation to the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the fruit of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-phala*), the explanations of conditions, the correct [cause], and arising have already been concluded.
As explained above,
that nature-pure fruit realizes the extinction of conditions; therefore,
it cannot be described in terms of conditions, nor in terms of correctness, nor in terms of arising.
One simply knows that equality is not of the nature of cause and effect.
When the Buddha was originally in the state prior to realization, it is conventionally described as the cause;
when he subsequently attained realization, it is described as the fruit.
Furthermore, at the time of subsequent realization, one reaches the understanding that there was originally no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because there is no object-condition, the original state is neither a cause nor is it now an effect.
Next, one determines its cause by looking toward the fourth type of *nirvāṇa*, which is characterized by the relative nature of essence and function.
Within this category, the purity of the essence of *nirvāṇa* is termed "purity of nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
Nirvana is purified through the skillful means of purity.
This refers to the cause as explained above in contrast to the essence of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
One should know that what is called "purity through skillful means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*) is as follows:
This refers to the nirvana of transformation through response.
There are two kinds of such response:
first, the response of the Dharma.
Second is retribution and response,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"The Great Parinirvāṇa can establish great meanings and manifest various transformations."
This is the principle of their dharma.
The various manifestations produced by the power of the vow of great compassion are termed "retribution-response" (pao-ying).
Now, in contrast to these two, their cause is established.
There are two kinds of discrimination:
first, discrimination that takes the correct as its object;
second, discrimination that arises from birth.
As for what constitutes the correct [teaching]:
the Dharma school takes the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) gate within the Tathāgatagarbha as the standard.

Just as in the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], the various Dharma-gates sought by the youth Sudhana have their arising function precisely because they take this fundamental power of great compassionate vows as their condition;
although those dharmas exist, it is through this that their functional utility can be activated.
