Just as obtaining an object is termed "non-object," the Tathāgata may further,
according to specific circumstances, take it away;
he proclaims that the nirvāṇa attained by the two vehicles possesses only bliss and purity, but lacks self and permanence.
As stated in the seventh chapter on virtues of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have attained the untainted Eightfold Noble Path,
they possess bliss and purity.
Furthermore, because the causes of delusion are extinguished, it is said that there is purity;
because the suffering of segmented existence (*paricchinna-duḥkha*) has been abandoned, it is said that there is bliss.
Because the essence of that limited nirvāṇa is not real and its functioning is not sovereign, it is not called "self" (*ātman*).
The body and consciousness that have been extinguished will arise once more;
therefore, they are not called permanent. Question:
Once the body and consciousness have been extinguished,
by what cause would they arise again? He replied:
That birth is itself the fruit of transformation;
by means of the cause of previously cultivated untainted karma,
with ignorance as its condition, it can arise again.
Regarding "conditioned by ignorance":
at the time of entering nirvana, the deluded consciousness-mind remains.
This deluded mind of the seven consciousnesses is the ground of ignorance.
Because this deluded mind is not severed, retribution arises in dependence upon it,
just as a dream-body arises in dependence upon a sleeping mind.
[The questioner] asks:
If the nirvāṇa attained by śrāvakas involves the extinction of body and cognition such that they arise again,
then the afflictions that were extinguished should also subsequently arise. To this,
the commentary says:
This is inconsistent.
Afflictions are extinguished because one perceives the principle;
thus, after the nirvana without remainder of the two vehicles, [afflictions no longer arise].
When mental images arise, one must also necessarily perceive the principle.
Therefore, the afflictions previously severed in the past cannot arise again;
however, those not yet severed may subsequently manifest.
The source of the body and wisdom is not a cessation through the perception of principles;
rather, it is a cessation through quiescence, not a cessation through treatment, and therefore may arise again later.
Furthermore, the essence of the nirvāṇa attained by the two vehicles is not ultimate.
Since one must ultimately undergo transition and proceed toward the Mahāyāna,
it cannot be called permanent.
If that which undergoes subsequent transition cannot be called permanent, then it likewise should not be called blissful or pure.
For what reason is it said that there is pleasure and purity?
The principle should likewise be equal;
the meaning of this equality is as stated above.
However, pleasure and purity are not definitive characteristics of permanence;
therefore, they are described according to their respective degrees of attainment.
Permanence, by contrast, is a definitive characteristic.
That which never shifts from beginning to end through skillful means is called "permanent.
Since that [other type] ultimately tends toward the Great [Vehicle] but is not eternally fixed,
it is not called "permanent."
The distinction between the large and the small regarding the presence or absence of clarity has been briefly analyzed in this manner;
such are the four meanings.
Next, five [qualities] are further explained:
permanence, bliss, self, purity, and existence.
These five are taught as the opposites of birth-and-death, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity.
To translate "emptiness" (śūnyatā) as "existence" (astitva) is a reversal; the other meanings can be understood accordingly.
What difference is there between emptiness and selflessness (nairātmya), such that they must be translated separately?
Accordingly, following the *Vimalakīrti*, that which is the emptiness of sentient beings is termed "selflessness," while the emptiness of the essence of phenomena is directly termed "emptiness.
Thus, that sutra says:
Sentient beings are the site of enlightenment because one knows there is no self;
all phenomena are the site of enlightenment because one knows that all phenomena are empty.
Now, in response to these two points:
Therefore, speaking from the perspective of nirvāṇa, I say that there is a self;
whereas for sentient beings within saṃsāra who lack a self, the Buddha—the True Person—is taken as the self.
"Self" is a specific designation for such a person.
Therefore, I shall explain it:
because the essence of phenomena within the cycle of birth and death is empty,
one speaks of the phenomenon of nirvāṇa as existing by taking this [emptiness] as its basis.
Furthermore, the essence of the phenomena of birth and death is empty and unreal, which is termed "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
Their lack of autonomy is termed "non-self" (*anātman*).
Because it is the opposite of these two, it is said within *nirvāṇa* that "I" exist.
Because its substance is truly not empty, it is termed "existence" (sat).
Because its function is sovereign, it is spoken of as "self" (ātman).
Next, six kinds [of self] are further explained.
By adding one more wholesome [state] to the aforementioned five,
they may be divided into eight,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The first is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).
Exhaustion is synonymous with cessation.
Because all faults are exhausted and extinguished, it is called exhaustion.
The second is called "wholesome nature" (*kuśala-svabhāva*). It is termed "wholesome" because it is free from evil;
furthermore, that which is conducive and beneficial is also called wholesome.
The third is called "real" (satya),
as it is free from the realm of falsehood.
The fourth is called "true" (tattva).
To abandon delusive sentiments and further distance oneself from the four inversions is called "reality. To emerge from thought,
perception, and view, and to regard the three inversions and false discourses as true, is [the opposite].
The five constants, the six joys, the seven selves, and the eight purities are explained as above.
It is asked:
"If the Nirvana of the Tathāgata is thus..."
Furthermore, what is the ultimate nirvana of the two vehicles?
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that it possesses six characteristics,
the first of which is liberation.
It is called "wholesome nature" (kuśalatva) for two reasons: because it is free from all suffering,
and because it is capable of providing benefit and support.
The third is called unreal;
the fourth is called untrue.
The Buddha himself explained these terms as follows.
Because they have not yet attained bodhi, they are called unreal;
because they are unreal, they are called untrue.
The fifth is called bliss.
The sixth is called "purity.
The Buddha himself explained that it is because one cultivates the untainted Eightfold Noble Path.
They may also be described as eight by adding "pleasant" and "pure" to the six types mentioned above;
these are combined with the preceding eight to form [the ten]. Furthermore, by adding impermanence and non-self, they become eight in total.
The Buddha himself explained:
"Because one shall attain Bodhi, it is called impermanent.
The meaning of non-self is fully explained as above.
Question: If the nirvāṇa of the noble ones is thus,
what is the meaning of the nirvāṇa of ordinary beings?
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is taught that there are eight characteristics.
What is the nirvāṇa of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?
The sūtra says:
For sentient beings who sever afflictions by means of the mundane path, this is nirvana.
As for what are called the eight aspects:
the first is named liberation.
Because it is free from afflictions,
it is called "virtuous" (kuśala) in the second sense;
because it opposes all evils and is conducive to benefit.
The third is called unreal;
the fourth is called untrue.
The Buddha himself explained these terms as follows:
Because they are impermanent, they are neither true nor real.
The fifth is called impermanence;
the sixth is called the absence of pleasure.
The seventh is called "selflessness" (anātman);
the eighth is called "impurity" (aśubha).
The Buddha himself explained this, saying:
Because the afflictions to be abandoned arise again,
there is impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
these can also be explained as nine.
If one adds one more existence to the aforementioned eight types,
they may also be said to be ten; namely:
It is free from ten characteristics.
As for these ten characteristics, they are:

the characteristics of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and the characteristics of male and female. Including the preceding [three], these are said to be ten.
Among these ten, the first five are the characteristics of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The next three are mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*).
These eight constitute the characteristics of dharmas.
The characteristics of the latter two are severed in nirvāṇa; therefore,
they are said to be ten.
It can also be divided into thirteen by adding the sensations of suffering,
pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure to the preceding ten;
thus there are thirteen.
As stated in the "Noble Practices" (*āryacaryā*) section of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
if subdivided according to their specific distinctions, they are likewise immeasurable.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
To speak of immeasurable names for a single name-dharma,
and to speak of immeasurable meanings within a single meaning—
such is the analysis of their characteristics.
Within the fifth section, there is a detailed analysis of miscellaneous meanings.

This consists of seven parts: first, the analysis of existence and non-existence; second, the analysis of pervasiveness and limitation; third, the analysis of the Great and Small Vehicles; fourth, the analysis according to stages; fifth, the analysis according to time; sixth, the identity or difference between the essence of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; and seventh, the identity or difference between the essences of the nirvāṇa of various Buddhas.
First, the meaning of existence and non-existence is clarified.

Within this, the characteristics of existence and non-existence are distinguished by way of the nirvana of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), the nirvana of skillful means (*upāya*), and the nirvana of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
The nirvana of intrinsic purity clarifies both existence and non-existence.
That which is called "existence" is the essence of the true consciousness-mind;
it is the nature of all meritorious virtues.
In the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, it is described as the dharma of all essential meritorious virtues.
Śrīmālādevī states that there are dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
when the mind is falsely obscured by them, it is called Buddha-nature,
and it is also called Dharma-nature.
When delusion ceases, the essence is revealed; this is described as the "all-encompassing" and designated by the virtue of "existence.
That which is called "non-existence" is the state of being free from characteristics and free from intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "leaving behind marks," this means that upon realizing the truth, one looks back and sees that from the beginning there has been no delusion.
Since there is no deluded defilement to be eliminated,
there is likewise no mark of purity as an antidote to arise.
Because both defilement and purity are simultaneously extinguished, it is called "without opposition.
Since the characteristics of defilement do not exist,
the characteristics of purity likewise do not exist.
The simultaneous vanishing of both defilement and purity is called "transcending characteristics.
As for "transcending nature," it has already been explained above.
Within the Great Nirvana, the dharma-realm is of a single essence; thus, there is not a single dharma that separately maintains its own nature.
Next, regarding the skillful means, the existence and non-existence are clarified.
That which is called "existence" refers to being fully endowed with the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom;
this is designated as existence.
Furthermore, being endowed with the dharma-body, liberation, and prajñā,
it is also called "existence.
Because it extinguishes the suffering of afflictions and is characterized by the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of severed virtues, it is designated as "non-existence."
Next, regarding the emanated body (nirmāṇakāya), we clarify its existence and non-existence.
The nirvāṇa of the emanated body is both universal and specific.
Discussing it universally, it arises based on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra.
Regarding their functional significance, one need not inquire whether they are contrary or compliant, defiled or pure;
all such functions are termed "Nirvana of Responsive Transformation.
Within this Nirvana, there is both presence and absence.
That which is currently severed as afflictions and currently extinguished as body and wisdom is called "non-existent";
all else is entirely "existent."
If explained according to the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it arises based on the Great Nirvāṇa;
in its meaning, it possesses all functions.
Within this, one selectively takes the present severance of afflictions and the present extinction of body and wisdom as the Nirvāṇa that is to be attained.
The remaining [terms] are further given alternative names according to their meaning.
If one follows this principle, the nirvāṇa of transformation is neither non-existent nor existent;
such is the case regarding existence and non-existence. Thus concludes this first section.
Next, the universal and the particular are explained.
Within this, they are distinguished according to five types of persons: ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
Regarding these persons, there are four aspects of the universal and the particular.
Generally speaking from the ultimate perspective,
these five types of persons all equally possess nirvana,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Ordinary worldlings, relying on the mundane path, sever the fetters through the six modes of practice;
this is called the "nirvāṇa of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
Obtaining a small amount of food and drink is called "nirvana," and so forth;
these two are the nirvana of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
The nirvana obtained by practicing the Eightfold Noble Path and severing the four abidings (*catasraḥ sthitayaḥ*) is [the true nirvana].
What is called the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is,
for the bodhisattva, the cultivation and eradication of the stages of ignorance and so forth, which is described as their nirvāṇa.
Realizing that the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent— having never arisen from the beginning and not ceasing now.
This refers to the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*.
Second, it distinguishes the noble from the ordinary;
the noble possess it while the ordinary do not.
As stated in the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra),
within the three vehicles there is definitely nirvāṇa;
this is called "right certainty" (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Those outside the stage of ordinary beings certainly do not possess it;
this is termed "wrong certainty" (mithyā-niyata).
For those within the three vehicles who are ordinary beings, it exists prior to their formal entry [into the path]; thus it is termed "existent."
If, after the expectation, it is said that [the object] does not exist, this is called "indeterminate.
Third, this distinguishes the Great [Vehicle] as distinct from the Small.
The Great Vehicle has it substantially, while the Small Vehicle has it nominally. Within the Mahāyāna teachings, nirvāṇa exists in reality;
within the Hīnayāna teachings, it exists provisionally but does not exist in reality.
Therefore, the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"That Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and others attain nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s skillful means.
This is clearly understood.
In truth, there is none.
Furthermore, that sutra states that Arhats and others are far removed from nirvana.
It is clearly known that they do not truly exist.
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
If there were no Buddha in the world, it would not be that the two vehicles do not attain the two types of nirvāṇa;
rather, in all worlds, there is only the single Buddha vehicle, and no separate attainment of nirvāṇa through the two vehicles.
Therefore, know that they do not truly exist;
thus the Sūtra says.
When Bodhisattvas abide in Great Nirvana, the Buddhas are likewise;
this is clearly known.
There are four aspects of this "Greatness."
The fruit is distinct from its cause;
only the Buddha alone attains nirvana,
while for all others it is entirely non-existent.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
it is therefore said in that seventh merit:
"Although a bodhisattva has severed the afflictions, they are not yet called 'nirvāṇa'."
The fact that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to afflictions is what is called nirvāṇa.
Therefore, nirvāṇa exists exclusively in the Buddha. Question:
Why is it that the mere severing of afflictions is not called *nirvāṇa*,
whereas the non-arising of afflictions is alone termed *nirvāṇa*?
The Buddha himself explained this, saying:
*Nir* means "non-arising" (*aniṣṭha*),
and *vāṇa* means "arising.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to afflictions.
This refers to the meaning of non-arising in accordance with parinirvāṇa;
therefore, the Buddha possesses it.
Although a bodhisattva has severed the afflictions, they do not yet possess the meaning of non-arising in accordance with parinirvāṇa.
Regarding this statement that [phenomena] are non-existent, it is asked:
For what reason is the bodhisattva’s severance of the fetters not called "non-arising"?
The Buddhas sever all fetters and are specifically termed "non-arising.
There are three meanings to this "explanation":
first, it is discussed in terms of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although a Bodhisattva has severed the fetters, he does not sever them completely;
because residual fetters and adventitious afflictions still arise within his mind, it is not the case that they do not arise.
Once the Buddha has severed them, they are exhausted and can no longer arise.
Therefore, it is said that they are "unborn.
Second, regarding liberation through the mind:
although the Bodhisattva has severed the afflictions, the seven consciousnesses still remain.
Because the nature of the mind undergoes arising and ceasing, it is not non-arising.
The Buddha has severed the afflictions, and thus the deluded mind is also exhausted;
because the true mind is eternally quiescent, it is called non-arising.
Third, the explanation according to principle:
The Bodhisattva perceives that there are afflictions to be severed;
because they did not originally fail to arise, they are not "unborn."
The Buddhas have exhausted the ultimate reality and realized that delusion is fundamentally empty;
there is no affliction that can arise, nor is there anything that can be severed.
Therefore, it is said that they are "unborn."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Phenomena were originally not so;
now they do not cease."
This is the meaning of quiescence (*śānti*).
Because it possesses these three meanings, the Buddha alone has them, while others do not. Question:
If non-arising exists exclusively in the Tathāgata,
then this nirvāṇa should belong only to the Buddha.
For what reason was it previously stated that bodhisattvas also possess it?
The commentary states:
The interpretation of the meaning [of the term] is both general and specific.
Discussing it generally, *nirvāṇa* is named "extinction" (*nirodha*).
The Bodhisattva’s severing of fetters is precisely the meaning of cessation; therefore,
it is said that this applies universally,
whereas in a restricted sense, it does not exist.
Nirvāṇa means the sense of quiescence.
Only that which is neither born nor extinguished is truly quiescent;
therefore, it belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
Because there is arising and ceasing, and because there is agitation and a lack of tranquility,
it is said that they are restricted to non-existence. He asked:
Generally speaking, nirvana is called cessation.
For Bodhisattvas and followers of the Two Vehicles who have attained the penetrations,
their cessation of afflictions through these penetrations should likewise be uniform.
Why was the former [teaching] distinguished as being vastly different from the small [vehicle] and not applicable to the Two Vehicles?
The explanation states:
within the meaning of "extinction" (nirodha), there is both that which is universal and that which is restricted.
In a general sense, everything that is extinguished is termed *nirvāṇa*;
thus, it was previously stated generally that both the two vehicles possess it. In a restricted sense, however, it refers specifically to the severance of afflictions.
Discriminating the conditions for the cessation of breath and attaining the reality of immovability is only then called nirvana.
Therefore, it is said that there is "great existence.
Although those of the Two Vehicles have severed a small portion of their fetters, they have not yet extinguished the conditions for their antidotes;
because they do not attain the reality of dharmas, it is said that [existence] is non-existent for them.
Question: Regarding the general sense, anything that can be extinguished is termed *nirvāṇa*.
This applies to those who have attained the commonality of the two vehicles as well as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It would also be appropriate for this [attainment] to universally eliminate afflictions.
Why, then, did the former [section] distinguish the noble ones from ordinary beings and not apply to ordinary beings?
The explanation is as follows:
This meaning also possesses both universal and specific applications.
In the former case, everything that has something to be extinguished is termed *nirvāṇa*;
thus, the former is a universal statement, whereas the latter is restricted even to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Only when there is eternal cessation can it be called *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is said that the noble ones possess it;
whereas the cessation of ordinary persons is merely temporary and not eternal liberation.
Therefore, it is said that they do not exist.
Such is the distinction between the universal and the particular; this concludes the two gates.
Next, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles is analyzed by way of ordinary beings, the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
Among these people, there are three distinctions.
First, distinguishing the noble ones from the ordinary;
for ordinary persons, nirvana is termed "small."
The nirvāṇa of the noble ones is all termed "Great.
The noble one is a great person;
because it is that which is attained by a great person, it is called "Great."
Furthermore, regarding that single Great Nirvana, it is divided into the three vehicles;
because the root subsumes the branches, they are all termed "Great.
Thus, a sutra says:
The Mahāyāna gives birth to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, a sūtra says:
"That which you practice is the bodhisattva path."
Such are these [distinctions].
Second, distinguishing the Great from the Small:
that which is attained by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is called "Small."
The nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas is great;
therefore, it is proclaimed in the sūtras that bodhisattvas abide in great nirvāṇa.
The vehicles attained by the two vehicles abandon compassion and vows;
because they cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings,
they are called "small."
Furthermore, because they have not yet realized or attained the dharma-gate of the samādhi of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) that establishes the Great Meaning,
it is called "small.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, however, are able to attain nirvāṇa while not abandoning their compassionate vows to extensively benefit all beings.
Therefore, it is called "Great.
Thus, the *Dichilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"Without abandoning great compassion, one manifests great *nirvāṇa* through the power of great vows."
Furthermore, because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize the true nature of phenomena,
they are able to establish great benefit through the power of this gateway of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), accomplishing everything that can be done;
therefore, it is called "Great."
Third, distinguishing the fruit from its cause:
only the *nirvāṇa* of a Buddha is termed "Great," while all others are termed "Small."
This is explained in detail within the seventh virtue of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It states: "Because the bodhisattva does not perceive the Buddha-nature, they sever the afflictions."
The nirvāṇa thus attained possesses only bliss and purity, but lacks self and permanence;
therefore, it is not called "Great.
The Buddhas, having realized their nature, have severed all afflictions.
The nirvāṇa thus attained is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
therefore, it is called "Great.
Bodhisattvas, according to their respective capacities, also perceive the nature [of reality] to a slight degree.
Because their vision of the Buddha is not yet clear,
they say they do not see him;
yet there are those who have severed the afflictions.
Therefore, it is called "pure.
Because one attains a portion of nirvana, it is said to be "blissful.
"Eternal" is the meaning of its dharma-body.
Because its nature is not perceived and it does not manifest as a body, it is not called "permanent";
this is the meaning of "I" being the Buddha. That [self] is not yet the Buddha.
Because they lack the eight masteries (*vaśitā*), they are not called "Self" (*ātman*);
for this reason, they are "small.
The Buddha is not like this.
This is why it is "great.
The three gates concerning the great and the small are thus concluded.
Next, we shall discuss them according to their positions.
Within the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), there are three distinct stages.
The first is the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
which precedes the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
There is that which is equal-intelligence (sāmānyajñāna), the abandonment of fetters, and nirvāṇa;
the second is the stage of the noble ones (ārya),
from the path of vision (darśanamārga) upward.
There is that which possesses the outflow-free cessation of fetters and nirvana, yet is not fully perfected;

and there is that which possesses the outflow-free cessation of fetters and nirvana, which is ultimately and completely fulfilled. This refers to the three stages of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are five distinct stages.
The first is the stage of the ordinary person (bālapṛthagjana) who is constantly submerged;
by attaining conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), they sever the fetters and realize nirvāṇa.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
regarding the eight matters of the ordinary person’s nirvāṇa:
two of these pertain to the stage of the external ordinary person in the happy realms.
One attains the nirvana that severs the fetters by taking the consciousness of phenomena as its object and contemplating the outflow-free;
for within this stage, one cultivates the causes of outflow-free karma through the consciousness of phenomena in order to sever the afflictions.
Above the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra), one experiences the fruit of transformation (pariṇāmika).
Above the three types of spiritual lineages, at the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala),
there arises false consciousness that takes as its object the untainted (anāsrava) antidote, thereby severing the fetters and attaining nirvāṇa.
By contemplating phenomena, the mind gives rise to equanimity because it abandons external conditions.
Fourth, at the stage of the true sages from the first bhūmi upward,
the cultivation that pacifies conditions gradually subsides, and the direct realization of reality gradually manifests.
One attains the true realization of the dharma-nature nirvana, yet it is not yet fulfilled;
the fifth is the stage of Buddhahood,
wherein one realizes that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, such that purity is not manifested through antidotes.
The *dharmatā-nirvāṇa* is perfectly complete;
it is designated as the fifth by taking the beginning as the end.
Upon reaching the time of its attainment, there are no four stages prior to it.
This is not the fifth; these four gates are concluded.
Next, [the distinctions] are explained in terms of time.
Specifically regarding the Mahāyāna, the temporal distinctions are numerous.
Roughly categorized, there are three:
first, the period prior to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), which may also be understood as the stage prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).
The second is the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), from the lineage (*gotra*) upward,
which may also include the stages of realization (*bhūmi*).
The third is the stage of the Buddha, situated at the final limit.
When discussing the Buddha, he possesses the three types of nirvāṇa:
the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), the nirvāṇa of skillful means (*upāya*), and the nirvāṇa of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), as fully explained above.
During his time as a holy being, he likewise possessed the threefold divisions of nirvāṇa.
Yet it is not yet fulfilled.
When one is still an ordinary being, the two kinds of nirvana—through skillful means and through transformation—are neither existent nor non-existent;
from the very beginning, they possess the sense of being capable of arising.
It is called "not non-existent" because it has not yet been cultivated and attained; thus it is said to be "not existent.
It is like a seedling within a tree: neither existent nor non-existent.
This is also the case here.
It is not that there is no nirvāṇa through the severance of fetters even within the state of the happy realms;
however, because it is minimal, it is not mentioned in this coarse classification.
Regarding the indeterminate nature of existence and non-existence in the *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity),
there are three interpretations.
The first is a distinction made by considering conditions in relation to reality.
Speaking of reality in terms of conditions, at this time,
reality is concealed by the false and thus is not yet called nirvāṇa;
it can only be termed the "nature of nirvāṇa" or "buddha-nature."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The cause of nirvāṇa is what is called buddha-nature.
Furthermore, the Sūtra proclaims:
Nirvāṇa is called the fruit of the clarifying cause;
therefore, this [fruit] does not exist.
Discussing reality in terms of reality, there is no object of cognition external to reality.
Who comes to cover me?
There is no condition with which to correspond.
With whom can it be designated as a cause?
Since there is no object to confront, for whom could it be called a fruit?
Thus, nirvāṇa is neither cause nor fruit; it has been thus from the beginning.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Great Parinirvāṇa has existed inherently from the beginning;
it is not something that has come into being only now."
Second, distinguishing between the two types of persons— the ordinary being and the Buddha—
[it is seen that] for an ordinary being, reality is obscured by afflictions;
as long as it has not been made manifest, it is not called nirvana.
It can merely be called a "cause," yet it also receives the name of "nature.
If one views the essence of sentient beings with the Buddha-eye as being fundamentally undefiled from the beginning,
this is itself nirvana.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha knows that sentient beings are ultimately quiescent and grasp the mark of nirvāṇa;
yet they do not undergo further extinction, for what more would they need to wait for? This is not called nirvāṇa."
Third, regarding the distinction between the beginning and end for a single individual:
at the outset, while still an ordinary person, one has not yet perceived the dharma-nature;
thus, the nature is obscured by delusion.
It has not yet been named Nirvana.
Later, when one attains Buddhahood, looking back at birth-and-death, one realizes it has never existed from the beginning.
By what could the truth have been obscured?
The true essence is eternally pure and does not depend on external conditions or adornments;
therefore, it is primordially and eternally nirvana.
It is like a person who, upon being freed from delusion, finally beholds the cardinal directions.
When it is actually seen, it has always been inherently correct.
Such is the conclusion regarding these five gates concerning time.
Next, we shall discuss whether saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are identical or distinct.
How are they identical or different?
There are three ways to distinguish them.
First, explaining conditions in terms of conditions.
One severs the substance of birth and death to attain the nature of nirvana;
the essential natures of birth and death and nirvana are entirely distinct,
as stated in the sutras.
"That which existed originally is now non-existent; that which was originally non-existent is now existent.
To claim that dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time is impossible.
This refers precisely to this point.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that the mutual non-existence of nirvāṇa also pertains to this gate;
these two points discuss reality in terms of conditions.
The very substance of birth and death is transformed into nirvana;
it is not an entirely separate entity.
This is because, during delusion, one mistakes the nature of nirvana for birth and death.
Therefore, at the time of realization, one realizes that the very essence of birth and death is itself nirvana.
It is like when a person is deluded, the cardinal directions appear distorted;
yet upon reaching the point of realization, those same distorted directions are immediately seen as correct.
It is also like seeing a rope as a snake in the darkness of night,
yet when it becomes bright later, the snake is simply the rope.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
For ordinary beings who have not yet attained the enlightenment of a Buddha, afflictions are [obstacles];
for sages who have attained Buddhahood, afflictions are themselves enlightenment.
As it is with enlightenment, so it is with nirvana.
Third, when discussing reality in terms of reality, the very substance of birth and death is itself nirvāṇa;
it cannot be turned back or transformed,
just as a snake is [in fact] a rope.
How could one wait until dawn?
Such is the relationship between birth-and-death and nirvana regarding their identity or difference.
One must not, having finished these six gates, grasp them in a biased manner.
Next, the identity or difference among the nirvāṇas of all Buddhas is explained.
If nirvāṇa were one,
then when one person attains it, others should also attain it.
Furthermore, if it were a single entity,
then once one person had attained it, others would have no share in it; if nirvāṇa were distinct [for each], [the same fault would follow].
If they were distinct, they would not be the same;
there would then be this and that, more and less, increase and decrease, and boundaries that could be counted,
which would mean they are impermanent.
What is the meaning of this?
It is as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
where the meaning of the Buddha-nature is explained as being neither identical nor different.
Nirvana is likewise:
it is neither identical nor different.
This [practice] is cultivated and this [attainment] is realized; that [practice] is cultivated and that [attainment] is realized.
Therefore, they are not definitively one;
yet, since there is no distinction in what is attained,
they are not definitively different.
For example, one who has studied a sutra understands it, whereas one who has not studied it does not;
thus, the sutras are not the same.
Yet, as for what they understand, their essence is no different.
It may be said that they are not different;
this case is likewise.
Furthermore, one may discuss their actual nature by way of conditions.
Because they arise from distinct conditions, they are truly different;
therefore, they are not necessarily one.
Discussing reality in terms of reality, there is no person apart from these realities.
I understand.
Furthermore, from whom did he say that?
Is what he said not different [from yours]?
The meaning of *nirvāṇa* is profound and difficult to fathom to its ultimate limit.
For now, I have sought out its expressions through analogies and provided this brief description.

206. The Meaning of Unsurpassed Bodhi (18): An Exposition by Way of Seven Gates. I. Explaining the Name. II. Determining the Essence. III. Distinguishing the Characteristics. IV. Attainment and Non-attainment. V. Universality and Limitation according to Stages. VI. Distinctions according to Time. VII. Identity and Difference between Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. First, Explaining the Name.
"Bodhi" is a term from the language of India;
here it is translated as "path.
Because the qualities of the fruit are perfected and all-pervading, it is called the "path."
There are five aspects of the Way and its Meaning.
First, the distinction regarding obstacles:
when the accumulation of obstructions is exhausted, the essence of virtue is free from hindrance.
It is called "penetration" (tong).
Because it penetrates, it is called the "path" (dao).
Second, [the path] is distinguished according to its essential nature (ti).
Realizing that one has been free from defilement since the beginning,
and that one's own essence is inherently pure, unobstructed, and sovereign—
this is called "penetration" (abhijñā).
Because it penetrates, it is called the "path.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The intrinsic nature of the noble path of all Buddhas is eternally quiescent."
It is not that there was first defilement which was later abandoned.
Third, regarding the classification by means of virtues:

within the path to enlightenment, all virtues are of the same essence; through the principle of dependent origination, they are mutually constitutive, such that the perfection of one constitutes the perfection of all.
When all things become one,
empty and harmonious without obstruction,
this is called "pervasion" (tong).
It is called the "Path" (mārga) because it leads through [to liberation]. Fourth, an analysis according to its meaning:
the categories of practice, such as ethical discipline (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā), each differ in their enumeration.
The Path (mārga) is like a track; it is broad and pervasive according to four meanings.
Because it is pervasive, it is called the "Path.
The fifth [meaning] distinguishes it according to persons.
It enables practitioners to reach the place of nirvāṇa;
because it serves as a passage, it is called "passage" (tong). Because it is a passage, it is called the "path" (dao).
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
"The Path is the cause;
by practicing this Path, one can reach the state of the noble ones."
It is called the Noble Path.
Question: The Sūtra states that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is also called the Path.
It is also called bodhi and also called nirvāṇa.
Since the meanings of "path" (mārga) and "awakening" (bodhi) should be distinct,
for what reason is bodhi now explained as a synonym for the path?
The commentary states:
In foreign lands, the term for "Path" has many names;
it is called *bodhi*, and it is also called *mārga*.
Just as the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) among the Four Noble Truths is called *mārga*,
this term is abbreviated here;
therefore, it is translated in its entirety as "the Path."
In those foreign lands, both *nirvāṇa* and *vinaya* are termed "extinction" (*nirodha*),
and their meaning is similar.
In the sūtras, it is proclaimed that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called the "path" (*mārga*).
This path of practice is called bodhi;
it is the path to enlightenment.
This is because both [terms] are designated as "the Way" (mārga).
Therefore, one may translate *bodhi* as "the Way. Question:
What is the difference between bodhi and that mārga?
In general explanation, they are one;
together they are like eyes.
They differ only in name; within them,
there are indeed distinctions that are not without difference,
as was explained previously in the section on the Path (mārga-varga).
Now, let us further discuss this: there are four kinds of distinctions.
First, the distinction between cause and fruit:
all causal paths are termed *mārga*.
All paths of fruition are said to be bodhi.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"For those who have attained skillful means, it is the path cultivated and studied by all bodhisattvas."
What is called "attaining the meaning" refers to unsurpassed bodhi.
Second, the distinction between the universal and the specific:
*mārga*, or the path, applies to both cause and fruit.
Therefore, the Truth of the Path includes all paths;
yet the path to enlightenment (bodhi-mārga) is specifically situated within the fruit.
This is truly because enlightenment is specifically situated within the fruit.
To realize the Buddha-way is called attaining bodhi.
Third, there is the threefold distinction between the general and the specific: the specific paths consisting of the three matters of precept, concentration, and wisdom.
It is called bodhi.
This very matter is the supreme path; because it conveys one across all meanings like a vehicle, it is explained as mārga.
Because mārga provides universal passage, [it is so named].
One who perceives the Truth of the Path universally severs all afflictions that delude one regarding the path;
because enlightenment is specific,
although one contemplates it, one cannot universally sever the fetters that delude one regarding the path.
This is also called the "discrimination between phenomena and principles" (dharma-artha-vibhāga).
It is the discrimination of the four modes of practice.
All dharmas of the path are termed *mārga*.
The Dharma of the Four Noble Truths does not manifest through [mere] practice; rather,
all paths of practice are termed *bodhi* (enlightenment).
To discuss virtue in terms of persons is not to discern the Dharma;
such is the nature of bodhi.
The term "unsurpassed" (anuttara) is an expression of praise for excellence.
There are three types of bodhi: first, that which is attained by śrāvakas; [the second is that of pratyekabuddhas; and the third is that of buddhas].
Second, that attained by the pratyekabuddhas;
third, that attained by the buddhas.
What the Tathāgata has attained surpasses the former two.
Because the former two are not such, they are called "unsurpassed.
Question: Is it not the case that "bodhi" (awakening) is what is termed "unsurpassed"?
The essence is identical.
Although the stage of abiding in ignorance is called "ignorance," its essence is not clarity.
What is the meaning of this?
The commentary states:
There are two types of discourse—speaking of existence and speaking of non-existence.
First, one says "non-existent" to others.
Second, regarding the negation in terms of essence:
supreme enlightenment is said to be non-existent in relation to others;
that is, outside of me, there is nothing superior to me.
It is called "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because it is not superior by virtue of its essential nature; as for the term "ignorance" (avidyā),
it is spoken of as "non-existent" (avidyamāna) with respect to its essential nature.
Its essence is not luminous wisdom;
therefore, it is called ignorance (avidyā),
and its essence is darkness.
The incongruity lies herein.
It is asked:
The Sūtra says:
The path practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is neither high nor low;
therefore, it is called the Middle Way.
For what reason, then, do you now proclaim that the essence of bodhi is "high"?
The explanation says:
it is because the objects addressed differ that [the teachings] are thus;
this is what is proclaimed in the *Nirvāṇa*.
Regarding that which is called the Middle Way— neither high nor low—
it is therein proclaimed that for the deluded and inverted mind, there are the three miserable realms below toward which one may tend.
That which is called the lower path is so named because there is bodhi above it toward which one may aspire;
that is called the higher path.
The path practiced by the Buddha cannot lead to regression or descent into the three miserable realms (trāya).
Nor does it regress to become something attained by ordinary beings;
therefore, it is not termed "downward."
Because there is no direction above toward which it tends, it is not called "above.
Because it neither ascends nor descends, it is described as "middle."
Now, regarding the term "superior":
it is called superior because the Buddha’s virtues are exceptionally sublime when contrasted with the bodhi attained by the two lower vehicles.
The explanation of names and meanings concludes this first section.
Next, we shall determine its essence.
Its qualities and essence are boundless.
Now, this will be briefly analyzed by way of three gates:
first, the analysis according to the three gates of matter, mind, and that which is neither matter nor mind;
second, the analysis of primary and attendant factors.
Third, regarding the distinction between the purity of nature and skillful means:
the initial statement concerning "form and mind" versus "non-form and non-mind" has been extensively analyzed above in the chapter on *Nirvāṇa*.
Now, I shall briefly elucidate this:
within the essence of bodhi, there is both the meaning of form and the meaning of mind.
There is also the meaning of that which is neither form nor mind.
As for what is called "form," the Buddha is endowed with the three bodies (trikāya).
Among these three bodies— the Dharma-body,
the Reward-body, and the Response-body— all possess the significance of form (*rūpa*).
As for the form of the Dharma-body:
Within the tathāgatagarbha are present dharmas such as the eyes and ears that exceed the sands of the Ganges;
therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra states:
"Within the bodies of sentient beings are the eyes, ears, and other faculties of a Tathāgata."
Like an image within a mold—
these are taught as the Dharma-gates of the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The Buddha-nature is also form;
that which is form is seen by the eye.
That form, being clearly manifest, is described as the form of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
"nature-seed" (*prakṛtisthagotra*) refers to the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) which has been naturally so from beginningless time; this is its meaning.
The form of this Dharma-body is merely a dharma of form, yet it lacks the characteristics of form;
it is like the form of a bhikṣu’s unmanifest precepts (avijñapti-śīla), which possesses form but lacks [visible] characteristics.
As for the form of the Reward-body (saṃbhoga-kāya):
The Tathāgata, having cultivated the karma of the primary and secondary marks over a vast period, has attained the fruit of those marks.
Within each individual mark of that response body (nirmāṇakāya),
there are each infinite and boundless oceans of marks.
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
although these marks exist, they cannot be seen;
it is like the jewel atop the crown of the Brahmā King, which exists yet is invisible.
Regarding the color of the response body (nirmāṇakāya):
it manifests as various forms and images according to the objects [of perception]. Such is the nature of the dharma of form (rūpadharma).
Regarding what is called "mind," its differentiation is also threefold:
first, the dharma-mind; second, the retribution-mind; and third, the response-mind.
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the essence of the true consciousness, which is the nature of cognition—
like the nature of awareness possessed by a person who is in a state of deep sleep.
Because it is by nature wisdom, the Sūtras speak of it as mind (*citta*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).
That mind is described as the manifestation of all the qualities of the Buddhas in every respect;
however, this is merely a dharma-gate of the nature of mind (*cittatva*) and is devoid of any characteristics of mind (*cittalakṣaṇa*).
Just as a chick within an egg has no differentiated characteristics,
that which is called the "retributive mind" is the true mind manifested through the accumulated power of the Tathāgata’s vast cultivation of causes and conditions for pure karma.
It causes the birth of immeasurable virtues such as wisdom, samādhi, and dhāraṇī within the true mind;
yet, although it possesses these virtues, it remains free from discrimination.
What is called "conforming to the mind" refers to the manifestation of various diverse knowledges in accordance with the transformation of the world.
The mental factors are thus.
Regarding that which is said to be neither form nor mental factors,
there are two types of distinctions.
First, the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation;
second, the principle of the emptiness of dharmas.
Within these two, there is neither form nor mind.
When subdivided according to their meaning, there are also three types:
the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body.
As for what is called the "Dharma-body":
The true essence of bodhi cannot be grasped by form nor can it be grasped by mind;
it is called neither form nor mind.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
Enlightenment cannot be attained by means of the body or the mind.
What is the meaning of this?
It is that the true essence of enlightenment is free from the characteristics of form and mind.
Therefore, it cannot be attained by body or mind.
Furthermore, the essence of bodhi is empty, quiescent, unconditioned, and free from the nature of form and mind;
therefore, it cannot be attained by body or mind.
Regarding what is called "being free from characteristics," it is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
although the minds of sentient beings exist, they lack characteristics such as large or small, blue, yellow, red, or white, and long or short.
The Way, as well as bodhi and nirvāṇa, are likewise.
Although their substance exists, they possess no single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because they are without characteristics, they cannot be grasped by means of characteristics.
Therefore, it cannot be attained by means of the body nor attained by means of the mind.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Quiescence is bodhi."
Because all marks are extinguished,
awakening is not perceived;
because it is free from all conditions.
Non-practice is bodhi,
because it is free from recollection.
Severance is bodhi.
Enlightenment is free from this because it involves relinquishing all views;
it is free from this because it is devoid of conceptual construction.
Obstruction is bodhi,
because it obstructs all vows; non-entry is bodhi.
Because there is no attachment.
For this reason, it cannot be apprehended by the mind.
The sutra further states:
Enlightenment is not a non-meeting,
for the sense-bases do not meet;
enlightenment is not a union.
Because it is free from the habitual tendencies of affliction,
awakening has no location; because it is devoid of form and color, it has no location.
Provisional names are bodhi,
because names are empty.
That which is like a magical transformation is bodhi.
Because there is no grasping or rejecting.
For this reason, it cannot be attained by the body.
As for the term "separation from nature":
Within the essence of bodhi, all virtues are of one substance, mutually arising and mutually constituting through dependent origination.
When the particular is subsumed into the universal, all virtues are fully present;
yet when the universal is divided into particulars, everything is entirely absent.
Because there is no cause, it is devoid of intrinsic nature. Such is the essence of phenomena.
As for what is called "retribution":
Having severed and abandoned all afflictions, karma, and suffering,
one realizes quiescent unconditionedness, which is termed "neither form nor mind.
As for what is called "responsive":
In accordance with the scope of his transformation, he demonstrates that there is something to be severed;
the direct realization of the unconditioned is termed "neither form nor mind.
Such is the first gate.
Next is the second gate, the distinction between the principal and the attendant:
the primary essence is the principal,
while the manifest aids are called attendants.
The primary and its attendants are not fixed;
there are six distinct meanings.
First, they are distinguished according to mental factors (*caitasika*).
The mind of true consciousness is precisely the essence of the Way;
it is said to be the master.
Wisdom and all other mental factors, which are virtues that follow the mind, are all termed its attendants.
Second, regarding the classification by way of cultivation:
mindfulness is the primary leader,
while all others are its companions.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment take mindfulness as their primary guide.
The Vinaya and the sūtras likewise say:
Since one can attain liberation from all streams by taking mindfulness as the primary guide,
we know that the mind of mindfulness is the master of all conditioned phenomena.
The remaining formations follow and revolve according to mindfulness,
just as the fourfold army follows the will of its commander; therefore,
they are called "companions."
Third, regarding the classification of the karmic actions performed:
volition (cetanā) is the primary agent,
while all others are its companions.
The mind of volition (cetanā) is precisely the nature of formative activity;
therefore, it is said to be the sovereign.
All other mental formations (saṃskāra) are that which is produced by volition.
Because they arise in accordance with volition, they are called "companions.
Fourth, they are distinguished according to their arising causes and their movement toward the fruit,
with the bodhicitta serving as the primary leader.
Because of this seed of the bodhicitta,
all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that follow the mind toward its fruition are collectively termed "companions.
Fifth, they are distinguished according to the strength or weakness of their active qualities.
The practice of wisdom is the most powerful and constitutes the true essence of the Path;
it is designated as the "master" because it possesses great power to eliminate obstacles and enter into the Dharma. Therefore, the other practices assist wisdom.
All are termed "companions.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The retinue of wisdom refers to dāna and the other perfections."
Sixth, regarding the analysis of the constituent aspects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
all conditioned phenomena act as mutual masters and as mutual companions.
Within the gateway of *dāna*, the meaning is distinguished such that *dāna* itself is the primary master and the other practices are its companions.
Distinguishing the meaning of the gateway of precepts:
the precepts are the primary master,
while the other practices are their companions.
In this way, there are these six types, differing according to whether they are primary or secondary.
Now, regarding what is called the "virtue of bodhisattva conduct," it is primarily explained as the practice of wisdom, with the others serving as its attendants. These two sections are concluded.
Next, the third gate, the nature-purity expedient (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-upāya*),
is analyzed through two gates,
as taught in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
He explains that the enlightenment obtained through the cause of production is called "purity of expedient means," while that manifested by the cause of revelation is called "purity of nature."
The meanings of these two terms are exactly as explained previously in the section on *nirvāṇa*;
they shall now be briefly distinguished.
[These are] skillful means (*upāya*) and awakening (*bodhi*).
Accumulation arises from conditions;
accomplishment originates from substance;
the gathering of virtues follows conditions—all arise from conditions.
Just as ornaments are fashioned by a goldsmith,
so too the gathering of virtues arises from the essence and is entirely the work of the true mind of Buddha-nature;
it is like ornaments made of pure gold.
Although conditions can act,
their action must depend on a substance;
although a substance can function, its functioning must rely upon conditions.
Generally speaking, these two are both termed the "producing cause" (*janakahetu*) and that which is produced.
Within this, specifically distinguishing the aspect of external dependent origination, it is called the "active cause" (*kārakahetu*),
just as a worldly craftsman produces ornaments.
The designation of "causal condition" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the aspect of the arising of Buddha-nature, it is called the "producing cause" (*janana-hetu*);
this is because within Buddha-nature there exists the sense of being capable of arising, and thus it serves as the producing cause.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Although the Buddha-nature is non-existent, it is not the same as a rabbit's horn;
although it cannot be produced by means of infinite expedient methods, it exists."
The Buddha-nature can be produced;
because it can be produced, it is called the "cause of production.
It may also be so described.
Regarding the external aspect of dependent origination, it arises with a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, there is a productive cause."
The six pāramitās lead to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because they arise from the Buddha-nature, they are called "causes" and "conditions.
Thus, the *Dì jīng* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) says:
Just as pure gold is fashioned into ornaments, the Buddha-nature, the true mind, produces all merits.
This nature-pure bodhi has existed from antiquity; it arises only through conditions.
Within this, there are two types of analysis:
first, from the perspective of conditions, it is argued that reality only begins to manifest through conditions;
second, based on reality itself, conditions are transcended such that there is neither concealment nor manifestation, yet it manifests through conditions.
The meaning of "middle" is distinguished into two types:
first, manifestation through conditions;
second, manifestation through essence.
When virtues are subsumed within their essence, they are all manifestations of that essence.

Although there are manifestations among the conditions, they must necessarily rely upon the essential nature. If within the essential nature there were no meaning that could be manifested, [the conditions would have nothing upon which to depend].
Although one cultivates various practices, nothing is ultimately manifested.
While the nature may be manifestable, manifestation necessarily depends upon conditions;
if the manifold conditions are absent, it will never be manifested.
Just as within a dark room or amidst the seven treasures,
if there is no lamp to illuminate them, they have no way to manifest themselves;
these two cases, when discussed together, are both termed "that which is realized" by the enabling cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*).
External conditions are the "cause of manifestation" (*vijñapti-hetu*) because they clarify its distinct characteristics,
just as a lamp illuminates objects.
Buddhahood (*buddhadhātu*) is the "cause of manifestation" because it is its own essence that can be manifested.
Just as a lamp within a jar has the quality of being visible, yet it becomes visible once the jar is broken,
so too does the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* state:
"Although the Buddha-nature differs from empty space, [it is nonetheless revealed through the removal of obstructions]."
Although space cannot be seen despite immeasurable skillful means,
the Buddha-nature can be seen;
because it can be seen, it is called the "revealing cause" (pariniṣpatti-hetu).
This means that the Buddha-nature, having been present from the very beginning as something capable of being realized, is termed the "cause of realization" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*).
It is not that it has already been realized;
rather, within this [nature], one separately distinguishes the aspect of realizing external objects, which is termed the "cause of realization" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) in its manifestation.
When the Buddha-nature is manifested, it is termed the "causal nature" (*dharmatā-hetu*).

Such is the case from the perspective of conditions. However, according to the ultimate reality, conditions are transcended; within this state where there is neither concealment nor manifestation, the distinctions in meaning are likewise twofold.
First, regarding the discourse on the abandonment of dharmas:
the nature of dharmas is fundamentally quiescent and has from the beginning been without conditions;
indeed, there are no conditions external to reality.
Understood.
Furthermore, based on what are the hidden and the manifest, the cause and the fruit explained?
This can be subsumed within the gate of the principle of *dharmatā-bodhi*.
This has no bearing on their practice or virtue.
Second, regarding the inclusion of the Dharma through the person: the preceding nature of phenomena (dharmatā) reaches its realization only upon attaining Buddhahood;
once realized, one looks back toward the source, where there was originally no object-condition.
Because it is fundamentally without conditions, the fundamental is not defiled;
because it is not newly purified, it is identical to the preceding *dharmatā*.
It is neither hidden nor manifest, neither cause nor fruit.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Conformity is bodhi,
for it conforms to the Dharma."
Abiding is bodhi, because abiding is the dharma-nature;
arriving is bodhi.
Because it reaches the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
the meaning lies herein. This single gateway,
which subsumes all phenomena from the perspective of persons, is called "the practice of virtues."
Although their names differ, their practice and virtue are no different from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As stated in the *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra*:
"One knows that the intrinsic nature of the noble path is eternally quiescent."
It is not that there was defilement first and it is abandoned at a later time;
therefore, one must say that definitive cessation is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
This precisely accords with this teaching.
The wondrous mystery of the skillful means of intrinsic purity resides herein;
one should reflect upon this with careful scrutiny.
Such is the nature of reality. This concludes the two gates.
Next, the third section extensively distinguishes its characteristics.
Within this, first it is discussed in terms of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*),
and subsequently in terms of skillful means (*upāya*).
The characteristics of intrinsically pure bodhi are distinguished into two types:
first, the characteristic of emptiness;
second, the characteristic of existence.
Regarding the characteristic of emptiness,
as it is taught in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"There is not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended."
This is called bodhi.
This dharma is equal, without high or low;
this is called bodhi.
Because there is no sentient being, no person, and no life-span, one attains the equality of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such instances as these constitute the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That no dharma can be apprehended and that there is no high or low constitutes the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of phenomena (dharmas) is twofold.
First, that which is grasped by deluded cognition:
the fruits and virtues of the Buddhas fundamentally do not exist within the ultimate principle.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness.
Second, the true nature of bodhi is wondrously quiescent and free from characteristics;
therefore, it is called "emptiness."
Because the nature and characteristics of that Buddha-fruit are both empty,
there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained.
Furthermore, within this emptiness, there are no distinctions among the fruits and virtues of the three vehicles.
Therefore it is said that equality has no high or low.
This emptiness is precisely the meaning of "emptiness as it truly is" within the essence of bodhi;
hence it is named bodhi.
The designation of "non-arising," "no person," "no life-span," and so forth as bodhi refers to the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*).
This is analyzed into two types:
first, that which is grasped by deluded cognition.
The principle that "I" and "sentient beings" can attain bodhi is fundamentally non-existent;
therefore, it is called emptiness.
Second, the true nature of bodhi is a synthesis formed through dependent origination.
Because the self, sentient beings, and so forth are equal to the true,
eternal, and quiescent, they are called "empty.
If one were to maintain the marks of self, person, sentient being, and so forth, as distinct from one another, [they would not be empty].
It cannot be called equanimity.
To maintain a self is to deviate from the Way and fail to attain Bodhi,
for there is no self, person, or sentient being.
There is no distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas, nor between self and other;
this is called attaining equality.
There is no person, and no separate path.
There is no distinction between the Way and ordinary persons;
the human way is without separation.
That one is said to have attained Bodhi is because the meaning of emptiness is thus.
Regarding what is called "not empty," as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is also called bodhi,
also called the path (*mārga*),
and also called nirvāṇa.
Such dharmas as these both exist and are empty.
If they did not exist, how could one sever all afflictions?
Because they do exist, the bodhisattva understands and perceives them with complete clarity.
Therefore, one knows that it exists; how so?
Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, all Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, are fully present.
Because those dharmas are clearly explained as the qualities of all aspects of enlightenment (bodhi),
they are called "existent.
Existence and non-existence are thus [defined].
If one wishes to explain this in detail, it is as Vimalakīrti said:
"Nirvana-bodhi is because all marks have been extinguished;
non-contemplation of bodhi is because it is free from all conditions."
One does not practice awakening because there is no recollection;
such is the case. To summarize:
it is wondrously quiescent, free from marks, and perfectly complete in all its meanings.
This is the characteristic of bodhi;
its nature is pure in this way.
Next, the discussion concerns skillful means.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of three gates:
first, the analysis of the severance of practice;
second, the analysis of the real and the responsive.
Third is the classification according to meaning.
Regarding the term "cessation" (prahāṇa):
the state in which afflictions, karma, and suffering are exhausted and no longer exist is called cessation.
This refers to the dharmas such as the non-dharmakāya, prajñā, and liberation;
to speak of them as being "practice" is to say they exist.
Analyzing their specific characteristics, their cessation is the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya).
This is not bodhi.
Cultivating virtue is the Way;
only then is it bodhi.
Regarding the summary statement, both the gate of cultivation and the gate of abandonment are *bodhi*.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"The two abandonments and the two knowledges are called *bodhi*."
The two abandonments are abandonment;
the two knowledges are practice.
The meaning is as explained later.
Both of these are termed "purification through skillful means" because they sever hindrances by practicing the application of skillful means.
Such is the practice of severance.
Next, we shall distinguish them according to the two gates of the True (Dharmakāya) and the Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya).
That which is attained through self-correspondence is called "True" (zhen);
that which manifests and transforms according to sentient beings is called "Responsive" (ying).
The True is purified through the practice of skillful means, and is thus termed "Purified by Skillful Means" (fāngbiàn jìng).
It should likewise be the same in this case.
Furthermore, the term "purification through skillful means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*) should be applied to abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
However, the meaning of "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) possesses both general and specific senses.
Generally speaking, all transformative functions arising from true enlightenment (bhūta-bodhi) are termed "responsive and transformative enlightenment" (nirmāṇa-bodhi),
because they are the functioning of enlightenment.
Specifically, this refers to the manifestation of the Buddha-way through the eight phases of appearance.
This corresponds to bodhi;
as for the other transformations such as monkeys, deer, horses, and so forth, they are designated by names according to their distinct characteristics and are not called bodhi.
What are the eight aspects?
As stated in the sūtras:
first, ascending to Tuṣita.
Second, descending from the realm of gods to enter the womb;
third, abiding within the womb;
fourth, being born.
Fifth, leaving the household life;
sixth, attaining the Way of Buddhahood;
seventh, turning the wheel of the Dharma.
There are eight types of *parinirvāṇa*.
Each of these is explained in detail as in the sūtras.
Among these eight, the sixth—manifesting the attainment of the Buddha-way—is precisely the essence of the responsive and transformative (*nirmāṇa*) bodhi.
The first five are the preparatory means;
the latter two are the functions.
It is truly thus.
Next, the third section provides a detailed analysis according to the meaning;
there are six distinct categories of meaning,
as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*.
1. The meaning of its essential nature; 2. The meaning of its unsurpassedness;
3. The merit of its renown; 4. The merit of recollecting it.
Fifth is the meaning of capability;
sixth is the meaning of supremacy.
Among these six, the first two are its own virtues.
Regarding the latter four transformed virtues (*nirmāṇa-guṇa*),
among their own attributes, the first— the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—
is precisely the substance of virtue itself.
The latter one is unsurpassed.
This reveals the excellence of its qualities; among the qualities of transformation, the first three constitute its essential nature, while the latter one is the most supreme.
To manifest its extraordinary excellence,
I shall now provide an analytical exposition according to this sequential framework.
First, regarding the "essential nature" (*svabhāva*), I shall clarify the fundamental character of the virtues of the bodhi-practice.
Therefore, it is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Within this, there are briefly three categories of discernment:
first, ultimate liberation.
Second, the perfection of prajñā;
third, the ultimate fulfillment of the dharmakāya.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* teaches that these three meanings constitute Great Nirvāṇa.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains this as the nature of enlightenment (*bodhikṛtva*).
That treatise proclaims that the two abandonments and the two knowledges constitute liberation.
The two types of abandonment are themselves unconditioned liberation;
therefore, the treatise concludes by naming them "great liberation.
What are these two types of abandonment?
First, the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*):

this refers to the severance and separation from the afflictions that constitute the fetters of the five stages of existence (*pañcavihāra*). Second, the severance of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
To sever matters without knowledge constitutes the two types of conditioned liberation.
What are these two types of knowledge?
First, the abandonment of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
which is the knowledge that all afflictions no longer continue. Second, the abandonment of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The unobstructed wisdom regarding all that is knowable.
That treatise explains that pure wisdom, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), unimpeded wisdom (*apratihata-jñāna*), and so forth, are precisely *prajñā*.
The wisdom of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas that realizes suchness (*tathatā*)—which is able to extinguish afflictions and is pure, clear, and penetrating—is "pure wisdom" (*viśuddha-jñāna*).
To thoroughly know all phenomena in every aspect according to conventional truth is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
To possess mastery in knowing all phenomena within the scope of that omniscience,
such that the mind is awakened without relying on expedient means, is called unimpeded knowledge (*jñānāsaṅga*).
These three will be analyzed in detail later in the chapter on the three types of knowledge.

It is said that the Tathāgata possesses one hundred and forty unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as the Buddha’s vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
This is called bodhi;
it is the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s dharma-body.
As for what are called the one hundred and forty unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma):
That which is called the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics constitutes one hundred and twelve.
When combined with the four kinds of universal purity mentioned previously, they total one hundred and sixteen.
The ten powers (*daśabala*) together with the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), when combined with the preceding [qualities], total one hundred and thirty.
Adding the three applications of mindfulness (*trismṛtyupasthāna*) and the three forms of non-protection (*trirakṣa*), they total one hundred and thirty-six.
7. Great Compassion;
8. The quality of non-forgetfulness;
9. The eradication of all habitual tendencies.
The tenth is the wondrous wisdom of all modes;
these combined total one hundred and forty [qualities].
These belong exclusively to the Buddha and do not extend to the two vehicles.
The "unshared dharmas" (*āveṇika-dharma*) shall be explained in detail later.
The Tathāgata’s "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (*praṇidhijñāna*) and "knowledge of non-contention" (*araṇājñāna*) have been fully explained in the previous chapter on the five knowledges.
The four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) are also explained as above.
Such is its intrinsic nature.
As for the term "unsurpassed," it means that the Buddha’s virtues are preeminent and transcend those of the two vehicles.
Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.
There are seven distinctions:
first, the unsurpassed body.
The primary and secondary marks are exceptionally sublime;
this refers to the unsurpassed nature of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks among the previously mentioned one hundred and forty characteristics.
Second, the Unsurpassed Path:
having crossed over oneself and leading others across,
one delivers many beings, out of compassion for the world, bringing benefit, peace, and security to devas and humans.
This refers to the unsurpassed nature of the aforementioned practices such as great compassion.
Third is the correct unsurpassedness;
fourth is the correct accomplishment.
These are right precepts, right view, dignified conduct, and right livelihood.
"Right precepts" refers to remaining far removed from natural transgressions.
"Right view" refers to remaining far removed from false slanders.
"Right deportment" means being free from all transgressions such as drinking alcohol and so forth.
"Right livelihood" means being free from all other forms of wrong livelihood for one's sustenance.
This refers to the unsurpassed nature [of these practices] in relation to the three types of non-restraint previously mentioned, as well as the abandonment of habitual tendencies and so on.
The four supreme knowledges refer to the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
This constitutes the unsurpassed excellence in terms of the previously mentioned four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Fifth is the unsurpassed excellence of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), which consists in the accomplishment of the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
This refers to the unsurpassed nature as explained in relation to the aforementioned pure wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, the ten powers, and so forth;
for these various forms of wisdom constitute its universal essence.
Sixth is the unsurpassed abandonment.
This refers to the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is described as "unsurpassed" with reference to these aforementioned abandonments.
The seventh is the unsurpassed dwelling.
There are three types of dwellings:
namely, the noble dwelling, the celestial dwelling, and the Brahma dwelling.
The noble dwellings consist of the meditative attainments of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and cessation.
The Brahma-dwellings are the four immeasurables.
The celestial dwellings are the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
As explained extensively above,
this too is spoken of as "unsurpassed" with reference to the aforementioned all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus is the unsurpassed.
The former clarifies the quality of virtue;
the latter elucidates the quality of transformation.
Within this, the first three [sections] clarify the essence of the quality of transformation.
The final one reveals his excellence.
Among the first three, the first clarifies that his fame and meritorious renown are manifested externally, causing people to take refuge in him with reverence.
The second clarifies his merit of recollecting [him], whereby he manifests transformations in accordance with such recollection.
Third is the one capable of bringing vast benefit alone,
whose name is Virtue (*guṇa*).
This refers to the ten titles of the Tathāgata, which are called virtues.
Beginning from the Tathāgata down to the tenth title, Bhagavān— also called Lokajyestha—
as will be explained in detail later.
Regarding the recollection of his qualities:
In accordance with the differing mental inclinations of sentient beings,
he manifests at all times and in all places;
this is the meaning of "capability."
In a single trichiliocosm, a single Tathāgata alone is able to bring about vast benefit;
the appearance of a second Buddha would serve no further purpose.
This is the meaning of "supreme."
Excellence is of two kinds:
first, excellence of qualities,
which refers to the various distinctions among the transformation marks of all Tathāgatas.
Because their actual qualities are equal,
that text states: "In all Tathāgatas,
there is no sign of increase or decrease, except for four matters."
It is not other merits.
Regarding the four matters,
the first is longevity.
First, lifespans vary in length;
second, reputations vary in their reach,
being either far-reaching or limited.
Third is caste and lineage,
whether high or low;
fourth is the physical body.
Their physical forms may differ in size;
only these [physical attributes] increase or decrease,
while all other qualities, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, are entirely equal.
It is superior because it is equal [to all].
Second, the body is superior:
all the sense faculties and marks of excellence are entirely preeminent.
