One cannot attain the Buddha-way in a female body. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata already relinquished his female body during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
How much more so under the Bodhi tree,
where what was previously abandoned is now absent;
therefore, one does not attain Buddhahood in a female body.
Furthermore, women by nature possess many afflictions and have accomplished evil wisdom.
One does not attain Buddhahood through afflictions or evil wisdom;
rather, it is because one is free from them.
Each of these has been explained in detail according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*;
here they are stated only briefly. This concludes the third section.
Next, the fourth section distinguishes the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*).
The cultivation and arising of expedient means and bodhi depend upon conditions;
they are invariably attained because one attains bodhi by severing birth and death.
Regarding the intrinsically pure bodhi, it is both attained and unattained.
From the perspective of characteristics, when one discusses the reality of its attainment: by extinguishing ignorance, one obtains the blazing lamp of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi);
this is termed "attainment."
Since realization is found to have been devoid of conditions from the very beginning,
from what could wisdom further cultivate or realize bodhi? Therefore,
there is nothing to be attained.
The meaning of "non-attainment" is distinguished into five aspects.
First, there is no separate self or person external to the essence of bodhi who can attain it;
this constitutes non-attainment.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"In truth, there is neither one who attains nor one who falls back.
This is because where there is a person, it is not bodhi; only where there is no person is it truly so."
Therefore, there is no attainment.
Apart from the essence of the two types of bodhi, there is no separate dharma capable of attaining bodhi;
for this reason, there is no attainment.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Awakening cannot be attained by means of the body or the mind.
This is because where there is a body, it is not awakening; only where there is no body is it awakening."
Therefore, it cannot be attained by means of the body;
for as long as there is a mind, it is not bodhi—it is only when there is no mind that it truly is.
Therefore, it cannot be attained by means of the mind.
The essence of the three types of enlightenment is like the wondrous tranquility that is free from characteristics and beyond grasping or abandoning;
therefore, there is nothing to be attained.
Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There is not even the slightest dharma to be attained."
This is called bodhi;
therefore, it cannot be apprehended.
The essence of the four types of bodhi is of an eternal nature, existing from antiquity and not produced through conditions.
Because this is non-attainment,
the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"The nature of wisdom is eternal and does not arise from causes and conditions."
World-Honored One, for what reason may one inquire into its causes and conditions?
Because it is without conditions, there is no capacity to attain it;
it is eternally not something produced through cultivation.
Therefore, there is nothing to be attained.
Since the five types of awakening have no abiding place that can be sought,
they are thus unattainable.
Therefore, the goddess said:
"Because awakening has no location, there is nothing that can be attained. She asked:
"Bodhi exists at the limit of the future.
Why is it said to have no location? He explained:
If one judges by means of ordinary beings, then birth-and-death is here and bodhi is there;
yet if one discusses it according to the true nature of bodhi, there are no ordinary beings here.
With reference to whom was that said?
Therefore, there is no abiding place.
[The opponent] asks:
The *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds) states that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in all places.
How could there be no place?
The meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
Speaking of reality in terms of conventional characteristics, one attains bodhi everywhere;
yet from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is nowhere it can be found.
Therefore, it is said that there is nowhere.
Because there is no locus, it cannot be apprehended.
This brief exposition on the meaning of "attaining non-attainment" concludes these four gates.
Next, the fifth gate follows: the analysis of the universal and the specific.
Distinguishing it according to its stages:
the intrinsically pure bodhi has both universal and specific aspects;
when analyzed, there are three types.
First, from the perspective of the comprehensive discussion of reality,
its essence permeates both the defiled and the pure;
it is present even within the causal stage.
Therefore, the sutra states:
"All sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi.
Second, this is discussed in terms of the reality of persons.
The true nature of Bodhi is fully realized in the Buddha;
when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha looking back toward its origin, it has always been so,
for it is fundamentally free from the delusive defilements that could obscure or obstruct it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"For ordinary beings who have not yet attained the bodhi of a Buddha, afflictions are [afflictions];
for noble ones when they have attained Buddhahood, afflictions are bodhi."
This meaning is similar to what is taught in the sūtras: that the Buddha knows sentient beings are already in the state of nirvāṇa and do not need to be extinguished further.
Third, distinguishing the real by means of its characteristics:
during the stage of the cause, it is merely called "buddha-nature" and is not yet called "bodhi."
Only when the fruit is fully manifested is it termed *bodhi*.
This is because *bodhi* is the realization of cause and effect.
As for the *bodhi* of skillful means (*upāya*), it is entirely absent during the ordinary stage.
If one speaks of "existence," it refers only to the sense that there is the potential for arising within the essence of the Buddha-nature’s true mind;
as yet, no dharma-essence has come into being.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
That which existed originally is now non-existent;
that which was originally non-existent is now existent. It is impossible for a dharma to exist throughout the three periods of time.
As for what is called "existing originally":
Originally, when one was an ordinary person, there were only the phenomena of birth-and-death and conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
As for the statement that these do not exist now:
it means that while birth-and-death currently exists, the world-transcending virtues of bodhi-practice do not exist therein.
Regarding the statement "originally non-existent":

when originally in the state of an ordinary being, there were no supramundane practices or virtues of bodhi. Regarding the statement "now existent": [supramundane practices and virtues of bodhi now exist].
Regarding the statement that when there is no manifestation of the merit of awakening, there is only birth and death,
and that it is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time:
this is because it is impossible for the dharmas of birth and death to exist eternally throughout the three periods of time.

It is impossible for the noble to exist and ordinary beings not to exist, because the conduct and virtues of bodhi exist eternally throughout the three periods of time; therefore, it is the case that the noble exist while ordinary beings do not.
The sutra commentary explains it thus:
some say that both skillful means and bodhi exist even during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
This interpretation is not correct.
If it were the case that awakening already existed during the stage of an ordinary person and is now absent, or that it was previously absent and is now present,
what would such verses as these intend to reveal?
It is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time;
how, then, could they exist prior [to arising]?
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
The causal basis for the arising of expedient means and bodhi is that which was originally non-existent but now exists;
how can one say it "arises"?
That which previously existed and is now manifested is the causal basis for realization.
How can it be said that [enlightenment] arises?
Furthermore, within the Nirvāṇa-sūtra, the relationship between cause and effect is extensively illustrated through analogies such as milk and curd, or seeds and the growth of trees.
If bodhi were already present during the stage of an ordinary being (pṛthagjana), [how could these analogies hold?]
Milk should contain curd;
within the seed of a tree, there should already be the tree.
[Thus,] curd would exist within the milk, and the tree within the seed.
The Buddha has already refuted this extensively;
by extension, the same applies here.
Why labor to establish it by force?
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"If one says that there is no Buddha-nature at all within the body, one commits a pārājika offense;
if one says that bodhi already exists within the body from the outset, one commits a pārājika offense."
This sin is fearsome;
what is the use of speaking of its existence?
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
If it is said that there previously existed permanence, bliss, self, and purity— which are unconditioned and unborn—
yet they could not be seen because they were obscured by afflictions,
and only after destroying those afflictions does one see them.
This is what is called slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Such a sin of slander is not light;
what benefit is there in establishing it by force?
Furthermore, within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, four types of Buddha-nature are distinguished.
There is a certain Buddha-nature that exists in icchantikas but not in those who possess roots of goodness.
There is a Buddha-nature that those with roots of goodness possess, while those who are icchantikas do not;
there is also a Buddha-nature [that both possess].
Both may possess it; or both may lack the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the meaning of these four phrases,
how can you all interpret them in such a one-sided manner?
Such is the scriptural text.
If one says that both the intrinsically pure nature and the bodhi of skillful means are co-emergently present from the beginning,
how can it be said that icchantikas lack them?
And how can it be said that both types of persons lack them?
The commentary further explains:
It is because they are not manifest that they do not exist; it is not that they lack a substantial nature entirely.
If one says they are non-existent, this "non-existence" is merely a name for their non-manifestation.
That which exists for both parties should be manifest;
the existence that is not manifest is called "knowledge of existence.
That which does not exist is not hidden; it is called "non-existence."
Furthermore, the fruit of bodhi through skillful means is precisely the *saṃbhoga-buddha*. It is called "retribution" (*saṃbhoga*) because it recompenses causes;
it has existed eternally from the beginning, without having previously had a cause.
To whom can this be repaid?
This serves as proof that seeking the original [nature] through such means involves a grave error;
it should not be further established.
Question: The sutras state that within the bodies of sentient beings, the faculties such as the Tathāgata’s eyes and ears, as well as all Buddha-dharmas, are fully present.
Now, why do you say that the bodhi of skillful means is entirely non-existent during the stage of an ordinary person?
To explain: the sūtra states that it is endowed with all dharmas.
This is the Buddha-nature of the Dharma.
Regardless of skillful means,
the distinction between the ordinary and the sage regarding its universality and limitation is thus.
If we consider only the noble ones (ārya) in terms of their universal or limited attainment, there are five categories.
First, according to the most universal perspective,
the worthy and noble ones (ārya) of all three vehicles (triyāna) all attain bodhi.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Śrāvakas attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
pratyekabuddhas attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
"Bodhisattvas attain unsurpassed bodhi," and so forth.
Second, distinguishing the Great Vehicle from the Small Vehicle.
Bodhi is great and does not apply to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Therefore,
the *Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* speaks of five types of bodhi,
which pertain exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
The meaning of the five types of bodhi has been explained extensively above;
here they are listed briefly.
First, the bodhi of generating the mind of awakening (cittotpāda-bodhi).
While within the immeasurable ocean of birth and death, one generates the bodhicitta;
established in the realms of happy rebirths,
this is the second, the bodhicitta of the subdued mind.
Within the stage of the lineage and the patience of subduing,
one realizes the bodhi of the three knowledges of the mind;
this occurs upon the first bhūmi.
Because Prajñā increases further, it is called "clarity" (vidyā).
The four types of emergence and arrival at bodhi occur on the seven stages (bhūmi) and above.
Transcending existence and non-existence, one arrives at the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The five unsurpassed enlightenments reside in the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).
By these five points, it is clearly shown that [these qualities] belong exclusively to the Mahāyāna and do not apply to the Hīnayāna.
Third, regarding the distinction of "differentiation" and "retrogression":
bodhi is restricted to those above the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Therefore, it is said in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding the stage of the "seed of practice" (*śikṣā-bīja*) that "one attains perfect enlightenment as soon as the initial resolve is made.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
The *srotāpanna* reaches it in eighty thousand *kalpas*,
and so on up to the *pratyekabuddha*, who reaches *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in ten thousand *kalpas*. This reaching—
from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upwards— is what is called "reaching bodhi."
When one contemplates within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) based on the superior stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
the true mind of the eight consciousnesses manifests as the subtle obstructions subside;
by relying upon this, one accomplishes virtue.
Therefore, it is upon the spiritual lineage (gotra) that one is said to attain enlightenment (bodhi);
previously, this was not the case,
which is why it was not mentioned.
Fourth, distinguishing the noble from the ordinary:
bodhi is restricted to those from the first bhūmi upward and does not extend to the stages prior to the bhūmis.

Therefore, it is proclaimed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that upon hearing the teaching on the lifespan, a bodhisattva may attain great enlightenment after eight births, or even after a single birth.
The treatise states:
Those who attain awakening after eight births, up to those who attain it after one birth,
clearly understand this through the realized wisdom of the first stage.
Awakening (bodhi) is localized on the stages (bhūmi).
Because, from the first stage onward, within the seven consciousnesses,
the objectifying contemplation gradually ceases and true wisdom gradually manifests, it is called "attaining awakening."
Before the stages (bhūmi), they are not yet identical; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Fifth, this distinguishes the fruit from its cause.
Bodhi resides in the Buddha and does not extend to other persons; therefore,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Attaining skillful means" refers to the path cultivated and studied by all bodhisattvas.
"Attaining the meaning" refers to unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). This should be clearly understood.
Enlightenment (bodhi) resides exclusively in the fruit of Buddhahood.
Such is the distinction between the universal and the particular; this concludes the five gates.
Next, the sixth gate distinguishes [enlightenment] according to time.
"Time" refers to the three periods.
Based on these three periods, awakening (bodhi) is distinguished;
thus, awakening is not fixed.
There is the principle of being both the three times and not the three times.
Regarding what are called the "three times," there are two kinds:
first, the three times as the transformation of substance.
That is to say:
first, the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) undergoes transformation and change according to the beings it converts;
second, with respect to the obstacles of afflictions, there is a sequence of before and after.
There are also two ways to understand why it is not of the three periods of time: first,
because its essence is neither arising nor ceasing,
it is not of the three periods of time.
Turning back toward the first gate:
second, because realization of the truth transcends conditions and wondrously eliminates formal dependencies,
it does not belong to the three periods of time.
Turning back toward the rear gate,
the Sūtra therefore says:
"The Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is neither past, nor future, nor present."
Furthermore, the Sūtra also says:
"I contemplate the Tathāgata as not coming from the past limit, not going to the future limit, and not abiding in the present.
It is like this and so forth.
It is precisely because bodhi possesses this indeterminacy that the Sūtra states:
"According to conventional terminology, one speaks of the three periods of time."
It is not meant that bodhi has past, future, or present.
What is the meaning of this?
Generally, there are four ways of explaining it.
First, regarding the distinction between the True [Body] and the Responsive [Body]: because the responsive transformation has temporal occurrence,
it is subsumed within the three periods of time.
True virtue is eternally abiding;
it is like space, devoid of past, future, or present.
Second, there is a distinction made by contrasting the intrinsic purity of the true nature with skillful means.
The *upāya-bodhi* (expedient bodhi) arises through cultivation based on conditions;
because its arising has a sequence of before and after, it is subsumed within the three periods of time.
Although the *prakṛti-viśuddha-bodhi* (naturally pure bodhi) also arises from the cultivation of contemplation, [it is not so subsumed].
The nature has existed from antiquity;
it does not arise from conditions and is neither past, future, nor present.
This third point directly addresses the purity of this very nature.
This is distinguished according to cultivation and realization.
Innately pure bodhi is manifested through the cultivation of conditions;
because cultivation involves sequential stages, this purity is not simultaneous.
Therefore, there are the three periods of time.
Having attained realization, one looks back and finds that from the beginning there has been nothing hidden;
the present is not something newly manifested. Being neither cause nor effect, by this principle it is neither past, future, nor present.
This one meaning is similar to what is said regarding *nirvāṇa*:
having relinquished conventional compassion (*saṃvṛti-maitrī*), one attains ultimate compassion (*paramārtha-maitrī*);
yet this ultimate compassion does not arise from causes and conditions. The phrasing is thus analogous.
The fourth [point] directly addresses the essence of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
It makes a distinction by considering conditions in relation to reality:
from the perspective of conditions relative to reality, reality exists apart from conditions.
When the reality of external conditions ceases, one realizes them through conditions;
because there is a sequence before and after this realization, there are the three periods of time.
Speaking of reality according to reality, there is no object external to reality;
since objects fundamentally do not exist,
who could come to obscure me?
Therefore, there was nothing hidden originally, and there is nothing hidden now being revealed.
How could there be anything manifested now?
The true nature is eternally quiescent and does not undergo transformation in accordance with conditions.
For this reason, there is no past, future,
or present. Possessing these many meanings,
bodhi is likewise the three periods of time.
The sixth section concerning time is thus concluded.
Next, the seventh section distinguishes between identity and difference by correlating [the subject] with nirvāṇa;
identity and difference are not fixed.
Why is this so? There are two types of dharma-gates: first, the gate of differentiated characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the gate of the two aspects of inclusion:
from the perspective of distinguishing their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the two gates of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are distinct;
however, when discussed from the perspective of inclusion, the two essences of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are one.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of two gates:
first, the analysis of the two virtues in terms of the abandonment of practice;
second, the analysis in terms of intrinsic purity and expedient means.
To speak of the characteristics within the gate of the cultivation of abandonment:
all cultivated virtues are termed bodhi,
for such cultivation is the path.
All virtues of abandonment are uniformly termed *nirvāṇa*,
because abandonment is cessation.
If one considers them according to their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
All of these are aspects of bodhi, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Thus, that text states:
"The two abandonments and the two knowledges are called bodhi."
Question: Bodhi is translated here as "the Path" (mārga).
Cultivating virtues is the Path.
It may be called bodhi;
however, the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) is not the path. For what reason is it also called bodhi?
The term "liberation" (mokṣa) has three meanings.
First, cessation is the fruit of the path;
the fruit is designated according to its cause.
Therefore, it is called bodhi.
It is like the expression "life-sustaining fruit," where life is spoken of as food.
Second, because the meaning of abandonment is the virtue of being free from faults within the family of bodhi,
and because these virtues are subsumed within its essence, it is called bodhi.
Just as all mental factors that are attendants of wisdom are collectively termed "wisdom," so it is with all such cases.
Third, because the essence of the virtue of abandonment is free from obstruction.
This is precisely the meaning of the Path.
Because of this Path, it is called Bodhi.
The practice that severs [defilements] and the virtue [of cessation] together constitute Nirvana.
As it is stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, that text proclaims:
"The extinction of all afflictions is called nirvāṇa."
This is its abandonment.
To proclaim that the three things constitute Great Nirvāṇa is its practice.
Question: Nirvāṇa is translated here as "extinction" (miè).
Since the virtue of cessation is extinction, it may be called nirvāṇa.
The practice of virtue is not extinguished.
For what reason is it called *nirvāṇa*?
There are also three ways of explaining this.
First, because practicing virtue is the cause of its cessation,
and since the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Just as food is said to be life because it is the cause of life,
so too, as stated in the *Dharaṇī*, pleasure is the cause [of happiness];
although the cause is not itself pleasure, it is the cause of pleasure.
Therefore, it is also called "pleasure.
This case is likewise the same.
Second, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the counteractive practices and virtues for the home of nirvāṇa, they are its retinue.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it subsumes all virtues within its essence.
Third, it is called *nirvāṇa* because all conditioned phenomena possess the sense of being free from faults and being quiescent.
The abandonment of the formations is thus.
Next, regarding the distinction between the nature-purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and the skillful means (*upāya*),
if one speaks in terms of their differentiated characteristics, the fruit of nature-purity is entirely *nirvāṇa*.
Because its nature is pure, its essence is quiescent, and it possesses the characteristic of the unconditioned;
the fruits of skillful means are all for the sake of bodhi,
for the practice of skillful means enables one to penetrate to the bodhi and nirvāṇa of the person.
This same point is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Therefore, it is proclaimed there that the qualities of enlightenment are both the causes for their arising and the results produced by them.
The virtue of nirvāṇa is manifested through its causes of arising.
Since skillful means (upāya) alone refers exclusively to bodhi without ambiguity,
there is no need to establish a separate category for it by means of skillful means.
Since the virtue of intrinsic purity (prakṛti-viśuddhi) is unique to nirvāṇa, there is no ambiguity in speaking of it as such;
therefore, there is no need to establish a separate category for "intrinsic purity.
Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, although all forms of bodhi are expedient means, they are not designated as "expedient means."
Although all nirvāṇa is inherently pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), it is not designated as "inherently pure" alone.
When the characteristics are subsumed, both inherent purity and the skillful means (*upāya*) are termed *bodhi*,
and both are likewise called *nirvāṇa*.
Both are termed bodhi.
As it is said in that *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
within that text, the manifestation of the fundamental nature and the discourse on quiescence are called "naturally pure bodhi."
The treatise on the cultivation of merit produced through practice is currently termed "expedient means for bodhi.
This is because both types are indeed bodhi;
they must be distinguished by means of the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and expedient means (*upāya*).
Question: When one practices through skillful means (*upāya*) so that the cultivation of merit leads a person to the fruit,
there is the principle of a path that may be called *bodhi*.
The virtue of intrinsic purity does not possess such a meaning.
For what reason is it also called *bodhi*?
There are three meanings to this explanation.
First, it is the fruit realized by the Daoists.
Because the fruit is designated according to its cause, it is called the "Dao" (Way).
Because it is this Dao, it is termed "bodhi" (enlightenment).
Second, regarding the essence of the Daoist school:
because the essence is subsumed within virtue, it is called bodhi.
Third, the essence of the virtue of intrinsic purity is universally pervasive and unobstructed.
Because it is the meaning of the Path, it is called bodhi.
Both the purity of nature and skillful means are nirvāṇa, as stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
This characteristic also appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In that sutra, the fruit of the pure nature is termed "permanent," while the fruit of the retribution of skillful means is described as "nature.
The Buddha himself said:
If one can cultivate these two characters, "permanently abiding" (nitya), as the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa),
for such a person I have entered parinirvāṇa; for them,
it is the characteristic of cessation.
Relying on foreign languages, the two characters "constant" (chang) and "abiding" (zhu) are cultivated as the characteristic of cessation; this is precisely still the characteristic of nirvana.
Thus it is known.
Both types are indeed *nirvāṇa*.
Precisely because both are *nirvāṇa*, they must be distinguished by means of their intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and their skillful means (*upāya*).
Question: The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inherently pure and its essence is quiescent; it may be termed nirvāṇa.
However, the merit of skillful means is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
Cultivating that which has not yet arisen and that which is not tranquil— by what meaning is it named *nirvāṇa*?
There are three meanings to this explanation.
First, it is the cause of the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity;
because the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, it is called "nirvāṇa.
Second, it is the virtue belonging to the category of nirvāṇa.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it subsumes all virtues within its essential nature.
Furthermore, the cultivation and arising of meritorious qualities also possess the meaning of being free from signs and quiescent; thus, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Because these meanings are pervasive, the essence of naturally pure bodhi is itself naturally pure *nirvāṇa*.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is also called bodhi and also called nirvāṇa.
Because the essence of skillful means (upāya-bodhi) is itself the skillful means of nirvāṇa,
the cultivation of retribution is eternally attained as the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa).
The identity or difference between bodhi and nirvāṇa is thus.
The essence and nature of the virtue of bodhi are profound and vast;
its meaning is difficult to fathom or exhaust.
Furthermore, let us briefly examine this according to the explanations provided in the analogies.
This concludes Volume Eighteen of the *Dacheng yizhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna).
*Mahāyāna-artha-khaṇḍa*, Scroll Nineteen, compiled by Dharma Master Yuan.
Within the section on the Dharmas that are the Fruits of the Collection of Pure Dharmas, this scroll contains nine gates: [1] the Meaning of the Pure Land; [3] the Meaning of the Three Buddhas.

The meaning of the three knowledges; the meaning of the three forms of non-protection; the meaning of the three foundations of mindfulness; the meaning of the four kinds of purity in all aspects; the meaning of the two knowledges; the meaning of the four knowledges; and the meaning of the four fearlessnesses.

207. The Meaning of the Pure Land (19). The Meaning of the Pure Land: An Exposition through Sixfold Categorization. I. Distinguishing Characteristics. II. Clarifying the Causes. III. Clarifying the Land in Terms of the Body. IV. The Presence or Absence of Ordinary and Holy Beings. V. Examining Their Similarities and Differences. First: Explaining the Names.
Regarding what is called the "Pure Land," in the sutras it is at times termed a "Buddha-field" (buddhakṣetra) and at other times referred to as a "Buddha-realm" (buddhaviṣaya).
Some call it the Buddha-land;
some call it the Buddha-field;
others further describe it as the pure realm, the pure sphere, the pure country, or the pure land.
*Kṣetra* is a term from the language of India;
it has no direct equivalent in this region [of China].
It is essentially a specific name for "everywhere."
Distinguishing the location by way of the Buddha,
it is called a "Buddha-field" (buddhakṣetra).
As for a "Buddha-world" (buddhaloka):
"World" (*loka*) refers to the realms and territories of the mundane world;
the place where sentient beings flourish is called the "receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) signifies a distinct sphere.
The dwelling place of the Buddha differs from that of other persons; therefore, it is called a distinct realm (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, the places where the Buddha resides according to his transformative teachings (*nirmāṇa*) each differ.
It is also called "distinction of realms" (*dhātu-vibhāga*).
When distinguished according to the Buddha,
it is termed the "Buddha-world" (*buddha-loka*).
What is called a "Buddha-land" refers to a place where people are gathered;
it is designated as a "land."
It is called a "Buddha-land" because it is distinguished by means of the Buddha;
as for the term "Buddha-field," [it refers to the same].
The place where one dwells in peace is called a "land" (*kṣetra*).
According to the Buddha's analysis, there are lands.
It is called a buddha-field.
If one discusses such a land,
there are those who rule it as kings.
Those who do not rule have no territory;
it is not so for those who possess a body, for all such beings have [a body].
The meanings of "kṣetra" (field) and "dhātu" (realm) are interchangeable;
because this [land] is free from impurity,
it is entirely termed "pure."
The nature-seas of lands, lotuses, Sumerus,
and all such like— these are the various designations for their breadth and narrowness.
Question: Since both the land and the sentient beings exist together,
why is it specifically called the "Buddha-land"?
Now, it is called a "Buddha-field" because no other [fields] are spoken of here,
and because the Buddha is the sovereign.
Thus it is named a Buddha-field.
The explanation of the names and meanings of this single section is thus concluded.
Next, its characteristics will be distinguished;
in order to clarify the Buddha-fields, other meanings will also be distinguished.
There are three types of differentiation:
first, the pure land of phenomena;
second, the pure land of characteristics.
Third, the truly pure lands.
Within the category of phenomenal purity, there is a threefold analysis.
First, a general explanation of their characteristics.
Second, they are specifically revealed;
third, they are determined by way of the truths.
What is their general characteristic?
Regarding "purity of affairs," this refers to the realm inhabited by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Ordinary persons attain a pure sphere through their impure yet pure karma (*sāsrava-śukla-karman*).
The adornment of various jewels and the excellence of their physical characteristics are called "purity of phenomena" (*vastu-śuddhi*).
However, regarding this purity of phenomena at the time of cultivating its causes:
Sentient beings have distinct limitations;
at the time of receiving retribution, the lands they inhabit have specific boundaries and frontiers that differ from one another.
Furthermore, during this period of cultivation...
When grasping at signs and clinging to them as fixed,
at the time of receiving retribution,
the various characteristics of the adornments of the land are each determined.
The general characteristics are thus.
Next, they are specifically explained.
There are two types of purity of phenomena (*vastu*).
First, there are lands obtained through pure karma by ordinary beings seeking existence (*bhava*),
such as the abodes of the various devas mentioned above;
these are acquired because they result from wholesome karma that seeks existence.
At the time of enjoyment,
it again gives rise to the afflictions, fetters, and karma of the three realms of existence;
it does not give rise to the path leading out of existence, but rather to further birth within existence.
It arises specifically through the power of the instruction of virtuous friends;
it is not due to the power of the objects of experience one encounters.
The second refers to the pure lands obtained by ordinary beings seeking liberation through their roots of goodness,
such as the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī) or the World of Fragrant Treasures (Gandhavatī).
These are attained because they arise from supramundane wholesome karma.
When enjoyed, it can give rise to the path to liberation,
like the rice of many fragrances.
Those who consume it extinguish delusion and give rise to the Way;
such is the case with these and others like them.
Question: Are the realms of the devas in this land exclusively populated by those born through karma that seeks existence (*bhava*),
or can there also be those who attain supramundane goodness?
The principle also encompasses both [aspects].
Therefore, within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
the Buddha expounded the meaning of "self."
It is clearly understood that immeasurable birds and beasts, upon hearing this teaching, gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and were reborn among the devas; however,
because those who emerge from goodness and are reborn in [the higher realms] are few, they are not discussed here.
The specific characteristics are thus.
Next, their characteristics are defined by way of the Four Noble Truths;
this concerns the cause within the first of the two preceding sections.
This is exclusively the truth of origination (samudaya-satya),
because it is the cause of the segmented [existence] and is the fruit of the first gateway.
Its essence is exclusively the Truth of Suffering,
as it is the fruit of the conditioned existence of the mundane realm; it is the cause for the subsequent category.
It possesses two capacities:
first, it directly evokes the fruit of Buddhahood;
second, it indirectly summons rebirth in a Pure Land.
Directly encountering the Buddha,
it is exclusively non-accumulative and capable of generating the virtues of a Buddha.
Because one does not accumulate the fruits of birth-and-death and the various realms of existence,
one is reborn in the borderlands; furthermore,
one accumulates both the non-accumulated and the accumulated.
Manifesting as the cause at the initial gate before one, it may be said that it is not the accumulation [of suffering];
it seeks out the roots of goodness.
Because this is subsumed under the Truth of the Path that resembles [the Truth of Cessation], it is a discourse on reality according to its specific category;
its essential nature is accumulation (*samudaya*).
Because it can bring about the fruits of conditioned arising and cessation,
the fruit of the latter category differs from that of the former in not being suffering.
Because it is a fruit that resembles the supramundane,
the treatise declares that the Land of Immeasurable Life does not belong to the three realms.
Because it is free from craving and desire, it is not the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Because it exists on the ground, it is not called the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Because it possesses form and color, it is not the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because these resemble the fruits of the Path,
they are subsumed under the category of the Path;
therefore, they are not called suffering.
Resembling the pure land of a Buddha,
it is subsumed within the path to enlightenment;
this is the definitive discourse on its own specific category.
Its essence is the Truth of Suffering,
because it is the fruit of arising and ceasing,
and because it is the locus upon which the retributive body with outflows depends.
The purity of the object is thus established.
Next, the purity of the characteristics is analyzed,
which is likewise distinguished by means of three gates.
First, a general explanation of the characteristics;
second, a specific elucidation;
third, a definitive determination based on the truths.
What is the general characteristic?
Regarding "purity of marks," this refers to the lands inhabited by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas.
As Nāgārjuna has said:
there exists a wondrous pure land that transcends the three realms.
These Arhats shall be reborn therein;
such are these various noble ones and sages.
Through the cultivation of contemplation on conditions as an antidote, one attains a realm that is adorned with sublime marks,
free from defilement, and utterly pure; yet, although the land is thus purified, [it remains a conditioned state].
The deluded mind arises like what is seen in a dream;
it is false and not real.
Because it is free from defilement among the marks, it is called "purity of marks.
Now, regarding this purity of marks at the time of cultivating its causes:
Sentient emotions have no fixed distinctions;
when retribution is received,
there are no spatial boundaries to the lands.
Furthermore, during this cultivation, the mind is free from fixed attachment;
whatever objects are attained revolve in accordance with the mind.
They are like magical illusions;
they have no fixed direction.
Such is their general characteristic.
Next, it will be explained specifically.
There are two distinct sections:
first, the classification according to practice.
Second, the classification according to mind.
Regarding the phrase "according to practice," there are two distinct types of practice.
First, there is the land obtained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas through the roots of goodness for their own benefit;
it is empty, quiescent, and formless.
Just as there are places where beings dwell in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
A question is asked:
How can there be places in the formless realm?
The commentary states:
In the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), there is merely an absence of coarse matter (rūpa),
but it is not that subtle matter is absent.
Therefore, there is a basis for this;
thus the Sūtra proclaims that the olfactory faculty of a Bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the formless palaces.
As Nāgārjuna said:
there is a wondrous pure land that transcends the three realms.
This refers precisely to the case of the Arhat who, while among the living, heard the Lotus Sūtra.
Because it arises from one's own roots of goodness,
at the time of its enjoyment,
it gives rise only to the roots of goodness of renunciation regarding one's own conduct.
They are unable to spontaneously give rise to the compassionate vow to act for the benefit of others;
even if such a thought should arise,
it is due to the power of the Buddha’s and Bodhisattvas’ transformative teachings.
It is not obtained through the power of the objects of experience; rather,
it is the land obtained from the roots of goodness of various bodhisattvas who transform others,
never abandoning sentient beings.
One receives them according to the objects [offered],
just as in the room of Vimalakīrti;
this is because they arise from the roots of goodness cultivated for the sake of transforming others.
At the time of enjoyment,
one is naturally able to initiate virtuous practices for the benefit of others;
such is the case with respect to conduct.
Regarding the phrase "abbreviating the mind," there are two distinct types of mind: first,
within the *saviṣayavijñāna* (consciousness with objects), by contemplating the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [states], one can attain the Pure Land.
Within the two types of deluded consciousness, the object-observing (yuan-guan) untainted consciousness can attain the Pure Land;
as for the activity-consciousness (shi-shi),
its untainted state is of two kinds.
First, the pure land attained through the contemplation of increasing signs (*vṛddhi-nimitta-bhāvanā*),
which is maintained in continuous succession and relinquished only upon the realization of truth (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).
Second, the pure land attained through the contemplation of ceasing signs (*nirodha-nimitta-bhāvanā*).
Manifesting momentarily like an illusion,
the deluded consciousness is also of two kinds when it is untainted (anāsrava).

First, the pure land attained through the contemplation of increasing signs (*vṛddhi-nimitta-bhāvanā*) is maintained in continuous succession and only relinquished upon the realization of truth (*tattva-sākṣātkriyā*).
Second, the pure land attained through the contemplation of ceasing signs (*nirodha-nimitta-bhāvanā*).
Manifesting briefly, they immediately perish;
such are their distinct characteristics.
Next are the three successive gates.
Established by way of the truths,
it is the cause for the purification of characteristics;
its form precedes and is not the accumulation.
Because it is subsumed within the Truth of the Path,
it is "origination" in its own right;
because it is the cause of transformation, it is origination.
The fruit of the purification of the marks is not suffering as previously defined,
because it is subsumed within the fruit of the Path.
Just as in the Buddha’s Pure Land, which is subsumed within the path to enlightenment,
when analyzed according to its specific divisions, the essential nature of reality is suffering;
yet, because it is a fruit of transformation, its characteristics are pure in this way.
Next, the true purity is elucidated through an analysis of its four gates:
first, a general analysis of its characteristics;
second, a specific manifestation of them.
Third, the determination according to the truths;
fourth, the detailed analysis according to their meanings.
What, in general terms, is this?
That which is called "truly pure" refers to the lands where those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, up to all Buddhas, abide.
It is the land obtained through the roots of goodness realized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The true nature of dependent origination is wondrously pure and free from defilement,
for it is eternal and unchanging.
Therefore, it is called "True Purity.
Yet this True Purity arises because there is no conditioned thought;
where there is no conditioned thought, the land has no conditioned thought, and the land has no phenomenal characteristics.
It is like the jewel atop the head of Brahmā, the Lord of Gods: although its substance exists, it does not manifest the characteristics of blue, yellow, red, white, or other colors.
It is also like the unmanifested precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) of a bhikṣu: although their substance is form (*rūpa*), they possess no single characteristic.
It exists yet lacks signs; this is the subtlety of the land.
Furthermore, because this true land is free from fixed attachments, the land has no fixed location.
Because it is free from discrimination,
the land has no distinctions of "this" and "that," or "self" and "other.
Such is its general characteristic.
Next, it is specifically elucidated.
Within this, there are three analytical sections.
The first concerns false conceptualization.
True practice is of two kinds.
The first is the true [practice] that is free from delusion,
which preserves the true practices accomplished by all bodhisattvas.
Though separated from delusion,
the true land one attains nevertheless merges back with delusion.
Like the sky amidst mist,
within this gateway,
the lands vary in their stages and levels according to their respective positions.
As one progresses through the various stages of the path, [the realization] gradually increases stage by stage;
the false lands gradually vanish while the true lands gradually manifest,
just as when mist gradually dissipates, the empty sky becomes increasingly apparent.
Second is the purity of the true realm,
which refers to the lands where the Buddha-Tathāgata resides;
these are purely true and without admixture.
Just as pure space,
although the land is pure, should still be conjoined with defilement;
these two are distinguished according to their activity.
The essential practices are only two:
first, wisdom; second, compassion.
Wisdom is established by relying on emptiness.
Gathering practice through wisdom,
all practices are free from signs;
such is the land attained.
It is identical to that cause:
wondrously quiescent, free from marks,
and like empty space.
Compassion arises in accordance with the existence of sentient beings. One gathers all practices through compassion,
and every practice is performed for the sake of others.
The land thus obtained corresponds to its cause;
it manifests according to the objects [of perception].
It is like a pure jewel;
no color appears within it.
Therefore, the *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds) says:
Although one knows that all Buddha-lands are like space,
one nevertheless contemplates the practice of the infinitely adorned lands.
Third, the classification according to phenomena.
Within that true *tathāgatagarbha*,
there are two gateways to the Dharma:
first, the gateway of quiescence.
Based on this, one attains the land,
which likewise accords with that Dharma— quiescent and devoid of characteristics.
Second is the dharma-gate of the functioning of conditions.
Based upon this, lands arise,
manifesting everything without exception.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which manifests everything according to whatever is sought by the mind.
The specific characteristics are thus.
Next, we shall discuss them in terms of the Truths within this section.
Regarding the causes of the Pure Land:
whether they are the path (*mārga*) or cessation (*nirodha*),
when the causal substance arises through practice, it is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The arising through the power of the Dharma-gate is subsumed under the Truth of Cessation;
its fruit is likewise so.
Alternatively, it is included within the fruit of the Path, as it is comprised by Bodhi.
Alternatively, because it is subsumed under the fruit of cessation within nirvāṇa,
it resembles the Buddha’s dharmakāya;
such is the case with respect to the [Four] Truths.
Next, the fourth section provides a detailed analysis according to the meaning.
Within this, the opening and closing, as well as the expansion and abbreviation, are not fixed;
sometimes they are consolidated into one.
There is but one Buddha-land;
yet it is sometimes divided into two,
namely the True and the Responsive, as designated by those who boast of their own [doctrines].
It is called "True" (Sambhogakāya);
it is called "Responsive" (Nirmāṇakāya) because it manifests diversely according to others.
That true land is precisely the land of the Dharma-gate of equality;
it is wondrously quiescent and free from marks.
Perfectly embodying all meanings,
its form has no fixed location;
there is nowhere it does not abide.
This is like the principles of the Yin and Yang and the Five Elements;
this analogy resembles the Dharma.
One should maintain it with careful mindfulness.
Since the earth is thus,
how could its various marks and adornments be apprehended as something separate?
Although there is no distinct form,
one cannot say that earth does not exist;
likewise, although it is wondrously quiescent, it possesses the nature of functioning as a condition.
All things arise in dependence upon it;
its transformations respond to what is entrusted to them,
just as the principles of the Yin and Yang and the Five Elements can create all the material forms of the world.
The true land is thus;
as for its manifested lands,
they appear according to the dispositions of sentient beings, exhibiting localized distinctions.
The defiled and pure bodies differ in form;
the various marks of good and evil, as well as their adornments, are distinct and diverse.
It is thus with the lands they inhabit.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three:
first, the Dharma-nature land;
second, the land of true retribution.
Third is the Perfectly Accomplished Land (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*).
As for the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*),
it is the fundamental nature of the land.
All phenomena share the same essence;
they are empty, harmonious, and unimpeded,
like the net of Indra.
It is also like space— unimpeded, immovable, non-existent, and so forth.
This is the analysis of the meaning of the single essence,
the characteristic of the true meaning as taught in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
This is precisely its meaning:
the fundamental nature of all worlds is eternally thus,
yet the deluded thoughts of sentient beings obscure their minds.
One brings about obstruction through self-inflicted conditioning;
within the state of non-obstruction,
one perceives fixed obstructions.
Where there is existence, it is definitively existent; where there is non-existence, it is definitively non-existent;
where there is defilement, it is definitively defiled.
The element of space is fixed as space;
the element of earth is fixed as earth;
the element of water is fixed as water.
In this way, all such [notions] are subsequently stilled;
that is the true nature of that land.
The manifestation that accomplishes my function is called the Dharma-nature Land (dharmatā-kṣetra).
As for the Land of Actual Reward (vipāka-bhoga-kṣetra):
When the Bodhisattva manifests the land of the dharma-nature before him,
he extensively cultivates inexhaustible practices within the dharma-realm;
by the power of the merit generated through these pure deeds, [he attains this state].
Within that realm of the boundless pure dharma-dhātu,
the arising of immeasurable and diverse adornments is termed the "Land of True Reward.
This Land of True Reward—
The meaning is distinguished into three types,
which are identical to the subsequent *saṃbhogakāya*. The first is according to the teaching based on the Dharma.
It returns to the same dharma-nature;
adorned with all marks,
it is fused and unimpeded like the ten characteristics of the ocean.
"Pervading each and all,
perfectly corresponding to the lands" refers to the two aforementioned true lands.
It is like a pure jewel that can manifest in various different ways according to sentient beings.
Because it is utilized without deficiency,
it is called the Perfectly Responsive Land (pariśuddha-kṣetra).
Alternatively, it may be divided into seven.
As stated in the *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra*:
first, purity of the same essence;
second, purity of mastery.
Third, purity of adornment;
fourth, purity of enjoyment;
fifth, purity of the sentient beings inhabiting the dwelling place.
Sixth is purity of cause;
seventh is purity of result.
Among these seven, the first four clarify the characteristics of the essence of the land.
The fifth type relies upon others to manifest its excellence;
this refers to the final two gates.
Citing the cause to reveal the result:
among the preceding four [categories],
this concerns the first two gates.
The first section clarifies the substance of that land;
the third section distinguishes the characteristics of that land.
Regarding the latter one [of the three] as the function and the former two as the essence:
the first clarifies that there is no distinction in the essence of those lands.
The latter one reveals that the substance of that land is pure.
Regarding "purity of identical substance":
the obstruction of phenomena by one another is termed impurity.
The state in which they are identical in essence and interfuse is called "purity.
What is meant by being identical in essence?
There are three distinctions.
First, the distinction between root and branch:
the land of the Dharma-nature is its root.
Retribution is the secondary aspect;
all retribution has the dharma-nature as its essence.
Therefore, they are said to be of the same substance.
Second, one must distinguish between the true and the responsive;
this applies to all lands of response.
Because they take the True [Dharmakāya] as their essence,
they are called "identical in essence.
Third, regarding the various lands within the realm of response, they are compared with one another.
They are of the same substance and without distinction; therefore, they are called "of the same substance.
Thus it is with the various kinds of sentient beings in this Sahā world-system.
Regarding the various different views concerning this land,
they are like King Śaṅkhacūḍa’s vision of the jewel-adorned [palace], and so forth.
The various lands they perceive all share the same substance as this Sahā world;
such is the case for all of them.
Therefore, they are said to be of the same substance. Thus, a sutra states:
"All Buddha-fields are one Buddha-field."
One is all. The three meanings are as before.
Regarding "mastery and purity":
Generally speaking, there are two kinds of purity:
the first is purity of characteristics.
Adorned with various jewels, it is pure, magnificent, and beautiful,
like the realm of Sukhāvatī or the land of Gandhavatī;
this is the purity of the two masteries.
It is like a pure jewel,
in which beauty and ugliness both appear;
what appears therein is without obstruction.
Therefore, it is called "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*).
Because the essence of the land is pure,
one is able to exercise such unimpeded sovereignty.
By manifesting the essence through its function,
it is termed "sovereign purity.
The meaning discussed here corresponds to the latter category.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All lands are equally pure; they are lands of pure characteristics."
That which is defiled and this which is pure cannot be called equal.
As for that which is pure by its own mastery:
Defilement and purity are perfectly interfused;
the Dharma-realm is uniformly equal.
Therefore, it is called "equality."
The adornment and purity of the substance of these two lands constitute their characteristic marks.
In general, there are three types:
first, those who adorn themselves,
namely superior and virtuous sentient beings.
Dwelling therein, the land is called Pure.
Regarding the purity of sentient beings in the five lower abodes:
This is precisely its meaning.
Adorned with these two dharmas,
one is endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
That land is named Pure;
thus the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
"It is adorned by persons and all dharmas."
Adorned with these three things,
the five desires are exquisite and sublime.
Among these three kinds:
The *Bhūmi-sūtra* specifically explains one matter: adornment.
Regarding the adornment of the pure land, there are three types.
First is the adornment of supernormal powers,
wherein all objective realms are manifested without obstruction.
Second is the adornment of radiant light.
It is constantly possessed of radiance that dispels all darkness;
it is adorned with the three marks and embellished with various jewels.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Those who enjoy purity are fully endowed with the majestic marks of light and the adornments of supernormal powers."
This is the functional utility of that land;
it is the enjoyment at the time of experiencing the realm of the Pure Land.
It can extinguish afflictions and give rise to the Path;
these preceding four kinds clarify the essential characteristics of the land.
Regarding the purification of sentient beings in the fifth dwelling place:
this is manifested through the excellence of human beings—
sentient beings possessing immeasurable merit and wisdom.
It is completely filled with these;
therefore, the land is superior.
Furthermore, because virtuous people dwell within it, the land is pure.
Within the latter two gates,
regarding the first, "purity of cause," the cause is cited to manifest the result.
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the practice of deeds for the pure land,
namely, generosity and the observance of precepts.
The practice of deeds is as explained by Vimalakīrti.
Second is the merit of the pure land,
namely, the dharma-gate of the Pure Land Samādhi.
Because one has attained this gate,
all objective realms revolve in accordance with the mind.
Such as the samādhi of the essential nature of the Buddha-lands entered by Vajragarbha;
these are examples of abiding within the midst of the midst.
Because they rely exclusively on the rear gate,
he further states:
"They enter the wondrous state of equality within the Buddha-land."
This is called the "Purity of Causes.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Lands of all Buddhas is called the "Supremely Wondrous and Equal Realm."
When a bodhisattva enters into realization,
they are able to manifest various transformations;
this is called the purity of the cause.
Regarding the term "purity of the fruit":
in contrast to the cause,
the fruit is generally discussed as being of two types.
The fruit of purity in a single aspect:
by extensively cultivating practices for the pure land,
the bodhisattva attains a wondrously pure land.
The adornment of various marks is able to purify and remove all defilements;
this is the second fruit of mastery,
which relies upon the merit and activity of the aforementioned samādhi of the pure land.
The meaning explained in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding various diverse manifestations will be addressed in a subsequent section.
In that sutra, manifesting [the Buddha] in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings is called "purity of fruition.
This is explained in detail according to specific treatises.
It may also be immeasurable.
The analysis of its characteristics is thus.
Next is the third section.
To discern and determine its cause,
we shall first establish that cause by way of the three lands,
beginning with the analysis of the causes according to the Dharma-body and Reward-body lands.
This shall be explained separately later.
As for the characteristics of the causes of the two lands—the Dharma-realm land and the Reward land—how are they distinguished? They are discussed according to their distinct characteristics.
The beginningless dharma-nature is the cause of the dharma-realm;
it consists of the various perfections and other practices.
This is the cause of the reward land (*vipākakṣetra*).
To summarize its characteristics,
both lands alike take the beginningless *dharmatā* and the various *pāramitās* as their cause.
Within this, the meaning is divided into the conditioned (sappaccaya) and the correct (sammā).
Regarding the contrast between the conditioned and the correct, there are two gates to the underlying crookedness (*vaṅka*): first, the explanation by way of specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*).
The land of the dharma-nature takes the beginningless dharma-nature as the direct cause and the various perfections (pāramitās) as the contributory cause.
In the land of true retribution,
the various practices such as the perfections constitute the direct cause,
for they are what directly give birth [to that land].
The dharma-nature serves as the condition.
This is explained through two general characteristics:
both lands equally employ the beginningless dharma-nature as the direct cause.
Although both take the dharma-nature as their direct cause,
they differ in their specific causes:
the cause for the Dharma-body and the cause for the Land.
The essential nature of the dharmas as they exist inherently is no different from that at the time of their subsequent manifestation;
there is neither increase nor decrease in their essence,
only the difference between concealment and manifestation.
Regarding the cause of the land of retribution:
fundamentally, there is no intrinsic nature of dharmas;
it merely arises upon the aforementioned cause of the dharma-land.
From the very beginning,
there has been the principle of dependent origination through which things can arise;
upon encountering conditions, they are born.
Just as gold within ore has the potential to be fashioned into ornaments, which it then becomes upon meeting with the necessary conditions,
yet there was no pre-existing entity of that form contained within it beforehand.
In both lands, the practices of the various pāramitās are equally employed as contributory causes (pratyaya-hetu).
Although in both cases the various pāramitās serve as contributory causes, [there is a distinction].
When subdivided therein,
their meanings also differ.
How do these differing characteristics manifest?
The various practices of the perfections possess the capacity to produce [results];
they are therefore described as the conditions for the land of retribution.
Just as earth, water, and so forth are able to produce all things,
the various practices such as the perfections (pāramitās) have the capacity to realize the ultimate meaning;
therefore, they are described as the conditions for the Dharma-nature land (dharmatā-kṣetra).
The preceding two [cases] are thus.
Next, we shall discuss the lands of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). Regarding the causes for these lands of transformation, their presence or absence is not fixed.
Function is subsumed within its substance;
there is no further distinct cause.
This is, for example, like how worldly people hold that because of a form there is a shadow, yet the shadow is not a separate entity.
The differences in the lands perceived through karma are not due to my own agency;
they are distinctions of function within a single substance.
It is also said that they possess causes, because they are effects.
There are two kinds of causes.
The homogeneous cause likewise takes that which is to be practiced as its corresponding cause.
Thus it is with all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Having attained this land long ago,
he now cultivates various practices to adorn the realm.
It is like the land of Amitābha Buddha, which was manifested through the cultivation of the forty-eight great vows and various practices that adorned the Western World;
such is the case here as well.
Second, the cause of a different category:
practicing the true Dharma serves as the cause for the Land of Response (*saṃbhogakāya*).
However, within the Land of Response, there are two distinct meanings.
First, by the power of the dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Purity of the Buddha-land,
various realms are manifested;
second, it is due to retributive response.
By means of the causal conditions of his original vow of great compassion,
he manifests various lands;
such is the distinction in their meaning.
These two are distinct divisions:
the land of the Dharma-correspondence and the pure land dharma-gate within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Taking this as the cause,
through the land of retribution and response and the power of great compassionate vows.
Taking this as the cause and making compassionate vows the primary factor,
one governs and integrates all practices.
All of these serve as causes.
Such is the analysis of their individual characteristics. To speak in terms of their inclusive characteristics:
Second, one should employ both the Dharma-gate of Pure Land and compassionate vows as the causes.
In terms of their meaning, these are further divided into the circumstantial and the primary.
The conditions are correct yet indeterminate;
if we discuss the principles of the Dharma,
it concerns the dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
One considers the right cause as the primary cause and great compassion, vows, and so forth as the contributory causes. If there were no compassion and vows,
[enlightenment would not arise].
Those dharmas cannot arise independently of their appropriate conditions.
For example, although a fire-gem can produce fire, it must depend upon seeing the sun;
likewise, although a water-gem can produce water, it must require seeing the moon.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because a distinct phenomenon exists, another distinct phenomenon arises;
because a distinct phenomenon does not exist, another distinct phenomenon ceases and perishes."
In this land of retribution,
the Great Compassionate Vow serves as the direct cause,
while the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land serves as the contributory cause.
If those dharmas were absent,
although one possessed compassion and vows, one would not be born in that land;
it is like how sound, though capable of producing an echo, must necessarily depend upon a mountain valley.
A face can produce a reflection only by depending on water or a mirror.
[The opponent] asks:
Should not the land arise from the power of the dharma-gate of true compassion and vows?
Why is it not called "Real" (Bhūta),
but rather explained as "Conformity" (Anurūpa)?
The commentary states:
Through the power of great compassion, vows, and practice,
one truly attains the true land;
through the power of superior conditions, one simultaneously gives rise to the responsive land.
Because it does not arise correctly, it is not called "real.
It arises through the combined power of conditions,
causing people to see and hear it.
Therefore, it is said to be "appropriate.
The analysis of the cause is thus.
Next follow four gates.
Explaining the lands by way of the body,
therein there are three gates of analysis. First,
explaining the mutual dependence of the body and the land, as well as their primary and secondary aspects.
Second, the mutual dependence of body and land regarding their breadth and narrowness;
third, the mutual dependence of body and land regarding their totality and particularity.
As for the terms "root" and "branch":
Speaking according to conventional characteristics,
the physical retribution depends upon the land; yet,
when investigating the ultimate reality, [it is found that]...
Since the land depends upon the body,
the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"Clouds of jewel flowers, fragrances, and various articles of adornment."
All emerge from within the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is also said that the kalpas of the three periods of time and all the Buddha-fields [arise therefrom].
Everything is manifested within a single Buddha-body;
this is precisely the supporting body of that land. Since the Buddha-land is thus, [so too is its supporting body].
It is the same for all lands.
Discussing them according to their characteristics:
the retribution body relies upon the land.
Ultimate reality is likewise the body upon which the land depends;
thus the Sūtra says:
"It is proclaimed that the three realms are illusory and are produced solely by the mind."
The root and the branches are thus.
Next, the breadth and narrowness will be clarified;
their meaning is not fixed.
There are four types of distinctions.
First, the land is broad while the body is narrow,
as is commonly seen.
It is because the body is one's individual retribution that it is narrow and limited;
whereas the land is a collective fruit.
They mutually rely upon one another,
which is why [the realm] is so vast and expansive.
In the case of the two bodies, the bodies are broad while the lands are narrow.
As it is said in the sūtras:
there are some buddha-fields that abide within the pores of a buddha or bodhisattva.
Or they dwell within the folds of the Bodhisattva’s robes;
or they dwell within the Bodhisattva’s celestial crown;
such are the various instances.
The three bodies and their lands are both vast.
According to the ultimate reality,
the body is like empty space.
The land is likewise. In these four cases, both the bodies and the lands are narrow;
they manifest in accordance with the beings to be transformed.
Sometimes they manifest small bodies,
and sometimes they dwell in lands of skillful means;
their breadth and narrowness are thus.
Next, the mutual dependence of the bodies and lands is explained in terms of both the general and the specific. To discuss them according to their general characteristics:
the three bodies constitute one body and three lands.
Although there is but one Buddha-body based upon one Buddha-land,
it is divided according to its various meanings;
thus, by means of those three bodies, they respectively rely upon three lands.
The Dharma-nature body abides in the Dharma-nature land;
the Body of True Reward [abides in] the Land of True Reward.
Based on the true recompense land,
the responsive transformation body still relies upon the responsive land.

Question: What is the distinction between the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and the Dharma-nature land (dharmatā-bhūmi), and how do they relate to the teaching on the mutual dependence [of form and emptiness]?
The commentary states:
Although the nature of the body and the land is without distinction,
they are differentiated according to their characteristics.
Therefore, they attain mutual dependence.
The true nature of the body is called the *dharmakāya*;
the true nature of the land is called the *dharmatā*, and so forth.
This also involves the meaning of being of the same substance while having distinct aspects that depend upon one another,
just as the ten characteristics of the ocean are of the same substance and mutually dependent.
It is asked:
The response body (nirmāṇakāya) likewise relies upon the response land;
this relying body first manifests as an ordinary being and subsequently manifests as a noble one.
Why is it that the land upon which they rely does not likewise remain constant from beginning to end, being initially defiled and subsequently pure?
The commentary states:
This is because the manifestations of transformation are not uniform;
alternatively, the lands follow the bodies [of the Buddhas].
Just as the land of Amitābha Buddha was base and defiled before he attained buddhahood,
yet after his attainment of buddhahood, the realm became majestic and pure,
and that Buddha now dwells therein.
Because the objects are indeterminate;
thus it is in all such cases.
Alternatively, the body conforms to the land.
Thus, although Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood long ago,
throughout immeasurable past eons he dwelt in bodies within defiled lands.
They manifest as ordinary beings and do not attain perfect enlightenment;
all such cases may involve a difference between the body and the land.
Now, although Śākyamuni dwells in a defiled land and manifests as a Buddha,
this land is a manifestation of his retribution;
once retribution is fixed, it is difficult to alter.
Therefore, from beginning to end it is always defiled;
it is like the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya),
which manifests as a result of karmic retribution.
Constant from beginning to end,
it consists of wisdom, conduct, and merit;
it is a skillful means, not a karmic retribution.
This is because there is a subsequent transformation;
that which initially appears as ordinary subsequently transforms into the holy.
This rough analysis based on the correspondence between body and land is thus concluded.
The fifth section in sequence clarifies the meaning of the existence or non-existence of ordinary beings and sages. Regarding this,
the explanations provided by various schools since ancient times have each differed.
As Master Daosheng said:
"The Buddha has no form-body, nor does he have a pure land;
it is solely for the purpose of transforming sentient beings."
"One should manifest and abide within the realms of sentient beings. Thus it is said:
sentient beings possess realms.
The Buddhas have none;
this is what Master Kumārajīva found peculiar.
The Buddhas possess lands.
Sentient beings do not exist at all;
it is only that the Buddha manifests different lands according to his transformative teachings.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
It is for the sake of transforming sentient beings that this land is manifested as impure.
Furthermore, others say:
The Buddhas and sentient beings each have their own distinct lands,
for they each dwell within the fruits of their respective karma;
such is what has been taught.
The meaning is such that it encompasses both perspectives and cannot be definitively fixed to one side alone. What is this meaning?
There are three types of discrimination:
first, subsuming reality under appearances,
whereby sentient beings possess lands.
The Buddhas have no lands,
for they manifest their dwelling in accordance with the places where sentient beings are to be transformed.
Therefore, a sutra says:
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva relies upon suchness and does not rely upon Buddha-fields;
since Samantabhadra is thus, [others are likewise].
The same applies to all Buddhas.
Master Sheng’s established doctrine corresponds to this gate.
Second, subsuming the characteristics according to reality.
The Buddhas possess lands;
sentient beings have no land.
Within a single Buddha-land...
According to their various karmic actions, there are diverse perceptions;
this is just as sentient beings perceive the single body of a Buddha differently.
Thus, a sutra says:
The Buddha-land is as pure as a mani jewel,
appearing in various different ways according to the diverse dispositions of sentient beings.
Vimalakīrti also said:
"My land is eternally pure.
It is only because I wish to deliver these inferior beings that I manifest this world as a place of manifold evils and impurity."
What Master Kumārajīva has stated is precisely what the meaning requires here;
since the sutra teaches it thus, it must be so.
According to the position established by Master Sheng,
the Buddha has no form-body (rūpakāya) and possesses no pure land (śuddhāvāsabhūmi) whatsoever.
This interpretation is incorrect.
That the Buddha possesses no form-body has been refuted in detail in the preceding chapter on Nirvāṇa.
Since the body is not non-existent,
how could the land not exist?
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
The Bodhisattva’s cultivation of all modes of conduct serves as the cause for purifying the Buddha-field;
the Sūtras state that there is such a cause.
How can there be no fruit?
Others also offer this defense:
"It is not that the realms are entirely non-existent."
It must simply not be real.
If the land and its fruits were [merely] so, they would necessarily not be real,
as Vimalakīrti has said.
All modes of conduct are the causes for purifying the Buddha-land;
they should be practiced accordingly.
Since the cultivation of causes is already genuine,
how could the fruit not be true?
If you yourself do not understand this, [you will fail].
One should only inquire further;
how could one dare to slander it rashly?
To slander the fruit-virtues of the Buddha is [unjustified].
The gravity of this offense is extreme;
do not speak of it again later.
This is the second summary of characteristics according to reality.
The three aspects differ in their reality;
sentient beings and Buddhas each have their own distinct lands.
How is this meaning explained? It is by subsuming the fruit within karma.
Since the fruit varies according to the distinctions of karma, all [beings] and the Buddha each have their own distinct lands.
Just as hungry ghosts see the waters of the Ganges as fire,
the Tathāgata sees them as water.
The hungry ghosts, through the karmic force of fire, perceive it as fire;
the Buddha, through the karmic force of water, perceives it as water.
Each perceives the fruit of their own karma and clings to it, not seeing the reality of what others see.
The Buddha-field is likewise:
Śikhin, whose mind was pure, saw the land as pure;
Śāriputra, whose mind was defiled, saw the land as impure.
Thus, this has been a brief differentiation regarding the existence or non-existence of ordinary beings and sages.
Next is the sixth section.
To clarify what is seen and examine its similarities and differences,
there are two parts. First, a classification according to location.
Second, the classification according to the phenomena.
Regarding the classification according to the locations, there are four types.
They dwell together while holding divergent views,
just as within a single world there are various differing views according to the diversity of karma.
Just as in the Ganges River,
worldly people see water,
while hungry ghosts see fire.
Or they may see empty pits;
in all such cases, two people see the same thing in different locations.
Just as in the Sahā world,
although the locations of the ten billion heavens differ, what is seen therein is similar;
in three respects, they are identical in location and identical in vision.
Sentient beings with similar karma perceive the same object in one place; for example,
immeasurable sentient beings alike perceive and know the water of the Ganges.
In this way, all such cases involve different locations and different perspectives,
as in the case of the Sahā world and the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
What is seen is distinct for each;
in this manner, it is so with respect to all locations.
Next, regarding the discussion of the actual entities:
within a single locus, they are divided into four according to their respective meanings.
First, there is the single substance with diverse perceptions.
For example, regarding a single piece of land in this Sahā world-system,
sentient beings therein have various different perceptions of it.
Some see it as water;
others see it as fire;
others see various jewels.
Or one may see empty space;
all such cases are instances of different substances being perceived as the same.
Within a single location,
according to what various people perceive, there appear diverse lands;
yet when a group of sentient beings perceives it, they see it as only a single field and world-system.
In all such cases, there is one substance and one perception;
sentient beings of the same class collectively perceive a single object.
