The Meaning of the Three Non-Defenses (19). The Meaning of the Three Non-Defenses. The Meaning of the Three Non-Defenses.
As it is said in the sūtras:
"The three karmas of the Tathāgata are purely clean and free from fault."
There is no need for protection; this is called the "threefold lack of need for protection.
Although the three types of action of all Arhats are pure, [they do not require guarding].
One must constantly practice protection in order to be able to remain free from faults;
the Tathāgata is different from such persons,
and for this reason, he proclaims the three ways in which he requires no protection.
Question: For what reason do the Tathāgata’s actions of body, speech, and mind not require protection? Answer:
Because he has long cultivated pure precepts and their nature is fully perfected.
Because they abide eternally in profound meditative concentration and never emerge from it;
because their three karmas always follow the movement of wisdom;
and because they dwell in great nirvana in perpetual quiescence.
Therefore, there is no need to guard the three types of action;
this concludes the brief explanation of the meaning of the "three non-guardings."
211. The Meaning of the Three Applications of Mindfulness (19). Regarding the meaning of the three applications of mindfulness, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"All sentient beings..."
This is the sphere of the Tathāgata’s arising of mindfulness;
therefore, it is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). These foundations of mindfulness are not the same.
According to the objects [of the assembly], there are three divisions: first, the correct assembly;
second, the heterodox assembly.
Third, it is neither correct nor incorrect.
The Tathāgata knows that his own Dharma is the most supreme;
nevertheless, he does not give rise to a mind of attachment toward those who receive it.
This is the first foundation of mindfulness.
Not giving rise to a mind of anger toward those who do not accept [one's teaching] is the second foundation of mindfulness.
Within that state which is neither felt nor un-felt, one remains capable of receiving people;
without giving rise to deluded indifference,
one constantly attains a pure mind.
Regarding the third foundation of mindfulness,
since it is divided into three categories— namely, the false, the correct, and so forth— [the same applies here].
Among the three types of persons— enemies, relatives, and neutral parties—
one can likewise distinguish three [levels of practice]:
namely, being free from anger toward enemies.
This is the first application of mindfulness;
regarding those who are neither loved nor disliked is the second application of mindfulness.
A person of neutral temperament does not give rise to delusion.
This is the third application of mindfulness. Question:
For what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata attain the three foundations of mindfulness?
Because he has long cultivated a mind of equanimity and great relinquishment toward sentient beings,
and because he deeply contemplates that sentient beings are devoid of self or personhood.
Because they thoroughly understand that the nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent,
they attain a mind of equanimity toward the three groups of beings.
This is the meaning of the three foundations of mindfulness.
This is a brief summary. 212.
The Meaning of the Fourfold Purity in All Aspects (19). Regarding the meaning of the fourfold purity in all aspects: there are four types of purity in all aspects.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
the Buddha’s virtues are free from defilement;
this is termed "purity."
The purities differ according to their respective meanings;
they are explained as four through a single gateway.
What are these four names?
First is purity of body;
second is purity of the objective sphere;
third is purity of mind.
Fourth is the purity of wisdom.
These four ultimately consist of nothing but body and mind;
the first two pertain to the body.
The latter two are mind;
they are merely divided into two based on the difference in the nature of their objects within the body.
Within the mind, according to the differences in their respective merit and wisdom,
they are further divided into two;
thus, combined, there are four.
Regarding the "purity of the body":
the habitual tendencies of the afflictions are forever extinguished without remainder,
and one attains the supreme body with mastery over arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is called the purity of the body.
When the body of afflictive habit-energies is forever extinguished without remainder,
one attains the supreme body, the purity of the true body.
Mastery over arising and ceasing is the purity of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Furthermore, attaining the upper body is the purity of the physical body;
mastery over arising and ceasing is the purity of bodily function.
Regarding the purity of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-viśuddhi*): the various manifestations and transformations, as well as all that is spoken,
being unimpeded and sovereign, is called the purity of the objective sphere.
The various manifestations are the sphere of the body,
and that which is spoken is the sphere of speech;
furthermore, the sphere of various manifestations is the sphere of phenomena.
Furthermore, that which is spoken is the realm of principle;
within this realm, one possesses mastery over its functioning.
The absence of obstruction within conditions is called the purity of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-viśuddhi*).
As for what is termed the purity of the mind (*citta-viśuddhi*):
This clarifies the purity of the Buddha’s adornment of merit.
All merits have the mind as their sovereign.
This is established by emphasizing the primary factor;
therefore, it is said that "the mind is pure.
Thus, the text states:
To be entirely free from afflictions and to have perfected the roots of goodness is called purity of mind;
to be entirely free from afflictions is the purity of the virtue of abandonment.
The accomplishment of roots of goodness is the purity of conduct and virtue.
As for the "purity of wisdom," it clarifies the purity of the adornments of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Therefore, that text states:
"Having abandoned all the defilements of ignorance,
one possesses unimpeded mastery over all that is knowable."
It is called the purity of wisdom.
It is the abandonment of all the defilements of ignorance and the removal of the stage of ignorance;
it is the purity of wisdom regarding ultimate truth.
He is unimpeded and sovereign regarding all that is knowable;
he has severed ignorance concerning phenomena;
his conventional wisdom is pure.
The four purities are thus. 213.
The Meaning of the Two Knowledges (19). Regarding the meaning of the two knowledges: the first is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Second is the wisdom of skillful means.
Regarding what is called "wisdom of reality," there are generally two interpretations.
First, to understand all phenomena as they truly are is called "real wisdom" (bhūta-jñāna);
it is not a case of being ignorant while falsely claiming to know.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Wisdom free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is called 'knowledge as it truly is' (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
This knowledge as it truly is stands in opposition to that conceited mind of false cognition."
It does not accord with skillful means. Within this context,
all the Buddha’s omniscience is termed true wisdom.
Without discriminating among skillful means,
knowing the true dharma is called "real wisdom" (bhūta-jñāna). Within this,
there are five meanings for the analytical differentiation of "crookedness" (vaṅka).
To know that which is falsely perceived as real is called true wisdom;
to know that the dharmas arising from the deluded mind of false discrimination are unreal is called true wisdom.
Just as knowing the truth of suffering is called the knowledge of suffering,
so it is for all [the other truths] within this framework.
True wisdom stands in contrast to that deluded wisdom;
it does not stand in contrast to skillful means.
These two stand in contrast to the provisional in order to clarify the ultimate reality.
Knowing the dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*);
knowing the dharma of conventional designations (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called provisional wisdom (*prajñapti-jñāna*).
Within this framework:
Actual knowledge (bhūtajñāna) is contrasted with that conventional knowledge (prajñaptijñāna),
not with skillful means (upāya).
These three pairs clarify actuality through their characteristics.
To know the reality of the single ultimate truth is called true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
To know the characteristics of existence and non-existence within that single truth is called characteristic wisdom (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*).
To know the dharmas of conventional truth as provisional designations is called provisional wisdom (*prajñapti-jñāna*).
Within this context, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is contrasted with the knowledge of signs (*nimittajñāna*);
it may also be said to be contrasted with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in relation to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
It does not accord with the provisional means.
Regarding the four [categories], it clarifies the reality through the teachings.
To realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called "real wisdom" (bhūta-jñāna).
Investigating words at the initial stage of learning is called "knowledge of the teaching" (śāstrajñāna). Within this context,
true knowledge (bhūtajñāna) is contrasted with that knowledge of the teaching.
It is not [to rely] on expedient means.
However, if one takes the wisdom of verbal instruction as the expedient means,
there is likewise no harm.
The fifth pair clarifies the provisional in light of the real.
To know the true Dharma of the One Vehicle is called real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*);
to thoroughly understand the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles is called skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Within this gateway, actual wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) is contrasted with that skillful means wisdom (upāya-jñāna); here,
we shall discuss actual wisdom.
This is based on what follows.
Regarding the wisdom of skillful means (upāya-jñāna),
there are generally four interpretations.
First is the skillful means of advancing toward [the goal],
such as the seven preparatory stages prior to the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
which advance toward the fruit.
It is called "expedient means" (upāya) because it serves as the basis for attaining the fruit;
this single expedient means is directed toward the fruit and not toward ultimate wisdom (bhūtajñāna).
If one takes the name of "fruition-virtue" as the reality itself,
there is no contradiction in meaning.
Second, the application of skillful means through the two types of giving.
It is like the *upāya-pāramitā* among the ten *pāramitās*.
Because one acts with skillful means regarding that which is practiced,
it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Within these skillful means, there are three types of flexibility (*vaṅka*).
First is skillfulness regarding the matters of practicing the taught skillful means, as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Grounds of Yogic Practice).
The twelve skillful means are precisely this matter.
Second is the expedient means of verifying practice:
contemplating emptiness without attachment.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
the meaning of this is the wisdom of the ten skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*).
Third is the skillful means of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-upāya*).
They skillfully traverse both the mundane and the supramundane;
as stated in the *Dilun*,
they remain untainted by the expedient means of the mundane and the supramundane.
The meaning is that it consists in dwelling with skillfulness.
These three are all the skillful means for performing giving (*dāna*).
This one skillful means stands in contrast to the lack of skillful means, which is characterized by ignorance and clumsiness.
It does not accord with true knowledge;
it is the skillful means of the three accumulations,
wherein all phenomena are of one essence.
It is the skillful integration of all characteristics;
therefore, it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
How is it skillfully accomplished?
Within the single true mind, there are fully and expansively present all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the dharma-realm;
these Buddha-dharmas exist because they share the same essence.
Taking wisdom as the gateway,
other dharmas assist in its accomplishment;
taking meditative concentration as the gateway.
The remaining meanings assist in its accomplishment; thus,
all such things are called "expedient means" (*upāya*) because they are skillfully integrated through phenomena of identical essence.
Therefore, the *Dichilun* states:
"This dharma is accomplished through skillfulness;
for this reason, it is called 'expedient means' (*upāya*)."
Furthermore, the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* states:

"One employs as a skillful means the general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, characteristics of formation, and characteristics of disintegration of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
This, too, is a method for integration.
This single method corresponds to all phenomena such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
it does not correspond to ultimate wisdom.
Therefore, in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), within the analysis of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), it is stated that "phenomena are excluded.
Phenomena refer to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
These four skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) are, in reality, without such phenomena.
Because it is skillfully applied, it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Within this, there are three types of distinctions regarding its subtlety:
the first is skillfulness of body (kāya-vaicakṣaṇya).
This refers to the Buddha’s manifestations as monkeys, deer, horses, and so forth;
second, it refers to skillfulness of speech.
In reality, there are no three vehicles.
It is taught according to the needs of those being transformed.
The third is skillfulness of mind,
which refers to the wisdom of expedient means (*upāya-prajñā*).
He gives rise to the two kinds of skillful transformations of body and speech,
as described in the Lotus Sūtra:
"Recalling the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past."
"The path that I have now attained should likewise be explained as the three vehicles," and so forth.
Now, it is said that skillfulness of mind constitutes the wisdom of means (upāya-jñāna).
This wisdom of means can be contrasted with the aforementioned wisdom of reality (tattva-jñāna).

The sutras speak of the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths.

Now, the four wisdoms are elucidated.
Why not rely on that? Instead,

The explanations of the Dharma-gates are manifold;
they cannot be fixed as one.
The Sūtras teach the Four Noble Truths according to the method of attraction and aversion,

For this reason, the cessation of the origin [of suffering] is clarified first,

Regarding the subsequent result:
first one extinguishes present faults,

"I shall not undergo further existence.

For this reason, the cultivation of the path is clarified first, followed by the manifestation of the abandonment of the origin [of suffering].

within each and every wisdom...

Within the teachings of the Small Vehicle:
The four knowledges attained by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas possess both substance and characteristics;

the characteristics of those four wisdoms are fully endowed with the four conditions.

When the noble wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifests in a single moment,

This essence and its characteristics are largely the same as those of the Hīnayāna.
However, within the Hīnayāna, regarding essence (*tattva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the sequence is such that entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is termed "essence."
Upon emerging from contemplation, one perceives these marks; in the Mahāyāna Dharma,
essence and marks are simultaneous.
The Buddha perceives both truths simultaneously and manifestly, without alternation;
therefore, within this simultaneity,
the wisdom of ultimate truth is designated as his essence.
The worldly observation of names and signs also possesses these four meanings within their own essence.
Yet, while there are no four conditions [for the mind],
those characteristics themselves also possess the four conditions.
Yet it lacks the four meanings.
How is it that within its essence the four meanings are fully present, yet the four conditions are absent?
It is through that wisdom of reality as it is.
In the manifestation of a single thought-moment,
one can sever the infinite causes and effects of birth and death;
this is described as "my births have been exhausted, and I shall not undergo further existence."
When this wisdom is attained,
the practice of the path is perfected and the realization of cessation is consummated;
it is then declared that the holy life has been established and what was to be done has been accomplished.
For this reason, one attains the possession of these four meanings; yet,
even though one possesses these meanings...
The mind that realizes suchness is precisely merged with principle;
it is devoid of the conceptual discrimination of [notions] such as "my births are exhausted" or "the holy life is established."
For this reason, there are no four conditions.
How is it that those characteristics possess the four conditions yet lack the four meanings?
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
within the context of conventional truth,
[possess] the noble wisdom obtained through their own realization of the cessation of conditions.
One gives rise to the thought that the four knowledges have reached their ultimate fulfillment.
There are four conditions for the realization that "birth has been exhausted" up to "there will be no further existence.
However, this is the mind of this world.
Because it cannot cause one to realize that "birth has been exhausted" up to "there will be no further existence," there are no four meanings.
Such is the nature and characteristic [of this path]; these two sections are concluded.
Next is the third section.
This is analyzed in relation to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Within this, first the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising are distinguished;
subsequently, they are analyzed in relation to the four knowledges.
The *Jinwushengzhi jing* (Sūtra on the Knowledge of the Exhaustion of Non-arising) and its commentaries differ.
According to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*),
the present exhaustion of all causes and effects of birth and death is entirely termed "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
This knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is attained by all those beyond training (aśaikṣa), whether of sharp or dull faculties;
there is none among them for whom it is not present.
Because there is that which has been severed, the one possessing the knowledge of non-arising [regards] the causes and effects of birth and death that were previously severed.
The definitive realization that one will never again give rise [to afflictions] is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This is the knowledge of non-arising.
Only those with sharp faculties attain it; those with dull faculties do not.
He explains that for those with dull faculties, there is the possibility of regression.
Because, according to what has been severed,
it may yet arise again; for this reason.
There is no wisdom regarding non-arising;
one benefits others without regressing,
according to what has been severed.
They will never again arise.
For this reason, there is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The meaning is as such.
What are its essence and characteristics?
For a person of dull faculties:
When the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises in a continuous succession of many moments, all are termed "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
For a person of sharp faculties, however,
the first moment of the mind of one beyond training is termed "exhaustion."
The moment after the second thought-moment is designated as "non-arising.
Nevertheless, because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) correctly takes the principle of the truths as its object and is capable of bringing about that which is to be exhausted,
it is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
It does not take their cessation as its object;
the same applies to non-arising.
It correctly takes the principle of the Truths as its object.
It is called "non-arising" because that which has been severed will not arise again;
it does not mean that it takes non-arising as its object-condition.
Question: To which truths do these two conditions pertain?
In the *Vibhāṣā*, various explanations are given.
One school of thought says:
"It takes only the Truth of Suffering as its object. Why is this so?"
When first entering the state of sainthood, one first takes the Truth of Suffering as an object; therefore,
when subsequently emerging from it, [one does so in the same order].
It still takes suffering as its object;
it is like when a person takes medicine—the one that enters first is the last to exit.
Thus it was proclaimed by one school.
It is subsumed within the Truth of Origination.
Why is this so? Because at the very moment one first enters the state of a noble one (ārya).
First one takes the fruit as the object;
later, when emerging from the noble state,
one must take its cause as the object.
Therefore, it is taught by one school that the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination are not fixed; they take each other as conditions.
One school proclaims that the Four Truths are not fixed;
such is the Abhidharma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
there is no principle whatsoever for the regression of any one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
it is not possible to differentiate them based on whether they are of sharp or dull faculties.
To know only how to sever the causes of birth and death is called the knowledge of exhaustion;
it is the severing of the fruits of birth and death.
To never again undergo [rebirth] is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
It is the same for the Mahāyāna.
Because the Buddha has no regression,

the distinctions between the characteristics of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are roughly as described above. Next, they shall be distinguished by way of the four knowledges.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
among these four [knowledges], "my births have been exhausted" is taken as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
and "there will be no further existence" is taken as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The Mahāyāna is likewise.
Furthermore, within the *Mahādharmāvadāna*, it is stated that the knowledge of the exhaustion of one's own births constitutes the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, it is described as the knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhakṣayajñāna*).
Therefore, it is said that not taking up further existence constitutes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This is because the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* describes it as the knowledge of the abandonment of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-prahāṇa-jñāna*). According to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), however:
Within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), four distinct knowledges are included;
the same is true for the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). If these two are considered together, they comprise these four.
How can one distinguish between the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*)? As Nāgārjuna said:

"He proclaims his own realization: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.'"
This is their knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Those of sharp faculties give rise to a resolute intention regarding what has been previously attained.
Birth for me has been exhausted; I shall not be born again.
The holy life has been established; there is no need for further practice.
What was to be done has been accomplished; I shall never again do what must be undone.
The firm resolve that one will not undergo further existence and shall never again be reborn—
such a definitive intention is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
These are the four knowledges.

215. The Meaning of the Four Fearlessnesses (19). The Explanation of the Meaning of the Four Fearlessnesses through Sevenfold Analysis. I. Defining their Essential Nature and Distinguishing their Objects and Endowments. II. Analysis by Way of Knowledge and Abandonment. III. Analysis by Way of Self-Benefit and Benefit for Others. IV. Manifesting Their Virtues by Way of Contrast. V. Distinguishing Their Similarities and Differences in Relation to the Ten Powers. VI. Differences in What is Taught in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. VII. First, the Explanation of the Names.
A mind of wisdom that is not timid is called fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
Fearlessness is not uniform;
it is divided into four according to its specific meanings.
What are these names?
First, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge;
second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows.
The third is the fearlessness in being able to teach the obstacles to the path;
the fourth is the fearlessness in being able to teach the path that exhausts suffering.
Universally illuminating all phenomena is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
Based on one's own possession of wisdom,
being undaunted before others is called the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*).
Having thus concluded the discussion on folly, it is termed the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
To illuminate one's own exhaustion [of outflows] and to be undaunted regarding others is called the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).
To be capable of declaring faults and obstacles is called the ability to speak of the hindrances to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-deśanā-śakti*).
Being confident in one's own capability and not being intimidated by others is called the fearlessness regarding the path that exhausts suffering;
these are the latter two types.
He is fearless regarding others because he relies on his own capability;
it is not because of the disciples' wisdom or their abandonment [of defilements].
The explanation of names and meanings concludes this first section.
Next, the second section shall determine their essential nature and distinguish their objects and attributes.
The essential nature has two aspects:
first, the essence of wisdom;
second, the essence of mind.
To inwardly illuminate that one possesses four virtues,
which are truly existent and not false— this is wisdom.
That one’s mind remains calm and undaunted when faced with difficult words from others is what constitutes this state of mind.
As it is said in the treatise:
The universal illumination of wisdom is called fearlessness;
it is this very wisdom that is courageous and undaunted.
It is named "Fearlessness," which is precisely that mind. Question:
The function of fearlessness has wisdom (*jñāna*) as its essence.
Wisdom is a factor of discernment (*prajñā-skandha*) that takes the mind (*citta*) as its essence.
What numerical category does this mind belong to?
According to the Abhidharma,
among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
there is no separate establishment of a distinct category of "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Inferring from this principle:
everything that is encompassed by the sensation of fear and suffering is entirely devoid of fearlessness.
It should be subsumed under pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
If one follows the school that establishes many mental factors (*caitta*),
both fear (*bhaya*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) are distinct factors.
Such is its essential nature.
Since there are two such natures,
they are established in relation to these respective natures.
Regarding the completeness of the objects of discourse, such completeness is not fixed.
What are their characteristics?
If one says that wisdom constitutes its essence,
there are four ways to distinguish its meanings in relation to this essence.
The first is its essence itself.
The second is function;
the third is the object;
the fourth is the condition.
The essence (*tǐ*) is the wisdom of inward illumination.
This inward illumination of oneself possesses both wisdom and its exhaustion, and is endowed with these two capacities.
The function (*yòng*) is the mind that is free from timidity.
Based on the prior knowledge of one's own nature,
and knowing that one possesses virtue,
one then gives rise to the function of courageous and undaunted resolve toward external challenges.
The "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the four kinds of virtues within oneself.
Because one's own wisdom, as well as abandonment and the two capacities, are that which is illuminated by wisdom,
they are termed "objects."
"Conditions" refers to the four difficult objections raised by non-Buddhists;
it is by responding to those objections that the Buddha's virtues are revealed.
Those four are the conditions for the manifestation of his virtues.
Therefore, it is called "condition.
If one speaks of a courageous and undaunted mind,
that is taken as its essence.
In defining the meaning based on this essence, there are also four aspects: first, the essence;
second, the function.
The third is the object;
the fourth is the equipment.
Its essence is a mind that is not timid.
This mind is precisely the meaning of fearlessness;
therefore, it is called the essence (*tī*).
Its function is the wisdom of inward illumination.
Because one knows for oneself through illumination that one possesses virtue and is not empty of it,
one is not timid toward others;
therefore, this is called "function."
"Object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the four difficult challenges posed by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
A mind free from fear is precisely that which,
when confronted by those challenges, remains undaunted.
Therefore, it is called that "objection.
Taking this as its object,
the "endowment" refers to one's own four kinds of virtues.
Maintaining one's own four virtues, one is not timid toward others;
therefore, these are called "one's own virtues. This concludes the exposition on these two gateways.
Next, the third section is the analysis of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). In terms of their general characteristics, they are roughly divided as follows:
the second [of the four analytical knowledges] is abandonment, while the other three are wisdom.
When subdivided further,
the first two pertain to one's own virtue and the latter two to the benefit of others.
Within the former, regarding one's own virtue:
First comes wisdom, followed by abandonment;
among the benefits for others,
these are what are sought.
He is able to explain the obstacles to the Path;
he explains these obstacles to show them to people,
leading them to sever and eliminate them.
He causes them to attain severance;
he is able to proclaim the path to its end,
and he teaches and demonstrates the path to others.
To cause others to practice and study,
so that they may attain wisdom,
according to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.
It is not like that.
How do they explain it? They are able to explain the obstacles to the Path so that others may recognize those obstacles.
Except for the Buddha’s attainment of the Way;
that attainment of the Way is wisdom,
which is able to explain the exhaustion of the Way.
One causes others to recognize the path that exhausts suffering and practices it so as to exhaust suffering.
Exhausting suffering is abandonment.
Such is the knowledge of abandonment; thus ends this section on the three doors.
Next, the fourth section is the analysis of the two practices of benefiting oneself and benefiting others,
categorized according to their specific characteristics.
The first two [perfections] benefit oneself, while the latter two benefit others.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Those first two types are the path for one's own peace."
The latter two types constitute the path for establishing others;
yet, when considered generally,
both are for one's own benefit.
Because one's own mind is stable and fearless,
this universally constitutes benefiting others,
as stated in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Stages of Yogic Practice).
Regarding the benefit of others,
the first [of the two types of omniscience], the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), is primarily intended to transform bodhisattvas.
Because Bodhisattvas seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), they specifically transform [beings] for that purpose.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"All-knowledge is fearless."

In order to transform the various bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna, [the Buddha] teaches the fearlessness of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya) specifically to those of the two vehicles (dviyāna).
This is because those of the two vehicles predominantly seek nirvāṇa; therefore, he specifically transforms them.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"The fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows is for the sake of transforming those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles."
The remaining two fearlessnesses apply universally to the transformation of both the Great and Small Vehicles;
followers of both vehicles alike seek liberation from obstacles.
Therefore, it is said that the obstacles to the path are taught so that they may be severed,
and the way out is sought; thus,
the path of exhaustion is taught so that it may be cultivated and studied.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"The Buddha taught the Sūtras for Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas as the path leading out of suffering;
those who compiled the scriptures [recorded them]."
These are compiled into two collections:
that which explains all the practices of śrāvakas is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
and that which proclaims all the practices of bodhisattvas is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The fourfold analysis of self-benefit and benefit for others is thus concluded.
Next is the fifth section,
which reveals the virtues by means of contrast.
Discussing them collectively,
all of the Buddha’s virtues surpass all others.
When distinguished according to their specific characteristics,
those four fearlessnesses are for the most part directed toward non-Buddhists.
The ten powers are directed against Māra;
the eighteen unique qualities are directed against those of the two vehicles.
This meaning is as explained in that *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Why is it that fearlessness specifically addresses non-Buddhists?
Because the knowledge of non-Buddhists is false.
The Buddha’s lack of virtue is challenged;
his four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) manifest his own possession of virtue, thereby overturning those erroneous challenges.
Therefore, the four fearlessnesses specifically counteract the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*),
while the ten powers specifically counteract the various Māras;
for Māra gives rise to defilement and corruption.
They destroy the roots of goodness in others;
yet the Ten Powers remain firm and cannot be destroyed by Māra.
Therefore, they are countered individually.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Regarding all māras..."
The abandonment [of faults] and the attainment of excellence are called "powers.
For what reason are the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) specifically contrasted with those of the two vehicles?
Because the minor virtues of the two vehicles might be confused with those of the Tathāgata from above,
they are described as "unshared" (āveṇika).
To distinguish it from the two vehicles,
it is specifically addressed to them.
It is asked:
It was previously stated that non-Buddhists (tīrthika) challenge the Buddha’s lack of merit and his four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and that the Buddha refutes them in response.
For what reason do the non-Buddhists challenge the Buddha’s lack of merit?
And how does the Tathāgata explain it?
The general explanation states:
the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) raise objections based on their attachment to superficial traces,
while the Tathāgata provides a comprehensive resolution by revealing the ultimate reality.
For what reason do the non-Buddhists challenge the Buddha-Tathāgata, claiming he lacks omniscience?
At times, within the traces of his speech,
it appears as though he does not possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, he raises this objection.
What is the meaning of this?
At times, the Tathāgata...
There were some disciples who came from afar;
the Buddha then questioned them.
"How is it that in that region they dwell in peace and happiness, with roads clear and tranquil, and the four great elements at ease?
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:
if a person goes to a city or village and asks for its name,"
I say that this person is not omniscient.
This was the question posed by the Buddha previously.
It appears as if there were no wisdom;
non-Buddhists cling to this,
which is why they raise such an objection.
The Buddha replied to him:
"I follow the ways of the world;
it is for the sake of providing comfort that we exchange greetings with one another."
The disciple has come from afar;
it would be improper for me to remain silent,
which is why I ask this.
It is not that he does not know; there are also instances in the world where one asks a question intentionally despite already knowing,
yet this is not due to a lack of wisdom.
The Buddha is likewise;
when responding to such challenges,
he has no fear of others.
For this reason, he proclaims the fearlessness of omniscience.
For what reason do the non-Buddhists challenge the Tathāgata, saying that his outflows are not yet exhausted?
At times, the Tathāgata says:
Within the traces [of the Buddha's life], it appears as if outflows were not yet exhausted;
for this reason, it is difficult [to reconcile].
What is the meaning of this?
At times, the Tathāgata spoke kindly to Rāhula,
appearing as if driven by the latent tendency of attachment;
yet he reviled Devadatta with harsh words.
It appears as though there is an underlying tendency toward anger;
at times, he praises himself as being superior to men, gods, and elephants,
which appears as though there is an underlying tendency toward pride.
Furthermore, he instructed his disciples:
"Uphold my Dharma well,
as if holding a bowl of oil."
It appears as though there are latent tendencies of views;
because non-Buddhists cling to this,
they find it difficult to accept that the Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows.
The Buddha replied to Śakra:
"I have no afflictions; it is only because I act in accordance with my transformations that it appears so."
There are some sentient beings who receive the Dharma through gentle words;
for this reason, [the Buddha speaks thus].
"Kind speech, Rāhula,
is not characterized by attachment.
Or, there may be sentient beings..."
Harsh speech conforms to the Vinaya; for this reason,
he reviled and scolded Devadatta.
It is not that he harbors anger;
rather, he desires to cause sentient beings to give rise to the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
For this reason, he personally praises the human-flower and the human-elephant.
This is not due to pride.
Furthermore, the Buddha-Tathāgata praises his own virtues as few though they are many;
therefore, it is not pride.
It circulates according to worldly convention;
I say that upholding my Dharma is like holding an oil bowl,
not that there is any [substantial] view.
In the world, there are also those who are free from afflictions yet whose speech resembles that of one with afflictions;
the Buddha is likewise so.
This is how the objection is resolved.
He is not intimidated by others;
therefore, he proclaims the fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).
For what reason would non-Buddhists challenge the Buddha, the Tathāgata, [claiming] that he is unable to explain the obstacles?
It is observed that even among the noble disciples of the Tathāgata,
there still remain afflictions and ignorance;
the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has skillfully taught the obstacles so that they may be abandoned.

Furthermore, although the Buddha-Tathāgata has taught that greed and other such afflictions can obstruct the Noble Path, [this applies to those who have not yet attained] the stage of Srotāpanna and so forth.
One constantly practices lust yet attains the noble path;
this is clearly known.
Thus has the Tathāgata spoken of the dharmas that obstruct the path.
It cannot obstruct the Path.
Because it does not obstruct the Path,
the Buddha said that it is incapable [of doing so].
The non-Buddhists cling to this and thus raise an objection;
the Buddha responds to and resolves it.
I am able to explain the hindrances so that people may sever them; however,
the strength of my disciples is not yet sufficient for such severance.
It is not that I am incapable;
furthermore, I have stated that obstacles truly can obstruct the Path.
Therefore, the treatise says:
If desire resides in the mind, the Dharma will not be granted;
one must first eliminate desire before attaining the Way.
However, the obstacles presented by the various afflictions (kleśa) differ from one another.
The afflictions practiced by those such as the Srotāpannas obstruct the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
but do not hinder their realization through vision (darśana).
Because it does not obstruct vision,
it does not hinder the attainment of the Path; because it obstructs the cultivation of the Path, [it hinders its progress].
I say that the dharmas which obstruct are truly able to obstruct the Path;
because they truly obstruct the Path,
I declare them to be such.
When resolving this objection, one is not intimidated by others; therefore,
the fearlessness of being able to teach the obstacles to the path is established.
For what reason do the non-Buddhists challenge the Buddha, claiming he cannot fully explain the path to the exhaustion of suffering,
when we clearly see the Tathāgata’s noble disciples,
such as the srotāpannas and others?
Although one may attain the fruits of sainthood,
there still remain the sufferings of birth and death within the realms of humans and devas;
this is clearly understood.
The Tathāgata taught that the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering cannot exhaust suffering;
because it does not exhaust suffering, the Buddha said it is incapable [of doing so].
The non-Buddhists cling to this.
This is why it is considered difficult.
The Buddha explained to Śreṇika:
"I declare that the Noble Path is truly capable of exhausting suffering."
However, because the disciples have cultivated it but little,
their various sufferings are not exhausted;
it is not that the Path is incapable of doing so.
For example, the medicinal nature of ghee is capable of dispelling heat;
yet, because one has taken only a small amount, the feverish illness is not cured.
It is not that ghee lacks the power to do so.
What has been said is thus:
because the Path is truly able to exhaust all suffering,
I say that it is capable [of this].
When resolving this objection,
one is not intimidated by others;
therefore, one establishes the fearlessness of being able to preach the path that exhausts suffering.
The comparison regarding these five gates is thus concluded.
Next, the second gate distinguishes their similarities and differences based on the ten powers (*daśabala*).
As for what are called the "ten powers":
First, the power of the possible and the impossible;
second, the power of the knowledge of one's own karma;
third, the power of meditative concentration.
Fourth is the power of the faculties;
fifth is the power of aspiration;
sixth is the power of nature.
Seventh is the power of knowing the destinations of beings;
eighth is the power of recollecting past lives;
ninth is the power of the divine eye.
The tenth is the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*). Its meaning will be explained later.
Regarding the powers of fearlessness and the powers of the noble ones (*ārya-bala*), there are both similarities and differences.
What is the common characteristic?
As explained in the Abhidharma,
it is initially like the first power.
The second is like the tenth;
the remaining two are like the second and seventh.
This is called the "Fearless Abiding."
Although this is what the treatise states,
one must further analyze it.
Within the first [of the four] fearlessnesses:
There exists an object and an essence;
the Buddha’s omniscience is that object.
Internally illuminating that one possesses all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā) is its essence (tattva).
This is the relationship between this object and its essence.
There is nothing that is not subsumed within the essence of the first power (*bala*),
because the wisdom encompassed by the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) is vast. Thus,
the second fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) possesses both its objective domain and its essential substance.
The Buddha’s quality of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is its object;
the wisdom that illuminates this exhaustion is its essence.
As for the object, it is subsumed within the domain of the tenth power (*bala*).
Since they both take the exhaustion of outflows as their object,
their essence is subsumed within the essence of the tenth power (*bala*).
They are identical in that they both take the wisdom that illuminates and exhausts [the outflows] as their essence.
Therefore, although this object and its essence are similar,
they differ in their breadth and narrowness;
the nature of fearlessness is known only by oneself.
The meaning of that [previous power] is narrow;
that tenth power observes its objects in a general manner.
Its meaning is broad. How is it broad?
As stated in the *Bhūmisaṃgraha* (Earth-Holding Treatise).
The tenth power is: knowing for oneself the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), knowing the exhaustion of outflows in others,
and knowing whether the means for the exhaustion of outflows have been applied or not yet applied.
Furthermore, it is called "broad" because one knows whether or not the conceit of having attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) has arisen.
The third fearlessness possesses both an object and a substance;
its object is the teaching that there are obstacles to the Path.
Illuminating one's own capacity is its essence (*tattva*).
This essence is subsumed under the initial power,
because the wisdom that discerns what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*) is so vast.
The objective sphere is subsumed under his second power;
that second power knows karma and afflictions.
The second is the fearlessness in proclaiming the obstacles to the Path.
This refers to knowing that karma and afflictions are the factors that obstruct the Path;
its meaning is largely the same [as the preceding].
Therefore, it is subsumed under that power (*bala*).
Since the Abhidharma treats this in terms of its object (*viṣaya*),
the third fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) is proclaimed in the same manner as the second power.
The fourth fearlessness possesses both an object and an essence.
Its object is the ability to fully expound the path;
its essence is the illumination of one's own capacity [to do so].
The essence is also subsumed under the first power,
because within that first power, the encompassing wisdom is vast;
the objective sphere is subsumed under the seventh power.
That seventh power consists in knowing the path leading to those states;
the fourth [fearlessness] is the ability to proclaim the path to the exhaustion [of suffering].
They also understand the Path;
its meaning is largely the same,
and therefore it is subsumed under those powers.
In the Abhidharma, because it proceeds by way of objects,
it states that the fourth [knowledge] is like the seventh power;
such is the Abhidharma.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the first fearlessness consists of the preceding nine powers,
because all nine are omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The second fearlessness is identical to the tenth power (*bala*);
its meaning has been explained above.
As for the latter two fearlessnesses:
The treatise does not discuss this at all.
If one wishes to analyze it,
it is the same as in the Abhidharma.
The same applies to their shared characteristics (*sādharmya*). As for what is called their difference (*vaidharmya*),
it is as explained in the *Abhidharma* and the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The essence of wisdom is power;
the universal illumination of the light of wisdom is called fearlessness.
It abides having fully encountered its conditions.
Because wisdom and abandonment, along with their two capacities, are present,
it is said that they "universally illuminate.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
Abiding securely in this power with valor and without cowardice constitutes fearlessness.
The Ten Powers are truly like a demon;
because they cannot be destroyed, they are called "abiding securely."
Because they are firmly established,
they are called powers;
[they prevail] over external obstacles and difficulties.
To be courageous and not timid is called fearlessness;
this is proclaimed as one proceeds forward.
The universal illumination of wisdom is called "fearlessness";
that is, wisdom constitutes the essence of fearlessness.
Now it is said:
Fearlessness is defined as the absence of timidity;
it is a mind that is secure and free from fear,
which constitutes the essence of fearlessness.
The treatise further states:
"The cause is called power;
the fruit is called fearlessness."
Because fearlessness arises from the mind that follows the powers,
the similarities and differences regarding the ten powers are as described above. This concludes the six gates.
Next is the seventh section,
clarifying the differences between what the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools teach.
There are five such differences.
The essence of the single mind differs:
the Hīnayāna proclaims that the Tathāgata’s fearlessness has *vijñāna* (consciousness) as its essence,
whereas the Mahāyāna proclaims that the Tathāgata’s fearlessness has the true mind (*bhūtamanas*) as its essence.
Because upon reaching Buddhahood there is no longer any other mind or consciousness;
because the objects of the two minds differ;
and because the Śrāvakayāna proclaims that the mind of *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness) is fearless.
Grasping at objects through conceptual discrimination,
one relies upon those external challenges and gives rise to fearlessness.
The Mahāyāna proclaims that the mind of true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) is fearless;
like space, the mind is free from conceptual discrimination,
possessing the virtue of non-discrimination.
Because it is difficult to manifest clearly,
he elucidates it by means of the four types of refutations used against non-Buddhists.
It is like using a measuring rod to reveal the high and low points of empty space.
The three types of wisdom function differently;
the Hīnayāna proclaims that the Tathāgata’s fearlessness has ten types of wisdom as its essence.
The ten knowledges are as described above.
Regarding the "all-knowing" (sarvajña) that illuminates all things at the beginning and the middle,
it possesses the nature of the ten knowledges.
The wisdom that is able to illuminate is exclusively of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
because it universally takes [all phenomena] as its object.
Regarding the second [of these],
that which is illuminated as "exhaustion" is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The wisdom that is capable of illuminating [the object] is not subsumed under the ten knowledges;
it corresponds to the nature of six knowledges within the tenth power (*bala*).
That which is called the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and conventional knowledge— now,
in response to the objection that these are predominantly of the nature of conventional knowledge,
we shall address this within the third [section].
Regarding the ability to explain the obstacles to the path,
only the second power (the power of knowing the thoughts of others) should possess the nature of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Now, based on the explanation of its arising,
the wisdom that is capable of illuminating [objects] possesses the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) alone.
Within the fourth [power],
it is only the seventh power that can explain the path to the end of suffering.
It possesses the nature of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
Now, based on its arising, it is said to possess the nature of many knowledges;
it is the wisdom (*prajñā*) capable of illuminating [the object].
It is also of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Such is the case in the Hīnayāna.
In the Mahāyāna, it is taught that the Buddha’s virtue of fearlessness is the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
As Nāgārjuna said:
"That pure wisdom is omniscience."
Unimpeded knowledge is this.
The meaning of "knowledge as it truly is" has been explained above.
Regarding the "all-knowing one" within the first fearlessness:
It has as its essence the three types of wisdom— pure wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñāna*),
and unimpeded wisdom (*asanga-jñāna*). The insight capable of illuminating these is subsumed within all-encompassing wisdom and unimpeded wisdom.
Regarding the second [category],
that which is illuminated— the exhaustion of outflows—
is not subsumed within the three knowledges.
The wisdom capable of illuminating is subsumed under omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅgajñāna*).
Regarding the latter two:
The ability to explain what obstructs the path and the ability to explain the exhaustion of suffering are subsumed under omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*);
the same applies to their capacity for illumination.
This is the third difference in the modes of wisdom.
Fourth is the difference in the illumination of objects,
as explained in the Hīnayāna teachings.
The Buddha’s fearlessness merely illuminates the objects before him and does not illuminate his own essence;
such is the nature of the discriminating mind.
Because it is unable to illuminate its own substance;
the Mahāyāna is not so,
for it can illuminate both external objects and its own substance.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
even the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) of a bodhisattva is capable of seeing itself.
How much more so for the Buddha’s wisdom, which does not fail to illuminate itself?
Fifth, the attainment of the state differs;
within the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle...
It is said that the Buddha’s fearlessnesses are attained only at the time he achieves enlightenment under the Bodhi tree;
this is not the case in the Mahāyāna,
where they are perfected in the Buddha.
From the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra) upward,
one attains liberation according to one's capacity;
thus it is proclaimed in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
At the moment of first generating the mind of awakening during the ten stages, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment,
becoming fully endowed with the body of wisdom and equal to all Tathāgatas.
As it is with the fearlessnesses,
so it is with all other virtues;
such is the meaning of the four fearlessnesses.
